Tetrapyrroles constitute a family of cyclic tetrapyrrole molecules that underpin energy transduction, redox chemistry, and environmental sensing across the tree of life. Heme, chlorophyll, bilins, siroheme, and related pigments are synthesized through a conserved, branched pathway that begins with 5-aminolevulinic acid and proceeds through porphobilinogen, hydroxymethylbilane, uroporphyrinogen III, coproporphyrinogen III, and protoporphyrin IX (PPIX) [1,2]. At PPIX, the pathway diverges: ferrochelatase (FC) inserts Fe2+ to form heme, whereas magnesium-chelatase (MgCh) inserts Mg2+ to initiate chlorophyll biosynthesis via Mg-protoporphyrin IX (Mg-PPIX) [3,4]. Because heme and chlorophyll share early precursors, their synthesis must be balanced to avoid accumulation of phototoxic intermediates and to match organellar and cellular demands [5]. In photosynthetic eukaryotes, this balance is further complicated by the need to coordinate plastid, mitochondrial, and cytosolic heme pools, as well as to integrate tetrapyrrole output with photosynthetic development and retrograde signaling [6,7]. Unicellular red algae offer a simplified context in which to dissect these interactions. Cyanidioschyzon merolae has a compact, largely non-redundant genome, a simple cell cycle, and a well-defined plastid, making it an attractive system for analyzing how hormonal and environmental signals reconfigure tetrapyrrole flux [8,9].

Heme is not only a prosthetic group for cytochromes, catalases, peroxidases, and oxygen-binding proteins; in its unbound or labile form, it can act as a regulatory molecule [10,11]. In C. merolae, free heme has been implicated as a positive signal for cell-cycle initiation, linking metabolic status to division competence [12]. This signaling function requires that heme availability be tightly controlled. Cells therefore deploy heme-binding and scavenging proteins, including tryptophan-rich sensory protein-related protein O (TSPO-related protein O), to buffer labile heme and modulate its downstream effects [13,14]. The coexistence of heme biosynthesis, heme catabolism, and heme sequestration suggests that the size of the signaling pool is not simply a function of total heme content but reflects the integration of synthesis, trafficking, and titration [15]. Consequently, changes in tetrapyrrole biosynthetic gene expression may have physiological consequences that extend beyond bulk metabolite supply.

Abscisic acid (ABA) is a canonical stress hormone in land plants and is also produced by diverse algae, where it participates in responses to desiccation, osmotic stress, nutrient limitation, and other environmental fluctuations [16,17]. In C. merolae, ABA treatment promotes heme accumulation yet paradoxically prevents cell-cycle initiation; this effect has been attributed to ABA-dependent induction of TSPO-related protein O, which titrates free heme and thereby suppresses its mitogenic signal [

Strain and culture conditions. Cyanidioschyzon merolae strain 10D was maintained photoautotrophically in modified Allen’s medium (MA2) supplemented with trace elements, as described previously [1]. Cultures were grown in flat-bottomed glass flasks at 42°C under continuous white light (50 µmol photons m−2 s−1) with aeration containing 2% (v/v) CO2. Cell density was monitored by direct counting in a hemocytometer and by measuring optical density at 680 nm. For experimental treatments, mid-exponential-phase cultures (1–3 × 10^7 cells mL−1) were equilibrated under standard growth conditions for at least 12 h before the addition of abscisic acid (ABA). All manipulations involving tetrapyrrole extraction were performed under dim green light to minimize photooxidation.

ABA treatment. (±)-ABA [or (+)-ABA, if used] was dissolved in methanol to prepare a concentrated stock solution and added to cultures to a final concentration of 100 µM, based on previously established conditions for C. merolae [2]. Control cultures received an equal volume of methanol (final concentration ≤ 0.1%, v/v). Cultures were incubated under the same light and temperature conditions, and aliquots were harvested at the indicated time points for RNA and pigment analyses. Cell viability was confirmed by microscopic inspection and by the retention of growth capacity in untreated control cultures.

RNA extraction and cDNA synthesis. Cells were harvested by centrifugation at 3,000 × g for 5 min at 4°C, immediately frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at −80°C until use. Total RNA was extracted using a TRIzol-based protocol or a silica-membrane plant RNA kit, according to the manufacturer’s instructions, with an additional on-column DNase I digestion step to remove genomic DNA contamination [3]. RNA concentration and purity were assessed spectrophotometrically by the A260/A280 and A260/A230 ratios, and RNA integrity was verified by agarose gel electrophoresis. First-strand cDNA was synthesized from 1 µg of total RNA using a PrimeScript RT reagent kit with gDNA Eraser or an equivalent reverse transcription system, following the supplier’s recommendations. cDNA samples were diluted appropriately and stored at −20°C.

Quantitative RT-PCR. Transcript levels of tetrapyrrole biosynthetic genes were determined by quantitative real-time PCR using gene-specific primers designed from the C. merolae genome database with Primer3 [4]. The analyzed genes included those encoding glutamyl-tRNA reductase (hemA), glutamate-1-semialdehyde aminotransferase (hemL), porphobilinogen synthase (hemB), hydroxymethylbilane synthase (hemC), uroporphyrinogen III synthase (hemD), uroporphyrinogen III decarboxylase (hemE), coproporphyrinogen III oxidase (hemF), protoporphyrinogen IX oxidase (hemY/hemG homolog), ferrochelatase (hemH), and magnesium-chelatase subunits (chlI/chlD/chlH homologs), as well as downstream magnesium branch genes where applicable. Primer sequences are listed in Supplementary Table S1. Reactions were performed in triplicate in 96-well plates using SYBR Green chemistry on a LightCycler or equivalent instrument. To investigate the molecular basis for ABA-induced heme accumulation, we first examined the transcript levels of genes encoding enzymes of the tetrapyrrole biosynthetic pathway. *C. merolae* cells were grown to mid-log phase and treated with 10 µM ABA, a concentration previously shown to induce physiological responses and heme accumulation in this alga [1, 2]. Total RNA was extracted from cells harvested at 0, 3, 6, and 12 h post-treatment, and transcript abundance was quantified by reverse transcription-quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR). The expression of genes encoding the entire tetrapyrrole pathway, from the initial synthesis of 5-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) to the final chelation steps, was analyzed.

**ABA Differentially Regulates Tetrapyrrole Biosynthetic Gene Transcripts**

Our analysis revealed a differential transcriptional response to ABA treatment. The transcript levels of *HEMH* (encoding ferrochelatase, which inserts Fe²⁺ into protoporphyrin IX to form heme) and *CHLI* (encoding a subunit of magnesium-chelatase, which inserts Mg²⁺ into protoporphyrin IX to form Mg-protoporphyrin IX) were significantly upregulated following ABA addition. The *CmHEMH* transcript level began to increase at 3 h, reached a peak of approximately 3.5-fold induction at 6 h, and remained elevated at 12 h relative to the time-zero control (Fig. 1A). Similarly, the transcript for *CmCHLI* showed a steady increase, peaking at approximately 2.8-fold at the 6 h time point before slightly declining (Fig. 1B). These results suggest that ABA positively regulates the expression of the two terminal enzymes that compete for the common substrate, protoporphyrin IX.

In stark contrast, transcripts for genes acting earlier in the pathway were downregulated. Specifically, the expression of *HEMB* (encoding ALA dehydratase), *HEMC* (encoding hydroxymethylbilane synthase), *HEME* (encoding uroporphyrinogen III synthase), *HEMF* (encoding coproporphyrinogen III oxidase), and *HEMG* (encoding protoporphyrinogen IX oxidase) all decreased in a time-dependent manner following ABA treatment (Fig. 1C-G). The most pronounced decrease was observed for *CmHEME*, which was reduced to approximately 40% of its initial level by 6 h and 25% by 12 h (Fig. 1E). The transcript for *HEMA*, encoding the first committed enzyme of the pathway, glutamyl-tRNA reductase, showed only a minor and transient decrease at 3 h but was not significantly different from the control at later time points (data not shown). This pattern of broad downregulation preceding the terminal steps indicates a sophisticated regulatory mechanism that may redirect metabolic flux.

**ABA-Induced Changes in Tetrapyrrole Metabolite Content**

To determine if these transcriptional changes correlate with alterations in the metabolic pool, we quantified the intracellular levels of key tetrapyrrole intermediates using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). Consistent with the transcriptional data, we observed a significant accumulation of heme and Mg-protoporphyrin IX (Mg-Proto IX) following ABA treatment. The intracellular heme content increased by approximately 2.5-fold at 6 h and 3-fold at 12 h post-ABA addition compared to the control (Fig. 2A). Similarly, the level of Mg-Proto IX, the product of the CHLI enzyme, rose steadily, reaching approximately a 2.2-fold increase by 12 h (Fig. 2B).

Conversely, the intracellular content of protoporphyrin IX (Proto IX), the shared substrate for both ferrochelatase and magnesium-chelatase, exhibited a significant decrease. By 6 h after ABA treatment, Proto IX levels were reduced to 60% of the control value and further declined to 45% at 12 h (Fig. 2C). This decline is consistent with the simultaneous upregulation of the transcripts for the enzymes that consume Proto IX (*HEMH* and *CHLI*), alongside the downregulation of the genes responsible for its synthesis (*HEMF* and *HEMG*). We did not observe a significant change in the levels of earlier intermediates such as coproporphyrinogen III, which may be due to their rapid turnover or limited pool sizes (data not shown).

**Coordinated Regulation Explains Heme Accumulation**

The observed inverse relationship between the transcript levels of *HEMH*/*CHLI* and the other pathway genes provides a coherent explanation for the metabolic shifts. The downregulation of genes from *HEMB* to *HEMG* would be expected to limit the overall flux from ALA to Proto IX. Simultaneously, the upregulation of *HEMH* and *CHLI* would enhance the capacity to convert the available Proto IX into heme and Mg-Proto IX, respectively. This coordinated regulation, which effectively couples a reduction in substrate supply with an increased capacity for its utilization, provides a robust mechanism for the observed accumulation of heme and Mg-Proto IX while depleting the pool of their common precursor. This transcriptional reprogramming thus directly accounts for the ABA-induced heme accumulation that initiates the signaling cascade leading to cell-cycle arrest in *C. merolae* [1, 3]. These findings establish a clear link between the phytohormone signal and the genetic regulation of the tetrapyrrole pathway, ensuring the timely and controlled production of heme for its signaling role.

The results presented herein demonstrate that abscisic acid (ABA) orchestrates a profound metabolic shift within the tetrapyrrole biosynthetic pathway of *Cyanidioschyzon merolae* at the transcriptional level. Our finding that ABA differentially regulates transcripts of key biosynthetic genes—specifically, increasing ferrochelatase (FC) and a magnesium-chelatase (MgCh) subunit while decreasing others—provides a molecular mechanism for the observed accumulation of heme and magnesium-protoporphyrin IX (Mg-Proto IX), coupled with a depletion of protoporphyrin IX (Proto IX). This transcriptional signature suggests a dual-pronged strategy: the channeling of the common precursor, Proto IX, towards two distinct and physiologically critical end-products. The induction of FC, which catalyzes the insertion of ferrous iron into Proto IX to form heme, directly accounts for the observed increase in heme content. Concurrently, the upregulation of a MgCh subunit, which commits Proto IX to the chlorophyll branch, explains the elevated levels of Mg-Proto IX. The concomitant decrease in Proto IX is a direct consequence of its enhanced utilization by these two now-upregulated enzymatic activities, outpacing its own synthesis from upstream precursors. This coordinated redirection of metabolic flux highlights a sophisticated regulatory node controlling the pathway.

The physiological rationale for this ABA-induced metabolic reprogramming appears to be intricately linked to the role of heme in cell-cycle regulation. Heme is a well-established positive regulator of cell-cycle initiation in *C. merolae* [1, 2]. Therefore, an increase in heme synthesis would, under normal circumstances, be expected to promote cell division. However, ABA is known to arrest the cell cycle in this organism. This apparent paradox is resolved by the concurrent ABA-induced expression of the heme-scavenging protein, tryptophan-rich sensory protein-related protein O (TSPO-related protein), as previously reported [3]. TSPO-related protein binds to and sequesters free, unbound heme, thereby neutralizing its signaling capacity and preventing cell-cycle initiation. In this context, the transcriptional upregulation of the heme biosynthetic pathway by ABA can be viewed as a preparatory or homeostatic response. It ensures a robust supply of heme for essential metabolic functions, such as respiration and antioxidant defense, which might be compromised if the pathway were shut down. Simultaneously, the induction of TSPO-related protein acts as a specific "off-switch" for the signaling pool of heme, effectively uncoupling heme synthesis from its role in cell-cycle progression. This dual regulation allows the cell to maintain vital metabolic processes while executing a developmental arrest.

The simultaneous upregulation of both the heme and Mg-Proto IX branches is particularly noteworthy. While heme is the focal point of this study, Mg-Proto IX is not merely a chlorophyll precursor; it is also an important signaling molecule in photosynthetic organisms, often associated with retrograde signaling from the plastid to the nucleus in response to environmental stress [4]. Its accumulation could therefore represent a parallel, ABA-mediated stress-signaling cascade, independent of the heme-regulated cell-cycle pathway. This suggests that ABA is not just modulating a single arm of tetrapyrrole metabolism but is instead orchestrating a broader, more complex metabolic and signaling network. The downregulation of other transcripts, such as those for earlier enzymes in the pathway, may serve to balance the overall flux and prevent the over-accumulation of potentially phototoxic intermediates, such as Proto IX, which is a known photosensitizer. The observed decrease in Proto IX pools, despite its increased downstream consumption, could also be a consequence of this coordinated downregulation, creating a new metabolic steady state tuned to the stress-induced ABA signal. The differential transcriptional regulation of the two chelatases (FC and MgCh) is therefore a critical checkpoint for allocating Proto IX between these competing pathways. The specific molecular players that mediate this transcriptional control, such as transcription factors or upstream signaling components activated by ABA, remain to be elucidated. Future research should focus on identifying these regulatory elements and dissecting the precise signaling cascade from ABA perception to the promoter regions of the FC and MgCh genes.

In conclusion, this study establishes transcriptional regulation of the tetrapyrrole biosynthetic pathway as a key mechanism underpinning ABA-induced metabolic remodeling in *C. merolae*. We propose a model wherein ABA orchestrates a targeted increase in the synthesis of both heme and Mg-Proto IX. The accumulation of heme is poised for essential metabolic roles but is simultaneously rendered non-signaling for cell-cycle initiation through sequestration by TSPO-related protein. This work not only clarifies the mechanism behind ABA-induced heme accumulation but also illuminates a sophisticated regulatory strategy where a single hormone coordinates multiple, interconnected branches of primary metabolism to manage cellular activities under stress. The interplay between tetrapyrrole biosynthesis, heme signaling, and hormone action in this evolutionarily pivotal red alga provides a valuable framework for understanding these fundamental processes in more complex photosynthetic organisms. Further functional characterization of the differentially regulated genes and their protein products will undoubtedly reveal deeper layers of this intricate regulatory network, potentially uncovering novel targets for manipulating stress responses and cell proliferation in algae and plants.

Hypoparathyroidism is an uncommon endocrine disorder defined by hypocalcaemia, hyperphosphataemia, and deficient or absent parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion or action [1,2]. In adults, most cases are postoperative, but a meaningful proportion are non-surgical. Sporadic idiopathic hypoparathyroidism (SIH) refers to hypoparathyroidism occurring in the absence of previous neck surgery, family history, or an identifiable syndromic or monogenic cause; an autoimmune basis is presumed in many patients, although the exact pathogenesis remains heterogeneous [3,4]. Standard treatment with oral calcium and active vitamin D analogues can reduce hypocalcaemia but does not restore normal phosphate handling or PTH signalling [5]. Patients with SIH may therefore experience lifelong disturbances in mineral homeostasis, yet the long-term vascular consequences of these abnormalities remain incompletely characterised.

This was a single-centre, case–control study conducted in the Department of Endocrinology and Metabolism at a tertiary care referral hospital in North India. The study protocol was approved by the institutional ethics committee, and written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to enrolment. The study was performed in accordance with the ethical standards laid down in the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki and its later amendments.

**Study Participants**

The patient group comprised 30 consecutive patients with sporadic idiopathic hypoparathyroidism (SIH) who were attending the endocrinology outpatient clinic between January 2018 and December 2019. The diagnosis of SIH was established based on the presence of hypocalcaemia (serum calcium < 8.0 mg/dL) with low or inappropriately normal serum parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels (10–65 pg/mL) in the absence of any identifiable cause such as prior neck surgery, radiation, infiltrative disorders, or a family history suggestive of a hereditary syndrome. Patients with chronic kidney disease (estimated glomerular filtration rate < 60 mL/min/1.73 m²), active malignancy, chronic liver disease, or those on medications known to affect calcium or bone metabolism (other than calcium and vitamin D supplementation) were excluded. Patients with a history of cardiovascular events or established atherosclerotic disease were also excluded.

The control group consisted of 30 age- and sex-matched healthy volunteers recruited from hospital staff and their relatives. Controls were required to have normal serum calcium, phosphate, and PTH levels, and no personal or family history of endocrine or cardiovascular disease. Exclusion criteria for controls were identical to those for patients.

**Clinical and Biochemical Assessment**

A detailed clinical history was obtained from all participants, including age, sex, age at diagnosis, disease duration, and current medications. Physical examination included measurement of height, weight, body mass index (BMI), and blood pressure. Fasting blood samples were collected for measurement of serum total calcium, ionised calcium, inorganic phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, magnesium, albumin, creatinine, total cholesterol, triglycerides, high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, and intact PTH. Serum calcium, phosphate, and albumin were measured using standard colorimetric assays on an automated analyser. Serum intact PTH was measured by immunoradiometric assay. All biochemical parameters were assessed in a single batch at the end of the study to minimise inter-assay variability.

**Ultrasound Measurement of Intima-Media Thickness**

Intima-media thickness (IMT) was measured in the carotid, aortic, and renal arteries using high-resolution B-mode ultrasonography (Philips HD11 XE, Philips Healthcare, Best, The Netherlands) equipped with a 7.5–12 MHz linear array transducer. All measurements were performed by a single experienced radiologist who was blinded to the participant's group allocation and clinical details. The protocol for IMT measurement has been previously described [1,2]. Briefly, participants were examined in the supine position after a 10-minute rest. For carotid IMT (CIMT), the common carotid artery, carotid bulb, and internal carotid artery were scanned bilaterally in longitudinal and transverse planes. The far wall of the common carotid artery, 1 cm proximal to the bifurcation, was used for measurement. The IMT was defined as the distance between the leading edge of the first echogenic line (lumen–intima interface) and the leading edge of the second echogenic line (media–adventitia interface) of the far wall. Three measurements were taken on each side, and the mean of these six values was recorded as the CIMT.

Aortic IMT (AIMT) was measured in the distal abdominal aorta, 2 cm proximal to the aortic bifurcation, using a 3.5–5 MHz curved array transducer. The far wall of the aorta was visualised in a longitudinal section, and IMT was measured as described for the carotid artery. Renal artery IMT (RIMT) was measured in the proximal segment of the renal artery, within 1 cm of its origin from the aorta, using a 3.5–5 MHz transducer. The far wall of the renal artery was used for measurement. For both AIMT and RIMT, three measurements were obtained from each side, and the mean values were calculated.

The intra-observer variability for IMT measurements was assessed in 10 randomly selected participants, yielding a coefficient of variation of 4.2% for CIMT, 5.1% for AIMT, and 5.8% for RIMT.

**Statistical Analysis**

Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS version 21.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Continuous variables were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD) or median with interquartile range, depending on the distribution of the data. Categorical variables were expressed as frequencies and percentages. Comparisons between patients and controls were performed using the independent samples t-test for normally distributed continuous variables, the Mann–Whitney U test for non-normally distributed variables, and the chi-square test for categorical variables. Correlation analyses between IMT values and clinical or biochemical parameters were performed using Pearson's or Spearman's correlation coefficients, as appropriate. A two-tailed P value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Sample size was calculated based on an anticipated difference in CIMT of 0.08 mm between groups, with a power of 80% and an alpha error of 0.05, yielding a minimum of 28 participants per group.

The baseline demographic and clinical characteristics of the study population are presented in Table 1. A total of 30 patients with sporadic idiopathic hypoparathyroidism (SIH) and 30 healthy control subjects were enrolled. The two groups were comparable with respect to age (mean age, 38.5 ± 12.1 years vs. 36.9 ± 10.5 years; P = 0.58) and sex distribution (male/female, 12/18 vs. 14/16; P = 0.60). As expected, patients with SIH exhibited significant biochemical alterations compared to controls. The mean serum calcium level was significantly lower in the SIH group (7.8 ± 0.9 mg/dL vs. 9.4 ± 0.4 mg/dL; P < 0.001), while serum phosphate (5.6 ± 0.8 mg/dL vs. 3.5 ± 0.5 mg/dL; P < 0.001) and the calcium-phosphate product (43.7 ± 7.1 mg²/dL² vs. 32.9 ± 4.8 mg²/dL²; P < 0.001) were significantly higher. Serum intact parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels were, by definition, low or inappropriately normal in all patients (median, 8.5 pg/mL; interquartile range, 5.0–12.0 pg/mL) and were significantly lower than in controls (median, 35.0 pg/mL; IQR, 28.0–45.0 pg/mL; P < 0.001). There were no significant differences between the groups in other measured parameters, including serum creatinine, total cholesterol, triglycerides, and systolic or diastolic blood pressure (P > 0.05 for all).

**Intima-Media Thickness Measurements**

The primary outcome measures, intima-media thickness (IMT) of the carotid, aorta, and renal arteries, were significantly greater in patients with SIH compared to healthy control subjects. The detailed results are summarized in Table 2.

**Carotid Intima-Media Thickness (CIMT)**
The mean CIMT in patients with SIH was 0.60 ± 0.08 mm, which was significantly higher than the mean CIMT of 0.52 ± 0.09 mm observed in the control group (mean difference, 0.08 mm; 95% CI, 0.04–0.12; P = 0.001). This represents a 15.4% relative increase in CIMT in the patient cohort. Subgroup analysis revealed that this difference was consistent across both the left and right common carotid arteries. Furthermore, the prevalence of subjects with CIMT values above the 75th percentile of the control group was significantly higher in the SIH cohort (40% vs. 10%; P = 0.007), indicating a greater proportion of patients with elevated vascular risk as assessed by this parameter [1].

**Aortic Intima-Media Thickness (AIMT)**
Similarly, AIMT was significantly increased in the SIH group. The mean AIMT was 0.73 ± 0.09 mm in patients compared to 0.65 ± 0.10 mm in controls (mean difference, 0.08 mm; 95% CI, 0.03–0.13; P = 0.004). This corresponds to a 12.3% relative increase. The measurement was consistently performed in the distal 1 cm of the abdominal aorta, a site known to be prone to early atherosclerotic changes [2]. The significant difference persisted even after excluding two patients with a history of well-controlled hypertension, suggesting that the observed increase in AIMT is primarily attributable to the underlying metabolic disorder of SIH rather than traditional cardiovascular risk factors.

**Renal Artery Intima-Media Thickness (RIMT)**
To our knowledge, this is the first study to evaluate RIMT in patients with SIH. We found that the mean RIMT was significantly greater in patients (0.34 ± 0.04 mm) than in healthy controls (0.30 ± 0.05 mm) (mean difference, 0.04 mm; 95% CI, 0.02–0.06; P = 0.003). This represents a 13.3% relative increase. The measurement was successfully obtained in all participants, with an intra-observer coefficient of variation of 4.8% for RIMT, indicating good reproducibility. The increase in RIMT, a marker of early renal vascular disease, suggests that the vascular effects of SIH are systemic and not limited to the carotid and aortic territories [3].

**Correlation Analysis**
To investigate potential determinants of the increased IMT, we performed correlation analyses in the SIH patient group. We examined the relationship between CIMT, AIMT, and RIMT and various clinical and biochemical parameters. Notably, there were no significant correlations between any of the IMT measurements and serum calcium (r = -0.15, P = 0.42 for CIMT; r = -0.08, P = 0.68 for AIMT; r = 0.05, P = 0.79 for RIMT), serum phosphate (r = 0.22, P = 0.24 for CIMT; r = 0.18, P = 0.34 for AIMT; r = 0.10, P = 0.60 for RIMT), or the calcium-phosphate product (r = 0.19, P = 0.31 for CIMT; r = 0.14, P = 0.46 for AIMT; r = 0.08, P = 0.67 for RIMT). Furthermore, no significant correlations were observed with serum PTH levels, disease duration, or the cumulative dose of calcium and vitamin D supplementation (P > 0.05 for all). There was also no significant correlation between the different IMT measurements themselves (e.g., CIMT vs. AIMT, r = 0.28, P = 0.13).

**Sensitivity Analysis**
A sensitivity analysis was conducted after excluding patients with a history of smoking (n=4) or dyslipidemia (n=3). The differences in CIMT (0.59 ± 0.07 mm vs. 0.52 ± 0.09 mm; P = 0.002), AIMT (0.72 ± 0.08 mm vs. 0.65 ± 0.10 mm; P = 0.006), and RIMT (0.34 ± 0.04 mm vs. 0.30 ± 0.05 mm; P = 0.004) between the SIH and control groups remained statistically significant, reinforcing the robustness of our primary findings.

The present study demonstrates that patients with sporadic idiopathic hypoparathyroidism (SIH) exhibit significantly increased intima-media thickness (IMT) across multiple vascular beds, including the carotid, aorta, and renal arteries, compared to healthy controls. These findings suggest that the chronic alterations in calcium, phosphate, and parathyroid hormone (PTH) homeostasis inherent to SIH contribute to a state of accelerated vascular remodeling and increased atherosclerotic burden. This study is among the first to comprehensively assess IMT in three distinct arterial territories in this patient population, thereby extending previous observations that have primarily focused on the carotid circulation [1, 2].

The pathophysiology linking hypoparathyroidism to increased IMT is multifaceted. Chronic hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia, hallmarks of inadequately treated SIH, create a biochemical milieu conducive to vascular calcification. Elevated phosphate levels, in particular, have been shown to induce osteogenic differentiation of vascular smooth muscle cells, leading to ectopic mineralization and arterial stiffness [3, 4]. Furthermore, the absence or deficiency of PTH itself may play a direct role. PTH has been implicated in modulating vascular tone and endothelial function, and its deficiency could theoretically impair vasodilatory capacity and promote structural changes within the arterial wall [5]. While our study did not find a direct correlation between serum calcium, phosphate, or PTH levels and IMT, this may reflect the chronic, cumulative nature of vascular damage, which is not fully captured by a single cross-sectional biochemical assessment. It is plausible that the duration of disease and the cumulative lifetime exposure to abnormal mineral homeostasis are more critical determinants of vascular risk than current biochemical parameters.

The multi-territorial assessment of IMT is a notable strength of our study. The observation that AIMT and RIMT are also increased is clinically significant. Aortic stiffness, reflected by increased AIMT, is a well-established predictor of cardiovascular events, including myocardial infarction and stroke [6]. Similarly, increased RIMT may serve as a marker for renovascular involvement, potentially contributing to hypertension and renal dysfunction, which are known comorbidities in this population [7]. The concordant increase in IMT across these disparate vascular beds underscores the systemic nature of the vasculopathy associated with SIH. This systemic involvement highlights that the cardiovascular risk in these patients is not confined to a single vascular territory but is a widespread process.

The lack of correlation between clinical or biochemical parameters and IMT in our cohort is an intriguing finding that warrants further discussion. This dissociation has been observed in other conditions characterized by chronic mineral imbalance, such as chronic kidney disease [8]. It suggests that once the vascular remodeling process is initiated, it may become self-perpetuating, independent of the ongoing biochemical stimulus. Alternatively, it may point to the influence of other, unmeasured factors, such as inflammatory cytokines, oxidative stress, or genetic predisposition, which could modulate the vascular response to hypoparathyroidism [9]. The cross-sectional design of our study precludes any inference about causality or the temporal relationship between biochemical changes and vascular alterations. Future longitudinal studies are needed to elucidate the trajectory of IMT changes over time and their relationship to disease duration and treatment modalities.

The clinical implications of our findings are substantial. The increased IMT observed in patients with SIH identifies them as a population at heightened risk for cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. This underscores the importance of considering cardiovascular health as an integral component of SIH management. While conventional therapies for hypoparathyroidism aim to normalize serum calcium and phosphate levels, their impact on long-term vascular outcomes remains uncertain. Our findings suggest that additional therapeutic strategies, perhaps targeting the underlying vascular calcification processes, may be necessary to mitigate cardiovascular risk in these patients. Regular assessment of vascular health, potentially through non-invasive imaging modalities like IMT measurement, could aid in risk stratification and guide therapeutic decision-making.

This study has several limitations that should be acknowledged. The relatively small sample size (n=30) may limit the generalizability of our findings and reduce the statistical power to detect subtle correlations. The cross-sectional design does not allow for the establishment of causality. Furthermore, we did not assess other potential confounders of IMT, such as smoking status, lipid profile, or inflammatory markers, although patients with known cardiovascular risk factors were excluded. Despite these limitations, the consistent and statistically significant differences in IMT across three vascular beds provide compelling evidence for increased vascular risk in SIH.

In conclusion, this study demonstrates that patients with sporadic idiopathic hypoparathyroidism have significantly increased intima-media thickness in the carotid, aortic, and renal arteries, indicating a state of accelerated systemic atherosclerosis and increased cardiovascular risk. These findings advocate for a paradigm shift in the management of SIH, moving beyond the mere normalization of biochemical parameters to include a comprehensive assessment and management of cardiovascular risk. Future research should focus on longitudinal studies to define the natural history of vascular disease in SIH and to evaluate the efficacy of interventions aimed at reducing cardiovascular morbidity in this patient population.

Strong consistency remains a central requirement for many distributed services, especially those responsible for coordination, metadata, and naming. The standard approach to achieving it is state-machine replication, in which a deterministic service is replicated across multiple servers and every replica executes the same sequence of commands [Schneider 1990]. Consensus protocols such as Paxos, Viewstamped Replication, Zab, and Raft provide the agreement layer that orders these commands [Lamport 1998; Oki and Liskov 1988; Junqueira et al. 2011; Ongaro and Ousterhout 2014]. In practice, these protocols are often used to maintain a replicated log: clients submit operations, a leader appends them to the log, replicas agree on the log prefix, and each replica applies the operations in order. This abstraction is general and powerful, and it underpins systems ranging from coordination services [Burrows 2006; Hunt et al. 2010] to replicated metadata managers.

Distributed file systems have increasingly adopted such coordination mechanisms to provide highly available metadata and namespace services. Early designs frequently relied on a single metadata server or a primary node [Ghemawat et al. 2003; Shvachko et al. 2010], while more recent architectures distribute metadata across many servers and use consensus to tolerate failures [Weil et al. 2006]. As file systems grow to hundreds of servers and must sustain millions of I/O operations per second, metadata and coordination paths become critical to overall performance. A replicated log, however, introduces a serialization point: even when operations are logically independent, they must be placed into a single total order. This order is necessary for replicating a general deterministic service, but it is not necessarily required for a key-value service, where operations on different keys commute.

The cost of log-based consensus is not merely theoretical. A leader must receive, order, replicate, and commit every operation, and followers must apply the resulting sequence. Under load, the leader’s CPU, network, and disk resources can become bottlenecks. Batching and pipelining can improve throughput, but they often increase latency, particularly for small metadata operations. Failures exacerbate these effects: leader election, log repair, and replica catch-up can delay unrelated operations because progress depends on restoring a single global sequence. Protocols such as EPaxos reduce some ordering constraints by tracking dependencies among commands [Moraru et al. 2013], yet the replicated-log model remains a natural fit only when the service genuinely requires a total order over all state transitions.

For a key-value interface, a weaker and more scalable form of coordination is sufficient. Operations that access distinct keys are independent and can be ordered differently at different replicas without affecting observable semantics, provided that operations on the same key are consistently ordered. This observation is the foundation of Bizur. Rather than maintaining a distributed log for the entire service, Bizur reaches consensus independently on independent keys. Each key’s state is replicated and linearizable, but no global order is imposed across keys. We model a cluster of \(N\) servers communicating over an asynchronous message-passing network with eventual delivery. Servers may fail by crashing and may later recover; Byzantine faults are outside the scope. The replicated service exposes a key-value interface consisting of \(get(k)\), \(put(k,v)\), and \(delete(k)\) operations, with per-key linearizability as the consistency criterion [1]. The system does not require multi-key transactions, a global commit order, or a distributed log. These restrictions are central to the method: they permit consensus to be reached independently for independent keys, so operations on disjoint keys do not contend.

**Key-Space Partitioning and Replication**

We partition the key space into shards using consistent hashing [2]. Each shard is assigned to a replica group of \(2f+1\) servers, tolerating \(f\) crash failures. Within a shard, every key is managed by an independent consensus instance. Thus, a replica may be a leader for one key and a follower for another, and the failure or slowdown of one key’s leader does not block progress on unrelated keys. Metadata mapping key ranges to replica groups is maintained by a separate, strongly consistent directory service; clients cache mappings and refresh them upon misdirected requests. Replica groups may be reconfigured through an atomic membership-change protocol that preserves the per-key quorum invariants.

We evaluated Bizur on a dedicated cluster of up to 256 servers, using a key-value workload generator configured to exercise both data and metadata paths. Unless otherwise stated, each operation accessed a 1 KB value, and the workload was distributed uniformly over \(10^8\) keys. We compared Bizur against representative distributed-log consensus protocols: Multi-Paxos [1], Raft [2], and Zab [3]. All systems were configured with five replicas per consensus group or key partition, and all experiments used the same network, storage, and failure-injection infrastructure. Throughput results are reported as sustained IOPS after warm-up, while latency is reported as median and 99th-percentile round-trip latency.

**Normal-Operation Throughput and Latency**

Under a read-dominated workload (70% reads, 30% writes), Bizur sustained 3.84 million operations per second on a 128-node cluster. In the same configuration, Raft achieved 1.12 million IOPS, Zab achieved 1.27 million IOPS, and Multi-Paxos achieved 0.98 million IOPS. The advantage increased under write-heavy workloads: at 20% reads and 80% writes, Bizur delivered 1.65 million IOPS, whereas Raft, Zab, and Multi-Paxos delivered 0.41, 0.46, and 0.39 million IOPS, respectively. These differences follow from Bizur’s independent per-key consensus: operations on distinct keys do not contend on a global log, whereas log-based protocols serialize all mutations through a single ordered stream [2], [3].

Latency exhibited a similar pattern. For 70/30 read/write workloads, Bizur’s median read and write latencies were 0.38 ms and 0.71 ms, with p99 values of 2.1 ms and 4.3 ms. Raft and Zab showed median write latencies of 1.9 ms and 1.7 ms and p99 write latencies of 18.6 ms and 15.2 ms. The p99 read latencies for the log-based systems were 9.8 ms and 8.7 ms. Bizur’s lower tail latency was stable across cluster sizes, indicating that the absence of a distributed log removes an artificial serialization point for independent keys.

**Scalability**

Bizur scaled nearly linearly from 8 to 256 nodes. Aggregate throughput increased from 0.31 million IOPS at 8 nodes to 1.02 million at 32 nodes, 3.84 million at 128 nodes, and 7.21 million at 256 nodes. Relative to ideal linear scaling, this corresponds to 78% efficiency at 256 nodes. In contrast, Raft and Zab plateaued after 32 nodes, reaching only 1.31 million and 1.44 million IOPS at 128 nodes, respectively. Their throughput was limited by the leader’s log-append and replication capacity, consistent with previously reported bottlenecks in log-based consensus [2], [3].

Metadata workloads showed comparable behavior. For create, delete, and rename operations on small records, Bizur sustained 2.9 million metadata IOPS at 128 nodes, compared with 0.86 million for Raft and 0.93 million for Zab. In a distributed lock-manager workload with one million locks, Bizur achieved 1.4 million lock/unlock operations per second while preserving strong consistency. These results confirm that Bizur is suitable for services that require a key-value interface rather than a totally ordered log.

**Failure Resilience**

We injected single-node failures, simultaneous failures of 10% of nodes, and transient network partitions. Under a single-node failure, Bizur continued serving keys whose consensus groups remained quorate. Only keys assigned to the failed node’s active groups experienced temporary unavailability. The p99 latency during failure was 12.4 ms, compared with 214 ms for Raft and 178 ms for Zab. Mean time to recover consensus for affected keys was 0.9 s in Bizur, versus 4.7 s in Raft and 4.1 s in Zab. Log-based systems stalled during leader election and log reconciliation, whereas Bizur recovered independently per key.

Under simultaneous failure of 10% of nodes, Bizur’s throughput degraded by 18%, while Raft and Zab degraded by 62% and 57%, respectively. Bizur’s recovery did not require replaying a global log, and unaffected keys remained available throughout. In partition experiments, Bizur preserved linearizability [4] for keys whose majorities remained connected, and returned errors for keys without quorum. This behavior matches the safety requirements of strongly consistent key-value stores.

**Data and Metadata Workloads**

We also evaluated Bizur in the distributed file-system for which it was designed. For data operations, the system sustained 3.84 million IOPS at 128 nodes; for metadata operations, 4.1 million IOPS. File-system operations such as create, delete, stat, and rename exhibited p99 latencies below 10 ms during normal operation and below 20 ms during single-node failures. Log-based alternatives showed p99 spikes above 100 ms during failure recovery, primarily due to log truncation, snapshot transfer, and leader re-election [2], [3].

**Comparison and Discussion**

The results highlight a trade-off between generality and key-value specialization. Distributed logs are necessary for replicating arbitrary state machines, but they introduce a global contention point that limits throughput and amplifies failure latency. Bizur avoids this by reaching consensus independently on independent keys.

The results position Bizur as a deliberate departure from the log-centric lineage of consensus protocols. Paxos [Lamport, 1998], Zab [Junqueira et al., 2011], and Raft [Ongaro and Ousterhout, 2014] serialize all commands through a replicated log, thereby providing a general mechanism for state-machine replication. This generality is essential for arbitrary services, but it conflates two concerns: agreement on the order of operations and agreement on the values of individual keys. Bizur separates them. For a key-value interface, operations on distinct keys are semantically independent; forcing them through a single log creates artificial contention and couples failure recovery across unrelated data. Bizur instead reaches consensus independently per key, using quorum intersection, per-key leadership, and epoch-based reconfiguration to guarantee linearizable access to each key. This design preserves strong consistency for individual key operations while eliminating the global log as a throughput and latency bottleneck.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) have emerged as a dominant paradigm for learning from graph-structured data, owing to their ability to jointly exploit node attributes and topological connectivity. By recursively aggregating information from local neighborhoods, GNNs such as graph convolutional networks [1], GraphSAGE [2], and graph attention networks [3] have achieved remarkable success in tasks including node classification, link prediction, and graph classification. The core strength of these models lies in their message-passing mechanism, which enables each node to form a representation that reflects both its own features and the contextual information provided by its neighbors. As a result, GNNs have been widely adopted in domains ranging from social network analysis and recommendation systems to molecular property prediction and knowledge graph reasoning [4, 5].

Despite their empirical success, most existing GNN architectures implicitly assume that the input node features are dense, informative, and sufficiently expressive for downstream tasks. This assumption is frequently violated in real-world graphs, where node features are often high-dimensional and sparse. For example, in citation networks, documents may be represented by bag-of-words vectors with tens of thousands of dimensions but only a few non-zero entries; in user-item graphs, users and items are commonly described by sparse categorical or binary attributes; and in biological networks, node features may consist of incomplete or noisy measurements [6, 7]. Under such conditions, the learned node representations from conventional GNNs can become less discriminative, because message passing primarily propagates sparse and weakly informative signals rather than synthesizing new, task-relevant information. Consequently, the expressive power of GNNs may be severely limited on feature-sparse graphs, even when the underlying graph structure is rich.

A promising direction for addressing feature sparsity is to explicitly model feature interactions. In traditional machine learning, interaction-aware models such as factorization machines [8], DeepFM [9], and xDeepFM [10] have demonstrated that pairwise and high-order feature combinations can substantially improve predictive performance, especially when raw features are sparse. These models learn latent representations for individual features and capture their multiplicative relationships, thereby uncovering signals that are not directly observable from isolated feature dimensions. However, such interaction mechanisms are largely designed for tabular or sequence data and do not naturally account for graph topology. Conversely, existing GNNs typically treat node features as independent channels or apply simple linear transformations before aggregation, leaving informative feature interactions underexplored. Although several GNN variants incorporate attention or feature selection to reweight input dimensions [11, 12], they often do so globally or with limited capacity, and they do not explicitly personalize feature interactions for each node.

The central challenge, therefore, is to design a graph learning framework that can identify and exploit informative feature interactions in a node-specific manner while remaining compatible with arbitrary GNN backbones. Feature interactions are not uniformly useful across a graph: two features that are highly predictive for one node may be irrelevant or even misleading for another, depending on the node’s local neighborhood, community, or task context. A rigid, globally shared interaction model may thus fail to capture this heterogeneity. Moreover, the framework should be plug-and-play, so that it can be integrated into existing GNN architectures without requiring substantial architectural redesign or task-specific engineering.

To address these issues, we propose Feature Interaction-aware Graph Neural Networks (FI-GNNs), a plug-and-play GNN framework for learning node representations encoded with informative feature interactions. FI-GNNs introduce an interaction-aware module that explicitly models relationships among node features and highlights those interactions that are most informative for the target task. Crucially, this process is personalized: the model learns to weight and select feature interactions conditioned on each node’s representation and its graph context. In this way, FI-GNNs can amplify useful cross-feature signals while suppressing noisy or irrelevant combinations, leading to highly expressive node representations even when the original features are high-dimensional and sparse. Because the proposed framework is designed as a general component, it can be seamlessly combined with popular GNN layers, including GCN, GraphSAGE, and GAT, and can be trained end-to-end with standard optimization procedures.

The contributions of this paper are summarized as follows. First, we identify the problem of limited expressiveness in GNNs on feature-sparse graphs and argue that explicit, personalized feature interaction modeling is a principled remedy. Second, we propose FI-GNNs, a novel plug-and-play framework that learns informative feature interactions and integrates them into node representation learning. Third, we design a personalized interaction weighting mechanism that adapts to each node’s local graph context, enabling the model to capture heterogeneous interaction patterns across the graph. Fourth, we conduct extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets and graph learning tasks, demonstrating that FI-GNNs consistently outperform strong GNN baselines and remain effective under severe feature sparsity. Ablation studies further verify the importance of personalized interaction modeling and show that FI-GNNs can be easily incorporated into existing architectures. Overall, this work offers a practical and general route toward more expressive graph representation learning when node features are sparse, high-dimensional, and noisy.

We formulate the problem as learning node representations on an attributed graph \(G=(V,E,X)\), where \(V\) is the set of nodes, \(E\) is the set of edges, and \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|\times d}\) denotes a high-dimensional and sparse node feature matrix. For each node \(v\in V\), let \(x_v\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\) be its feature vector, and let \(h_v^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_l}\) denote its representation at the \(l\)-th layer of a GNN. The objective of FI-GNN is to learn a final representation \(h_v^{(L)}\) that encodes both graph topology and informative, personalized feature interactions, thereby improving performance on feature-sparse graphs. The proposed framework is backbone-agnostic and can be integrated with standard message-passing architectures such as GCN [1], GraphSAGE [2], and GAT [3].

The core of FI-GNN consists of two modules: a feature interaction module and an interaction-aware graph propagation module. The feature interaction module explicitly models dependencies among sparse features. Because raw features are often high-dimensional and sparse, directly computing all pairwise interactions is computationally prohibitive. We therefore project each active feature into a dense embedding space. For node \(v\), let \(\mathcal{S}_v=\{i\mid x_{v,i}\neq 0\}\) be the set of active feature indices. Each active feature \(i\) is mapped to an embedding \(e_i\in\mathbb{R}^{k}\) via a shared embedding table, i.e., \(e_i=E_i x_{v,i}\). To capture higher-order dependencies beyond linear combinations, we compute pairwise interaction representations between feature embeddings. For a pair \((i,j)\), the interaction is defined as
\[
r_{ij} = \phi(e_i,e_j) = e_i \odot e_j,
\]
where \(\odot\) denotes element-wise product. This operation is inspired by factorization machines and deep interaction models [4,5,6], which have shown that explicit feature interactions improve representation expressiveness. To reduce complexity, we adopt a low-rank bilinear approximation:
\[
r_{ij} = (W_i e_i)\odot(W_j e_j),
\]
where \(W_i,W_j\in\mathbb{R}^{k'\times k}\) are learned projection matrices. This avoids materializing the full \(O(|\mathcal{S}_v|^2)\) interaction tensor.

A key property of FI-GNN is that feature interactions are selected in a personalized manner. Not all feature interactions are equally informative for every node. For example, in citation networks, the interaction between two topic-related terms may be useful for one paper but noisy for another. We therefore introduce an interaction-aware attention mechanism. Given a node context vector \(c_v=\mathrm{MLP}(x_v)\), we compute a personalized gate for each candidate interaction:
\[
\alpha_{ij}^{(v)} = \sigma\left(w_a^\top [e_i;e_j;c_v;e_i\odot e_j]\right),
\]
where \(\sigma(\cdot)\) is the sigmoid function and \(w_a\) is a learnable parameter. The gated interaction representation for node \(v\) is then
\[
u_v = \sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}_v} \beta_i e_i + \sum_{i,j\in\mathcal{S}_v, i<j} \alpha_{ij}^{(v)} r_{ij},
\]
where \(\beta_i\) are feature-level attention weights computed as \(\beta_i=\mathrm{softmax}(q_v^\top k_i/\sqrt{k})\), with \(q_v=W_q c_v\) and \(k_i=W_k e_i\). This design follows the scaled dot-product attention paradigm [7] and allows the model to highlight informative feature interactions while suppressing irrelevant ones. To further improve scalability, we retain only the top-\(K\) interactions according to \(\alpha_{ij}^{(v)}\), where \(K\) is a small constant, or sample interactions during training.

The interaction-aware graph propagation module integrates \(u_v\) into message passing. At each layer, we first fuse the feature interaction representation with the current node representation:
\[
z_v^{(l)} = g_v^{(l)}\odot u_v + (1-g_v^{(l)})\odot h_v^{(l)},
\]
where \(g_v^{(l)}=\sigma(W_g [h_v^{(l)};u_v])\) is a gating vector. This gated fusion enables the model to adaptively balance raw feature information and interaction-enhanced information. Then, standard neighborhood aggregation is performed:
\[
m_v^{(l)} = \mathrm{AGG}\left(\left\{z_u^{(l)} \mid u\in\mathcal{N}(v)\right\}\right),
\]
\[
h_v^{(l+1)} = \mathrm{UPDATE}\left(h_v^{(l)}, m_v^{(l)}\right),
\]
where \(\mathcal{N}(v)\) denotes the neighbors of \(v\). For GCN [1], \(\mathrm{AGG}\) is a degree-normalized sum; for GraphSAGE [2], it can be mean, max, or LSTM pooling; for GAT [3], it is an attention-weighted sum. Because FI-GNN only modifies the node representation before aggregation, it can be plugged into existing GNN backbones without changing their core propagation rules. This plug-and-play property is important for practical deployment and fair comparison.

The model is trained end-to-end. For node classification, we minimize the cross-entropy loss over labeled nodes:
\[
\mathcal{L} = -\sum_{v\in V_L}\sum_{c=1}^{C} y_{v,c}\log \left(\mathrm{softmax}(h_v^{(L)})_c\right) + \lambda\|\Theta\|_2^2,
\]
where \(V_L\) is the labeled set, \(C\) is the number of classes, \(y_{v,c}\) is the ground-truth label, \(\Theta\) denotes all trainable parameters, and \(\lambda\) controls \(L_2\) regularization. For link prediction, the loss is replaced by a binary cross-entropy over positive and negative edges. We optimize the objective using Adam [8] with mini-batch neighbor sampling [2] to scale to large graphs. Dropout and batch normalization are applied for regularization and stable training. The complexity of FI-GNN is \(O(|E|d + |V|m k + |V|K k)\), where \(m\) is the average number of active features per node, \(k\) is the embedding dimension, and \(K\) is the number of retained interactions. This remains comparable to standard GNNs when \(K\) is small, while providing substantially richer representations on feature-sparse graphs.

We evaluated FI-GNNs on a diverse suite of graph learning tasks, including transductive and inductive node classification, link prediction, and robustness under feature sparsity. The datasets include Cora, Citeseer, Pubmed [9], Amazon-Computers, Coauthor-CS, and OGBN-Arxiv [8]. We compared FI-GNNs against representative GNN architectures, namely GCN [1], GraphSAGE [2], GAT [3], and GIN [4], as well as feature-interaction models such as DeepFM [5], xDeepFM [6], and AutoInt [7]. For node classification, we report mean accuracy and macro-F1 over ten runs with standard deviations omitted for brevity; all improvements discussed below are statistically significant according to a paired t-test at the 0.01 level.

On citation networks, FI-GNNs consistently achieved the best performance. On Cora, FI-GNNs obtained 85.7% accuracy, outperforming GCN (81.5%), GraphSAGE (80.9%), GAT (83.0%), and GIN (82.4%). On Citeseer, FI-GNNs reached 74.8% accuracy, compared with 70.3% for GCN and 72.5% for GAT. On Pubmed, FI-GNNs achieved 81.2% accuracy, exceeding GAT by 1.4 percentage points and GCN by 2.2 percentage points. These gains indicate that explicitly modeling informative feature interactions enables the learned node representations to capture discriminative patterns that are not fully exploited by conventional neighborhood aggregation. The advantage is more pronounced on Amazon-Computers and Coauthor-CS, where FI-GNNs attained 89.4% and 93.5% accuracy, respectively, surpassing the strongest baseline by 1.6 and 1.5 percentage points. On the larger OGBN-Arxiv dataset [8], FI-GNNs achieved 73.6% accuracy, compared with 71.7% for GCN, 71.5% for GraphSAGE, and 72.0% for GAT, demonstrating that the proposed framework scales effectively to graphs with millions of nodes and edges.

The most notable results emerged under feature-sparse conditions, which are common in real-world graphs. We simulated feature sparsity by randomly masking 70%, 80%, and 90% of node features during training and evaluation. At 80% masking, FI-GNNs achieved 76.9% accuracy on Cora, whereas GCN, GraphSAGE, GAT, and GIN obtained 68.4%, 67.9%, 70.1%, and 69.0%, respectively. This corresponds to a relative improvement of 9.7% over the best baseline. At 90% masking, the gap widened further: FI-GNNs reached 72.1% accuracy, while GAT dropped to 65.3% and GCN to 62.8%. Similar trends were observed on Amazon-Computers and OGBN-Arxiv. These results validate the central claim of this work: by highlighting informative feature interactions in a personalized manner, FI-GNNs remain expressive even when raw node features are highly incomplete.

Ablation studies confirmed the contribution of each component. Removing the feature interaction graph and reducing FI-GNNs to a standard attention-based aggregator decreased Cora accuracy by 4.6 percentage points. Replacing personalized interaction weighting with uniform weighting reduced accuracy by 2.8 percentage points, suggesting that not all feature interactions are equally useful across nodes. Eliminating the gating mechanism, which filters noisy or redundant interactions, led to a 1.9 percentage point drop. Removing the residual connection caused a 2.3 percentage point decrease, likely due to optimization difficulties in deeper interaction layers. We also varied the number of interaction layers and found that two layers yielded the best trade-off; three layers produced comparable results, while four layers led to over-smoothing and a 1.7 percentage point drop on Pubmed. The experimental findings presented in this work provide consistent evidence that feature interaction-aware modeling offers a principled and effective route to improving graph neural network performance under high-dimensional and sparse node-feature regimes. Across the evaluated datasets and graph learning tasks, FI-GNNs consistently outperform representative GNN baselines, including architectures that primarily aggregate neighborhood information without explicitly accounting for informative feature interactions [1], [2]. The gains are particularly pronounced on feature-sparse graphs, where conventional message-passing schemes tend to produce less expressive node representations because the available feature signals are weak, noisy, or unevenly distributed. By identifying and emphasizing informative feature interactions in a personalized manner, FI-GNNs mitigate this limitation and enable node representations to encode richer semantic relationships than those obtained through standard feature transformation and neighborhood aggregation alone.

A central observation from the empirical analysis is that the benefits of FI-GNNs are not merely attributable to increased model capacity. Ablation studies indicate that the feature interaction selection mechanism and the personalized interaction weighting scheme are both important contributors to the observed improvements. When informative interactions are suppressed or uniformly treated, performance degrades, suggesting that the proposed framework’s capacity to distinguish useful from redundant or noisy interactions is critical. This is consistent with the broader literature on feature interaction modeling in deep learning, where explicit interaction learning has been shown to improve representational power in sparse and high-dimensional settings [3], [4]. In the graph domain, our results further suggest that such interactions should be conditioned on node-specific characteristics rather than learned as a single global interaction pattern, since different nodes may rely on different feature subspaces to support downstream prediction.

The plug-and-play nature of FI-GNNs is another important aspect of the proposed framework. Because the interaction-aware module can be integrated into existing GNN architectures, the approach offers a practical pathway for enhancing established models without requiring a complete redesign of the message-passing pipeline. This modularity is valuable both scientifically and practically: scientifically, it helps isolate the contribution of feature interaction modeling from other architectural choices; practically, it allows practitioners to retain well-understood GNN backbones while improving their expressiveness on feature-sparse graphs. The experimental results support this claim, as FI-GNN variants built upon different backbone architectures exhibit stable improvements, indicating that the benefits are not tied to a single specific GNN design.

Despite these promising results, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the additional interaction modeling introduces computational and memory overhead relative to standard GNNs. Although the proposed framework is designed to remain practical, the cost of evaluating and weighting feature interactions may become non-negligible on very large graphs or in latency-sensitive applications. Second, the current study focuses primarily on static, homogeneous graphs with predefined node features. Many real-world systems involve dynamic graphs, heterogeneous entity types, or multi-modal features, where the notion of an informative feature interaction may evolve over time or vary across relation types. Third, while the personalized interaction mechanism improves expressiveness, it may also increase model complexity and sensitivity to hyperparameter choices, such as the number or sparsity level of selected interactions. Finally, although the empirical results are encouraging, a more rigorous theoretical characterization of when and why feature interaction-aware GNNs improve generalization on sparse graphs remains an important open question.

These limitations suggest several directions for future work. One promising direction is the development of adaptive and efficient interaction selection mechanisms that can reduce computational overhead while preserving expressiveness, for example through sparse gating, low-rank approximation, or differentiable pruning. Another direction is to extend FI-GNNs to dynamic and heterogeneous graphs, where feature interactions could be conditioned on temporal context or relation type. It would also be valuable to investigate self-supervised and contrastive objectives for learning interaction-aware representations, particularly in settings with limited labeled data. In addition, robustness to noisy or adversarially perturbed features deserves further attention, since feature sparsity and noise often co-occur in real-world applications. Finally, integrating FI-GNNs with scalable mini-batch training and distributed graph learning frameworks would help establish their applicability to industrial-scale graphs.

In conclusion, this paper introduced Feature Interaction-aware Graph Neural Networks, a plug-and-play framework for learning node representations enriched with informative feature interactions. The proposed approach addresses a key limitation of existing GNNs on high-dimensional and sparse graphs by highlighting personalized feature interactions and incorporating them into the representation learning process. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superior capability of FI-GNNs across various graph learning tasks, and ablation studies confirm the importance of interaction-aware modeling. The framework’s modularity, generality, and empirical effectiveness make it a useful contribution to the growing effort to design more expressive and robust graph neural architectures. At the same time, the limitations discussed above indicate that feature interaction-aware graph learning remains a rich area for further research, with important opportunities in efficiency, theoretical understanding, dynamic and heterogeneous graphs, and large-scale deployment.

Postoperative adhesion formation remains a clinically significant sequela of abdominopelvic surgery, particularly after operative laparoscopy for endometriosis and other inflammatory pelvic conditions [1,2]. Although laparoscopy reduces peritoneal trauma compared with laparotomy, it does not eliminate adhesionogenesis; serosal injury, desiccation, thermal damage, foreign-body reaction, and local ischemia initiate a cascade of fibrin deposition, impaired fibrinolysis, and subsequent collagen-rich adhesion band formation [3,4]. Such adhesions may remain asymptomatic, but they can produce chronic pelvic pain, dyspareunia, bowel obstruction, and subfertility, and they substantially complicate repeat surgery by obscuring anatomical planes and increasing the risk of visceral injury [5,6].

The ovary and ovarian fossa are especially vulnerable to postoperative adhesion development. In endometriosis, endometriotic implants, endometriomas, and stripping of the ovarian cortex create opposing raw surfaces within a confined anatomical space. When the ovary remains in the ovarian fossa during peritoneal re-epithelialization, fibrinous bridges may mature into dense adhesions between the ovarian capsule and the fossa peritoneum [7,8]. These adhesions can distort ovarian position, restrict ovarian motility, impair follicular development and ovum release, and interfere with transvaginal oocyte retrieval. Even after complete surgical excision of endometriosis, adhesion recurrence may compromise ovarian reserve and fertility outcomes, making adhesion prevention a central objective of conservative pelvic surgery [9,10].

Several strategies have been proposed to reduce postoperative ovarian adhesions, including meticulous microsurgical technique, minimal use of electrocoagulation, copious irrigation, and the application of anti-adhesion barriers such as hyaluronic acid–carboxymethylcellulose, oxidized regenerated cellulose, icodextrin, and polytetrafluoroethylene membranes [11,12]. However, these agents have limitations, including cost, handling characteristics, incomplete surface coverage, variable efficacy, and, in some cases, infectious or inflammatory risks. Moreover, barrier agents may not reliably maintain separation between the ovary and the ovarian fossa during the critical early healing phase, when the ovary is mobile and adjacent peritoneal surfaces are still raw [13].

Temporary ovarian suspension (TOS) to the anterior abdominal wall has emerged as a mechanical alternative designed to address this specific problem. The principle is straightforward: at the conclusion of operative laparoscopy, the ovary is elevated away from the ovarian fossa and fixed to the anterior abdominal wall for a finite period, allowing the peritoneal surfaces within the fossa to heal without direct apposition to the ovarian capsule [14,15]. After the suspension suture is absorbed or removed, the ovary is expected to return to its anatomical location. TOS has been described in several surgical contexts, including after laparoscopic excision of deep endometriosis, ovarian cystectomy, and adnexal surgery, with variations in suture material, caliber, fixation technique, and duration of suspension [16,17]. Despite growing interest, standardized protocols remain lacking, and comparative evidence regarding optimal suture choice is limited.

The choice of suture material is a key technical consideration. Absorbable sutures, such as plain catgut, provide temporary support and obviate the need for postoperative removal; however, they lose tensile strength relatively quickly and may elicit an inflammatory response during degradation. If absorption occurs before adequate peritoneal healing, the ovary may return prematurely to the ovarian fossa, potentially reducing the protective effect [18]. Non-absorbable monofilament sutures, such as nylon, maintain tensile strength for a longer period and may provide more reliable suspension, but they generally require removal and carry theoretical risks of suture migration, infection, sinus formation, chronic pain, and, rarely, bowel herniation through a persistent suture loop [19,20]. The comparative safety and efficacy of absorbable versus non-absorbable sutures for TOS therefore remain uncertain.

Safety is a paramount concern when suspending the ovary. Suture placement must avoid the ovarian hilum and vascular pedicle to prevent bleeding, hematoma, venous congestion, or compromise of ovarian perfusion. Fixation to the anterior abdominal wall must also avoid inferior epigastric vessels and ensure that no bowel or omentum is interposed within the suture loop, which could lead to obstruction or strangulation [21,22]. Postoperative monitoring must confirm that the ovary has returned to its anatomical position and that no adnexal complications have occurred. Given these technical demands, TOS must be simple, reproducible, and safe if it is to be widely adopted.

The present investigation was therefore designed to compare the safety and efficacy of TOS to the anterior abdominal wall using absorbable versus non-absorbable suture after operative laparoscopy. The study focused on patients undergoing surgery for advanced endometriosis and other selected indications, in whom adhesion prevention between the ovary and ovarian fossa is clinically relevant. Specific objectives included assessment of intraoperative and postoperative complications, documentation of ovarian position after suture absorption or removal

This retrospective cohort study was conducted using surgical records, hospital charts, and outpatient follow-up data from a tertiary referral centre for minimally invasive gynaecological surgery between January 1998 and December 2017. The study was designed to evaluate the safety and efficacy of temporary ovarian suspension (TOS) to the anterior abdominal wall after operative laparoscopy, with the aim of displacing the ovaries from the ovarian fossa and thereby reducing postoperative adhesion formation [1,2]. The Institutional Review Board approved the study protocol. Because data were collected retrospectively and analysed anonymously, the requirement for written informed consent was waived. All procedures were performed in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.

Patients were eligible if they had undergone operative laparoscopy for advanced endometriosis or another benign gynaecological indication and had received TOS at the conclusion of surgery. Advanced endometriosis was defined according to revised American Society for Reproductive Medicine criteria [3]. Patients with malignancy, pregnancy, active pelvic infection, previous pelvic radiotherapy, or insufficient follow-up data were excluded. A total of 152 patients were identified. One hundred forty-two patients (93.4%) underwent operative laparoscopy for advanced stages of endometriosis, and 10 patients (6.6%) underwent surgery for other indications. Group allocation was based on the suture material used for TOS and reflected a change in surgical practice over the study period rather than randomisation. Group 1 comprised 78 patients in whom the ovaries were suspended to the anterior abdominal fascia using absorbable 3-0 plain catgut sutures. Group 2 comprised 74 earlier patients in whom non-absorbable 3-0 monofilamentous nylon sutures were used for the same purpose. Baseline demographic, surgical, and reproductive characteristics were extracted from the medical records.

Patient characteristics and operative indications
The analysable cohort consisted of 152 women who underwent operative laparoscopy with temporary ovarian suspension (TOS) to the anterior abdominal wall between 1998 and 2017. Group 1 comprised 78 patients in whom the ovaries were suspended to the anterior abdominal fascia using absorbable 3-0 plain catgut sutures; Group 2 comprised 74 patients treated at an earlier period in whom non-absorbable 3-0 monofilament nylon sutures were used. The groups were comparable with respect to median age (32.4 ± 5.1 vs 33.1 ± 5.6 years; p = 0.42), body mass index (24.1 ± 3.7 vs 24.8 ± 4.0 kg/m²; p = 0.29), parity, and history of prior abdominopelvic surgery (p = 0.51). Indications for surgery were advanced endometriosis in 142 patients (93.4%) and other benign gynaecological conditions in 10 patients (6.6%). In Group 1, 73 patients had endometriosis and 5 had other indications; in Group 2, 69 patients had endometriosis and 5 had other indications. Among those with endometriosis, the majority had revised American Society for Reproductive Medicine stage III or IV disease, consistent with the referral pattern for operative laparoscopy in this cohort [1,2].

Operative and suspension techniques
All procedures were performed under general anaesthesia by the same surgical team using standard laparoscopic access. After completion of adhesiolysis, excision or ablation of endometriotic deposits, and ovarian surgery where indicated, the ovaries were elevated away from the ovarian fossa and suspended to the anterior abdominal wall. In Group 1, a single 3-0 plain catgut suture was passed through the ovarian cortical stroma or utero-ovarian ligament and anchored to the anterior abdominal fascia. In Group 2, an identical suspension technique was used with 3-0 monofilament nylon. The suspension sutures were either allowed to absorb or were removed at the first postoperative visit, approximately one week after surgery. No intraoperative difficulty related to suture placement, anchoring, or tension was recorded in either group. There were no conversions to laparotomy attributable to the suspension technique, and no patient required additional port placement or intraoperative reintervention for suture-related issues.

Safety outcomes
No major intraoperative complications occurred in either group. Specifically, there were no cases of significant bleeding requiring transfusion, no visceral injury related to suture passage, and no vascular or bowel injury attributable to the suspension procedure.
