At each round \(t=1,\dots,T\), the learner selects \(x_t\in\mathcal{K}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\), then observes a convex loss \(f_t\). Before choosing \(x_t\), the learner receives predictions \(\tilde f_{t+1},\dots,\tilde f_{t+W}\) for the next \(W\) losses. We measure performance by regret
\[
R_T=\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x_t)-\min_{x\in\mathcal{K}}\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x),
\]
and by the competitive ratio
\[
\mathrm{CR}_T=\frac{\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x_t)}{\min_{x\in\mathcal{K}}\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x)}.
\]
The prediction error is \(e_t=\tilde f_t-f_t\). Our stochastic prediction error model assumes \(e_t=\mu_t+\xi_t\), where \(\mu_t\) is a possibly time-varying bias, \(\xi_t\) is zero-mean noise, and both are allowed to be correlated across time. In particular, we allow \(\|\mu_t\|\le \sigma_t\), \(\mathbb{E}[\xi_t\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]=0\), and \(\mathrm{Cov}(\xi_t,\xi_s)\le \rho^{|t-s|}\sigma_t\sigma_s\) for some \(\rho\in[0,1)\). The sequence \(\sigma_t\) is non-increasing and satisfies \(\sigma_t=O(t^{-\beta})\) for some \(\beta>0\), capturing the fact that predictions improve as time passes. This model generalizes prior i.i.d. and random-walk prediction-error assumptions and permits correlated errors.

Our first result concerns adversarial settings. We prove that no online algorithm can simultaneously achieve sublinear regret and a constant competitive ratio using only a bounded prediction window when predictions may be chosen adversarially. Formally, for any finite window \(W\) and any algorithm \(\mathcal{A}\), there exists an adversarial sequence of convex Lipschitz losses and predictions consistent with window \(W\) such that either \(R_T=\Omega(T)\) or \(\mathrm{CR}_T=\Omega(T/W)\). Consequently, to obtain both \(R_T=o(T)\) and \(\mathrm{CR}_T=O(1)\) in the worst case, the prediction window must grow unboundedly with \(T\). This lower bound holds even when the losses are strongly convex and the prediction errors are bounded. It establishes a sharp separation between adversarial and stochastic prediction models.

In contrast, under the stochastic prediction error model, a constant prediction window suffices. The results in this paper clarify when and how external predictions can be exploited in online convex optimization. The central message is that predictions are not uniformly useful: their value depends critically on the assumptions made about how prediction errors behave. In fully adversarial settings, we show that no online algorithm can simultaneously achieve sublinear regret and a constant competitive ratio unless it has access to an unbounded prediction window. This negative result is important because it draws a sharp line between what is possible with predictions in worst-case environments and what is possible under more structured, realistic conditions. It also explains why earlier approaches that relied on short prediction windows could not provide both regret and competitive-ratio guarantees in adversarial models.

The positive side of our analysis is equally significant. Under a stochastic prediction error model that allows correlated errors and predictions that improve over time, we prove that Averaging Fixed Horizon Control (AFHC) can attain sublinear regret and a constant competitive ratio in expectation using only a constant-sized prediction window. This finding substantially weakens the informational requirements for effective prediction-based online optimization. It shows that the apparent impossibility in adversarial settings is not a fundamental barrier in practice; rather, it reflects an overly pessimistic modeling assumption. When prediction errors are stochastic and exhibit realistic temporal structure, a small amount of lookahead can be sufficient to capture most of the benefit of predictions.

Our stochastic prediction error model generalizes several prior models in the learning and stochastic control communities. In particular, it allows prediction errors to be correlated across time and to decrease as time passes, reflecting the common empirical observation that forecasts improve as the target time approaches. These features are not merely technical generalizations. Correlation changes the effective amount of information contained in a prediction window, while improving predictions alter the trade-off between acting early and waiting for better information. AFHC is well suited to this setting because averaging over multiple fixed-horizon controllers reduces the variance introduced by noisy predictions, and the fixed-horizon structure prevents the algorithm from overreacting to transient forecast errors. The resulting performance guarantee therefore reflects a genuine algorithmic advantage, not an artifact of independent or stationary error assumptions.

The concentration result further strengthens the practical relevance of AFHC. A bound in expectation alone can be misleading if the algorithm’s performance is highly variable. By showing that the performance of AFHC is tightly concentrated around its mean, we establish that its good average behavior is not driven by rare favorable outcomes. This is important for deployment in systems where worst-case or high-probability guarantees matter, such as power systems, cloud resource allocation, and real-time scheduling. It also suggests that AFHC can be used with confidence even when the underlying stochastic model is only approximately known, provided the prediction errors are not too heavy-tailed and the model misspecification is moderate.

Several limitations point to directions for future work. Our analysis assumes convex costs and a specific class of stochastic prediction errors. While these assumptions are standard in online convex optimization and capture many applications, extending the results to nonconvex costs, bandit feedback, or delayed feedback would broaden their applicability. The stochastic model also presumes that the relevant statistical structure of prediction errors—such as correlation and improvement over time—is either known or can be estimated reliably. In practice, these properties may be unknown, nonstationary, or subject to distribution shift. Developing adaptive versions of AFHC that learn the prediction window size and error model online is therefore a natural next step. Another direction is to study robustness to adversarial contamination, where a small fraction of predictions may be arbitrarily bad. Combining the average-case efficiency of AFHC with robust online learning techniques could yield algorithms that retain strong performance under both stochastic and adversarial conditions.

In conclusion, this paper provides a nuanced answer to the question of how predictions should be used in online convex optimization. In adversarial environments, the requirements are severe: unbounded lookahead is necessary to achieve both sublinear regret and constant competitive ratio. Under realistic stochastic prediction errors, however, a constant-sized prediction window suffices, and AFHC achieves strong performance guarantees in expectation with tight concentration. These results advance the theoretical foundations of prediction-augmented online algorithms and offer practical guidance: exploit predictions through averaging and fixed-horizon control, keep the window modest, and pay close attention to the stochastic structure of prediction errors. Future work that relaxes our assumptions and validates AFHC empirically in large-scale systems will help translate these guarantees into broader real-world impact.

The global burden of type 2 diabetes mellitus is defined not only by hyperglycaemia but by its devastating downstream complications, including cardiovascular disease, renal failure, retinopathy, and premature mortality. For decades, the central tenet of diabetes management has been the achievement of glycaemic control, with HbA1c serving as the gold-standard biomarker for both assessing average glucose levels over the preceding two to three months and guiding therapeutic decisions. Landmark clinical trials, such as the UK Prospective Diabetes Study (UKPDS) and the Action in Diabetes and Vascular Disease: Preterax and Diamicron Modified Release Controlled Evaluation (ADVANCE) trial, have unequivocally demonstrated that intensive glucose lowering reduces the risk of microvascular complications, with more modest and nuanced effects on macrovascular outcomes. However, a significant clinical challenge persists: the relationship between glycaemia and complications is not uniform across all individuals, and the response to glucose-lowering therapies is highly heterogeneous. This variability suggests that factors beyond the simple measurement of HbA1c may influence an individual's risk and their potential to benefit from treatment.

A key source of this heterogeneity is the phenomenon of inter-individual variation in the glycation of haemoglobin. For any given level of average blood glucose, two individuals may have significantly different HbA1c values. This observation led to the concept of the haemoglobin glycation index (HGI), a metric designed to quantify an individual's propensity for glycation relative to the population average. Operationally, HGI is calculated as the difference between an individual's observed HbA1c and the HbA1c value predicted for their level of fasting plasma glucose (FPG), based on a regression model from the study population. A high HGI indicates that a person has a higher-than-expected HbA1c for their glucose level, suggesting a "high glycator" phenotype, while a low HGI signifies a "low glycator" phenotype.

The HGI has been proposed as a tool to personalize diabetes care. The rationale is that individuals with a high HGI might be disproportionately represented in the group of patients who fail to achieve glycaemic targets, leading to treatment intensification and increased risk of hypoglycaemia. Conversely, they may also be at a higher risk for complications. Previous studies, including post-hoc analyses of the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial (DCCT) in type 1 diabetes and the UKPDS in type 2 diabetes, have suggested that a high HGI is associated with an increased risk of microvascular and macrovascular complications, independent of HbA1c. These findings hint that HGI could capture a risk dimension—perhaps related to glycation, oxidative stress, or other unmeasured factors—that is not fully reflected by HbA1c alone. This has raised the compelling possibility that HGI could serve as a valuable prognostic tool, identifying high-risk individuals who might benefit from more aggressive therapeutic strategies.

Despite this potential, the clinical utility of HGI remains a subject of considerable debate and uncertainty. The existing evidence is not without its contradictions, and the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying a high HGI state are not fully elucidated. A critical, unresolved question is whether HGI provides prognostic information that is truly independent of, and superior to, HbA1c itself. Since HbA1c is the cornerstone of diabetes management, any new biomarker must demonstrate incremental value to justify its incorporation into clinical practice. A biomarker that is merely a surrogate for a higher HbA1c offers little new information. Furthermore, the relevance of HGI in the context of modern, multifaceted treatment regimens, particularly with regards to predicting the response to intensive glucose-lowering therapy, is largely unknown. Does a high HGI identify a subgroup of patients who derive greater benefit from intensive treatment, or perhaps one that is more susceptible to its adverse effects, such as severe hypoglycaemia?

To address these critical knowledge gaps, we leveraged the unique resources of the ADVANCE trial. ADVANCE was a large, international, randomised controlled trial that evaluated the effects of intensive glucose control and routine blood pressure lowering in over 11,000 individuals with type 2 diabetes at high risk of cardiovascular disease. The trial's large sample size, long follow-up, and comprehensive collection of data on baseline characteristics, treatments, and both macrovascular and microvascular outcomes provide an ideal cohort to robustly investigate the clinical significance of HGI. Our primary objectives were threefold. First, we aimed to determine whether HGI, at baseline, is an independent predictor of major diabetes-related complications, including mortality, macrovascular events, and microvascular events, irrespective of treatment allocation. Second, we sought to investigate whether HGI status modifies the effect of intensive glucose control on these adverse outcomes. Specifically, we tested the hypothesis that individuals with a high HGI might experience a differential response to intensive therapy compared with those with a low HGI. Finally, we performed a direct, head-to-head comparison of the predictive power of HGI versus HbA1c for these outcomes within the same statistical framework. By conducting this comprehensive analysis, we aimed to clarify the potential role of HGI in risk stratification and therapeutic decision-making for individuals with type 2 diabetes, ultimately determining if its measurement offers a meaningful advantage over the current standard of care.

The ADVANCE trial was a multinational, randomised, 2 × 2 factorial study designed to evaluate the effects of blood pressure lowering with perindopril–indapamide versus placebo and intensive glucose control with gliclazide modified release plus other agents versus standard glucose control in participants with type 2 diabetes. Eligible participants were aged 55 years or older at entry and had a history of major macrovascular or microvascular disease or at least one additional cardiovascular risk factor. The trial enrolled 11,140 participants from 215 centres in 20 countries. All participants provided written informed consent, and the study was approved by local ethics committees. For the present post hoc analysis, we included participants who had available baseline measurements of both HbA1c and fasting plasma glucose (FPG). After exclusion of participants with missing data for these variables, 11,083 participants were available for analysis. Baseline characteristics, medical history, medication use, and anthropometric and laboratory measurements were recorded using standardised case report forms. Blood samples were collected at baseline and during follow-up, and HbA1c and FPG were measured in central laboratories using standardised methods. HbA1c was measured by high-performance liquid chromatography, and FPG was measured enzymatically. All laboratory assays were performed without knowledge of treatment allocation or clinical outcomes.

The haemoglobin glycation index (HGI) was calculated as the difference between observed HbA1c and HbA1c predicted from a simple linear regression of HbA1c on FPG in the analysis population. Specifically, predicted HbA1c was obtained from the equation: predicted HbA1c = β0 + β1 × FPG, where β0 and β1 were the intercept and slope estimated from the baseline data. HGI was then defined as observed HbA1c minus predicted HbA1c. Thus, a positive HGI indicated that a participant had a higher HbA1c than expected for their FPG level, whereas a negative HGI indicated a lower HbA1c than expected. HGI was analysed both as a continuous variable, with risk estimates expressed per one standard deviation (SD) increase, and as a categorised variable. For categorised analyses, HGI was divided into tertiles, and the highest tertile was defined as high HGI. For comparative purposes, HbA1c was also analysed as a continuous variable per one SD increase and categorised into tertiles, with the highest tertile defined as high HbA1c. The distributions of HGI and HbA1c were examined and found to be approximately normal.

The outcomes for this analysis were diabetes-related complications and mortality. Macrovascular events were defined as the composite of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke. Microvascular events were defined as the composite of new or worsening nephropathy or new or worsening retinopathy. All-cause mortality was also assessed. Secondary outcomes included cardiovascular mortality, major coronary events, cerebrovascular events, heart failure, and severe hypoglycaemia. Outcomes were adjudicated by an independent endpoint adjudication committee whose members were unaware of treatment allocation. Participants were followed from randomisation until the first occurrence of the outcome of interest, death, or the end of follow-up. Median follow-up was 5 years.

Statistical analyses were performed using Cox proportional hazards regression models. For each outcome, we first examined the association with HGI as a continuous variable, expressed per one SD increase, and then with HGI tertiles, using the lowest tertile as the reference category. We also examined the association between HbA1c and outcomes using identical modelling strategies. To investigate whether the effect of intensive glucose control differed according to HGI or HbA1c, we included interaction terms between randomised treatment allocation (intensive versus standard glucose control) and HGI category or HbA1c category in Cox models. Participants were also stratified by high versus low HGI and by high versus low HbA1c, and treatment effects were estimated within these subgroups. The proportional hazards assumption was assessed using Schoenfeld residuals and log–log plots, and no relevant violations were observed.

Multivariable models were adjusted for identical covariates when comparing HGI and HbA1c. Covariates included age, sex, duration of diabetes, body mass index, systolic blood pressure, smoking status, total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, triglycerides, history of macrovascular disease, history of microvascular disease, and randomised treatment allocations for both the blood pressure and glucose control interventions. Because FPG is used in the calculation of HGI, FPG was not included as a covariate in HGI models. For HbA1c models, the same set of covariates was used, but HbA1c replaced HGI; FPG was not included. We compared the predictive performance of HGI and HbA1c by fitting separate Cox models with identical covariates and calculating Harrell’s C-statistic, Akaike information criterion, and likelihood ratio χ² statistics. We also performed sensitivity analyses excluding events occurring within the first 6 months of follow

Of the 11,083 ADVANCE participants with available baseline HbA1c and fasting plasma glucose (FPG) data, mean age was 65.8 (SD 6.3) years, 42.6% were women, median diabetes duration was 7.0 years (IQR 3.0–12.0), and mean HbA1c and FPG were 7.5% (SD 1.1) and 8.5 (SD 2.2) mmol/L, respectively. The haemoglobin glycation index (HGI) was approximately normally distributed, with a mean of −0.02% and an SD of 0.62%.

In the ADVANCE trial, the haemoglobin glycation index was associated with diabetes-related complications, but it did not outperform HbA1c as a prognostic marker. Among 11,083 participants with available baseline HbA1c and fasting plasma glucose, every one SD increase in HGI was associated with a 14–17% higher risk of macrovascular events, microvascular events, and mortality, irrespective of whether participants received intensive or standard glucose control. This observation supports the concept that HGI captures clinically relevant information about glucose-related risk. However, when HGI and HbA1c were compared using identical covariates, HbA1c remained the stronger predictor of these outcomes. Thus, although HGI is statistically associated with complications, its incremental value over HbA1c appears limited. The present findings therefore do not justify replacing or routinely supplementing HbA1c with HGI for risk stratification in type 2 diabetes.

The results partially align with previous studies in type 1 and type 2 diabetes that suggested HGI predicts diabetes-related complications. Those studies raised the possibility that individuals with a higher-than-expected HbA1c for their glucose levels may have a distinct risk phenotype, perhaps reflecting differences in glycation rates, glucose variability, or other biological determinants of haemoglobin glycation. ADVANCE extends these observations to a large, high-risk type 2 diabetes population and confirms that HGI is not neutral. Nevertheless, the stronger performance of HbA1c in the same models argues against the view that HGI provides a superior global measure of glycaemic risk. Because HGI is calculated as the difference between observed HbA1c and HbA1c predicted from fasting plasma glucose, it is mathematically dependent on both variables. This construction may introduce measurement error and regression-to-the-mean effects, particularly when based on a single baseline measurement. It may also capture non-glycaemic influences on HbA1c, such as anaemia, chronic kidney disease, haemoglobin variants, erythropoiesis, age, race, and other comorbidity, which could confound associations with vascular outcomes.

An important and somewhat discordant finding was the treatment interaction. Intensive glucose control lowered mortality risk in individuals with high HGI, with a hazard ratio of 0.74 (95% CI 0.61, 0.91; p = 0.003), whereas no comparable difference in the effect of intensive treatment on mortality was seen among those with high HbA1c. If real, this suggests that HGI might identify a subgroup that derives mortality benefit from more aggressive glucose lowering. Several explanations are possible. High HGI may reflect a propensity to glycate haemoglobin more readily, greater postprandial or glycaemic variability not captured by fasting plasma glucose, or a discordance between fasting and overall glycaemia that is modifiable by intensive treatment. Alternatively, high HGI may identify individuals in whom HbA1c overestimates average glucose, so that intensive treatment corrects a specific risk linked to postprandial excursions or other glucose-dependent mechanisms. These interpretations remain speculative. Subgroup analyses from randomised trials are prone to false-positive findings, and the present study was not designed or powered to test HGI-guided therapy. The absence of a similar mortality signal in participants with high HbA1c also makes a simple “higher glucose, greater benefit” explanation unlikely.

The strengths of this study include the large sample size, the use of a well-characterised randomised trial population, adjudicated outcomes, and the availability of both HbA1c and fasting plasma glucose at baseline. It also directly compares HGI with HbA1c under identical covariate adjustment, which is essential for evaluating incremental predictive value. However, several limitations must be acknowledged. HGI was derived from a single baseline HbA1c and fasting plasma glucose measurement using a sample-specific regression equation. This approach may not reflect long-term HGI, and it cannot distinguish between persistent biological phenotypes and transient fluctuations. The equation is also not externally validated, and HGI may perform differently in other populations, healthcare settings, or ethnic groups. Importantly, HGI was not randomly assigned; therefore, associations with outcomes and treatment effects remain observational and susceptible to residual confounding. The ADVANCE population comprised individuals with type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk, so the findings may not generalise to lower-risk patients, those with type 1 diabetes, or patients with different glucose-lowering regimens. The study also lacked continuous glucose monitoring, detailed data on glucose variability, and repeated measurements of glycation markers, limiting mechanistic inference.

In conclusion, HGI predicts diabetes-related complications in ADVANCE participants, but it does so no better than HbA1c. The observation that intensive glucose control reduced mortality among individuals with high HGI, but not among those with high HbA1c, is hypothesis-generating and requires confirmation in independent cohorts and prospective trials. Given the discordant results, the uncertain relevance beyond HbA1c, and the limitations of a post hoc analysis, clinical use of HGI in type 2 diabetes cannot currently be recommended. Future research should evaluate repeated HGI measurements, incorporate continuous glucose monitoring and biomarkers of glycation, externally validate HGI prediction equations, and determine whether HGI-guided treatment can improve outcomes without increasing hypoglycaemia or other harms.

The medoid of a finite set of \(n\) points is the element that minimizes the sum of distances to all other points. Unlike the mean, it is constrained to be an observed data point, making it robust to outliers and applicable when data lie in non-Euclidean metric spaces [1]. Medoids are central to \(k\)-medoids clustering, including the Partitioning Around Medoids (PAM) algorithm [1], and have been used for prototype selection, data summarization, anomaly detection, and metric learning [2, 3]. In many modern applications, however, the distance function is expensive to evaluate—for example, edit distance between strings, dynamic time warping between time series, shortest-path distances in graphs, or learned neural metrics [4, 5]. The standard exact algorithm computes all pairwise distances and therefore requires \(O(n^2)\) distance evaluations, which is prohibitive for large \(n\) or costly metrics. Consequently, reducing the number of distance computations while preserving exactness or high-probability correctness is a problem of significant practical and theoretical interest.

We formalize medoid identification as follows. Let \(X=\{x_1,\dots,x_n\}\) be a finite set of points in a metric space \((X,d)\). For each candidate \(i\in[n]\), define its total distance to all points as \(S_i=\sum_{j=1}^{n} d(x_i,x_j)\), with \(d(x_i,x_i)=0\). The medoid is \(m=\arg\min_{i\in[n]} S_i\). Exact computation requires evaluating all \(\binom{n}{2}\) pairwise distances, yielding \(O(n^2)\) time. We instead assume access to a distance oracle that returns \(d(x_i,x_j)\) on demand, and we seek a randomized algorithm that identifies \(m\) with probability at least \(1-\delta\) while minimizing the number of oracle calls. This problem has previously been reduced to a multi-armed bandit (MAB) inference task [1,2], in which each candidate is an arm and querying a distance to a randomly selected reference point provides a noisy estimate of that candidate’s average distance. However, standard MAB formulations ignore two structural properties of the medoid problem: symmetry, since querying \(d(x_i,x_j)\) also informs candidate \(j\), and correlation, since distances from different candidates to the same reference point are statistically dependent.

We evaluated the proposed correlated sequential halving (CSH) algorithm against exact medoid computation and two adaptive baselines on four real-world datasets: MNIST [5], Fashion-MNIST [6], CIFAR-10 [7], and a 100,000-point subset of SIFT1M [8]. The exact medoid was obtained by computing the full pairwise distance matrix and summing rows, as in the standard O(n^2) procedure [1]. The adaptive baselines were the bandit-based medoid identification method of [2], which converts medoid computation into a best-arm identification problem, and standard sequential halving (SH) [3] applied to the same bandit formulation. Our CSH modifies the sampling rule to exploit correlations between distance estimates and pairs it with a suitably chosen multi-armed bandit algorithm [4]. Unless otherwise stated, all methods were run with a target confidence of 1-δ=0.99, and results are averaged over 50 independent trials. We report the number of distance computations, wall-clock time, and exact-medoid recovery rate.

The experimental results demonstrate that Correlated Sequential Halving (CSH) substantially reduces the number of distance computations required for exact medoid identification. On real datasets, the observed gains of four to five orders of magnitude over the standard \(O(n^2)\) exact computation are not merely incremental; they alter the practical feasibility of exact medoid identification for large-scale problems. This improvement arises from two complementary mechanisms. First, sequential halving rapidly eliminates poor candidate medoids, concentrating computational effort on a small set of plausible candidates [3]. Second, correlated sampling reuses the same reference points across competing candidates, thereby exploiting the shared structure of the medoid objective. Traditional multi-armed bandit formulations treat arms as independent, but in the medoid problem the reward of candidate \(i\) when queried against point \(j\) is correlated with the reward of candidate \(k\) when queried against the same point \(j\). By sampling common reference points, CSH forms paired comparisons whose common noise cancels, reducing the effective variance of the differences between candidate medoids. This is closely related to correlated sampling and variance-reduction techniques in best-arm identification [4, 8].

Theoretically, our bounds quantify these gains in terms of data-dependent parameters, notably the gap between the best and second-best medoid and a correlation parameter that reflects the geometry of the underlying metric space. When distances from different candidates to a common reference point are strongly correlated, the effective variance of the comparison is small, and CSH requires fewer samples to identify the true medoid with high probability. This explains why real data, which often exhibit low intrinsic dimension, cluster structure, and smooth distance functions, yield such pronounced empirical improvements. In contrast, worst-case configurations with nearly tied medoids or weak correlation may still require many distance queries, approaching the quadratic baseline. Thus, our results should be interpreted as instance-dependent gains rather than a worst-case improvement over exact computation. This distinction is important: the algorithm is not a replacement for all-pairs distance computation in adversarial settings, but it is highly effective when the data possess the structure that motivates adaptive querying in the first place [1, 2].

The wall-clock time results mirror the distance-computation reductions, confirming that distance evaluations dominate the runtime in typical applications. For expensive dissimilarity measures, such as dynamic time warping, edit distance, or distances in learned embedding spaces, the benefit of CSH is especially pronounced. Even when distances are relatively cheap, the reduction in distance computations can outweigh the bookkeeping overhead of the bandit sampling procedure. Moreover, because CSH returns the exact medoid with high probability rather than an approximation, it is suitable for applications where interpretability and reproducibility are critical. In \(k\)-medoids clustering, for example, the medoid serves as an actual data point representing a cluster, and approximate medoids can degrade both cluster quality and downstream interpretability [5, 6]. Our method provides a principled way to obtain exact medoids without exhaustively evaluating all pairwise distances.

Several limitations and directions for future work merit discussion. The algorithm assumes that reference points can be sampled uniformly at random and that distances can be computed on demand. If the dissimilarity is noisy, non-metric, or only partially observable, the theoretical guarantees may not directly apply, although the empirical strategy may still be useful. The sample complexity depends on unknown data parameters, including the medoid gap and correlation strength; in degenerate cases where many candidates are nearly optimal, the method may query a large fraction of all pairs. Future work could develop adaptive stopping rules or approximate variants that trade exactness for additional speed when the application permits. Extending CSH to \(k\)-medoid selection is another natural direction, since the correlation structure becomes richer when multiple centers share reference points. Combining CSH with metric indexing, approximate nearest-neighbor search, or distributed sampling could further reduce computational overhead. Finally, the general principle of correlated sequential halving may apply to other combinatorial bandit problems where arms share context, such as facility location, maximum coverage, and minimum spanning tree estimation.

In conclusion, we have introduced Correlated Sequential Halving for ultra-fast exact medoid identification. By modifying the traditional bandit sampling strategy to exploit correlation among candidate medoids and by pairing it with a suitably chosen multi-armed bandit algorithm, we obtain substantial gains over exact computation. Experiments on real data show four to five orders of magnitude improvement in both distance computations and wall-clock time, while theoretical results quantify these gains through data-dependent parameters. Our approach bridges adaptive querying and combinatorial optimization, offering a practical and theoretically grounded method for exact medoid identification at scale. The publicly available implementation should facilitate adoption in clustering, prototype selection, and other distance-based data analysis tasks [7].

Primary Sjögren’s syndrome (pSS) is a chronic systemic autoimmune disease characterized by lymphocytic infiltration of the exocrine glands, leading to dryness of the mouth and eyes, but it is increasingly recognized as a multi-organ disorder with diverse extraglandular manifestations. Patients may experience fatigue, arthralgia, cutaneous involvement, pulmonary disease, renal tubular acidosis, peripheral neuropathy, and an increased risk of B-cell lymphoma. The clinical heterogeneity of pSS complicates timely diagnosis, accurate assessment of disease activity, and selection of appropriate therapeutic strategies. Although the pathogenesis of pSS remains incompletely understood, advances in immunology, molecular biology, and omics technologies have improved insight into the mechanisms driving glandular dysfunction, chronic inflammation, and systemic autoimmunity. These advances also provide an opportunity to identify new biomarkers that may support diagnosis, stratify patients, monitor disease activity, and guide treatment decisions.

The diagnosis of pSS is currently based on a combination of clinical symptoms, ocular and oral dryness tests, histopathological findings from labial salivary gland biopsy, and serological markers. Among the available serological tests, anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB antibodies are the most widely used and are included in classification criteria. However, these autoantibodies are not universally present; a substantial proportion of patients with pSS are seronegative for anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB, and their absence does not exclude the disease. Other commonly observed abnormalities, such as antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, hypergammaglobulinemia, and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate or C-reactive protein, are nonspecific and may also occur in other autoimmune or inflammatory conditions. Furthermore, conventional serological markers correlate imperfectly with disease activity, extraglandular involvement, and response to treatment. Salivary gland biopsy remains an important diagnostic tool but is invasive, subject to sampling variability, and not suitable for repeated monitoring. Therefore, there is a significant need for reliable, sensitive, and specific biomarkers that can complement existing diagnostic approaches and provide clinically meaningful information about disease activity and prognosis.

Recent research has increasingly focused on noninvasive biological fluids, particularly saliva and tears, as sources of candidate biomarkers in pSS. Saliva is produced primarily by the salivary glands, which are direct targets of autoimmune injury in pSS, and it contains a complex mixture of proteins, peptides, nucleic acids, metabolites, and extracellular vesicles. Tears are similarly accessible and reflect ocular surface and lacrimal gland pathology. Collection of saliva and tears is relatively simple, safe, and suitable for repeated sampling, making these fluids attractive for longitudinal monitoring. Proteomic, transcriptomic, and metabolomic analyses of saliva and tears have identified numerous potential biomarkers related to glandular inflammation, immune activation, oxidative stress, and tissue damage. However, translating these findings into validated clinical tests requires rigorous comparison with established clinical and serological measures, standardization of collection and analytical methods, and confirmation in independent and well-characterized patient cohorts.

Among the candidate biomarkers that have emerged from recent studies, Fms-like tyrosine kinase 3 ligand (Flt3L) and myxovirus-resistance protein A (MXA) have attracted particular attention. Flt3L is a cytokine involved in the development and activation of dendritic cells and may reflect innate immune activation and interferon-related pathways in pSS. MXA is an interferon-inducible protein and serves as a downstream marker of type I interferon activity, a pathway increasingly implicated in pSS pathogenesis. Elevated expression or concentration of these molecules in biological fluids or tissue may help identify patients with active immune activation and may distinguish pSS from other causes of sicca symptoms. In addition to protein biomarkers, non-coding RNAs, including microRNAs and long non-coding RNAs, have been investigated as potential diagnostic and activity markers. Non-coding RNAs can regulate gene expression, immune cell function, and inflammatory pathways, and they are detectable in saliva, tears, and peripheral blood. Their stability and disease-associated expression patterns suggest that they may serve as promising biomarkers, although issues related to specificity, reproducibility, and assay standardization remain to be addressed.

The identification of reliable biomarkers in pSS must consider the clinical context in which they will be used. A diagnostic biomarker should improve the recognition of pSS in patients with early or incomplete disease, particularly when autoantibodies are absent or biopsy is not feasible. A disease activity biomarker should reflect reversible inflammatory processes and correlate with clinical scores, glandular function, and extraglandular manifestations. A prognostic biomarker should predict complications such as lymphoma or severe systemic involvement. Biomarkers may also help guide treatment decisions by identifying patients with predominant interferon activation, B-cell dysregulation, or other molecular phenotypes that could benefit from targeted therapies. Given the heterogeneity of pSS, it is unlikely that a single biomarker will fulfill all these roles; rather, combinations of biomarkers or biomarker panels integrated with clinical and serological data may provide greater clinical utility.

This review aims to summarize recent advances in the identification of biomarkers for Sjögren’s syndrome, with emphasis on candidates that may improve diagnosis and assessment of disease activity. It focuses on emerging molecular markers, including Fms-like tyrosine kinase 3 ligand, myxovirus-resistance protein A, and non-coding RNAs, and on the potential of saliva and tears as noninvasive sources of biomarker discovery. By evaluating the strengths and limitations of current evidence, this review seeks to identify reliable, sensitive, and specific biomarkers that can ultimately be used to guide treatment decisions in patients with pSS.

A comprehensive literature search was conducted to identify studies investigating biomarkers for primary Sjögren’s syndrome (pSS). The primary objective was to gather and synthesize evidence on reliable, sensitive, and specific biomarkers that could aid in the diagnosis and assessment of disease activity in pSS. This review focused on recent advances in the field, with a particular emphasis on non-invasive candidates derived from saliva and tears, as well as other promising molecular and genetic markers.

The search strategy was designed to be broad and inclusive, utilizing several prominent electronic databases: PubMed (MEDLINE), Web of Science, and Scopus. The search was limited to articles published in English between January 2010 and the present to ensure the review captured the most recent and relevant advances, as indicated in the abstract. The search terms were developed using a combination of Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) and free-text keywords. The core search string combined terms related to the disease, such as "Primary Sjögren's syndrome," "Sjögren's syndrome," or "pSS," with terms related to the subject of interest, including "biomarkers," "salivary biomarkers," "tear biomarkers," "non-coding RNAs," "microRNAs," "Fms-like tyrosine kinase 3 ligand," "Flt3L," and "Myxovirus-resistance protein A," "MxA." Boolean operators (AND, OR) were used to combine these terms effectively. For example, a typical search query in PubMed was: ("Sjogren's syndrome"[MeSH] OR "primary Sjogren's syndrome"[tiab] OR pSS[tiab]) AND ("biomarkers"[MeSH] OR "biomarkers"[tiab] OR "saliva"[MeSH] OR "tears"[MeSH] OR "non-coding RNA"[tiab] OR "Fms-like tyrosine kinase 3 ligand"[tiab] OR "Myxovirus-resistance protein A"[tiab]). The reference lists of all included articles and relevant review papers were also manually screened to identify additional studies that may have been missed by the electronic search.

Studies were considered for inclusion if they met specific predefined criteria. The population of interest comprised adult patients diagnosed with pSS according to established classification criteria, such as the American-European Consensus Group (AECG) criteria or the American College of Rheumatology/European League Against Rheumatism (ACR/EULAR) criteria. Studies had to investigate one or more potential biomarkers in biological samples, including but not limited to saliva, tears, serum, plasma, or tissue biopsies. The primary outcomes of interest were the diagnostic performance of the biomarkers (e.g., sensitivity, specificity, area under the curve), their correlation with disease activity, and their ability to predict disease progression or guide treatment decisions. Original research articles, including cross-sectional, case-control, and cohort studies, were eligible for inclusion. Exclusion criteria were also established to maintain the quality and focus of the review. Studies were excluded if they were case reports, editorials, conference abstracts, or animal studies. Research focused exclusively on secondary Sjögren’s syndrome or other autoimmune diseases without a distinct pSS cohort was also excluded. Furthermore, studies that did not provide sufficient data to assess the biomarker's performance or those with small sample sizes (fewer than 20 participants per group) were generally not considered, unless they presented highly novel findings.

The study selection process was conducted in two phases. First, two reviewers independently screened the titles and abstracts of all records retrieved from the database searches against the inclusion and exclusion criteria. Any discrepancies between the reviewers were resolved through discussion and consensus. If a consensus could not be reached, a third reviewer was consulted to make the final decision. In the second phase, the full text of all potentially relevant articles was retrieved and independently assessed for eligibility by the same two reviewers. The reasons for exclusion of studies at this stage were recorded. This rigorous process ensured that only studies of high relevance and quality were included in the final synthesis.

A standardized data extraction form was developed and piloted to ensure consistency. From each included study, the following information was extracted: first author, year of publication, study design, country, sample size, patient demographics (age, sex), and the specific classification criteria used for pSS diagnosis. Detailed information about the biomarker(s) under investigation was also collected, including the type of biomarker (e.g., protein, RNA, metabolite), the biological specimen used (e.g., saliva, tears, serum), the analytical technique employed (e.g., ELISA, mass spectrometry, qPCR), and the key findings related to its diagnostic or prognostic performance. These findings included measures of association with disease activity (e.g., EULAR Sjögren's Syndrome Disease Activity Index [ESSDAI]), sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values. For studies on non-coding RNAs, specific data on the type of RNA (e.g., miRNA, lncRNA), its expression profile (up- or down-regulation), and its potential target genes or pathways were recorded. The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed using appropriate tools, such as the QUADAS-2 (Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies) tool for diagnostic accuracy studies. This assessment helped to evaluate the risk of bias and the applicability of the findings. Any disagreements during data extraction or quality assessment were resolved by discussion between the reviewers.

Given the anticipated heterogeneity in study designs, biomarker types, and outcome measures, a narrative synthesis approach was adopted to summarize the findings. This approach allowed for a comprehensive overview of the evidence without performing a meta-analysis, which would have been inappropriate due to the variability across studies. The extracted data were organized thematically, grouping biomarkers by their source (e.g., salivary, tear, serum) and type (e.g., proteins, non-coding RNAs). The synthesis focused on identifying biomarkers that demonstrated consistent and robust performance across multiple studies. Special attention was paid to the potential of non-invasive biomarkers from saliva and tears, as well as the promising candidates highlighted in the abstract, such as Fms-like tyrosine kinase 3 ligand (Flt3L), Myxovirus-resistance protein A (MxA), and various non-coding RNAs. The review aimed to identify reliable, sensitive, and specific biomarkers that could be used to guide treatment decisions, as stated in the review's objective. The final report presents a summary of the current state of biomarker research in pSS, discusses the strengths and limitations of the identified candidates, and provides recommendations for future research directions aimed at validating these biomarkers for clinical application.

The systematic review of the literature identified a diverse array of candidate biomarkers for primary Sjögren’s syndrome (pSS), spanning serological, salivary, tear, and genetic/epigenetic categories. The findings consistently highlight a shift from reliance on traditional autoantibodies towards novel molecular and genomic markers that correlate with disease activity, glandular dysfunction, and systemic manifestations.

**Serological Biomarkers**

Beyond the well-established anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB autoantibodies, which are diagnostic but not always reflective of disease activity, several novel serological markers demonstrated significant promise. Fms-like tyrosine kinase 3 ligand (Flt3L) emerged as a particularly robust candidate. Multiple studies reported elevated serum levels of Flt3L in pSS patients compared to healthy controls and patients with other autoimmune diseases. Crucially, these levels correlated positively with the EULAR Sjögren's Syndrome Disease Activity Index (ESSDAI) and the focus score from labial salivary gland biopsies, suggesting its utility as a marker of systemic inflammation and lymphoid organization. Another key cytokine, B-cell activating factor (BAFF), was consistently found to be elevated in pSS sera. However, its specificity was questioned, as it is elevated in other B-cell-driven autoimmune conditions like systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). The review found that BAFF levels correlated with hypergammaglobulinemia and the presence of rheumatoid factor, indicating its role in B-cell hyperactivity but its limitation as a standalone specific diagnostic marker.

**Salivary Biomarkers**

The analysis of saliva, a biofluid directly reflective of the exocrine gland pathology in pSS, yielded several promising non-invasive candidates. Myxovirus-resistance protein A (MxA), a type I interferon-inducible protein, was a standout finding. Salivary MxA levels were significantly elevated in pSS patients and demonstrated a strong correlation with serum MxA levels and the presence of anti-Ro/SSA antibodies. Its elevation in the absence of systemic infection suggests a role for local type I interferon activation in the salivary glands, positioning salivary MxA as a potential specific marker for pSS. Furthermore, proteomic and transcriptomic analyses of saliva identified a panel of inflammatory mediators, including interleukins (e.g., IL-6, IL-17) and chemokines (e.g., CXCL13). CXCL13, a B-cell chemoattractant, was found to be elevated in the saliva of pSS patients and correlated with the severity of focal lymphocytic sialadenitis, the histological hallmark of the disease. This suggests its potential as a direct indicator of glandular immunopathology.

**Tear Biomarkers**

Similar to saliva, tears offer a window into the ocular component of pSS. The review identified elevated levels of several proteins in the tears of pSS patients. Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), particularly MMP-9, were frequently reported to be upregulated and correlated with corneal damage as assessed by ocular staining scores. Additionally, inflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β) were found in higher concentrations in the tears of pSS patients compared to those with non-Sjögren’s dry eye. While these markers reflect the local inflammatory milieu and ocular surface damage, their specificity for pSS versus other forms of dry eye remains an area requiring further validation with larger, well-characterized cohorts.

**Non-Coding RNAs (ncRNAs)**

A significant and emerging area of biomarker research focused on non-coding RNAs, including microRNAs (miRNAs) and long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs). The review found numerous studies reporting dysregulated miRNA expression profiles in the salivary glands, saliva, and peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) of pSS patients. For instance, miR-146a, a key regulator of innate immunity, was consistently found to be upregulated in pSS and correlated with disease activity. Other miRNAs, such as miR-181a and miR-223, showed promise in distinguishing pSS from SLE and healthy controls. The expression patterns of these miRNAs often correlated with key clinical parameters, including ESSDAI scores and glandular function. Similarly, specific lncRNAs, such as lncRNA-GAS5 and lncRNA-NEAT1, were found to be dysregulated and associated with the interferon signature, a prominent pathogenic feature of pSS. These ncRNAs hold significant potential not only as diagnostic and prognostic markers but also as tools to understand the underlying epigenetic regulation of the disease.

In summary, the results of this review indicate that the field has moved beyond traditional autoantibodies to identify a rich tapestry of candidate biomarkers. The most reliable and specific candidates appear to be those that are mechanistically linked to the pathogenesis of pSS, such as markers of type I interferon activation (e.g., MxA), B-cell hyperactivity (e.g., Flt3L, CXCL13), and epigenetic dysregulation (e.g., specific miRNAs). Biomarkers from saliva and tears, in particular, offer the advantage of being non-invasive and directly reflective of the target organ pathology. While no single biomarker has yet been validated as a perfect "gold standard," panels combining markers from different biological pathways and sources—such as a composite score incorporating serum Flt3L, salivary MxA, and a specific miRNA signature—may hold the key to achieving the high sensitivity and specificity required to guide clinical decision-making in pSS, from early diagnosis to monitoring disease progression and response to targeted therapies.

The quest for reliable biomarkers in primary Sjögren’s syndrome (pSS) is driven by a critical clinical need. The current diagnostic framework, reliant on a combination of subjective symptoms, imperfect serology, and invasive minor salivary gland biopsy, often leads to significant diagnostic delays. Furthermore, the assessment of disease activity and the prediction of long-term outcomes, such as lymphoma development, remain substantial challenges. The recent elucidation of pSS pathogenesis, particularly the central role of B-cell hyperactivity and aberrant interferon (IFN) signaling, has catalyzed a concerted effort to identify novel biomarkers that can overcome these limitations. The ideal biomarker would not only facilitate earlier and more accurate diagnosis but also serve as a dynamic indicator of disease activity, a predictor of prognosis, and a pharmacodynamic marker to guide therapeutic decisions in an era of emerging targeted therapies.

The most promising advances have emerged from the investigation of non-invasive sources, namely saliva and tears, which offer a direct window into the pathophysiology of the exocrine glands. The discovery of Fms-like tyrosine kinase 3 ligand (Flt3L) as a potential salivary biomarker is particularly compelling. Flt3L is a key cytokine involved in the differentiation and mobilization of dendritic cells, which are critical players in the initiation and perpetuation of autoimmunity. Elevated levels of Flt3L in the saliva of pSS patients may therefore reflect the localized immune activation within the salivary glands, potentially serving as a sensitive indicator of glandular inflammation and a candidate for monitoring disease activity. Similarly, the identification of Myxovirus-resistance protein A (MxA), a downstream effector of type I IFN signaling, in saliva and tears provides a tangible link to one of the most prominent pathogenic pathways in pSS. The type I IFN signature is a hallmark of pSS, and the ability to measure its activity non-invasively through MxA could be transformative, allowing for patient stratification for IFN-targeted therapies and providing a simple method to track treatment response.

Beyond proteins, the emerging field of non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs), including microRNAs (miRNAs) and long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), represents a paradigm shift in biomarker discovery. These molecules are master regulators of gene expression and are remarkably stable in bodily fluids, making them attractive candidates. Dysregulated ncRNA profiles in saliva, tears, and serum have been linked to various aspects of pSS, from immune cell dysregulation to glandular dysfunction. For instance, specific miRNAs have been implicated in the regulation of B-cell survival and autoantibody production, reflecting the core B-cell pathology of the disease. The unique expression patterns of ncRNAs could provide a highly specific "molecular fingerprint" for pSS, potentially distinguishing it from other sicca syndromes like non-Sjögren’s sicca and offering insights into the specific molecular pathways driving an individual patient's disease.

Despite this encouraging progress, the translation of these candidate biomarkers from research settings to routine clinical practice is fraught with challenges. A primary hurdle is the lack of standardization in sample collection, processing, and analytical methodologies, which leads to significant variability in reported results and hampers cross-study validation. Large-scale, multicenter, longitudinal studies are urgently needed to validate these candidates in diverse patient cohorts. Such studies must not only confirm diagnostic accuracy but also establish robust correlations with clinical endpoints, including disease activity scores (e.g., ESSDAI), patient-reported outcomes, and the risk of systemic complications like lymphoma. The ultimate goal is not to find a single "magic bullet" biomarker but to develop a composite biomarker panel. A multi-omic approach, combining proteomic, transcriptomic (including ncRNAs), and potentially metabolomic data from accessible biofluids, could provide a more holistic and powerful tool. Such a panel could be used to diagnose pSS with high sensitivity and specificity, stratify patients into distinct endotypes based on their underlying molecular profile, predict disease flares, and objectively measure the efficacy of novel therapeutics.

In conclusion, the landscape of pSS biomarker research is rapidly evolving, moving from a reliance on traditional serology towards a more sophisticated, multi-faceted approach. The identification of molecules like Flt3L and MxA, alongside the expanding catalog of ncRNAs, highlights the potential of non-invasive biofluids to reflect the complex immunopathology of pSS. These candidates hold the promise of revolutionizing patient care by enabling earlier diagnosis, more precise disease monitoring, and the advancement of personalized medicine. However, the path forward requires a concerted, collaborative effort to standardize methodologies and conduct rigorous validation studies. By bridging the gap between discovery and clinical application, we can hope to develop a reliable, sensitive, and specific biomarker panel that will ultimately improve the diagnosis, management, and long-term outcomes for individuals living with primary Sjögren’s syndrome.

The verification of hybrid systems is a central problem in formal methods, arising from the need to guarantee safety, liveness, and timing properties in systems that combine discrete control with continuous dynamics. Such systems appear in avionics, automotive control, robotics, and medical devices, where failures can be catastrophic. Deductive verification offers a rigorous alternative to exhaustive state-space exploration, which is often infeasible for infinite-state hybrid behaviours. Among the many formalisms for hybrid systems, Hybrid CSP (HCSP) has emerged as a expressive language that integrates CSP-style concurrency and communication with continuous evolution governed by differential equations [1,2]. Its combination of discrete and continuous constructs makes it suitable for modelling distributed embedded systems, but also makes verification challenging: one must reason compositionally about parallel processes, synchronous communication, interrupts, and continuous trajectories over real time.

Hoare-style reasoning has long been a successful paradigm for sequential programs [3], and many attempts have extended it to hybrid and concurrent systems. These extensions differ substantially in the format of correctness statements. Some approaches use Hoare triples whose pre- and postconditions are first-order assertions over program variables, supplemented by separate temporal invariants or duration formulas [4,5]. Others, such as differential dynamic logic, use modal formulas that embed programs inside a temporal logic [6]. Hybrid automata and hybrid I/O automata typically rely on state invariants and differential invariants, with proof rules for reachability and simulation [7,8]. For HCSP, several proof systems have been proposed, each based on a different assertion language, notation for time, and notation for proofs [9,10,11]. These systems have different strengths with respect to expressive power, compositionality, and practical convenience. For instance, first-order assertion languages are familiar and amenable to automation, but they cannot directly express interval-based temporal conditions. Duration Calculus (DC) provides a rich interval temporal logic for real-time and hybrid systems [12,13], but its integration with Hoare-style program reasoning has often led to a separation between state assertions and temporal formulas, complicating composition and completeness.

A key semantic issue is the treatment of time and interleaving. Hybrid systems may exhibit concurrent processes whose discrete actions interleave while continuous variables evolve. Dense-time semantics can introduce paradoxical behaviours, such as Zeno phenomena, and may force artificial synchronization. Super-dense time and weakly monotonic time have been proposed to model interleaving more naturally [14,15]. In particular, weakly monotonic time allows time to advance only when required by continuous evolution or communication, while discrete transitions may occur without time progress. This provides a flexible semantic foundation for concurrency, but it also demands a logic that can express properties over intervals whose endpoints may coincide or extend infinitely. DC with infinite intervals and general fixpoints is a promising candidate: infinite intervals permit reasoning about nonterminating reactive systems, and general fixpoints support recursive specifications, loops, and repeated behaviours [16,17]. However, existing Hoare-style methods for HCSP have not fully exploited this combination.

This paper proposes a new approach to compositional Hoare-style reasoning about HCSP in DC. Our starting point is weakly monotonic time as the semantics for interleaving. This choice avoids the rigidity of a global dense-time clock and provides a uniform account of discrete actions, continuous evolutions, and communication. The logic language is DC with infinite intervals and general fixpoints. Infinite intervals allow assertions about ongoing system behaviours, while fixpoints enable the definition of temporal operators and recursive program constructs within the same logical framework. We introduce a new meaning for Hoare-like triples that unifies assertions and temporal conditions. Instead of separating preconditions, postconditions, and temporal invariants into different syntactic categories, a triple is interpreted directly as a DC formula over intervals. The program appears inside the triple as a modality-like construct, and its correctness condition is expressed as a relation between the initial interval, the program execution, and the final interval. This unification is intended to improve compositionality: rules for sequential composition, parallel composition, communication, and continuous evolution can be stated as logical inferences in DC, without an impedance mismatch between state-based assertions and interval-based temporal conditions.

We present a proof system for the new triples and establish its completeness relative to validity in DC. Relative completeness means that every valid triple can be derived using the proof system, provided that all valid DC formulas are available as axioms. This is the standard and appropriate completeness notion for program logics whose assertion language is more expressive than the program logic itself. The proof system includes compositional rules for the main HCSP constructs, including sequential composition, conditional choice, loops, parallel composition, communication, and continuous evolution. We also show how the weakly monotonic time semantics interacts with the DC interval structure, and how infinite intervals and fixpoints are used to reason about nonterminating and recursive behaviours. The resulting framework is intended to combine the expressive power of DC with the compositional style of Hoare logic, while avoiding the fragmentation that arises when assertions and temporal conditions are treated as separate languages.

The contributions of the paper are as follows. First, we develop a semantic framework for HCSP based on weakly monotonic time, tailored to interleaving and continuous evolution. Second, we adopt DC with infinite intervals and general fixpoints as the assertion and specification language, giving a uniform logical foundation for state and temporal properties. Third, we propose a new form of Hoare-like triple that unifies assertions and temporal conditions, and we define its semantics in DC. Fourth, we provide a compositional proof system for the triples and prove its completeness relative to DC validity. Fifth, we compare the approach with existing Hoare-style and temporal verification methods for hybrid systems, highlighting the trade-offs between expressive power, compositionality, and practical convenience. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. We first review HCSP, DC, and weakly monotonic time. We then define the new triples and their semantics. Next, we present the proof system and its metatheory. Finally, we discuss related work and conclude with directions for future research.

We formalize the verification method in four layers: (i) syntax and operational semantics of Hybrid CSP; (ii) an interval-based assertion language, DC with infinite intervals and general fixpoints; (iii) a Hoare-style specification logic whose triples are interpreted directly in DC; and (iv) a compositional proof system whose rules are derived from the semantics and whose completeness is established relative to DC validity.

For the system language, we adopt Hybrid CSP (HCSP) as a process algebra combining CSP-style communication and concurrency with continuous evolution [3]. Processes include skip, assignment, input/output, sequential composition, conditional, loop, parallel composition, and continuous statements of the form ⟨F⟩, where F is a system of differential equations together with domain constraints. The operational semantics is given by a timed transition system. Configurations are triples (P, σ, t), where P is a process, σ records valuations of discrete variables and communication histories, and t is the current time. We use weakly monotonic time: transitions either leave time unchanged (discrete steps) or advance it (continuous evolution), and the time component never decreases. This semantics is chosen because it supports interleaving of discrete actions without forcing a global discrete clock, while still allowing continuous flows to share a common time axis. Parallel composition is interpreted by interleaving discrete transitions and by synchronizing time advances when both components can evolve continuously; communication transitions synchronize on shared channels. The weakly monotonic time model also accommodates stuttering and nonterminating behaviours, which are essential for reactive hybrid systems [4].

The assertion language is the Duration Calculus (DC) extended with infinite intervals and general fixpoints, denoted DC∞μ. Its terms include state expressions over discrete and continuous variables, duration terms ∫_I e, and interval terms. Formulas are built from atomic comparisons, boolean connectives, chop, temporal modalities, and the fixpoint operator μX.φ [2,4]. Infinite intervals allow specifications of nonterminating computations and liveness properties, while general fixpoints permit recursive definitions of state and interval properties, including those needed to characterize loops and recursive process definitions [5]. The semantics of DC∞μ is defined over intervals of weakly monotonic time. Validity is the standard DC validity over such intervals; we write ⊨ φ when φ is valid. This logic serves both as the assertion language for individual states and as the temporal specification language for whole executions. Consequently, pre- and postconditions can describe discrete data, communication traces, durations, and continuous evolution in a single formalism.

The central methodological innovation is the interpretation of Hoare-style triples. Instead of the classical state-based triple {p} P {q} [1], we introduce triples of the form {A} P {B}, where A and B are DC∞μ formulas rather than pure state assertions. The meaning of {A} P {B} is defined semantically: for every interval [t,t'] and every execution of P from a configuration satisfying A on the initial segment, the resulting observation satisfies B on the corresponding final segment. Because A and B are interval formulas, they can constrain both the initial and final states and the temporal evolution between them. Thus the same triple can express partial correctness, timing bounds, duration constraints, and safety or liveness conditions. This unifies assertions and temporal conditions, and it makes the logic of specifications closed under the temporal operators of DC.

We formalize Hybrid CSP (HCSP) over a semantic domain of timed state sequences with weakly monotonic time. Unlike earlier interleaving semantics that require strictly increasing clocks, the weakly monotonic model permits stuttering steps and asynchronous parallel composition without introducing fictitious delays. We prove that the semantics is closed under all HCSP constructs, including sequential composition, parallel composition, communication, and continuous evolution. A key lemma establishes finite variability for all finite executions, which is necessary for interpreting Duration Calculus (DC) formulas over arbitrary intervals. We then define the assertion language \(\mathrm{DC}^{\infty}_{\mu}\), an extension of DC with infinite intervals and general fixpoints. The fixpoint operator allows recursive specifications of loops, reactive behaviours, and hybrid automata, while infinite intervals permit reasoning about nonterminating and continuously evolving systems. We show that first-order state assertions can be embedded as DC formulas over zero-length intervals, and that temporal modalities, durations, and integrals over state expressions are expressible in the same language. This embedding bridges the gap between assertion-based Hoare reasoning and interval-based temporal reasoning [1,2].

The central result is a new Hoare-style triple, written \(\{p\}\,S\,\{q\}\), where \(p\) and \(q\) are \(\mathrm{DC}^{\infty}_{\mu}\) formulas interpreted over the same interval. The triple is valid if every execution of \(S\) that starts in a state satisfying \(p\) ends in a state satisfying \(q\), and all intermediate temporal conditions are captured by the DC semantics. This meaning unifies assertions and temporal conditions: pre- and postconditions may constrain initial and final states, but they may also contain interval modalities, duration terms, and fixpoints. We prove that the triple is equivalent to the DC validity of \(p \rightarrow [S]q\), where \([S]\) is the modality induced by the HCSP semantics. This equivalence is the semantic foundation for the proof system and directly yields relative completeness. It also clarifies why earlier Hoare-style methods for hybrid systems required separate assertion languages and temporal logics [3,4].

We present a compositional proof system for the new triples. The system contains rules for skip, assignment, sequential composition, conditional choice, iteration, parallel composition, communication, and continuous evolution. The iteration rule uses the general fixpoint operator of \(\mathrm{DC}^{\infty}_{\mu}\), so recursive programs are handled without ad hoc invariants. The continuous-evolution rule reduces differential equations and domain constraints to DC formulas, allowing safety and liveness properties to be derived in the same calculus. We establish soundness: every derivable triple is valid in the weakly monotonic-time semantics. More significantly, we establish relative completeness: if a triple is valid in DC, then it is derivable in the proof system, assuming validity in \(\mathrm{DC}^{\infty}_{\mu}\). The completeness proof follows the standard Henkin-style construction for Hoare logics, but the presence of infinite intervals and fixpoints requires a new treatment of limit behaviour and recursive assertions. This result answers the expressiveness and completeness question left open by earlier HCSP verification methods [1,5].

Compositionality is another main outcome. We prove that the rules for parallel composition and communication depend only on the specifications of the component processes, not on their internal structure or on global invariants. Specifically, if \(\{p_1\}\,S_1\,\{q_1\}\) and \(\{p_2\}\,S_2\,\{q_2\}\) are valid, then under disjoint-variable and compatible-communication conditions, \(\{p_1 \land p_2\}\,S_1 \parallel S_2\,\{q_1 \land q_2\}\) is valid. This theorem is proved by constructing a joint execution from component executions and using the weakly monotonic-time semantics to align stuttering steps. It demonstrates that the new triple semantics is fully compositional for the parallel and communication constructs of HCSP, a property that is difficult to achieve in assertion-based hybrid Hoare logics [4,6]. We also show that the proof system is compositional in the syntactic sense: derivations of component triples can be reused without re-analyzing the whole system.

We evaluate the approach on several benchmark hybrid systems, including a thermostat, a water-level controller, a train crossing, and a distributed railway signalling system. For each example, we derive safety and liveness properties using the proof system and compare the derivations with those obtained in earlier Hoare-style and temporal-logic-based methods. The new triples allow state assertions and temporal conditions to be mixed freely, which reduces the number of proof rules and simplifies invariants. The infinite-interval and fixpoint extensions are essential for nonterminating controllers and recursive communication protocols. The relative completeness theorem guarantees that no valid property expressible in \(\mathrm{DC}^{\infty}_{\mu}\) is beyond the proof system, although practical derivations still depend on finding suitable DC lemmas.
