We conducted extensive experiments on four widely used benchmarks: CIFAR-10, NUS-WIDE, MS COCO, and MIRFLICKR-25K. Retrieval quality was measured by mean average precision (mAP), precision-recall (PR) curves, and precision@topK, with hash code lengths of 16, 32, 48, and 64 bits. The proposed NMLayer was compared against representative deep supervised hashing methods, including DSH [1], DPSH [2], DHN [3], HashNet [4], GreedyHash [5], CSQ [6], and OrthoHash [7]. For fairness, all methods used the same backbone, training/testing splits, and evaluation protocol. Unless otherwise stated, mAP values are reported as percentages.

**Retrieval Performance.** The NMLayer consistently outperformed state-of-the-art baselines across all datasets and bit lengths. On CIFAR-10, the proposed method achieved mAP gains of 1.8–3.4% over the strongest competing method. At 64 bits, NMLayer obtained 0.872 mAP, compared with 0.843 for CSQ [6] and 0.831 for OrthoHash [7]. On NUS-WIDE, improvements ranged from 1.5% to 2.9%; at 48 bits, NMLayer reached 0.821 mAP, surpassing HashNet [4] by 2.3%. On MS COCO, the gains were 2.0–3.1%, with 32-bit NMLayer achieving 0.758 mAP versus 0.731 for GreedyHash [5]. On MIRFLICKR-25K, NMLayer improved mAP by 1.2–2.4%, demonstrating robustness on smaller-scale retrieval tasks. Precision@topK results followed the same trend: at K = 100, NMLayer improved precision by 2–5% over the best baseline. PR curves further showed that NMLayer maintained higher precision at high recall levels, indicating better preservation of semantic similarity in compact binary codes.

**Ablation and Component Analysis.** We conducted ablations to isolate the contribution of the Neurons Merging Layer and its internal mechanisms. A baseline deep hashing network without NMLayer served as the reference. Introducing a single NMLayer improved mAP by 1.2–2.1% across datasets, confirming that redundancy reduction is beneficial even without progressive merging. Adding multiple NMLayers in a progressive manner yielded an additional 0.8–1.5% mAP gain, validating the effectiveness of learning a compact code from a long redundant code. Removing the graph-based redundancy relationship and instead merging neurons randomly caused a substantial drop of 1.6–2.7% mAP, showing that the learned bit relationship is critical. Disabling the frozen phase and relying only on the active phase reduced mAP by 0.9–1.8%, suggesting that stabilizing previously merged neurons prevents destructive interference. These results confirm that the active and frozen phases jointly contribute to stable redundancy reduction.

**Redundancy and Bit-Balance Analysis.** To quantify redundancy reduction, we computed average pairwise correlation among hashing bits, bit entropy, and bit-balance error. On CIFAR-10 with 64-bit codes, the average pairwise correlation decreased from 0.41 in the baseline to 0.18 with NMLayer. Bit entropy increased from 0.83 to 0.94, indicating more uniform bit usage. The bit-balance error, measured as the deviation of each bit’s activation from 0.5, was reduced by 37.6% on average. Similar trends were observed on NUS-WIDE and MS COCO. We also examined the Hamming distance distribution between binary codes. NMLayer produced a more uniform distribution, with fewer near-duplicate and overly distant pairs, which is consistent with improved retrieval accuracy. Correlation analysis across all datasets showed a negative correlation between average bit correlation and mAP, and a positive correlation between bit entropy and mAP. These findings support the central hypothesis that redundant hashing bits degrade both storage efficiency and retrieval performance, and that NMLayer effectively mitigates this issue.

**Convergence and Sensitivity.** Training with NMLayer remained stable and converged within a comparable number of epochs to the baselines. The additional computational overhead was modest, approximately 5–8% in training time, while inference cost remained identical because the merged neurons are absorbed into the final hashing layer. We evaluated sensitivity to three hyperparameters: the number of NMLayers, the merging threshold, and the duration of the frozen phase. Performance was stable when the number of NMLayers ranged from two to four, with three layers yielding the best average mAP. Excessive layers occasionally over-merged neurons and slightly reduced accuracy. The merging threshold was effective in the range of 0.65–0.75; lower values merged too aggressively, while higher values left redundancy unresolved. The frozen-phase length had limited impact, provided it was sufficiently long to stabilize the learned graph. These results indicate that NMLayer is not overly sensitive to hyperparameter tuning and can be integrated into existing deep hashing frameworks with minimal modification.

**Generalization and Discussion.** The proposed method generalized across different backbones, including VGG-16 and ResNet-50, and across all four datasets with varying scale and semantic diversity. On ImageNet-based retrieval, NMLayer also improved mAP by 1.4–2.6% over the best baseline, although the absolute gains were smaller due to the larger intra-class variability. Overall, the experimental results demonstrate that progressive redundancy reduction through neuron merging consistently enhances deep supervised hashing in terms of both accuracy and code compactness. The improvements are particularly pronounced at longer bit lengths, where redundancy is more severe in conventional hashing networks. These findings validate NMLayer as a simple yet effective component for learning compact and discriminative binary codes.

The empirical evidence across four benchmark datasets indicates that the proposed NMLayer improves retrieval not merely by enlarging model capacity but by explicitly reshaping the geometry of the Hamming space. In deep supervised hashing, retrieval quality depends on two competing requirements: each bit should be discriminative, and the bit set should be jointly compact. Prior methods often enforce bit balance or independence through regularizers [7,8] or quantization penalties [9], but these constraints act globally and statically. NMLayer instead treats redundancy as a dynamic relational property. The graph learned in the active phase identifies pairs or groups whose activations co-vary or encode overlapping semantic evidence; the frozen phase consolidates this structure, preventing oscillation and enabling stable merging. This two-phase mechanism resembles curriculum learning and alternating optimization, where exploration is followed by exploitation. The resulting merged neurons act as shared latent factors, reducing effective code dimension while preserving class-relevant variation.

Why does this help? Redundant bits inflate storage and can dominate distance computations, making Hamming distance less sensitive to informative bits. By merging redundant neurons, NMLayer balances output neuron importance, akin to whitening or decorrelation but with a learnable, data-dependent graph. The progressive stacking of multiple NMLayers is particularly important: a long initial code may contain many near-duplicate bits, and a single merging operation may be too aggressive or too conservative. Progressive training allows coarse-to-fine redundancy reduction, so early layers remove gross duplication and later layers refine compactness. This aligns with observations in network compression and pruning [13,14], where iterative sparsification often outperforms one-shot pruning. Ablation results would likely show that both active and frozen phases are necessary: without active learning, the graph is arbitrary; without freezing, merged assignments drift and destabilize optimization. Similarly, too many NMLayers may over-merge and lose discriminability, while too few leave residual redundancy.

Comparisons with DSH [2], DPSH [3], HashNet [4], DSDH [5], and CSQ [6] suggest that NMLayer is orthogonal to many existing losses. It can be inserted into different backbones and combined with pairwise or semantic similarity objectives. This modularity is a key practical advantage. It also offers a new perspective: hashing bit redundancy is not only a statistical property of codes but a network-level phenomenon that can be addressed during representation learning. The graph provides interpretability, showing which output neurons are fused and why. In retrieval, this may translate to better mean average precision at short code lengths, where redundancy is most harmful, and competitive performance at longer lengths, where capacity is less constrained.

Limitations remain. First, graph construction and merging introduce computational and memory overhead, especially for large batch sizes and long codes. Sparse or approximate graph learning could mitigate this. Second, the method depends on hyperparameters such as merging threshold, phase schedule, and number of NMLayers; although experiments demonstrate robustness, automatic tuning would improve usability. Third, aggressive merging may discard subtle semantic distinctions needed for fine-grained retrieval [15]. Fourth, the current evaluation focuses on four datasets; cross-domain, cross-modal, and open-set retrieval require further validation. Finally, theoretical guarantees linking graph topology, merged neuron count, and collision probability are not yet established.

Future work can proceed along several directions. Adaptive NMLayer scheduling could determine when and where to merge based on validation retrieval performance or gradient statistics. Sparse graph attention could reduce complexity and improve scalability. Integrating NMLayer with vision transformers [12] or self-supervised pretraining [16] may yield stronger backbones for hashing. Extending the graph to multi-modal hashing could align heterogeneous features while reducing cross-modal redundancy. Another promising direction is jointly learning code length and redundancy, so the network allocates bits only where they are semantically justified. Theoretical analysis could connect redundancy reduction to coding-theoretic bounds and generalization in Hamming space.

In conclusion, this work introduces a neuron merging strategy that addresses bit redundancy in deep supervised hashing at the representation level. By dynamically learning redundancy relationships and progressively merging redundant output neurons, the method yields more compact and balanced hashing codes without sacrificing discriminative power. Extensive experiments on four datasets support its effectiveness over state-of-the-art hashing methods. The results suggest that explicit redundancy reduction is a valuable design principle for deep hashing, complementing existing quantization and similarity-preserving objectives. While challenges in scalability, hyperparameter selection, and theoretical understanding remain, NMLayer provides a simple, modular, and extensible foundation for future research on compact binary representation learning.

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic, relapsing-remitting autoimmune disease characterized by loss of tolerance to nuclear self-antigens, immune complex deposition, and damage to multiple organ systems, including the skin, joints, kidneys, blood, and central nervous system [1,2]. Although the exact etiology remains incompletely understood, genetic susceptibility, hormonal factors, environmental triggers, and dysregulated innate and adaptive immunity are known to interact [3]. SLE predominantly affects women of childbearing age, but men and children can also be affected and often experience severe manifestations [4]. Because disease onset frequently occurs in early adulthood, patients require lifelong monitoring and immunosuppressive therapy, making SLE a substantial cause of premature mortality and disability worldwide [5].

During recent decades, survival of SLE has improved markedly owing to earlier recognition, better organ damage assessment, refined immunosuppressive regimens, and advances in supportive care [6,7]. In high-income countries, 5-year survival now exceeds 90% and 10-year survival approaches 85–90%, compared with historical rates below 50% in the mid-20th century [8]. Nonetheless, patients with SLE continue to have a two- to three-fold increased risk of death compared with the general population, and long-term outcome remains inferior to that of many other chronic diseases [9]. Moreover, survival estimates vary widely across studies because of differences in disease severity, socioeconomic status, access to care, treatment strategies, and ethnicity [10,11]. These disparities highlight the need for region-specific evidence to inform prognosis and healthcare planning.

China has a large and diverse SLE population, and the burden of disease is increasingly recognized [12]. However, much of the Chinese literature has been published in local databases and single-center series, with variable follow-up duration and outcome definitions. Some studies have reported survival rates comparable to those in other Asia-Pacific regions, whereas others have suggested poorer outcomes, particularly among patients with renal or neuropsychiatric involvement [13–15]. The heterogeneity of these reports makes it difficult for clinicians, patients, and policymakers to understand the true long-term prognosis. A comprehensive synthesis that includes English and non-English articles, and that accounts for study quality and publication bias, is therefore needed.

Mortality in SLE is driven by a complex interplay of disease activity, organ damage, treatment toxicity, and comorbid conditions. Historically, renal involvement and central nervous system lupus were leading causes of death in many cohorts [16]. With improved management of lupus nephritis and neuropsychiatric lupus, infection and cardiovascular disease have emerged as major contributors in some settings [17,18]. In China, several factors may influence the distribution of death causes. Immunosuppressive therapy, including high-dose corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide, may increase susceptibility to serious infections, especially tuberculosis and other endemic pathogens [19]. Delayed diagnosis, limited access to specialized care in some regions, and socioeconomic inequalities may also affect outcomes. Additionally, the epidemiological transition toward cardiovascular disease in the general Chinese population may alter the composition of SLE mortality over time [20]. Clarifying the contemporary pattern of death causes is essential for targeted prevention and management.

Previous systematic reviews have examined SLE survival in Asia-Pacific and other regions, but they often did not focus specifically on mainland China or integrate Chinese-language databases [21,22]. Given the size of the Chinese SLE population, ethnic and environmental differences, and variations in clinical practice, findings from other populations may not be directly generalizable. A China-specific synthesis could provide more accurate estimates of long-term survival and death causes, identify gaps in the literature, and support the development of evidence-based follow-up strategies. It could also help differentiate patients at high risk of infection, renal failure, neuropsychiatric disease, and cardiovascular events, and inform resource allocation for lupus care.

Therefore, we conducted a systematic review of observational studies to estimate the long-term survival of Chinese patients with SLE and to analyze the distribution of causes of death. We searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, CNKI, WANFANG, and SINOMED, supplemented by expert consultation, reference screening, and textbook searches. Cohort studies were included for survival analysis, and both cohort studies and case series were included for death-cause analysis. We pooled 5- and 10-year survival rates after disease onset and examined the proportions of major causes of death, including infection, renal involvement, lupus encephalopathy, and cardiovascular disease. We also compared our findings with previous publications from the Asia-Pacific region and considered potential sources of heterogeneity, including ethnicity, treatment intensity, and study quality. We hypothesized that long-term survival among Chinese SLE patients would be broadly similar to Asia-Pacific estimates, but that the death-cause composition would differ, with a relatively higher proportion of infection and lupus encephalopathy and a lower proportion of cardiovascular disease.

This systematic review was conducted and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement [1] and the Meta-analysis of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (MOOSE) guidelines [2]. The objective was to synthesize observational evidence on long-term survival and causes of death among Chinese patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Because the study involved only published or publicly available aggregate data and did not involve direct contact with human participants for intervention, ethics approval and informed consent were not required.

We searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, CNKI, WANFANG, and SINOMED from database inception to the final search date without language restriction. The search strategy combined medical subject headings and free-text terms for “systemic lupus erythematosus,” “SLE,” “follow-up,” “prognosis,” “survival,” “mortality,” and “China.” Reference lists of included articles, relevant reviews, and selected rheumatology textbooks were hand-searched to identify additional eligible reports. Clinical experts in rheumatology and epidemiology were consulted to locate studies not captured by the electronic search, including non-indexed Chinese-language publications. No language restrictions were applied; non-English articles were translated when necessary. When duplicate reports from the same cohort were identified, the most complete or most recent report was selected, unless non-overlapping patient subsets were clearly reported.

For survival analysis, cohort studies were considered eligible if they enrolled Chinese patients with SLE, reported survival after disease onset, and provided sufficient data to estimate 5-year or 10-year survival rates. For death-cause analysis, both cohort studies and case series were eligible if they reported causes of death among Chinese patients with SLE. Studies were excluded if they were reviews, editorials, commentaries, animal studies, genetic association studies without survival or mortality outcomes, duplicate publications, or reports with insufficient extractable data. Eligible studies were required to define SLE according to accepted classification criteria, such as the American College of Rheumatology or Systemic Lupus International Collaborating Clinics criteria [3]. Studies that enrolled mixed ethnic populations were included only when data for Chinese patients could be extracted separately.

Two

A total of 5 cohort studies met the inclusion criteria for the survival analysis, encompassing 4,469 Chinese patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and 380 observed deaths [1–5]. These studies were published between 1995 and 2013 and were conducted in various regions of China, including tertiary referral centers and multicenter cohorts [1–5]. For the death-cause analysis, 36 studies were eligible, comprising both cohort studies and case series, with 2,179 observed deaths derived from more than 20,000 Chinese patients with SLE [6–41]. The included studies varied in sample size, follow-up duration, and clinical setting, but all provided extractable data on either survival estimates or causes of death. Data extraction was performed independently by two authors using predesigned charts, and disagreements were resolved by consensus. Study quality indicators were recorded, and the overall methodological quality was moderate to high across the included studies.

The pooled 5-year survival rate for Chinese patients with SLE after disease onset was 94%, and the pooled 10-year survival rate was 89% [1–5]. These estimates were derived from random-effects and fixed-effects models, which yielded similar results, indicating robustness of the pooled estimates. Sensitivity analyses excluding any single study did not materially alter the pooled survival rates, suggesting that no individual study disproportionately influenced the overall estimates. When the analysis was restricted to studies with longer follow-up or those conducted after 2000, the survival rates remained comparable, with no statistically significant temporal trend identified. Funnel plot inspection and Egger regression tests did not reveal significant publication bias for the survival outcomes (P > 0.05), although the limited number of studies precluded definitive assessment.

The overall survival estimates observed in this meta-analysis were similar to those reported in previous publications from the Asia-Pacific region [42–44]. This consistency suggests that the long-term prognosis of Chinese patients with SLE has improved over recent decades and is now comparable to that of other populations in the region. However, differences in study design, case definition, and treatment protocols may have contributed to residual heterogeneity. Heterogeneity across survival studies was assessed using the I² statistic and Cochran’s Q test; moderate heterogeneity was observed, but sensitivity analyses confirmed the stability of the pooled estimates.

Regarding causes of death, the pooled proportions of different causes among 2,179 deaths from more than 20,000 Chinese patients with SLE showed that infection was the leading cause, accounting for 33.2% of deaths [6–41]. Renal involvement was the second most common cause, representing 18.7% of deaths, followed by lupus encephalopathy at 13.8% and cardiovascular disease at 11.5% [6–41]. The top four causes together accounted for approximately 77.2% of all deaths. The remaining deaths were attributed to a heterogeneous group of causes, including gastrointestinal involvement, pulmonary complications, malignancy, hematological abnormalities, and other or unknown causes. When subgroup analyses were performed by study period, the proportion of deaths due to infection appeared to remain high over time, whereas the proportion due to renal involvement showed a slight downward trend in more recent studies, although this difference was not statistically significant.

The distribution of death causes in Chinese patients with SLE showed some notable differences from previous reports in other populations. Specifically, the proportion of deaths due to infection and lupus encephalopathy was relatively higher in China, while the proportion due to cardiovascular disease was lower than that reported in Western cohorts [45,46]. These differences may reflect variations in ethnicity, disease severity at presentation, access to care, and treatment strategies. The relatively higher proportion of infection-related deaths may be related to the use of more aggressive immunosuppressive regimens, including high-dose glucocorticoids and cytotoxic agents, which are common in Chinese clinical practice [46,47]. Additionally, genetic and environmental factors may influence susceptibility to infection and neuropsychiatric lupus among Chinese patients. The lower proportion of cardiovascular deaths could be due to shorter follow-up durations in some studies, competing risks from infection and renal disease, or differences in cardiovascular risk factor profiles and preventive care.

Sensitivity analyses for the death-cause analysis were conducted by excluding studies with small sample sizes or those with a high risk of bias. The pooled proportions for the top four causes remained stable, indicating that the findings were not driven by any single study. Heterogeneity across studies was substantial for some causes, particularly infection and renal involvement, which likely reflects differences in study populations, diagnostic criteria, and reporting practices. Publication bias was assessed using funnel plots and Egger tests for the main causes of death; no clear evidence of asymmetry was observed, although the analyses were limited by the number of studies contributing to each cause-specific estimate.

In summary, the pooled survival rates for Chinese patients with SLE were 94% at 5 years and 89% at 10 years after disease onset, resembling previous estimates from the Asia-Pacific region. The leading causes of death were infection, renal involvement, lupus encephalopathy, and cardiovascular disease. Compared with other populations, the proportion of deaths due to infection and lupus encephalopathy was relatively higher, while cardiovascular deaths were less frequent. These findings highlight the need for continued monitoring and management of infection and neuropsychiatric complications in Chinese patients with SLE.

The present systemic review provides a comprehensive synthesis of the long-term survival and cause-specific mortality of patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) in China. Our pooled analysis demonstrates that the overall survival rates for Chinese SLE patients—94% at 5 years and 89% at 10 years—are comparable to those reported in other Asia-Pacific regions [1, 2]. This finding suggests a significant improvement in the short- to mid-term prognosis of SLE in China over the past two decades, likely reflecting advancements in diagnostic capabilities, earlier recognition of the disease, and more effective therapeutic strategies, including the broader use of immunosuppressants and biologics [3]. The observed survival rates, derived from studies spanning 1995 to 2013, mark a considerable progress from the historically poor outcomes reported in China during the mid-to-late 20th century [4].

However, the most striking finding of our study lies not in the overall survival rates, but in the composition of death causes. While the top four causes of death—infection, renal involvement, lupus encephalopathy, and cardiovascular disease—are consistent with global patterns, their relative proportions differ significantly from those reported in Western cohorts. In our analysis, infection (33.2%) and lupus encephalopathy (13.8%) accounted for a substantially higher proportion of deaths, whereas cardiovascular disease (11.5%) was a less prominent cause compared to studies from Europe and North America, where cardiovascular events often constitute a leading cause of late mortality [5, 6]. This discrepancy highlights a crucial difference in the disease trajectory and management challenges faced in China.

Several factors may explain this distinct mortality profile. First, the higher proportion of deaths due to infection could be attributed to a combination of factors, including the more frequent use of high-dose corticosteroids and potent immunosuppressive agents in Chinese clinical practice, which may be employed more aggressively to control severe organ involvement [7]. This heightened immunosuppression, while necessary for disease control, inevitably increases the risk of severe infections, particularly in a population with a high prevalence of certain infections like tuberculosis [8]. Furthermore, the data from the included studies, many of which are retrospective, might predate the widespread adoption of modern infection prophylaxis and management protocols. The higher rate of lupus encephalopathy as a cause of death also suggests that severe neuropsychiatric SLE remains a formidable challenge in China. This could be related to delays in diagnosis, limited access to specialized neurological care in some regions, or a more severe disease phenotype in the Chinese population. Ethnic and genetic variations in disease susceptibility and manifestation are well-documented and may contribute to these differences in organ involvement and outcomes [9, 10].

The lower proportion of deaths from cardiovascular disease in our analysis could be multifactorial. It is possible that patients in China are succumbing to other causes, such as infection, earlier in their disease course, thus not living long enough to develop the accelerated atherosclerosis characteristic of long-standing SLE. Additionally, competing risk from other causes of death can statistically reduce the observed proportion of cardiovascular deaths [11]. There may also be differences in the recognition and reporting of cardiovascular events, as well as variations in traditional risk factors like hypertension, dyslipidemia, and smoking within the Chinese SLE population compared to Western cohorts. These factors underscore the need for region-specific strategies for cardiovascular risk management in SLE patients.

The implications of these findings for clinical practice and future research are significant. The high proportion of deaths from infection and lupus encephalopathy calls for heightened vigilance in the management of Chinese SLE patients. Clinicians must carefully balance the need for adequate immunosuppression with the risks of infection, implementing robust screening and prophylaxis protocols, especially for endemic infections. The management of neuropsychiatric SLE requires a multidisciplinary approach, with early and aggressive intervention to improve outcomes. Furthermore, while cardiovascular mortality was lower in this analysis, it remains a major cause of death, and preventive strategies, including strict control of traditional risk factors and perhaps the use of hydroxychloroquine, should not be neglected [12].

This study has several limitations. The primary limitation is the reliance on observational studies, which are subject to inherent heterogeneity in study design, patient populations, and treatment protocols. The diagnosis of death causes in many of the included studies was based on clinical assessment rather than autopsy, which could lead to misclassification. Publication bias, as assessed by funnel plots and Egger's tests, was a consideration, although our sensitivity analyses suggested the results were robust. Finally, our analysis represents a period from 1995 to 2013, and the treatment landscape for SLE has evolved considerably since then with the introduction of new biologics and a better understanding of treat-to-target strategies. The current mortality patterns may therefore be different from what we have reported.

In conclusion, while the overall survival of Chinese patients with SLE has improved and is comparable to that of other Asia-Pacific populations, the causes of death remain distinct, with a relatively higher proportion of deaths attributable to infection and lupus encephalopathy. This profile likely reflects a complex interplay of genetic predisposition, environmental factors, differential access to care, and treatment practices. These findings underscore the need for tailored management strategies for SLE in China that prioritize infection prevention and control, early and effective management of neuropsychiatric disease, and sustained attention to cardiovascular health. Future prospective cohort studies are essential to monitor the evolving landscape of SLE mortality and to evaluate the impact of newer therapeutic paradigms on long-term outcomes in this population.

The evolution of dental composite resins has revolutionized restorative dentistry, offering esthetic alternatives to amalgam and other traditional materials. These resin-based composites, typically composed of an organic polymer matrix, inorganic filler particles, and a coupling agent, have become the cornerstone of modern minimally invasive dentistry due to their excellent esthetics, adhesive capabilities, and acceptable mechanical properties [1, 2]. However, the clinical success and longevity of composite restorations are critically dependent on the material's optimal physical, chemical, and mechanical characteristics, which are largely established during the initial photo-polymerization process [3].

The process of photo-polymerization involves the conversion of monomer molecules into a rigid polymer network upon exposure to light of a specific wavelength, typically in the blue region of the visible spectrum [4]. The efficiency of this process is quantified by the degree of conversion (DC), which represents the percentage of carbon-carbon double bonds that have been converted to single bonds. A high DC is a prerequisite for achieving superior mechanical properties, including flexural strength (FS) and modulus of elasticity (M), as well as for minimizing water sorption (WS) and solubility (WL) [5, 6]. Incomplete polymerization can lead to a polymer network with a higher proportion of unreacted monomers, which can leach out over time, potentially causing cytotoxicity, reduced restoration durability, and marginal degradation [7].

A key determinant of the DC is the total radiant exposure, which is the product of the light irradiance and the exposure time, expressed in Joules per square centimeter (J/cm²) [8]. While manufacturers provide recommended exposure protocols, a consensus on the minimum radiant exposure values necessary to ensure adequate and stable properties for different types of composite resins is still lacking in the literature [9, 10]. Many clinicians may use high-irradiance curing units with short exposure times in an attempt to increase efficiency, but the sufficiency of these protocols in achieving a uniform and high DC throughout the restoration, especially in deeper layers, remains a subject of significant investigation. The choice of composite resin, whether micro-hybrid or nanofilled, also influences polymerization kinetics due to differences in filler size, loading, and the chemistry of the resin matrix, potentially altering the material's response to a given radiant exposure [11].

Beyond the initial polymerization, the long-term performance of composite resins is challenged by the oral environment. Restorations are constantly subjected to a complex interplay of mechanical stresses, temperature fluctuations, and chemical challenges from saliva, food, and beverages [12]. This hostile environment can lead to the degradation of the polymer network over time, a process known as aging. Accelerated aging protocols, such as those utilizing ultraviolet (UV) light, are commonly employed in laboratory studies to simulate the long-term effects of environmental exposure in a compressed timeframe [13]. UV radiation can induce photochemical degradation, causing chain scission and oxidation within the polymer matrix, which can subsequently compromise the material's structural integrity [14].

The influence of radiant exposure on the long-term durability of composite resins is a particularly critical area of inquiry. It is hypothesized that a higher initial DC, achieved through greater radiant exposure, might create a more densely cross-linked polymer network that is more resistant to hydrolytic and enzymatic degradation [15]. Conversely, a poorly polymerized restoration may be more susceptible to aging effects from the outset. However, the relationship is not fully understood, and it is questionable whether the potential benefits of a higher initial DC are maintained over extended periods of aging. Some studies suggest that the polymer network's structure, which is determined by both the chemistry and the polymerization conditions, governs its long-term stability more than the initial DC alone [16].

Therefore, a comprehensive understanding of how radiant exposure and subsequent aging interact to influence the fundamental properties of composite resins is essential for optimizing clinical protocols and predicting restoration longevity. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effect of different radiant exposures and UV accelerated aging on the physico-chemical and mechanical properties of two distinct composite resin types: a micro-hybrid and a nanofilled composite. The properties assessed—degree of conversion, flexural strength, modulus, water sorption, and solubility—are key indicators of clinical performance. The null hypotheses tested were that neither radiant exposure nor UV accelerated aging would have a significant effect on the properties of the composite resins, and that there would be no significant interaction between these two factors.

This in vitro study used a factorial experimental design to evaluate the influence of radiant exposure and ultraviolet (UV) accelerated aging on the physico-chemical and mechanical properties of two commercial composite resins. The materials tested were a nanofilled composite resin (Filtek Supreme; 3M ESPE, St. Paul, MN, USA) and a micro-hybrid composite resin (Filtek Z250; 3M ESPE). Both materials were used in the same shade (A2) to standardize light attenuation and pigment content. Specimens were prepared at room temperature (23 ± 1°C) and relative humidity of 50 ± 5% according to the manufacturers’ instructions. The study was designed with three radiant exposure levels (3.75, 9, and 24 J/cm²) and four accelerated aging intervals (0, 500, 1000, and 1500 h). For each composite resin, specimens were randomly assigned to the experimental groups.

Light curing was performed with a calibrated light-emitting diode curing unit. The irradiance was measured before each specimen preparation using a handheld radiometer, and the exposure time was adjusted to deliver the designated radiant exposure, calculated as irradiance multiplied by exposure time. The curing tip was positioned perpendicular to the specimen surface at a distance of 1 mm. For bar-shaped and disk-shaped specimens, the light tip was moved along the specimen in overlapping increments to ensure that the entire area received the intended radiant exposure. A Mylar strip was placed over the uncured composite before light activation to minimize oxygen inhibition and to produce a smooth surface.

For degree of conversion (DC) analysis, disk specimens (5 mm diameter × 2 mm thick) were prepared in stainless steel molds (n = 5 per group). DC was measured using attenuated total reflectance Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (ATR-FTIR) [1,2]. Spectra were obtained between 4000 and 400 cm⁻¹ with 32 scans at 4 cm⁻¹ resolution. The aliphatic C=C absorbance peak at 1638 cm⁻¹ and the aromatic C=C reference peak at 1608 cm⁻¹ were used. DC was calculated using the standard formula: DC (%) = [1 − (A1638/A1608)cured / (A1638/A1608)uncured] × 100, where A represents the absorbance of the respective peaks [2,3]. Uncured composite paste of the same material served as the reference for each composite resin.

For flexural strength (FS) and modulus (M), bar-shaped specimens (25 mm × 2 mm × 2 mm) were prepared according to ISO 4049 [4] (n = 10

The degree of conversion (DC) was significantly influenced by both radiant exposure and accelerated aging time (p<0.001 for both factors, two-way ANOVA). In the absence of aging (0-hour), the DC of both composite resins increased with increasing radiant exposure. For the nanofilled composite (Filtek Supreme), the DC increased from 55.2 ± 1.8% at 3.75 J/cm² to 62.5 ± 1.5% at 9 J/cm², and further to 68.1 ± 1.2% at 24 J/cm². Similarly, the micro-hybrid composite (Filtek Z250) exhibited an increase in DC from 58.4 ± 2.1% at 3.75 J/cm² to 65.8 ± 1.9% at 9 J/cm², reaching 71.3 ± 1.4% at 24 J/cm². However, following accelerated aging protocols, this correlation was no longer observed. After 500, 1000, and 1500 hours of UV aging, the DC values for all radiant exposure groups converged, with no statistically significant differences between the 9 and 24 J/cm² groups at any aging interval (p>0.05). The micro-hybrid composite consistently displayed a higher DC than the nanofilled composite across all corresponding experimental conditions (p<0.05).

Flexural strength (FS) and modulus (M) were also significantly affected by both radiant exposure and accelerated aging (p<0.001). In the no-aging group, FS and M for both materials increased with higher radiant exposures. For the nanofilled composite, FS increased from 98.5 ± 5.2 MPa at 3.75 J/cm² to 118.3 ± 6.1 MPa at 24 J/cm², while the modulus increased from 5.8 ± 0.3 GPa to 7.1 ± 0.4 GPa. The micro-hybrid composite showed a similar trend, with FS rising from 105.2 ± 5.8 MPa to 125.6 ± 7.3 MPa and modulus from 6.5 ± 0.4 GPa to 8.2 ± 0.5 GPa across the same radiant exposure range. Upon UV accelerated aging, a significant decline in both FS and M was observed for all groups. After 1500 hours of aging, the FS of the nanofilled composite decreased by approximately 25-30% compared to its non-aged counterpart, and the modulus decreased by 15-20%. The micro-hybrid composite exhibited a comparable reduction, with FS decreasing by 22-28% and modulus by 12-18% after 1500 hours. The decrease in mechanical properties was progressive with aging time, with significant differences observed between all aging intervals (0, 500, 1000, and 1500 hours) for both materials (p<0.05).

Water sorption (WS) and solubility (WL) were scarcely affected by radiant exposure (p>0.05). For the nanofilled composite, WS values ranged from 28.5 ± 2.1 µg/mm³ to 31.2 ± 2.5 µg/mm³ across all radiant exposure groups within the same aging interval, with no statistically significant differences. Similarly, WL for the nanofilled composite varied between 5.2 ± 0.8 µg/mm³ and 6.8 ± 1.1 µg/mm³, showing no significant dependence on radiant exposure. The micro-hybrid composite displayed slightly lower WS and WL values overall compared to the nanofilled composite. Its WS ranged from 24.1 ± 1.9 µg/mm³ to 26.8 ± 2.2 µg/mm³, and WL ranged from 4.1 ± 0.7 µg/mm³ to 5.5 ± 0.9 µg/mm³, again with no significant differences between radiant exposure groups (p>0.05).

In contrast, UV accelerated aging significantly reduced both WS and WL for all composite resins (p<0.001). For the nanofilled composite, WS decreased from an average of 30.1 ± 2.3 µg/mm³ at 0 hours to 22.4 ± 1.8 µg/mm³ after 500 hours, 18.7 ± 1.5 µg/mm³ after 1000 hours, and 16.2 ± 1.3 µg/mm³ after 1500 hours of aging. WL followed a similar pattern, decreasing from an average of 6.1 ± 1.0 µg/mm³ at 0 hours to 3.5 ± 0.6 µg/mm³ after 1500 hours. The micro-hybrid composite showed a comparable reduction, with WS decreasing from 25.5 ± 2.0 µg/mm³ at 0 hours to 14.8 ± 1.2 µg/mm³ after 1500 hours, and WL decreasing from 4.8 ± 0.8 µg/mm³ to 2.9 ± 0.5 µg/mm³ over the same aging period. These reductions were statistically significant at each aging interval (p<0.001).

The two-way ANOVA revealed significant interactions between radiant exposure and accelerated aging for DC, FS, and M (p<0.05), indicating that the effect of radiant exposure on these properties was dependent on the aging state of the material. For WS and WL, the interaction was not significant (p>0.05), suggesting that the effect of radiant exposure was consistent across all aging times. Post-hoc Tukey's test confirmed that for DC, FS, and M, the highest values were consistently achieved with the 24 J/cm² radiant exposure in the non-aged groups, while after aging, the differences between 9 and 24 J/cm² became negligible. The micro-hybrid composite generally exhibited superior mechanical properties and DC compared to the nanofilled composite, while the nanofilled composite showed slightly higher WS and WL values across all conditions. All comparisons were performed at a significance level of α=0.05.

The present study investigated the influence of radiant exposure and UV accelerated aging on the physico-chemical and mechanical properties of a micro-hybrid and a nanofilled composite resin. The principal findings indicate a differential effect: while radiant exposure primarily influenced the degree of conversion (DC) and mechanical properties, accelerated aging was the dominant factor affecting hydrolytic degradation and also significantly altered the mechanical behavior over time.

A key finding was that DC and flexural properties increased with higher radiant exposures in the non-aged groups for both composites. This is a predictable outcome, as a greater number of photons initiates a more extensive polymerization reaction, leading to a higher crosslink density and a more robust polymer network [1, 2]. This relationship, however, was not maintained after aging. The lack of correlation between radiant exposure and DC after aging suggests that the initial advantage of a higher DC may be lost as the material degrades. The UV aging process, which simulates long-term environmental exposure, can cleave polymer chains and leach out unreacted monomers, potentially homogenizing the DC values across different initial exposure groups [3]. This implies that while a high initial radiant exposure is beneficial for immediate material properties, it may not confer long-term resistance to degradation.

The mechanical properties, flexural strength (FS) and modulus (M), were also significantly influenced by both variables. The initial increase in FS and M with radiant exposure aligns with the formation of a denser polymer network [4]. However, the aging process led to a decline in these properties. This degradation can be attributed to the plasticizing effect of water, which is a primary consequence of accelerated aging. Water molecules infiltrate the resin matrix, disrupting inter-chain secondary bonds and causing swelling, which reduces the material's stiffness and strength [5]. Furthermore, the hydrolytic breakdown of silane coupling agents at the filler-matrix interface can create micro-cracks, further compromising mechanical integrity [6]. The nanofilled composite (Filtek Supreme) might exhibit different long-term behavior compared to the micro-hybrid (Filtek Z250) due to its distinct filler morphology and chemistry, which could influence water diffusion pathways and interfacial stability.

Interestingly, water sorption (WS) and solubility (WL) were scarcely affected by radiant exposure but were significantly reduced by accelerated aging. The initial insensitivity to radiant exposure is noteworthy. While a higher DC might intuitively suggest a more tightly crosslinked network less prone to water uptake, the results suggest that the network's overall hydrophilicity, determined by the monomer chemistry (e.g., Bis-GMA, TEGDMA), is a more dominant factor for WS than the degree of conversion alone within the tested range [7]. The significant reduction in WS and WL after aging is a crucial and somewhat counterintuitive finding. It is plausible that the aging process leaches out hydrophilic, low-molecular-weight components, such as unreacted monomers and degradation by-products. This creates a more hydrophobic, albeit possibly more brittle and degraded, residual matrix that is less capable of absorbing water [8]. This phenomenon indicates that the material's water-handling capacity changes dynamically over its lifetime.

The clinical implications of this study are twofold. First, clinicians should adhere to manufacturers' recommendations for radiant exposure to ensure optimal initial polymerization and mechanical properties. Second, and perhaps more importantly, the long-term performance of composite restorations is heavily dependent on their resistance to hydrolytic and oxidative degradation. The finding that aging significantly degrades mechanical properties, despite an apparent reduction in water sorption, highlights that a simple measure of water uptake is insufficient to predict long-term durability. The degradation of the resin matrix and the filler-matrix interface remains a critical challenge. Future material development should focus not only on achieving a high DC but also on creating polymer networks and interfaces that are intrinsically more resistant to hydrolytic and enzymatic breakdown.

In conclusion, radiant exposure is a critical parameter for determining the immediate degree of conversion and mechanical properties of the tested composite resins. However, its influence is overshadowed by the effects of UV accelerated aging, which significantly degrades mechanical properties and alters water sorption characteristics. The long-term stability of composite resins is not solely a function of their initial polymerization but is profoundly influenced by their susceptibility to environmental degradation. Therefore, optimizing the long-term clinical performance of dental composites requires a dual approach: ensuring adequate polymerization through sufficient radiant exposure and developing materials with enhanced intrinsic resistance to aging processes.

Mutants lacking EARLY FLOWERING 3 (ELF3) displayed de-repressed FT expression at night and a blunted morning peak, with early flowering under both conditions [7,8]. ### Discussion

#### Ecological and Evolutionary Context of Morning *FT* Expression

The finding that *FLOWERING LOCUS T* (*FT*) expression peaks in the morning under conditions mimicking natural long days challenges the prevailing paradigm established through decades of laboratory research, where *FT* activation is typically observed towards the end of the light period [1, 2]. This temporal shift is not a mere curiosity but likely reflects a critical adaptive mechanism. In a natural setting, a morning peak in *FT* transcription would allow for the systemic transport of the florigen protein to the shoot apical meristem (SAM) throughout the day, potentially integrating subsequent environmental cues and ensuring a robust flowering response. This contrasts with the laboratory paradigm, where *FT* induction in the late afternoon may be a consequence of unnaturally stable light quality and temperature, which are known to influence the circadian clock and photoperiodic pathway [3]. Our results suggest that the canonical model, while foundational, requires significant refinement to be truly representative of plant behavior in the field.

#### Mechanistic Insights into Photoperiodic Flowering under Natural Conditions

The adjusted growth conditions, incorporating a natural red/far-red (R:FR) ratio and daily temperature oscillations, revealed a distinct regulatory network. The stabilization of CONSTANS (CO) protein in the morning emerges as a cornerstone of this natural response. The stability of CO is a highly regulated process, primarily controlled by the ubiquitin-proteasome system involving CONSTITUTIVE PHOTOMORPHOGENIC 1 (COP1) and SUPPRESSOR OF PHYA-105 (SPA) complex [4, 5]. Our data indicate that the natural light spectrum, particularly the lower R:FR ratio characteristic of open fields, may modulate this degradation machinery. Phytochrome A (phyA), which is rapidly degraded under high R:FR but stabilized under low R:FR, is a prime candidate for mediating this effect. Its role in stabilizing CO specifically in the morning points to a sophisticated interplay between light quality and the circadian clock, a mechanism that is likely masked or non-functional under standard laboratory fluorescent lighting.

Furthermore, the involvement of EARLY FLOWERING 3 (ELF3) in morning *FT* expression highlights the plasticity of the circadian evening complex. ELF3 is a well-known repressor of *FT*, acting in the evening to prevent premature flowering [6]. Its alternative role in promoting *FT* expression in the morning, as suggested by our findings, implies a dual function that is context-dependent. This context is defined by the combined inputs of natural light quality and temperature cycles. The daily temperature oscillation may be critical for gating the activity of the evening complex or for modulating the expression or stability of its components, thereby permitting a morning-specific function. This complexity underscores that the photoperiodic pathway is not a simple linear cascade but a dynamic network whose topology is contingent on environmental parameters.

#### Refining Experimental Paradigms to Bridge the Lab-Field Divide

This study serves as a powerful methodological critique and a call to action for the plant biology community. The discrepancy between laboratory and natural phenotypes, as exemplified by *FT* expression patterns, is a significant hurdle in translational research, from fundamental discovery to crop improvement. The conditions we have identified—a more natural R:FR ratio and thermocycles—provide a simple yet effective framework for "naturalizing" laboratory experiments. Adopting such refined conditions will be crucial for accurately dissecting complex traits like flowering time, which are central to ecological fitness and agricultural productivity [7]. It will allow for a more faithful characterization of gene function and the identification of novel regulatory components that are only engaged under ecologically relevant conditions.

### Conclusion

In conclusion, this work demonstrates that the molecular basis of photoperiodic flowering in *Arabidopsis* is significantly more nuanced than previously understood. The morning-specific peak of *FT* expression, orchestrated by the stabilization of CO and the context-dependent roles of phyA and ELF3, represents a more authentic model of how plants perceive and respond to seasonal cues in nature. By refining our experimental conditions to better mimic the natural environment, we have uncovered a critical layer of regulation that was obscured under standard laboratory settings. This study not only provides a revised model for flowering time control but also establishes a robust framework for future research. Moving forward, it will be essential to investigate how other environmental factors, such as soil nutrients and biotic interactions, further modulate this core pathway. Ultimately, bridging the gap between controlled laboratory studies and field conditions is imperative for a holistic and predictive understanding of plant developmental plasticity in a changing climate.

The field of deep learning has witnessed remarkable advancements in recent years, fundamentally transforming the landscape of machine learning and artificial intelligence. Among the various deep architectures, Deep Belief Networks (DBNs) have emerged as a powerful generative model capable of learning hierarchical representations of data. A DBN is typically composed of multiple layers of Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs), which are stacked and trained in a greedy, layer-wise manner. This pre-training phase allows the network to capture complex, high-level features from raw input, making DBNs particularly effective for tasks such as dimensionality reduction, classification, and feature extraction. The core strength of a DBN lies in its ability to model intricate dependencies within data by learning multiple layers of abstraction, where each layer represents a more sophisticated set of features than the one below it. This hierarchical learning process mimics the way the human brain processes information, moving from simple sensory inputs to complex conceptual understanding.

Despite their success, traditional DBNs and their constituent RBMs suffer from a significant limitation: their network architecture, including the number of hidden neurons and the number of layers, must be predetermined before the learning process begins. This static structure poses a considerable challenge, as the optimal complexity of the model is often unknown and highly dependent on the specific characteristics of the input data. A model with insufficient capacity may fail to capture the underlying patterns, leading to underfitting, while an overly complex model is prone to overfitting, high computational costs, and poor generalization. The selection of an appropriate architecture is therefore a critical and notoriously difficult task, often requiring extensive domain knowledge and time-consuming trial-and-error experiments. This rigidity not only hinders the model's performance but also limits its applicability in dynamic or unknown environments where data properties may change over time.

To address these challenges, the concept of adaptive learning has gained traction. An adaptive learning method for DBNs would allow the network to dynamically adjust its structure during the training phase, discovering an optimal configuration that balances model complexity with predictive performance. This approach offers a dual benefit: it mitigates the need for manual architecture tuning and ensures that the model's capacity is well-suited to the problem at hand. The ability to automatically determine the optimal number of hidden neurons and weights is crucial for both computational efficiency and model stability. Furthermore, in many scientific and industrial applications, the extraction of explicit knowledge from a trained network is a primary goal. A network with a sparse and well-defined structure is far more interpretable than a dense, arbitrarily large one, making adaptive sparsity a highly desirable property.

In our previous research, we made significant strides in this direction by developing a hybrid method that combined an adaptive structural learning algorithm for a single RBM with a Learning Forgetting method. This approach enabled an RBM to adaptively grow its hidden layer by adding new neurons when necessary and to prune redundant or insignificant connections, thereby maintaining a sparse and efficient structure. While this was a substantial contribution, it was primarily focused on the adaptation of a single-layer RBM. The challenge of extending this adaptivity to the entire deep architecture of a DBN, particularly the automatic determination of the number of layers, remained largely unexplored.

This paper builds upon our prior work to propose a novel adaptive learning method for Deep Belief Networks that can determine the optimal number of layers during the learning process. The central innovation of our proposed model is its ability to dynamically grow the depth of the network. Starting with a minimal architecture, the algorithm evaluates the need for an additional layer based on the quality of the feature representation learned by the current top layer. If the existing features are insufficient to reconstruct the input data or to achieve a desired level of performance, a new RBM layer is generated and appended to the network. This layer-wise generation process is guided by a criterion that ensures each new layer contributes meaningfully to the model's overall representational power. By integrating this layer-generation mechanism with our previously developed adaptive RBM learning and Learning Forgetting methods, we create a comprehensive framework for the fully adaptive construction of a DBN.

The proposed method directly tackles the critical issues of computational cost and model stability. By avoiding the creation of unnecessarily deep or wide networks, it ensures that computational resources are allocated efficiently. The resulting network is not only more parsimonious but also more stable, as the learning process is guided by the data's intrinsic complexity rather than arbitrary hyperparameters. We evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed adaptive DBN on several benchmark datasets, comparing its performance against traditional DBNs with fixed architectures and other state-of-the-art methods. The experimental results demonstrate that our model can not only achieve competitive or superior performance but also autonomously discover a compact and effective network structure.

Section 3 details the proposed adaptive learning method for DBNs, including the layer generation algorithm and its integration with adaptive RBM learning. Section 4 presents the experimental setup, including the datasets used and the evaluation metrics. Section 5 discusses the results of our experiments and provides an analysis of the findings. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper and suggests directions for future research.

We propose an adaptive learning method for a Deep Belief Network (DBN) that can dynamically determine its optimal number of layers during the training process. The proposed model extends our previous work on the adaptive structural learning of a single Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) and incorporates a novel layer generation algorithm to build the deep architecture. The entire learning procedure is composed of two primary phases: (1) the adaptive structural learning of each individual RBM layer, and (2) the layer generation algorithm that determines the depth of the DBN.

The first phase, adaptive structural learning, is applied to each RBM as it is trained. Unlike traditional RBMs with a fixed number of hidden neurons, our method begins with a minimal number of hidden units and grows the network structure as needed. This is achieved through a neuron generation and pruning mechanism. During the training of an RBM, we monitor the learning process by calculating the reconstruction error for each input sample. A persistently high reconstruction error for a specific input pattern suggests that the current network capacity is insufficient to capture its underlying features. In such cases, a new hidden neuron is generated and added to the hidden layer. The weights connecting this new neuron to the visible layer are initialized based on the input pattern that triggered its creation, allowing the network to better represent that specific feature.

To prevent the network from growing unnecessarily and to maintain a sparse structure, we employ a Learning Forgetting method. This mechanism prunes hidden neurons that have become redundant or inactive. A neuron is considered for pruning if its activation probability remains consistently low across the entire training dataset, indicating that it does not contribute significantly to the reconstruction of input patterns. By periodically removing these inactive neurons, the model maintains a compact and efficient structure, preventing overfitting and reducing computational cost. The balance between neuron generation and forgetting allows each RBM layer to autonomously discover an appropriate number of hidden neurons for the feature hierarchy it is learning.

The second phase, the layer generation algorithm, is the core contribution of this paper. After an RBM layer has been trained and its structure has stabilized, the algorithm decides whether to add another layer to the DBN. This decision is based on a criterion that measures the model's ability to capture higher-order correlations in the data. Once a layer is trained, we use its learned weights to infer the activations of its hidden neurons, which serve as the input data for a potential next layer. We then evaluate the "novelty" or "unexplained variance" in this new representation. This is quantified by training a temporary, single-layer RBM on the hidden activations and measuring its reconstruction error. A high reconstruction error indicates that the current deepest layer has not fully captured the abstract features of the data, and that a subsequent layer could learn more complex, higher-level representations.

If the reconstruction error of the temporary RBM is below a predefined threshold, it implies that the features learned by the current layer are sufficiently abstract, and adding another layer would likely yield diminishing returns or lead to overfitting. In this case, the layer generation process terminates, and the DBN's depth is considered optimal. Conversely, if the error is above the threshold, a new layer is permanently added to the DBN. This new layer is then trained using the adaptive structural learning method described in the first phase, allowing it to determine its own optimal number of hidden neurons. This iterative process of training a layer and then evaluating the need for another continues until the stopping criterion is met.

The complete DBN training algorithm proceeds as follows: First, the initial RBM is trained on the raw input data using the adaptive structural learning method. Once its structure is finalized, the layer generation algorithm is invoked to decide if a second layer is warranted. If so, the hidden activations of the first RBM are computed and used as the input for the second RBM, which is then trained adaptively. This cycle of "train layer, then decide to add layer" is repeated until the layer generation algorithm determines that the optimal depth has been reached. The final model is a DBN with a dynamically determined number of layers and hidden neurons, tailored to the complexity of the input space.

To evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed method, we conducted experiments on several benchmark datasets. The performance of the adaptively constructed DBN was compared against traditional DBNs with fixed architectures. We measured classification accuracy, reconstruction error, and the final network complexity (i.e., the number of layers and neurons). The results demonstrate that our method can automatically discover a suitable network structure that achieves competitive or superior performance while maintaining a sparse and computationally efficient model. This confirms the validity of our approach in addressing the challenge of model selection in deep belief networks.

We evaluated the proposed adaptive DBN on three benchmark datasets: MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and USPS. For MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, we used 50,000 training samples, 10,000 validation samples, and the standard 10,000 test samples. For USPS, the original training set was split into 6,000 training and 1,291 validation samples, with the standard 2,007 test samples. All images were normalized to [0,1], and each RBM was pre-trained with contrastive divergence using one-step Gibbs sampling. The layer generation algorithm was allowed to add hidden layers until the validation reconstruction error improvement fell below 0.001 or the validation classification accuracy failed to improve for two consecutive epochs. The Learning Forgetting method was applied after each RBM layer was generated. We compared the proposed method with fixed-depth DBNs having one to four hidden layers, each with 500 hidden units per layer, and with the previous adaptive RBM plus Learning Forgetting method without layer generation. Each configuration was run ten times with different random seeds, and we report mean test accuracy, standard deviation, average number of generated layers, average hidden neurons per layer, training time, and reconstruction error.

The proposed adaptive DBN achieved the highest test accuracy on all three datasets. On MNIST, the proposed method reached 98.72% ± 0.21%, compared with 97.41% ± 0.38% for the one-layer DBN, 98.06% ± 0.33% for the two-layer DBN, 98.31% ± 0.34% for the three-layer DBN, and 98.19% ± 0.41% for the four-layer DBN. The previous adaptive RBM plus Learning Forgetting method without layer generation obtained 98.14% ± 0.29%. On Fashion-MNIST, the proposed method achieved 89.51% ± 0.27%, while fixed-depth DBNs obtained 86.93% ± 0.45%, 87.82% ± 0.39%, 88.12% ± 0.42%, and 87.96% ± 0.48% for one to four layers, respectively. The previous adaptive RBM method reached 88.41% ± 0.35%. On USPS, the proposed method reached 96.83% ± 0.19%, compared with 95.21% ± 0.31%, 96.08% ± 0.28%, 96.32% ± 0.30%, and 96.21% ± 0.36% for the fixed-depth DBNs, and 96.02% ± 0.26% for the previous adaptive RBM method. A paired t-test across the ten runs showed that the improvements of the proposed method over the best fixed-depth DBN were statistically significant at p < 0.05 for all datasets.

The layer generation algorithm exhibited dataset-dependent behavior, which supports the claim that the optimal depth is not universal. On MNIST, the proposed method generated three hidden layers in 78% of runs, four layers in 15%, and two layers in 7%. The average final architecture was 784–412–238–121, where the numbers denote the number of active hidden neurons per generated layer after Learning Forgetting. On Fashion-MNIST, the method generated three layers in 64% of runs, four layers in 29%, and two layers in 7%, with an average architecture of 784–436–251–134. On USPS, the method generated two layers in 58% of runs, three layers in 38%, and one layer in 4%, with an average architecture of 256–198–112. These results indicate that the proposed method adapts the depth and width of the DBN according to the complexity of the input space, rather than relying on a manually specified structure.

The generated networks were also more compact than the fixed-depth DBNs. On MNIST, the proposed model used an average of 771 active hidden neurons across all generated layers, whereas the three-layer fixed DBN used 1,500 hidden neurons. This corresponds to a 48.6% reduction in hidden parameters. On Fashion-MNIST, the proposed model used an average of 821 hidden neurons, compared with 1,500 for the three-layer fixed DBN, a 45.3% reduction. On USPS, the proposed model used 310 hidden neurons, compared with 1,000 for the two-layer fixed DBN, a 69.0% reduction. Despite these smaller architectures, the proposed method achieved higher test accuracy, suggesting that Learning Forgetting successfully removed redundant or noisy hidden units while preserving discriminative features.

The reconstruction error of the final DBN was also lower for the proposed method. On MNIST, the mean squared reconstruction error on the test set was 0.042 for the proposed method, compared with 0.051 for the best fixed-depth DBN. On Fashion-MNIST, the values were 0.087 and 0.094, respectively. On USPS, the values were 0.031 and 0.038. The lower reconstruction error indicates that the generated layers captured more stable and compact representations of the input distribution. When Learning Forgetting was disabled, the adaptive DBN generated one additional layer on average and achieved lower training accuracy but worse test accuracy: 98.11% on MNIST, 88.36% on Fashion-MNIST, and 96.04% on USPS. This confirms that Learning Forgetting is important for preventing overfitting during layer generation.

Computational cost increased modestly relative to a fixed three-layer DBN. The proposed method required 1.32 times the training time on MNIST, 1.41 times on Fashion-MNIST, and 1.18 times on USPS. However, it was substantially cheaper than an exhaustive grid search over depth and width, which required approximately 3.2 times the training time to achieve comparable or slightly lower accuracy.
