On each trial, monkeys viewed a moving-dot stimulus, indicated their perceived direction with a saccade, and received a liquid reward for correct choices; errors ended without reward. We analyzed behavioral performance on trial n as a function of the outcome and difficulty of trial n−1. Current-trial accuracy was significantly higher after an error than after a correct response, demonstrating a post-error improvement in performance. This effect was present in both monkeys and was accompanied by longer reaction times after errors. A trial-by-trial logistic regression confirmed that n−1 outcome, but not n−2 outcome, predicted current choice accuracy. The present results demonstrate that the outcome of the immediately preceding trial exerts a strong influence on both behavior and neuronal activity in the ventral premotor cortex (PMv) during perceptual decision-making. In the current trial, monkeys adjusted their performance according to whether the previous choice was correct or incorrect, and single PMv neurons changed their firing patterns as a function of that previous outcome. Importantly, this effect was temporally specific: the outcome of trial n−2 had little or no measurable impact on either behavior or PMv activity. This pattern suggests that PMv does not merely represent the ongoing decision process but also participates in a short-lived evaluative mechanism that uses the most recent outcome to shape upcoming behavior. The fact that difficult trials produced larger behavioral adjustments and recruited a greater proportion of PMv neurons further supports the idea that this area is particularly engaged when the decision process requires closer monitoring and when the outcome carries greater instructional value.

A central question concerns why the previous outcome should modulate PMv activity at all. PMv has traditionally been associated with action selection, motor preparation, and sensorimotor transformations. However, accumulating evidence indicates that PMv also represents abstract decision variables, including the accumulation of sensory evidence, choice confidence, and the evaluation of the decision process after feedback. Our findings extend this view by showing that PMv activity is not confined to the current trial’s sensorimotor contingencies. Instead, neurons in this area carry information about the recent past and use that information to influence the future. This is consistent with the proposal that PMv contributes to a distributed network for adaptive decision-making, in which outcome evaluation is transformed into adjustments in strategy, response caution, or evidence weighting. The short temporal window of the effect—restricted to trial n−1—may reflect a local eligibility trace that tags recent decisions for updating before the information is either consolidated elsewhere or allowed to decay.

The difficulty-dependent modulation is especially informative. When the preceding decision was difficult, the outcome was less predictable and therefore more informative. A correct outcome on a difficult trial may signal that a weak or ambiguous evidence state was resolved appropriately, whereas an error may indicate that the decision process failed under uncertainty. Either way, difficult trials provide a richer teaching signal than easy trials, in which the outcome is largely expected. The greater recruitment of PMv neurons after difficult outcomes suggests that PMv dynamically allocates resources according to the informativeness of the feedback. This is consistent with reinforcement learning and performance-monitoring frameworks in which prediction errors, conflict, and uncertainty modulate the strength of learning. In this sense, PMv may act as a cortical node that evaluates the decision process and broadcasts an update signal to circuits involved in future action selection.

The absence of an n−2 effect places important constraints on the underlying mechanism. If PMv were simply maintaining a long-lasting trace of reward history, one would expect older outcomes to influence current activity. Instead, the influence was limited to the most recent trial. This suggests that PMv is involved in rapid, trial-by-trial adaptation rather than in maintaining a prolonged reward or error history. Longer-term adjustments may depend on other structures, such as prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, or basal ganglia circuits, which could integrate PMv outcome signals over time. Alternatively, the n−1 effect may reflect a transient working-memory or attentional set that is overwritten once the next outcome is processed. Future experiments combining PMv recordings with simultaneous measurements in connected areas will be needed to determine how this short-lived signal is transmitted and whether it is transformed into more durable changes in behavior.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. Our results are correlational: they show that PMv activity and behavior covary with the previous outcome, but they do not establish that PMv activity causes the behavioral adjustment. Causal perturbation methods, such as optogenetics, chemogenetics, or microstimulation, will be necessary to test whether disrupting outcome-related PMv signals impairs trial-by-trial adaptation. In addition, the present task cannot fully disentangle outcome valence, surprise, decision difficulty, and motor error. Future work should vary reward magnitude, feedback timing, and task contingencies to determine which components are encoded by PMv. It will also be important to test whether similar effects appear in other decision-making contexts and whether PMv neurons encode an abstract evaluation signal or a more specific sensorimotor update.

In conclusion, these findings provide strong support for the hypothesis that PMv neurons evaluate the decision process and use that evaluation to modify future behavior. The previous trial’s outcome, particularly when it follows a difficult decision, changes both behavioral performance and the activity of single PMv neurons in the next trial. The rapid decay of this effect indicates a short-lived credit-assignment mechanism that is well suited to trial-by-trial adaptive control. Errors, therefore, are not merely failures to be avoided; they are salient teaching signals that reshape the decision system. By linking recent outcomes to upcoming choices, PMv may help transform experience into improved performance.

Polar codes, introduced by Arikan, are the first class of explicit channel codes proven to achieve the symmetric capacity of binary-input discrete memoryless channels with low-complexity encoding and decoding. Owing to their capacity-achieving property and recursive structure, polar codes have attracted significant attention in both academia and industry, and have been adopted for control channels in 5G New Radio. The standard decoder for polar codes is successive cancellation (SC) decoding, which processes the received signal sequentially and makes hard decisions on information bits in a bit-by-bit manner. Its complexity is O(N log N) for block length N, making it attractive for practical implementation. However, at short and moderate block lengths, SC decoding suffers from a non-negligible performance loss compared with maximum-likelihood decoding. The main reason is error propagation: because SC decoding is sequential, an incorrect estimate of any prior unfrozen bit affects all subsequent decisions, often causing a burst of errors and degrading the block error rate (BLER).

To mitigate this problem, successive cancellation list (SCL) decoding was proposed

We consider a polar code of length \(N\), information set \(\mathcal{A}\), and frozen set \(\mathcal{A}^c\). The encoder maps an information vector \(u_1^N\) to a codeword \(x_1^N\), and the decoder observes a noisy channel output \(y_1^N\). Under successive cancellation (SC) decoding, bit decisions are made sequentially from index \(1\) to \(N\). Once an unfrozen bit is estimated incorrectly, the error propagates through subsequent decisions, making it difficult to recover the correct codeword. The proposed method therefore focuses on identifying and correcting the first error as early as possible, and then recursively correcting additional independent errors that remain after the first correction.

The first component of the method is the construction of a critical set \(S\) of unfrozen bit indices. For each unfrozen bit \(i \in \mathcal{A}\), we estimate the probability \(p_i\) that \(i\) is the first erroneous decision in an SC decoding attempt under the target channel condition. These probabilities are obtained offline by density evolution, Gaussian approximation, or Monte Carlo simulation of SC decoding over the desired signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) range. The critical set is then formed by sorting the unfrozen indices in descending order of \(p_i\) and selecting the smallest subset whose cumulative first-error probability exceeds a prescribed threshold, typically \(0.99\). Thus, with high probability, the first SC error occurs at an index contained in \(S\). The set \(S\) is stored at both encoder and decoder and is independent of the received vector. In practice, a small critical set is sufficient because the first-error distribution is highly concentrated on a limited number of unfrozen positions.

The second component is the construction of layered critical sets. After a candidate first error at index \(i_1 \in S\) is flipped, the decoder resumes SC decoding from the remaining undecoded subtree associated with that decision. The next independent error, if any, is not uniformly distributed over all remaining unfrozen bits; its distribution depends on the already decoded prefix and on the correction applied at \(i_1\). Therefore, for each \(i_1 \in S\), we construct a second-layer critical set \(S^{(2)}_{i_1}\) using the remaining undecoded subtree rooted after \(i_1\). This set is obtained by the same offline procedure as \(S\), but restricted to the unfrozen bits that have not yet been decoded and conditioned on the previous flipped index. More generally, for a sequence of previously flipped indices \((i_1,\ldots,i_{\ell-1})\), the \(\ell\)-th layer critical set \(S^{(\ell)}_{i_1,\ldots,i_{\ell-1}}\) is constructed from the remaining undecoded subtree associated with the previous layer. The level \(\ell\) therefore corresponds to the number of independent errors that the decoder is allowed to correct.

The progressive bit-flipping decoder operates as follows. First, a standard SC decoding pass is performed to obtain an initial estimate \(\hat{u}_1^N\). If the appended cyclic redundancy check (CRC) is satisfied, the estimate is declared successful. Otherwise, the decoder enters level 1 and considers each index \(i_1 \in S\). For each candidate, the hard decision at \(i_1\) is flipped, and SC decoding is resumed from the next position using the stored channel log-likelihood ratios and partial sums. If the resulting codeword passes the CRC, decoding terminates. If no level-1 candidate succeeds, the decoder proceeds to level 2. For each previously tried first flip \(i_1\), it traverses the corresponding second-layer critical set \(S^{(2)}_{i_1}\), flips a second index \(i_2\), resumes SC decoding, and checks the CRC. This process continues up to a maximum level \(L_{\max}\). At level \(\ell\), the decoder maintains a stack of flipped positions \((i_1,\ldots,i_\ell)\) and explores only the layered critical set associated with the current prefix. This progressive search avoids the combinatorial explosion of testing all \(\ell\)-bit combinations and ensures that each additional flip targets a likely independent error location.

To reduce complexity, several pruning rules are applied. Candidates whose reliability metric, such as the absolute LLR or path metric, is above a threshold may be skipped. If a partial path already violates a CRC check or a parity constraint, its descendants are discarded. The decoder also stops early once the CRC is satisfied. Because the critical sets are small and the first error is usually corrected at a low level, the average number of SC resumes remains modest, especially at medium to high SNR.

The computational complexity of the proposed decoder consists of an offline construction cost and an online decoding cost. The offline construction is performed once per code and SNR region and is negligible for practical deployment. Online, each SC resume can be implemented efficiently by storing intermediate LLRs and partial sums at the flip position; the cost of a resume is proportional to the size of the remaining decoding subtree. The initial SC pass has complexity \(O(N\log N)\). Each additional flip attempt adds a similar but often smaller cost. At medium to high SNR, the average complexity is close to that of standard SC decoding and is significantly lower than that of a successive cancellation list (SCL) decoder. For example, a level-4 progressive bit-flipping decoder can achieve block error rate performance comparable to a CRC-aided SCL decoder with list size \(L=32\), while requiring far fewer path expansions on average. The frozen set was obtained by Gaussian approximation, and the critical set \(S\) was constructed offline for each signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) region of interest. For the CA-SCL benchmark, a 24-bit cyclic redundancy check was appended to the information bits; the proposed progressive bit-flipping (PBF) decoder operated directly on the same polar code construction without relying on CRC for error detection. Unless otherwise stated, the block error rate (BLER) was evaluated after a minimum of \(10^5\) block transmissions, and the average complexity was measured in SC-equivalent decoding attempts, where one SC-equivalent attempt corresponds to the computational cost of a conventional successive cancellation decoding pass.

The first set of experiments evaluated the reliability of the critical set \(S\). Across the SNR range from 1.0 to 4.0 dB, the probability that \(S\) contained the first erroneous unfrozen bit exceeded \(99\%\), consistent with the design target. At 1.5 dB, the first-error inclusion probability was \(99.12\%\); at 2.5 dB, it increased to \(99.54\%\); and at 3.5 dB, it reached \(99.71\%\). The average size of \(S\) was approximately \(84\) unfrozen bits, corresponding to about \(16.4\%\) of the \(K=512\) unfrozen positions. This compact size is important because it limits the number of candidate bit flips that must be tested at each level. When the first error fell outside \(S\), the level-1 decoder could not correct it, and the block was declared in error; however, such events were rare and became negligible at medium to high SNR.

The progressive bit-flipping decoding algorithm presented in this work addresses a fundamental challenge in the practical deployment of polar codes: the gap between the excellent performance of list-based decoders and the low complexity of the standard successive cancellation (SC) decoder. Our discussion centers on the implications of the results, the underlying mechanisms that drive the performance, and the potential pathways for future research and application.

The core contribution of this paper, the layered critical set, provides a systematic method for identifying the most probable locations of the first decoding error. The finding that a single critical set $S$ can contain the first error with a probability exceeding 99% validates the underlying premise that errors in SC decoding are not uniformly distributed but are concentrated in specific, predictable bit-channels. This high probability is the cornerstone of the proposed algorithm's success. It ensures that the initial bit-flipping attempt is highly likely to be successful if only a single error has occurred. The construction of this set, based on the intrinsic reliability metrics of the polarized channels, is a static, code-specific property, which lends itself to efficient pre-computation and avoids any online complexity overhead.

The progressive, multi-level nature of the algorithm is what elevates it from a simple single-error corrector to a powerful competitor against state-of-the-art decoders like CA-SCL. The concept of iteratively constructing new critical sets from the remaining undecoded subtrees is particularly effective. When a bit-flip at level $l$ successfully corrects an error, the subsequent decoding path is altered. The new critical set for level $l+1$ is then tailored to this new path, focusing on the most probable error locations within the corrected subtree. This recursive refinement allows the decoder to correct multiple, independent errors that may occur at different stages of the decoding process. The term "independent" is crucial here; the algorithm is designed to handle errors that are not direct consequences of a single prior error, but rather distinct events that would each derail the SC decoder. The performance results, where a level-4 decoder rivals a CA-SCL decoder with a list size of $L=32$, are highly significant. This demonstrates that for a moderate number of independent errors, the targeted search strategy of progressive bit-flipping can achieve a performance level comparable to the broad, parallel search of a list decoder, but with a fraction of the computational cost.

This complexity advantage is arguably the most compelling aspect of the proposed decoder. The average complexity, which is similar to that of a standard SC decoder at medium to high signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs), is a direct result of its progressive nature. In the vast majority of cases, especially at high SNR, the SC decoding attempt is successful, and no bit-flipping is required. When an error does occur, the first level of bit-flipping is attempted. The complexity only increases if multiple errors are present, which becomes increasingly rare as SNR improves. This is in stark contrast to SCL decoding, whose complexity is a fixed multiple (proportional to the list size $L$) of the SC decoder's complexity, regardless of the channel conditions. This makes the progressive bit-flipping decoder an attractive candidate for applications where energy efficiency and low average latency are paramount, such as in machine-type communications or mobile devices.

However, the proposed algorithm is not without its limitations, which also illuminate avenues for future work. The performance is intrinsically linked to the quality of the critical sets. While the initial set is highly effective, the construction of subsequent layers relies on the remaining undecoded subtree, and its effectiveness could degrade as more errors are corrected. A potential research direction could involve optimizing the construction of these layered sets, perhaps by incorporating dynamic information from the received signal or by using a more sophisticated metric than the static channel reliability. Furthermore, the algorithm's performance in the presence of a burst of errors, rather than independent ones, is an open question. The current framework is designed for independent errors, and its efficacy might be reduced if errors are correlated.

Another area for exploration is the trade-off between performance and complexity. The paper compares a level-4 decoder to a CA-SCL decoder with $L=32$. It would be valuable to investigate the performance of higher-level progressive decoders and compare them to CA-SCL decoders with larger list sizes. This would help define the practical limits of the bit-flipping approach. Additionally, the hardware implementation of such a decoder, particularly the control logic for managing the progressive levels and the bit-flipping process, presents an interesting engineering challenge that warrants further study.

In conclusion, this paper has introduced a novel and efficient decoding algorithm for polar codes that successfully bridges the performance-complexity gap. By intelligently identifying and correcting errors through a progressive, multi-level bit-flipping scheme over layered critical sets, the proposed decoder achieves a block error rate performance that is competitive with CA-SCL decoding, while maintaining an average complexity close to that of standard SC decoding. The key strengths of this approach lie in its targeted error correction strategy and its favorable complexity profile, which is particularly advantageous in the medium-to-high SNR regime. This work not only provides a practical alternative to existing decoders but also opens up new research directions in the design of low-complexity, high-performance decoding algorithms for polar codes and other advanced forward error correction schemes. The principles of progressive, targeted error correction demonstrated here could potentially be adapted to other code families where error propagation is a significant concern.

Psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory dermatosis that affects approximately 2–3% of the global population and significantly impairs quality of life [1,2]. It is clinically characterized by well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale, commonly involving extensor surfaces, scalp, trunk, and nails. Although the disease is primarily driven by dysregulated adaptive immunity, particularly the IL-23/IL-17 axis, increasing evidence indicates that innate immune effectors, including neutrophils, contribute substantially to lesion formation and maintenance [3,4]. Psoriatic plaques exhibit epidermal hyperproliferation, abnormal keratinocyte differentiation, angiogenesis, and a mixed inflammatory infiltrate composed of T cells, dendritic cells, macrophages, and neutrophils [5]. The histological hallmarks of psoriasis include acanthosis, parakeratosis, absence of the granular layer, dilated tortuous capillaries in the dermal papillae, and accumulation of neutrophils within the epidermis and stratum corneum, where they form Munro microabscesses and Kogoj spongiform pustules [6,7]. These features suggest that neutrophil recruitment and activation are not merely epiphenomena but may actively participate in the inflammatory cascade.

Neutrophils are short-lived phagocytes that are rapidly recruited to sites of inflammation in response to chemotactic signals such as CXCL8/IL-8, leukotriene B4, complement C5a, and IL-17-induced chemokines [8,9]. Upon activation, neutrophils release a variety of granule enzymes and reactive oxygen species (ROS) that mediate host defense but can also cause tissue injury. Myeloperoxidase (MPO) is a heme-containing enzyme abundantly expressed in azurophilic granules of neutrophils. It catalyzes the reaction between hydrogen peroxide and chloride to generate hypochlorous acid, a potent microbicidal oxidant [10,11]. Beyond its antimicrobial function, MPO promotes oxidative modification of lipids and proteins, activates latent matrix metalloproteinases, inactivates protease inhibitors, and amplifies inflammatory signaling pathways [12,13]. Elevated MPO levels and activity have been reported in the serum and lesional skin of patients with psoriasis, and MPO may correlate with disease severity and systemic inflammation [14,15]. However, the precise contribution of MPO to psoriatic tissue damage and its functional relationship with other inflammatory mediators remain incompletely defined.

Nitric oxide (NO) is a gaseous signaling molecule synthesized from L-arginine by nitric oxide synthase (NOS). The inducible isoform of NOS (iNOS/NOS2) is transcriptionally upregulated in response to proinflammatory cytokines, microbial products, and oxidative stress in macrophages, neutrophils, keratinocytes, and endothelial cells [16,17]. While physiological NO participates in vasodilation, neurotransmission, and immune defense, excessive iNOS-derived NO can react with superoxide to form peroxynitrite, a powerful nitrating and oxidizing agent that causes lipid peroxidation, protein tyrosine nitration, DNA damage, and cellular dysfunction [18,19]. iNOS expression has been demonstrated in psoriatic plaques, particularly in keratinocytes and inflammatory infiltrates, and NO metabolites are increased in the serum and skin of affected individuals [20,21]. Nevertheless, whether iNOS activation is primarily a downstream consequence of neutrophil-derived oxidants or an independent driver of psoriatic inflammation remains unclear.

MPO and iNOS are functionally interconnected. MPO can consume NO and thereby modulate its bioavailability, while MPO-derived hypochlorous acid and ROS can activate redox-sensitive transcription factors such as NF-κB, AP-1, and mitogen-activated protein kinases, leading to iNOS induction [22,23]. Conversely, iNOS-derived NO may influence neutrophil recruitment, degranulation, and MPO release, creating a feed-forward loop of oxidative and nitrosative stress [24]. This case-control study was conducted in the Department of Dermatology of a tertiary referral center during a 12-month recruitment period. Fifty adult patients with chronic plaque-type psoriasis vulgaris and 25 healthy controls were enrolled. The diagnosis of psoriasis was established by at least two experienced dermatologists on the basis of characteristic clinical features, including well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale, and was supported by histopathological findings when diagnostic uncertainty existed [1]. Patients were eligible if they were aged 18 years or older, had stable chronic plaque psoriasis involving at least 5% of the body surface area, and had not received systemic antipsoriatic therapy, phototherapy, or biologic agents within 4 weeks before enrollment. Exclusion criteria were other forms of psoriasis, active psoriatic arthritis requiring systemic treatment, topical antipsoriatic therapy within 2 weeks before sampling, pregnancy or lactation, active infection, malignancy, known autoimmune or inflammatory disease other than psoriasis, and current smoking, because smoking may influence myeloperoxidase (MPO) and nitric oxide metabolism. Healthy controls were matched for age and sex and had no personal or family history of psoriasis, no inflammatory dermatosis, no systemic inflammatory disease, and no recent infectious illness. The study was approved by the institutional ethics committee and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki [2]. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants before any study procedure.

Peripheral venous blood samples were collected from all participants after an overnight fast. Blood was allowed to clot at room temperature for 30 minutes and then centrifuged at 3,000 rpm for 10 minutes. Serum was separated, aliquoted, and stored at −80°C until analysis. Serum MPO and inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) concentrations were measured using commercially available enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits according to the manufacturers’ instructions [3,4]. All samples were assayed in duplicate, and a standard curve was generated for each plate. Absorbance was read at 450 nm using a microplate reader. Concentrations were calculated by interpolation from the standard curve and expressed as ng/mL for MPO and pg/mL for iNOS. The intra-assay and inter-assay coefficients of variation were below 5% and 8%, respectively. All serum assays were performed in a single batch by an investigator blinded to the clinical status of the participants.

Skin biopsy specimens were obtained from each patient with psoriasis. After local anesthesia with 2% lidocaine without epinephrine, two 4-mm punch biopsies were taken: one from the center of a representative active psoriatic plaque and one from uninvolved skin at least 5 cm away from any visible lesion. The uninvolved specimen served as an internal normal control. Healthy controls did not undergo skin biopsy. Each specimen was fixed in 10% neutral buffered formalin for 24 hours, processed routinely, and embedded in paraffin. Serial 4-µm sections were cut onto poly-L-lysine-coated slides for immunohistochemical analysis.

Sections were deparaffinized in xylene, rehydrated through graded ethanol, and subjected to antigen retrieval using 10 mM citrate buffer (pH 6.0) in a microwave oven. A total of 50 patients with chronic plaque psoriasis and 25 healthy controls were enrolled. Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics were comparable between groups. The present study was designed to elucidate the contribution of neutrophils to the pathogenesis of psoriasis by investigating the systemic and local expression of myeloperoxidase (MPO) and inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS). Our findings demonstrate a significant elevation of serum MPO levels in patients with chronic plaque psoriasis compared to healthy controls, alongside intense immunohistochemical staining for both MPO and iNOS within psoriatic lesions. Interestingly, while tissue-level iNOS was prominent, serum iNOS levels did not show a statistically significant difference between the two groups. These results suggest a pivotal role for neutrophil-derived MPO in the local inflammatory milieu of psoriasis, which may, in turn, drive the local synthesis of iNOS, contributing to the disease's pathogenesis.

The significant increase in circulating MPO levels observed in our patient cohort aligns with the established understanding of psoriasis as a systemic inflammatory disease, not merely a cutaneous disorder [1]. Neutrophils, a key component of the innate immune system, are abundant in psoriatic lesions and are known to release MPO upon activation. This enzyme is a potent catalyst for the production of hypochlorous acid, a powerful oxidant that can cause significant tissue damage [2]. The elevated serum MPO we detected likely reflects the heightened state of neutrophil activation and degranulation occurring systemically in these patients. This systemic inflammation is a known contributor to the comorbidities often associated with severe psoriasis, such as cardiovascular disease and metabolic syndrome [3]. Therefore, MPO could serve as a valuable biomarker for both disease severity and the risk of associated systemic conditions.

A key finding of our study is the intense staining for MPO in the leukocytes infiltrating the psoriatic epidermis, the formation of Munro microabscesses being a hallmark histological feature [4]. This confirms that the neutrophils recruited to the skin are actively engaged in releasing MPO directly into the lesion. This local release of MPO and the subsequent oxidative stress are likely major contributors to the characteristic epidermal hyperproliferation and aberrant differentiation seen in psoriasis. The resulting tissue damage and release of pro-inflammatory cytokines can further perpetuate the inflammatory cycle, creating a feedback loop that sustains the psoriatic plaque [5].

The role of iNOS in psoriasis is more complex. Our immunohistochemical analysis revealed intense iNOS staining in psoriatic skin, corroborating previous reports of increased nitric oxide (NO) production in psoriatic lesions [6]. NO is a pleiotropic molecule involved in vasodilation, immune regulation, and inflammation. The high local expression of iNOS suggests that it is a significant source of NO within the psoriatic microenvironment. However, the lack of a significant difference in serum iNOS levels between patients and controls is noteworthy. This discrepancy between local and systemic iNOS expression has been observed in other inflammatory conditions and could be explained by several factors. It is plausible that iNOS induction is predominantly a localized phenomenon, driven by the specific cytokine milieu within the skin, and that any NO or iNOS that enters the circulation is rapidly metabolized or diluted, preventing a detectable systemic increase [7]. Alternatively, the regulation of iNOS in circulating leukocytes may differ from that of tissue-resident cells or infiltrating cells in the skin.

Our findings suggest a potential mechanistic link between MPO and iNOS. The oxidative stress generated by MPO-derived hypochlorous acid can lead to the activation of various transcription factors, including nuclear factor kappa-B (NF-κB), a master regulator of inflammatory gene expression [8]. NF-κB is a known potent inducer of the iNOS gene. Therefore, it is plausible that the MPO released by neutrophils in the psoriatic lesion indirectly triggers the synthesis of iNOS in various cell types, including keratinocytes, macrophages, and endothelial cells. This creates a self-amplifying loop where neutrophil recruitment and activation lead to MPO release, which in turn promotes iNOS expression and NO production, further enhancing vasodilation, immune cell infiltration, and tissue inflammation [9]. This pathway highlights a synergistic interaction between two key inflammatory mediators, placing neutrophils at a central nexus in the pathogenesis of psoriasis.

The translational implications of these findings are significant. The central role of MPO in the inflammatory cascade of psoriasis identifies it as a promising therapeutic target. Current treatments for moderate-to-severe psoriasis are largely focused on modulating the adaptive immune system, particularly T-cells and their associated cytokines like TNF-α, IL-17, and IL-23 [10]. While highly effective, these therapies are not universally successful and can be associated with significant side effects. Targeting the innate immune system, specifically neutrophil function and MPO activity, could offer a novel and complementary therapeutic strategy. Inhibitors of MPO or agents that block its synthesis or release could potentially reduce the local oxidative damage and break the inflammatory feedback loop, thereby alleviating the clinical manifestations of psoriasis [11]. This approach could be particularly beneficial for patients who do not respond adequately to conventional therapies.

This study has several limitations that should be acknowledged. The sample size was moderate, and all patients had chronic plaque psoriasis, so our findings may not be generalizable to other forms of the disease, such as pustular or guttate psoriasis. Furthermore, we measured serum levels and tissue expression at a single time point, which does not capture the dynamic changes in these mediators over the course of the disease or in response to treatment. Future studies with larger cohorts, longitudinal sampling, and investigation of different psoriasis subtypes are warranted to confirm and extend our findings. It would also be valuable to explore the specific cell types responsible for iNOS expression in the skin and to directly test the hypothesis that MPO inhibition leads to reduced iNOS expression and clinical improvement in psoriasis.

In conclusion, this study provides compelling evidence for the active involvement of neutrophils in the pathogenesis of psoriasis through the systemic and local release of MPO. The intense local expression of iNOS, potentially driven by MPO-mediated pathways, underscores the complex interplay between innate immune cells and inflammatory mediators within the psoriatic lesion. Our results strengthen the rationale for targeting MPO and its downstream effects, including iNOS synthesis, as a novel therapeutic strategy for psoriasis. Such an approach could complement existing treatments by addressing the innate immune component of this multifaceted disease, offering new hope for patients. Further research into the precise mechanisms linking MPO and iNOS in psoriasis is essential to fully realize the potential of this therapeutic avenue.

Oral squamous cell carcinoma of the tongue remains one of the most common malignancies of the oral cavity, and its incidence has been rising, particularly among younger patients without traditional risk-factor profiles [1,2]. In early-stage disease, defined as pT1 and pT2 tumors with clinically negative neck nodes (cN0), the primary therapeutic decision concerns adequate resection of the lingual lesion and the management of the clinically uninvolved neck [3,4]. Although elective neck dissection is increasingly advocated for patients with early oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma (OTSCC), a substantial proportion of cN0 patients harbor occult cervical nodal metastases, while others may be overtreated if all necks are addressed surgically [5,6]. This therapeutic dilemma has driven the search for reliable preoperative biomarkers that can stratify patients according to their risk of nodal dissemination and thereby inform the extent of neck management.

Tumor thickness (TT) has emerged as a robust histopathological predictor of nodal metastasis, locoregional recurrence, and survival in OTSCC [7,8]. TT is generally defined as the maximum perpendicular distance from the mucosal surface or the reconstructed epithelial surface to the deepest point of tumor invasion, whereas depth of invasion (DOI) is measured from the level of the adjacent normal basement membrane [9,10]. The eighth edition of the American Joint Committee on Cancer staging system incorporated DOI into the T category for oral cavity cancers, underscoring the prognostic importance of this parameter [11]. Multiple studies have identified a TT threshold of approximately 4 mm as a clinically meaningful cut-off, above which the risk of occult nodal metastasis increases substantially [12,13]. Consequently, accurate preoperative estimation of TT could guide decisions regarding elective neck dissection, sentinel lymph node biopsy, or close observation in patients with early OTSCC.

Histopathological examination of the glossectomy specimen remains the gold standard for TT measurement, but it is inherently postoperative and cannot inform the initial surgical plan [14]. Intraoperative measurement from fresh specimens may provide useful information, yet it also occurs after primary resection and may be subject to tissue distortion, orientation difficulties, and sampling error [15]. Therefore, preoperative imaging modalities capable of reliably measuring TT are of considerable clinical interest. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) offers excellent soft-tissue contrast and has been used to assess tumor depth and tongue invasion, but its routine use may be limited by cost, availability, motion artifacts, dental amalgam artifacts, and longer acquisition times [16,17]. Computed tomography (CT) is widely available and rapid, but it provides inferior soft-tissue resolution for superficial lingual lesions and exposes patients to ionizing radiation [18]. These limitations have prompted investigation into ultrasonography (USG) as a practical alternative for preoperative locoregional assessment.

High-frequency intraoral ultrasonography allows real-time, multiplanar evaluation of superficial oral tongue lesions with good spatial resolution and without ionizing radiation [19,20]. Because the probe can be placed directly on the tongue mucosa, USG can delineate the mucosal surface and the deep tumor margin, permitting TT measurement in a manner that approximates histopathological assessment [21]. Neck ultrasonography can also be performed in the same setting to evaluate cervical lymph nodes, making USG a potentially cost-effective and comprehensive preoperative tool [22]. Nevertheless, the accuracy of USG-derived TT depends on operator experience, transducer frequency, lesion accessibility, and the presence of inflammation or fibrosis adjacent to the tumor [23]. Previous studies have reported variable correlation coefficients between USG and histopathological TT, and the optimal threshold for predicting occult nodal metastasis in early OTSCC remains incompletely defined [24,25]. Moreover, many series have combined oral cavity subsites or included advanced-stage tumors, limiting their applicability to the specific clinical scenario of early, clinically N0 oral tongue cancer.

From a management perspective, the clinical value of preoperative TT measurement lies not merely in its numerical agreement with microscopy but in its capacity to predict pathological nodal status and thereby alter treatment decisions. If a noninvasive, reproducible, and inexpensive imaging method could identify patients with TT below a safe threshold, those patients might be spared elective neck dissection and its associated morbidity [26]. Conversely, patients with TT above the threshold could be counseled more accurately regarding the likelihood of occult metastasis and the benefits of elective nodal treatment [27]. This risk-adapted approach is particularly relevant in resource-constrained settings, where access to MRI and sentinel lymph node biopsy may be limited, and where USG is already widely used for head and neck evaluation [28,29].

Despite the theoretical advantages of USG, prospective data specifically addressing early OTSCC remain sparse. Most published studies are retrospective, include heterogeneous patient populations, or lack standardized measurement protocols for both USG and histopathology [30,31]. There is also uncertainty regarding the magnitude of agreement between USG and microscopic TT, the direction and limits of bias, and the clinical significance of small measurement discrepancies [32]. Furthermore, the relationship between USG-derived TT and occult nodal metastasis has not been consistently evaluated in patients who are clinically N0 and uniformly treated with elective neck dissection, which is necessary to validate the true predictive capacity of the imaging parameter [33,34].

The present study was therefore designed to address these gaps by prospectively evaluating preoperative intraoral and neck ultrasonography in patients with early OTSCC and clinically negative necks. The specific objectives were twofold: first, to assess the statistical correlation and agreement between TT measured by USG and TT measured by microscopic examination of the glossectomy specimen; and second, to evaluate the predictive capacity of USG-derived TT for detecting occult cervical nodal metastasis. By correlating a practical preoperative imaging biomarker with definitive histopathological outcomes, this study aimed to clarify whether ultrasonography can serve as a reliable and cost-effective tool to guide neck management in early oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma.

Study design and setting. This was a prospective, single-institution, observational diagnostic study conducted in a tertiary-care academic center over a 2-year period from January 2012 to December 2013. Consecutive patients diagnosed with early oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma (OTSCC) were screened for eligibility. The study was designed in accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) recommendations for observational research [1] and was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Institutional ethics committee approval was obtained before patient enrollment, and written informed consent was obtained from all participants.

Participants. Adults aged 18 years or older with histopathologically confirmed squamous cell carcinoma of the oral tongue and clinically early-stage disease (pT1 or pT2, clinically N0, M0) according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer staging system [2] were eligible. Patients were required to have no prior history of head and neck surgery, radiotherapy, or chemotherapy; no synchronous second primary malignancy; and no contraindication to surgical resection or elective neck dissection. Patients with recurrent disease, non-squamous histology, inadequate ultrasonographic visualization of the primary lesion, or distant metastasis at presentation were excluded. All included patients underwent preoperative clinical examination, imaging, and routine staging investigations as per institutional protocol.

Preoperative ultrasonography. Preoperative intraoral and neck ultrasonography (USG) was performed within 7 days before surgery by an experienced head and neck radiologist using a high-frequency linear-array transducer (7–12 MHz) or an intraoral hockey-stick probe, depending on lesion accessibility.
