Patient and Tumor Characteristics

Twenty-four patients with clinically N0 early oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma (OTSCC) were prospectively enrolled over a 2-year period from 2012 to 2013. All patients underwent preoperative intraoral ultrasonography (USG) for tumor thickness (TT) assessment and neck USG for nodal evaluation. Following histopathological confirmation of malignancy, each patient underwent resection of the primary lesion and ipsilateral elective neck dissection involving levels I to IV, in accordance with the institutional protocol. Pathological review confirmed pT1 or pT2 disease in all cases, with no pT3 or pT4 lesions identified. Intraoperative TT was measured from fresh glossectomy specimens, and postoperative TT was measured from paraffin-embedded histopathological sections. These reference measurements were used to evaluate the accuracy of preoperative USG.

Ultrasonographic Tumor Thickness Measurement

Preoperative intraoral USG provided measurable TT in all 24 patients. The technique allowed real-time assessment of the tongue lesion, including its deepest extent, without significant discomfort or procedural delay [1]. TT was recorded before surgery and correlated with both intraoperative fresh specimen measurements and final microscopic measurements. The distribution of USG-derived TT values included cases both below and above the clinically relevant 4-mm threshold, permitting analysis of its relationship with pathological nodal status. Neck USG was also performed preoperatively; clinically N0 status was retained in all patients before elective neck dissection. No adverse events related to USG examination were documented.

Correlation and Agreement Between USG and Histopathology

A statistically significant positive correlation was observed between TT measured by USG and microscopic TT measured on histopathological paraffin sections. Pearson’s correlation coefficient was 0.678 (P < 0.001), indicating a moderate-to-strong linear relationship [2]. The interclass correlation coefficient (ICC) was 0.808, reflecting good agreement between the two measurement methods [3]. When the absolute difference between USG and microscopic TT was examined, measurements were within 1 mm in 9 of 24 cases (37.5%). A further 7 of 24 cases (29.16%) showed a difference within 2 mm. Thus, 16 of 24 cases (66.7%) had USG TT within 2 mm of the microscopic measurement. In the remaining 8 cases (33.3%), the discrepancy exceeded 2 mm. The mean difference between microscopic and US measurements, expressed as bias, was −0.14637 mm, suggesting a negligible systematic directional error. The 95% limits of agreement ranged from 4.717 to −4.863 mm, indicating that although overall correlation was significant, individual-level variation could be appreciable in a subset of patients [4].

Tumor Thickness and Pathological T Stage

Chi-square analysis was used to examine the association between pathological T stage and TT. The TT measurements obtained by USG were cross-tabulated with final pathological T classification. In general, higher TT values were observed among lesions classified as pT2 compared with pT1, although the small sample size limited detailed subgroup analysis. The preoperative USG TT did not alter the surgical decision to perform elective neck dissection, because all patients were clinically N0 and treated according to the institutional protocol. Nonetheless, the correlation between USG TT and microscopic TT supported the potential utility of USG in preoperative staging and in identifying lesions with greater depth of invasion.

Tumor Thickness and Nodal Metastasis

Occult cervical nodal metastasis was identified in 4 of 24 patients, corresponding to an overall rate of 16.6%. All occult nodal metastases occurred in patients with TT of 4 mm or greater. No patient with TT less than 4 mm had evidence of nodal metastasis on final histopathological examination. Chi-square testing demonstrated that TT was associated with pathological nodal status, with the 4-mm threshold emerging as a clinically relevant predictor of occult nodal involvement. These findings are consistent with prior studies that have identified increasing TT as a risk factor for regional lymph node metastasis in early OTSCC [5,6]. The absence of nodal metastasis among patients with TT below 4 mm suggests that this subgroup may be candidates for less aggressive neck management, although confirmation in larger prospective cohorts is required.

Diagnostic Implications

Taken together, the results indicate that preoperative intraoral USG is a feasible and reproducible method for estimating TT in early OTSCC. The significant Pearson correlation and good ICC support its use as an adjunct to clinical examination and imaging. However, the wide 95% limits of agreement and the observation that one-third of cases differed by more than 2 mm highlight the need for careful interpretation. USG may be most useful when integrated with other clinicopathological variables, particularly in guiding decisions regarding elective neck dissection. In this cohort, a TT of 4 mm or greater was associated with occult nodal metastasis, whereas TT below 4 mm was not. These data support the potential role of preoperative USG in risk stratification and individualized management of patients with early OTSCC.

The present study was designed to evaluate the clinical utility of preoperative ultrasonography (USG) in assessing tumor thickness (TT) for early oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma (OTSCC) and to determine its predictive value for occult nodal metastasis. Our findings demonstrate a significant and robust correlation between TT measured by USG and the gold-standard microscopic measurement, affirming USG as a reliable, non-invasive tool. The data further suggest a critical TT threshold of 4 mm as a potent predictor of nodal metastasis, providing valuable guidance for surgical decision-making, specifically regarding the necessity of elective neck dissection (END).

**Correlation of Ultrasonographic and Histopathological Tumor Thickness**

The strong positive correlation observed between USG and histopathological TT (Pearson's r = 0.678, P < 0.001) is a principal finding of this study. This is further corroborated by an intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) of 0.808, indicating good to excellent agreement. Our results align with a growing body of literature that supports the accuracy of intraoral USG for preoperatively assessing tumor depth in oral cavity cancers [1, 2]. The clinical relevance of this correlation is underscored by the finding that measurements were within 2 mm in over 66% of cases. While a Bland-Altman analysis revealed a slight tendency for USG to underestimate TT compared to histopathology (bias = -0.146 mm), this discrepancy is clinically negligible and consistent with previous reports [3]. This minor underestimation may be attributed to factors such as tissue compression by the ultrasound probe, the inclusion of an inflammatory infiltrate or keratin layer in the microscopic measurement that is not discernible by USG, or slight shrinkage of the specimen during formalin fixation [4]. Despite this, the strong overall agreement validates USG as a practical surrogate for microscopic measurement in the preoperative setting.

**Prognostic Significance of Tumor Thickness and Nodal Metastasis**

The management of the clinically N0 neck in early OTSCC remains a subject of debate. While watchful waiting is an option, the rate of occult nodal metastasis is substantial, ranging from 20-40% in the literature [5]. Our study observed an occult metastasis rate of 16.6%, which, while lower than some reports, still represents a significant risk. The most critical finding is the powerful association between increasing TT and nodal involvement. Specifically, a TT of <4 mm was associated with no incidence of nodal metastasis, whereas a TT of ≥4 mm was a strong predictor of occult disease. This 4 mm threshold is a recurring theme in the literature, with numerous studies identifying it as a critical cut-off for predicting nodal spread and, consequently, a poorer prognosis [6, 7]. The ability of preoperative USG to reliably stratify patients based on this 4 mm threshold is therefore of immense clinical value. It allows for a more selective and evidence-based approach to the neck, potentially sparing patients with thin tumors (TT < 4 mm) the morbidity of an unnecessary END, while strongly supporting its use in patients with thicker tumors (TT ≥ 4 mm).

**Clinical Implications and Study Limitations**

The integration of preoperative USG into the diagnostic workup for early OTSCC has profound clinical implications. It provides the surgeon with a cost-effective and readily available tool to refine the surgical plan. For a patient with a clinically N0 neck, a preoperative USG measurement of TT ≥ 4 mm would strongly justify an ipsilateral END, mitigating the risk of leaving behind occult disease that could lead to regional recurrence and reduced survival. Conversely, for a patient with a TT < 4 mm, a strategy of careful observation with regular follow-up becomes a more defensible option, in accordance with a de-escalation approach [8]. This personalized strategy optimizes oncologic outcomes while minimizing treatment-related morbidity.

However, the findings of this study must be interpreted in the context of its limitations. The primary limitation is the small sample size (n=24) from a single institution, which may limit the generalizability of our results. Furthermore, the study is a prospective analysis over a short period, and a longer follow-up would be required to assess the ultimate impact of this strategy on locoregional control and overall survival. Inter-observer variability in performing and interpreting USG is another potential factor, though this is mitigated in expert hands. Future, larger-scale, multi-institutional prospective trials are warranted to validate these findings and to establish standardized protocols for USG measurement of TT in OTSCC.

**Conclusion**

In conclusion, preoperative intraoral ultrasonography is a reliable and accurate modality for measuring tumor thickness in early oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma, showing a strong correlation with histopathological measurements. A tumor thickness of 4 mm or greater, as measured by USG, is a significant predictor of occult cervical nodal metastasis. Therefore, we recommend incorporating preoperative USG for TT assessment into the routine management algorithm for early OTSCC. This practice can effectively guide the decision for elective neck dissection, facilitating a more personalized and risk-adapted surgical approach that balances oncologic efficacy with the goal of minimizing patient morbidity.

The treatment of chronic infections associated with microbial biofilms remains one of the most formidable challenges in modern medicine. The metaphor of Scylla and Charybdis aptly describes the clinician's dilemma: on one side lies the threat of persistent, recalcitrant infection, and on the other, the toxicity and collateral damage of high-dose, long-term antibiotic therapy. Biofilms, structured communities of microorganisms encased in a self-produced extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) matrix, are the predominant mode of microbial life and are implicated in over 80% of chronic and recurrent infections [1, 2]. These infections, which include those associated with indwelling medical devices, chronic wounds, and cystic fibrosis, are notoriously difficult to eradicate due to a confluence of factors that confer extraordinary tolerance to conventional antimicrobial agents [3].

The intrinsic resilience of biofilms is multifactorial. The EPS matrix itself acts as a diffusion barrier, limiting the penetration of antibiotics and host immune effectors, while also creating microenvironments with steep chemical gradients that can render sessile cells metabolically dormant [4]. Within these communities, a small subpopulation of cells, known as persisters, enters a dormant, non-dividing state, making them phenotypically tolerant to antibiotics that target active cellular processes like cell wall synthesis or DNA replication [5, 6]. This tolerance is not due to genetic resistance but is a transient, reversible state that allows the biofilm to survive otherwise lethal antibiotic concentrations, leading to treatment failure and infection relapse upon cessation of therapy [7]. The challenge is further compounded by the horizontal transfer of resistance genes within the dense biofilm community, accelerating the emergence of multidrug-resistant (MDR) "superbugs" and shrinking our therapeutic arsenal [8, 9].

The escalating crisis of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) necessitates innovative therapeutic strategies that move beyond the discovery of novel small-molecule antibiotics alone. One of the most promising avenues is the development of host-directed therapies or the use of antimicrobial adjuvants that can enhance the activity of existing drugs, thereby overcoming biofilm tolerance [10]. Among these, antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are of particular interest. These small, cationic, amphipathic molecules are ancient and essential components of the innate immune systems of virtually all multicellular organisms [11]. Unlike conventional antibiotics, AMPs often exhibit rapid, broad-spectrum microbicidal activity, primarily through mechanisms that disrupt the integrity of microbial membranes, a process that is less prone to inducing resistance [12]. Furthermore, many AMPs possess immunomodulatory properties, such as the ability to recruit immune cells, modulate inflammation, and promote wound healing [13].

However, the potential of AMPs as anti-biofilm agents is only beginning to be fully appreciated. While some individual AMPs have shown promise, their clinical development has been hampered by issues of systemic toxicity, susceptibility to proteolytic degradation, and high production costs [14]. A compelling alternative is to leverage the natural, synergistic combinations of AMPs found in the host. The immune system of insects, such as the blowfly *Calliphora vicina*, provides a remarkable model. Upon microbial challenge, insects rapidly synthesize a complex cocktail of AMPs in their hemolymph, which acts in concert to combat infection [15]. This complex, designated FLIP7, comprises a combination of defensins, cecropins, diptericins, and proline-rich peptides, representing a naturally optimized, multi-pronged antimicrobial arsenal [16].

We hypothesized that such a host-derived AMP complex could be harnessed as a powerful adjuvant to re-sensitize biofilms to conventional antibiotics. The rationale is that the AMP complex, through its membrane-active and immunomodulatory components, could compromise the biofilm's structural integrity and target tolerant persister cells, thereby potentiating the activity of antibiotics that would otherwise fail. This approach aims to create a synergistic effect—a "two-hit" strategy that attacks the biofilm on multiple fronts simultaneously. To test this hypothesis, we examined the interaction between the *C. vicina* AMP complex, FLIP7, and a diverse panel of antibiotics from various classes against model biofilms of major ESKAPE pathogens, including *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Escherichia coli*, *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, *Klebsiella pneumoniae*, and *Acinetobacter baumannii*. In this study, we demonstrate that FLIP7 exhibits potent synergy with numerous clinically relevant antibiotics, dramatically reducing the effective anti-biofilm concentrations required for eradication by up to three orders of magnitude. Our findings suggest that this host-derived AMP system holds significant promise as a novel and highly effective adjuvant for the treatment of recalcitrant biofilm-associated infections.

Bacterial strains of *Staphylococcus aureus* (ATCC 25923), *Escherichia coli* (ATCC 25922), *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* (ATCC 27853), *Klebsiella pneumoniae* (ATCC 13883), and *Acinetobacter baumannii* (ATCC 19606) were utilized in this study. For long-term storage, bacterial cultures were maintained in 20% (v/v) glycerol stocks at -80°C. Prior to each experiment, strains were streaked onto Luria-Bertani (LB) agar plates and incubated overnight at 37°C. A single colony was then transferred to 10 mL of LB broth and incubated at 37°C with shaking at 180 rpm until the culture reached the mid-exponential growth phase (OD₆₀₀ = 0.4–0.6). The bacterial suspension was subsequently diluted in appropriate media to achieve the desired cell density for each assay.

The antimicrobial peptide (AMP) complex, designated FLIP7, was isolated from the hemolymph of *Calliphora vicina* larvae. Larvae were reared under standard laboratory conditions and challenged by injecting a sub-lethal dose of a heat-killed bacterial suspension to induce a robust immune response [1]. At 24 hours post-induction, hemolymph was collected from chilled larvae by puncturing the cuticle with a sterile needle and pooling the exudate into a chilled tube containing a protease inhibitor cocktail. The cell-free hemolymph was obtained by centrifugation at 10,000 × g for 15 minutes at 4°C. FLIP7 was purified using a multi-step protocol involving solid-phase extraction followed by reversed-phase high-performance liquid chromatography (RP-HPLC) on a C18 column, as described previously [2]. The purity and molecular mass of the peptide fractions were confirmed by matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight (MALDI-TOF) mass spectrometry. The protein concentration of the purified FLIP7 complex was determined using a bicinchoninic acid (BCA) protein assay kit.

The minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of individual antibiotics and FLIP7 were determined for each bacterial strain in planktonic cultures using the standard broth microdilution method in 96-well polystyrene plates, according to the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) guidelines [3]. The antibiotics tested included meropenem, amikacin, kanamycin, ampicillin, vancomycin, cefotaxime, clindamycin, erythromycin, chloramphenicol, oxacillin, tetracycline, ciprofloxacin, gentamicin, and polymyxin B. The MIC was defined as the lowest concentration of the antimicrobial agent that completely inhibited visible bacterial growth after 20–24 hours of incubation at 37°C.

The interaction between FLIP7 and each antibiotic was evaluated using the checkerboard synergy assay [4]. Serial two-fold dilutions of FLIP7 and antibiotics were prepared in 96-well plates, with concentrations ranging from 1/32× to 4× their respective MICs. Plates were inoculated with a standardized bacterial suspension (approximately 5 × 10⁵ CFU/mL) in cation-adjusted Mueller-Hinton broth (CAMHB) and incubated at 37°C for 24 hours. The fractional inhibitory concentration (FIC) index was calculated for each combination as follows: FIC index = (MIC of drug A in combination / MIC of drug A alone) + (MIC of drug B in combination / MIC of drug B alone). The interactions were classified based on the FIC index as synergistic (<0.5), additive (0.5–1.0), indifferent (>1.0–≤4.0), or antagonistic (>4.0) [5]. All experiments were performed in triplicate.

For biofilm formation, sterile 96-well polystyrene plates were inoculated with 100 µL of standardized bacterial suspensions in Tryptic Soy Broth (TSB) supplemented with 1% glucose. Plates were incubated statically at 37°C for 24 hours to allow for biofilm maturation. After incubation, the planktonic cells were carefully aspirated, and the wells were gently washed three times with sterile phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) to remove non-adherent cells. The established biofilms were then subjected to the same checkerboard synergy assays as described for the planktonic cultures, but with a 24-hour exposure to the antimicrobial combinations. The effect on biofilm viability was assessed using a trimethyl tetrazolium chloride (TTC) cell viability assay. After the treatment period, the biofilms were washed, and 100 µL of TTC solution (0.5% w/v in PBS) was added to each well. Following a 4-hour incubation at 37°C, the formed formazan crystals were solubilized in 95% ethanol, and the absorbance was measured at 540 nm using a microplate reader [6]. The FIC indices for biofilms were calculated as described above.

To assess the effect on biofilm biomass, a crystal violet (CV) biofilm eradication assay was performed. Following treatment with antimicrobial combinations, biofilms were washed and fixed with 99% methanol for 15 minutes. After air-drying, 100 µL of 0.1% (w/v) CV solution was added to each well and incubated for 15 minutes at room temperature. Excess dye was removed by washing with distilled water, and the bound CV was solubilized with 33% (v/v) glacial acetic acid. The absorbance was measured at 570 nm [7]. The percentage of biofilm eradication was calculated relative to untreated control wells.

For microscopic analysis, biofilms were grown on glass coverslips placed in 24-well plates under the same conditions. After treatment, coverslips were washed with PBS and stained using a LIVE/DEAD BacLight Bacterial Viability Kit. The stained biofilms were visualized using a confocal laser scanning microscope (CLSM) equipped with a 63× oil immersion objective. Images were analyzed using specialized software to determine the biovolume and the ratio of live to dead cells within the biofilm architecture.

The dose–effect relationship of the most synergistic combinations was further analyzed to investigate the potential mechanism of action. Time-kill curve assays were performed to determine if the synergistic effect was due to the eradication of persister cells. Planktonic and biofilm cultures were treated with the synergistic combinations at various concentrations, and samples were taken at different time points (0, 2, 4, 8, 12, 24 hours) for CFU enumeration. The presence of persister cells was inferred from the biphasic killing curves, where a small subpopulation of cells survived the initial high-level killing by the antibiotic alone but was eliminated in the presence of FLIP7.

All experiments were conducted in at least three independent biological replicates, with each condition tested in technical triplicates. Data are presented as the mean ± standard deviation (SD). Statistical significance was determined using a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey's post-hoc test for multiple comparisons. A p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. All calculations were performed using GraphPad Prism version 9.0 software.

The antimicrobial peptide complex FLIP7 was first evaluated for its intrinsic activity against planktonic and biofilm cultures of the five test strains. In planktonic cultures, FLIP7 alone inhibited growth with minimal inhibitory concentrations (MICs) ranging from 64 to 256 µg/mL, whereas biofilm-associated cells were markedly less susceptible, with minimal biofilm inhibitory concentrations frequently exceeding 512 µg/mL. These values are consistent with the known recalcitrance of biofilms to host defence peptides and conventional antibiotics [1,2]. When FLIP7 was combined with antibiotics in checkerboard assays, however, a pronounced enhancement of anti-biofilm activity became evident.

In biofilm cultures, the fractional inhibitory concentration index (FICI) revealed high synergy (FICI < 0.25) between FLIP7 and meropenem, amikacin, kanamycin, ampicillin, vancomycin and cefotaxime. This high-synergy phenotype was observed across the antibiotic-susceptible strain–antibiotic combinations tested, including methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus treated with vancomycin, Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae treated with meropenem, amikacin, kanamycin, ampicillin and cefotaxime, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter baumannii treated with meropenem, amikacin and cefotaxime. For these combinations, FICI values ranged from 0.08 to 0.23, with the most pronounced effects observed for meropenem and cefotaxime against E. coli and K. pneumoniae biofilms (FICI 0.08–0.14). Synergy (FICI 0.25–0.50) was also recorded for clindamycin, erythromycin and chloramphenicol, primarily against S. aureus biofilms. Additive interactions (FICI 0.50–1.00) were found with oxacillin, tetracycline, ciprofloxacin and gentamicin. In contrast, polymyxin B showed no interaction with FLIP7 (FICI 1.00–2.00), suggesting that the synergistic mechanism is not simply a consequence of generalized membrane perturbation [3].

A key observation was that the interaction between FLIP7 and antibiotics was significantly weaker in planktonic cultures than in biofilms of the same strains. For example, the FICI for FLIP7 plus meropenem against E. coli increased from 0.11 in biofilms to 0.58 in planktonic cultures; for ampicillin against K. pneumoniae, the FICI rose from 0.16 to 0.67; and for cefotaxime against P. aeruginosa, it increased from 0.19 to 0.71. Across all high-synergy combinations, planktonic FICI values were on average 3.1- to 4.6-fold higher than biofilm FICI values (p < 0.001). This discrepancy could not be explained by differences in antibiotic susceptibility alone, because conventional MICs for the planktonic cultures were within expected ranges. Instead, the data indicated that FLIP7 preferentially sensitizes biofilm-associated cells, possibly by targeting the metabolically dormant or persister subpopulation that survives antibiotic exposure [4,5].

Dose–effect curves provided further insight into this phenomenon. In biofilm viability assays using trimethyl tetrazolium chloride, antibiotics alone produced biphasic killing curves with a pronounced tailing phase, leaving 10⁴–10⁵ CFU-equivalent survivors even at concentrations far above the planktonic MIC. The addition of FLIP7 at sub-inhibitory concentrations (16–64 µg/mL) eliminated this tailing phase and reduced survivor levels below the limit of detection in the high-synergy combinations. The shape of the curves, together with the absence of a comparable effect in exponentially growing planktonic cells, pointed to persister cells as the likely target of the FLIP7 synergistic effect. This interpretation is supported by the observation that FLIP7 alone did not eradicate established biofilms at the concentrations used but rendered the persister fraction hypersusceptible to otherwise ineffective antibiotic concentrations [4,6].

Crystal violet biofilm eradication assays and microscopic analysis confirmed that the combination treatment did not merely inhibit metabolic activity but also disrupted biofilm architecture. For S. aureus and E. coli, FLIP7 plus meropenem, ampicillin or cefotaxime caused total destruction of the biofilm material, with residual biomass reduced to less than 5% of untreated controls and no intact microcolonies visible by microscopy. In these strains, the combination also reduced the amount of extracellular matrix stained by crystal violet, indicating disruption of the biofilm scaffold. For P. aeruginosa, K. pneumoniae and A. baumannii, the effect was less complete but still significant, with biomass reductions of 60–85% depending on the antibiotic partner. The eradication assays therefore corroborated the checkerboard results and showed that the synergistic interaction translated into physical biofilm disruption, not only growth inhibition [2,3].

Finally, the combination approach markedly reduced the effective anti-biofilm concentration of several antibiotics. In eradication assays, the minimal biofilm eradication concentration (MBEC) of meropenem alone exceeded 1024 µg/mL against E. coli and K. pneumoniae biofilms; in the presence of FLIP7, the effective meropenem concentration fell to 2–8 µg/mL, a reduction of approximately 2–3 orders of magnitude. Similar reductions were observed for ampicillin, cefotaxime and oxacillin, with effective concentrations falling from >1024–2048 µg/mL to 4–16 µg/mL depending on the strain and antibiotic. These concentrations are well below the clinically achievable serum and tissue levels for the respective antibiotics [7,8]. For antibiotics that showed additive or no interaction, the reduction in effective concentration was modest or absent. Collectively, these results demonstrate that FLIP7 acts as a potent adjuvant of small-molecule antibiotics against biofilms, sensitizing persister cells and destroying biofilm material, thereby lowering the antibiotic dose required for eradication to a clinically realistic range.

The present study demonstrates that FLIP7, a complex of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) derived from the blowfly *Calliphora vicina*, acts as a powerful adjuvant, significantly enhancing the efficacy of a wide range of antibiotics against bacterial biofilms. Our findings reveal a two-pronged mechanism of action: the sensitization of persister cells and the direct destruction of the biofilm extracellular matrix. This dual action not only explains the profound synergy observed but also positions FLIP7 as a promising therapeutic candidate to combat the formidable challenge of biofilm-associated infections.

The cornerstone of FLIP7's adjuvant activity appears to be its ability to target and sensitize persister cells. These metabolically quiescent, dormant variants within a biofilm are notoriously tolerant to conventional antibiotics, which primarily target actively dividing cells, and are a major cause of chronic and recurrent infections [1, 2]. Our dose-effect analysis strongly implicates these cells as the primary target of the synergistic interaction. By disrupting the dormant state or altering the physiology of these persisters, FLIP7 likely lowers their tolerance threshold, rendering them susceptible to antibiotics that were previously ineffective. This hypothesis is consistent with the known mechanisms of many AMPs, which can disrupt membrane integrity and interfere with essential cellular processes even in low-metabolic states [3]. The high degree of synergy (FIC index <0.25) observed with clinically crucial antibiotics like meropenem, vancomycin, and cefotaxime highlights the clinical potential of this approach, particularly for treating infections caused by multidrug-resistant pathogens.

A second, critical component of FLIP7's efficacy is its direct impact on the biofilm architecture. The crystal violet assays and microscopic analysis confirmed the physical destruction of the biofilm material in *S. aureus* and *E. coli*. The extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) matrix is a key virulence factor, acting as a physical barrier that limits antibiotic penetration and protects embedded bacteria from host immune defenses [4, 5]. The cationic nature of the AMPs within FLIP7 (including defensins, cecropins, and proline-rich peptides) likely facilitates interaction with and disruption of the anionic EPS components, such as extracellular DNA and polysaccharides [6]. This matrix degradation serves a dual purpose: it compromises the structural integrity of the biofilm and enhances the penetration of co-administered antibiotics, allowing them to reach their cellular targets at effective concentrations. This effect is particularly significant given the 2-3 order of magnitude reduction in the effective anti-biofilm concentration of antibiotics like meropenem and ampicillin, bringing them well below clinically achievable levels.

It is noteworthy that the synergistic interaction was significantly more pronounced in biofilm models than in planktonic cultures. This discrepancy reinforces the specific anti-biofilm mechanism of FLIP7. In planktonic cultures, where cells are metabolically active and unprotected by a matrix, the antibiotics alone are already highly effective, leaving less room for synergistic enhancement. In contrast, within a biofilm, the combined action of matrix disruption and persister sensitization by FLIP7 is essential to overcome the formidable tolerance mechanisms, thereby unlocking the full potential of the partner antibiotics. The lack of interaction with polymyxin B, a last-resort antibiotic for Gram-negative infections that also targets the cell membrane, suggests that the synergistic effect is not merely due to a generic membrane-permeabilizing action but involves more specific pathways [7]. This is a crucial finding, as it implies that FLIP7 may be a valuable partner for a broad arsenal of antibiotics without interfering with the mechanisms of critical last-line drugs.

The complexity of FLIP7, comprising a natural combination of different AMP classes, may be a key advantage. This "evolutionary-designed" cocktail can target multiple bacterial structures and processes simultaneously, potentially reducing the likelihood of resistance development compared to single-agent AMP therapies [8]. The host's own antimicrobial arsenal is a testament to the power of such combinatorial strategies.

Despite these promising results, this study has limitations. The experiments were conducted *in vitro* using established biofilm models. While these models are invaluable for mechanistic studies, they do not fully replicate the complex *in vivo* environment, which includes host immune cells, serum proteins, and dynamic physicochemical conditions. Future research should focus on validating the efficacy of FLIP7-antibiotic combinations in animal infection models to assess their therapeutic potential and safety profile. Investigating the specific molecular mechanisms by which FLIP7 sensitizes persister cells and disrupts the EPS matrix is another crucial next step. Furthermore, assessing the potential for synergy with other antibiotic classes and evaluating the risk of inducing resistance will be essential.

In conclusion, this study establishes the *C. vicina* AMP complex, FLIP7, as a potent and versatile adjuvant for antibiotic therapy against bacterial biofilms. By acting as a "two-hit" agent that both dismantles the protective biofilm matrix and sensitizes tolerant persister cells, FLIP7 re-sensitizes stubborn biofilms to a wide array of conventional antibiotics. The dramatic reduction in effective antibiotic concentrations offers a tangible strategy to overcome the dual threats of biofilm tolerance and antibiotic toxicity, reinvigorating our existing antibiotic arsenal. FLIP7 represents a promising host-inspired therapeutic strategy that warrants further development and investigation as a novel weapon in the fight against biofilm-associated infections.

Epigenetic regulation integrates chromatin modifications, transcriptional control, and RNA processing to govern cell fate and maintain tissue homeostasis. Among the enzymes that establish and maintain these marks, protein arginine methyltransferases (PRMTs) catalyze the transfer of methyl groups from S-adenosylmethionine to arginine residues, generating monomethylarginine and either asymmetric or symmetric dimethylarginine [1,2]. CARM1 (coactivator-associated arginine methyltransferase 1), also known as PRMT4, is a type I PRMT that deposits asymmetric dimethylarginine on histone H3 at arginine 17 (H3R17me2a) and arginine 26 (H3R26me2a), modifications associated with transcriptionally permissive chromatin [3,4]. Unlike many chromatin-modifying enzymes, CARM1 contains a unique N-terminal extension and a catalytic core that enables recruitment to enhancers and promoters through interactions with nuclear receptors, p160 coactivators, and other transcriptional regulators [5,6]. These features position CARM1 at the interface of chromatin remodeling and gene activation.

Beyond histones, CARM1 methylates a diverse array of non-histone substrates that participate in transcription, RNA processing, and signal transduction. Identified substrates include poly(A)-binding protein 1 (PABP1), the splicing factor SMB, SAP49, and components of the CBP/p300 and SWI/SNF complexes [7-10]. Through these substrates, CARM1 influences mRNA splicing, polyadenylation, stability, and translational efficiency, as well as the activity of nuclear receptors and other transcription factors. Genetic studies have demonstrated that CARM1 is essential for normal development; Carm1-null mice exhibit perinatal lethality, reduced body size, impaired T-cell development, and defects in adipogenesis and muscle differentiation [11-13]. These observations establish CARM1 as a pleiotropic regulator of gene expression with roles extending beyond a single histone mark.

CARM1 overexpression and dysregulation have been reported in multiple human cancers, including breast, prostate, colorectal, lung, pancreatic, and hepatocellular carcinoma [14-18]. In breast cancer, CARM1 cooperates with the p160 coactivator AIB1 (SRC-3) and methylates CBP, thereby amplifying estrogen receptor-dependent transcription and promoting proliferation and invasion [14,19]. In prostate cancer, CARM1 acts as a coactivator for the androgen receptor and contributes to castration-resistant growth [15,20]. Additional studies have linked CARM1 to epithelial-mesenchymal transition, cancer stem cell maintenance, DNA damage repair, and resistance to chemotherapy [16,21,22]. Collectively, these findings support the concept that CARM1 is a bona fide oncogenic dependency in selected tumor contexts, although the mechanistic basis for its tumor-specific functions remains incompletely defined.

Multiple myeloma (MM) is a clonal plasma cell malignancy characterized by accumulation of monoclonal immunoglobulin, bone marrow failure, lytic bone lesions, renal impairment, and immunodeficiency [23,24]. Despite substantial improvements in outcome with proteasome inhibitors, immunomodulatory agents, anti-CD38 antibodies, and BCMA-directed therapies, MM remains largely incurable, and patients inevitably relapse with increasingly refractory disease [25-27]. The genetic and epigenetic heterogeneity of MM, together with the adaptive plasticity of plasma cells, underscores the need for therapeutic strategies that target non-genetic dependencies. Assays were performed in triplicate, and percentage inhibition was normalized to vehicle and no-enzyme controls.

Cell culture and reagents. Multiple myeloma cell lines RPMI-8226, MM.1S, U266, NCI-H929, and AMO-1 were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection or the Deutsche Sammlung von Mikroorganismen und Zellkulturen [4]. Cells were maintained in RPMI-1640 medium supplemented with 10–20% fetal bovine serum, 2 mM L-glutamine, 100 U/mL penicillin, and 100 µg/mL streptomycin at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO2. Cell line identity was confirmed by short tandem repeat profiling, and cultures were routinely tested for mycoplasma contamination. EZM2302 was dissolved in dimethyl sulfoxide for in vitro studies and in 0.5% methylcellulose with 0.2% Tween-80 for oral administration.

Cell proliferation and viability assays. Cells were seeded in 96-well plates at densities of 5 × 10³ to 2 × 10⁴ cells per well and treated with EZM2302 at concentrations ranging from 0.1 nM to 10 µM for 72 h. Cell viability was determined using CellTiter-Glo reagent according to the manufacturer’s instructions [5]. Luminescence was measured on a microplate reader, and IC50 values were calculated using GraphPad Prism. For cell cycle analysis, cells were fixed in 70% ethanol, stained with propidium iodide, and analyzed by flow cytometry [6]. Apoptosis was evaluated by Annexin V–fluorescein isothiocyanate and propidium iodide staining followed by flow cytometry.

Immunoblotting and methylation analysis. Cells were lysed in radioimmunoprecipitation assay buffer supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitor cocktails. Protein concentrations were determined by bicinchoninic acid assay. Equal amounts of protein were resolved by sodium dodecyl sulfate–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis and transferred to polyvinylidene difluoride membranes. Membranes were blocked and incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies against asymmetric dimethylarginine motifs on PABP1 and SMB, total PABP1, total SMB, CARM1, and β-actin [7]. After incubation with horseradish peroxidase–conjugated secondary antibodies, signals were visualized by enhanced chemiluminescence. Densitometric quantification was performed using ImageJ, and methylated protein levels were normalized to total protein and β-actin.

Selectivity profiling. To confirm selectivity beyond histone methyltransferases, EZM2302 was screened against a broad panel of kinases, G-protein–coupled receptors, ion channels, and proteases at a single concentration of 10 µM [8]. Follow-up dose–response assays were performed for any targets showing greater than 50% inhibition. In addition, cellular selectivity was assessed by measuring global histone methylation marks, including H3K4me2, H3K9me2, H3K27me2, and H3K36me2, by immunoblotting after treatment with EZM2302.

In vivo xenograft studies. All animal procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee and conducted in accordance with institutional and national guidelines. Female CB17-SCID mice aged 6–8 weeks were subcutaneously inoculated with RPMI-8226 cells (5 × 10⁶ cells per mouse) suspended in Matrigel [9]. When mean tumor volume reached approximately 150–200 mm³, mice were randomized into vehicle and treatment groups. EZM2302 was administered orally twice daily at doses of 10, 30, or 100 mg/kg for 21 consecutive days. Tumor volume was measured twice weekly with calipers and calculated as 0.5 × length × width². Body weights were recorded to assess tolerability. At study termination, tumors were harvested, snap-frozen, and processed for pharmacodynamic analyses.

Pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic analyses. Blood samples were collected at predetermined time points after oral dosing, and plasma concentrations of EZM2302 were quantified by liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry [10]. Tumor tissue was homogenized, and EZM2302 concentrations were determined similarly. Pharmacodynamic inhibition of CARM1 was evaluated by immunoblotting for methylated PABP1 and SMB in tumor lysates. Dose-dependent changes in methylation were correlated with plasma and tumor drug exposures.

Statistical analysis. Data are presented as mean ± standard error of the mean unless otherwise indicated. IC50 values were derived from nonlinear regression. Comparisons between two groups were made using unpaired two-tailed Student’s t tests, and multiple group comparisons were performed by one-way or two-way analysis of variance followed by appropriate post hoc tests. A p value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. All analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism software.

Identification and biochemical characterization of EZM2302
A focused methyltransferase inhibitor campaign using recombinant human CARM1 and a biotinylated histone H3 peptide substrate identified EZM2302 (GSK3359088) as a potent, concentration-dependent inhibitor of CARM1-mediated asymmetric arginine dimethylation (IC50 = 6 nM; Hill slope ≈ 1.1) [Fig. 1A]. The inhibitory activity was confirmed in orthogonal biochemical formats, including radiometric and AlphaLISA assays, with comparable low-nanomolar potency. Selectivity profiling against a panel of recombinant histone methyltransferases, including PRMT1, PRMT5, PRMT7, EZH2, G9a, SETD7, SETD8, and MLL1, revealed no substantial inhibition at concentrations up to 10 µM, corresponding to greater than 1,000-fold selectivity for CARM1 over these enzymes [Fig. 1B; 1]. EZM2302 also showed negligible activity against a broad kinase panel, consistent with a selective chemical probe suitable for cellular and in vivo interrogation of CARM1 biology [2].

Cellular inhibition of CARM1 substrates in multiple myeloma cells
We next evaluated whether EZM2302 engages CARM1 in multiple myeloma (MM) cells. Western blot analysis of MM cell lines (RPMI-8226, MM.1S, U266, and NCI-H929) treated with EZM2302 for 24–72 h demonstrated dose-dependent reductions in asymmetric dimethylarginine (ADMA) modifications on established CARM1 substrates PABP1 and SMB [3,4]. Inhibition was observed at nanomolar concentrations, with half-maximal effects on PABP1 and SMB methylation ranging from approximately 40 to 250 nM across cell lines [Fig. 2A–C]. Total PABP1 and SMB protein levels and CARM1 protein expression were unchanged, indicating that the effect was due to inhibition of catalytic activity rather than altered substrate or enzyme abundance. Time-course experiments showed maximal substrate demethylation by 24 h, with sustained suppression for at least 72 h after a single treatment [Fig. 2D]. To confirm on-target activity, siRNA-mediated depletion of CARM1 phenocopied the reduction in PABP1 and SMB methylation, whereas EZM2302 treatment did not alter methylation of PRMT1 or PRMT5 substrates [Fig. 2E; 5]. These data establish that EZM2302 inhibits CARM1-dependent methylation in intact MM cells.

Anti-proliferative effects of CARM1 inhibition in MM cell lines
Having confirmed cellular target engagement, we assessed the phenotypic consequences of CARM1 inhibition. Treatment with EZM2302 for 72 h resulted in concentration-dependent inhibition of proliferation across a panel of MM cell lines, with IC50 values in the nanomolar range (approximately 30–300 nM) [Fig. 3A]. In contrast, normal peripheral blood mononuclear cells were markedly less sensitive, with >10 µM required for significant growth inhibition, suggesting a preferential effect on MM cells [Fig. 3B]. Cell cycle analysis of MM.1S and RPMI-8226 cells treated with EZM2302 showed an increase in the G1 fraction and a corresponding decrease in S-phase cells, without a substantial increase in sub-G1 or annexin V-positive cells, consistent with cytostatic rather than cytotoxic activity [Fig. 3C,D]. The development of EZM2302 (GSK3359088) represents a significant advancement in the field of epigenetic pharmacology, providing a much-needed tool to dissect the biological functions of CARM1 in both health and disease. Prior to this work, the study of CARM1 in in vivo models was hampered by a lack of potent, selective, and bioavailable inhibitors. While earlier compounds demonstrated some utility in vitro, their limited selectivity and poor pharmacokinetic properties precluded a rigorous assessment of CARM1's role in complex biological systems [1, 2]. Our identification and characterization of EZM2302, a highly potent and selective inhibitor of CARM1, directly addresses this critical gap. The biochemical potency (IC50 = 6 nM) and exceptional selectivity of EZM2302 against a broad panel of other histone methyltransferases (HMTs) establish it as a superior chemical probe, enabling more definitive conclusions about CARM1-specific biology [3].

The cellular effects of EZM2302 confirmed the on-target engagement of CARM1 and provided mechanistic insights into its role in cancer. The dose-dependent inhibition of key CARM1 substrates, including PABP1 and SMB, directly links the compound's biochemical activity to its cellular function. The resulting anti-proliferative effects observed across multiple myeloma (MM) cell lines, with IC50 values in the nanomolar range, are consistent with the hypothesis that CARM1 is a critical dependency in this malignancy. This finding is particularly noteworthy as it provides the first demonstration of a role for CARM1 in MM, a disease characterized by complex genetic and epigenetic heterogeneity [4]. The induction of cell stasis, rather than immediate cytotoxicity, suggests that CARM1 inhibition may primarily modulate transcriptional programs essential for maintaining the proliferative drive of MM cells. This is mechanistically plausible given CARM1's established role as a transcriptional co-activator, where it methylates histone H3 at arginine 17 (H3R17me2) and H3R26me2, thereby facilitating the assembly of co-activator complexes on target gene promoters [5, 6]. The inhibition of PABP1 methylation further implicates CARM1 in post-transcriptional regulation, including mRNA stability and translation, which are also known to be dysregulated in cancer [7].

The most compelling evidence for the therapeutic potential of CARM1 inhibition comes from our in vivo studies. Oral administration of EZM2302 in an MM xenograft model resulted in dose-dependent inhibition of CARM1, as evidenced by a reduction in methylated PABP1 and SMB in tumor tissues. This target engagement translated into significant anti-tumor activity, validating CARM1 as a druggable target in a physiologically relevant setting. This in vivo validation is a crucial step forward, as it bridges the gap between in vitro observations and potential clinical application. It provides the necessary proof-of-concept to pursue the development of CARM1 inhibitors, potentially derived from the EZM2302 scaffold, as a novel therapeutic strategy for MM, particularly for patients who have become refractory to existing standards of care [8].

Despite these promising findings, several important questions remain. The precise mechanism by which CARM1 inhibition leads to cell stasis in MM requires further elucidation. Future studies should employ transcriptomic and proteomic profiling of EZM2302-treated cells to identify the specific gene networks and signaling pathways that are most sensitive to CARM1 depletion. For instance, it will be important to determine whether the anti-proliferative effect is linked to the downregulation of key MM oncogenes such as IRF4 or MYC, which are known to be regulated by epigenetic modifiers [9]. Furthermore, the potential for combination therapies should be explored. Given its role in transcriptional regulation, CARM1 inhibition may synergize with other targeted agents, such as proteasome inhibitors (e.g., bortezomib) or immunomodulatory drugs (IMiDs), which are the cornerstones of MM treatment [10]. Investigating these combinations could reveal potent new regimens and potentially overcome mechanisms of resistance.

In conclusion, this study introduces EZM2302 as a first-in-class, potent, and selective chemical probe for CARM1. We have demonstrated its efficacy in inhibiting CARM1 activity in biochemical, cellular, and in vivo settings, and have used it to uncover a previously unrecognized role for CARM1 in the pathogenesis of multiple myeloma. EZM2302 not only serves as an invaluable tool for the broader research community to further explore CARM1 biology but also provides a strong rationale for the clinical development of CARM1 inhibitors as a promising new class of therapeutics for MM and potentially other cancers driven by CARM1 overexpression or dependency.

Recommender systems have become an integral part of modern digital platforms, shaping how users discover movies, music, products, news, jobs, and social connections. Their widespread adoption stems from their ability to leverage collective user behavior—clicks, ratings, purchases, and other interactions—to deliver personalized recommendations that often outperform generic or popularity-based alternatives. By learning latent representations of users and items, collaborative filtering and related techniques can surface items that match individual tastes, reduce information overload, and create economic value for service providers. As a result, recommender systems are now deployed in domains as diverse as entertainment, e-commerce, employment, and online education.

However, the same data-driven nature that makes recommender systems effective also makes them vulnerable to inheriting and propagating biases present in user behavior. Users do not interact with items in a vacuum; their preferences are shaped by social norms, historical inequalities, demographic stereotypes, and structural constraints. For example, if a hiring dataset contains fewer female applicants for technical roles, or if movie ratings reflect gendered genre preferences, a recommender trained on that data may learn to associate certain items with certain user groups. Such learned associations can lead to recommendations that systematically disadvantage or stereotype particular groups. In many cases, the recommender does not merely reflect the bias in the input data; it may amplify it. This phenomenon—where the bias in the recommendations diverges from and often exceeds the bias in the original user preferences—is what we refer to as bias disparity.

Bias disparity is distinct from, though related to, other fairness concerns in recommendation. Much existing work on fair recommendation focuses on outcomes such as demographic parity, equal opportunity, or calibrated exposure, asking whether different user groups receive comparable quality or representation. Bias disparity instead asks a relative question: given the level of bias already present in a user’s historical preferences or in the training data, how much more (or less) biased are the items that the recommender chooses to present? A recommender may exhibit high bias disparity even if it appears fair under some aggregate metric, because the disparity is measured against the input distribution rather than an absolute ideal. Conversely, a recommender that reduces bias relative to the input may still produce biased recommendations if the input itself is heavily skewed. Understanding this distinction is important for diagnosing when and why recommenders worsen existing inequalities.

The consequences of bias disparity extend beyond immediate fairness violations. Recommender systems operate in dynamic environments where their outputs become future inputs. When a user receives recommendations, their subsequent interactions—clicks, ratings, purchases—are influenced by what they were shown. These new interactions are then used to retrain or update the recommender, creating a feedback loop. If the recommender amplifies bias, the loop can gradually shift user preferences and item popularity in the direction of that amplification, leading to homogenization, filter bubbles, polarization, and the erosion of diverse exposure. In employment or commerce, such loops may entrench occupational segregation or unequal access to opportunities. In entertainment, they may narrow the range of cultural products that users encounter. Thus, bias disparity is not only a static property of a single recommendation list but also a dynamic force that can reshape the data ecosystem over time.

Despite growing interest in fairness and bias in recommender systems, several questions remain open. Under what conditions does a recommender exhibit bias disparity? How do data characteristics, such as the strength and distribution of bias, the level of sparsity, and the number of users and items, affect the degree of disparity? Do different recommendation algorithms—memory-based, model-based, or neural—differ in their tendency to amplify bias? What happens over repeated recommendation cycles: does bias disparity stabilize,

We conducted a series of controlled experiments on synthetic data to isolate the conditions under which a recommender system exhibits bias disparity and to examine how repeated recommendations reshape data bias over time. The synthetic setting allowed us to manipulate data-generating parameters directly, including preference bias, item-group representation, interaction sparsity, and user-group composition. We generated a population of N = 1,000 users and M = 500 items. Each item i was assigned a binary sensitive or semantic attribute z_i ∈ {0, 1}, representing membership in one of two item groups, such as a majority versus minority content category. Each user u was associated with a latent preference vector p_u ∈ R^K and each item with a latent factor vector q_i ∈ R^K, with K = 10. The base affinity between user u and item i was computed as s_ui = p_u · q_i + β z_i + ε_ui, where β controlled the global preference bias toward group 1 items and ε_ui was zero-mean Gaussian noise. To induce user-specific bias, we also varied β by user group: users in group A received β_A and users in group B received β_B. Observed interactions were sampled from a softmax distribution over s_ui, yielding implicit feedback matrices with controlled sparsity. Unless otherwise stated, we retained 80% of interactions for training, 10% for validation, and 10% for testing.

We evaluated three recommender families: a popularity baseline, a matrix factorization model optimized with Bayesian personalized ranking (MF-BPR), and a neural collaborative filtering model. For each model, we generated top-N recommendation lists for every user, with N ∈ {5, 10, 20}. Models were trained on the observed interaction matrix only, without access to the sensitive item attribute during training, so that any disparity arose from learned user preferences and data imbalance rather than explicit group-aware optimization. Hyperparameters were selected on the validation set to maximize NDCG@N, and all experiments were repeated over five random seeds.

Bias disparity was quantified by comparing the group distribution in recommendations to the group distribution in the input data. For a given user u, let B_in(u) denote the proportion of group 1 items among the items with which u interacted in the training data, and let B_rec(u) denote the proportion of group 1 items in u’s top-N recommendation list. The bias disparity for user u was defined as D(u) = B_rec(u) − B_in(u). Positive values indicate that the recommender amplifies the existing bias toward group 1 items, while negative values indicate suppression. We also computed aggregate disparity D = mean_u D(u), as well as group-specific disparities D_A and D_B for the two user groups. Recommendation accuracy was measured using Recall@N and NDCG@N to ensure that disparity reduction did not come at an unacceptable cost to utility.

To study long-term effects, we implemented an iterative feedback-loop simulation. At round t = 0, the recommender was trained on the initial synthetic interaction matrix. At each subsequent round, the system recommended top-N items to each user. Users accepted or interacted with recommended items according to a probabilistic choice model based on their true latent preferences, with an exploration rate ε ∈ {0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2}. Accepted interactions were added to the training data, and the recommender was retrained at each round. We ran T = 20 rounds and tracked the input bias B_in(t), recommendation bias B_rec(t), and bias disparity D(t). This procedure allowed us to observe whether bias disparity diminished, persisted, or amplified as the recommender and the data co-evolved.

We also implemented a simple post-processing re-ranking algorithm to reduce bias disparity. Given an initial ranked list of candidate items for user u, the algorithm selected items iteratively. At each step, it chose the item that maximized s_ui − λ · max(0, C_z − C_target_z), where s_ui was the original recommendation score, C_z was the current count of selected items from group z, and C_target_z was the target count implied by a desired group distribution. The parameter λ controlled the trade-off between relevance and group calibration. We considered two targets: matching the input bias B_in(u) and matching a balanced distribution, B_target = 0.5. The value of λ was tuned on the validation set to minimize |D| subject to an NDCG@N loss of no more than 2% relative to the unconstrained recommender.

Finally, we examined data disparity on a real-world dataset, MovieLens 1M, to contextualize the synthetic findings. We treated user gender as a demographic attribute and item genres as semantic item groups. We computed input data disparity metrics, including differences in interaction frequency, item coverage, and genre distribution across user groups. These observations were descriptive and were used to assess whether the levels of bias manipulated in the synthetic experiments were plausible relative to naturally occurring disparities. All synthetic experiments were averaged over seeds, and statistical comparisons used paired tests across seeds or users where appropriate.

The results of our preliminary study suggest that bias disparity is not an inevitable property of every recommender, but rather emerges from an interaction between data characteristics, model design, and the dynamics of the recommendation loop. In synthetic experiments, recommenders trained on biased user–item interactions tended to reproduce the existing bias in their input data. This alone is expected: a model that learns from biased preferences will inherit them. More concerning is the subset of conditions under which the recommender amplifies bias. We found amplification to be strongest when the training data were sparse, when a small number of users or items dominated the interaction history, and when the model had enough capacity to memorize group-specific preferences. Under these conditions, recommendations for minority or underrepresented groups became increasingly concentrated on a narrow set of items, while majority groups received more diverse and more favorable recommendations. Bias disparity therefore appears to be a systemic outcome of feedback loops rather than a simple reflection of static data bias.

Our long-term simulations provide additional evidence for this view. When we simulated repeated cycles of recommendation, user choice, and retraining, bias disparity compounded over time. Early disadvantages in exposure translated into fewer interactions for certain groups or items, which in turn made those groups or items even less visible in later training rounds. This created a self-reinforcing cycle: the recommender did not merely reflect the initial bias but helped to reshape the data in a way that made future bias more severe. The effect was especially pronounced when users were assumed to follow recommendations closely, because the recommender then had greater control over the feedback it later learned from. When user choice included more randomness or external influence, amplification slowed, though it did not disappear. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating recommender systems longitudinally. A model that appears fair or only mildly biased in a single static evaluation may still produce substantial disparity after several rounds of deployment.

We also examined a simple re-ranking algorithm as a potential mitigation. The algorithm adjusted the final recommendation lists to reduce disparity between groups, without retraining the underlying model. In our synthetic setting, this approach reduced bias disparity in the top-k recommendations at a modest cost in conventional accuracy. The reduction was largest when the disparity penalty was tuned carefully and when the candidate pool contained enough relevant items from underrepresented groups. However, re-ranking was not a complete solution. When the penalty was too weak, disparity persisted; when it was too strong, recommendation quality degraded noticeably. Moreover, because re-ranking operated only at the output stage, it did not directly correct the biased training data or the model’s internal representations. In the long-term simulations, re-ranking slowed the compounding of bias but did not prevent it entirely. This suggests that re-ranking can be a useful short-term safeguard, particularly when combined with other fairness-aware interventions, but it should not be treated as a substitute for addressing bias at the data, model, and feedback-loop levels.

Our observations on real data further reinforce the need to distinguish between data disparity and bias disparity. Before applying any recommender, we found measurable imbalances in the interaction data, including uneven representation of user groups and unequal exposure of items. These imbalances varied across domains and were often intertwined with popularity effects, activity differences, and missing or noisy user attributes. When recommenders were trained on such data, they tended to inherit and sometimes magnify these patterns. However, real data also revealed complications that synthetic simulations did not capture, such as implicit feedback, temporal drift, and confounding between group membership and item popularity. These factors make it difficult to attribute bias disparity to a single cause and underscore the need for careful, context-specific measurement.

Several limitations qualify our conclusions. Our study is preliminary and primarily based on synthetic data, which cannot fully represent the complexity of real user behavior or the diversity of recommender architectures. We tested a limited set of models, metrics, and one simple re-ranking strategy. The long-term effects we observed depend on assumptions about how users respond to recommendations, and different assumptions could yield weaker or stronger amplification. Nevertheless, the general pattern is clear: recommender systems can actively participate in the production and amplification of bias, not just passively reflect it.

In conclusion, bias disparity is a dynamic and consequential phenomenon in recommendation systems. It arises when biased data, model learning, and feedback loops interact, and it can worsen over time if left unmonitored. A simple re-ranking algorithm can reduce disparity in the short term, but sustainable mitigation requires a more integrated approach: measuring bias at multiple stages, evaluating systems in closed-loop settings, and combining output-level corrections with data collection practices, model regularization, and long-term fairness objectives. Future work should extend these preliminary findings to larger real-world datasets, multiple recommendation algorithms, and longer deployment horizons, while also considering the trade-offs among accuracy, diversity, fairness, and user satisfaction.

The pursuit-evasion problem occupies a central place in mathematical game theory, control theory, and robotics. Since the classical lion-and-man problem [1], researchers have sought to characterize when a pursuer can guarantee capture of an evader under various assumptions on speed, sensing, environment, and kinematics. Early investigations established deep connections between pursuit-evasion games and geometry, leading to strategies based on Voronoi partitions, Apollonius circles, and visibility regions [2], [3]. In robotics, related formulations arise in surveillance, target tracking, adversarial search, and security applications, where autonomous agents must intercept or evade opponents in real time [4], [5]. The majority of these studies, however, assume idealized holonomic motion, instantaneous changes of direction, or a pursuer that is strictly faster than the evader. Such assumptions are often violated by physical robots.

A differential drive robot (DDR) is one of the most common mobile platforms in practice. Its motion is nonholonomic: it cannot translate sideways, and its heading can change only at a bounded angular rate. These constraints are fundamental rather than incidental, and they significantly restrict the set of feasible trajectories [6], [7]. By contrast, an omnidirectional evader can instantaneously choose any direction of motion within its speed bound. When both players have the same maximum speed, the evader appears to possess a decisive advantage: it can exploit lateral mobility to slip around the DDR while the DDR must spend time turning. Indeed, many pursuit strategies developed for holonomic pursuers rely on instantaneous alignment with the evader’s bearing, a maneuver that a DDR cannot perform [8]. This raises a natural and practically important question: can a single DDR with equal speed capture an omnidirectional evader, or does the evader’s kinematic advantage make evasion possible indefinitely?

Prior work on nonholonomic pursuit-evasion has largely focused on settings where the pursuer is faster than the evader, where the evader is constrained, or where multiple pursuers cooperate. For example, capture strategies have been proposed for a faster nonholonomic pursuer against a slower omnidirectional evader [9], and bounded-curvature pursuit has been studied under assumptions of superior speed or known evader trajectories [10]. When speeds are equal, negative results are common: in unbounded planar environments, an omnidirectional evader can often maintain separation by mirroring or circling the pursuer [11]. Cooperative teams of nonholonomic pursuers can overcome individual kinematic limitations through encirclement and containment [12], but single-pursuer capture remains elusive. Convex environments introduce boundaries that restrict the evader’s motion and can, in principle, compensate for the pursuer’s turning constraints. Yet the evader may use the boundary as a geometric resource, turning sharply along walls while forcing the DDR to execute wide arcs. Whether convexity alone is sufficient to guarantee capture under equal speed and bounded turning rate has, to the best of our knowledge, remained open.

This paper answers that question affirmatively. We study a pursuit-evasion game in which both players are unit disks moving in a convex environment. The evader is omnidirectional and has a bounded maximum speed. The DDR has the same maximum speed but can change its motion direction only at a bounded rate. The DDR wins if it collides with the evader at any time instant; the evader wins if it avoids capture forever. Despite the DDR’s nonholonomic constraint, we show that it can capture the evader. The result is perhaps counterintuitive, because the evader can instantaneously choose any heading while the DDR cannot. The key observation is that convexity and the positive radius of the players create a geometric coupling: the evader cannot exploit lateral mobility without eventually approaching the boundary or entering a configuration where the DDR’s bounded turning rate is sufficient to close the gap. Our strategy combines direct pursuit with boundary-aware maneuvering, using a potential function that measures both the center-to-center distance and the relative bearing. The analysis accounts for the DDR’s minimum turning radius and shows that the evader’s possible escape directions shrink over time.

The contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we formalize a continuous-time pursuit-evasion game between a DDR and an omnidirectional evader in a convex environment, with equal speed bounds and a bounded angular velocity for the DDR. Second, we propose a capture strategy that respects the DDR’s nonholonomic constraints and prove that it guarantees capture in finite time from any initial configuration in which the evader is not already in contact with the DDR. Third, we analyze the role of convexity and disk geometry in the proof, showing that capture does not require the DDR to match the evader’s instantaneous maneuverability. These results extend the classical pursuit-evasion literature to a practically relevant robotic setting and provide a constructive foundation for interception with differential drive platforms.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II presents the problem formulation and notation. Section III develops the proposed capture strategy and the geometric lemmas underlying its analysis. Section IV establishes the main capture guarantee and discusses the effects of speed and turning-rate bounds. Section V provides concluding remarks and directions for future work, including sensing uncertainty, non-convex environments, and multiple evaders.

The evader is an omnidirectional unit disk with center \(p_e(t) \in W\), whose velocity \(v_e(t) \in \mathbb{R}^2\) satisfies \(\|v_e(t)\| \le 1\). The pursuer is a differential drive robot (DDR) with center \(p_d(t) \in W\) and orientation \(\theta(t) \in \mathbb{S}^1\). Its kinematics are given by
\[

\dot{y}_d = v \sin\theta,\qquad
\dot{\theta} = \omega,
\]
where \(p_d = (x_d,y_d)\), and the control inputs satisfy \(|v| \le 1\) and \(|\omega| \le \omega_{\max}\). Both players are unit disks; capture occurs when \(\|p_d(t)-p_e(t)\| \le 2\). The evader wins if it avoids capture for all \(t \ge 0\). We assume perfect state information, simultaneous control, and deterministic dynamics. The game is formulated in the framework of pursuit-evasion differential games with state constraints [1], [2].

We evaluated the proposed pursuit strategy through a combination of theoretical analysis and numerical experiments. The main result establishes that the differential drive robot (DDR) can capture an omnidirectional evader in any compact convex environment, despite the DDR’s bounded turning rate and the evader’s ability to change its motion direction instantaneously. This finding contrasts with classical equal-speed pursuit-evasion results in unbounded domains, where an omnidirectional evader can avoid capture indefinitely by moving directly away from the pursuer [1], [4]. The convexity of the environment is therefore essential: it restricts the evader’s reachable set and allows the DDR to convert its bounded curvature into a separating advantage.

The evader is holonomic, while the DDR has turning-rate bound \(\omega_{\max}>0\). The DDR wins if the distance between the centers of the two disks becomes at most \(2\). We first formalize the game and then state the capture guarantee.

Because the DDR can turn at a positive bounded rate, it cannot instantaneously match arbitrary evader headings; however, Lemma 1 shows that the heading error can be driven below a critical threshold \(\theta_c = \arcsin(v/(v+\delta))\) for some \(\delta>0\) whenever the evader remains in the interior of \(\Omega\). Since \(\Omega\) is bounded, only finitely many such boundary encounters can occur before the evader’s reachable set collapses to a singleton, at which point capture follows from the DDR’s speed and turning constraints. The central contribution of this work is the proof that a Differential Drive Robot (DDR), despite its nonholonomic constraints, can guarantee the capture of a faster or equally fast omnidirectional evader within a compact convex environment. This result stands in contrast to classical pursuit-evasion games, where the pursuer's limited maneuverability often precludes a guaranteed win against a more agile opponent [1], [2]. Our analysis demonstrates that the constraints of the environment and the specific kinematics of the DDR can be leveraged to overcome the evader's superior directional agility. The key insight is that by employing a strategy that balances direct pursuit with a containment policy, the DDR can progressively restrict the evader's accessible region, eventually forcing a capture. This finding extends the known results in pursuit-evasion for differential drive systems, which have often focused on scenarios with a faster pursuer or simpler environmental constraints [3], [4].

The implications of this result are twofold. From a theoretical perspective, it enriches the field of pursuit-evasion games by providing a constructive strategy for a nonholonomic pursuer against an omnidirectional evader of equal speed. The proof relies on a Lyapunov-like argument, where a carefully chosen potential function, representing a measure of the evader's "escape space," is shown to be non-increasing under the DDR's control law. This potential function is derived from the geometric properties of the convex environment and the relative positions of the two players. The strategy ensures that the evader is either driven towards the boundary of the environment or is directly captured. This contrasts with strategies that might rely on pure pursuit, which can be unstable or lead to indefinite evasion in open environments [5]. The bounded turning rate of the DDR is the critical parameter; our analysis shows that capture is guaranteed as long as this rate is non-zero, a significant relaxation of previous assumptions that often required a minimum turning radius or a speed advantage [6].

From a practical standpoint, this research provides a robust and implementable control policy for autonomous robotic systems tasked with capture or herding objectives. Applications range from security and surveillance, where a robot must intercept an intruder, to multi-robot systems where a DDR might be used to corral a target [7]. The strategy's reliance on the environment's convexity is a limitation, but many real-world scenarios, such as warehouses, factory floors, or designated arenas, can be approximated as convex or decomposed into convex sub-regions. Furthermore, the result is robust to small errors in sensing and actuation, as the underlying strategy is based on a continuous feedback law. However, the assumption of perfect information and an evader with equal speed is an idealization. Future work should address scenarios with sensing uncertainty, where the DDR must estimate the evader's state, and games where the evader possesses a speed advantage, which would require a more sophisticated strategy, perhaps involving predictive control or learning-based approaches [8], [9].

A critical discussion point is the nature of the evader's optimal strategy. While our proof shows that the DDR's strategy guarantees capture, it does not fully characterize the evader's best response. It is plausible that the evader's optimal policy is to retreat directly away from the DDR towards the environment's boundary, but a formal game-theoretic analysis could reveal more complex behaviors, such as feinting or attempting to exploit the DDR's turning limitations in specific geometric configurations. The convexity of the environment is another key factor. In non-convex environments, the evader might use obstacles or corners to break the DDR's containment strategy, potentially leading to an indefinite evasion. Extending this work to non-convex environments would likely require a topological approach, where the environment is decomposed into a graph of convex regions, and the pursuit is framed as a game on this graph [10].

In conclusion, this paper has established that a Differential Drive Robot can successfully capture an omnidirectional evader of equal speed in a convex environment. We have provided a constructive, non-anticipative strategy for the DDR and proven its efficacy using a potential function argument. This result challenges the conventional wisdom that a nonholonomic pursuer is at a fundamental disadvantage against a holonomic evader. The findings have significant implications for the design of autonomous interception and herding systems. The limitations of our study, particularly the assumptions of convexity and equal speed, pave the way for several promising avenues of future research. These include extending the analysis to non-convex environments, considering evaders with superior speed or sensing capabilities, and addressing the challenges of implementing these strategies on physical robots with real-world constraints such as sensor noise and actuator delays. Ultimately, this work contributes a foundational building block towards a comprehensive theory of pursuit-evasion with nonholonomic agents.
