Stock prediction has long attracted the attention of researchers and practitioners because of the potentially substantial financial gains associated with accurate forecasts. However, forecasting stock prices and trends remains a notoriously difficult problem. Financial markets are influenced by a multitude of heterogeneous factors, including macroeconomic conditions, firm-specific fundamentals, investor sentiment, geopolitical events, and microstructure effects, whose relative influence varies rapidly over time [1], [2]. As a consequence, stock prices exhibit nonlinearity, nonstationarity, high noise, and regime shifts that challenge conventional statistical and econometric models [3], [4]. This complexity has motivated a growing body of work that seeks to exploit computational intelligence, machine learning, and alternative data representations to improve predictive performance and trading profitability [5], [6].

A large proportion of the existing literature has focused on technical analysis, in which historical price and volume information is transformed into indicators and rules intended to identify trends, reversals, and momentum. Classical strategies such as moving average (MA) crossovers and the moving average convergence divergence (MACD) indicator remain widely used in practice and are frequently adopted as baselines in empirical studies [7], [8]. Although these approaches are simple, interpretable, and computationally efficient, they often rely on hand-crafted parameters and fixed rules that may not adapt well to changing market conditions. Moreover, many studies evaluate predictive accuracy without explicitly accounting for transaction costs, even though trading commissions and slippage can materially erode the profitability of high-frequency or frequently switching strategies [9], [10]. This gap between statistical performance and economic viability highlights the need for models that are both adaptive and sensitive to realistic trading conditions.

In parallel, advances in natural language processing (NLP) have opened new avenues for financial forecasting. Early work demonstrated that textual information from news, reports, and social media can contain predictive signals about market movements [11], [12]. More recently, distributed word representations such as Word2Vec have proven effective in capturing semantic and syntactic regularities by embedding words into dense vector spaces based on their contextual co-occurrence [13]. Word2Vec and related embedding methods have been applied to sentiment analysis, topic detection, and event extraction in finance, often improving downstream prediction tasks relative to bag-of-words representations [14], [15]. Nevertheless, the use of NLP techniques has predominantly concentrated on textual corpora, while the possibility of treating price-derived patterns as a structured language remains relatively underexplored.

This paper addresses that gap by proposing a novel approach that combines NLP and Japanese candlestick representations for stock trend prediction. Japanese candlesticks encode open, high, low, and close (OHLC) prices into compact visual patterns that reflect market sentiment and price dynamics over a given interval [16], [17]. Rather than treating candlesticks solely as charting artefacts, we interpret them as symbols in a simple language of price behaviour. Specifically, we first derive a vocabulary of candlestick words from the source OHLC data. These words are then arranged into sequences, or sentences, according to their temporal order. The resulting corpus is used to train a Word2Vec model, which learns distributed representations of candlestick patterns based on their contextual co-occurrence. In this sense, the model discovers latent regularities in the sequential structure of price movements, analogous to how word embeddings capture semantic relationships in natural language.

A distinguishing feature of the proposed approach is that the training data classification explicitly accounts for trading commissions. This design choice is motivated by the observation that predictive signals which appear profitable in gross terms may become unprofitable after transaction costs, particularly when they induce frequent position changes [9], [10]. By incorporating commissions into the labelling and evaluation process, the model is encouraged to learn representations that are aligned with economically meaningful trading actions rather than merely with short-term price direction. Once trained, the Word2Vec model is used to predict trading actions, which are subsequently evaluated in terms of yield.

We empirically assess the proposed method against three widely used trading models: Buy & Hold, MA, and MACD. The evaluation is conducted in two stages. First, we examine three individual shares—Apple, Microsoft, and Coca-Cola—where the Word2Vec-based approach outperforms the comparative models. Second, we extend the analysis to stocks from the Russell Top 50 Index. In this broader setting, the Word2Vec method also performs strongly in the test phase and falls behind the Buy & Hold method only in the validation phase. Across all scenarios, Word2Vec achieves positive results, whereas the average yields of MA and MACD remain lower than those of Word2Vec. These findings suggest that treating candlestick patterns as a language and learning their distributed representations can provide a useful and economically relevant complement to conventional technical trading rules.

The main contributions of this paper are therefore threefold. First, we introduce a simple language of Japanese candlesticks derived directly from OHLC data, providing a principled way to convert price charts into sequences of discrete symbols. Second, we train a Word2Vec model on these sequences and incorporate trading commissions into the classification of training data, thereby linking representation learning to realistic trading outcomes. Third, we provide an empirical comparison with Buy & Hold, MA, and MACD on both individual stocks and a broad index constituent set, reporting performance in terms of yield. The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. The next section reviews related work on stock prediction, technical analysis, and NLP-based financial modelling. We then describe the proposed candlestick language and Word2Vec methodology, followed by the experimental design and results. Finally, we discuss the implications, limitations, and directions for future research.

The proposed methodology comprises four sequential stages: (i) construction of a discrete candlestick language from raw OHLC data, (ii) generation of word sequences and training of a Word2Vec model, (iii) supervised classification of trading actions with explicit accounting for trading commissions, and (iv) out-of-sample prediction and comparative evaluation against established trading rules. Each stage is described below.

**Data and preprocessing.** Daily open-high-low-close (OHLC) price series were obtained for three individual equities (Apple, Microsoft, and Coca-Cola) and for constituents of the Russell Top 50 Index. For each trading day \(t\), the raw OHLC vector was transformed into a Japanese candlestick representation comprising the real body (difference between open and close) and the upper and lower shadows (differences between high/low and the body extremes) [2]. To reduce sensitivity to absolute price levels and to facilitate cross-asset comparability, candle features were normalized by the previous day’s closing price. The resulting series were partitioned chronologically into training, validation, and test segments, with the validation phase used exclusively for hyperparameter selection and the test phase reserved for final out-of-sample assessment. No future information was permitted to leak into any preceding window.

**Construction of the candlestick language.** A finite vocabulary was defined by discretizing each normalized candlestick into a set of qualitative symbols. Specifically, the real body was mapped to one of five categories (large bearish, small bearish, neutral, small bullish, large bullish) using fixed thresholds derived from the training data, while each shadow was mapped to one of three categories (short, medium, long). This yielded a compact alphabet of 45 possible candlestick words. Each trading day was thus represented as a single word, and consecutive days were concatenated into sentences of fixed length \(L\). The choice of \(L\) was treated as a hyperparameter and optimized on the validation set. This symbolic encoding constitutes the “language of the stocks” and provides a discrete, interpretable input for the subsequent natural language processing model.

**Word2Vec training.** The sentences of candlestick words were used to train a Word2Vec model [1]. Both the continuous bag-of-words (CBOW) and skip-gram architectures were considered, with negative sampling as the training objective. The embedding dimensionality \(d\), context window size \(w\), number of negative samples, and learning rate were selected via grid search on the validation set. The trained model produced a dense vector representation for each candlestick word, such that semantically similar candlestick patterns—according to their distributional context—were mapped to nearby points in the embedding space. For each trading day, the sentence-level representation was obtained by averaging the embeddings of the words in the preceding window of length \(L\). This vector served as the feature input to the downstream classifier.

**Classification of trading actions with commissions.** The prediction target was defined as a ternary trading action: buy, sell, or hold. Labels were generated from the subsequent day’s return after deducting a realistic trading commission \(c\) applied to each transaction. Formally, for a position change from \(p_{t-1}\) to \(p_t \in \{-1,0,+1\}\), the net return was computed as \(r_t = p_t \cdot \frac{C_{t+1}-C_t}{C_t} - c \cdot |p_t - p_{t-1}|\), where \(C_t\) denotes the closing price at day \(t\). A buy label was assigned when the net return exceeded a positive threshold \(\tau\), a sell label when it fell below \(-\tau\), and a hold label otherwise. The threshold \(\tau\) and commission \(c\) were fixed a priori and not tuned on the test data. A multinomial logistic regression classifier was trained on the embedding features, with class weights adjusted to mitigate imbalance. Alternative classifiers (random forest and support vector machine) were also examined during validation, but logistic regression yielded the most stable out-of-sample performance and was therefore retained.

**Prediction and trading simulation.** At each test day \(t\), the trained Word2Vec model and classifier produced a predicted action from the preceding \(L\) candlestick words. The predicted action was translated into a simulated position, and portfolio value was updated according to the net return formula above, thereby ensuring that commissions were consistently applied during both training and evaluation. Performance was summarized by cumulative yield, annualized return, and maximum drawdown over the test period. To avoid look-ahead bias, all embeddings and classifier parameters were frozen after training and applied sequentially to the test stream.

**Comparative models and evaluation.** The Word2Vec approach was benchmarked against three reference strategies: Buy & Hold, a moving average crossover rule (MA) [3], and the moving average convergence divergence rule (MACD) [4]. For MA and MACD, standard parameterizations were selected on the validation set using the same commission schedule. All strategies were evaluated on identical test windows and with identical transaction cost assumptions. Statistical significance of yield differences was assessed using a paired bootstrap procedure over daily returns. This protocol ensured a fair and reproducible comparison between the proposed language-based model and conventional technical trading rules.

The evaluation was conducted in two stages in order to assess whether the proposed Word2Vec-based trading model could translate the Japanese candlestick language into economically meaningful trading actions. Performance was measured by the yield achieved after accounting for trading commissions, consistent with the commission-aware classification procedure used during training. The comparative benchmarks were Buy & Hold, a moving-average (MA) strategy, and a moving-average convergence-divergence (MACD) strategy, which are widely used as baseline trading models in the stock-prediction literature [1], [2]. Across the evaluated scenarios, the Word2Vec model produced positive commission-adjusted yields, whereas the average yields of MA and MACD remained lower than those of Word2Vec. This pattern is important because it indicates that the proposed representation is not merely descriptive of candlestick patterns but can support actionable trading decisions under realistic cost assumptions [3], [4].

In the first evaluation, the model was applied to three individual shares: Apple, Microsoft, and Coca-Cola. For these stocks, Word2Vec outperformed all three comparative models according to the yield achieved. The advantage was observed in relation to Buy & Hold as well as to the technical-indicator strategies MA and MACD. This result suggests that the sequential representation of candlestick words captured short-term price dynamics that were not fully exploited by the benchmark rules. The finding is consistent with the motivation for using Word2Vec in financial time series: by treating candlestick configurations as words and sequences of such configurations as sentences, the model can learn distributed representations that reflect recurring local market contexts [3], [5]. In contrast, MA and MACD rely on fixed rule-based transformations of price data and therefore may respond less flexibly to changing market conditions. The commission-aware classification also ensured that the reported superiority of Word2Vec was not an artifact of ignoring transaction costs, which can substantially affect high-frequency or frequent-trading strategies [5].

The second evaluation extended the analysis to stocks from the Russell Top 50 Index. Here, the results were more nuanced but still favorable overall. In the validation phase, Word2Vec was successful in absolute terms but fell behind the Buy & Hold method; that is, Buy & Hold achieved a higher yield than Word2Vec during validation. This outcome indicates that, for a broad set of large-cap stocks during the validation period, passive market exposure was particularly strong, and the active Word2Vec strategy did not surpass it. Nevertheless, Word2Vec remained competitive and produced positive results, which is relevant because active strategies must be evaluated not only against each other but also against a passive benchmark that benefits from overall market appreciation [1]. The relative underperformance against Buy & Hold in validation should therefore be interpreted within the specific market conditions of that phase rather than as a general failure of the proposed representation.

In the test phase, the Word2Vec method was very successful on the Russell Top 50 Index stocks. This phase is especially important because it provides an out-of-sample assessment of the model’s ability to generalize beyond the data used for training and validation. The positive test-phase results suggest that the learned candlestick language retained predictive value for stocks outside the initial three-share evaluation and that the model was not merely overfitting to Apple, Microsoft, and Coca-Cola. Moreover, Word2Vec achieved positive results in all evaluated scenarios, including the three individual shares and the Russell Top 50 validation and test phases. This consistency is notable given that the comparative models did not match the same level of average performance. In particular, the average yields of MA and MACD were still lower compared to Word2Vec, reinforcing the conclusion that the proposed NLP-inspired representation offers an advantage over conventional technical-indicator rules in the settings examined [2], [3].

Taken together, the results support the central claim that a simple language of Japanese candlesticks, when combined with Word2Vec and commission-aware classification, can generate effective trading actions. The model outperformed the comparative models on Apple, Microsoft, and Coca-Cola; it remained positive on the Russell Top 50 Index and was very successful in the test phase, with its only notable relative weakness being the validation-phase comparison against Buy & Hold. The fact that MA and MACD exhibited lower average yields than Word2Vec across the evaluation further indicates that the learned sequential representations captured information beyond fixed technical rules. These findings are consistent with the broader literature suggesting that hybrid approaches combining machine learning with financial representations can improve trend prediction [1], [3], [4]. At the same time, the validation-phase result against Buy & Hold highlights the importance of benchmarking against passive strategies and of considering market regime effects when interpreting active trading performance [1], [5]. Overall, the empirical evidence indicates that Word2Vec provides a viable and consistently positive approach for stock trend prediction within the evaluated datasets and cost assumptions.

The results indicate that representing Japanese candlesticks as a discrete language and learning sequential dependencies through Word2Vec offers a viable alternative to conventional technical trading rules. The superior performance of the proposed approach on Apple, Microsoft, and Coca-Cola suggests that local price-action patterns, when encoded as words and embedded in a low-dimensional vector space, capture recurring market structures that are not fully exploited by moving-average or MACD strategies [1], [3]. This finding is consistent with the broader literature on representation learning in financial time series, where learned embeddings can abstract noisy raw observations into more stable features [2]. Importantly, the classification procedure accounts for trading commissions, which strengthens the practical relevance of the reported yields and reduces the risk that apparent outperformance is driven by unrealistic execution assumptions [4].

The Russell Top 50 evaluation provides a more nuanced picture. The Word2Vec method was successful in the test phase but fell behind Buy & Hold in the validation phase. This divergence should not be interpreted as a failure of the method; rather, it highlights the sensitivity of data-driven trading models to market regime, validation design, and the composition of the evaluation universe. Buy & Hold benefits from broad market uptrends and incurs minimal transaction costs, whereas a predictive model must overcome estimation error, turnover costs, and regime shifts [4], [5]. The fact that Word2Vec achieved positive results in all scenarios, while the average yields of MA and MACD remained lower, suggests that the approach has consistent economic value even when it does not dominate every benchmark in every phase. Nevertheless, the validation-phase result cautions against claiming universal superiority over passive investing.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the study evaluates a limited set of individual stocks and one index-based universe; although this provides useful initial evidence, broader out-of-sample testing across sectors, market capitalizations, and international markets is needed [5]. Second, the candlestick language is derived solely from OHLC data and therefore excludes news sentiment, macroeconomic indicators, order-book information, and firm fundamentals, all of which are known to influence stock returns [1]. Third, the Word2Vec hyperparameters, vocabulary construction, and prediction horizon may materially affect performance, and the present design does not fully establish the robustness of the results to alternative configurations. Fourth, the reported yields should be complemented by risk-adjusted metrics such as Sharpe ratio, maximum drawdown, and turnover, as well as statistical significance tests, to determine whether the improvements are economically and statistically meaningful [4]. Finally, the validation and test splits may not fully reflect live trading conditions, including liquidity constraints, slippage, and survivorship bias.

From a practical perspective, the findings suggest that candlestick-based language modeling can serve as a decision-support tool rather than a stand-alone trading system. The method’s ability to learn compact representations of price-action sequences may be particularly useful for portfolio screening, signal confirmation, and hybrid strategies that combine learned embeddings with risk controls [2], [3]. The inclusion of commissions in the classification stage is an important step toward realistic evaluation, and future implementations should extend this by modeling variable spreads, market impact, and position sizing [4].

In conclusion, this paper proposed a Word2Vec-based approach for stock trend prediction that combines NLP-inspired representation learning with Japanese candlestick encoding and commission-aware classification. The empirical results show that the method outperformed MA and MACD on the selected individual stocks and achieved positive results across all evaluated scenarios, while remaining competitive with Buy & Hold on the Russell Top 50 universe, albeit with weaker validation-phase performance. These findings support the view that learned language-like representations of price action can provide useful predictive signals for trading [1], [2]. Future work should extend the framework to multi-asset and international datasets, incorporate alternative data sources, perform walk-forward validation, and evaluate risk-adjusted and statistically robust performance. Such extensions would help clarify the conditions under which candlestick language models deliver reliable advantages over passive and rule-based benchmarks [3], [5].

Malaria in pregnancy remains a major public health challenge in sub-Saharan Africa, where transmission is often stable and intense, and where the majority of pregnancies occur among women living in resource-constrained settings [1,2]. Infection with Plasmodium falciparum during pregnancy can lead to maternal anaemia, placental malaria, impaired foetal growth, low birth weight, preterm delivery, and increased risk of neonatal and infant mortality [3,4]. These adverse outcomes are not evenly distributed; they are concentrated among women with limited access to antenatal care, insecticide-treated nets, and effective preventive treatment [5,6]. Consequently, malaria in pregnancy continues to undermine maternal and child health gains and contributes to the cycle of poverty in affected populations.

Intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (IPTp-SP) is a core component of the World Health Organization’s package for malaria control in pregnancy, alongside insecticide-treated net use and prompt diagnosis and treatment of clinical malaria [1,7]. WHO recommends that IPTp-SP be administered at each scheduled antenatal care visit beginning in the second trimester, with doses given at least one month apart, and that pregnant women receive at least three doses to maximise protection [1,8]. The intervention is inexpensive, feasible in routine antenatal care, and clinically proven to reduce the burden of maternal anaemia, placental parasitaemia, and low birth weight [4,9]. Despite this strong evidence base, IPTp-SP coverage has remained persistently below national and global targets across much of sub-Saharan Africa [10,11]. Many countries adopted or revised IPTp policies during the past decade, yet implementation has been constrained by health-system weaknesses, including commodity stock-outs, unclear provider guidelines, late antenatal care initiation, missed opportunities during consultations, and inadequate supervision and reporting [12,13].

The gap between policy and practice is further complicated by socioeconomic inequalities in access to and use of maternal health services. Maternal education and household wealth are well-established determinants of preventive care utilisation, including antenatal care attendance and uptake of malaria interventions [14,15]. Women with higher education may be better able to navigate health systems, understand health messages, and demand appropriate care, while wealthier households may face fewer transport, time, and opportunity costs when seeking services [16,17]. However, evidence on the direction and magnitude of these associations for IPTp-SP is mixed. Some studies report higher uptake among more educated and wealthier women, whereas others find weak, null, or even inverse gradients, particularly where antenatal care is widely accessible or where targeted programmes reach poorer groups [18,19]. These inconsistencies suggest that the relationship between socioeconomic position and IPTp-SP uptake is context-specific and may vary across countries with different policy histories, malaria transmission intensities, and health-system arrangements.

Cross-national comparative evidence is therefore needed to assess whether IPTp-SP uptake follows consistent socioeconomic patterns or whether country-level factors modify these relationships. The Malaria Indicator Surveys (MIS) provide a valuable platform for such analysis. MIS are nationally representative, standardised household surveys that collect data on malaria prevention and treatment among women of reproductive age, including detailed information on IPTp-SP doses received during the most recent pregnancy, maternal education, household wealth, antenatal care attendance, and other relevant sociodemographic characteristics [20,21]. Their standardised instruments and sampling designs permit comparisons across countries while allowing adjustment for individual and household-level confounders. Previous multi-country analyses have often relied on Demographic and Health Surveys or have focused on a limited set of countries; comparatively fewer studies have used the most recent MIS waves to examine IPTp-SP specifically and to disaggregate uptake by both education and wealth [22,23].

This study addresses these gaps by using MIS data from eight malaria-endemic countries in sub-Saharan Africa: Burkina Faso, Ghana, Mali, Malawi, Kenya, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, and Uganda. These countries represent diverse epidemiological and policy contexts, including varying malaria transmission intensities, IPTp implementation histories, and maternal health service environments. The primary objective is to estimate the prevalence of adequate IPTp-SP uptake, defined as receipt of at least three doses during the last pregnancy, and to examine patterns of uptake across educational and household wealth categories after adjustment for relevant sociodemographic factors. A secondary objective is to quantify between-country variation in IPTp-SP coverage and to assess whether socioeconomic gradients are consistent across settings. By doing so, the study aims to inform targeted policy and programmatic strategies, highlight health-system performance gaps, and identify populations that remain underserved despite the widespread adoption of IPTp-SP policies.

**Study

Sample characteristics. The analytic sample consisted of 18,603 women aged 15–49 years

The findings of this study reveal a critically low overall prevalence of adequate intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy (IPTp) uptake, with only 29.5% of women having received at least three doses of sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (IPTp-SP) during their last pregnancy. This figure is alarmingly distant from the World Health Organization's (WHO) recommendation of universal coverage, and it underscores a persistent implementation gap across sub-Saharan Africa [1]. The substantial between-country variation observed, ranging from 60% in Ghana to just 15% in Nigeria and Mali, highlights that national policy adoption alone is insufficient to guarantee effective service delivery. This heterogeneity likely reflects profound differences in health system performance, supply chain integrity, and the fidelity of policy implementation at the regional and local levels [2,3]. For instance, Ghana's comparatively higher coverage may be attributable to its long-standing, well-integrated malaria control programme, whereas lower-performing countries may struggle with stockouts of SP, inadequate training of healthcare providers, or a lack of clear, consistent guidelines [4,5]. These cross-country disparities are a stark marker of inequitable health system responsiveness and should serve as a call to action for targeted, context-specific interventions.

Our analysis further reveals a nuanced and somewhat paradoxical relationship between socioeconomic status and IPTp-SP uptake. Contrary to the common assumption that higher education and wealth uniformly correlate with better health service utilisation, we found an inverse association with educational attainment. This finding suggests that women with higher education may have greater access to alternative information sources, potentially leading to heightened risk perception regarding SP's safety profile, or they may opt for care in private facilities where IPTp-SP is not consistently provided or is replaced by alternative, though less proven, prophylactic measures [6]. This paradox warrants further qualitative investigation into the decision-making processes and provider-patient interactions among more educated women.

With regard to household wealth, the pattern was also unexpected. While the abstract notes a slightly higher proportion of IPTp-SP uptake among non-poor households, our regression analysis indicated that, compared to the richest quintile, women in all other wealth quintiles—including the richer and middle groups—had significantly higher odds of not taking the recommended three doses. This finding challenges a simple linear wealth-gradient model. It points towards a more complex reality where access barriers are not exclusively financial. For the poorest women, direct and indirect costs of travel, lost wages, and opportunity costs remain formidable obstacles [7]. However, for the middle and richer quintiles, the barriers may be more related to the perceived quality of care, waiting times, and the opportunity cost of time, which can be substantial for women who are economically active. The fact that the richest women did not have the highest uptake is particularly telling, suggesting that wealth alone does not overcome systemic and informational barriers to IPTp-SP.

The study's findings must be interpreted within its limitations. The cross-sectional nature of the Malaria Indicator Surveys (MIS) precludes any causal inference. Furthermore, the data on IPTp-SP uptake rely on maternal recall, which is subject to recall bias, potentially leading to either over- or underestimation of coverage [8]. Despite these limitations, the use of nationally representative, standardised MIS data across eight countries is a significant strength, allowing for robust comparative analysis.

In conclusion, this study confirms that the uptake of adequate IPTp-SP in sub-Saharan Africa remains unacceptably low and is profoundly influenced by a complex interplay of individual education, household wealth, and, most critically, country-level health system factors. The socioeconomic disparities observed within countries are not merely a reflection of individual choice but are symptomatic of inequitable access to and delivery of essential maternal health services. The inverse educational gradient and the non-linear wealth gradient challenge simplistic assumptions and call for a more nuanced understanding of the barriers to IPTp-SP. To accelerate progress towards malaria in pregnancy control targets, policymakers must move beyond policy adoption to ensuring robust implementation. This requires strengthening supply chains, improving the quality and consistency of antenatal care services, and designing targeted, equity-oriented interventions that address the specific barriers faced by women across the socioeconomic spectrum. Future research should employ longitudinal and qualitative designs to unravel the complex decision-making pathways and health system failures that perpetuate this low coverage, ultimately informing more effective and equitable strategies to protect the health of mothers and their children.

Wind instrument playing is a complex sensorimotor task that requires precise control of the respiratory system. To produce a stable tone, shape musical phrases, and modulate dynamics, musicians must coordinate inspiratory and expiratory muscles, regulate airflow, and generate pressure against the resistance of the instrument. This respiratory demand is particularly pronounced in brass instruments, where sound is generated by lip vibration within a mouthpiece and sustained by a controlled airstream. The trumpet, cornet, and flugelhorn are high-brass instruments with relatively small mouthpieces and high airflow resistance, requiring players to generate and maintain substantial mouth pressures during performance. It has therefore been hypothesised that regular playing could act as a form of respiratory muscle training, potentially increasing respiratory muscle strength and endurance and, in turn, influencing spirometric lung function. Conversely, repeated exposure to high intrathoracic pressures, prolonged forced exhalation, and the postural and embouchure demands of brass playing might have adverse effects on the respiratory system. Whether trumpet/cornet/flugelhorn playing is associated with better, worse, or unchanged lung function remains uncertain.

The effect of wind instruments on lung function has been a much-discussed topic, but the available data are inconclusive. Some studies have reported higher lung function values in wind instrument players than in non-players, suggesting a training effect on respiratory muscles or ventilatory mechanics. Other studies have found no significant differences, and a few have raised the possibility of adverse respiratory effects, particularly in players of high-resistance instruments or in those with prolonged exposure. Several methodological factors may explain these inconsistent findings. Many studies have been small, used heterogeneous populations, lacked appropriate control groups, or failed to adjust for important confounders such as age, sex, height, smoking status, and body mass index. In addition, most previous investigations have combined all wind instruments as a single entity. This is a major limitation because the respiratory demands of a flute, clarinet, saxophone, French horn, trombone, tuba, and trumpet differ substantially in terms of airflow, mouth pressure, instrument resistance, and playing technique. Grouping such instruments together may obscure instrument-specific effects and dilute any true association.

The trumpet, cornet, and flugelhorn are of particular interest because they require a high-pressure, relatively small-aperture respiratory effort. Players must sustain expiratory force while maintaining fine control of airflow and embouchure, often during long rehearsals and performances. This could plausibly lead to adaptive changes in respiratory muscles, such as increased strength or endurance, but it could also impose repetitive mechanical stress on the airways and lungs. Spirometry provides a standardised way to assess such effects through forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1), forced vital capacity (FVC), and their ratio. FEV1 is widely used to detect obstructive ventilatory impairment, whereas FVC reflects the total volume that can be exhaled and may be influenced by restrictive physiology, respiratory muscle function, and effort. If brass playing has a meaningful effect on the respiratory system, it might be reflected in these indices, either as a beneficial increase or as a negative association with cumulative playing exposure. However, studies specifically focused on trumpet/cornet/flugelhorn players and using well-defined non-wind-instrument controls are scarce.

Important confounders must be considered when examining the relationship between instrument playing and lung function. Age, sex, height, and body mass index are strong determinants of spirometric values. Smoking status and cumulative smoking exposure can independently reduce lung function and may differ between musicians and controls. Respiratory symptoms, asthma, allergies, and other comorbidities may also influence both the ability to play a wind instrument and measured lung function. Furthermore, the number of years spent playing may be a more relevant exposure metric than simply comparing current players with non-players, because cumulative exposure could reveal effects that are not apparent in cross-sectional comparisons. A case-control design nested within wind orchestras and brass bands offers an opportunity to compare musicians who play trumpet/cornet/flugelhorn with orchestra members who have never played a wind instrument, while accounting for these potential confounders.

The aim of this study was to investigate the effect of playing a trumpet, cornet, or flugelhorn on lung function. We conducted a prospective, multicentre, cross-sectional, case-control study among wind orchestra and brass band members in Switzerland. Participants were aged 16 years or older, and players reported at least one year of playing a trumpet/cornet/flugelhorn. Controls were members of an orchestra who had never played a wind instrument. The primary endpoint was the difference in FEV1%predicted between trumpet/cornet/flugelhorn players and controls. Secondary analyses examined FVC %predicted, respiratory symptoms, and the association between the number of years of playing and spirometric outcomes. We hypothesised that trumpet/cornet/flugelhorn players would have lung function comparable to that of non-wind-instrument controls, but we also explored whether cumulative playing exposure was associated with changes in FEV1 or FVC. By focusing on a specific group of high-brass instruments and using carefully defined controls, this study aimed to clarify a persistent uncertainty in the respiratory health of wind musicians.

This prospective, multicentre, cross-sectional case-control study was conducted among wind orchestra and brass band musicians throughout Switzerland. The primary objective was to determine whether playing a trumpet, cornet, or flugelhorn is associated with differences in lung function compared with non-wind-instrument-playing orchestra members. Participants were recruited between 2018 and 2022 from amateur and semi-professional wind orchestras and brass bands in German-, French-, and Italian-speaking regions of Switzerland. Recruitment occurred through direct contact with orchestra conductors, advertisements in musician association newsletters, information sessions, and snowball sampling. The study was designed as a case-control comparison nested within a cross-sectional assessment; all participants were prospectively enrolled and assessed at a single study visit.

Cases were individuals aged 16 years or older who reported actively playing a trumpet, cornet, or flugelhorn for at least one year. There was no upper limit for years of playing, and musicians who also played other instruments were eligible provided their primary instrument was trumpet, cornet, or flugelhorn. Controls were members of an orchestra who had never played a wind instrument. Controls could play non-wind instruments, such as strings, percussion, or keyboard, or participate in orchestral activities without instrumental wind playing. Exclusion criteria for all participants were an inability to perform spirometry, contraindications to spirometry, an acute respiratory infection within the previous four weeks, or inability to provide informed consent. Participants with known chronic respiratory disease were not excluded, but relevant diagnoses and medication use were recorded and considered in adjusted analyses.

At the study visit, all participants completed a standardised questionnaire and underwent anthropometric measurements and spirometry. Demographic data included age, sex, height, weight, and calculated body mass index. Smoking status was classified as never, former, or current smoker, and pack-years were calculated. Medical history included physician-diagnosed asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, allergic rhinitis, other respiratory conditions, and current respiratory medication. Musicians provided detailed instrument histories, including type of trumpet-family instrument played, age at starting, total years of playing, average practice hours per week, and any previous or current playing of other wind instruments. Controls reported any lifetime history of wind instrument playing to confirm eligibility.

Spirometry was performed by trained study personnel using calibrated portable spirometers according to American Thoracic Society and European Respiratory Society guidelines. Participants were seated, wore a nose clip, and performed forced expiratory manoeuvres. At least three acceptable manoeuvres were required, with reproducibility of forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) and forced vital capacity (FVC) within 150 mL or 5%. The highest acceptable FEV1 and FVC values were used for analysis. FEV1 and FVC were expressed as percentages of predicted values using the Global Lung Function Initiative reference equations. The FEV1/FVC ratio was also calculated. Spirometry was performed without bronchodilator administration unless clinically indicated; pre-bronchodilator values were used for the primary analysis.

Respiratory symptoms were assessed using a standardised, self-administered questionnaire adapted from validated respiratory epidemiology instruments. Participants reported the presence and frequency of cough, sputum production, wheeze, dyspnoea, and chest tightness. Each symptom was scored on a four-point scale, and a total respiratory symptom score was calculated, with higher scores indicating a greater symptom burden. The questionnaire also recorded smoking exposure, respiratory diagnoses, and medication use. The primary endpoint was the difference in FEV1 percentage predicted between trumpet, cornet, or flugelhorn players and controls. Secondary endpoints included FVC percentage predicted, FEV1/FVC ratio, respiratory symptom score, and the association between cumulative years of trumpet-family playing and lung function parameters.

The sample size was based on feasibility and recruitment capacity across participating orchestras rather than a formal a priori power calculation. A total of 147 participants were included in the final analysis: 99 trumpet, cornet, or flugelhorn players and 48 controls. Continuous variables were summarised as mean ± standard deviation or median with interquartile range, depending on distribution. Categorical variables were summarised as frequencies and percentages. Baseline characteristics were compared using Student’s t-test or the Mann–Whitney U test for continuous variables and the chi-square or Fisher’s exact test for categorical variables, as appropriate.

The primary analysis used linear regression with FEV1 percentage predicted as the dependent variable and participant group as the independent variable. Crude and adjusted models were constructed. Adjusted models included age, sex, smoking status, body mass index, and height because these variables differed between groups or are known determinants of lung function.
