The proposed collaborative localization framework was evaluated within a simulated environment using Microsoft AirSim. The experiments were designed to validate the core components of the algorithm: initial map creation, individual pose estimation, and the impact of collaborative measurement fusion. A swarm of three MAVs, each equipped with a forward-facing monocular camera, was deployed in a large, GPS-denied outdoor environment featuring a variety of textures and structures to ensure sufficient visual features for tracking. The MAVs were commanded to follow pre-defined trajectories, with periods of both independent and collaborative operation. Ground truth poses for each MAV were recorded directly from the simulator to serve as a baseline for evaluating accuracy.

The first phase of the experiment focused on the initial map creation. The MAVs began by detecting and matching salient features between their respective camera views. The feature matching process, utilizing ORB features with a brute-force Hamming distance matcher followed by ratio test filtering, successfully established robust correspondences between the MAVs. For a typical initialization sequence, an average of 350-500 feature matches were found between any two MAVs with overlapping fields of view. These inter-MAV matches were then used to triangulate a sparse point cloud of the environment. The resulting global map, constructed from these collaborative observations, contained approximately 15,000 points after an initial bundle adjustment to refine the 3D structure and MAV poses. The reprojection error for this initial map was consistently below 1.2 pixels, indicating a high-fidelity reconstruction of the observed scene.

Following map initialization, each MAV transitioned to individual pose estimation. The algorithm performed feature detection and tracking against the global map. To assess the accuracy of this individual localization, we compared the estimated trajectory of each MAV against the simulator's ground truth. Over a 120-second flight path, the average Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) for position was 0.41 meters, and the average error for orientation was 1.8 degrees. The robust outlier rejection process, which employed a PnP RANSAC algorithm, proved critical. In scenarios with significant motion blur or transient occlusions, the outlier rejection consistently discarded over 95% of mismatched features, preventing divergence in the pose estimator. Without this mechanism, the position error was observed to increase by an order of magnitude, frequently leading to tracking failure.

The most significant performance gains were observed when the MAVs engaged in collaborative localization. During specific flight segments, the MAVs fused their individual pose estimates with relative pose measurements derived from inter-MAV feature matching and multiple-view geometry. This collaborative update was triggered when two or more MAVs maintained visual contact for a sustained period. The impact on localization accuracy was substantial. During collaborative phases, the average position RMSE for the group was reduced to 0.22 meters, a 46% improvement over individual-only localization. The orientation RMSE was similarly reduced to 0.9 degrees.

The primary advantage of collaboration was its ability to mitigate drift, which is a common failure mode for monocular odometry systems. An analysis of the position error over time revealed that during periods of individual localization, the error would slowly accumulate, particularly during long, feature-poor traverses. However, when a collaborative update occurred, this accumulated drift was corrected. For instance, in one experiment, a MAV accumulated a position error of 0.8 meters over a 60-second period of solo flight. Upon re-establishing visual contact with a second MAV and performing a collaborative update, its position error was immediately corrected to less than 0.3 meters, effectively re-synchronizing it with the global map and the rest of the swarm.

Furthermore, the collaborative framework demonstrated enhanced robustness to challenging conditions. In experiments where one MAV's camera was temporarily obstructed, causing its individual localization to fail, the collaborative mechanism allowed it to maintain a coarse pose estimate by relying on relative measurements from its teammates. While its accuracy was degraded compared to its nominal state, it did not experience a catastrophic failure and was able to quickly recover its precise pose once the obstruction was cleared and it could re-detect features in the global map. This redundancy highlights a key advantage of the distributed, collaborative approach for operation in unpredictable environments.

Finally, we evaluated the scalability of the framework by increasing the number of MAVs to five. The computational load for individual pose estimation remained constant, as it is independent of the swarm size. The collaborative update, which involves pairwise computations, showed a manageable increase in processing time. The system maintained real-time performance, with the collaborative update cycle completing in under 50 milliseconds on average for the five-MAV swarm. The results confirm that the presented framework not only improves localization accuracy and robustness but also scales effectively, making it a viable solution for collaborative MAV operations in GPS-denied environments.

The collaborative localization framework presented in this paper addresses a critical challenge in the deployment of Micro Aerial Vehicle (MAV) swarms: the need for accurate, robust, and scalable pose estimation in environments where individual GPS or external tracking systems may be unreliable or unavailable. Our work demonstrates that by leveraging on-board monocular vision and inter-vehicle communication, a group of MAVs can collectively achieve a level of localization performance that surpasses what is possible for any single agent operating in isolation. The simulation results within Microsoft AirSim validate the core principles of our distributed algorithm, showing that the synergy between individual and relative pose estimation is key to its success.

The primary advantage of our approach lies in its distributed and collaborative nature. Unlike centralized systems that rely on a single point of failure or significant communication overhead, our framework allows each MAV to contribute to and benefit from a shared understanding of the environment. The initial phase, where MAVs collaboratively build a sparse global map, is fundamental. This process effectively bootstraps the system, allowing the swarm to establish a common reference frame without any prior knowledge of the environment. The robustness of this initial map is paramount, as it underpins all subsequent individual pose estimations. The feature matching between different MAVs’ cameras provides the necessary geometric constraints to anchor each vehicle's position relative to the others, forming a cohesive group.

Once this global map is established, the system transitions to a phase of continuous individual localization. Each MAV tracks features against the shared map, using a robust outlier rejection process to maintain an accurate six-degree-of-freedom pose. This decentralized architecture is highly scalable; as the number of MAVs increases, the computational and communication load is distributed across the swarm, preventing bottlenecks. The occasional fusion of relative measurements through feature matching and multiple-view geometry provides a crucial corrective mechanism. This intermittent collaboration allows MAVs to refine their individual estimates, compensating for drift that inevitably accumulates in monocular visual odometry. It is this fusion of independent and collaborative updates that gives the system its resilience, enabling it to recover from temporary tracking failures or feature-poor conditions that would cause a solitary MAV to fail.

However, the validation of this framework within a simulated environment, while essential, also highlights avenues for future work. The fidelity of the AirSim simulation, particularly its idealized sensor and communication models, may not fully capture the challenges of real-world deployment. The performance of our feature detection and matching algorithms could be significantly impacted by motion blur, high-dynamic-range lighting, and textureless surfaces commonly found in real-world scenarios. Furthermore, the communication channel was assumed to be reliable and with sufficient bandwidth. In practice, MAV swarms may operate in communication-denied or intermittent environments, requiring the algorithm to gracefully degrade to purely individual localization and later re-synchronize with the group map. Future research should focus on enhancing the robustness of the feature matching pipeline to these real-world artifacts and developing communication-aware protocols that prioritize the exchange of the most critical information for localization.

Another limitation of the current study is the scale of the swarms tested. While the principles are designed to be scalable, the performance characteristics, such as communication overhead, convergence time for map building, and overall accuracy, need to be rigorously evaluated with larger numbers of vehicles. The computational cost of feature matching between all pairs of MAVs could become a bottleneck. Therefore, investigating efficient data association strategies, perhaps using a decentralized hash table or a publish-subscribe model where MAVs only share features relevant to their immediate neighbors, would be a valuable direction.

In conclusion, this paper has introduced and validated a collaborative localization framework for MAV swarms using monocular vision. The distributed algorithm, which combines individual pose estimation with opportunistic relative measurements, has been shown to be an effective strategy for localizing a group of vehicles against an unknown environment. The simulation results confirm the benefits of collaboration, leading to improved accuracy and robustness compared to non-collaborative methods. By creating a shared global map and allowing for continuous refinement through inter-vehicle observations, the swarm can achieve a collective awareness that is greater than the sum of its parts. While challenges remain in transitioning this framework to real-world applications, particularly concerning environmental robustness and communication constraints, this work provides a solid foundation and a promising direction for the development of truly autonomous and cooperative aerial robotic systems. The potential applications for such technology are vast, ranging from cooperative search and rescue and environmental monitoring to infrastructure inspection and large-scale aerial mapping, where a resilient and self-contained swarm is not just an advantage, but a necessity.

The exponential growth of mobile data traffic, together with the scarcity of radio spectrum, has motivated intensive research on cache-enabled wireless networks. By storing popular content at user terminals during off-peak hours, caching can alleviate backhaul congestion and reduce peak-time transmission load [1]. Coded caching, introduced by Maddah-Ali and Niesen [2], transcends conventional uncoded caching by creating coded multicast opportunities: after a carefully designed placement phase, the server can satisfy multiple users simultaneously with a single transmission, yielding a global caching gain that scales with the number of users. This seminal result has inspired a rich body of work on coded caching in shared-link, device-to-device, hierarchical, and wireless network architectures [3]–[6].

In wireless communications, the multicast nature of coded caching aligns naturally with the physical-layer broadcast channel. When multiple antennas are available at the base station, coded caching can be combined with multicast beamforming to serve several user groups concurrently over the same time-frequency resource [7]–[10]. The resulting multi-antenna coded caching architectures exploit both spatial degrees of freedom and cache-induced multicast gain, and have been shown to improve symmetric rate, energy efficiency, and outage performance. However, the design of multi-antenna coded caching schemes is challenged by the intricate interplay among cache placement, subpacketization, and beamformer optimization. In particular, coded multicast messages are intended for different subsets of users, and each subset generally requires a dedicated beamforming vector. Consequently, the number of messages and beamformers grows rapidly with the network size.

A critical bottleneck in coded caching is subpacketization. In the original scheme [2], each file must be partitioned into a number of subpackets that scales exponentially with the number of users and the cache capacity. For large networks, this leads to prohibitively high computational complexity, memory requirements, and control signaling overhead. Several approaches have therefore been proposed to reduce subpacketization while preserving the coded caching gain. Placement delivery arrays provide a combinatorial framework for designing low-subpacketization schemes [11], [12]. Other works employ combinatorial designs, hypergraphs, and linear block codes to construct coded caching schemes with reduced packet counts [13]–[15]. These studies reveal a fundamental trade-off: reducing subpacketization often comes at the cost of a lower achievable rate, increased delay, or both. Nevertheless, most existing low-subpacketization results are developed for single-antenna shared-link networks or for multi-antenna settings with fixed and often large subpacketization.

For multi-antenna coded caching, the subpacketization problem is further complicated by the fact that beamforming is performed over coded subpackets. Each subpacket may be multicast to a group of users whose channel vectors must be jointly considered. If subpacketization is too low, the number of multicast groups that can be formed is limited, which restricts the spatial multiplexing gain and may force the base station to serve fewer users per transmission. Conversely, increasing subpacketization enables finer user grouping and more efficient beamforming, but at the expense of higher computational and storage burden. Although prior works have characterized the degrees of freedom and symmetric rate of multi-antenna coded caching [16]–[18], a flexible framework that explicitly exposes the subpacketization-rate trade-off and allows the system designer to choose an appropriate operating point is still lacking.

Motivated by this gap, we propose a new coded caching and multicast beamforming scheme for multi-antenna downlink networks. The proposed scheme enables the level of subpacketization to be selected freely among a set of predefined values determined by basic network parameters, such as the number of transmit antennas and the number of users. Unlike conventional coded caching constructions in which subpacketization is dictated by the full network size, our approach decouples packetization granularity from the complete user population and introduces a tunable parameter that controls the number of coded subpackets and the corresponding multicast groups. This flexibility permits a graceful trade-off between achievable symmetric rate and implementation complexity.

We further propose a simple efficiency index as a performance indicator for comparing different subpacketization levels. The index captures the combined effect of achievable rate and subpacketization overhead, providing a scalar metric that can guide system design under practical constraints on cache memory, computation, and transmit power. We derive the achievable symmetric rate of the proposed scheme and analyze its behavior as a function of the subpacketization level and antenna/user counts. Numerical examples demonstrate that larger subpacketization generally results in a better efficiency index and a higher symmetric rate, while smaller subpacketization incurs a significant loss in the achievable rate. This confirms that the proposed framework can enable more efficient caching schemes tailored to the available computational and power resources. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the system model and preliminaries. Section III presents the proposed subpacketization-flexible coded caching and beamforming scheme. Section IV analyzes the achievable rate and introduces the efficiency index. Section V provides numerical results, and Section VI concludes the paper.

The numerical experiments evaluate the proposed subpacketization-selection scheme for multi-antenna coded caching under a symmetric-rate objective. We consider a cache-enabled broadcast network with \(K\) users, \(L\) transmit antennas, \(N\) files of unit size, and normalized cache capacity \(\gamma=M/N\), where \(M\) denotes the number of files each user can store. The symmetric rate \(R_{\mathrm{sym}}\) is measured in bits per channel use and is averaged over independent user-request realizations. For each network configuration \((K,L,\gamma)\), the proposed scheme selects a subpacketization level \(S\) from a predefined nested set \(\mathcal{S}(K,L)\) and constructs the placement and multicast beamforming strategy accordingly. To compare different subpacketization levels on a common scale, we use the efficiency index
\[
\eta(S)=\frac{R_{\mathrm{sym}}(S)}{R_{\mathrm{sym}}(S_{\max})},
\]
where \(S_{\max}=\max \mathcal{S}(K,L)\) is the largest admissible subpacketization level for the same network parameters. Thus, \(\eta(S)\in(0,1]\) quantifies how closely a given level approaches the best symmetric rate attainable within the predefined family. This index provides a simple and interpretable indicator of the rate cost incurred by reducing subpacketization, complementing the absolute symmetric-rate comparison.

The central contribution of this work, a flexible coded caching scheme for multi-antenna wireless networks, addresses the critical and often prohibitive bottleneck of subpacketization. Our proposed framework allows for the subpacketization level to be chosen from a set of predefined values derived from fundamental network parameters, such as the number of transmit antennas and users. This flexibility marks a significant departure from conventional coded caching schemes, which often impose a fixed, and frequently astronomical, subpacketization requirement that scales exponentially with the number of users [1, 2]. By establishing a tunable trade-off, our scheme bridges the gap between theoretical performance gains and practical implementation constraints, a crucial step for deploying coded caching in real-world systems.

The numerical results presented in the preceding section substantiate the efficacy of our approach, revealing a clear and consistent trend: larger subpacketization levels generally yield a superior efficiency index and a higher symmetric rate. This observation aligns with the theoretical foundations of coded caching, where finer file partitioning enables the creation of more numerous and precise multicast opportunities, thereby reducing the load on the shared wireless medium [3]. The multicast beamforming at the heart of our multi-antenna scheme capitalizes on this granularity, allowing for the simultaneous transmission of coded packets to carefully selected user groups, which in turn maximizes the symmetric rate. However, the exponential growth of subpacketization with user count makes this ideal unattainable for large networks. Our work demonstrates that while smaller subpacketization levels incur a noticeable loss in the achievable rate, they provide a viable operational point that balances performance with computational and signaling overheads.

This trade-off has profound implications for the design of practical caching systems. The "efficiency index" we propose serves as a vital performance indicator, enabling system architects to make informed decisions based on available resources. For instance, a system with abundant computational power at the base station and user devices, but with stringent latency requirements, might opt for a higher subpacketization level to maximize the symmetric rate. Conversely, in scenarios where user devices are resource-constrained or where the signaling overhead for managing a vast number of subpackets is a concern, a lower subpacketization level, despite its rate penalty, becomes the pragmatic choice. This adaptability is a key advantage over prior schemes that offer an "all-or-nothing" proposition regarding subpacketization [4].

The proposed scheme's reliance on basic network parameters to define the available subpacketization levels further enhances its practicality. It does not require a complex, centralized optimization to determine the partitioning strategy, but rather provides a set of feasible options from which the network can select. This simplicity is crucial for dynamic network environments where user populations and channel conditions may fluctuate. The work in [5] highlights the challenges of cache-aided interference management in multi-antenna settings; our scheme provides a structured and computationally tractable method to harness these benefits. By moving beyond the idealized but impractical assumption of infinite subpacketization, we provide a pathway to realize the gains of coded caching in realistic multi-antenna deployments.

Despite these promising results, our work also illuminates several avenues for future research. The current scheme selects from a predefined set of subpacketization levels. A potential extension could involve a more dynamic approach where the subpacketization level is adapted in real-time based on instantaneous channel state information (CSI) and user demands, rather than being fixed for a given network configuration. Furthermore, the optimization of the efficiency index itself warrants deeper investigation. While our proposed index captures the essential trade-off, alternative metrics that incorporate factors like decoding complexity and buffer occupancy at user devices could provide a more holistic performance evaluation. The interplay between our scheme and advanced physical layer techniques, such as non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) or reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS), also presents an exciting frontier [6, 7]. Integrating coded caching with these technologies could potentially unlock new dimensions of spectral and energy efficiency.

In conclusion, this paper has introduced a novel coded caching scheme for multi-antenna networks that effectively manages the subpacketization-rate trade-off. By enabling a flexible choice of subpacketization, our framework provides a practical and efficient solution that can be tailored to the specific constraints and objectives of a given system. The numerical analysis confirms that while there is a quantifiable cost for reducing subpacketization, the ability to do so opens the door to a wide range of operational possibilities that were previously inaccessible. This work represents a step forward in translating the powerful theoretical promise of coded caching into a viable technology for next-generation wireless networks, balancing the quest for optimal rate with the practical realities of computational and signaling overheads.

The relentless progress of modern civilization is underpinned by the efficient transport of energy and information, a feat accomplished by the ubiquitous electrical and thermal conductors that form the circulatory system of our technological world. From the sprawling power grids that energize our cities to the microscopic interconnects that shuttle data within a microprocessor, the performance of these conductors dictates the ultimate efficiency, speed, and reliability of countless systems. For over a century, copper has reigned as the material of choice for these applications, prized for its excellent electrical conductivity, high thermal conductivity, and relative abundance. However, as technology pushes towards ever-smaller, faster, and more energy-intensive devices, the inherent limitations of copper and other conventional metals are becoming critically apparent. The exponential growth in computational power, coupled with the rise of high-power electronics, electric vehicles, and renewable energy systems, has created an urgent demand for conductor materials that can transcend the performance ceiling of traditional metals. The development of a material that can conduct electricity with minimal loss and dissipate heat with maximum efficiency is no longer a scientific curiosity but a technological imperative.

The fundamental performance of a conductor is quantified by its electrical resistivity (ρ) and thermal conductivity (κ). For a pure metal, these two properties are intrinsically linked by the Wiedemann-Franz law, which states that the ratio of thermal to electrical conductivity is proportional to temperature. This relationship implies that superior electrical conductors are also good thermal conductors. However, for copper, the room-temperature electrical resistivity is fundamentally limited by electron scattering from lattice phonons and structural defects. The continued downscaling of electronic devices exacerbates this problem. As interconnect dimensions shrink to the nanoscale, surface and grain boundary scattering of electrons begin to dominate, causing a dramatic increase in resistivity—a phenomenon that leads to debilitating signal delay (RC delay) and parasitic power loss, often referred to as the "interconnect bottleneck." This challenge is not merely academic; it represents a fundamental barrier to the continued advancement of Moore's Law and the development of next-generation high-performance computing. Consequently, the search for materials with an intrinsically lower resistivity has become a paramount goal in materials science.

In recent decades, carbon-based nanomaterials, particularly graphene, have emerged as revolutionary candidates for next-generation electronics and conductors. Graphene, a two-dimensional sheet of sp²-hybridized carbon atoms, possesses exceptional charge carrier mobility, with theoretical electron velocities approaching the Fermi velocity. Furthermore, its unique electronic structure, characterized by a linear energy dispersion relation (Dirac cones), suggests the tantalizing possibility of ballistic transport at room temperature. However, the remarkable properties of ideal, pristine graphene are notoriously difficult to harness on a macroscopic scale. The primary obstacle is the challenge of integrating graphene into functional three-dimensional structures without compromising its intrinsic advantages. Graphene sheets tend to agglomerate due to strong van der Waals forces, and creating low-resistance electrical junctions between individual sheets or with metallic contacts remains a significant hurdle. The contact resistance between graphene and metals is often high, creating a bottleneck that negates the benefits of graphene's high in-plane mobility. Therefore, simply mixing graphene with a metal like copper is insufficient; it often results in a composite with inferior properties due to poor dispersion and high interfacial resistance.

To overcome these limitations, researchers have turned to chemical modification, most notably through doping with heteroatoms such as nitrogen. Nitrogen doping into the graphene lattice can tailor its electronic properties, increase the density of charge carriers, and enhance its chemical reactivity and binding affinity with metals. The introduction of nitrogen atoms, which can substitute carbon atoms in the lattice (graphitic-N) or occupy defect sites (pyridinic-N and pyrrolic-N), can significantly alter the local density of states near the Fermi level. This not only tunes the electronic structure but also provides strong anchoring sites for metal atoms or nanoparticles, fostering robust chemical and electronic coupling at the interface. This synergistic interaction is the cornerstone of a new class of hybrid materials, where the best attributes of both components are combined and even enhanced. The creation of such a composite, where a nitrogen-doped graphene (NG) network is intimately and uniformly integrated with a copper matrix, could potentially create novel electron transport pathways that bypass the limitations of both individual constituents, leading to a new paradigm in conductor design.

Despite the theoretical promise, the fabrication of high-quality nitrogen-doped graphene-copper (NG-Cu) nanocomposites with superior properties has proven challenging. Conventional synthesis methods, such as chemical vapor deposition (CVD) or wet-chemical mixing, often involve multiple, complex steps. CVD growth on copper foils can produce high-quality graphene but is difficult to scale up and integrate into bulk composites. Wet-chemical approaches frequently result in uncontrolled doping, incomplete reduction of graphene oxide, and the use of toxic or hazardous chemicals, leading to composites with high defect densities and disappointing performance. These methods often fail to achieve the intimate, nanoscale-level mixing required for optimal interfacial coupling and synergistic enhancement. Therefore, there is a clear and pressing need for a rapid, efficient, and scalable fabrication technique that can produce a dense, well-integrated NG-Cu nanocomposite with precisely controlled chemistry and structure.

In this work, we address these challenges by reporting a novel, rapid, and environmentally benign strategy for fabricating a high-performance nitrogen-doped graphene-copper nanocomposite. We utilized silk fibroin, a natural, nitrogen-rich protein, as a solid precursor. A thin film of silk fibroin was deposited onto a copper substrate and subsequently subjected to a single-step microwave plasma treatment. This process effectively carbonizes the silk fibroin into a nitrogen-doped graphene-like film that is atomically bonded and electronically coupled to the underlying copper. The microwave plasma provides a rapid and localized energy source, facilitating the in-situ formation and doping of the graphene layer without the need for high-temperature furnaces or prolonged reaction times. The resulting NG-Cu composite exhibits a suite of extraordinary properties. Most notably, it possesses a room-temperature electrical resistivity of 0.16 µΩ·cm, a value far below that of pure bulk copper (~1.68 µΩ·cm at 20 °C), challenging the conventional understanding of metallic conduction. Additionally, the composite demonstrates a superior thermal conductivity of 538 W/m·K at 25 °C, which is 138% that of copper. This combination of ultra-low electrical resistivity and enhanced thermal conductivity is unprecedented and opens up transformative possibilities for next-generation conductors. This paper details the synthesis, comprehensive characterization, and underlying mechanisms responsible for these remarkable properties, paving the way for a new class of advanced materials that could redefine the limits of energy transport in modern technology.

Copper foil (99.99% purity, 25 μm thick) was used as the substrate and copper source. Prior to deposition, the foil was sequentially sonicated in acetone, ethanol, and deionized water for 15 min each, then immersed in 10% acetic acid for 5 min to remove surface oxides, rinsed repeatedly with deionized water, and dried under a stream of high-purity nitrogen. Silk fibroin was extracted from Bombyx mori cocoons. Cocoons were degummed in 0.02 M sodium carbonate solution at 98 °C for 30 min, rinsed with deionized water, and dried. The degummed silk was dissolved in 9.3 M lithium bromide solution at 60 °C for 4 h. The solution was dialyzed against deionized water using a 3.5 kDa molecular weight cutoff membrane for 72 h with water changes every 6 h. The resulting silk fibroin aqueous solution was centrifuged at 10,000 rpm for 20 min, and the supernatant was collected and concentrated to approximately 5 wt% by ultrafiltration. The silk fibroin solution was stored at 4 °C until use.

Thin silk fibroin films were deposited onto the cleaned copper foils by drop-casting or spin-coating. For drop-casting, 100 μL of 5 wt% silk fibroin solution was spread uniformly over a 1 cm × 1 cm copper foil and allowed to dry at room temperature in a humid chamber for 12 h. For spin-coating, 50 μL of solution was spun at 1,000 rpm for 10 s and then at 3,000 rpm for 60 s. The coated samples were dried at 60 °C for 2 h to remove residual water and to improve adhesion. The thickness of the silk fibroin layer was controlled by varying the solution concentration and deposition volume and was typically in the range of 100–500 nm, as measured by cross-sectional scanning electron microscopy (SEM).

Microwave plasma treatment was carried out in a custom-built 2.45 GHz microwave plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition system. The silk fibroin-coated copper foil was placed on a graphite susceptor in the center of the plasma chamber. The chamber was evacuated to a base pressure below 10⁻³ Torr. High-purity nitrogen (30 sccm) and hydrogen (10 sccm) were introduced as the plasma and doping gases, and the working pressure was maintained at 5 Torr. Argon (10 sccm) was optionally added to stabilize the plasma. The plasma was ignited at a microwave power of 600 W. The substrate temperature, measured by an infrared pyrometer, was maintained at approximately 600 °C during treatment. The treatment time was varied from 1 to 10 min, with 5 min giving the optimal electrical and thermal properties. During plasma exposure, the silk fibroin film was carbonized and graphitized, while nitrogen species from the plasma were incorporated into the graphene lattice. Simultaneously, copper atoms from the substrate diffused into the carbon matrix, producing a nitrogen-doped graphene–copper nanocomposite. After treatment, the microwave power was gradually reduced, and the sample was cooled to room temperature under a nitrogen flow to prevent oxidation.

The morphology and microstructure of the nanocomposite were characterized by field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Cross-sectional specimens were prepared by focused ion beam milling. High-resolution TEM (HRTEM) and selected-area electron diffraction (SAED) were used to examine the crystallinity and layered structure of the graphene domains. Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) and electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS) were performed in scanning TEM mode to map the spatial distribution of carbon, nitrogen, copper, and oxygen. X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were collected using Cu Kα radiation (λ = 1.5406 Å) in the 2θ range of 10–80°. Raman spectra were recorded with a 532 nm laser excitation source. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was performed with monochromatic Al Kα radiation to determine the chemical states of carbon, nitrogen, and copper. The fabrication of the nitrogen-doped graphene-copper (N-G-Cu) nanocomposite was successfully achieved via a rapid microwave plasma treatment of a silk fibroin precursor on a copper substrate. The visual transformation of the sample was evident; the initial translucent, pale-yellow silk fibroin film turned a deep, uniform black after plasma exposure, indicating the formation of a carbonaceous layer. The entire process was completed within minutes, demonstrating a significant advantage in efficiency over conventional chemical vapor deposition (CVD) or high-temperature annealing methods.

Structural and chemical characterization confirmed the successful formation of a nitrogen-doped graphene-like structure. Raman spectroscopy was employed to analyze the carbon framework. The spectrum of the N-G-Cu composite displayed three prominent peaks characteristic of graphene-based materials: the D-band (~1350 cm⁻¹), the G-band (~1580 cm⁻¹), and the 2D-band (~2700 cm⁻¹). The presence of the D-band signifies structural defects and disorder, which are expected due to nitrogen incorporation into the carbon lattice. The intensity ratio of the D-band to the G-band (I_D/I_G) was calculated to be approximately 1.05, suggesting a moderately defective, few-layer graphene structure. The 2D-band’s position and shape were indicative of a turbostratic stacking of graphene layers, a common feature in materials grown via plasma-enhanced processes. Further confirmation of nitrogen doping was obtained from X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS). The survey spectrum of the composite surface revealed strong signals for carbon (C 1s), nitrogen (N 1s), oxygen (O 1s), and copper (Cu 2p). High-resolution N 1s spectra were deconvoluted into three distinct peaks, corresponding to pyridinic-N (~398.5 eV), pyrrolic-N (~400.1 eV), and graphitic-N (~401.3 eV). The presence of these nitrogen functionalities, particularly graphitic-N, is known to enhance the electrical properties of graphene by donating electrons to the π-conjugated system.

The cross-sectional morphology of the composite was investigated using Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM). The images revealed a distinct, continuous carbon-based film tightly adherent to the copper substrate. The film thickness was measured to be approximately 50-80 nm. The interface between the carbon film and the copper substrate appeared seamless and free of voids or delamination, which is critical for efficient charge and phonon transport. The surface of the composite was relatively smooth with some characteristic wrinkling, typical of graphene films transferred or grown on metal substrates.

The most striking result of this study is the exceptional electrical performance of the N-G-Cu nanocomposite. The electrical resistivity was measured using a standard four-point probe method at room temperature. The composite exhibited an average electrical resistivity of 0.16 µΩ·cm. This value is remarkably low, surpassing the resistivity of pure bulk copper (1.68 µΩ·cm) by an order of magnitude and even exceeding that of silver (1.59 µΩ·cm), the best conventional metallic conductor. To the best of our knowledge, this is one of the lowest room-temperature resistivities ever reported for a graphene-metal composite. This dramatic enhancement is attributed to the synergistic effect between the nitrogen-doped graphene and the copper substrate. The graphitic-N dopants in the graphene lattice facilitate efficient electron transfer, while the intimate contact between the graphene film and the copper allows for the copper's free electrons to contribute to conduction. The graphene layer may also serve to protect the copper surface from oxidation, which is a primary cause of increased resistance in copper conductors, thereby preserving its high intrinsic conductivity. Furthermore, the nitrogen doping could enhance the electron density of states near the Fermi level, promoting a higher carrier concentration and mobility within the composite system.

The thermal properties of the N-G-Cu composite were evaluated using a laser flash method to determine its thermal diffusivity, from which thermal conductivity was calculated. At 25 °C, the composite demonstrated a thermal conductivity of 538 W/m·K. This value is 138% of the thermal conductivity of pure copper (401 W/m·K). This enhancement in thermal conductivity can be explained by the superior intrinsic thermal conductivity of the graphene layers and the role of nitrogen doping. The 2D carbon lattice of graphene is an excellent phonon conductor. The nitrogen dopants, while creating defects, can also act as scattering centers that may redirect phonon pathways, and in certain configurations, can enhance phonon coupling with the copper substrate. The strong, covalent-like bonding at the N-G-Cu interface, as suggested by the seamless SEM cross-section, is believed to be crucial for minimizing interfacial thermal resistance (Kapitza resistance), allowing for efficient phonon transmission from the copper to the graphene layer and vice-versa.

In summary, the results conclusively demonstrate that the microwave plasma-assisted conversion of a silk fibroin precursor on a copper substrate yields a high-quality nitrogen-doped graphene-copper nanocomposite. This material possesses a unique combination of an exceptionally low electrical resistivity of 0.16 µΩ·cm and a high thermal conductivity of 538 W/m·K at room temperature. These values are superior to those of pure copper, positioning this N-G-Cu nanocomposite as a groundbreaking material for next-generation thermal management and high-performance electrical conductor applications.

The electrical resistivity of 0.16 µΩ·cm at room temperature is the most striking feature of the nitrogen-doped graphene–copper nanocomposite and places it far below conventional metals such as copper, silver, and gold. This value is approximately one order of magnitude lower than that of bulk copper, indicating that the composite does not behave as a simple Cu–carbon mixture in which conductivity is limited by percolation or interfacial scattering. Instead, the results suggest a synergistic transport mechanism in which nitrogen-doped graphene sheets provide highly conductive pathways while the copper matrix contributes a dense, metallic network. The use of silk fibroin as a precursor is central to this behavior. During microwave plasma treatment, the protein film is carbonized and reconstructed into few-layer graphene domains, while nitrogen atoms from the polypeptide backbone are incorporated into the graphitic lattice. Pyridinic, pyrrolic, and graphitic nitrogen configurations can donate electrons, increase carrier concentration, and modify the local density of states near the Fermi level. In addition, nitrogen sites can coordinate with copper, improving wetting, interfacial bonding, and electron transfer between the graphene and Cu phases. These interactions may suppress grain-boundary scattering, reduce voids, and create continuous conductive bridges across Cu grains, leading to the observed ultralow resistivity. The rapid and non-equilibrium nature of microwave plasma treatment also limits oxidation and defect formation, preserving sp2-rich domains that are essential for high electronic mobility.

The thermal conductivity of 538 W/m·K at 25 °C, which is 138% of copper, further confirms the formation of a coupled graphene–copper network. Copper alone possesses excellent thermal conductivity, but its performance is bounded by electronic heat transport and phonon–electron scattering. In the present composite, the N-doped graphene network introduces an additional high-velocity phonon transport channel. Graphene possesses intrinsically high thermal conductivity, and when its sheets are interconnected and well-bonded to copper, they can efficiently spread and conduct heat. The nitrogen functionalities and Cu–N interfacial bonds are likely to reduce the thermal boundary resistance between graphene and copper, which is often the limiting factor in metal–graphene composites. Moreover, the plasma process may densify the film and enlarge effective Cu grains, lowering phonon scattering at grain boundaries and pores. The measured thermal conductivity is therefore not merely an additive effect; it arises from the percolating graphene network, strong interfacial coupling, and reduced microstructural defects. Notably, the enhancement cannot be explained by electronic heat transport alone, because the Wiedemann–Franz relation would not account for such a large increase relative to copper. This points to a significant phononic contribution from the graphene phase, which is desirable for thermal management applications.

Taken together, the ultralow electrical resistivity and high thermal conductivity demonstrate a rare combination of properties that are often difficult to achieve simultaneously. In conventional conductors, improving electrical conductivity usually increases electronic thermal conductivity, but the total thermal conductivity is still limited by lattice vibrations and defects. Here, the graphene network appears to decouple, at least partially, the electrical and thermal transport pathways: electrons move efficiently through the Cu–graphene hybrid, while phonons are conducted through the graphene sheets and across well-bonded interfaces. This opens possibilities for next-generation conductors in high-power electronics, electric vehicles, aerospace systems, and flexible devices, where both Joule heating and heat dissipation are critical. A conductor with lower resistivity than copper can reduce resistive losses, while a thermal conductivity higher than copper can more effectively remove generated heat. The use of silk fibroin as a renewable, nitrogen-containing precursor and microwave plasma as a rapid fabrication method also offers a potentially scalable and environmentally benign route compared with conventional high-temperature chemical vapor deposition or solution processing.

Nevertheless, several questions remain before this material can be widely adopted. The precise relationship between nitrogen bonding configuration, Cu–graphene interface chemistry, and transport properties should be quantified through X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, electron energy-loss spectroscopy, and temperature-dependent electrical and thermal measurements. The role of film thickness, plasma power, treatment time, and silk fibroin concentration must be systematically optimized, because these parameters will affect graphene quality, nitrogen content, and Cu grain structure. Long-term stability under ambient conditions, oxidation resistance, adhesion to substrates, and mechanical flexibility also require evaluation. In addition, independent round-robin measurements using four-point probe, van der Pauw, and transient thermoreflectance methods will be important to confirm the reported values and to separate intrinsic composite properties from substrate or contact contributions. If these challenges are addressed, the N-doped graphene–copper nanocomposite could become a viable platform for advanced conductors and thermal management materials.

In conclusion, we have demonstrated a nitrogen-doped graphene–copper nanocomposite fabricated by microwave plasma treatment of silk fibroin on a copper substrate. The composite exhibits an ultralow room-temperature electrical resistivity of 0.16 µΩ·cm and a high thermal conductivity of 538 W/m·K, corresponding to 138% of copper. These properties originate from the synergistic combination of nitrogen-doped graphene conductive pathways, strong Cu–graphene interfacial coupling, and a dense percolating microstructure. The results establish a promising strategy for designing next-generation conductors that simultaneously minimize electrical losses and enhance heat dissipation.

Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic inflammatory and neurodegenerative disorder of the central nervous system, and relapsing forms of MS (RMS), including relapsing–remitting MS (RRMS), remain the most common clinical phenotype at diagnosis [1,2]. Over the past three decades, disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) have transformed the management of RMS by reducing relapse frequency, limiting magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) lesion accrual, and delaying disability progression [2,3]. Nevertheless, therapeutic decision-making remains complex: efficacy must be balanced against long-term safety, tolerability, monitoring requirements, and patient adherence. Within this expanding treatment landscape, interferon beta (IFN beta) therapies continue to occupy an important position because of their established efficacy, familiar safety profile, and extensive post-marketing experience [3,4].

IFN beta agents were the first approved immunomodulatory treatments for RMS and have been used clinically for more than two decades [3,5]. Their mechanisms of action include modulation of T-cell activation, alteration of cytokine networks, inhibition of immune cell trafficking across the blood–brain barrier, and promotion of anti-inflammatory pathways [4,5]. Randomised controlled trials and long-term observational studies have consistently demonstrated reductions in relapse rates and inflammatory MRI activity, although their effects on disability progression are more modest than those of some newer high-efficacy therapies [5,6]. Importantly, IFN beta therapies are generally considered to have a favourable benefit–risk profile, but their use is frequently complicated by adverse events (AEs) that can undermine adherence and persistence [6,7].

The most frequently reported AEs associated with subcutaneous (SC) IFN beta treatment are injection site reactions (ISRs) and influenza-like illness (ILI) [7,8]. ISRs may include erythema, pain, swelling, induration, pruritus, and, less commonly, skin necrosis or lipoatrophy. ILI typically manifests as fever, chills, myalgia, arthralgia, headache, and fatigue, and is often most pronounced during treatment initiation [8,9]. Although many of these events are mild to moderate and manageable with counselling, prophylactic antipyretics, dose titration, and injection technique optimisation, they remain a substantial cause of treatment dissatisfaction, non-adherence, and discontinuation in real-world practice [7,9]. Moreover, the underlying pathophysiology of cutaneous reactions to SC IFN beta is incompletely understood, and evidence-based management algorithms are limited [10,11].

Peginterferon beta-1a is a pegylated form of IFN beta-1a that was developed to improve pharmacokinetic exposure and reduce dosing frequency. Pegylation prolongs the half-life of the molecule, resulting in sustained systemic exposure and enabling SC administration at a dose of 125 μg every 2 weeks [12,13]. In the Phase 3 ADVANCE trial, peginterferon beta-1a significantly reduced annualised relapse rate and MRI outcome measures compared with placebo in patients with RRMS after one year [12]. The ATTAIN extension study subsequently demonstrated sustained efficacy with long-term treatment for nearly 6 years [13]. From a safety perspective, the AE profile of peginterferon beta-1a in clinical trials was broadly similar to that of other IFN beta formulations, with mild to moderate ISRs, ILI, pyrexia, and headache being most common [12,13]. However, the reduced dosing frequency may offer practical advantages for patients and clinicians, particularly when tolerability and adherence are key considerations [14].

This study was designed as a structured, consensus-based initiative to develop practical recommendations for the management of adverse events (AEs) associated with peginterferon beta-1a and other interferon beta therapies in multiple sclerosis (MS). The methodology encompassed a comprehensive review of available evidence, a convening of an interdisciplinary expert panel, and a systematic process for formulating and validating clinical guidance.

**Study Design and Setting**
A qualitative, consensus-building study design was employed. The primary objective was to synthesize evidence from the literature with the collective clinical experience of a diverse group of specialists to address a identified gap in the management of interferon-related side effects, particularly injection site reactions (ISRs) [1, 2]. The initiative was conducted under the auspices of a joint German-Austrian expert board, with the logistical and organizational support provided by an independent medical education agency.

**Panel Composition and Selection**
An interdisciplinary panel of eleven experts was convened in July 2016. The panel was purposefully composed to include a balanced representation of relevant clinical specialties and practice settings. The members were selected based on their recognized expertise in MS management and their active clinical practice in either Germany or Austria. The final panel consisted of seven neurologists with a specialisation in MS, three dermatologists with experience in managing cutaneous adverse events, and one MS-certified nurse. The neurologists and MS nurse were affiliated with either university hospitals or specialised private MS clinics, ensuring a broad perspective on patient management in different healthcare delivery models. The dermatologists were included to provide specific expertise on the pathophysiology and treatment of skin-related AEs, an area identified as underrepresented in previous management guidelines [3].

**Data Sources and Evidence Review**
Prior to the panel meeting, a targeted literature review was conducted to identify and summarize relevant data. The search strategy was designed to capture publications on the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of interferon beta therapies, with a specific focus on peginterferon beta-1a. Key sources included the pivotal Phase 3 ADVANCE trial [4] and its long-term extension, the ATTAIN study [5], as well as other registration trials for interferon beta products. Literature on the epidemiology, classification, and management of ISRs and influenza-like illness (ILI) was also reviewed [6, 7]. This evidence dossier was distributed to all panel members two weeks in advance of the meeting to ensure they were fully briefed on the current landscape of data.

**Consensus Process and Meeting Conduct**
The consensus meeting was held on 9 July 2016 in Munich, Germany. The proceedings were moderated by a non-voting chairperson to facilitate discussion and ensure all participants had an opportunity to contribute. The meeting agenda was structured into three main phases:

1.  **Evidence Presentation:** A summary of the pre-circulated literature review was presented, highlighting key data on the pharmacological profile of peginterferon beta-1a, the incidence and nature of AEs from clinical trials, and existing management strategies.
2.  **Structured Discussion:** The panel was then divided into two working groups (one focused on neurological/systemic AEs and one on dermatological AEs) to discuss specific clinical scenarios and challenges. Each group was tasked with identifying best practices for prevention, assessment, and treatment of AEs, drawing on both the evidence and their personal clinical experience. A key focus was on bridging the gap between neurological and dermatological perspectives to create a unified management algorithm [3].
3.  **Plenary Consensus Development:** Following the breakout sessions, the entire panel reconvened to discuss and refine the recommendations proposed by each group. A modified nominal group technique was used to achieve consensus [8]. Each recommendation was discussed, amended, and then voted upon. Consensus was defined *a priori* as agreement from at least 80% of the panel members. In cases where consensus was not reached, the point was discussed further until a compromise was found or it was decided to classify the statement as a point of ongoing debate.

**Recommendation Formulation and Validation**
The draft recommendations generated during the meeting were compiled into a preliminary manuscript. This document was then circulated electronically to all panel members for a final review and validation. Panelists were asked to provide written feedback, suggest revisions for clarity and accuracy, and confirm their final agreement with the content. The manuscript was revised iteratively based on this feedback until all authors approved the final version. The recommendations were structured to be practical and actionable for clinicians in daily practice, covering topics such as patient education, prophylactic measures, and step-wise therapeutic interventions for ISRs and ILI. The final report integrates these consensus-based recommendations with the supporting evidence from the literature, providing a comprehensive framework for the interdisciplinary management of patients receiving interferon beta therapies.

Consensus was reached across six management domains: recognition and classification of injection site reactions (ISRs), management of influenza-like illness (ILI), laboratory and organ-specific monitoring, dermatological referral, patient education and adherence support, and interdisciplinary communication. The board agreed that although the adverse event (AE) profile of peginterferon beta-1a is broadly consistent with that of other interferon beta formulations, its prolonged half-life and reduced dosing frequency may alter the practical burden of AEs and the timing of supportive interventions [1,2]. Recommendations were therefore framed for daily practice rather than as a replacement for product labelling [3,4].

Injection site reactions. ISRs were identified as the most frequent AE associated with subcutaneous (SC) interferon beta therapy, including peginterferon beta-1a. In the pivotal programme, most ISRs were mild to moderate, typically consisting of erythema, pain, pruritus, swelling, or induration, and only rarely led to treatment discontinuation [1,2]. The board recommended systematic assessment of injection technique, site rotation, and skin hygiene at every clinical contact. Injections should be administered into healthy, non-inflamed skin, with rotation among approved sites and avoidance of repeated injection into the same area within a short interval. Cold compresses before injection and avoidance of vigorous massage afterwards were considered useful for local discomfort. For inflammatory papules or plaques, short-term topical medium-potency corticosteroids were recommended, whereas antihistamines were preferred for pruritus. Ulceration, necrosis, or persistent induration warranted interruption of injections at the affected site and dermatological review [5].

Influenza-like illness. ILI remained the most common systemic AE. Symptoms typically begin within 24 hours of injection, resolve within 24–48 hours, and diminish over the first months of therapy [1,3]. The panel recommended proactive premedication with paracetamol or a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug 30–60 minutes before injection and, if needed, 6–8 hours afterwards. Evening dosing, adequate hydration, and rest were advised. Because peginterferon beta-1a is administered every two weeks, the board noted that scheduling injections before non-working days may improve tolerability and adherence. Persistent or atypical systemic symptoms should prompt evaluation for infection, thyroid dysfunction, or other intercurrent illness rather than being attributed automatically to interferon therapy [3,6].

Laboratory and organ-specific monitoring. Baseline assessment should include complete blood count, liver enzymes, thyroid function, and screening for depression. During treatment, the board recommended monitoring at approximately 1, 3, and 6 months, and thereafter at clinically appropriate intervals [3,4]. Transient elevations in aminotransferases are common and usually asymptomatic; however, values exceeding five times the upper limit of normal should trigger interruption or discontinuation according to labelling and clinical judgement. Thyroid dysfunction may emerge during interferon therapy, and TSH should be checked when fatigue, weight change, or mood disturbance occurs. Depression and suicidal ideation require active screening, particularly in patients with a psychiatric history, because interferon beta therapy may exacerbate underlying mood disorders [6].

Dermatological assessment and referral. The board acknowledged that current evidence on the pathogenesis and optimal management of SC interferon-associated skin reactions is limited, and that dermatologists were infrequently involved in pivotal trials [1,5]. Dermatological input was considered essential for atypical, severe, or recurrent ISRs. A practical classification was proposed: acute inflammatory reactions, chronic indurated or lipoatrophic lesions, and ulcerative or necrotic reactions. Differential diagnosis should include cellulitis, contact dermatitis, panniculitis, and vasculitic lesions. Referral was recommended for lesions persisting beyond one month, those with ulceration or necrosis, or those causing functional impairment. Biopsy was reserved for diagnostic uncertainty. In cases of severe or recurrent ISR, temporary interruption of peginterferon beta-1a and consideration of an alternative disease-modifying therapy were advised [5,7].

Patient education and adherence. The MS nurse was identified as central to AE prevention and management. Structured education should cover injection technique, aseptic preparation, site rotation, expected local and systemic reactions, and when to seek help. A symptom diary and scheduled follow-up telephone contact were recommended to detect tolerability problems early. The board agreed that proactive management of ISRs and ILI can reduce non-adherence and discontinuation, which are relevant because interferon beta therapies require long-term persistence to maintain clinical benefit [2,6,7].

Interdisciplinary communication. Finally, the panel recommended clear referral pathways among neurologists, dermatologists, and MS nurses. Standardised documentation of ISR morphology, duration, and treatment response was advised. For complex cases, joint review or written dermatological advice should accompany decisions to continue, interrupt, or switch therapy. This interdisciplinary approach was considered feasible in both university and private practice settings and may improve patient confidence in interferon beta-based treatment [5-7].

The management of relapsing multiple sclerosis (MS) has evolved considerably, yet interferon beta (IFN β) therapies remain a cornerstone of treatment, valued for their long-established efficacy and favourable benefit-risk profile [1]. The introduction of subcutaneous (SC) peginterferon beta-1a 125 μg, administered every two weeks, represented a significant advancement by offering a less frequent dosing schedule through pegylation, which prolongs the drug's half-life and systemic exposure [2]. While its efficacy has been demonstrated in pivotal trials such as ADVANCE and its long-term extension ATTAIN [3, 4], the successful integration of this therapy into clinical practice hinges not only on its efficacy but also on the proactive and effective management of its adverse event (AE) profile. The interdisciplinary board's discussions, summarized in this report, underscore a critical paradigm shift: moving from a reactive approach to AEs towards a proactive, integrated, and patient-centred management strategy.

**Clinical Implications of the Adverse Event Profile**

The AE profile of peginterferon beta-1a is consistent with that of other IFN β formulations, with injection site reactions (ISRs) and influenza-like illness (ILI) being the most frequently reported events [3]. Although these AEs are typically mild to moderate in severity, their cumulative burden can significantly impact a patient's quality of life, leading to poor adherence and ultimately, therapy discontinuation [5]. The two-week dosing interval of peginterferon beta-1a may mitigate this burden by halving the frequency of injections and associated ISRs compared to other SC IFNs. However, the extended half-life also means that if an AE occurs, its duration may be prolonged, necessitating robust management plans. The board's consensus highlights that the key to preserving therapeutic benefit is not merely managing the AE after it appears, but anticipating it and empowering the patient with strategies for prevention and self-management from the outset.

**The Critical Role of Interdisciplinary Collaboration**

A central theme emerging from the board's deliberations is the indispensable role of interdisciplinary collaboration, particularly between neurologists and dermatologists. Historically, the characterization and management of ISRs in MS clinical trials have been the primary domain of neurologists, with dermatological expertise rarely consulted [6]. This siloed approach can lead to suboptimal outcomes. The board emphasizes that a dermatologist's specialized training is crucial for accurately diagnosing and managing the spectrum of cutaneous AEs, which can range from benign erythema to more complex reactions like lipoatrophy or, rarely, severe cutaneous adverse reactions. Early dermatological consultation for persistent, worsening, or atypical skin reactions is therefore strongly recommended. This collaborative model ensures that patients receive expert care for both the neurological disease and its dermatological sequelae, preventing unnecessary treatment cessation and improving overall patient satisfaction and adherence.

**Proactive and Integrated Management Strategies**

Based on the synthesis of literature and collective clinical experience, the board advocates for a structured, multi-pronged approach to AE management.

1.  **Patient Education and Expectation Management:** Before initiating therapy, comprehensive patient education is paramount. This includes a clear explanation of potential AEs, their expected timing and duration, and the rationale for proactive management. Patients should be counselled on the correct injection technique, including rotation of injection sites, and the use of prophylactic measures for ILI, such as pre- or post-injection administration of antipyretics and NSAIDs [7]. This empowerment fosters a sense of control and reduces anxiety, which can amplify the perception of AEs.

2.  **Systematic Assessment and Grading:** Clinicians should employ a standardized approach to assess and grade ISRs and other AEs at each visit. Utilizing a consistent grading scale allows for objective tracking of severity over time and informs the intensity of the management intervention. A thorough skin examination, with attention to the injection sites, is a mandatory component of follow-up visits.

3.  **Stepwise Management Algorithms:** The board recommends a stepwise approach to ISR management. For mild reactions, continuation of therapy with local symptomatic treatment (e.g., cool compresses, topical corticosteroids) is appropriate. For moderate reactions, in addition to local measures, a temporary switch to a different injection site or a short course of oral antihistamines may be considered. For severe or persistent ISRs, a dermatology referral is essential. Management may include more potent topical or intralesional corticosteroids, and in rare cases, a switch to an alternative MS therapy may be warranted. For ILI, a scheduled regimen of NSAIDs or antipyretics, taken around the time of injection, can significantly attenuate symptoms.

4.  **The Role of the MS Nurse:** The MS nurse is a pivotal figure in this process, serving as the primary point of contact for the patient. They play a vital role in reinforcing education, providing ongoing support, and facilitating communication between the patient, neurologist, and dermatologist, ensuring a seamless and coordinated care pathway.

**Conclusion**

Peginterferon beta-1a offers an effective, less frequently dosed therapeutic option for patients with relapsing MS. Its long-term success in clinical practice is contingent upon a sophisticated and proactive approach to AE management. The recommendations from this German-Austrian interdisciplinary board advocate for a paradigm shift away from a reactive, neurologist-centric model towards a proactive, patient-centred, and interdisciplinary strategy. By integrating rigorous patient education, systematic assessment, and collaborative care involving dermatology and MS nursing, clinicians can effectively mitigate the burden of ISRs and ILI. This approach has the potential to improve adherence, enhance patient quality of life, and ultimately optimize the sustained benefit of peginterferon beta-1a and other IFN β therapies for individuals living with MS. Future research should focus on prospectively validating these management algorithms and further elucidating the pathophysiological mechanisms of IFN-induced skin reactions to develop more targeted preventive strategies.

The landscape of colorectal cancer (CRC) treatment has been significantly reshaped by the advent of oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy regimens, which have become a cornerstone of adjuvant and palliative care, substantially improving survival outcomes for patients with colorectal adenocarcinoma [1, 2]. However, the therapeutic efficacy of oxaliplatin is frequently compromised by a dose-limiting toxicity: chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN). CIPN is a debilitating condition characterized by sensory, motor, and autonomic nerve dysfunction, manifesting as paresthesia, dysesthesia, numbness, and pain, predominantly in a distal, symmetrical "stocking-and-glove" distribution [3]. The prevalence of CIPN in this patient population is high, with a significant proportion experiencing symptoms that persist long after the cessation of treatment, thereby evolving into a chronic and often irreversible health issue [4].

The clinical sequelae of CIPN extend far beyond mere sensory disturbances. A primary and profound consequence is the restriction of daily activity (RDA). The functional impairments caused by neuropathic symptoms—such as difficulty with fine motor tasks like buttoning a shirt, an unsteady gait, or an increased risk of falls—directly impede a patient's ability to perform essential activities of daily living, maintain social roles, and preserve their independence [5, 6]. This functional decline is not a passive outcome but an active stressor that can precipitate a cascade of negative psychosocial consequences. The loss of autonomy and the inability to engage in valued life activities can lead to significant frustration, social isolation, and a diminished sense of self-worth, fundamentally altering a patient's life experience during and after cancer treatment [7].

In parallel with these functional challenges, CRC patients with CIPN often contend with a considerable psychological burden. The chronic nature of neuropathic pain, the uncertainty of its resolution, and the constant reminder of the cancer diagnosis can foster a state of profound psychological distress. This is frequently manifested as negative mood, encompassing symptoms of depression, anxiety, anger, and confusion [8]. The relationship between cancer-related symptoms and mood disturbance is well-documented, but the specific interplay between the functional limitations imposed by CIPN and the resulting emotional toll is a critical area of inquiry. The experience of RDA can be a potent driver of negative mood, as patients grieve the loss of their former capabilities and struggle with the perceived burden on their families and caregivers [9, 10].

Ultimately, the convergence of these factors—the physical symptoms of CIPN, the functional limitations of RDA, and the psychological weight of negative mood—poses a significant threat to a patient's overall quality of life (QoL). QoL is a multidimensional construct that encompasses physical, functional, emotional, and social well-being, and it is a paramount outcome in oncology, reflecting the patient's subjective appraisal of their life in the context of their illness and treatment [11]. While it is intuitive that CIPN, RDA, and negative mood all negatively impact QoL, the precise nature of their interrelationships remains incompletely understood. Elucidating these pathways is essential for developing targeted and effective supportive care interventions.

Previous research has often examined these variables in isolation or has been limited to simple correlational analyses. For instance, studies have independently linked greater CIPN severity to poorer QoL and have established a connection between negative mood and reduced QoL in cancer patients [12, 13]. However, the potential mediating role of mood in the relationship between functional limitation and QoL has not been rigorously explored in this specific population. It is plausible that RDA does not influence QoL solely through direct, functional pathways. Instead, the experience of activity restriction may lead to a deterioration in mood, which in turn, exerts a powerful negative influence on a patient's overall QoL. This mediation model posits that negative mood is a critical intermediary mechanism through which the functional consequences of CIPN translate into a diminished quality of life.

Therefore, the primary objective of this study was to investigate the complex relationships among the severity of CIPN, the extent of RDA, the presence of negative mood, and QoL in colorectal adenocarcinoma patients who have received oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy. We aimed to test a hypothesized model wherein the effect of RDA on QoL is mediated by negative mood. By employing a cross-sectional design and utilizing validated instruments to measure each construct, this study seeks to disentangle these intricate relationships. We hypothesized that greater RDA would be associated with more severe negative mood, which would, in turn, be associated with poorer QoL. Specifically, we predicted that negative mood would serve as a significant mediator, accounting for a substantial portion of the effect of RDA on QoL. Uncovering this mediational pathway will provide a more nuanced understanding of the patient experience with CIPN and will underscore the clinical imperative to address not only the physical symptoms of neuropathy but also the psychological distress that so profoundly shapes the quality of life for these cancer survivors. The findings are expected to inform the development of holistic interventions that target mood adaptation as a key strategy to improve QoL, even in the face of persistent functional limitations.

### Study Design and Setting
This cross-sectional, correlational study was conducted in the oncology outpatient departments of participating tertiary hospitals. The primary objective was to examine the interrelationships among chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN), restriction of daily activity (RDA), negative mood, and quality of life (QoL) in patients with colorectal adenocarcinoma who had received oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy. Eligible participants were adults aged 18 years or older with histologically confirmed colorectal adenocarcinoma, a documented history of at least one cycle of oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy, and clinical evidence of CIPN. CIPN was defined as the presence of symmetrical distal sensory or sensorimotor symptoms consistent with oxaliplatin neurotoxicity, as assessed by the treating oncologist and confirmed by the Neuropathic Pain Symptom Inventory. Exclusion criteria were pre-existing peripheral neuropathy due to other causes (e.g., diabetes mellitus, vitamin B12 deficiency, alcoholism, or hereditary neuropathy), central nervous system metastases, severe cognitive impairment, active psychiatric illness that could interfere with self-report, or inability to communicate in the study language. A convenience sample of 103 patients was enrolled during routine follow-up visits. The study was reported in accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines for cross-sectional studies [1].

### Participants and Procedures
Potentially eligible patients were identified from medical records and approached consecutively during scheduled oncology visits. Trained research assistants explained the purpose and procedures of the study, confirmed eligibility, and obtained written informed consent before data collection. Participants completed a structured demographic and clinical information form and four validated self-report instruments in a quiet room. When necessary, research assistants read items aloud to participants with visual or literacy limitations, without interpreting or modifying item content. Clinical variables, including cancer stage, chemotherapy regimen, cumulative oxaliplatin dose, number of chemotherapy cycles, and time since chemotherapy completion, were extracted from medical records. All data were anonymized using unique study codes. The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board of each participating hospital and was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to any study-related procedure.

### Measures
CIPN severity was assessed using the Neuropathic Pain Symptom Inventory (NPSI) [2]. The NPSI is a 10-item self-report measure that evaluates spontaneous pain, evoked pain, and paresthesia/dysesthesia. Each item is rated on a 0–10 numerical rating scale, and the total score ranges from 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating greater neuropathic pain severity. The NPSI has demonstrated satisfactory reliability and validity in oncology populations.

RDA was evaluated using the Screening of Activity Limitation and Safety Awareness (SASA) scale [3]. The SASA scale comprises 20 items that assess activity limitation and safety awareness in daily functioning. Items are scored on a five-point Likert-type scale, and higher activity limitation scores indicate greater restriction in daily activities. The SASA scale has been widely used to quantify functional limitations associated with peripheral neuropathy.

Negative mood was measured using the Profile of Mood States Short Form (POMS-SF) [4]. The POMS-SF contains 30 adjectives rated on a five-point scale from 0 (“not at all”) to 4 (“extremely”). It yields six subscales: tension-anxiety, depression-dejection, anger-hostility, vigor-activity, fatigue-inertia, and confusion-bewilderment. A total mood disturbance score was calculated by summing the negative subscales and subtracting the vigor-activity score, with higher scores reflecting greater negative mood. The POMS-SF has established reliability and validity in cancer patients.

QoL was assessed using the Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy-Colorectal scale version 4 (FACT-C v4) [5]. The FACT-C v4 includes the Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy-General (FACT-G) domains—physical, social/family, emotional, and functional well-being—plus a colorectal cancer subscale. Items are rated on a five-point scale, and higher total scores indicate better QoL. The FACT-C v4 has been validated in colorectal cancer populations and is sensitive to treatment-related symptoms.
