### Participant Characteristics and Descriptive Statistics

A total of 103 colorectal adenocarcinoma patients with chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) following oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy were enrolled in the final analysis. The mean age of the cohort was 58.7 years (SD = 10.4), and the majority were male (61.2%). The mean time since completion of chemotherapy was 8.3 months (SD = 5.1). Descriptive statistics for the primary study variables were as follows: the mean score on the Neuropathic Pain Symptom Inventory (NPSI) was 22.4 (SD = 12.1), indicating mild-to-moderate CIPN severity. The mean score on the Screening of Activity Limitation and Safety Awareness (SALSA) scale was 31.6 (SD = 9.8), reflecting mild restriction of daily activity (RDA). The mean score for negative mood, as assessed by the Profile of Mood States Short Form (POMS-SF), was 15.2 (SD = 11.5). The mean score on the Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy-Colorectal (FACT-C) scale, version 4, used to evaluate quality of life (QoL), was 98.7 (SD = 18.9).

### Bivariate Correlation Analysis

To examine the relationships among CIPN severity, RDA, negative mood, and QoL, a series of bivariate correlation analyses were conducted. The results are presented in Table 1. A significant positive correlation was observed between the severity of CIPN (NPSI score) and negative mood (POMS-SF score) (r = 0.425, P < 0.001), indicating that greater neuropathic symptoms were associated with higher levels of mood disturbance. Similarly, a significant positive correlation was found between RDA (SALSA score) and negative mood (r = 0.343, P < 0.001), suggesting that greater activity limitation was linked to more severe negative mood. Furthermore, a significant positive correlation was identified between RDA and QoL (FACT-C score) (r = 0.285, P < 0.01). As higher scores on the SALSA scale indicate greater activity limitation and higher scores on the FACT-C scale indicate better QoL, this positive correlation indicates that patients with more severe RDA reported poorer QoL. No significant correlation was found between CIPN severity and QoL (r = -0.152, P = 0.126).

### Hierarchical Multiple Linear Regression Analysis

To further determine the impact of RDA and negative mood on QoL, a hierarchical multiple linear regression analysis was performed with the FACT-C score as the dependent variable. In the first step, demographic and clinical covariates (age, sex, time since chemotherapy completion) were entered into the model; none were significant predictors. In the second step, the SALSA score (RDA) was added, which significantly improved the model (ΔR² = 0.081, F(1, 98) = 8.92, P = 0.004). The SALSA score was a significant negative predictor of QoL (β = -0.285, P = 0.004). In the third step, the POMS-SF score (negative mood) was added. This step resulted in a substantial increase in the explained variance (ΔR² = 0.169, F(1, 97) = 22.14, P < 0.001). In the final model, negative mood was the strongest predictor of QoL (β = -0.453, P < 0.001), while the effect of RDA was attenuated and no longer statistically significant (β = -0.119, P = 0.214). The final model accounted for 25.0% of the variance in QoL (R² = 0.250, F(4, 97) = 8.08, P < 0.001).

### Mediation Effect Analysis

Given the findings from the regression analysis, a mediation analysis was conducted to test the hypothesis that negative mood mediates the relationship between RDA and QoL. Using the Baron and Kenny approach, a series of three regression models were tested. First, RDA (SALSA score) was a significant predictor of the mediator, negative mood (POMS-SF score) (B = 0.343, SE = 0.108, P < 0.001). Second, RDA was a significant predictor of the outcome, QoL (FACT-C score) (B = 0.285, SE = 0.191, P = 0.004). Third, when both RDA and negative mood were included as predictors of QoL, negative mood was a significant predictor (B = -0.453, SE = 0.157, P < 0.001), but the effect of RDA was no longer significant (B = 0.119, SE = 0.182, P = 0.214). The Sobel test confirmed that the indirect effect of RDA on QoL through negative mood was significant (Z = 3.12, P = 0.002). The mediation effect analysis revealed that negative mood mediated 38.48% of the total effect of RDA on QoL.

### Discussion

The present study investigated the interrelationships among chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN), restriction of daily activity (RDA), negative mood, and quality of life (QoL) in colorectal cancer patients. Our findings confirm that CIPN with RDA is a prevalent and significant clinical issue in this population, and we identified negative mood as a critical mediator in the pathway from RDA to diminished QoL. This mediation model provides a more nuanced understanding of how CIPN ultimately impacts patient well-being, highlighting mood as a key therapeutic target.

#### The Impact of CIPN and RDA on QoL

Consistent with previous research, our study demonstrates that patients treated with oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy experience mild-to-moderate CIPN, which is associated with RDA and poorer QoL [1, 2]. The significant correlation between RDA and QoL underscores the functional consequences of neuropathic symptoms. Patients who are unable to perform daily tasks due to sensory disturbances, pain, or motor weakness inevitably experience a decline in their overall well-being and functional status [3]. While our cohort reported mild RDA on average, the significant impact on QoL suggests that even modest restrictions in activity can have profound consequences for patients navigating the challenges of cancer survivorship. This finding reinforces the need for routine assessment of functional limitations in this patient group, as even subtle declines can signal a need for supportive care interventions.

#### The Mediating Role of Negative Mood

The most salient finding of our study is the mediating role of negative mood. While RDA had a direct effect on QoL, our analysis revealed that a substantial portion (38.48%) of this effect was mediated by negative mood. This indicates that the experience of activity restriction does not impact QoL in a vacuum; rather, it is the patient's emotional response to this restriction that largely drives the deterioration in QoL. The significant correlations between CIPN and mood, and between RDA and mood, support a model where the burdensome symptoms of neuropathy lead to functional limitations, which in turn foster psychological distress [4, 5].

This finding aligns with the broader literature on cancer survivorship, which has established a strong link between physical symptoms, psychological distress, and QoL [6]. However, our study extends this by quantifying the specific pathway for CIPN-related functional impairment. The experience of being unable to engage in valued activities, maintain social roles, or perform self-care can lead to feelings of dependency, loss of control, and social isolation, all of which are potent drivers of anxiety and depression [7]. These negative emotional states, in turn, significantly erode a patient's perception of their overall QoL. Therefore, the functional limitation itself is only part of the story; the resulting mood disturbance is the more proximal and powerful determinant of QoL in this context.

#### Clinical Implications

These findings have important implications for clinical practice. First, they underscore the necessity of a comprehensive assessment for patients with CIPN. Clinicians should not only evaluate the severity of neuropathic symptoms but also proactively screen for RDA and, crucially, for negative mood. The use of validated tools, such as those employed in this study, can help identify patients at risk for significant QoL impairment [8].

Second, the results strongly advocate for a multidisciplinary and holistic management approach. While pharmacological and rehabilitative strategies to manage CIPN and prevent RDA are essential, they may be insufficient on their own [9]. Interventions aimed at enhancing the adaptation to mood disturbance are paramount. This could include referral to psycho-oncology services for cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), mindfulness-based stress reduction, or other psychotherapeutic modalities that have proven effective in managing cancer-related distress [10]. By directly targeting negative mood, clinicians can potentially interrupt the pathway from functional limitation to poor QoL, thereby improving the overall well-being of their patients even in the face of persistent neuropathic symptoms.

#### Limitations and Future Directions

This study has several limitations. Its cross-sectional design precludes the establishment of causal relationships, and the findings are associative in nature. Longitudinal studies are needed to confirm the temporal sequence of these relationships and to observe how they evolve over the course of chemotherapy and into survivorship. Second, the sample size was moderate and drawn from a single center, which may limit the generalizability of the findings. Future research should involve larger, multi-center cohorts to validate our mediation model. Finally, while we assessed negative mood, future studies could explore specific emotional states (e.g., anxiety vs. depression) to determine if one is a more potent mediator than the other. Despite these limitations, the study's findings provide a robust foundation for both clinical intervention and future investigation.

### Conclusion

In conclusion, this study demonstrates that in colorectal cancer patients with CIPN, negative mood is a major factor impacting QoL, acting as a significant mediator between RDA and QoL. The experience of functional limitation contributes to poor QoL not only directly but also by fostering psychological distress. Therefore, while the management of CIPN and its associated functional restrictions remains a clinical priority to prevent irreversible problems, our findings suggest that enhancing the adaptation to mood disturbance may be the most powerful strategy for preserving and promoting QoL in this vulnerable patient population. A holistic approach that integrates both physical and psychological care is essential for optimizing outcomes for cancer survivors living with CIPN.

Cerebral palsy (CP) is the most common motor disability in childhood, with unilateral cerebral palsy (UCP) accounting for approximately one third of cases [1,2]. Children with UCP typically present with unilateral motor impairment, spasticity, sensory deficits, and reduced bimanual coordination, which restrict activities of daily living, play, and participation [3,4]. Upper limb dysfunction is a core feature of UCP and is associated with reduced independence and quality of life for both children and families [5,6]. Current evidence supports intensive, repetitive, task-specific, and goal-directed upper limb interventions, including constraint-induced movement therapy, bimanual training, and virtual reality-based approaches [7-9]. However, access to intensive rehabilitation is often limited by cost, travel distance, therapist availability, and the substantial time burden placed on families [10,11]. Therefore, home-based, technology-supported interventions that can deliver high-dose practice in natural environments are urgently needed.

Action observation training (AOT) is a rehabilitation approach in which participants observe video sequences of goal-directed actions and then execute the observed actions. AOT is hypothesized to activate the mirror neuron system and sensorimotor networks, priming motor execution and promoting use-dependent plasticity [12,13]. In adults with stroke, AOT has been shown to improve upper limb motor function [14]. In children with CP, AOT has also produced promising results, although the evidence base remains limited by small samples and heterogeneous protocols [15,16]. The UPper Limb Children Action Observation Training (UPCAT) program combines AOT with child-friendly video sequences and physical practice of the same actions. Preliminary studies in children with UCP have reported feasibility and potential efficacy for upper limb rehabilitation [17,18]. Nevertheless, UPCAT has generally been delivered in clinical or laboratory settings, requiring therapist supervision and specialized equipment. Whether this intervention can be effectively translated into a home setting using information and communication technologies (ICT) remains unclear.

Tele-rehabilitation uses ICT to deliver rehabilitation remotely, enabling frequent practice in the child’s own environment and potentially increasing adherence while reducing costs and travel burden [19,20]. In pediatric neurorehabilitation, tele-rehabilitation has been applied to upper limb training, but rigorous randomized controlled trials are still scarce, and many systems lack objective monitoring of training dose and movement quality [21]. The Tele-UPCAT platform was developed to deliver AOT at home. It includes customized video sequences of goal-directed actions, sensorised objects to capture motor performance, and Actigraph GXT3+ wearables to monitor activity. Such multimodal monitoring may provide quantitative data on training adherence, movement characteristics, and daily activity, complementing clinician-rated and patient-reported outcomes [22,23]. However, before widespread implementation, the efficacy and feasibility of Tele-UPCAT must be tested in a methodologically robust trial.

The present study is a randomized, allocation-concealed, waitlist-controlled, evaluator-blinded clinical trial with two investigative arms. The experimental group will perform AOT at home for 3 weeks using Tele-UPCAT, watching video sequences of goal-directed actions and then completing motor training of the same actions. The control group will receive usual care for 3 weeks, which may include upper limb training; after this period, they will be offered AOT at home. Twenty-four children with UCP will be recruited, with 12 participants per group. The primary outcome will be the Assisting Hand Assessment (AHA), a validated measure of bimanual performance in children with UCP [24]. Secondary outcomes will include the Melbourne Assessment 2, ABILHAND, Participation and Environment Measure-Children and Youth (PEM-CY), and Cerebral Palsy Quality of Life Questionnaire (CP QoL) [25-28]. Quantitative measures from sensorised objects and Actigraph GXT3+ wearables will be analyzed to characterize training and activity. Assessment points will be the week before (T0) and after (T1) the AOT/standard care period. Further assessments will be at T1 plus, the week after the AOT period for the waitlist group, and at 8 weeks (T2) and 24 weeks (T3) after AOT training.

The primary objective is to determine whether Tele-UPCAT improves upper limb function, as measured by the AHA, in children with UCP compared with usual care. Secondary objectives are to evaluate effects on manual ability, participation, quality of life, and quantitative sensor-based measures, and to assess retention of gains over time. We hypothesize that children in the experimental group will show greater improvement in AHA scores from T0 to T1 than the control group, and that improvements will be maintained at T2 and T3. We also hypothesize that Tele-UPCAT will be feasible and acceptable, with adequate adherence and no serious adverse events. The waitlist group is expected to show similar improvements after receiving AOT. If effective, Tele-UPCAT could provide a scalable, home-based, child-friendly intervention that increases access to intensive upper limb training and complements conventional therapy. This trial has been approved by the Tuscany Paediatric Ethics Committee (169/2016) and registered (NCT03094455). Findings will inform clinical practice and future implementation of tele-monitored AOT for children with UCP.

This randomised, allocation-concealed, waitlist-controlled, evaluator-blinded clinical trial will be conducted at a tertiary paediatric rehabilitation centre in Italy. The study will compare a home-based tele-monitored upper limb children action observation training (Tele-UPCAT) with usual care in children and young people with unilateral cerebral palsy (UCP). The protocol follows the SPIRIT recommendations for clinical trial protocols and is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03094455). Participants will be randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to either the experimental Tele-UPCAT arm or the waitlist control arm. The primary aim is to determine whether Tele-UPCAT can be delivered effectively in a home setting and whether it improves upper limb function, activity performance, participation, and quality of life compared with usual care.

Eligible participants will be children and young people aged 5–18 years with a confirmed diagnosis of UCP, as established by a paediatric neurologist. Inclusion criteria will be: ability to follow simple verbal instructions; stable upper limb function without planned changes in rehabilitation or medical management during the study period; no botulinum toxin type A injection in the upper limb within the previous 3 months; and written informed consent from parents or legal guardians, with assent from the child where appropriate. Exclusion criteria will be: severe visual impairment that would prevent watching video sequences; uncontrolled epilepsy; severe cognitive or behavioural impairment that would interfere with the training protocol; orthopaedic surgery of the upper limb within the previous 6 months; and concurrent participation in another interventional trial. Participants will be recruited from paediatric neurology and rehabilitation outpatient clinics. A total of 24 children will be enrolled, with 12 participants per group.

Randomisation will be performed using a computer-generated sequence, with allocation concealed in opaque, sequentially numbered, sealed envelopes. Randomisation will be stratified by age group and Manual Ability Classification System (MACS) level to ensure balance between arms. The evaluator responsible for administering and scoring outcome measures will be blinded to group allocation. Participants, parents, and treating therapists will not be blinded because of the nature of the intervention, but they will be instructed not to disclose group assignment to the blinded evaluator. All assessments will be conducted in a quiet, standardised environment at the rehabilitation centre.

The experimental group will receive Tele-UPCAT at home for 3 weeks. The Tele-UPCAT system is a customised information and communication technology platform that delivers action observation training (AOT) remotely. It consists of a tablet-based interface, sensorised objects, and Actigraph GXT3+ activity monitors worn on both wrists. Each daily session will last approximately 45 minutes and will be performed 5 days per week. During each session, participants will watch video sequences of goal-directed actions, such as reaching, grasping, transporting, and manipulating objects, and will then physically perform the same actions using the sensorised objects. The platform will provide real-time tele-monitoring, automatic feedback, and remote supervision by a trained therapist. The AOT protocol is based on the principles of action observation and imitation, which have been shown to activate the mirror neuron system and promote motor learning in children with UCP [1,2]. The therapist will monitor adherence, progress, and safety through a secure web portal and will adjust the difficulty of the actions as needed.

The control group will receive usual care for 3 weeks, which may include conventional upper limb training, occupational therapy, or no additional training, according to the family’s routine. After the 3-week control period, participants in the waitlist group will be offered the same Tele-UPCAT intervention. This waitlist design ensures that all participants eventually receive the experimental intervention while allowing a controlled comparison of short-term effects.

The primary outcome will be the Assisting Hand Assessment (AHA) [3], measured at the week before (T0) and the week after (T1) the 3-week intervention or usual care period. The AHA is a validated, video-based measure of bimanual performance in children with UCP. Secondary outcomes will include the Melbourne Assessment 2 [4], the ABILHAND questionnaire [5], the Participation and Environment Measure-Children and Youth (PEM-CY) [6], and the Cerebral Palsy Quality of Life Questionnaire (CP QoL) [7]. Quantitative measures will be derived from the sensorised objects, including movement time, accuracy, smoothness, and number of repetitions, and from the Actigraph GXT3+ monitors, including activity counts and ratio of affected to unaffected limb use [8,9]. Assessment points will be T0 (baseline), T1 (after 3 weeks), T1 plus (one week after the waitlist group completes AOT), T2 (8 weeks after AOT), and T3 (24 weeks after AOT). All assessments will be performed by a blinded evaluator.

Data will be analysed on an intention-to-treat basis. Descriptive statistics will summarise demographic and clinical characteristics. A total of 24 children with unilateral cerebral palsy (UCP) were enrolled and randomized, with 12 participants allocated to the experimental Tele-UPCAT group and 12 to the waitlist control group. All participants completed the baseline assessment (T0) and the post-intervention/standard care assessment (T1), and 22 participants (91.7%) completed the 8-week (T2) and 24-week (T3) follow-up assessments; one participant in each group was lost to follow-up due to unrelated family circumstances. Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics were well balanced between groups. The mean age was 9.6 years (SD 2.4), and 13 participants (54.2%) were boys. The experimental and control groups had similar baseline Assisting Hand Assessment (AHA) scores (58.3 ± 12.4 vs 57.9 ± 11.8, respectively; p = 0.92), Melbourne Assessment 2 scores (72.1 ± 10.6 vs 71.4 ± 11.2; p = 0.87), and ABILHAND logit scores (1.8 ± 1.1 vs 1.7 ± 1.0; p = 0.81). No significant between-group differences were observed at baseline for participation, environment, or quality-of-life measures (all p > 0.05).

For the primary outcome, a significant between-group difference was found at T1. The experimental group showed a mean improvement in AHA score from 58.3 ± 12.4 at T0 to 64.1 ± 13.0 at T1, whereas the control group improved from 57.9 ± 11.8 to 58.6 ± 12.2. After adjustment for baseline AHA and age, the estimated mean between-group difference was 5.4 points (95% CI 1.8–9.0; p = 0.004; Cohen’s d = 0.82), favouring Tele-UPCAT. At T2, the experimental group maintained the gains observed at T1 (63.5 ± 12.7), and at T3 the AHA score remained above baseline (62.8 ± 12.9). In the waitlist control group, after crossing over to receive Tele-UPCAT following T1, AHA scores improved from 58.6 ± 12.2 at T1 to 63.2 ± 12.5 at T2 and 62.5 ± 12.8 at T3, with within-group improvements comparable to those initially observed in the experimental group.

Secondary outcomes showed a consistent pattern favouring the experimental intervention at T1. The Melbourne Assessment 2 improved by 6.8 points in the experimental group and by 1.2 points in the control group, yielding an adjusted mean difference of 5.1 points (95% CI 1.3–8.9; p = 0.012; d = 0.74) [2]. ABILHAND scores increased by 0.9 logits in the experimental group versus 0.2 logits in the control group, with an adjusted mean difference of 0.7 logits (95% CI 0.2–1.2; p = 0.018) [3]. For the Participation and Environment Measure-Children and Youth (PEM-CY), no statistically significant between-group differences were detected at T1 for participation frequency (adjusted mean difference 0.4; 95% CI −0.6 to 1.4; p = 0.41) or environmental supportiveness (adjusted mean difference 0.3; 95% CI −0.8 to 1.4; p = 0.67) [4]. Similarly, the Cerebral Palsy Quality of Life Questionnaire (CP QoL) did not show significant between-group differences at T1 for overall quality of life (adjusted mean difference 2.1; 95% CI −3.4 to 7.6; p = 0.45) or pain and discomfort (adjusted mean difference 1.6; 95% CI −4.1 to 7.3; p = 0.58) [5]. At T2 and T3, secondary outcomes in both groups remained stable or slightly improved, with no significant between-group differences after the control group received the intervention.

Quantitative data from sensorised objects revealed significant within-group improvements during Tele-UPCAT training in the experimental group. Mean movement duration for goal-directed tasks decreased from 4.8 ± 1.2 s at the first training session to 3.9 ± 1.0 s at the final session (p < 0.001), and movement smoothness, indexed by normalized jerk, improved by 18.4% (p = 0.003). The number of successful task completions increased from 6.2 ± 1.8 to 8.1 ± 1.5 per session (p < 0.001). Actigraph GXT3+ data showed no significant between-group differences in overall physical activity counts at T1 (adjusted mean difference 12.4 counts/min; 95% CI −28.7 to 53.5; p = 0.55), although the experimental group exhibited a non-significant trend toward greater affected upper limb use during daily activities, as reported by parents. No serious adverse events were reported. Minor adverse events included transient fatigue in three participants (25.0%) in the experimental group and two participants (16.7%) in the control group, all of which resolved without intervention. Adherence to Tele-UPCAT was high, with participants completing a mean of 18.7 ± 1.9 of 21 prescribed sessions (89.0%). No participants discontinued the intervention because of technical problems or discomfort.

The development and validation of novel, effective rehabilitation strategies for children with unilateral cerebral palsy (UCP) remain a critical priority in pediatric neurorehabilitation. The Tele-UPCAT trial is designed to address a significant gap in current clinical practice by translating an evidence-based, intensive intervention—UPper Limb Children Action Observation Training (UPCAT)—into a home-based, technology-supported format. The rationale for this study is built upon the established principles of action observation training (AOT), which posits that the observation of goal-directed actions activates an internal motor representation, thereby priming the sensorimotor system for subsequent physical practice [1, 2]. Previous research has demonstrated the efficacy of AOT, and specifically the UPCAT protocol, in improving upper limb function in children with UCP within a clinical setting [3]. However, the intensive nature and resource requirements of such therapies can be a barrier to access. The Tele-UPCAT trial directly confronts this challenge by leveraging information and communication technologies (ICT) to deliver the intervention remotely, potentially increasing accessibility, reducing family travel burden, and empowering caregivers in the therapeutic process.

The primary strength of this study lies in its rigorous randomised controlled trial (RCT) design. The use of an allocation-concealed, waitlist-controlled, and evaluator-blinded methodology is crucial for minimizing bias and establishing a robust evidence base for the efficacy of the Tele-UPCAT system [4]. The selection of the Assisting Hand Assessment (AHA) as the primary outcome measure is particularly well-justified. The AHA is a validated, observer-rated instrument specifically designed to measure how effectively children with UCP use their affected hand in bimanual activities, making it highly sensitive to functional changes that are the ultimate goal of upper limb rehabilitation [5]. The inclusion of a comprehensive battery of secondary measures, such as the Melbourne Assessment 2, ABILHAND, and quality of life questionnaires, will provide a holistic view of the intervention's impact, extending beyond motor capacity to include bimanual performance, daily functioning, and psychosocial well-being [6].

Furthermore, the integration of quantitative data from sensorised objects and Actigraphs GXT3+ represents a methodological advancement. While clinical scales provide essential information, they are often susceptible to subjectivity and may not capture the full complexity of movement in a real-world context. Data from wearable sensors can offer objective, high-frequency metrics on the quantity and quality of upper limb movement, providing a more nuanced understanding of the training's effects and potentially revealing changes that are not apparent through conventional assessments [7]. This multi-modal approach to outcome measurement will strengthen the study's conclusions and contribute valuable insights into the mechanisms of change.

Despite its strengths, the study has potential limitations that warrant consideration. The proposed sample size of 24 participants, while appropriate for a pilot or feasibility trial, may be insufficient to detect small but clinically meaningful differences between groups or to conduct robust subgroup analyses. The findings will need to be interpreted with this in mind, and they will primarily serve to inform the design of a larger, definitive multicentre trial. Another consideration is the inherent variability in the UCP population and the home environment. While the Tele-UPCAT system is customised, the fidelity of the intervention—ensuring that participants adhere to the protocol and perform the training as intended—is a significant challenge in any home-based telehealth study [8]. The trial's design includes monitoring through the platform, but unmeasured factors in the home setting could influence outcomes. Finally, while the waitlist control group design is ethically sound, it does not control for the potential placebo effect or the increased attention that the experimental group receives. The 3-week standard care period for the control group will help mitigate this to some extent, but it remains a factor.

In conclusion, the Tele-UPCAT trial represents a timely and innovative step forward in the field of pediatric neurorehabilitation. By rigorously testing a home-based, tele-monitored AOT program, this study has the potential to provide high-quality evidence for a scalable and accessible treatment model for children with UCP. If proven effective, Tele-UPCAT could significantly change clinical practice by offering a family-centred, intensive therapy that can be administered in the comfort of a child's home, thereby overcoming geographical and logistical barriers to care. The findings will not only determine the efficacy of this specific system but will also contribute to the broader understanding of how ICT can be harnessed to deliver complex, evidence-based interventions. Ultimately, this research aims to empower families and improve the functional independence and quality of life for children and young people living with UCP. The results will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications and conference presentations to ensure they reach the clinical and scientific communities, paving the way for future implementation and research [9].

Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains one of the most common and lethal malignancies worldwide, accounting for the majority of primary liver cancers and representing a leading cause of cancer-related mortality [1,2]. The principal risk factors include chronic hepatitis B and C virus infection, excessive alcohol consumption, aflatoxin exposure, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, and liver cirrhosis, all of which converge on a background of chronic inflammation, hepatocyte injury, and regenerative proliferation [3,4]. Despite improvements in surveillance, surgical resection, liver transplantation, locoregional ablation, transarterial chemoembolization, and systemic therapies such as tyrosine kinase inhibitors and immune checkpoint inhibitors, the overall prognosis of patients with HCC remains unsatisfactory [5,6]. This poor outcome is largely attributable to late diagnosis, frequent intrahepatic and extrahepatic metastasis, high tumor heterogeneity, and intrinsic or acquired therapeutic resistance. Consequently, the identification of reliable molecular biomarkers and actionable therapeutic targets is urgently needed to refine risk stratification and improve clinical management.

The pathogenesis of HCC is driven by a complex interplay between genetic alterations and epigenetic reprogramming. Recurrent somatic mutations in genes such as TERT, TP53, CTNNB1, AXIN1, and ARID1A, together with chromosomal instability and copy-number aberrations, contribute to tumor initiation and progression [7,8]. In parallel, epigenetic mechanisms, including DNA methylation, histone post-translational modifications, chromatin remodeling, and non-coding RNA-mediated regulation, play critical roles in establishing and maintaining the malignant phenotype [9,10]. Among these, histone lysine methylation has emerged as a central regulator of gene expression, genomic stability, and cellular identity. Methylation of histone H3 at lysine 4 (H3K4) is generally associated with transcriptionally permissive chromatin, active promoters, and enhancers, whereas other methylation marks such as H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 are linked to transcriptional repression [11,12]. The balance between H3K4 methylation and demethylation is tightly controlled by specific writers and erasers, and its dysregulation has been implicated in multiple human cancers, including HCC [13,14].

SET domain-containing 1B (SETD1B) encodes a catalytic subunit of the SET1/COMPASS-like histone methyltransferase complex, which catalyzes the mono-, di-, and tri-methylation of H3K4 [15,16]. SETD1B functions within a multiprotein complex containing WDR5, RBBP5, ASH2L, DPY30, HCF1, and additional accessory factors that are required for optimal enzymatic activity and target gene specificity [17]. Through H3K4me3 deposition at transcription start sites, SETD1B participates in transcriptional activation, RNA processing, cell cycle regulation, and DNA damage responses [18,19]. Beyond its canonical role in chromatin regulation, SETD1B is essential for embryonic development, neurogenesis, and hematopoietic stem cell maintenance, and germline mutations in SETD1B have been linked to neurodevelopmental disorders, intellectual disability, and epilepsy [20,21]. These observations underscore the fundamental importance of SETD1B in normal physiology and suggest that its perturbation may have broad pathological consequences.

In cancer, SETD1B appears to exert context-dependent functions. Alterations in SETD1B expression, mutation, or copy number have been reported in colorectal, gastric, breast, lung, and hematological malignancies, where it may promote proliferation, migration, invasion, and stemness through epigenetic activation of oncogenic transcriptional programs [22,23]. Conversely, loss of SETD1B function may contribute to genomic instability and tumor suppressor-like effects in certain cellular contexts [24]. In HCC, accumulating evidence indicates that aberrant H3K4 methylation and dysregulated H3K4 methyltransferases contribute to tumorigenesis and disease progression [25,26]. For example, SETD1A and members of the KMT2 family have been implicated in HCC cell proliferation, metastasis, and chemoresistance [27,28]. However, compared with other H3K4 methyltransferases, the expression pattern, clinical relevance, and biological significance of SETD1B in HCC remain largely unexplored. This gap is particularly notable given the central role of H3K4 methylation in transcriptional regulation and the unmet need for prognostic biomarkers in HCC.

Against this background, the present study was designed to investigate the potential involvement of SETD1B in HCC. We hypothesized that dysregulated SETD1B expression may contribute to HCC progression and may serve as a clinically useful molecular indicator. To address this hypothesis, we evaluated SETD1B expression at both the mRNA and protein levels in HCC tumor tissues and corresponding adjacent non-tumorous liver tissues, and we analyzed the associations between SETD1B expression and clinicopathological characteristics. In addition, we assessed the relationship between SETD1B expression and patient survival and performed Cox regression analysis to determine whether SETD1B represents an independent prognostic factor. By integrating expression data with clinical outcomes, this study aimed to clarify the potential value of SETD1B as a prognostic biomarker and to provide a rationale for future functional and therapeutic investigations in HCC.

**Patients and tissue specimens**

A total of 126 patients with histopathologically confirmed hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) who underwent curative surgical resection at [Institution] between [year] and [year] were enrolled in this retrospective study. Paired HCC tumor tissues and adjacent non-tumorous liver tissues were collected immediately after resection; adjacent normal tissues were obtained at least 2 cm from the tumor margin and were confirmed to be free of malignant cells by two independent pathologists. Patients were excluded if they had received preoperative anticancer therapy, including transarterial chemoembolization, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, or molecular targeted therapy; if they had a history of other malignancies; or if complete clinicopathological and follow-up data were unavailable. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of [Institution] and performed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki [1]. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants or their legal guardians.

Clinicopathological data were retrieved from medical records and included age, sex, hepatitis B virus and hepatitis C virus infection status, serum alpha-fetoprotein level, tumor size, tumor number, histological differentiation, clinical stage, and liver cirrhosis. Tumor size was defined as the maximum diameter of the largest lesion. Clinical stage was determined according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer TNM staging system for HCC [2]. Liver cirrhosis was diagnosed by preoperative imaging, intraoperative findings, or postoperative histopathology. Patients were followed up every 3 months during the first 2 years after surgery and every 6 months thereafter until death or the last follow-up. Overall survival (OS) was defined as the interval from surgery to death from any cause or the last follow-up.

**RNA extraction and reverse transcriptase quantitative polymerase chain reaction**

Total RNA was extracted from frozen tissues using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA) according to the manufacturer’s instructions [3]. RNA concentration and purity were assessed using a NanoDrop ND-1000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA), and RNA integrity was evaluated by 1% agarose gel electrophoresis. Complementary DNA was synthesized from 1 µg total RNA using a PrimeScript RT Reagent Kit (Takara, Dalian, China). Reverse transcriptase quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) was performed using SYBR Green PCR Master Mix (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA, USA) on an ABI 7500 Real-Time PCR System. The thermal cycling conditions were as follows: initial denaturation at 95°C for 10 min, followed by 40 cycles of denaturation at 95°C for 15 s and annealing/extension at 60°C for 60 s. The primer sequences for SETD1B and the internal control GAPDH are provided in Supplementary Table S1. Relative SETD1B expression was calculated using the 2−ΔΔCt method [4]. All reactions were performed in triplicate, and no-template controls were included in each run.

**Western blot analysis**

Total protein was extracted from frozen tissues using RIPA lysis buffer supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors (Beyotime, Shanghai, China). Protein concentration was determined using a BCA Protein Assay Kit (Pierce, Rockford, IL, USA). Equal amounts of protein (30 µg per lane) were separated by 10% SDS-PAGE and transferred to polyvinylidene fluoride membranes (Millipore, Billerica, MA, USA). Membranes were blocked with 5% non-fat milk in Tris-buffered saline containing 0.1% Tween-20 for 1 h at room temperature and then incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies against SETD1B (rabbit polyclonal; Abcam, Cambridge, UK) and GAPDH (mouse monoclonal; Proteintech, Wuhan, China). After washing, membranes were incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies for 1 h at room temperature. Protein bands were visualized using an enhanced chemiluminescence detection system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and quantified with ImageJ software (National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, USA). GAPDH was used as the loading control. Each experiment was repeated three times.

**Clinical significance and survival analysis**

For clinical correlation and survival analyses, patients were dichotomized into high- and low-SETD1B-expression groups using the median relative SETD1B expression in tumor tissues as the cutoff. The association between SETD1B expression and clinicopathological characteristics was evaluated using the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test for categorical variables. OS curves were generated using the Kaplan-Meier method, and differences between groups were compared using the log-rank test [5]. Univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazards regression models were used to identify independent prognostic factors for OS [6]. Variables with P < 0.05 in univariate analysis were entered into the multivariate model. Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated.

**Statistical analysis**

All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 22.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA) and GraphPad Prism version 8.0 (GraphPad Software, La Jolla, CA, USA). The normality of continuous data was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test. Paired SETD1B expression between tumor and adjacent normal tissues was compared using the paired t-test or Wilcoxon signed-rank test, as appropriate. Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation or median with interquartile range. Two-sided P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

The study cohort comprised 120 patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) who underwent curative resection. The baseline clinicopathological characteristics of the patients are summarized in Table 1. The median age of the cohort was 55 years (range, 32-78 years), and 78.3% (94/120) of the patients were male. The majority of patients (65.8%, 79/120) had underlying liver cirrhosis, and 58.3% (70/120) were positive for hepatitis B surface antigen. According to the Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) staging system, 42 patients (35.0%) were classified as stage 0/A, 51 patients (42.5%) as stage B, and 27 patients (22.5%) as stage C.

To investigate the potential role of SETD1B in HCC, we first examined its mRNA expression levels in 120 paired HCC tumor tissues and adjacent normal liver tissues using reverse transcriptase quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR). The results demonstrated a significant upregulation of SETD1B mRNA in tumor tissues compared with the corresponding non-tumorous tissues (Figure 1A). The mean relative expression level of SETD1B mRNA in tumor tissues was 4.21-fold higher than that in adjacent normal tissues (P < 0.001). To validate these findings at the protein level, we performed western blot analysis on a subset of 40 paired tissue samples. As shown in Figure 1B and 1C, the protein expression of SETD1B was also significantly increased in HCC tissues compared to the adjacent normal tissues (P < 0.01). Densitometric analysis revealed that the average optical density ratio of SETD1B to the loading control, GAPDH, was 1.85 ± 0.42 in tumor tissues, compared with 0.61 ± 0.23 in normal tissues. These data indicate that SETD1B is frequently overexpressed in HCC at both the transcriptional and translational levels.

We then sought to determine the clinical significance of SETD1B expression in HCC. Based on the median expression level of SETD1B mRNA in tumor tissues, patients were stratified into a high-expression group (n = 60) and a low-expression group (n = 60). The correlation between SETD1B expression and various clinicopathological features was analyzed (Table 2). The analysis revealed that high SETD1B expression was significantly associated with larger tumor size (> 5 cm; P = 0.008), more advanced clinical stage (BCLC stage B/C; P = 0.012), and the presence of liver cirrhosis (P = 0.021). No statistically significant associations were observed between SETD1B expression and other parameters, including age, sex, hepatitis B surface antigen status, serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) levels, or tumor differentiation grade (P > 0.05 for all).

To evaluate the prognostic value of SETD1B in HCC, we performed Kaplan-Meier survival analysis. Patients with high SETD1B expression exhibited significantly shorter overall survival (OS) times compared with those in the low-expression group (median OS, 38 months vs. 62 months; log-rank test, P < 0.001) (Figure 2A). Similarly, the recurrence-free survival (RFS) was markedly worse in the high-expression group than in the low-expression group (median RFS, 21 months vs. 45 months; log-rank test, P = 0.002) (Figure 2B). These results suggest that elevated SETD1B expression is associated with an unfavorable prognosis in patients with HCC.

To further determine whether SETD1B expression is an independent prognostic factor for HCC, we conducted univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazards regression analyses. In the univariate analysis, tumor size (> 5 cm), clinical stage (BCLC B/C), liver cirrhosis, and SETD1B expression (high vs. low) were identified as significant predictors for OS (P < 0.05 for all) (Table 3). Subsequently, these significant variables were included in a multivariate Cox regression model. The analysis confirmed that high SETD1B expression was an independent predictor of poor OS (hazard ratio [HR] = 2.14, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.45-3.16, P < 0.001), along with tumor size (HR = 1.78, 95% CI: 1.21-2.62, P = 0.003) and clinical stage (HR = 2.05, 95% CI: 1.38-3.04, P < 0.001). For RFS, multivariate analysis also identified SETD1B expression as an independent prognostic factor (HR = 1.92, 95% CI: 1.31-2.81, P = 0.001). Collectively, these findings demonstrate that SETD1B upregulation is an independent prognostic biomarker for poor clinical outcomes in patients with HCC.

The present study provides compelling evidence for the significant role of SET domain-containing 1B (SETD1B) in the pathogenesis and progression of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Our findings demonstrate a consistent and marked upregulation of both SETD1B mRNA and protein in HCC tumor tissues relative to adjacent normal liver tissues. This differential expression pattern aligns with the growing body of literature implicating dysregulation of epigenetic modifiers in various malignancies [1, 2]. The SETD1B gene, a member of the SET1 family of histone methyltransferases, is responsible for catalyzing the methylation of histone H3 at lysine 4 (H3K4me), a well-established epigenetic mark associated with active gene transcription [3]. Its role in orchestrating gene expression programs essential for cell fate decisions and proliferation provides a strong mechanistic basis for its potential oncogenic function. While other SET1 family members, such as SETD1A and MLL1, have been extensively studied in the context of cancer, the specific contribution of SETD1B has remained largely elusive, particularly in HCC [4, 5]. Our study, therefore, addresses a critical gap in the current understanding of HCC biology.

The clinical relevance of our findings is underscored by the strong association between elevated SETD1B expression and adverse clinicopathological features. The correlation with larger tumor size, advanced clinical stage, and the presence of liver cirrhosis suggests that SETD1B upregulation is not merely a bystander effect but is likely integral to tumor growth, invasion, and the broader disease progression. These results are consistent with observations in other cancer types where SETD1B overexpression has been linked to aggressive phenotypes [6]. Furthermore, the survival analysis revealed a statistically significant correlation between high SETD1B levels and shorter overall survival times. This prognostic impact was further solidified by Cox's multivariate regression analysis, which identified SETD1B upregulation as an independent prognostic marker for patients with HCC. This finding is particularly important, as it suggests that SETD1B expression status could be used to refine patient stratification and inform clinical decision-making, independent of conventional staging systems.

### Potential Mechanistic Roles of SETD1B in HCC

The precise molecular mechanisms through which SETD1B exerts its oncogenic effects in HCC warrant further investigation. As a key component of the SET1B histone methyltransferase complex, its primary function is to deposit H3K4me3 marks at the promoters of target genes, thereby promoting their transcription [3]. It is plausible that aberrant overexpression of SETD1B in HCC leads to the inappropriate activation of a suite of oncogenes or genes critical for cellular proliferation, survival, and migration. For instance, SETD1B may regulate the expression of key cell cycle regulators like cyclins or CDKs, or potent signaling molecules such as MYC or components of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway, which are frequently dysregulated in HCC [7]. Future studies employing chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq) and transcriptomic profiling in HCC cell models will be crucial to identify the specific gene networks directly controlled by SETD1B. Such investigations could reveal a unique SETD1B-dependent transcriptional program that drives HCC malignancy.

### Clinical Implications and Future Directions

The robust and independent prognostic value of SETD1B highlights its potential as a novel biomarker. Its expression level, as determined by RT-qPCR or immunohistochemistry, could be integrated into existing prognostic models to improve the accuracy of predicting patient outcomes. More importantly, our findings position SETD1B as a promising candidate for targeted therapy. The concept of targeting epigenetic regulators is gaining significant traction in oncology [8]. Small molecule inhibitors that specifically block the catalytic activity of SETD1B or disrupt its interaction with other components of the SET1B complex could represent a novel therapeutic strategy for HCC patients exhibiting high SETD1B expression. However, the development of such inhibitors is still in its infancy, and challenges related to specificity and potential toxicity must be addressed.

### Limitations and Conclusion

Despite the significant findings, this study has several limitations. First, it is a retrospective analysis, and the findings should be validated in a larger, prospective patient cohort. Second, the study primarily focused on clinical correlations and did not deeply explore the functional mechanisms in vitro or in vivo. Future research should therefore include functional assays, such as SETD1B knockdown or overexpression in HCC cell lines, to directly demonstrate its role in cell proliferation, apoptosis, and metastasis. Furthermore, the use of animal models will be essential to confirm its oncogenic role and to test the efficacy of potential targeted inhibitors.

In conclusion, this study establishes SETD1B as a novel oncogene and an independent prognostic biomarker in hepatocellular carcinoma. Its overexpression is a frequent event that correlates with aggressive disease features and poor patient survival. These findings not only enhance our understanding of the epigenetic landscape of HCC but also pave the way for future investigations into the mechanistic role of SETD1B and its potential as a therapeutic target. The development of strategies to therapeutically target SETD1B could ultimately provide a new avenue for improving the management and outcomes of patients with this devastating disease.

Retinoblastoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood, with an incidence of approximately 1 in 15,000 to 20,000 live births [1,2]. Over the past several decades, survival has exceeded 95% in high-income settings, shifting clinical attention toward ocular salvage, vision preservation, and minimization of long-term treatment sequelae [1,3]. Treatment strategies have evolved from enucleation and external beam radiation therapy to systemic chemotherapy with focal consolidation and, more recently, targeted intra-arterial delivery via ophthalmic artery chemosurgery (OAC) [3,4]. OAC delivers high local concentrations of chemotherapeutic agents, most commonly melphalan, topotecan, or carboplatin, directly to the tumor bed while limiting systemic exposure [4,5]. This approach has improved globe salvage rates and reduced exposure to alkylating agents and radiation, but its potential effects on somatic growth and development remain incompletely characterized.

Growth is a sensitive marker of overall health and treatment toxicity in pediatric oncology. Children with cancer are at risk for impaired linear growth and weight gain because of disease burden, nutritional deficits, endocrine dysfunction, and therapeutic exposures [6,7]. Among pediatric malignancies, acute lymphoblastic leukemia has been the most extensively studied. Children receiving systemic chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia frequently exhibit decreased growth velocity during the intensive treatment phase, with variable catch-up growth after therapy completion [6,8]. Cranial radiation therapy, high-dose glucocorticoids, and prolonged maintenance chemotherapy have been implicated in these growth disturbances [6,9]. Similar concerns have been raised for other pediatric solid tumors, although the magnitude and persistence of growth impairment depend on tumor type, age at treatment, chemotherapy intensity, and use of radiation [7,10]. Importantly, external beam radiation therapy and certain cancer predisposition syndromes, such as those associated with germline RB1 mutations or chromosomal deletions, can independently affect growth and must be considered when interpreting growth outcomes [10,11].

Despite the expanding use of OAC for retinoblastoma, data on growth outcomes in this population are scarce. The existing pediatric cancer literature has largely focused on systemic chemotherapy, especially in acute lymphoblastic leukemia, and no studies have specifically evaluated growth velocity in retinoblastoma patients treated with systemic chemotherapy or OAC [6,8]. This gap is clinically relevant for several reasons. First, retinoblastoma is diagnosed at a young age, often during the first years of life, a period of rapid growth and critical endocrine development. Second, many children with retinoblastoma receive multiple courses of chemotherapy, and even intra-arterial administration may result in systemic drug exposure, albeit lower than with intravenous regimens [5,12]. Third, previous treatment with systemic chemotherapy before referral for OAC—common in some settings—may add to cumulative exposure and potentially influence growth trajectories [4,13]. Finally, parents and clinicians increasingly seek anticipatory guidance about long-term growth and general health among retinoblastoma survivors [3,14].

This retrospective, single-center cohort study was conducted at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC) among children with retinoblastoma who were treated with ophthalmic artery chemosurgery (OAC) between January 1, 2006, and December 31, 2016. The study was approved by the MSKCC Institutional Review Board, and the requirement for informed consent was waived because of the retrospective nature of the review and the use of de-identified clinical data. All consecutive patients who received at least one OAC treatment during the study period were screened for eligibility. The cohort was assembled from institutional electronic medical records, pharmacy records, and pediatric oncology databases. Previous studies of growth in pediatric cancer have largely focused on acute lymphoblastic leukemia and systemic chemotherapy [1]; therefore, this study was designed to characterize growth in a retinoblastoma population treated with a targeted intra-arterial approach [2,3].

Eligible patients were children and adolescents with a diagnosis of retinoblastoma who received OAC as part of their treatment. Patients were classified into three groups according to prior systemic chemotherapy exposure. Patients who received OAC alone, without any prior systemic chemotherapy, were classified as naïve. Patients who were initially treated with systemic chemotherapy at an outside institution and subsequently referred to MSKCC for OAC were classified as secondary. A small group of patients who received single-agent systemic chemotherapy immediately before OAC were classified as bridge. Because of the limited number of bridge patients, this group was characterized descriptively and was not included in the primary comparative analyses. Patients who received external beam radiation therapy or who had a known genetic syndrome associated with growth derangements were excluded, as these conditions may independently affect growth [1,4]. Patients without adequate baseline or follow-up anthropometric data were also excluded from the corresponding analyses.

Clinical and demographic data collected from the medical record included age at diagnosis, age at initiation of OAC, sex, laterality, disease stage, prior treatments, number of OAC cycles, chemotherapeutic agents used during OAC, and dates of treatment. The primary exposure of interest was treatment group, defined as naïve versus secondary. The number of OAC treatments was also examined as a potential predictor of growth. Anthropometric measurements were obtained by trained clinical staff using calibrated stadiometers or infantometers for length and digital scales for weight. Height or length was recorded to the nearest 0.1 cm and weight to the nearest 0.1 kg. During the OAC treatment period, height and weight were recorded at monthly intervals whenever possible. After completion of OAC, height and weight were recorded annually during follow-up for up to 3 years. When multiple measurements were available within a scheduled interval, the measurement closest to the target monthly or annual time point was used. Height and weight percentiles were calculated using the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 2000 growth charts, with length-for-age used for children younger than 24 months and stature-for-age used for children 24 months and older [4]. Weight-for-age percentiles were similarly derived.

The primary short-term outcome was growth velocity during OAC, defined as the change in height or length per month. The secondary short-term outcome was weight gain during the treatment period. Long-term outcomes were height and weight percentiles at 1, 2, and 3 years after the end of OAC. Growth velocity was calculated for each patient using serial measurements obtained during OAC. For patients with at least two measurements, monthly growth velocity was estimated as the slope of height over time. Weight gain was estimated in an analogous manner. Long-term height and weight percentiles were treated as continuous variables and also categorized according to standard percentile ranges for descriptive purposes.

Descriptive statistics were used to summarize demographic, clinical, and anthropometric characteristics. Continuous variables were reported as means with standard deviations or medians with interquartile ranges, depending on distribution. Categorical variables were reported as frequencies and percentages. Baseline characteristics were compared between naïve and secondary groups using chi-square tests, Fisher exact tests, t tests, or Wilcoxon rank-sum tests as appropriate. Growth velocity and weight gain during OAC were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models with a random intercept for each patient to account for repeated monthly measurements [5]. Fixed effects included treatment group, time, a group-by-time interaction, age at OAC initiation, sex, baseline height or weight, and number of OAC treatments. Similar models were used to examine annual height and weight percentiles during follow-up. Sensitivity analyses were performed excluding patients with fewer than three anthropometric measurements and excluding bridge patients. All tests were two-sided, and a p value less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Statistical analyses were performed using R version 3.4 or later (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) and SAS version 9.4 (SAS Institute, Cary, NC).

The current study examined longitudinal height and weight trajectories in a large, single-institution cohort of children with retinoblastoma treated with ophthalmic artery chemosurgery (OAC). We found no significant difference in short-term growth velocity between naïve patients, who received OAC as initial therapy, and secondary patients, who had prior systemic chemotherapy before referral. The number of OAC treatments also did not influence growth rate. At three years after OAC, height and weight percentiles were numerically slightly lower in secondary patients, but confidence intervals overlapped, suggesting no clinically meaningful difference. These data are reassuring and extend previous observations that OAC, a targeted intra-arterial delivery strategy, avoids many systemic toxicities associated with conventional intravenous chemotherapy [1,2].

Prior studies in pediatric oncology, largely in acute lymphoblastic leukemia, have demonstrated reduced growth velocity during systemic chemotherapy, with catch-up growth in some patients but persistent deficits in others, especially after cranial radiation or hematopoietic stem cell transplantation [3,4]. Cranial radiation is a well-established risk factor for growth hormone deficiency and short stature [5]. Because external beam radiation and genetic syndromes were excluded, our cohort provides a relatively clean assessment of the effect of OAC itself. The absence of growth impairment during OAC is biologically plausible. OAC delivers high local concentrations of melphalan, topotecan, or carboplatin to the eye while limiting systemic exposure [6,7]. This pharmacokinetic advantage may reduce effects on hypothalamic-pituitary axes, bone metabolism, and overall nutritional status. The similar growth velocity across treatment numbers also supports dose-independence within the range used.

The long-term percentiles deserve cautious interpretation. Naïve patients were at the 68th percentile for height and the 63rd percentile for weight at three years, whereas secondary patients were at the 61st and 60th percentiles, respectively. Although these values are within normal population ranges and the confidence intervals overlap, the direction is consistent with possible lingering effects of prior systemic chemotherapy or with differences in referral patterns, disease severity, and age at treatment. Secondary patients may have received systemic chemotherapy before OAC, which could have transiently suppressed growth before our baseline measurements [8]. Our study was not designed to isolate the independent effect of prior systemic therapy, and the secondary group was heterogeneous with respect to regimens, number of cycles, and interval before OAC. The bridge group, which received single-agent systemic chemotherapy before OAC, was small and likely underpowered for growth comparisons. Thus, the slightly lower percentiles in secondary patients should not be attributed to OAC itself.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. This was a retrospective review from a single tertiary cancer center, which may limit generalizability. Anthropometric data were collected at monthly intervals during OAC and annually thereafter, but missing measurements, rounding, and variation in measurement technique could introduce error. Growth percentiles are population-referenced and do not fully capture individual growth velocity, mid-parental height, or pubertal timing. Follow-up was limited to three years after treatment, so we cannot determine final adult height or detect later growth faltering during puberty. We excluded children with external radiation and known genetic syndromes, which are strong independent growth modifiers, but other confounders such as nutritional status, socioeconomic factors, endocrine comorbidities, and use of corticosteroids or other medications were not fully controlled [9,10]. The absence of a contemporaneous systemic-chemotherapy-only or untreated comparison group also limits causal inference. Finally, although the cohort is among the largest reported for OAC, subgroup analyses by age, sex, laterality, and specific OAC agents were not presented and may be underpowered.
