The potential for non-antiarrhythmic drugs to delay ventricular repolarization and thereby increase the risk of torsades de pointes remains a central concern in clinical drug development. Since the adoption of the International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use (ICH) E14 guideline in 2005, the dedicated thorough QT (TQT) study has served as the principal regulatory instrument for characterizing a drug’s effect on cardiac repolarization [1]. In a conventional TQT study, healthy volunteers receive therapeutic and supratherapeutic doses of the investigational drug, a positive control, and placebo, with intensive electrocardiogram (ECG) sampling around matched time points. The primary endpoint is the placebo- and baseline-adjusted change in the Fridericia-corrected QT interval (ΔΔQTcF), and the study is designed to exclude a mean effect exceeding 10 ms with a specified upper confidence bound [1,2]. Although this paradigm has been highly effective in preventing drugs with substantial QT liability from reaching the market, it is resource-intensive, typically conducted late in phase I or early phase II, and may not reflect exposure–response relationships across the full concentration range encountered in patients.

Over the past decade, regulatory thinking has shifted toward a more mechanistic and exposure-driven assessment of proarrhythmic risk. The 2015 revision of the ICH E14 Questions and Answers document permitted exposure–response (ER) modeling of intensive ECG data collected in early clinical development as a primary analysis tool, thereby offering an alternative to a dedicated TQT study [2]. In this framework, the relationship between drug concentration and placebo-corrected change in QT interval is characterized, most commonly as concentration–QTc (C–QTc) analysis. The central question is no longer whether a single dose or time point produces a statistically significant QT effect, but whether the upper bound of the two-sided 90% confidence interval for the predicted ΔΔQTc remains below 10 ms across the relevant therapeutic and supratherapeutic exposure range [3,4]. This concentration-based approach aligns with the pharmacological principle that QT prolongation is driven by drug exposure at the target ion channel, and it can accommodate variability in pharmacokinetics, formulation, food effects, drug–drug interactions, and intrinsic factors such as renal or hepatic impairment [5].

The regulatory acceptance of ER modeling as a primary analysis has been accompanied by specific methodological expectations. Studies intended to support a TQT waiver must include adequate characterization of the drug’s pharmacokinetic profile, intensive ECG sampling timed to capture peak and trough concentrations, and rigorous control of ECG acquisition, storage, and reading procedures [2,6]. A positive control is generally required to demonstrate assay sensitivity, either within the same study or through a separate, adequately powered comparison. Moxifloxacin is the most widely used positive control because its QT effect is well characterized, typically producing a mean ΔΔQTcF of approximately 5–10 ms at therapeutic doses [7]. The ER analysis itself must be pre-specified, with an appropriate mixed-effects model that accounts for baseline QTc, time-matched placebo effects, circadian variation, heart rate, and subject-level random effects. Model diagnostics, handling of missing data, and sensitivity analyses are critical because the conclusion of no clinically relevant QT effect depends on the validity of the exposure–response model [8].

Embedding ER analysis into early clinical development offers several practical advantages. First-in-human and subsequent single- and multiple-ascending-dose studies can be designed prospectively to collect intensive ECG and pharmacokinetic data, allowing the C–QTc relationship to be evaluated without a separate TQT study [9]. This integration can reduce cost, shorten timelines, and provide earlier information for dose selection. It also permits assessment of QT effects across a broader range of exposures than may be safely administered in a dedicated TQT study, including in patients who may have different pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles. Nevertheless, important challenges remain. Early-phase studies often enroll small numbers of subjects, use narrow dose ranges, and may not achieve supratherapeutic exposures. ECG quality can be compromised by motion artifact, autonomic variability, and inconsistent electrode placement. The choice of heart rate correction method, the presence of hysteresis between concentration and effect, and the potential for model misspecification can materially influence the estimated QT effect [10]. In addition, the implementation of a positive control in an early-phase study raises logistical and ethical considerations, particularly when the study population is not healthy volunteers.

Regulatory and scientific consensus continues to evolve. The 2022 ICH E14/S7B Questions and Answers further clarified expectations for integrated nonclinical and clinical assessment, including the use of concentration–QTc modeling and the circumstances under which a TQT study may be waived [3]. For drug developers, the decision to pursue an ER-based strategy rather than a dedicated TQT study requires careful consideration of the stage of development, the intended patient population, the available nonclinical data, and the planned regulatory pathway. The present review examines the current state of ER modeling of intensive ECG data in early clinical drug development, with particular attention to regulatory requirements, the role of positive controls, methodological and operational challenges, and the opportunities that this alternative paradigm affords for more efficient and informative cardiac safety evaluation.

This review employed a structured narrative synthesis to evaluate the methodological, regulatory, and operational dimensions of exposure-response (ER) modeling of intensive electrocardiogram (ECG) data in early clinical drug development. The review was designed to integrate evidence from peer-reviewed literature, regulatory guidance documents, and methodological white papers rather than to generate pooled quantitative estimates, given the anticipated heterogeneity in study designs, modeling approaches, and reporting standards. The methodological framework was informed by established principles for systematic review conduct where applicable, including a prespecified search strategy, explicit eligibility criteria, duplicate screening, structured data extraction, and thematic synthesis [1,2].

**Search strategy.** We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library from 1 January 2005 through 31 December 2024. The lower date bound was selected to coincide with the introduction of the International Council for Harmonisation E14 guideline, while the upper bound captured contemporary methodological developments, including the 2015 E14 Questions and Answers revision and subsequent regulatory and scientific discussions [1,2]. Search strings combined controlled vocabulary and free-text terms related to cardiac safety and early clinical development. The core search comprised (“exposure-response” OR “exposure response” OR “ER modeling” OR “concentration-QT” OR “concentration-QTc” OR “C-QTc”) AND (“early clinical development” OR “phase I” OR “phase 1” OR “dose escalation” OR “first-in-human”) AND (“QT” OR “QTc” OR “thorough QT” OR “TQT” OR “proarrhythmia” OR “cardiac safety” OR “positive control” OR “assay sensitivity”). We also searched the websites of the United States Food and Drug Administration, European Medicines Agency, Health Canada, Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Agency, and ICH for relevant guidance, concept papers, and public workshop materials [3,4]. Reference lists of included articles and guidance documents were hand-searched to identify additional sources.

**Eligibility criteria.** Records were eligible if they addressed ER modeling of intensive ECG data for assessment of drug-induced QT/QTc liability in early clinical drug development, including phase I dose-escalation studies, dedicated thorough QT studies used for methodological comparison, and regulatory or scientific documents describing requirements for positive controls and assay sensitivity. Eligible study designs included prospective clinical trials, retrospective analyses of clinical trial data, simulation studies, methodological reviews, and regulatory guidance documents. We excluded nonclinical studies, case reports, editorials without methodological content, and publications not available in English. No restriction was placed on drug class, route of administration, or therapeutic area, because the methodological principles of ER modeling are broadly applicable across development programs.

**Screening and data extraction.** Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts against the eligibility criteria. Full texts of potentially relevant records were then assessed independently. Disagreements were resolved by consensus or, when necessary, by a third reviewer. A standardized extraction form was piloted and used to capture study characteristics, including design, phase, population, sample size, dose levels, ECG collection schedule, number of replicate ECGs per time point, QT correction method, pharmacokinetic sampling strategy, ER model specification, covariates, and handling of baseline values. For regulatory and methodological documents, we extracted recommendations regarding positive control selection, assay sensitivity, the threshold of regulatory concern, and the statistical criteria used to exclude clinically relevant QT prolongation, including the upper bound of the 95% confidence interval for the predicted effect at supratherapeutic exposures [2,5].

**Methodological appraisal.** Because the review encompassed heterogeneous evidence types, quality appraisal was adapted to study design. Clinical and modeling studies were assessed for prespecification of the ER analysis, adequacy of ECG sampling, appropriateness of QT correction, handling of time-matched baseline, inclusion of covariates, model diagnostics, and sensitivity analyses [5,6]. Regulatory and guidance documents were assessed for authority, currency, and methodological transparency. Given the absence of a single validated appraisal tool for this mixed evidence base, appraisal domains were used descriptively to contextualize findings rather than to exclude studies solely on quality grounds.

**Synthesis.** A thematic synthesis was conducted. Extracted data were tabulated and categorized into five predefined domains: regulatory evolution and acceptance of ER modeling; design requirements for intensive ECG collection in early clinical development; use and interpretation of positive controls; statistical and pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic modeling considerations; and challenges and opportunities for implementation. Findings were mapped against ICH E14 and its Questions and Answers revision, as well as contemporary public-private research initiatives such as the Comprehensive in vitro Proarrhythmia Assay initiative [1,2,7]. Where studies reported concordance between ER modeling and dedicated thorough QT studies, results were summarized narratively. No meta-analysis was performed because of substantial variability in drugs, populations, dose ranges, ECG schedules, and model specifications.

**Ethical considerations.** This review used only published literature and publicly available regulatory documents. No human participants or identifiable private information were involved; therefore, institutional review board approval and informed consent were not required.

Regulatory and evidentiary landscape. Synthesis of the available guidance and case-study literature indicated that the regulatory position on exposure-response (ER) modeling for cardiac risk has shifted from a strictly dedicated thorough QT (TQT) paradigm toward a integrated model-informed approach [1–3]. The 2015 ICH E14 Questions and Answers document was consistently identified as the pivotal change, permitting intensive electrocardiogram (ECG) data collected during early clinical development to serve as primary evidence for excluding a large QT effect when supported by robust concentration-QTc analysis [2]. Across the reviewed programs, ER analyses were most informative when derived from single- and multiple-ascending dose studies that included placebo and at least three active dose levels, with triplicate 12-lead ECGs time-matched to pharmacokinetic sampling [3,4]. Studies that relied on sparse or non-matched ECG sampling generally produced imprecise slope estimates and were less able to support definitive conclusions regarding QT liability [4,5].

Statistical performance and assay sensitivity. The ER modeling literature consistently demonstrated that concentration-QTc analysis, typically implemented as a linear mixed-effects model with concentration as a continuous fixed effect and subject-specific random effects, provided greater sensitivity than time-matched mean analysis for detecting small drug-induced QTc changes [3,5]. Baseline adjustment and Fridericia or individual heart-rate correction reduced residual variability, and the upper bound of the two-sided 90% confidence interval for the predicted ΔΔQTc at supratherapeutic concentrations was the most commonly applied decision metric [2,5]. When delayed effects or hysteresis were present, effect-compartment models improved fit and reduced bias in slope estimation [4]. Assay sensitivity was addressed variably. Dedicated TQT studies uniformly included a positive control, most often moxifloxacin 400 mg, which produced the expected mean ΔΔQTcF of approximately 5–10 ms [5,6]. In ER-based early-development studies, a separate positive control arm was not always required; instead, assay sensitivity was inferred from the precision of the concentration-response relationship, prior model qualification, or simulation-based power analyses [2,6]. Nevertheless, regulatory feedback summarized in the reviewed documents indicated that omission of a positive control increased review uncertainty, particularly when the observed concentration range was narrow or when the study lacked a supratherapeutic exposure [2,7].

Operational and design findings. Early-phase studies that successfully supported ER-based QT assessment typically enrolled 20–60 subjects, collected serial ECGs around expected peak concentrations, and ensured close temporal alignment between ECG and plasma concentration measurements [3,4,7]. Within-subject variability was the dominant determinant of power; when residual standard deviation was low, sample sizes of approximately 20–30 subjects could exclude a 10 ms effect with adequate precision [4,7]. Common confounders included diurnal variation, food intake, postural changes, and heart-rate fluctuations, all of which were mitigated by time-matched placebo comparisons and by using QTcF or subject-specific correction [5,7]. Missing ECG or pharmacokinetic data, irregular dosing times, and insufficient sampling around peak concentrations were recurrent limitations in studies that failed to meet regulatory expectations [6,7].

Positive control requirements. The results of the review indicated that the role of the positive control differs between the dedicated TQT and ER paradigms. In a TQT study, the positive control is essential for demonstrating assay sensitivity [1,5]. In an ER-based approach, the requirement is less prescriptive: a positive control may be included to validate the study’s ability to detect a small QT effect, but it is not universally mandatory if the concentration-QTc model is prespecified, the exposure range is adequate, and the analysis demonstrates acceptable precision [2,6]. When moxifloxacin was included in early-phase ER studies, it consistently reproduced a detectable ΔΔQTcF effect, supporting the sensitivity of the ECG and pharmacokinetic sampling scheme [5,6]. Conversely, studies without a positive control often required additional justification, such as external validation or simulation, to satisfy regulators that a true small effect would not have been missed [2,7].

Challenges and opportunities. The principal challenges identified were the absence of a harmonized ER study protocol, heterogeneity in ECG acquisition and core laboratory methods, uncertainty in model selection, and variable regulatory acceptance across regions [3,7,8]. Opportunities included the use of model-informed drug development to waive dedicated TQT studies, integration of ER analysis into first-in-human and proof-of-concept trials, application of Bayesian and nonlinear mixed-effects approaches, and incorporation of digital or wearable ECG devices for denser sampling [8,9]. The reviewed evidence also suggested that ER modeling may be particularly valuable for drugs with delayed effects, oncology agents, pediatric populations, and programs in which a supratherapeutic dose cannot be safely administered [6,8]. Overall, the findings support ER modeling of intensive ECG data as a scientifically robust alternative to the dedicated TQT study, provided that assay sensitivity, concentration range, and statistical precision are prospectively addressed [2–4,9].

The transition from a dedicated thorough QT (TQT) study to exposure-response (ER) modeling of intensive electrocardiogram (ECG) data reflects a broader shift toward model-informed drug development and more efficient cardiac safety assessment. Rather than treating ER analysis as a simple statistical alternative, it should be understood as an integrated design, pharmacokinetic (PK), and electrocardiographic strategy that requires prospective planning and rigorous execution [1,2]. The central question is no longer whether ER modeling can substitute for a TQT study in principle, but under what conditions it provides sufficiently robust evidence to characterize a drug’s concentration-dependent effects on ventricular repolarization.

Methodological and regulatory considerations

The estimand of primary interest is the relationship between drug exposure and placebo-adjusted change in the QT interval corrected for heart rate (ΔΔQTc). In practice, this is commonly evaluated using a prespecified linear mixed-effects model with concentration as a fixed effect and subject-specific random effects, incorporating baseline QTc, time, and other covariates as appropriate [3]. Adequate characterization requires plasma concentrations that span the therapeutic range and, where feasible, supratherapeutic exposures, because the slope of the concentration-QTc relationship must be estimated with sufficient precision to predict effects at clinically relevant concentrations. The regulatory threshold remains an upper bound of the two-sided 90% confidence interval for predicted ΔΔQTc below 10 ms at the relevant supratherapeutic concentration [1,2].

Assay sensitivity is a critical requirement. A positive control, typically moxifloxacin 400 mg, is expected to demonstrate that the study can detect a small but definite QT effect. In early clinical development, this control may be incorporated as a separate treatment period, a nested cohort, or a crossover component within an ongoing dose-escalation study. However, the positive control must be administered under conditions that permit valid interpretation, including standardized ECG collection, controlled food and activity, and adequate PK sampling. Failure to demonstrate assay sensitivity can render otherwise informative concentration-QTc data inconclusive [4,5].

Challenges and opportunities

Several challenges limit the universal adoption of ER modeling. Early-phase studies often enroll small numbers of subjects per dose cohort, yielding sparse PK and ECG sampling that may not adequately define the concentration-QTc relationship. Confounding by circadian variation, food intake, posture, activity, and concomitant medications can bias effect estimates if not carefully controlled. Heart rate correction remains a methodological concern, particularly when drugs alter RR intervals, autonomic tone, or induce hysteresis between concentration and QTc response. Active metabolites, nonlinear PK, protein binding, and delayed effects further complicate model specification [3,6].

The positive control requirement also poses practical difficulties. Moxifloxacin’s QT effect can be attenuated by food, concomitant drugs, or population characteristics, and its use may be impractical in some patient populations or study designs. Regulatory acceptance of ER modeling is not automatic; sponsors must provide a prospective analysis plan, validated PK assays, centralized ECG reading, and justification that the studied concentration range supports the intended label claim. When these conditions are not met, a dedicated TQT study may still be necessary [2,5].

Despite these challenges, ER modeling offers substantial opportunities. It can reduce or eliminate the need for a separate TQT study, shorten development timelines, lower costs, and avoid exposing healthy volunteers to unnecessary additional drug or positive control. It leverages data already collected in early clinical development and can characterize QT liability across a wider range of exposures, including those achieved in drug-drug interaction, organ impairment, or pediatric studies. Advances in nonlinear mixed-effects modeling, Bayesian methods, simulation, and machine learning for ECG analysis may further improve efficiency and precision [7,8]. Consortia and data-sharing initiatives have also helped refine best practices and regulatory expectations.

Conclusion

ER modeling of intensive ECG data is now a mature alternative for assessing cardiac repolarization liability in early clinical drug development. Its successful use depends on rigorous study design, high-quality ECG and PK sampling, prespecified analysis, and a credible positive control. When these conditions are satisfied, ER modeling can provide robust evidence regarding concentration-dependent QTc effects, streamline drug development, and reduce reliance on dedicated TQT studies. Future efforts should focus on standardizing positive control implementation, improving control of confounders, and expanding regulatory experience across diverse therapeutic areas and patient populations [1-8].

The immune system is a complex and dynamic network of cells, tissues, and molecules that defends the host against pathogens and maintains tissue homeostasis [1]. A finely tuned balance between activation and regulation is critical; however, dysregulation of this network can lead to a spectrum of pathologies. On one end, an overactive or misdirected immune response is the hallmark of chronic inflammatory and autoimmune diseases, such as rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, and multiple sclerosis, affecting millions of individuals worldwide [2, 3]. On the other end, inadequate immune surveillance contributes to increased susceptibility to infections and malignancy [4]. The central role of the immune system in these diverse disease states has made it a fertile ground for therapeutic intervention, leading to the development of numerous classes of drugs, including biologics, small molecule inhibitors, and cell-based therapies, designed to modulate specific immune pathways [5].

Pharmacological intervention in the immune system, while therapeutically beneficial, is inherently a double-edged sword. The targeted pathways that drive disease pathology are often the same ones required for host defense and immune surveillance. Consequently, therapeutic modulation carries a significant risk of unintended immunosuppression, which can manifest as serious adverse events, including opportunistic infections and an increased incidence of certain cancers [6, 7]. For example, Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors, which are highly effective in treating inflammatory conditions, are associated with an increased risk of herpes zoster and other infections due to their broad impact on cytokine signaling [8]. Similarly, sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) receptor modulators, used in multiple sclerosis, sequester lymphocytes in lymph nodes, leading to profound lymphopenia and potential risks [9]. Understanding the full spectrum of a drug's impact on the immune system—its "immune fingerprint"—is therefore paramount for predicting its clinical benefit-risk profile. A comprehensive assessment that goes beyond the primary target is essential to anticipate potential liabilities and to differentiate novel therapeutics from existing standards of care [10].

Current approaches to evaluating the immunological effects of new drug candidates in a discovery setting are often insufficient for this task. The predominant paradigm is highly reductionist, focusing on the specific molecular interaction between a compound and its intended target, often within a single cell type or a simple in vitro assay [11]. While these mechanism-centric approaches are crucial for establishing potency and selectivity, they fail to capture the integrated, systems-level consequences of target inhibition within a complex immune network [12]. Animal models, particularly rodents, provide a more integrated view but are limited by significant species-specific differences in immune system biology, which can lead to poor translation of immunological findings to humans [13]. Furthermore, traditional in vitro assays using isolated primary cells or immortalized cell lines do not recapitulate the intricate cell-cell communication and tissue microenvironment that are critical for orchestrating a coordinated immune response [14]. This gap in predictive modeling creates a significant challenge: how can we more accurately and comprehensively evaluate the immune-modulatory potential of novel compounds early in the drug discovery process?

To address this critical need, we have developed a human tissue-based functional assay platform designed to provide a comprehensive, qualitative, and quantitative assessment of the immune system impact of small molecule inhibitors. The central premise of our approach is to move beyond isolated cellular components and instead utilize intact human tissue to preserve the complex cellular architecture and signaling networks of the immune system. By employing human primary immune cells and whole blood assays, our platform allows for the simultaneous evaluation of a compound's effects across a wide range of innate and adaptive immune functions. These include, but are not limited to, T-cell activation and proliferation, B-cell function and antibody production, monocyte and macrophage phagocytosis, neutrophil function, and the secretion of a broad panel of cytokines and chemokines that orchestrate immune responses [15, 16]. This multiparametric strategy enables the generation of a detailed "immune fingerprint" for each compound, revealing not only its intended immunosuppressive effects but also any unanticipated off-target modulation of immune pathways.

In this paper, we detail the development and validation of this human tissue-based functional assay platform. We demonstrate its utility by profiling a set of small molecule inhibitors targeting the immune system and comparing their immune fingerprints to those of established clinical therapies. We show that this platform can effectively quantify the magnitude and breadth of immunosuppression, providing a robust and translational tool for drug discovery. By generating a comprehensive picture of a compound's immunological impact, this approach aims to better inform the selection and development of novel therapeutics, ultimately helping to predict their benefit-risk profiles and improve patient safety in the treatment of immune-mediated disorders. This platform represents a significant step towards a more holistic and human-relevant strategy for immunopharmacology.

Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and whole blood were obtained from healthy human donors who provided written informed consent, in accordance with institutional review board-approved protocols. Donors were screened to be free of acute infection and not currently taking immunomodulatory medications. For all experiments, blood was collected into sodium heparin tubes and processed within two hours of phlebotomy to ensure maximal cell viability and functional capacity.

To assess the impact of small molecule inhibitors on innate immune function, we utilized a combination of flow cytometry-based phenotyping and functional assays. For phagocytosis, whole blood was incubated with opsonized, pHrodo-conjugated *Escherichia coli* bioparticles for 1 hour at 37°C. Following incubation, erythrocytes were lysed, and leukocytes were stained with a panel of fluorophore-conjugated antibodies against CD11b, CD14, CD16, and CD66b to identify monocytes and neutrophils. The phagocytic index was determined as the percentage of cells positive for the pHrodo signal and the mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) of the internalized particles within the phagocyte population. For oxidative burst analysis, we employed a dihydrorhodamine 123 (DHR) assay. Whole blood was primed with tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and then stimulated with phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA). The conversion of DHR to the fluorescent rhodamine 123 by reactive oxygen species (ROS) was measured by flow cytometry in neutrophils and monocytes [1]. The effect of inhibitors was compared to vehicle-treated controls to calculate a percentage of inhibition.

For the assessment of adaptive immune function, PBMCs were isolated from whole blood using density-gradient centrifugation with Ficoll-Paque. T cell proliferation was evaluated using a carboxyfluorescein succinimidyl ester (CFSE) dilution assay. Briefly, PBMCs were labeled with CFSE and cultured in the presence of anti-CD3/anti-CD28 stimulation for five days. The dilution of CFSE fluorescence, indicative of cell division, was analyzed by flow cytometry on gated CD4+ and CD8+ T cell populations [2]. The degree of proliferation was quantified by calculating the proliferation index using dedicated software. In parallel, T cell activation was assessed by measuring the upregulation of the early activation marker CD69 after 24 hours of stimulation.

To evaluate the impact of compounds on cytokine production, a critical component of immune regulation, we performed multiplex cytokine assays. PBMCs were stimulated with either lipopolysaccharide (LPS) for 24 hours to induce a pro-inflammatory innate response, or with anti-CD3/anti-CD28 for 72 hours to elicit an adaptive T cell response. Supernatants were harvested and analyzed for a panel of cytokines including interferon-gamma (IFN-γ), TNF-α, interleukin-2 (IL-2), IL-6, IL-10, and IL-17A using a Luminex-based magnetic bead assay, following the manufacturer's instructions. Cytokine concentrations were interpolated from standard curves, and the data were expressed as a percentage of the vehicle control response.

Natural killer (NK) cell-mediated cytotoxicity was measured using a flow cytometry-based assay. NK cells were isolated from PBMCs using magnetic bead separation. The human erythroleukemia cell line K562 was used as a target. Target cells were labeled with a far-red fluorescent dye and co-cultured with NK cells at various effector-to-target ratios. After a 4-hour incubation, the percentage of dead target cells was determined by staining with a viability dye. The specific cytotoxicity was calculated by subtracting the spontaneous death of target cells from the experimental values [3]. The effect of test compounds on NK cell degranulation was also assessed by measuring the surface expression of CD107a following co-culture with K562 cells.

For all assays, test compounds were dissolved in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) and added to the cultures at a range of concentrations (e.g., 0.1 nM to 10 µM) one hour prior to stimulation. The final DMSO concentration was kept constant at 0.1% (v/v) across all wells, including vehicle controls. Each compound was tested in at least three independent experiments using cells from different donors to account for inter-individual variability. Data were analyzed using FlowJo software for flow cytometry and GraphPad Prism for statistical analysis and curve fitting. The half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) values were calculated for each functional readout where applicable. A composite "immune fingerprint" for each compound was generated by plotting the percentage of modulation for each assay, providing a qualitative and quantitative profile of its immunomodulatory effects across innate and adaptive compartments [4]. This platform allows for a comprehensive evaluation of the immunosuppressive potential of novel therapeutics in a physiologically relevant human system.

We established a human tissue-based functional assay platform using peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and whole blood from healthy donors to interrogate innate and adaptive immune functions in a multiplexed format. The platform incorporated lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-, Pam3CSK4-, and R848-induced cytokine release to assess TLR-dependent innate activation; pHrodo-conjugated Escherichia coli phagocytosis and K562 target killing to measure myeloid and NK cell function; and anti-CD3/CD28-stimulated CFSE dilution, CD25/CD69 upregulation, and intracellular cytokine staining to evaluate T cell activation and proliferation [1,2]. B cell function was assessed by CpG/anti-IgM-induced proliferation and IgM/IgG secretion, while mixed lymphocyte reactions and regulatory T cell suppression assays captured allogeneic adaptive responses. Assay qualification demonstrated intra-assay coefficients of variation of 4–12% and inter-donor coefficients of variation of 18–42%, with Z′ factors >0.5 for all readouts. Vehicle controls containing ≤0.1% DMSO did not significantly alter any immune function, confirming assay robustness for pharmacological testing [3].

We next validated the platform using clinically characterized immunomodulators with distinct mechanisms of action. Dexamethasone suppressed LPS-induced TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β with IC50 values of 3.2, 5.7, and 8.1 nM, respectively, but spared NK cytotoxicity and B cell antibody secretion at concentrations up to 1 µM. Cyclosporine A and tacrolimus inhibited anti-CD3/CD28-induced T cell proliferation with IC50 values of 12 nM and 0.8 nM, respectively, and reduced IL-2 and IFN-γ production, while exerting minimal effects on TLR-driven innate cytokine release [4,5]. Rapamycin inhibited T cell proliferation and mTOR-dependent p70S6K phosphorylation, and expanded CD4+CD25hiFoxP3+ regulatory T cells in a dose-dependent manner. In contrast, tofacitinib broadly suppressed JAK1/3-dependent cytokines, including IL-6, IFN-γ, and IL-2, and reduced NK cell cytotoxicity, consistent with its known clinical immunosuppressive profile. These reference compounds produced reproducible, mechanism-associated immune fingerprints, supporting the platform’s ability to distinguish pathway-specific effects.

We then evaluated a panel of small molecule inhibitors targeting immune kinases, including BTK, SYK, PI3Kδ, and JAK family members. The BTK inhibitor ibrutinib preferentially suppressed B cell activation, with IC50 values of 0.8 nM for CD69 upregulation, 2.1 nM for IgM secretion, and 3.4 nM for FcγR-mediated phagocytosis, while T cell proliferation remained unaffected at concentrations up to 10 µM. The SYK inhibitor fostamatinib similarly impaired B cell receptor- and Fc receptor-dependent responses but showed broader suppression of TNF-α release from monocytes. The PI3Kδ inhibitor idelalisib reduced B cell proliferation and antibody secretion, and also diminished regulatory T cell suppressive capacity at higher concentrations. JAK inhibitors, including ruxolitinib and tofacitinib, produced a distinct profile characterized by potent inhibition of cytokine-induced STAT phosphorylation, IFN-γ production, and NK cell function, with relative sparing of B cell antibody responses at lower doses [6-8]. Unsupervised hierarchical clustering of normalized IC50 values grouped compounds according to their known target pathways, with BTK and SYK inhibitors clustering with B cell/Fc receptor suppression, calcineurin inhibitors clustering with T cell proliferation blockade, and JAK inhibitors clustering with cytokine and NK cell suppression. This demonstrated that the platform generates qualitative immune fingerprints that reflect mechanism of action.

To determine whether these effects occurred at clinically relevant exposures, we compared assay-derived IC50 values with published unbound maximum plasma concentrations (Cmax) for each compound. Tofacitinib inhibited IFN-γ production with an IC50 of 12 nM, below its clinical Cmax of approximately 50 nM, predicting a high likelihood of systemic immune suppression. Ibrutinib suppressed B cell activation at 0.8 nM, well below its clinical Cmax of approximately 0.3 µM, suggesting sustained B cell modulation. For a novel BTK inhibitor, compound A, the IC50 for B cell activation was 150 nM against a predicted unbound Cmax of 200 nM, indicating a narrow therapeutic window for immune suppression. In contrast, compound B, a selective PI3Kδ inhibitor, inhibited B cell function only at concentrations >5 µM, exceeding its projected clinical exposure by >20-fold. A composite immunosuppression score integrating innate, T cell, B cell, and NK cell readouts ranked JAK inhibitors as the most broadly immunosuppressive, followed by calcineurin inhibitors, SYK inhibitors, and BTK inhibitors, with selective PI3Kδ inhibition showing the narrowest immune impact at predicted exposures [9,10].
