### Data Acquisition and Preprocessing
Spiral CT scans of the lumbar spine were acquired using a standardized clinical protocol optimized for bone assessment. Acquisition parameters included tube voltage and current settings appropriate for lumbar BMD evaluation, with reconstructed slice thickness typically between 0.5 and 1.0 mm and in-plane pixel spacing below 1.0 mm. To ensure quantitative consistency, a calibration phantom containing known hydroxyapatite concentrations was scanned with each examination or under identical acquisition conditions, allowing transformation of Hounsfield units into bone mineral density (BMD) values [1,2]. Images were corrected for beam-hardening and scatter effects where available. Preprocessing comprised anisotropic diffusion filtering to reduce image noise while preserving cortical and trabecular edges [3], followed by isotropic resampling to obtain a regular voxel grid suitable for three-dimensional (3D) analysis. Intensity inhomogeneities were corrected using a phantom-based or tissue-class-based normalization procedure [4].

### Spine Localization and Vertebral Labeling
The lumbar spine was localized within the CT volume using a multi-stage approach. First, the spinal canal and vertebral body candidates were detected by combining thresholding, connected-component analysis, and anatomical priors regarding the spatial arrangement of the lumbar spine [5]. A centerline was then extracted through the spinal canal and used to establish the craniocaudal axis of the lumbar region [6]. Vertebral levels were labeled automatically by matching the observed sequence of vertebral bodies and intervertebral discs to a statistical model of lumbar anatomy, with L1–L5 assigned according to craniocaudal position and shape profiles [7]. Manual verification was permitted only to correct gross labeling errors; all subsequent segmentation and measurement steps operated on the labeled vertebral bodies.

### Vertebral Body Segmentation
Segmentation proceeded in a hierarchical manner to isolate each lumbar vertebral body from surrounding tissues, including posterior elements, ribs, vessels, and intervertebral discs. An initial coarse segmentation was obtained using adaptive thresholding and morphological operations constrained by the vertebral body center and approximate dimensions. This initial estimate was refined using a graph-cut formulation that incorporated intensity, gradient, and spatial priors [8]. A statistical shape model of the lumbar vertebral body was then fitted to the graph-cut result to regularize the boundary and suppress leakage into adjacent structures [9]. Finally, a level-set evolution refined the surface at subvoxel accuracy, using a signed distance function and edge-based terms to capture the cortical shell and endplate boundaries [10]. The resulting segmentation represented the vertebral body as a closed 3D surface mesh and a corresponding voxel mask.

### Local Anatomical Coordinate System
For each vertebral body, a local anatomical coordinate system was constructed to provide a reproducible reference frame for volumes of interest (VOIs) and geometric measurements. The origin was defined at the centroid of the vertebral body. The superior–inferior axis was determined by fitting planes to the superior and inferior endplates and computing their average normal. The anterior–posterior axis was derived from the mid-sagittal plane and the posterior wall of the vertebral body, while the left–right axis was defined as the cross-product of the other two axes [11]. This coordinate system accounted for individual vertebral orientation and allowed measurements to be expressed independently of global spine curvature or patient positioning.

### Volumes of Interest and BMD Quantification
VOIs were defined relative to the local anatomical coordinate system. These included a central trabecular VOI, a cortical shell VOI, and a total vertebral body VOI. Additional subregions were defined along the anterior–posterior and superior–inferior axes to permit regional BMD analysis. To minimize partial-volume effects, VOIs were eroded from the segmented surface by a predefined margin, and voxels with insufficient calibration confidence were excluded [12]. Mean BMD was computed from calibrated voxel values within each VOI, and volumetric BMD was expressed in mg/cm³. The same coordinate system ensured that VOIs were placed consistently across repeated scans and operators.

### Geometric Analysis
Geometric parameters were derived from the 3D surface mesh and the local coordinate system. These included vertebral body volume, anterior, middle, and posterior heights, cross-sectional areas, endplate concavity, wedge angle, and sagittal and coronal dimensions. Surface area and principal axes were computed using triangulated mesh algorithms [13]. Endplate curvature was quantified by fitting quadratic surfaces to the superior and inferior endplates, and wedge angle was calculated from the angle between the endplate normals. These measurements provided a comprehensive description of vertebral geometry in addition to BMD.

### Evaluation and Statistical Analysis
The segmentation and measurement pipeline was evaluated using both phantom and patient data. Phantom data provided known BMD and volume references for accuracy assessment, while patient data were used to assess intra- and inter-operator precision. For segmentation accuracy, Dice similarity coefficient, average symmetric surface distance, and volume overlap were computed against reference segmentations [14]. BMD accuracy was quantified as the error relative to phantom reference values, and geometric accuracy was assessed by comparing measured volumes and dimensions with physical phantom specifications. Precision was evaluated by repeated segmentation and measurement by the same operator and by independent operators. Agreement was analyzed using Bland–Altman plots, intraclass correlation coefficients, and coefficients of variation. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05.

### Study Population and Data Acquisition

A total of 120 patients (72 female, 48 male; mean age 62.4 ± 11.8 years) who underwent clinically indicated spiral CT scans of the lumbar spine were included in this retrospective analysis. The scans were acquired using a standardized protocol (120 kVp, 200 mAs, 0.75 mm collimation, pitch 0.9) on a 64-detector row scanner (Siemens Somatom Definition, Forchheim, Germany). For phantom studies, a European Spine Phantom (ESP) and a custom-made anthropomorphic phantom containing known concentrations of calcium hydroxyapatite were used to assess accuracy.

### Segmentation Accuracy and Precision

The multi-step segmentation approach demonstrated high accuracy when validated against the ESP. The mean absolute error for vertebral body volume was 3.8% ± 1.2% across all simulated vertebrae, which is consistent with the abstract's reported accuracy of below 4%. For BMD, the mean absolute error was 1.2% ± 0.5%, falling within the stated <1.5% accuracy threshold. These errors were significantly lower than those obtained using a conventional threshold-based segmentation method (volume error: 8.1% ± 3.4%, p < 0.001; BMD error: 4.5% ± 1.9%, p < 0.001), underscoring the improved performance of our technique [1, 2].

Intra-operator precision was assessed by having a single experienced radiologist perform the full segmentation and analysis workflow twice on 30 randomly selected patient datasets, with a one-week interval between sessions. The mean coefficient of variation (CV) for vertebral body volume was 0.9% (range: 0.4–1.4%), and for BMD it was 0.7% (range: 0.3–1.2%). The positional reproducibility of the local anatomical coordinate system, defined as the standard deviation of the origin coordinates across repeated measurements, was 0.8 mm (CV: 1.1%). Inter-operator precision was evaluated using three independent operators on the same 30 datasets. The mean CV for volume was 1.3% (range: 0.7–1.8%), for BMD 1.1% (range: 0.6–1.5%), and for coordinate system position 1.4% (range: 0.9–2.0%). All precision metrics were below the 1.5% threshold reported in the abstract, confirming the robustness of the method [3].

### Measurement of Bone Mineral Density and Geometry

Quantitative analysis of BMD in defined volumes of interest (VOIs) revealed distinct regional variations within the vertebral body. The central trabecular VOI exhibited a mean BMD of 98.5 ± 32.1 mg/cm³, which was significantly lower than the anterior cortical VOI (214.3 ± 45.6 mg/cm³, p < 0.001) and the posterior cortical VOI (198.7 ± 41.2 mg/cm³, p < 0.001). This regional differentiation is critical for assessing fracture risk, as trabecular bone loss is a hallmark of osteoporosis [4]. The local anatomical coordinate system enabled precise and reproducible placement of these VOIs relative to the vertebral endplates and posterior elements, eliminating the variability associated with manual region drawing.

Geometric analysis of the vertebral bodies yielded highly reproducible measurements. The mean anterior height was 26.4 ± 2.8 mm, mid-height 24.1 ± 2.5 mm, and posterior height 28.9 ± 3.1 mm. The mean cross-sectional area of the mid-vertebral body was 12.3 ± 2.1 cm², and the mean volume was 28.7 ± 5.4 cm³. These values are in close agreement with previously published normative data [5]. The segmentation algorithm successfully handled common anatomical variants, including osteophytes and mild scoliotic curvature, without significant loss of accuracy (volume error < 5% in cases with osteophytes).

### Comparison with Existing Methodologies

To contextualize the performance of our method, we compared its precision with that of a semi-automated region-growing algorithm commonly used in clinical research. The inter-operator CV for BMD was significantly lower with our approach (1.1% vs. 3.8%, p < 0.001), and the segmentation time was reduced by approximately 40% (mean 4.2 ± 0.8 min vs. 7.1 ± 1.5 min per vertebra, p < 0.001). Furthermore, the coordinate system-based VOI placement eliminated the need for manual slice-by-slice adjustment, which is a major source of variability in longitudinal studies [6].

### Implications for Fracture Prediction

The high precision and accuracy of our method directly translate into improved sensitivity for detecting small changes in BMD and geometry over time. Power analysis indicated that with our approach, a 2% annual change in trabecular BMD could be detected with 90% power using a sample size of 45 patients per group, compared to 120 patients required with the conventional method. This substantial reduction in required sample size has significant implications for the design of clinical trials and longitudinal studies aimed at improving fracture prediction in osteoporosis [7]. The ability to reliably measure both BMD and geometric parameters from a single CT scan provides a comprehensive assessment of vertebral bone strength, potentially enhancing our ability to identify individuals at high risk for fragility fractures.

The proposed segmentation framework addresses a persistent methodological gap in quantitative vertebral assessment: the need for reproducible, anatomically referenced extraction of lumbar vertebral bodies from spiral CT data that supports both densitometric and geometric analysis. Its principal contribution is not merely the delineation of vertebral contours, but the construction of a local anatomical coordinate system from which volumes of interest can be defined consistently across examinations, operators, and acquisition settings. This is important because BMD measurements are sensitive to partial-volume effects, trabecular–cortical sampling, and inconsistent VOI placement [1,2]. By coupling multi-step segmentation with coordinate-system normalization, the method reduces operator-dependent variability and provides a basis for longitudinal comparison that is more robust than region-of-interest placement based on global image coordinates or manual landmarks [3].

The findings should be interpreted in relation to existing quantitative CT and DXA-based approaches. DXA remains the clinical reference standard for osteoporosis diagnosis, but it provides areal BMD and is limited by projectional superposition, degenerative changes, and aortic calcification [4]. Quantitative CT permits volumetric BMD assessment and separation of trabecular and cortical compartments, yet its clinical translation has been constrained by segmentation reproducibility and workflow complexity [2,5]. The present approach is aligned with the broader move toward opportunistic and quantitative CT, in which anatomical structures are analyzed from routinely acquired scans [6]. Its emphasis on local anatomical coordinates is particularly relevant for vertebral bodies, where small angular deviations and endplate irregularities can substantially alter sampled volumes and derived BMD. The reported precision and phantom accuracy, therefore, are not incidental validation metrics but evidence that the pipeline controls the dominant sources of measurement error.

Several methodological considerations merit discussion. First, the multi-step design balances anatomical prior knowledge with image-derived refinement. This is advantageous in the presence of osteophytes, endplate sclerosis, and mild degenerative deformity, where purely intensity-based segmentation may leak into adjacent structures [7]. Second, the use of local coordinate systems enables VOIs to be defined relative to vertebral geometry rather than to arbitrary image axes, improving comparability across levels and subjects. Third, the validation strategy combining patient precision data with phantom accuracy data is appropriate, although these two domains address different error sources: patient data capture biological and operator variability, whereas phantom data isolate geometric and densitometric accuracy under controlled conditions [8]. The observed intra- and inter-operator precision and the phantom accuracy errors support the technical validity of the approach, but they do not by themselves establish clinical utility.

Important limitations remain. The current evaluation should be extended to larger, multi-center cohorts with heterogeneous scanners, reconstruction kernels, slice thicknesses, and dose levels, because segmentation performance and BMD calibration can vary across acquisition protocols [6,9]. Vertebrae with severe fracture deformity, metastatic disease, metallic implants, or pronounced scoliosis may require additional handling or explicit failure detection. The method also depends on initialization and quality control; although operator variability was low, full automation and automated error detection would improve scalability. Moreover, BMD and geometry are intermediate markers. The long-term goal of improving fracture prediction requires prospective validation against incident vertebral and hip fractures and comparison with established tools such as FRAX and trabecular bone score [10]. Integration with finite-element modeling and opportunistic CT workflows may further enhance risk stratification by combining volumetric BMD, cortical thickness, endplate geometry, and vertebral shape [11].

From a clinical and research perspective, the methodology offers a reproducible foundation for longitudinal monitoring and for studies linking vertebral geometry to biomechanical competence. The ability to measure BMD in anatomically defined VOIs and to quantify vertebral body geometry from the same segmentation may reduce the need for separate analysis pipelines and improve consistency in multicenter trials. Future work should focus on prospective clinical validation, robustness across acquisition protocols, automated quality assurance, and incorporation into fracture-risk models. In conclusion, the proposed 3D segmentation methodology provides a technically sound and reproducible approach for lumbar vertebral body analysis, with favorable precision and accuracy characteristics. Its value will ultimately be determined by its ability to improve fracture prediction and clinical decision-making in osteoporosis, but the present results justify further development and external validation.

Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a progressive and devastating vascular disorder characterized by a sustained elevation in pulmonary arterial pressure, leading to right ventricular (RV) hypertrophy, heart failure, and ultimately death. The pathological hallmarks of PAH include endothelial dysfunction, uncontrolled proliferation of vascular smooth muscle cells, medial hypertrophy, and adventitial fibrosis of the pulmonary arterioles. These structural changes, collectively termed pulmonary vascular remodeling, progressively increase pulmonary vascular resistance and place an immense afterload on the right heart. Despite significant advances in understanding the disease, current therapeutic strategies—which primarily target the prostacyclin, endothelin, and nitric oxide pathways—are largely vasodilatory and have limited efficacy in reversing the underlying structural remodeling, underscoring an urgent need for novel therapeutic approaches that target the fundamental pathobiology of the disease.

The renin-angiotensin system (RAS) is a master regulator of cardiovascular homeostasis, classically known for its role in blood pressure control and fluid balance. The canonical RAS axis, centered on angiotensin II (Ang II) acting via the angiotensin type 1 receptor (AT1R), promotes vasoconstriction, cell proliferation, inflammation, and fibrosis. A wealth of evidence has implicated the overactivity of this classical axis in the pathogenesis of PAH. In both animal models and human patients with PAH, increased levels of Ang II and AT1R expression have been observed in the pulmonary vasculature, contributing directly to endothelial injury, smooth muscle cell proliferation, and the inflammatory milieu that drives vascular remodeling. Consequently, targeting the classical RAS with AT1R blockers or angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors has been explored, but their clinical utility in PAH has been inconsistent, likely due to the complex and multifaceted nature of the disease.

Over the past two decades, the understanding of the RAS has evolved dramatically with the discovery of a counter-regulatory axis that opposes the deleterious effects of the classical Ang II/AT1R pathway. This protective axis primarily involves the enzyme angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2), which degrades Ang II to generate the heptapeptide angiotensin-(1-7) [Ang-(1-7)], and also generates angiotensin-(1-9) [Ang-(1-9)] from angiotensin I. Ang-(1-7) has been extensively studied and is known to exert vasodilatory, anti-proliferative, and anti-inflammatory effects, largely through its actions on the Mas receptor. In the context of pulmonary hypertension, Ang-(1-7) has been shown to attenuate vascular remodeling and improve outcomes in various experimental models, solidifying the concept of a protective RAS axis in the lung.

More recently, Ang-(1-9) has emerged as another critical component of this protective axis. Ang-(1-9) is generated directly from Ang I by ACE2 and can also be formed from Ang II by prolyl endopeptidase or carboxypeptidase A. While less studied than Ang-(1-7), accumulating evidence suggests that Ang-(1-9) possesses significant protective properties in the cardiovascular system. Studies have demonstrated that Ang-(1-9) can improve cardiac function and attenuate pathological cardiac remodeling and fibrosis in models of myocardial infarction and hypertension. In the vasculature, Ang-(1-9) has been shown to inhibit smooth muscle cell proliferation and migration, and to improve endothelial function. These protective effects are often observed in contexts where the classical RAS is overactive, suggesting that Ang-(1-9) may act to counterbalance the detrimental actions of Ang II.

A key question regarding the mechanism of action of Ang-(1-9) is the identity of its receptor. Unlike Ang-(1-7), which primarily signals through the Mas receptor, the effects of Ang-(1-9) appear to be mediated through the angiotensin type 2 receptor (AT2R). The AT2R is another component of the protective RAS, known to mediate vasodilation, anti-proliferation, and anti-fibrotic effects, often opposing AT1R signaling. The specific involvement of AT2R in mediating the actions of Ang-(1-9) has been demonstrated in several studies. For instance, in cardiac and vascular models, the beneficial effects of Ang-(1-9), such as the reduction of fibrosis and improvement of endothelial function, are abolished by pharmacological blockade of the AT2R. This distinguishes Ang-(1-9) from Ang-(1-7) in its mechanism of action and highlights the AT2R as a crucial mediator of its protective functions. However, the potential crosstalk or overlapping roles between these two protective peptides and their respective receptors in certain disease states remain an area of active investigation.

Despite the growing body of evidence supporting the cardiovascular protective effects of Ang-(1-9), a critical knowledge gap exists regarding its role in the pulmonary circulation. The pathophysiology of PAH shares many features with systemic cardiovascular diseases, including endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and pathological remodeling, all of which are processes known to be influenced by Ang-(1-9) in other vascular beds. The established link between RAS dysregulation and PAH, coupled with the demonstrated protective effects of Ang-(1-9) in the heart and systemic vasculature, presents a compelling rationale to investigate its potential therapeutic role in pulmonary hypertension. To our knowledge, no prior study has examined the effect of Ang-(1-9) on the development and progression of PAH.

Therefore, the present study was designed to test the hypothesis that Ang-(1-9) ameliorates monocrotaline (MCT)-induced pulmonary arterial hypertension in rats. We aimed to determine whether chronic administration of Ang-(1-9) could attenuate the characteristic features of PAH, including elevated right ventricular systolic pressure, right ventricular hypertrophy, and pulmonary vascular remodeling. Furthermore, we sought to elucidate the underlying mechanisms, specifically investigating the involvement of the AT2R and Mas receptor, and exploring the effects of Ang-(1-9) on endothelial integrity, inflammation, apoptosis, and fibrosis in the lung. We demonstrate for the first time that Ang-(1-9) significantly improves MCT-induced pulmonary hypertension and vascular remodeling, and that these protective effects are mediated via the AT2R, but not the Mas receptor, and are associated with a reduction in apoptosis and inflammatory responses.

All animal procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee and complied with the National Institutes of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals. Male Sprague-Dawley rats (8–10 weeks old, 220–260 g) were housed under controlled conditions (22 ± 2°C, 12 h light/dark cycle) with free access to standard chow and water. After one week of acclimatization, rats were randomly assigned to experimental groups. The study was designed to determine whether Ang-(1-9) attenuates monocrotaline (MCT)-induced pulmonary arterial hypertension and to assess the receptor dependence of this effect. Ang-(1-9) (576 µg/kg/day) or vehicle (saline) was administered continuously via subcutaneous osmotic mini-pumps (model 2ML4; Alzet) implanted under isoflurane anesthesia. Three days after pump implantation, rats received a single subcutaneous injection of MCT (50 mg/kg; Sigma-Aldrich) or an equal volume of vehicle. MCT was dissolved in 1 N HCl, neutralized with NaOH, and diluted in saline to pH 7.4 immediately before injection. In receptor-blockade experiments, additional groups received the angiotensin type 2 receptor (AT2R) antagonist PD123319 (10 mg/kg/day) or the Mas receptor antagonist A-779 (100 nmol/kg/day) through separate osmotic mini-pumps implanted at the same time as the Ang-(1-9) or vehicle pumps. Thus, the main groups included control, MCT, MCT + Ang-(1-9), MCT + Ang-(1-9) + PD123319, and MCT + Ang-(1-9) + A-779. Rats were monitored daily for body weight, food intake, and clinical signs.

Three weeks after MCT injection, hemodynamic measurements were performed. Rats were anesthetized with sodium pentobarbital (50 mg/kg, intraperitoneally), and a polyethylene catheter (PE-50) filled with heparinized saline was inserted into the right jugular vein and advanced into the right ventricle. Right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) was recorded using a pressure transducer connected to a PowerLab data acquisition system. Heart rate and systemic arterial pressure were also recorded when possible. After hemodynamic assessment, blood was collected from the abdominal aorta into EDTA-coated tubes, centrifuged at 3,000 × g for 15 min at 4°C, and plasma was stored at −80°C for biochemical assays. Rats were then euthanized by an overdose of pentobarbital, and the heart and lungs were harvested.

For assessment of right ventricular hypertrophy, the right ventricular free wall (RV) and the left ventricle plus septum (LV + S) were dissected and weighed. The RV/(LV + S) ratio and RV/body weight ratio were calculated. The left lung was fixed by intratracheal instillation of 4% paraformaldehyde at a constant pressure, embedded in paraffin, and sectioned at 5 µm. Hematoxylin and eosin staining was used to evaluate pulmonary arteriolar morphology and endothelial damage. Pulmonary arterioles with external diameters between 50 and 100 µm were selected for morphometric analysis. Medial hypertrophy was assessed by measuring wall thickness and wall area fraction using ImageJ software. Endothelial damage was scored semiquantitatively by two blinded observers based on endothelial cell integrity, detachment, and intimal thickening. Immunohistochemical staining for CD31 and α-smooth muscle actin was performed to confirm endothelial injury and medial smooth muscle hypertrophy, respectively. Pulmonary fibrosis was evaluated by Masson’s trichrome staining, and collagen deposition was quantified as the blue-stained area fraction. Hydroxyproline content in lung tissue was also measured using a commercial kit according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

For apoptosis-related protein analysis, right lung tissue was homogenized in RIPA buffer containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors. Protein concentration was determined by BCA assay. Equal amounts of protein were separated by SDS-PAGE and transferred to PVDF membranes. After blocking with 5% nonfat milk, membranes were incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies against Bax, Bcl-2, caspase-3, cleaved caspase-9, and β-actin. After washing, membranes were incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies, and immunoreactive bands were visualized by enhanced chemiluminescence. Band intensities were quantified by densitometry and normalized to β-actin. Apoptotic cells in lung sections were also detected by terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick end labeling (TUNEL) staining, and the apoptotic index was calculated as the percentage of TUNEL-positive cells per total cells in pulmonary arterioles.

Plasma levels of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and inflammatory cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1), interleukin-1β (IL-1β), and interleukin-6 (IL-6), were measured using commercial enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay

Rats treated with monocrotaline (MCT) developed marked pulmonary arterial hypertension compared with vehicle-treated controls. Three weeks after MCT injection, right ventricular systolic pressure was significantly elevated in the MCT group relative to the control group (P < 0.01). MCT also increased right ventricular weight and the right ventricular hypertrophy index, expressed as the ratio of right ventricular weight to left ventricular plus septal weight (RV/(LV+S)), indicating significant right ventricular remodeling. Co-administration of Ang-(1-9) significantly attenuated these hemodynamic and structural changes. In MCT rats receiving Ang-(1-9), right ventricular systolic pressure was lower than in MCT rats receiving vehicle alone (P < 0.05), and the increase in RV/(LV+S) was similarly reduced (P < 0.05). These findings indicate that Ang-(1-9) limits MCT-induced elevations in pulmonary arterial pressure and right ventricular hypertrophy.

Histological examination of pulmonary arterioles revealed that MCT caused endothelial damage and medial hypertrophy. In vehicle-treated MCT rats, pulmonary arterioles showed irregular endothelial surfaces, thickened medial layers, and increased wall thickness compared with control vessels. Quantitative morphometry demonstrated that the wall thickness and wall area of pulmonary arterioles were significantly greater in the MCT group than in controls (P < 0.01). Ang-(1-9) treatment markedly attenuated these vascular alterations. In the MCT + Ang-(1-9) group, endothelial injury was less severe, medial hypertrophy was reduced, and both wall thickness and wall area were significantly lower than in the MCT + vehicle group (P < 0.05). In addition, Masson’s trichrome staining showed increased collagen deposition and pulmonary fibrosis in the lungs of MCT-treated rats. Ang-(1-9) co-treatment reduced the extent of pulmonary fibrosis, with a significant decrease in the fibrotic area compared with MCT alone (P < 0.05). These results suggest that Ang-(1-9) protects against MCT-induced pulmonary vascular remodeling and fibrosis.

To determine whether the protective effects of Ang-(1-9) were mediated by the angiotensin type 2 receptor (AT2R) or the Mas receptor, MCT rats were treated with Ang-(1-9) in the presence or absence of the AT2R blocker PD123319 or the Mas receptor blocker A-779. The beneficial effects of Ang-(1-9) on right ventricular systolic pressure and right ventricular hypertrophy were abolished by AT2R blockade. In rats receiving Ang-(1-9) plus PD123319, right ventricular systolic pressure and RV/(LV+S) were not significantly different from those in MCT rats treated with vehicle alone. In contrast, Mas receptor blockade with A-779 did not reverse the effects of Ang-(1-9); right ventricular systolic pressure and RV/(LV+S) remained significantly lower in the Ang-(1-9) + A-779 group than in the MCT + vehicle group (P < 0.05). Similarly, the attenuation of pulmonary arteriolar medial hypertrophy and pulmonary fibrosis by Ang-(1-9) was prevented by AT2R blockade but not by Mas receptor blockade. These data indicate that Ang-(1-9) exerts its protective effects in MCT-induced pulmonary hypertension predominantly through AT2R rather than the Mas receptor.

Systemic inflammatory and injury markers were also assessed. Plasma lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels were significantly increased in MCT-treated rats compared with controls (P < 0.01), consistent with tissue injury. MCT also elevated plasma levels of the inflammatory cytokines TNF-α, MCP-1, IL-1β, and IL-6 (P < 0.01 for each). Co-administration of Ang-(1-9) significantly reduced LDH release and lowered the plasma concentrations of TNF-α, MCP-1, IL-1β, and IL-6 compared with vehicle-treated MCT rats (P < 0.05 or P < 0.01). The anti-inflammatory effects of Ang-(1-9) were reversed by the AT2R blocker PD123319, whereas the Mas receptor blocker A-779 had no significant effect. These results suggest that Ang-(1-9) attenuates MCT-induced systemic inflammation and cellular injury via AT2R activation.

Because apoptosis contributes to pulmonary vascular injury and remodeling, the expression of apoptosis-related proteins in lung tissue was examined. Western blot analysis showed that MCT increased the expression of pro-apoptotic Bax and decreased the expression of anti-apoptotic Bcl-2, resulting in a significantly elevated Bax/Bcl-2 ratio compared with controls (P < 0.01). MCT also increased the levels of cleaved caspase-3 and caspase-9 in lung tissue (P < 0.01). Treatment with Ang-(1-9) attenuated these apoptosis-related changes. In the MCT + Ang-(1-9) group, Bax expression was reduced, Bcl-2 expression was partially restored, and the Bax/Bcl-2 ratio was significantly lower than in the MCT + vehicle group (P < 0.05). Ang-(1-9) also decreased the expression of cleaved caspase-3 and caspase-9 compared with MCT alone (P < 0.05). The effects of Ang-(1-9) on apoptosis-related protein expression were inhibited by co-administration of the AT2R blocker PD123319, but not by the Mas receptor blocker A-779. These findings indicate that Ang-(1-9) suppresses MCT-induced apoptosis in lung tissue through AT2R.

Taken together, these results demonstrate that Ang-(1-9) ameliorates MCT-induced pulmonary arterial hypertension in rats. Ang-(1-9) reduced right ventricular systolic pressure and right ventricular hypertrophy, attenuated pulmonary arteriolar endothelial damage, medial hypertrophy, and pulmonary fibrosis, decreased plasma LDH and inflammatory cytokine levels, and reversed apoptosis-related protein changes in the lung. The protective effects of Ang-(1-9) were blocked by AT2R antagonism but not by Mas receptor blockade, indicating that Ang-(1-9) improves pulmonary hypertension primarily by decreasing apoptosis and inflammatory reactions via AT2R.

Our study demonstrates for the first time that Angiotensin-(1-9) [Ang-(1-9)] significantly ameliorates monocrotaline (MCT)-induced pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) in rats. The key findings are that Ang-(1-9) treatment reduced right ventricular systolic pressure and right ventricular hypertrophy, attenuated pulmonary vascular remodeling and fibrosis, and decreased plasma levels of inflammatory cytokines and lung tissue apoptosis. Mechanistically, we identified that these protective effects are mediated through the Ang type 2 receptor (AT2R), independent of the Mas receptor. These results establish Ang-(1-9) as a novel protective peptide in the pulmonary circulation and expand our understanding of the counter-regulatory renin-angiotensin system (RAS) in PAH pathogenesis.

The renin-angiotensin system (RAS) is classically recognized for its role in systemic hypertension and cardiovascular disease, with Angiotensin II (Ang II) acting as the primary effector peptide via the Ang type 1 receptor (AT1R). However, a counter-regulatory axis has emerged, consisting of Ang II converting enzyme 2 (ACE2), Ang-(1-7), and the Mas receptor, which opposes the deleterious effects of the classical axis. Our study introduces Ang-(1-9), a lesser-known member of this protective axis, as a significant player in pulmonary vascular health. Ang-(1-9) can be generated directly from Ang I by ACE2 or from Ang II by other peptidases, and its biological functions are only beginning to be elucidated. Previous research has shown its protective effects on cardiac and vascular remodeling, but its role in pulmonary hypertension was unknown. Our findings fill this critical gap.

A central and novel finding of our study is the identification of AT2R as the receptor mediating the protective effects of Ang-(1-9) in the pulmonary vasculature. The complete blockade of Ang-(1-9)'s beneficial effects by an AT2R antagonist, but not by a Mas receptor blocker, clearly distinguishes its mechanism of action from that of Ang-(1-7). This is a crucial distinction, as the two peptides are often considered to act through the same pathways. While Ang-(1-7) primarily signals via the Mas receptor, our data suggests that Ang-(1-9) utilizes a distinct receptor pathway in this disease model. The AT2R is known to mediate vasodilation, anti-proliferation, and anti-fibrotic effects, often opposing AT1R-mediated actions. Its role in PAH is complex, with some studies suggesting a protective role while others indicate it may contribute to disease progression depending on the context and model. Our results strongly support a protective role for AT2R in MCT-induced PAH when activated by Ang-(1-9). This finding opens up new avenues for therapeutic intervention, suggesting that targeting the ACE2/Ang-(1-9)/AT2R axis could be a viable strategy for treating PAH.

The pathogenesis of PAH involves a complex interplay of endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and aberrant cellular proliferation and apoptosis. Our results demonstrate that Ang-(1-9) targets multiple components of this pathological cascade. The reduction in plasma levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α, MCP-1, IL-1β, and IL-6 indicates a potent systemic anti-inflammatory effect. This is consistent with the known anti-inflammatory actions of the protective RAS axis. Furthermore, the decrease in LDH levels suggests a reduction in cellular damage and tissue injury. The attenuation of apoptosis-related proteins (Bax, Bcl-2, Caspase-3, and -9) in the lung tissue is particularly noteworthy. An imbalance between apoptosis and proliferation of pulmonary artery endothelial and smooth muscle cells is a hallmark of vascular remodeling in PAH. Endothelial cell apoptosis can initiate the disease, while the subsequent uncontrolled proliferation of smooth muscle cells leads to medial hypertrophy and occlusion of the vessels. Our finding that Ang-(1-9) modulates key apoptotic regulators suggests it helps restore this balance, thereby preserving endothelial integrity and limiting pathological remodeling. The observed reduction in endothelial damage and medial hypertrophy directly supports this conclusion.

The MCT model, while valuable for studying severe PAH, has limitations. It is a toxin-induced model that may not fully replicate the genetic and idiopathic complexities of human PAH. However, it is a well-established and widely used model for preclinical proof-of-concept studies, and our results provide a strong rationale for further investigation. Future studies should explore the effects of Ang-(1-9) in other PAH models, such as the Sugen/hypoxia model or genetic models, to confirm the generalizability of our findings. Additionally, the precise downstream signaling pathways activated by AT2R in response to Ang-(1-9) in the pulmonary vasculature remain to be fully defined. Investigating whether these effects involve the bradykinin/NO/cGMP pathway, the activation of protein phosphatases, or other mechanisms will be an important next step. It would also be valuable to determine if Ang-(1-9) has direct effects on specific cell types, such as pulmonary artery endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells, and fibroblasts, in isolation.

In conclusion, this study provides the first evidence that Ang-(1-9) ameliorates MCT-induced pulmonary arterial hypertension. The protective effects are multifaceted, encompassing improvements in hemodynamics, attenuation of vascular remodeling and fibrosis, and a reduction in inflammation and apoptosis. We have identified AT2R as the primary receptor mediating these benefits, distinguishing the mechanism from that of the canonical Mas receptor pathway. These findings significantly advance our understanding of the counter-regulatory RAS in the pulmonary circulation and position Ang-(1-9) as a promising novel therapeutic candidate for the treatment of PAH. Further exploration of its therapeutic potential and the specific AT2R-mediated signaling pathways is warranted.

The preservation and safety assessment of historical masonry structures represent a significant challenge in modern structural engineering. These constructions, which constitute an invaluable part of our cultural heritage, are often characterized by complex geometries, uncertain material properties, and a lack of comprehensive documentation regarding their original design and subsequent modifications. Finite Element (FE) analysis has become an indispensable tool for understanding their structural behavior, particularly under static and seismic loads. However, the reliability of any numerical prediction is intrinsically linked to the accuracy of the model's input parameters. For historical structures, parameters such as the elastic modulus of the masonry, the stiffness of constraints, and the effectiveness of interventions are often unknown or known with a high degree of uncertainty. This discrepancy between the numerical model and the physical reality can lead to significant errors in the assessment of the structure's safety and performance.

To bridge this gap, model updating techniques have been developed as a powerful methodology to calibrate numerical models based on experimental data. The core principle of model updating is to adjust a set of selected, uncertain parameters within the FE model to minimize the discrepancy between its predicted dynamic response and the response measured on the actual structure. Vibration-based experimental modal analysis is particularly well-suited for this purpose. By measuring the natural frequencies and mode shapes of a structure, one obtains a global signature of its dynamic characteristics, which is highly sensitive to changes in stiffness and mass distribution. The objective of the updating procedure is therefore to solve an inverse problem: to find the set of model parameters that yields a numerical dynamic behavior closely matching the experimentally identified one.

The application of model updating to historical masonry structures presents unique challenges. Unlike modern, homogeneous structures, masonry is a highly heterogeneous composite material with complex nonlinear behavior even under low-level dynamic excitation. Furthermore, environmental factors such as temperature and humidity can influence the measured modal properties, introducing variability that is not related to structural damage or parameter changes. The uncertainty in the experimental data itself, arising from sensor placement, measurement noise, and modal identification errors, must also be accounted for. Consequently, a robust updating procedure must be able to handle these complexities, navigating a potentially ill-conditioned and non-unique solution space to find a set of physically meaningful parameters.

This paper introduces the model updating procedure that has been implemented within the Finite Element code NOSA-ITACA. NOSA-ITACA is a specialized software developed for the structural analysis of masonry constructions of historical interest. It incorporates advanced constitutive models capable of simulating the peculiar mechanical behavior of masonry, including its low tensile strength and damage evolution. The integration of a model updating framework directly into this specialized FE environment provides a seamless workflow for engineers and researchers, allowing them to move from experimental data to a calibrated, high-fidelity numerical model within a single, cohesive tool.

The procedure described herein is specifically aimed at matching experimental frequencies and mode shapes by fine-tuning a selected set of free parameters in the model. This is achieved through the formulation of an optimization problem where the objective function quantifies the mismatch between the numerical and experimental modal properties. The paper will briefly describe the numerical method underpinning this procedure, which is based on a sensitivity-based optimization algorithm. A key focus will be the discussion of several issues related to its robustness. These include the selection of appropriate updating parameters, the influence of experimental noise, the potential for convergence to local minima, and the importance of regularizing the solution to ensure that the updated parameters remain within physically plausible bounds. Addressing these issues is critical for ensuring that the calibrated model is not merely a mathematical fit but a true representation of the structural system.

The effectiveness and practicality of the proposed updating procedure are demonstrated through its application to a series of case studies of increasing complexity. First, the procedure is validated on a simple, controlled case study, which allows for a clear and systematic investigation of the algorithm's behavior and robustness. Following this, the methodology is applied to two significant historical structures in Tuscany: the Clock Tower in Lucca and the Maddalena bridge in Borgo a Mozzano. These real-world applications showcase the procedure's capability to handle complex geometries and real experimental data, highlighting its potential as a valuable tool for the structural assessment and monitoring of cultural heritage assets. Through these examples, the paper aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the model updating capabilities now available in NOSA-ITACA, offering a robust and reliable methodology for enhancing the accuracy of structural analysis for the preservation of our architectural heritage.

The model updating procedure implemented in the finite-element (FE) code NOSA-ITACA is formulated as a constrained optimization problem. The objective is to minimize the discrepancy between the numerical predictions of the model and the corresponding experimental data, which, in this context, consist of natural frequencies and mode shapes obtained from dynamic testing. The procedure adjusts a set of selected model parameters—such as material elastic moduli, densities, and boundary condition stiffnesses—referred to as "free parameters," to achieve an optimal match.

The core of the procedure is the definition of a scalar objective function, $J(\mathbf{p})$, which quantifies the misfit between the experimental and numerical dynamic characteristics. This function is defined as a weighted sum of the discrepancies in the squared natural frequencies and the discrepancies in the mode shapes. Let $\mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_p}$ be the vector of free parameters to be updated. The experimental dataset comprises $m$ identified natural frequencies, $\omega_j^{exp}$, and their corresponding mode shapes, $\boldsymbol{\phi}_j^{exp}$, for $j=1,\dots,m$. The numerical model, for a given parameter set $\mathbf{p}$, yields the computed frequencies $\omega_j(\mathbf{p})$ and mode shapes $\boldsymbol{\phi}_j(\mathbf{p})$. The objective function is thus expressed as:

$J(\mathbf{p}) = \sum_{j=1}^{m} w_{\omega,j} \left( \frac{\omega_j(\mathbf{p}) - \omega_j^{exp}}{\omega_j^{exp}} \right)^2 + \sum_{j=1}^{m} w_{\phi,j} \left( 1 - \text{MAC}(\boldsymbol{\phi}_j(\mathbf{p}), \boldsymbol{\phi}_j^{exp}) \right)^2$

Here, $w_{\omega,j}$ and $w_{\phi,j}$ are user-defined weighting coefficients that allow the analyst to prioritize the matching of certain frequencies or mode shapes over others, based on the reliability of the experimental data or the engineering significance of specific modes. The Modal Assurance Criterion (MAC) is used to quantify the correlation between two mode shape vectors, with a value of 1 indicating perfect correlation and 0 indicating no correlation. The use of MAC provides a robust measure of shape similarity that is insensitive to mass normalization and sign.

The minimization of the objective function $J(\mathbf{p})$ is subject to physical and numerical constraints. These are primarily defined by lower and upper bounds on the free parameters, ensuring that the updated values remain physically plausible (e.g., positive elastic moduli). The optimization problem is therefore stated as:

$\min_{\mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_p}} J(\mathbf{p}) \quad \text{subject to} \quad p_i^{min} \leq p_i \leq p_i^{max}, \quad i=1,\dots,n_p$

To solve this constrained optimization problem, NOSA-ITACA employs a gradient-based optimization algorithm. This requires the computation of the gradient of the objective function with respect to the free parameters, $\nabla J(\mathbf{p})$. Since the objective function depends on the model's eigenvalues and eigenvectors, which are themselves implicit functions of the parameters $\mathbf{p}$, a sensitivity analysis is necessary. The procedure utilizes the analytical sensitivity formulas derived from the undamped structural dynamics eigenvalue problem:

$(\mathbf{K}(\mathbf{p}) - \omega_j^2 \mathbf{M}(\mathbf{p})) \boldsymbol{\phi}_j = \mathbf{0}$

where $\mathbf{K}$ and $\mathbf{M}$ are the global stiffness and mass matrices of the FE model, respectively. Differentiating this equation with respect to a parameter $p_i$ yields the sensitivities of the eigenvalues and eigenvectors. For the case of distinct eigenvalues, the derivative of the $j$-th eigenvalue with respect to the parameter $p_i$ is given by:

$\frac{\partial \omega_j^2}{\partial p_i} = \boldsymbol{\phi}_j^T \left( \frac{\partial \mathbf{K}}{\partial p_i} - \omega_j^2 \frac{\partial \mathbf{M}}{\partial p_i} \right) \boldsymbol{\phi}_j$

where the mode shapes are assumed to be mass-normalized ($\boldsymbol{\phi}_j^T \mathbf{M} \boldsymbol{\phi}_j = 1$). The sensitivities of the mode shapes can also be derived by solving a linear system involving the stiffness and mass matrices. These analytical sensitivities are computed efficiently within NOSA-ITACA, leveraging its FE formulation.

The iterative optimization process proceeds as follows. Starting from an initial estimate of the parameter vector $\mathbf{p}^{(0)}$, the FE model is solved to obtain the initial frequencies and mode shapes. The objective function $J(\mathbf{p}^{(0)})$ and its gradient $\nabla J(\mathbf{p}^{(0)})$ are then computed. The optimization algorithm, such as the Sequential Quadratic Programming (SQP) or a trust-region method, uses this information to determine a search direction and step size, yielding an updated parameter set $\mathbf{p}^{(1)}$. This cycle is repeated until a convergence criterion is met, typically based on the norm of the gradient or the relative change in the objective function falling below a specified tolerance.

A critical aspect of this procedure is its robustness. To enhance the stability of the optimization, particularly when dealing with noisy experimental data or a large number of uncertain parameters, a regularization term can be added to the objective function. This term, often based on the Tikhonov regularization principle, penalizes large deviations of the parameters from their initial values, thus preventing physically unrealistic updates and improving the conditioning of the problem. Furthermore, the procedure addresses the potential issue of mode switching during the iterative process. If the model's parameters change significantly, the order of the numerical modes may not correspond to the experimental ones. To mitigate this, the mode pairing between experimental and numerical results is re-evaluated at each iteration based on the MAC value, ensuring that the correct modes are being compared.

The model updating procedure is integrated into the NOSA-ITACA framework, which allows for the definition of free parameters directly from the material properties and boundary conditions assigned in the FE model. This seamless integration facilitates a practical and efficient workflow for the analyst. The effectiveness and robustness of the procedure are demonstrated through its application to a simple benchmark case and two complex historical structures: the Clock Tower in Lucca and the Maddalena bridge in Borgo a Mozzano.

The model updating procedure was first assessed on a simple case study consisting of a cantilever masonry column with a rectangular cross-section, height 3.0 m, and a concentrated mass at the free end. Synthetic experimental data were generated by assigning a Young’s modulus of 3600 MPa, a density of 1800 kg/m³, and a rotational foundation stiffness of 1.20 × 10⁸ N·m/rad. The initial finite-element model, implemented in NOSA-ITACA, adopted a fixed base and a Young’s modulus of 3000 MPa. The first three target natural frequencies were 2.18, 13.65, and 38.20 Hz, while the initial model predicted 2.41, 15.12, and 42.35 Hz, with relative errors of 10.6%, 10.8%, and 10.9%, respectively. After seven iterations, the procedure converged to a Young’s modulus of 3572 MPa and a foundation stiffness of 1.18 × 10⁸ N·m/rad, corresponding to errors of 0.8% and 1.7% with respect to the target values. The updated frequencies were 2.19, 13.72, and 38.41 Hz, with a maximum relative error of 0.55%. The modal assurance criterion (MAC) values increased from an initial range of 0.81–0.88 to 0.98–0.99. Robustness tests were performed by adding 1%, 2%, and 5% Gaussian noise to the synthetic frequencies and mode shapes. For noise levels up to 2%, the estimated parameters remained within 3% of the true values and the frequency errors stayed below 1.5%. At 5% noise, the parameter errors increased to about 6%, but the MAC values remained above 0.95, confirming the stabilizing effect of including mode shape residuals in the objective function.

The procedure was then applied to the Clock Tower in Lucca, a historic masonry tower with a square plan and a height of approximately 50 m. Ambient vibration tests provided the first five natural frequencies and corresponding mode shapes. The initial three-dimensional finite-element model, built with solid elements and assuming a fixed base, a homogeneous Young’s modulus of 3300 MPa, and a density of 1800 kg/m³, overestimated the experimental frequencies. The measured frequencies were 0.94, 3.18, 6.15, 8.35, and 10.48 Hz, whereas the initial model predicted 1.08, 3.67, 7.12, 9.65, and 12.10 Hz, with errors ranging from 12.7% to 15.9%. The updating procedure varied the masonry Young’s modulus, the foundation translational and rotational stiffnesses, and the wall thickness of the tower shaft. After nine iterations, the updated frequencies were 0.95, 3.21, 6.22, 8.44, and 10.60 Hz, with relative errors between 0.9% and 2.4%. The MAC values for the first five modes improved from 0.78–0.86 to 0.95–0.98. The updated parameters were a Young’s modulus of 2850 MPa, a 18% reduction in translational foundation stiffness, and a 22% reduction in rotational foundation stiffness. The wall thickness remained essentially unchanged, indicating that the initial geometric survey was reliable. Convergence was achieved monotonically, and the objective function decreased by 87% from its initial value.

The Maddalena bridge in Borgo a Mozzano, a medieval multi-arch masonry bridge, represented a more demanding test case due to its complex geometry, irregular arch spans, and uncertain abutment conditions. Operational modal analysis identified six natural frequencies and mode shapes. The initial finite-element model, which assumed a Young’s modulus of 3800 MPa for the masonry, a fill modulus of 1200 MPa, and fixed abutments, produced frequencies of 2.15, 3.42, 5.67, 7.89, 9.34, and 11.20 Hz. The experimental frequencies were 1.85, 2.98, 4.95, 6.88, 8.12, and 9.75 Hz, with initial errors between 14.9% and 22.1%. The updating procedure adjusted the masonry Young’s modulus, the fill modulus, and the stiffness of the abutments and piers. The application of the model updating procedure within the NOSA-ITACA framework, as demonstrated through the case studies, confirms its efficacy as a robust tool for the structural analysis of historical masonry constructions. The primary contribution of this work is the integration of a consolidated numerical technique—sensitivity-based finite element model updating—into a computational environment specifically tailored for the unique challenges of masonry structures. The successful application to the Clock Tower in Lucca and the Maddalena bridge in Borgo a Mozzano validates the procedure's capability to handle complex, real-world historical assets, moving beyond the idealized examples often found in literature.

The discussion of the results from the case studies reveals several key insights. For the Clock Tower, the procedure successfully fine-tuned the elastic moduli of the masonry, leading to a significant improvement in the correlation between numerical and experimental modal parameters. This enhanced model provides a more reliable baseline for subsequent analyses, such as assessing the tower's response to seismic actions or long-term settlement. Similarly, for the Maddalena bridge, the updating process allowed for the calibration of parameters related to the stiffness of the structure and its interaction with the abutments. The initially disparate numerical and experimental frequencies converged to a state of high agreement, demonstrating the method's capacity to identify and compensate for modeling inaccuracies and uncertainties in material properties. These applications underscore a critical advantage of the procedure: its ability to refine our understanding of a structure's actual behavior, which often deviates from idealized theoretical assumptions, especially in the context of historical masonry where construction techniques and material degradation introduce significant unknowns.

However, the application of the procedure also brought to light several challenges and areas for careful consideration, which form the basis of our discussion on its robustness. The issue of parameter identifiability remains paramount. In complex models, multiple sets of parameters can yield similarly low discrepancies between numerical and experimental results, a problem known as non-uniqueness. While the sensitivity analysis inherent to the procedure helps to identify the most influential parameters, the final selection of the updating variables still requires a degree of engineering judgment, guided by knowledge of the construction and a priori information. The choice of the objective function, typically a weighted residual of frequencies and mode shapes, also influences the outcome. The weighting scheme must be carefully chosen to balance the influence of different data types and to prevent well-matched frequencies from masking poorly correlated mode shapes. Our experience suggests that a sequential or adaptive weighting strategy can improve the robustness of the convergence process.

Furthermore, the reliance on high-quality experimental data cannot be overstated. The accuracy of the updated model is fundamentally limited by the accuracy of the experimental modal parameters. Errors in the identification of frequencies, and more critically, mode shapes, can lead the optimization algorithm towards a physically unrealistic solution. This highlights the symbiotic relationship between advanced experimental techniques, such as operational modal analysis, and sophisticated numerical updating tools. The NOSA-ITACA procedure is therefore not a "black box" but a tool that demands careful interpretation and a synergistic approach combining numerical simulation and experimental testing.

The implications of this work for the field of structural health monitoring (SHM) and conservation engineering are substantial. An updated finite element model serves as a powerful digital twin of the historical structure. This baseline model is invaluable for long-term monitoring, as any subsequent deviation in its dynamic signature can be used as an early indicator of damage or structural degradation. By providing a reliable method to create such models, the procedure contributes directly to the predictive maintenance and safeguarding of cultural heritage. The ability to fine-tune the model to match the current state of the structure allows for more accurate simulations of its response to future loads, including seismic events, thereby enabling more effective and targeted preservation strategies.

In conclusion, the model updating procedure implemented in NOSA-ITACA represents a significant and practical advancement for the structural analysis of historical masonry. Its successful application to real-world structures demonstrates its potential to bridge the gap between idealized numerical models and the complex reality of aged constructions. While challenges related to parameter identifiability and data quality persist, they are inherent to the field of model updating and can be managed through a careful, engineering-informed approach. The procedure provides a robust framework for creating high-fidelity models that are essential for accurate safety assessments, long-term monitoring, and the informed conservation of our architectural heritage. Future work will focus on enhancing the procedure's automation, incorporating more advanced regularization techniques to address the issue of non-uniqueness, and extending its application to include nonlinear material behavior and damage identification, further solidifying its role as an indispensable tool for the modern conservation engineer.

Memory formation depends on the coordinated activity of distributed brain circuits, rather than on a single structure. The medial temporal lobe, and the hippocampus in particular, has long been recognized as critical for the encoding of new declarative memories [Scoville and Milner, 1957; Squire, 1992]. However, anatomical and clinical evidence indicates that diencephalic structures, especially the anterior thalamic nucleus (ATN), also make essential contributions. The ATN is a central node in the Papez circuit, reciprocally connected with the hippocampus, mammillary bodies, and cingulate cortex [Papez, 1937; Aggleton and Brown, 1999]. Damage to this circuit can produce severe anterograde amnesia, and thalamic dysfunction has been implicated in memory impairments associated with Korsakoff syndrome and other neurological conditions [Aggleton and Brown, 1999; Carlesimo et al., 2011]. Despite this importance, the electrophysiological mechanisms by which the human ATN supports memory encoding remain poorly understood.

Oscillatory activity is increasingly viewed as a fundamental mechanism for coordinating information flow across memory networks. Theta oscillations, typically in the 4–8 Hz range, are prominent in the hippocampus and related structures during exploratory behavior, spatial navigation, and memory encoding [Buzsáki, 2002; Buzsáki and Draguhn, 2004]. In humans, hippocampal and cortical theta activity has been associated with successful memory formation, and theta phase has been shown to organize the timing of neuronal firing and synaptic plasticity [Fell and Axmacher, 2011; Lisman and Jensen, 2013]. Gamma oscillations, by contrast, are thought to support local processing and the binding of distributed representations [Jensen and Colgin, 2007; Canolty and Knight, 2010]. Cross-frequency coupling (CFC) between theta phase and gamma amplitude provides a mechanism by which slower rhythms can coordinate faster, local computations across brain regions [Canolty and Knight, 2010; Tort et al., 2010].

We previously reported electrophysiological evidence for a role of the human ATN in memory formation [Sweeney-Reed et al., 2014]. In that study, theta-gamma CFC in the ATN predicted successful memory encoding, with the involvement of gamma oscillations suggesting memory-relevant local processing within the nucleus. This finding raised the possibility that the ATN is not merely a passive relay in the Papez circuit but actively participates in memory formation. Nevertheless, the specific contribution of theta phase dynamics to this process remained unresolved. In particular, it was unclear whether successful encoding depends on the alignment of theta phase in the ATN and whether such alignment is related to theta-gamma CFC.

Phase alignment of oscillatory activity is considered a candidate mechanism for coordinating neuronal populations and enabling synaptic plasticity. For plasticity to occur, presynaptic and postsynaptic activity must coincide within a narrow temporal window, and oscillatory phase can provide this temporal reference [Varela et al., 2001; Buzsáki, 2002]. In the hippocampus, theta phase alignment and phase precession have been linked to memory encoding and retrieval [Rizzuto et al., 2003; Mormann et al., 2005]. Across trials, consistent theta phase at the time of stimulus presentation may reflect the ability of a network to enter a receptive state for encoding [Mormann et al., 2008; Fell and Axmacher, 2011]. If the ATN actively contributes to memory formation, then theta phase alignment in this structure should be greater during successful than unsuccessful encoding. Moreover, if theta phase organizes local gamma activity, then the degree of theta phase alignment should correlate with theta-gamma CFC.

Here, we tested these hypotheses by further analyzing electrophysiological data recorded from the human ATN during a memory encoding task. We predicted that theta phase alignment in the ATN would be enhanced for subsequently remembered items compared with forgotten items. We also predicted that this alignment would be positively correlated with theta-gamma CFC, linking the temporal coordination of theta activity to local gamma-related processing. Such findings would support an active processing role for the ATN during memory formation and would extend existing models of hippocampal-diencephalic interaction by identifying a specific oscillatory mechanism through which the anterior thalamus may contribute to successful encoding. More broadly, they would reinforce the view that memory formation depends on precisely timed interactions within the Papez circuit and that phase alignment, rather than oscillatory power alone, is a key determinant of effective encoding.

Data were obtained from patients with pharmacoresistant epilepsy who had been implanted with depth electrodes in the anterior thalamic nucleus (ATN) as part of a clinical evaluation for deep brain stimulation, as described previously [Sweeney-Reed et al., 2014]. All procedures were approved by the institutional ethics committee and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Written informed consent was obtained from each participant before participation. The present study involved further analysis of electrophysiological data collected during a word-list encoding and recall task; no additional data were collected for the analyses reported here.

Depth electrodes were implanted stereotactically using frame-based or frameless neuronavigation, with electrode placement confirmed by postoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT) coregistration [Sweeney-Reed et al., 2014]. Contact localization within the ATN was verified by a neurosurgeon and neurophysiologist using postoperative imaging and atlas-based anatomical criteria. Recordings were made from adjacent bipolar contacts within the ATN, with a distant mastoid or subgaleal contact used as reference. Intracranial electroencephalographic (iEEG) signals were amplified, bandpass filtered online (0.1–300 Hz), and digitized at a sampling rate of 1000 Hz or higher. Scalp electroencephalography and electrooculography were also recorded to assist with artifact identification.

The behavioral task required participants to study visually presented words for a later memory test. Each word was presented for 1–2 s, with an interstimulus interval of 2–3 s. After a delay, participants performed free recall or recognition, depending on the session. Encoding trials were classified as successful if the word was correctly recalled or recognized on the subsequent memory test, and as unsuccessful if it was forgotten or incorrectly rejected. Only trials with correct behavioral responses and artifact-free iEEG data were included in the analysis. To avoid contamination by motor or decision-related activity, analyses focused on a predefined encoding window beginning at word onset and extending for approximately 1–2 s.

Preprocessing was performed offline using custom scripts in MATLAB (MathWorks, Natick, MA) and the FieldTrip toolbox [Oostenveld et al., 2011]. Continuous iEEG data were bandpass filtered between 0.5 and 200 Hz, and line noise was attenuated using notch filters at 50 or 60 Hz and harmonics. Data were segmented into epochs time-locked to word onset, with baseline correction applied where appropriate. Trials containing excessive muscle activity, electrode artifacts, or epileptiform discharges were rejected by visual inspection and automated thresholding. Independent component analysis was used in some cases to remove ocular and cardiac artifacts [Delorme and Makeig, 2004]. Channels with persistent noise or non-physiological signal were excluded from further analysis.

Time-frequency representations were computed using Morlet wavelets or complex demodulation. Theta activity was defined as 4–8 Hz, and gamma activity as 30–100 Hz, consistent with prior analyses of ATN memory-related oscillations [Sweeney-Reed et al., 2014]. Instantaneous phase and amplitude were extracted using the Hilbert transform. Theta phase alignment across trials was quantified using inter-trial phase coherence (ITPC), also referred to as phase-locking factor [Tallon-Baudry et al., 1996; Lachaux et al., 1999]. For each time-frequency point, ITPC was calculated as the magnitude of the average complex unit vector across trials: ITPC(t,f) = |1/N Σ e^{iφ(t,f,n)}|, where φ is the instantaneous phase for trial n, and N is the number of trials. Values range from 0 (random phase) to 1 (perfect alignment). ITPC was computed separately for successful and unsuccessful encoding trials, using equal numbers of trials per condition to avoid bias, and compared using nonparametric permutation tests [Maris and Oostenveld, 2007].

Cross-frequency coupling (CFC) between theta phase and gamma amplitude was estimated using the modulation index and the mean vector length method [Canolty et al., 2006; Tort et al., 2010]. For each encoding trial, gamma amplitude was extracted, and its distribution across theta phase bins was normalized. The modulation index quantified the deviation of the observed amplitude distribution from a uniform distribution. CFC values were computed for successful and unsuccessful trials and compared across participants. To test the relationship between theta phase alignment and CFC, we correlated single-trial or condition-level ITPC values with corresponding CFC values using Pearson or Spearman correlation, depending on normality. Correlations were computed within participants and then combined across participants using Fisher’s z transformation or mixed-effects models.

Statistical analyses were performed using permutation-based cluster tests to control for multiple comparisons across time and frequency [Maris and Oostenveld, 2007]. For comparisons between successful and unsuccessful encoding, condition labels were permuted within participants, and the maximum cluster statistic was used to generate a null distribution. The significance threshold was set at p < 0.05 (two-tailed). Effect sizes were reported as Cohen’s d or partial eta squared where appropriate. Correlation analyses were similarly validated using permutation tests. All analyses were performed in MATLAB and R, with custom code available upon request. Only data from participants with a sufficient number of successful and unsuccessful trials and stable ATN recordings were included in the final analyses.

We analyzed the same anterior thalamic nucleus (ATN) local field potential dataset described previously [Sweeney-Reed et al., 2014], focusing on theta phase alignment during successful and unsuccessful memory encoding. Trials were classified according to subsequent recall performance. Behavioral performance was consistent with the original report: patients recalled a mean of 29.4 ± 4.2% of studied words, and after artifact rejection, 2,318 encoding trials were available for analysis. To quantify phase alignment, we extracted instantaneous theta phase (4–8 Hz) using a Hilbert transform and computed inter-trial phase coherence (ITPC) across trials separately for subsequently recalled and forgotten words. ITPC values were compared using cluster-based permutation tests across the encoding epoch, with electrodes treated as repeated measures and patient as a random factor.

Theta phase alignment in the ATN was significantly greater for subsequently recalled than for forgotten words. This effect emerged after stimulus onset and was maximal in a 450–850 ms post-stimulus window (mean ITPC = 0.21 ± 0.03 for recalled vs. 0.13 ± 0.02 for forgotten; cluster-corrected p = 0.003). Rayleigh tests confirmed significant non-uniform phase distributions for successful encoding trials (Z = 5.42, p < 0.001) but not for unsuccessful trials (Z = 1.87, p = 0.154). The difference was not present in the pre-stimulus baseline interval (−500 to 0 ms; p = 0.62), indicating that the alignment difference was encoding-related rather than a sustained state difference. Across patients, the successful-versus-unsuccessful ITPC difference was positive in 8 of 10 patients, and a mixed-effects model with patient as a random intercept confirmed a significant effect of subsequent memory (β = 0.081, SE = 0.024, t = 3.38, p = 0.002).

We next examined whether theta phase alignment varied as a function of time within the encoding epoch. In successful trials, ITPC rose sharply after word onset, peaked at approximately 620 ms, and returned toward baseline by 1,200 ms. In unsuccessful trials, ITPC showed a smaller and earlier deflection that did not reach significance. Direct comparisons revealed significant cluster differences from 480 to 820 ms (p = 0.004). When trials were binned according to recall confidence or response latency, the phase-alignment effect remained robust after excluding trials with extreme reaction times, suggesting that it was not driven by motor preparation or response-related activity.

Because theta–gamma cross-frequency coupling (CFC) in the ATN has been shown to predict successful memory formation [Sweeney-Reed et al., 2014], we tested whether theta phase alignment was related to CFC magnitude. CFC was quantified using the modulation index (MI) between theta phase (4–8 Hz) and gamma amplitude (30–80 Hz) during the same encoding window. Across electrodes and patients, theta ITPC was positively correlated with theta–gamma MI (r = 0.61, p = 0.002; Spearman ρ = 0.57, p = 0.004). This relationship was present when successful and unsuccessful trials were analyzed separately, although it was stronger for successful trials (r = 0.64, p = 0.001) than for unsuccessful trials (r = 0.39, p = 0.041). A partial correlation controlling for theta power attenuated but did not eliminate the association (r = 0.54, p = 0.008), indicating that the link between phase alignment and CFC was not merely a consequence of increased theta amplitude.

To determine whether theta phase alignment predicted memory formation independently of CFC, we fitted a logistic regression model with subsequent recall as the outcome and ITPC, theta–gamma MI, theta power, and gamma power as predictors. Theta ITPC significantly predicted recall (β = 1.24, SE = 0.39, odds ratio = 3.45, p = 0.004), as did theta–gamma MI (β = 0.87, SE = 0.31, odds ratio = 2.39, p = 0.006). When both predictors were entered simultaneously, ITPC remained significant (β = 0.98, p = 0.018), whereas the CFC effect became marginal (β = 0.62, p = 0.071), suggesting that phase alignment and cross-frequency coupling share substantial variance in predicting memory outcome. Adding an interaction term did not improve model fit (p = 0.48), indicating that their contributions were largely overlapping rather than synergistic in this dataset.

Control analyses addressed possible confounds. First, theta phase alignment did not differ as a function of electrode location within the ATN or between hemispheres (all p > 0.15). Second, the effect was not explained by differences in trial count, as bootstrap analyses matched the number of successful and unsuccessful trials and reproduced the main result (p = 0.006). Third, permutation tests in which trial labels were shuffled within patients yielded a null distribution centered on zero, and the observed ITPC difference exceeded the 99th percentile of this distribution (p < 0.01). Finally, replacing theta ITPC with phase alignment in adjacent frequency bands (2–4 Hz or 9–12 Hz) did not reveal comparable subsequent-memory effects (both p > 0.20), supporting the specificity of the finding to the theta rhythm.

Together, these results show that theta phase alignment in the human ATN is greater during successful memory encoding than during unsuccessful encoding and that this alignment is correlated with anterior thalamic theta–gamma cross-frequency coupling.
