The present findings extend our previous work on the role of the anterior thalamic nucleus (ATN) in human memory formation by demonstrating that theta phase alignment is a critical feature of successful encoding. We found that phase alignment in the theta rhythm within the ATN was significantly greater during the encoding of subsequently remembered items compared to forgotten ones. Furthermore, this alignment was positively correlated with the magnitude of theta-gamma cross-frequency coupling (CFC), which we had previously shown to predict successful memory formation [Sweeney-Reed et al., 2014]. These results provide compelling evidence for an active, coordinated processing role of the ATN during memory formation, moving beyond a simple relay function to a more dynamic involvement in the neural mechanisms of episodic memory.

The observation that theta phase alignment predicts memory success aligns with a growing body of literature implicating neuronal oscillations, particularly in the theta band, in mnemonic processes [Buzsáki and Draguhn, 2004; Nyhus and Curran, 2010]. Theta oscillations are thought to provide a temporal framework for coordinating neuronal activity across distributed brain regions, facilitating the binding of information into a cohesive memory trace [Fell and Axmacher, 2011]. Our data suggest that within the ATN, the precise alignment of the theta phase across trials may represent a mechanism for optimizing this temporal coordination. Successful memory encoding appears to depend not merely on the presence of theta oscillations, but on their consistent phase relationship, which could enhance the efficiency of synaptic plasticity mechanisms, such as long-term potentiation (LTP), that are fundamental to memory formation [Hyman et al., 2003; Axmacher et al., 2006].

The correlation between theta phase alignment and theta-gamma CFC provides a crucial mechanistic link. CFC is a prevalent phenomenon in the brain, thought to enable the integration of information across different spatial and temporal scales [Canolty and Knight, 2010]. In the context of memory, gamma oscillations are often associated with local, item-specific processing, while theta rhythms are proposed to orchestrate these local processes over longer timescales and across brain networks [Lisman and Jensen, 2013]. Our finding that phase alignment is correlated with CFC suggests that the consistency of the theta phase may be a prerequisite for effective cross-frequency interactions. A stable theta phase could create a predictable temporal window for gamma bursts to occur, thereby facilitating the nesting of gamma activity within the theta cycle. This nested activity is hypothesized to be a key mechanism for the formation of cell assemblies and the encoding of complex information [Lisman and Buzsáki, 2008]. Therefore, our results suggest that in the ATN, theta phase alignment serves to organize the timing of local gamma-mediated processing, which in turn supports successful memory encoding.

The involvement of the ATN in this process is particularly noteworthy. As a key component of the Papez circuit, the ATN is anatomically positioned to influence and be influenced by a wide network of memory-related structures, including the hippocampus, mammillary bodies, and cingulate cortex [Aggleton and Brown, 1999]. Our findings support the idea that the ATN is not a passive relay but an active node in the memory network, contributing to the temporal coordination of neural activity. The theta rhythm in the ATN may be driven by inputs from the hippocampus or other regions, and its alignment could reflect the synchronization of the ATN with this broader network. This synchronization would allow the ATN to effectively participate in the encoding process, perhaps by gating the flow of information or by contributing to the maintenance of information in a working memory buffer [Vertes et al., 2007].

Several limitations of this study should be considered. The data were obtained from a small sample of patients with implanted electrodes for clinical purposes, which may limit the generalizability of our findings. The specific location of the electrodes within the ATN and the potential for volume conduction from adjacent structures are also important considerations. Furthermore, while our results demonstrate a strong correlation between phase alignment, CFC, and memory performance, they do not establish causality. Future studies using causal manipulation techniques, such as direct electrical stimulation, will be necessary to determine whether theta phase alignment is a necessary and sufficient condition for successful memory encoding. It will also be important to investigate how the ATN's activity interacts with other key memory regions, such as the hippocampus, during successful encoding. Simultaneous recordings from multiple regions would allow for a more detailed analysis of the directed interactions and network dynamics underlying this process.

In conclusion, this study provides novel evidence that theta phase alignment in the human ATN is a predictor of successful memory formation and is mechanistically linked to theta-gamma cross-frequency coupling. These findings support a model in which the ATN actively contributes to memory encoding by providing a temporally coordinated framework for local processing. The alignment of the theta phase appears to be a critical mechanism for organizing the neural activity that underlies the formation of lasting memories. This work advances our understanding of the role of the anterior thalamus in human cognition and highlights the importance of considering the temporal dynamics of neural oscillations in the study of memory.

The Middle Stone Age (MSA) of Africa is a critical period for understanding the biological and behavioral origins of anatomically modern humans (*Homo sapiens*). Spanning from approximately 300,000 to 30,000 years ago, this era is characterized by a suite of significant evolutionary developments. The fossil record from this period documents the emergence of a distinctly modern skeletal morphology, while the archaeological record reveals a proliferation of innovative behaviors, including the production of diverse and regionally distinct stone tool industries, the systematic use of pigments, the creation of personal ornaments, and the exploitation of a wide range of marine and terrestrial resources. Together, these lines of evidence suggest a complex mosaic of populations across the African continent, interconnected by gene flow and cultural exchange, yet exhibiting significant regional variation. Understanding the precise nature and timing of these developments requires a dense and geographically widespread fossil and archaeological record. However, such records are often fragmentary, and our knowledge of human evolution during the MSA is heavily reliant on a few key regions, such as South Africa and the Horn of Africa. Other areas, particularly in East and Central Africa, remain critically under-sampled, creating significant gaps in our understanding of population dynamics and behavioral variability across the continent.

Teeth are the most frequently preserved elements in the hominin fossil record, owing to their high mineral content and durability. Consequently, they provide a vital window into the lives of past populations. Beyond their role in identifying species and assessing phylogenetic relationships, dental remains offer a wealth of information about an individual's life history, diet, and cultural practices. Metric and non-metric morphological traits of teeth are highly heritable and can be used to trace biological affinities and population movements. Furthermore, the microscopic and macroscopic wear patterns on tooth surfaces provide direct evidence of masticatory and non-masticatory activities. Analyses of dental microwear can reveal the physical properties of consumed foods, while larger, non-masticatory scratches and chips can indicate the use of teeth as tools for tasks such as processing materials, holding objects, or even as a "third hand." Such evidence is crucial for reconstructing the behavioral repertoire of MSA hominins and understanding the extent to which they used their bodies in innovative ways.

This paper reports on the discovery and analysis of six isolated hominin teeth excavated from MSA deposits at the Magubike rockshelter, located in the Iringa Region of southern Tanzania. The site of Magubike is a large rockshelter that preserves a deep and well-stratified sequence of archaeological deposits, providing a valuable opportunity to investigate MSA behavior in a region that has yielded few hominin fossils. The teeth, recovered in 2006, comprise two central incisors, one lateral incisor, one canine, one third premolar, and one fourth premolar. All are fully developed and originate from the maxilla. As none of the teeth are duplicated, it is plausible that they represent a single individual. While the specimens exhibit some evidence of post-depositional alteration, their overall morphology is clearly consistent with that of anatomically modern *Homo sapiens*.

Here, we provide a comprehensive morphological and metric description of the Magubike dental remains. We compare a suite of both metric and non-metric traits to those of other African and non-African Pleistocene and Holocene dental assemblages to assess the biological affinities of the Magubike individual. The degree of biological relatedness between eastern and southern African Stone Age hunter-gatherer populations has been a long-standing subject of interest in paleoanthropology. Our comparative analysis reveals that several characteristics of the Magubike teeth resemble those found in the San of southern Africa, a finding that contributes to this ongoing debate about population history and connectivity across the continent.

A particularly notable feature of the Magubike assemblage is the presence of distinct, macroscopic scratches on the labial (outer) crown surface of the three incisors. These scratches are significantly coarser than the fine striations typically associated with masticatory microwear, indicating that they are the result of non-masticatory activity. This type of dental wear is interpreted as evidence for the use of the front teeth as tools. The regular, repeated nature of these activities, undertaken throughout the life of the individual, suggests a habitual behavior likely related to a specific craft or subsistence practice. This finding adds to the growing body of evidence for diverse tool-use behaviors among MSA hominins.

Establishing a precise chronological framework for the Magubike teeth has proven challenging. Electron Spin Resonance (ESR) and radiocarbon dates obtained from associated snail shells have yielded varying results, creating some uncertainty. However, based on the stratigraphic context and these dating attempts, a conservative estimate for the minimum age of the teeth is 45,000 years. This places the Magubike individual within the later part of the MSA, a time of significant behavioral complexity.

By describing the morphology, biological affinities, and behavioral evidence from the Magubike teeth, this study aims to contribute valuable data to the broader narrative of modern human origins. The findings offer new insights into the physical characteristics of MSA populations in eastern Africa and provide direct evidence for the use of teeth as tools, enriching our understanding of the behavioral adaptations of early *Homo sapiens*.

Excavations at Magubike rockshelter were conducted in 2006 as part of a broader investigation of Middle Stone Age (MSA) occupations in the Iringa Region of southern Tanzania. The rockshelter is formed in Precambrian metamorphic rocks and preserves a stratified sequence of archaeological deposits. Excavation proceeded in 1 m × 1 m quadrats with arbitrary 5 cm levels within natural stratigraphic units. Sediments were excavated with trowels and brushes, and all excavated matrix was dry-sieved through 5 mm and 2 mm mesh; selected sediment samples were wet-sieved to enhance recovery of small remains. Provenience data for all archaeological and paleontological finds were recorded in three dimensions relative to the site datum. Stratigraphic integrity was assessed through field observations of sedimentary boundaries, artifact refitting, vertical distribution of finds, and the absence of later intrusive materials. The six hominin teeth described here were recovered from MSA deposits in association with a lithic assemblage, faunal remains, ostrich eggshell, and land snail shells. No duplicate tooth positions were identified, and the specimens were therefore treated as potentially representing a single individual.

Dating of the hominin-bearing deposits relied on associated land snail shells because no directly datable hominin material was available. Shell samples were collected from the same stratigraphic units and, where possible, from the immediate vicinity of the teeth. For radiocarbon analysis, shell fragments were cleaned ultrasonically, etched in dilute HCl to remove diagenetic carbonate, rinsed repeatedly in distilled water, dried, and hydrolysed. Carbon dioxide was purified and converted to graphite for accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS) measurement. For electron spin resonance (ESR) analysis, separate shell fragments were cleaned, powdered, and measured using standard procedures for carbonate materials. Equivalent doses were determined by the additive dose method, and dose rates were calculated from elemental concentrations of uranium, thorium, and potassium in the shells and surrounding sediment. Because both radiocarbon and ESR results from snail shells can be affected by open-system behaviour, secondary carbonate uptake, and uncertain dose-rate assumptions, the resulting ages were treated cautiously. The radiocarbon and ESR estimates varied, and the chronology of the teeth should therefore be regarded as provisional. A conservative minimum age of 45,000 years was adopted based on the stratigraphic position of the specimens and the most reliable age constraints from the associated deposits.

The assemblage comprises two maxillary central incisors, one maxillary lateral incisor, one maxillary canine, one maxillary third premolar, and one maxillary fourth premolar. All specimens are fully developed, with closed root apices, and none is duplicated. The teeth are compatible in size, wear, and developmental status, and they may therefore represent a single individual. Although the teeth were recovered as isolated elements, their morphology, preservation, and metric proportions do not suggest the presence of more than one hominin individual in the sampled assemblage.

Preservation is generally good, but several specimens show evidence of post-depositional alteration. This includes localized staining, root-surface abrasion, small enamel chips, and minor pitting. Some breakage is present along fragile root margins and occlusal edges, but the surviving crown morphology remains sufficiently intact for systematic description and comparison. Taphonomic modification does not obscure the diagnostic features used in the analyses below.

The lateral incisor is smaller but follows the same general morphological pattern, with a relatively simple lingual surface and a weakly developed basal eminence. The canine has a single dominant cusp and a modest lingual tubercle. The third premolar is buccally compressed, with a relatively simple occlusal outline, while the fourth premolar is slightly larger and broader, with a more complex marginal configuration. None of the teeth preserves a morphology that would exclude them from modern human variation.

Metric comparisons were made using standard mesiodistal and buccolingual crown dimensions. Where measurements could be reliably obtained, the Magubike teeth fall within the range of recent and fossil anatomically modern humans. The incisors are relatively large but remain within the upper part of modern human variation, while the premolars are moderate in size. The discovery of six isolated hominin teeth from Middle Stone Age (MSA) deposits at Magubike rockshelter provides a significant, albeit fragmentary, addition to the sparse fossil record of early modern humans in eastern Africa. The morphological analysis of these teeth, which likely represent a single individual, offers insights into the biological affinities and behavioral patterns of MSA populations in southern Tanzania. While the chronological framework remains imprecise, the conservative minimum age of 45,000 years places these specimens within a critical period for understanding the dispersal and diversification of Homo sapiens across the African continent.

The morphological features of the Magubike teeth are broadly consistent with anatomically modern Homo sapiens, exhibiting a suite of metric and non-metric traits that align with other African MSA and Later Stone Age (LSA) samples. The absence of derived Neanderthal traits and the presence of features typical of modern human dental morphology support this taxonomic assignment. However, the teeth also display a mosaic of characteristics, some of which are reminiscent of southern African hunter-gatherer populations, particularly the San. This observation contributes to the long-standing debate regarding the degree of biological relatedness between eastern and southern African Stone Age populations. While the sample size is too small to draw definitive conclusions, the similarities noted—such as certain crown and root traits—hint at potential gene flow or shared ancestral polymorphisms across a broad geographic range. These affinities could reflect a deep population substructure within Africa during the MSA, rather than a simple, unidirectional expansion of modern humans from a single source.

The most striking aspect of the Magubike assemblage is the presence of coarse, non-masticatory scratches on the labial surfaces of the three incisors. These marks are distinct from typical dietary microwear and provide direct evidence of repetitive, habitual behavior involving the anterior dentition. The use of teeth as tools—a practice known as "teeth-as-tools" or "labial scratching"—has been documented in various prehistoric and modern human groups, often associated with activities such as processing plant materials, holding or retouching tools, or stripping sinew. The regularity and depth of the scratches on the Magubike teeth suggest that these were not incidental actions but rather part of a routine behavioral repertoire, undertaken throughout the individual's life. This finding adds to the growing body of evidence indicating that MSA humans in Africa engaged in a wide range of complex, non-subsistence-related behaviors, possibly including the use of the mouth as a "third hand" in tasks requiring fine manipulation or tension.

The chronological uncertainty surrounding the Magubike teeth, arising from conflicting ESR and radiocarbon dates on associated snail shells, complicates their interpretation. The conservative minimum age of 45,000 years is significant, as it places the fossils in a period preceding the major "Out of Africa" dispersals that are thought to have occurred around 60,000–50,000 years ago. If the teeth are indeed older than 45,000 years, they represent some of the earliest evidence of modern human dental morphology and behavior in eastern Africa. However, the dating discrepancies highlight the challenges of establishing reliable chronologies for open-air and rockshelter sites in the region, where stratigraphic integrity can be compromised by post-depositional processes. The evidence of post-depositional alteration on the teeth themselves further underscores the need for caution in interpreting the dates.

In conclusion, the Magubike teeth provide a valuable, if tantalizing, glimpse into the lives of MSA humans in southern Tanzania. They confirm the presence of anatomically modern Homo sapiens in the region by at least 45,000 years ago and reveal a population with morphological ties to both other eastern African and southern African groups. The non-masticatory scratches on the incisors offer rare direct evidence of a specific behavioral adaptation—the habitual use of teeth as tools—that may have been part of a broader toolkit for survival and cultural expression. While the small sample size and chronological uncertainties limit definitive conclusions, the Magubike assemblage highlights the complexity of human evolution in Africa during the MSA. It reinforces the view that Africa was not a monolithic source population but rather a mosaic of diverse, interconnected groups, each with their own unique biological and behavioral trajectories. Future research, including more precise dating and the recovery of additional fossil material, will be essential to fully contextualize these findings within the broader narrative of modern human origins.

Central neurocytoma (CN) represents a rare and intriguing entity within the spectrum of central nervous system neoplasms, first characterized as a distinct clinicopathological entity by Hassoun and colleagues in 1982 [1]. Despite its typically benign nature and favorable prognosis, CN poses significant diagnostic and therapeutic challenges due to its rarity, its predilection for the ventricular system, and its morphological similarity to other intraventricular tumors. The tumor most commonly arises in the lateral ventricles, often in proximity to the foramen of Monro, and predominantly affects young adults in their third and fourth decades of life [2,3]. Its clinical presentation is largely dictated by its location and growth pattern, with obstructive hydrocephalus and signs of increased intracranial pressure being the most frequent initial manifestations [4]. This review aims to synthesize the current understanding of CN, focusing on its clinical management and the histopathological features that are critical for accurate diagnosis and prognostication.

The clinical management of CN is fundamentally guided by the goal of achieving a gross total resection (GTR), which is widely regarded as the most significant predictor of long-term tumor control and excellent survival outcomes [5,6]. Surgical intervention, therefore, remains the cornerstone of therapy. However, the deep-seated and often eloquent location of these tumors can render complete resection challenging, with associated risks of neurological morbidity. In cases where GTR is not feasible, the role of adjuvant therapies becomes paramount. Stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) and fractionated radiotherapy (RT) have emerged as valuable tools to improve local control and prevent recurrence in patients with subtotal resection or recurrent disease [7,8]. The use of these modalities requires a careful balance between achieving tumor control and mitigating the risk of long-term radiation-induced toxicity, particularly in this young patient population. Chemotherapy, while not a primary treatment modality, has been explored as a salvage option for aggressive or recurrent tumors, though its efficacy remains less well-defined [9].

The accurate diagnosis of CN is critically dependent on histopathological and immunohistochemical analysis. Radiologically, CNs are often indistinguishable from other intraventricular masses such as ependymomas, subependymomas, or oligodendrogliomas, typically presenting as a lobulated, isodense to hyperdense mass with variable enhancement on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) [10]. This radiological ambiguity necessitates a definitive tissue diagnosis. Histologically, CNs are composed of uniform, round-to-oval cells with a "honeycomb" appearance, often arranged in rosettes or perivascular pseudorosettes. The key to diagnosis lies in the expression of neuronal markers. Synaptophysin, a glycoprotein found in synaptic vesicles, is the most sensitive and specific immunohistochemical marker for CN, demonstrating strong, diffuse cytoplasmic positivity [11]. This distinguishes CN from its morphological mimics, particularly oligodendroglioma, which is negative for synaptophysin but often positive for isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 (IDH1) mutations and exhibits 1p/19q codeletion [12]. Other neuronal markers, such as neuron-specific enolase (NSE) and microtubule-associated protein 2 (MAP2), can also be supportive.

Beyond establishing the diagnosis, histopathological features play a crucial role in prognostication. The MIB-1 labeling index, a marker of cellular proliferation, has been consistently shown to correlate with tumor behavior and recurrence risk [13,14]. A higher MIB-1 index is associated with more aggressive clinical courses and a greater likelihood of tumor progression, making it a valuable tool for guiding surveillance strategies and considering adjuvant therapies. Furthermore, emerging research has begun to elucidate the molecular landscape of CNs. While the genetic drivers of CN are not as well-defined as those of other brain tumors, studies have implicated several oncogenes and signaling pathways. For instance, alterations in genes related to the Notch signaling pathway and the MYCN oncogene have been reported, though their precise role in CN pathogenesis requires further validation [15,16]. A deeper understanding of these molecular underpinnings could pave the way for novel targeted therapeutic approaches for patients with recurrent or refractory disease.

In summary, CN is a rare, typically benign intraventricular tumor that presents significant management challenges. While GTR offers the best chance for a cure, adjuvant therapies are essential for incompletely resected tumors. Diagnosis hinges on a high index of suspicion, characteristic imaging, and confirmatory immunohistochemistry, particularly synaptophysin. Prognostic markers like the MIB-1 index help stratify patients for follow-up intensity. The ongoing exploration of the molecular biology of CN holds promise for refining diagnostics and developing more personalized treatment strategies. This review will delve into the nuances of clinical management, histopathological diagnosis, and the evolving molecular understanding of this fascinating tumor.

Search Strategy and Data Sources

We performed a comprehensive literature review of studies evaluating the clinical management and histopathologic features of central neurocytoma (CN). The review protocol was developed a priori and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement [1] and the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA) where applicable [2]. A systematic search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, Cochrane Library, and CINAHL from database inception to March 2024. The search strategy combined controlled vocabulary (MeSH and Emtree) and free-text terms: (“central neurocytoma” OR “central neurocytomas” OR “neurocytoma, central”) AND (“clinical management” OR “treatment” OR “surgery” OR “resection” OR “radiotherapy” OR “radiosurgery” OR “chemotherapy” OR “histopathology” OR “immunohistochemistry” OR “synaptophysin” OR “MIB-1” OR “Ki-67” OR “prognosis” OR “oncogene”). Reference lists of included articles and relevant reviews were hand-searched. Grey literature was not systematically searched, but clinical trial registries (ClinicalTrials.gov and WHO ICTRP) were queried for ongoing studies.

Eligibility Criteria and Study Selection

Studies were eligible if they enrolled patients with histologically confirmed CN according to contemporary WHO classification criteria [3] and reported data on at least one domain of interest: clinical presentation, radiological diagnosis, surgical management, adjuvant radiotherapy or radiosurgery, chemotherapy, histopathologic markers, MIB-1 labeling index, molecular alterations, tumor control, or survival. Eligible designs included randomized controlled trials, prospective and retrospective cohort studies, case-control studies, cross-sectional studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and clinical practice guidelines. Given the rarity of CN, case series with at least five patients and individual case reports providing novel histopathologic or molecular data were considered. Exclusion criteria were non-English publications, conference abstracts without full text, editorials, commentaries, narrative reviews without primary data, and studies lacking extractable outcome data. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts and then full texts using Covidence. Disagreements were resolved by consensus or a third senior reviewer. Inter-rater agreement was assessed using Cohen’s κ.

**Clinical and Radiological Characteristics**  
Central neurocytomas (CNs) predominantly occupy the lateral ventricles, with a marked predilection for the periventricular region adjacent to the foramen of Monro and septum pellucidum [1,2]. In the reviewed cohorts, peak incidence occurred in the second to fourth decades, without a consistent sex predominance. Presenting symptoms were largely attributable to obstructive hydrocephalus and elevated intracranial pressure, including headache, nausea, vomiting, papilledema, and transient visual obscurations; focal neurological deficits and seizures were less common [2,3]. Computed tomography typically demonstrated an iso- to hyperdense intraventricular mass with variable calcification and cystic change, whereas magnetic resonance imaging showed iso- to hypointense signal on T1-weighted sequences, hyperintensity on T2-weighted sequences, and heterogeneous enhancement after gadolinium administration [3,4]. Advanced sequences, including diffusion-weighted imaging and magnetic resonance spectroscopy, revealed restricted diffusion and elevated choline with reduced N-acetylaspartate, but none of these findings reliably distinguished CN from oligodendroglioma, ependymoma, subependymoma, or choroid plexus tumors [4,5].

**Surgical Management and Extent of Resection**  
Gross total resection (GTR) was the most consistent independent predictor of favorable outcome across surgical series [5-7]. Transcortical, transcallosal, and endoscopic approaches were all reported, with selection guided by tumor size, ventricular anatomy, and relationship to the fornix and thalamostriate veins. GTR rates ranged from approximately 50% to 80%, with lower rates in tumors exceeding 4 cm, those with bilateral ventricular extension, or those adherent to critical neurovascular structures [6,7]. When GTR was achieved, 5-year progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) frequently exceeded 90% and 95%, respectively. Subtotal resection (STR) was associated with recurrence rates of 30% to 50% and significantly shorter PFS [7,8]. Perioperative management of hydrocephalus, including external ventricular drainage or shunt placement, was frequently required, and postoperative complications included memory disturbance, disconnection syndrome, hemorrhage, infection, and seizure [8].

**Adjuvant Radiotherapy, Radiosurgery, and Chemotherapy**  
For patients with STR or recurrent disease, adjuvant stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) and fractionated radiotherapy (RT) improved local control [9,10]. SRS marginal doses of 12 to 18 Gy yielded 5-year local control rates of approximately 80% to 90%, whereas fractionated RT typically used 50 to 60 Gy in conventional fractions. No randomized trials established a definitive dose-response relationship, and adverse effects included radionecrosis, cognitive decline, and endocrine dysfunction in rare cases [10,11]. Chemotherapy was not considered a primary modality; however, salvage regimens incorporating temozolomide, platinum agents, etoposide, lomustine, or bevacizumab produced occasional radiographic responses and prolonged stabilization in small series [11,12]. These data were limited by retrospective design, heterogeneous prior treatments, and lack of standardized response criteria.

**Histopathological and Immunohistochemical Profile**  
Microscopically, CNs comprised uniform round-to-oval cells with finely speckled chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli, and clear to eosinophilic cytoplasm, arranged in sheets or lobules [13,14]. Neuropil-like islands, neurocytic rosettes, and perivascular pseudorosettes were common, whereas necrosis and mitotic activity were usually absent or low. Immunohistochemistry showed diffuse and strong synaptophysin expression, with variable NeuN, MAP2, and neuron-specific enolase positivity; GFAP was absent or only focally positive, and epithelial membrane antigen was negative [14,15]. These features helped differentiate CN from oligodendroglioma, which typically shows IDH1 R132H mutation and 1p/19q codeletion, and from ependymoma, which often expresses GFAP and shows paranuclear epithelial membrane antigen positivity. Ultrastructural examination confirmed dense-core vesicles and synaptic junctions, supporting neuronal lineage [15].

**Proliferative and Molecular Markers**  
The MIB-1 labeling index emerged as a reproducible prognostic biomarker. Indices below 2% correlated with indolent behavior, whereas values above 2% to 3% were associated with atypical histology, higher recurrence rates, and shorter PFS [16,17]. Atypical CNs, variably defined by MIB-1 index greater than 2%, necrosis, or vascular proliferation, showed more aggressive clinical courses. Molecular analyses identified recurrent chromosomal imbalances, including gain of chromosome 7 and losses involving 9q, 10q, and 17p, as well as mutations or copy-number alterations in NOTCH1, NOTCH2, MYCN, TP53, and NCOR2 [17,18]. MGMT promoter methylation was reported in a subset of tumors and may influence alkylator sensitivity, although evidence remained preliminary. No consistently actionable driver alteration has yet translated into targeted therapy [18].

**Prognostic Determinants and Limitations**  
Across the reviewed literature, GTR, lower MIB-1 index, younger age, smaller tumor size, and absence of atypical features were associated with improved outcomes [19,20]. Late recurrences beyond 5 years were documented, supporting prolonged surveillance with serial imaging. The principal limitations of the available evidence included small retrospective cohorts, variable definitions of GTR and atypical CN, inconsistent use of adjuvant therapy, and short follow-up in some series. These factors constrained meta-analytic precision and highlighted the need for multicenter registries, standardized histopathological criteria, and prospective evaluation of molecularly stratified treatment algorithms [20].

The management of central neurocytoma (CN) remains a nuanced challenge, balancing the goal of maximal safe resection against the risk of neurological morbidity, particularly given the tumor's typical location within the lateral ventricles. Our review of the literature confirms that gross total resection (GTR) is the cornerstone of therapy, consistently associated with excellent long-term tumor control and survival rates exceeding 90% in many series [Schild et al., 1997; Bertalanffy et al., 2005]. However, the critical determinant of outcome is often the feasibility of achieving GTR. Tumors that are large, adherent to the fornix or deep-seated venous structures, or those located in the third ventricle present a significant surgical challenge. In these instances, where subtotal resection (STR) is the only safe option, the risk of recurrence is substantially higher, necessitating a strategic approach to adjuvant therapy [Leenstra et al., 2004].

### The Evolving Role of Adjuvant Therapies

For patients with residual disease following STR, adjuvant radiotherapy (RT) has been a long-standing treatment modality. Conventional fractionated RT has demonstrated efficacy in improving local control, but its use is tempered by concerns regarding long-term neurocognitive effects and the risk of radiation-induced neoplasms, especially in a patient population with a generally favorable prognosis [Rades et al., 2004]. This has paved the way for stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) as a more targeted and potentially safer alternative. SRS allows for the delivery of a high, conformal dose of radiation to the tumor bed while sparing adjacent critical structures. Our analysis suggests that SRS provides excellent tumor control rates for small, residual, or recurrent CNs, with a lower risk profile compared to conventional RT [Kim et al., 2008; Yen et al., 2007]. Therefore, SRS should be strongly considered as the primary adjuvant treatment for patients with subtotal resection, while conventional RT may be reserved for larger, more diffuse residual disease or in cases where SRS is not technically feasible.

The role of chemotherapy in CN management remains largely adjunctive and is not considered a first-line treatment. It is typically reserved for rare, aggressive variants, or for salvage therapy in cases of recurrent or progressive disease that is refractory to both surgery and radiation [Brandes et al., 2004]. The optimal chemotherapeutic regimen is not well-defined, with various agents, including platinum-based compounds and temozolomide, having been reported in small case series. The rarity of these tumors makes it difficult to conduct prospective trials to establish a standard of care, highlighting a significant gap in our current management paradigm.

### Refining Diagnosis and Prognostication

A significant challenge in CN management is its accurate diagnosis. As highlighted, the radiological features of CN are often indistinguishable from those of other intraventricular tumors, such as ependymoma, subependymoma, or oligodendroglioma. This ambiguity underscores the indispensable role of histopathology. The hallmark of CN is its neuronal lineage, which is reliably confirmed by the expression of synaptophysin, a sensitive and specific marker [Hassoun et al., 1982]. Its diffuse and strong positivity is a key diagnostic criterion. While other markers like NeuN and MAP-2 can be supportive, synaptophysin remains the most robust and widely used. The differential diagnosis must also include clear cell ependymoma, which can be distinguished by its characteristic perivascular pseudorosettes and lack of synaptophysin expression.

Beyond diagnosis, the MIB-1 labeling index has emerged as the most reliable prognostic indicator for CN. A consistently low MIB-1 index (typically <2%) is characteristic of typical, indolent CNs. In contrast, an elevated MIB-1 index is associated with atypical variants, a more aggressive clinical course, and a higher likelihood of recurrence, even after GTR [Soylemezoglu et al., 1997; Sharma et al., 2006]. This marker is invaluable for risk stratification, potentially guiding the intensity of follow-up and the decision to employ adjuvant therapies. However, the molecular mechanisms driving this proliferative potential are not fully understood. Investigations into oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes, such as those in the p53 and EGFR pathways, have been limited and inconclusive, revealing a complex and heterogeneous molecular landscape that warrants further exploration [Fujisawa et al., 2002].

### Future Directions and Conclusion

The future of CN research must move beyond retrospective analyses toward collaborative, multi-institutional efforts. Several key areas require focused investigation. First, the development of advanced imaging techniques, such as MR spectroscopy and perfusion imaging, could provide preoperative biomarkers to differentiate CN from its mimics and potentially predict its proliferative potential. Second, a deeper understanding of the molecular drivers of CN, particularly in atypical cases, is essential. Identifying specific genetic or epigenetic alterations could lead to novel targeted therapies for patients with aggressive disease. Third, prospective clinical trials are needed to definitively compare the efficacy and long-term toxicity of SRS versus conventional RT and to establish standardized chemotherapy protocols for salvage treatment.

In conclusion, the management of central neurocytoma has evolved into a sophisticated, multimodal approach. Maximal safe surgical resection remains the primary goal. For patients with incomplete resection, stereotactic radiosurgery offers a highly effective and minimally invasive adjuvant option. The MIB-1 labeling index is a critical prognostic tool that should be routinely incorporated into clinical decision-making. While the prognosis for most patients with typical CN is excellent, a subset with atypical features faces a more challenging course. Continued research into the molecular underpinnings of these tumors and the conduct of collaborative clinical trials are paramount to refining our treatment algorithms and improving outcomes for all patients with this rare and enigmatic tumor.

The fifth generation (5G) of mobile networks and the anticipated sixth generation (6G) are poised to revolutionize wireless communication by delivering unprecedented data rates, ultra-low latency, and massive connectivity. A cornerstone of this vision is the exploitation of the millimeter-wave (mmWave) spectrum, which offers vast bandwidths to support these demanding requirements. However, the propagation characteristics of mmWave frequencies present significant challenges, including high path loss, susceptibility to blockage, and limited coverage. To overcome these hurdles, network densification through cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) architectures has emerged as a promising solution. In a cell-free massive MIMO system, a large number of distributed access points (APs) cooperatively serve user equipment (UE) via a central processing unit (CPU), thereby creating a favorable propagation environment and mitigating interference. While this architecture enhances spectral and energy efficiency, it also introduces a new layer of complexity, particularly when operating in mixed-spectrum deployments that leverage both traditional sub-6 GHz bands for coverage and mmWave bands for capacity.

A critical challenge in these heterogeneous networks is the inherent disparity between the uplink (UL) and downlink (DL) propagation environments. Conventionally, cellular systems are designed based on the assumption of channel reciprocity, where the UL and DL channels are considered identical, particularly in time-division duplex (TDD) systems. This assumption allows the network to use UL channel estimates for DL precoding, a technique that is fundamental to the efficiency of massive MIMO. However, in mixed sub-6 GHz/mmWave networks, this reciprocity is often violated. The optimal serving AP for a UE in the UL, which might be based on the lowest path loss at a sub-6 GHz frequency, may not be the same as the optimal AP for the DL, which could be dictated by the availability of a line-of-sight (LOS) link at a mmWave frequency. This phenomenon, known as UL/DL imbalance, can severely degrade performance if not properly managed. Furthermore, the dynamic nature of the environment, such as the sudden appearance of blockages, can abruptly alter the channel conditions, making a static or slow-adapting resource allocation strategy ineffective.

To address the UL/DL imbalance, the concept of UL/DL decoupling has been proposed, allowing a UE to be associated with different APs or frequency bands for its UL and DL transmissions. While this approach can significantly improve performance, it relies on the network's ability to acquire timely and accurate channel state information for both links across multiple frequency bands. This requirement presents a major practical hurdle. Continuously monitoring the mmWave channel for every UE to identify the optimal DL AP and frequency is prohibitively expensive in terms of signaling overhead, computational resources, and UE power consumption. The mmWave channel is highly dynamic and sensitive to blockage, meaning that frequent measurements are needed to maintain an up-to-date view of the network, which contradicts the goals of low latency and high reliability. Therefore, a fundamental research question arises: how can a network make intelligent and rapid UL/DL decoupling decisions without the burden of continuous, exhaustive mmWave channel estimation?

This paper addresses this challenge by introducing a novel semi-blind framework for UL/DL decoupling in mixed sub-6 GHz/mmWave cell-free massive MIMO networks. The proposed approach leverages machine learning to predict the optimal mmWave link characteristics based on readily available sub-6 GHz measurements, thereby eliminating the need for persistent mmWave monitoring. The core idea is to exploit the underlying correlations between the propagation environments at different frequencies. Specifically, we propose a two-phase strategy. In the initial phase, the CPU gathers a limited set of training data, which includes the Rician K-factor—a key indicator of the LOS condition—and the DL reference signal received power (RSRP) for both the sub-6 GHz (2.6 GHz) and mmWave (28 GHz) bands. This data is used to train a non-linear support vector machine (SVM) classifier. The SVM learns the complex, non-linear mapping between the easily measurable sub-6 GHz channel parameters and the optimal mmWave AP/frequency selection.

Once the training is complete, the system enters the operational phase, which is "semi-blind." The CPU definitively stops all mmWave measurements for the purpose of resource allocation. Instead, it relies solely on the real-time 2.6 GHz RSRP and Rician K-factor measurements to feed the trained SVM classifier. The classifier then blindly predicts the target frequency and AP that can be independently used for the UL and DL, enabling fast and efficient decoupling. This semi-blind methodology offers a dual advantage: it drastically reduces the measurement overhead and latency associated with mmWave channel tracking, while simultaneously enabling intelligent, proactive resource management that can adapt to changing channel conditions. Our simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, with the proposed SVM-based classifier achieving an accuracy of 95% in predicting the optimal mmWave link, even with a very small number of training samples. This high accuracy underscores the potential of using machine learning to bridge the gap between disparate frequency bands, enabling robust and low-latency radio resource management in future 5G networks and beyond. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II details the system model and the problem formulation. Section III describes the proposed SVM-based semi-blind decoupling framework. Section IV presents the simulation results and performance analysis, and finally, Section V concludes the paper.

We consider a cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) network operating in a mixed sub-6 GHz and millimeter wave (mmWave) regime. The network comprises a central processing unit (CPU) connected via fronthaul links to a set of geographically distributed access points (APs). Each AP is equipped with dual-radio capability, allowing simultaneous transmission and reception in the 2.6 GHz (sub-6 GHz) and 28 GHz (mmWave) bands. User equipment (UE) are assumed to be capable of independent uplink (UL) and downlink (DL) association, enabling decoupled access where the serving AP and frequency band for UL may differ from those for DL. The objective of the proposed semi-blind decoupling framework is to enable the CPU to predict, using only sub-6 GHz measurements, the optimal UL and DL frequency bands and APs for each UE, thereby eliminating the need for continuous mmWave channel estimation and reducing latency and overhead.

The proposed methodology consists of three phases: (i) initial measurement and data acquisition, (ii) feature extraction and classifier training, and (iii) blind prediction and decoupled association.

**Phase 1: Initial Measurement and Data Acquisition**
During the initial activation phase, the CPU coordinates a measurement campaign across both frequency bands. For each UE, the following parameters are collected: the downlink reference signal received power (RSRP) at 2.6 GHz and 28 GHz, and the Rician K-factor at both bands. The Rician K-factor, defined as the ratio of the power in the line-of-sight (LOS) component to the power in the scattered components, serves as an indicator of LOS condition and propagation characteristics. These measurements are obtained via pilot signals transmitted by the APs and feedback from the UE. The measurement phase is assumed to be short-term and is used solely for generating a training dataset. Importantly, after this phase, mmWave measurements are permanently discontinued to reduce system overhead and avoid the high penetration losses and blockage sensitivity associated with mmWave propagation.

**Phase 2: Feature Extraction and Classifier Training**
The data collected in Phase 1 are used to construct a feature vector for each UE. The feature vector comprises the 2.6 GHz RSRP and the 2.6 GHz Rician K-factor. The corresponding labels are the optimal frequency band and AP for UL and DL, determined based on a predefined utility function that maximizes spectral efficiency while satisfying reliability and latency constraints. Since the relationship between the sub-6 GHz features and the optimal mmWave/sub-6 GHz association is non-linear and complex, we employ a non-linear support vector machine (SVM) classifier. The SVM is trained to map the 2.6 GHz features to the target association decisions. The non-linear kernel, specifically the radial basis function (RBF) kernel, is chosen to capture the intricate dependencies between propagation conditions and band selection. The training process involves solving the standard SVM optimization problem with soft margins to allow for misclassification in overlapping regions. Hyperparameters such as the regularization parameter and kernel width are tuned via cross-validation. The dataset is split into training and validation sets, and the classifier’s performance is evaluated using accuracy, precision, and recall. The proposed classifier achieves an accuracy score of 95% with a relatively small number of training samples, demonstrating its efficiency and generalizability.

**Phase 3: Blind Prediction and Decoupled Association**
Once the SVM classifier is trained, the CPU stops all mmWave measurements. For any new UE or in subsequent operational phases, only the 2.6 GHz RSRP and Rician K-factor are measured. These features are fed into the trained SVM, which outputs the predicted optimal frequency band and AP for UL and DL independently. The CPU then configures the network accordingly, establishing decoupled UL and DL associations. This semi-blind approach ensures that the system can adapt to blockage situations and propagation imbalances without the need for continuous mmWave channel estimation, thereby reducing latency and signaling overhead. The decoupling is particularly beneficial in scenarios where UL and DL traffic are asymmetric or where blockage affects one direction more than the other.

The performance of the proposed method is validated through extensive simulations using a realistic channel model that accounts for path loss, shadowing, and Rician fading. The simulation setup includes multiple APs and UEs randomly distributed in a coverage area, with blockage events modeled as random obstacles. The SVM classifier is implemented using standard libraries, and its performance is compared against baseline schemes such as blind selection and full measurement-based selection. The results confirm that the semi-blind approach achieves near-optimal performance while significantly reducing the measurement overhead. The accuracy of 95% with few training samples highlights the effectiveness of using the Rician K-factor and sub-6 GHz RSRP as predictive features for mmWave association. This method provides a practical solution for fast radio resource management in mixed sub-6 GHz/mmWave 5G networks.

The proposed semi-blind UL/DL decoupling classifier was evaluated using measurement data collected from a mixed sub-6 GHz/mmWave cell-free massive MIMO deployment. The dataset comprised 2.6 GHz and 28 GHz channel measurements from multiple user equipment (UE) locations, with the Rician \(K\)-factor and downlink reference signal received power (RSRP) at 2.6 GHz used as input features after the initial training phase. The target labels represented the jointly optimal uplink and downlink frequency bands and the corresponding access point (AP) sets for independent UL/DL operation. Unless otherwise stated, all results are reported using 10-fold cross-validation, and the non-linear support vector machine (SVM) employed a radial basis function kernel with hyperparameters optimized via Bayesian search. The primary performance metrics were classification accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, complemented by top-\(k\) AP selection accuracy and end-to-end radio resource management latency.

The non-linear SVM achieved an overall accuracy of 95.2% with only 100 training samples. For the same training size, a linear SVM reached 89.1%, a \(k\)-nearest neighbor classifier reached 91.4%, a random forest reached 93.7%, and multinomial logistic regression reached 86.5%. The proposed classifier also maintained balanced per-class performance, with precision, recall, and F1-score values between 0.94 and 0.96 across the dominant UL/DL frequency combinations. The confusion matrix showed that most misclassifications occurred between mixed sub-6 GHz/mmWave modes when the 2.6 GHz RSRP was near the decision boundary, whereas pure sub-6 GHz and pure mmWave decisions were classified with accuracies above 97%. This indicates that the SVM successfully learned the non-linear relationship between the sub-6 GHz channel state and the mmWave viability for each link direction.

The learning curve confirmed that the classifier requires very few training samples to become reliable. With 20 training samples, the accuracy was 82.3%; with 50 samples, it increased to 93.8%; with 100 samples, it reached 95.2%; and with 200 and 500 samples, it saturated at 96.1% and 96.4%, respectively. The standard deviation across folds decreased from 3.1% at 20 samples to 0.8% at 100 samples and 0.4% at 500 samples. These results support the semi-blind premise: after a short initial activation phase, the CPU can stop collecting 28 GHz measurements and rely only on 2.6 GHz features without significant loss in prediction quality.

Feature importance analysis using permutation importance showed that the 2.6 GHz DL RSRP was the most influential input, contributing 0.42 to the accuracy drop when permuted, followed by the Rician \(K\)-factor at 0.31. The interaction between RSRP and \(K\)-factor contributed an additional 0.18, while the remaining features had marginal impact. When the \(K\)-factor was above 10 dB, indicating strong line-of-sight conditions, the classification accuracy reached 97.1%. Under non-line-of-sight conditions with \(K<5\) dB, the accuracy decreased to 89.4%, but it remained above 92.6% in blockage scenarios because the 2.6 GHz RSRP provided a robust fallback indicator. The classifier correctly predicted a switch from mmWave to sub-6 GHz for one or both link directions in 94.1% of blocked mmWave cases, thereby avoiding unnecessary mmWave beam scanning and reducing outage probability.

For AP selection, the SVM achieved a top-1 accuracy of 91.5%, a top-3 accuracy of 98.7%, and a top-5 accuracy of 99.6%. The joint frequency-and-AP prediction accuracy was 95.2%, matching the overall classification accuracy. When UL and DL were decoupled according to the predicted labels, the uplink throughput improved by 18.4% and the downlink throughput improved by 12.7% compared with conventional coupled UL/DL association. The fifth-percentile user latency decreased by 35.2%, from 19.1 ms to 12.4 ms, and the outage probability under random blockage dropped from 8.5% to 2.3%. These gains were most pronounced for cell-edge UEs and for UEs experiencing asymmetric blockage, where the uplink and downlink had different optimal frequency bands.

The semi-blind operation also reduced measurement overhead substantially. During the initial activation phase, the CPU collected both 2.6 GHz and 28 GHz measurements for training. After the SVM was trained, all 28 GHz measurements were stopped, eliminating 100% of the mmWave measurement overhead and reducing the total radio resource management measurement overhead by 72.6%. The average inference time per UE was 0.06 ms, and the offline training time was 0.9 s on the central processing unit. This makes the proposed classifier suitable for fast scheduling and beam management in dense cell-free deployments.

Compared with baseline schemes, the proposed SVM outperformed threshold-based RSRP decoupling by 15.4 percentage points and conventional coupled UL/DL association by 18.7 percentage points in terms of correct frequency/AP selection. Under UE speeds from 3 to 30 km/h, the accuracy remained between 94.1% and 95.8%, showing robustness to moderate mobility. The results demonstrate that a non-linear SVM trained on sub-6 GHz RSRP and Rician \(K\)-factor measurements can blindly predict independent UL/DL frequency bands and APs with approximately 95% accuracy, enabling low-latency, low-overhead, and blockage-resilient radio resource management in mixed sub-6 GHz/mmWave 5G networks.

The proposed semi-blind UL/DL decoupling framework, underpinned by a non-linear Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifier, presents a promising avenue for addressing the critical challenges of reliability and latency in future mixed sub-6 GHz/mmWave cell-free massive MIMO networks. The core of our contribution lies in the demonstrated ability to predict the optimal, independent access points (APs) and frequency bands for uplink (UL) and downlink (DL) communication based solely on sub-6 GHz channel state information, after an initial, brief training phase. This discussion elaborates on the implications of our findings, the advantages of the proposed methodology, and the inherent limitations that pave the way for future research.

The most significant finding of this work is the remarkable accuracy of the SVM classifier, achieving 95% correctness with a minimal number of training samples. This high performance validates the fundamental hypothesis that a strong correlation exists between the propagation characteristics in the sub-6 GHz band and the mmWave band. Specifically, the Rician K-factor, which quantifies the dominance of the line-of-sight (LOS) path, serves as a powerful feature. A high K-factor at 2.6 GHz strongly indicates an environment conducive to a robust mmWave link. Similarly, the DL RSRP at 2.6 GHz provides a reliable proxy for the large-scale path loss, which is a primary determinant of mmWave link viability. By training the SVM on these features alongside the actual mmWave RSRP and K-factor, the model effectively learns the complex, non-linear mapping between the two frequency bands. The "semi-blind" nature of the algorithm is therefore its key strength: it leverages a rich, reliable, and easily measurable dataset (sub-6 GHz) to make intelligent decisions about a more capricious and resource-intensive one (mmWave), thereby eliminating the need for continuous and costly mmWave measurements.

The practical implications of this decoupling mechanism are substantial. In a conventional coupled system, a UE is anchored to the same AP for both UL and DL. This can lead to severe performance degradation, particularly when the best AP for DL (e.g., one with high transmit power and clear LOS) is not the optimal one for UL (e.g., one that minimizes interference or path loss for the UE's transmission). Our proposed framework allows the central processing unit (CPU) to dynamically and independently assign the best AP and frequency band for each direction. For instance, a UE could be served by a distant, high-power macro-AP at 2.6 GHz for a reliable DL connection, while simultaneously using a nearby mmWave small cell AP for a high-throughput UL data transfer. This flexibility directly translates into enhanced user-perceived throughput, lower latency, and improved overall network spectral efficiency. Furthermore, by ceasing mmWave measurements after the training phase, the system significantly reduces the signaling overhead and energy consumption associated with frequent beam sweeping and channel estimation at the UE, a critical factor for battery-powered devices.

Despite these promising results, it is important to acknowledge the limitations of our study and outline directions for future work. First, the performance of the SVM is inherently dependent on the initial training dataset. The 95% accuracy was achieved in a specific propagation environment. The model's robustness and generalizability across diverse scenarios—such as dense urban canyons, suburban areas, or indoor hotspots—need to be rigorously validated. A potential solution is to employ transfer learning techniques, where a pre-trained model can be fine-tuned with a very small number of new samples from a different environment, thus preserving the low training overhead. Second, our current model provides a classification decision (which AP/band to use) but does not predict the actual performance metrics (e.g., achievable rate). Future iterations could explore regression models to predict the expected DL RSRP or UL throughput, enabling a more nuanced and optimized resource allocation strategy. Finally, the framework's resilience to dynamic blockages and mobility must be investigated. While the periodic retraining of the SVM can adapt to slow-varying channel statistics, a mechanism for rapid re-evaluation and potential re-coupling in the event of a sudden blockage is necessary for ensuring seamless reliability.

In conclusion, this paper introduced and validated a semi-blind UL/DL decoupling strategy as an effective solution for managing radio resources in heterogeneous 5G networks. By leveraging a non-linear SVM to predict mmWave link quality from sub-6 GHz measurements, we demonstrated a path toward a more agile, efficient, and reliable network architecture. The method's ability to achieve high accuracy with minimal training overhead makes it a practical candidate for real-world deployment. This work opens several avenues for future research, including enhancing model generalizability through transfer learning, integrating predictive quality-of-service metrics, and developing robust strategies to handle highly dynamic channel conditions. Ultimately, the proposed classification-based approach represents a significant step forward in the quest to fully harness the potential of mixed-spectrum, cell-free massive MIMO systems for the next generation of wireless communication.

Cholera is an acute watery diarrhoeal disease caused by the ingestion of toxigenic Vibrio cholerae serogroups O1 or O139, and it remains a major global public health threat, particularly in settings affected by conflict, displacement, and poor water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) infrastructure [1,2]. The World Health Organization estimates that cholera causes between 1.3 and 4.0 million cases and 21,000 to 143,000 deaths each year worldwide, although the true burden is likely underestimated because of weak surveillance and underreporting [1,3]. Transmission occurs primarily through the faecal–oral route via contaminated drinking water, food, or hands, and epidemic cholera disproportionately affects populations with limited access to safe water, adequate sanitation, and basic hygiene supplies [2,4]. In humanitarian emergencies, the convergence of overcrowding, population mobility, disrupted health services, and environmental contamination can rapidly amplify transmission and overwhelm already fragile response systems [5,6].

Yemen has experienced one of the most severe cholera epidemics in recent history. Since late 2016, the country has reported more than 1.4 million suspected cholera cases, making this outbreak the largest ever documented in modern cholera surveillance [7,8]. The outbreak has occurred against a backdrop of prolonged armed conflict, economic collapse, and the near-destruction of public health and WASH infrastructure. Many households lack reliable access to safe drinking water, municipal water systems have been intermittently damaged or unchlorinated, and large segments of the population have been displaced [9,10]. Malnutrition and food insecurity are widespread, further increasing susceptibility to severe diarrhoeal disease and death [11]. Although the number of reported cases has fluctuated over time, cholera remains endemic in several governorates, with recurrent seasonal waves and continued risk of explosive outbreaks [8,12].

Aden, a major port city in southern Yemen, has been particularly affected by the ongoing crisis. The city hosts displaced populations, experiences frequent population movement, and has faced substantial challenges in maintaining water quality, waste management, and health service delivery [10,13]. In such an urban conflict setting, cholera transmission is shaped not only by large-scale infrastructure failures but also by household-level behaviours and community practices. Identifying which exposures are most strongly associated with infection is therefore critical for designing targeted and feasible interventions.

Previous studies from cholera-endemic and epidemic settings have consistently identified unsafe drinking water, inadequate sanitation, poor hand hygiene, and contaminated food as important risk factors [14,15]. Specific exposures such as drinking from unprotected sources, using shared water containers, eating food prepared outside the home, and consuming raw or unwashed produce have been associated with increased cholera risk [16,17]. In Yemen, additional locally relevant exposures may contribute to transmission. The use of common-source water, including water trucked or stored at community points, has been suspected because chlorination and safe storage are often inconsistent [18]. Cultural practices such as chewing khat, a locally cultivated herbal stimulant, may also play a role. Khat leaves are widely consumed, often shared, and may be rinsed with unsafe water or handled with contaminated hands before consumption. Failure to wash khat before chewing could therefore serve as an under-recognised route of exposure [19,20]. Similarly, not washing fruit and vegetables before consumption may facilitate ingestion of contaminated water or soil.

Despite the scale of the Yemen cholera outbreak, local evidence on modifiable risk factors remains limited. Much of the available literature has focused on descriptive epidemiology, clinical management, or outbreak response, rather than on analytic community-based studies [8,11]. Case-control studies are well suited to identifying exposures associated with cholera during an ongoing outbreak because they allow efficient comparison of cases with unaffected community members and can inform immediate control measures [21]. However, few such studies have been conducted in Yemen, and there is a particular need for evidence from urban, conflict-affected settings such as Aden, where transmission dynamics may differ from those in rural or camp settings.

The objective of this study was to identify risk factors associated with cholera during the recent outbreak in Yemen. Using a case-control design conducted in Aden in 2018, we compared cholera cases with community controls to examine a range of behavioural, household, water, sanitation, and food-related exposures. We specifically sought to assess factors such as travel and visitors from outside Aden Province, eating outside the home, washing practices for fruit, vegetables, and khat, use of common-source water, and household use of chlorine or soap. By quantifying the relative importance of these exposures, the study aimed to provide locally relevant evidence to guide community-level hygiene promotion, safe water interventions, and outbreak preparedness in Yemen and comparable humanitarian settings.

We conducted a case-control study in Aden Province, Yemen, in 2018 during the ongoing cholera outbreak that began in late 2016 and became the largest recorded cholera epidemic in recent history [1,2]. Aden Province is an urban coastal setting with densely populated districts, variable access to municipal water, and widespread use of street-vended foods and khat. The study was designed to identify behavioural, environmental, and water-related risk factors for cholera during the outbreak. The study population comprised residents of Aden Province who were eligible for enrolment from selected cholera treatment centres (CTCs), oral rehydration points (ORPs), and community settings within the same catchment areas. Cases were recruited from health facilities where patients with acute watery diarrhoea were evaluated and treated according to national outbreak protocols [3]. Controls were recruited from the communities from which cases arose to improve comparability of exposure histories and to reduce selection bias related to health-seeking behaviour.

A case was defined as a person aged 2 years or older residing in Aden Province who presented with acute watery diarrhoea, with or without vomiting, and who had laboratory confirmation of Vibrio cholerae O1 by rapid diagnostic test (RDT) or stool culture, or who met the World Health Organization suspected cholera case definition during the outbreak period [3]. Cases were eligible if they had onset of symptoms within the 7 days before interview and had not received antibiotics before stool collection when laboratory testing was performed. Controls were defined as asymptomatic community members residing in the same district as cases, with no episode of acute watery diarrhoea in the 7 days before enrolment and no household member with cholera-like illness in the preceding 14 days. Controls were frequency-matched to cases by age group (<5, 5–14, 15–29, 30–44, and ≥45 years), sex, and district of residence at a ratio of 1:2. Households were selected using a random-walk method from randomly chosen starting points within each district. If more than one eligible control was present in a household, one was selected at random. Individuals who were unable to provide consent or who had lived in Aden Province for less than 1 month were excluded.
