We evaluated the proposed LSTM Pose Machines on two large-scale video pose estimation benchmarks: Penn Action and JHMDB. Unless otherwise stated, all models were trained on the corresponding training splits and evaluated using the standard Percentage of Correct Keypoints at 0.2 (PCK@0.2) and Area Under the Curve (AUC) metrics. We compared against per-frame multi-stage CNN baselines, including the original unshared Convolutional Pose Machines (CPM), as well as several recently published video-based pose estimators. The results consistently show that imposing recurrent weight sharing and adding LSTM memory between frames substantially improves both accuracy and temporal stability.

On Penn Action, our full LSTM Pose Machine achieved 98.3% PCK@0.2, outperforming the strongest per-frame CPM baseline by 1.8 percentage points (96.5%) and the best optical-flow-augmented CNN baseline by 1.4 points (96.9%). The gains were especially pronounced on challenging joints and frames. For wrists and elbows, which are frequently affected by self-occlusion and fast motion, our method improved PCK@0.2 from 94.1% to 97.2% and from 95.8% to 98.0%, respectively. For ankles, the improvement was 2.7 points. When we partitioned the test set into easy and hard subsets based on motion blur and occlusion annotations, the hard subset showed a 4.3-point improvement over CPM (95.1% vs. 90.8%). This indicates that the LSTM memory is particularly effective when appearance evidence is degraded.

On JHMDB, our method reached 96.8% PCK@0.2 and 63.1% AUC. The corresponding CPM baseline obtained 94.2% PCK@0.2 and 58.7% AUC, while the best competing video method achieved 95.4% PCK@0.2 and 60.9% AUC. Thus, LSTM Pose Machines improved PCK@0.2 by 2.6 points and AUC by 4.4 points over CPM, and by 1.4 and 2.2 points over the strongest prior video-based approach. On the more difficult Sub-JHMDB split, which contains greater viewpoint variation and occlusion, our model achieved 94.5% PCK@0.2 compared with 91.3% for CPM. Per-action analysis showed consistent gains across all 21 action classes, with the largest improvements for actions involving rapid limb movement, such as kicking, swinging, and jumping.

Beyond static per-frame accuracy, we measured temporal stability. We computed jitter as the mean Euclidean distance between corresponding joint predictions in consecutive frames after global alignment, and flicker rate as the fraction of adjacent frame pairs with a joint displacement greater than 5 pixels. On Penn Action, LSTM Pose Machines reduced average jitter from 3.4 pixels for CPM to 2.1 pixels, a 38% reduction. Flicker rate dropped from 11.7% to 4.2%. On JHMDB, jitter decreased from 3.9 to 2.4 pixels, and flicker rate decreased from 13.5% to 5.1%. These improvements were even larger on occluded and blurred segments, where the memory mechanism could propagate reliable pose estimates across frames with missing or corrupted observations. For example, on occlusion-heavy Penn Action sequences, jitter was reduced from 5.1 to 2.8 pixels.

We conducted ablations to isolate the contributions of weight sharing, recurrence, and LSTM memory. Replacing the unshared multi-stage CNN with a shared-weight recurrent formulation without LSTM units improved Penn Action PCK@0.2 from 96.5% to 97.2% and JHMDB from 94.2% to 95.4%, while reducing the number of parameters by approximately a factor of six. Adding LSTM units between frames provided a further gain to 98.3% and 96.8%, respectively. A vanilla RNN variant performed worse than LSTM (97.4% and 95.9%), confirming that gated memory is important for handling long-range dependencies and appearance degradation. We also compared different recurrent update schedules. Updating the memory once per stage was inferior to updating it once per frame; the latter yielded the best accuracy and the lowest jitter, suggesting that frame-level memory is sufficient to enforce geometric consistency without overfitting to intermediate stage noise.

We analyzed the internal LSTM gates to understand why the memory helps. Averaged over the test set, the forget gate activations decreased when the input frame had high motion blur or occlusion scores, allowing the cell state to retain the previous pose representation for longer. The input gate activations increased when the current frame contained reliable limb evidence, permitting new observations to update the memory. The output gate modulated how much of the stored pose was exposed to the prediction layer, and its activation was higher for joints with stable motion. These patterns were consistent across actions and datasets. They suggest that the LSTM learns an adaptive trade-off between temporal smoothing and responsiveness to new evidence, rather than simply averaging predictions over time.

Finally, we measured computational cost. Because the multi-stage CNN is re-written as a recurrent network with shared weights, invoking the model on a video requires only one set of stage parameters. On an NVIDIA Titan X, our implementation processed 256×256 frames at 28 fps, compared with 11 fps for the unrolled six-stage CPM baseline. Memory footprint during inference was reduced to approximately one-sixth of the unshared model. These results confirm that LSTM Pose Machines not only improve accuracy and temporal consistency but also provide a more efficient architecture for video-based human pose estimation.

The experimental results support the central premise of this work: the multi-stage convolutional architecture that has driven recent progress in single-image human pose estimation can be reformulated as a recurrent network through weight sharing across stages, and this reformulation provides a principled and effective basis for video-based pose estimation. By decoupling the number of network invocations from the number of internal refinement stages, the proposed LSTM Pose Machine achieves a substantial reduction in computational cost when applied to video sequences, while preserving the representational capacity of multi-stage refinement. More importantly, the recurrent formulation creates a natural interface for memory. The LSTM units inserted between video frames allow the model to carry pose-related information forward in time, so that predictions are not made independently for each frame but are conditioned on the temporal context accumulated from preceding observations. This memory mechanism is particularly valuable under the conditions that most often degrade frame-by-frame pose estimation in video, including motion blur, partial occlusion, appearance changes, and short-term image quality degradation. The consistent gains observed on two large-scale video pose estimation benchmarks indicate that the benefits are not confined to a narrow setting but generalize across challenging sequences.

A key finding of this study is that the advantage of the LSTM Pose Machine is not merely computational. Although the weight-sharing reformulation makes video inference significantly faster by avoiding repeated stage-wise invocations, the more consequential effect is the imposition of sequential geometric consistency. In static-image multi-stage models, each frame is treated as an independent problem; consequently, small local ambiguities in individual frames can produce unstable joint predictions and visible flicker across time. The proposed recurrent model mitigates this failure mode by using memory to smooth and stabilize outputs while still allowing the network to respond to genuine motion. The experiments suggest that this stabilization does not come at the cost of excessive lag or over-smoothing, provided that the memory is appropriately integrated with the convolutional refinement process. The exploration of the internal LSTM memory cells further supports this interpretation. The memory appears to encode useful temporal context that helps disambiguate challenging joints, rather than simply averaging past predictions. This provides insight into why the mechanism benefits video-based pose estimation: the LSTM acts as a learned temporal prior that complements the spatial evidence available in the current frame, allowing the model to recover from transient corruption and to maintain coherent skeletal structure over time.

The results also have broader implications for the design of efficient video understanding systems. Many high-performance pose estimators are built around iterative refinement, and naively applying such models to every frame of a video is expensive and ignores temporal structure. The weight-sharing view adopted here suggests that iterative refinement and recurrent processing are closely related, and that architectures originally developed for static images can be reinterpreted as temporal models with relatively modest changes. This perspective may be useful beyond human pose estimation, particularly for other structured prediction tasks in video where spatial refinement and temporal consistency are both important. At the same time, the present study has limitations that should be acknowledged. The evaluation focuses on two-dimensional human pose estimation in video, and it does not fully characterize behavior in crowded multi-person scenes, severe long-term occlusion, or extreme camera motion. The memory mechanism is also bounded by the capacity and temporal span of the LSTM state; although it handles short- and medium-term degradation well, it may not retain information over very long gaps or recover from complete and prolonged absence of evidence. In addition, the current formulation assumes that temporal correspondence is available through the video sequence and does not explicitly model uncertainty or multiple plausible pose hypotheses. These limitations point to several directions for future work, including extending the recurrent formulation to multi-person tracking and pose estimation, incorporating longer-range memory or attention mechanisms, explicitly modeling uncertainty and occlusion, and exploring three-dimensional pose estimation in video. It would also be valuable to investigate adaptive memory updating, in which the network learns when to rely on temporal context and when to trust the current frame more strongly, as well as to evaluate the approach under real-time constraints and on a wider range of acquisition conditions.

In conclusion, this paper introduced LSTM Pose Machines, a recurrent reformulation of multi-stage convolutional pose estimators that couples spatial refinement with temporal memory. The proposed model addresses three central difficulties of video pose estimation: the computational burden of repeated multi-stage processing, the instability of frame-independent predictions, and the loss of geometric consistency under image degradation. By sharing weights across stages and introducing LSTM units between frames, the method retains the refinement power of multi-stage CNNs while enabling efficient recurrent inference and effective temporal integration. The experiments demonstrate that this design significantly outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods on two large-scale video pose estimation benchmarks, and the analysis of the LSTM memory provides evidence that learned temporal context plays a meaningful role in stabilizing and correcting pose predictions. These findings establish memory-augmented recurrent refinement as a promising direction for robust video-based human pose estimation and suggest that the relationship between iterative refinement and temporal recurrence deserves further attention in the design of efficient and reliable video understanding models.

Dementia, a debilitating neurodegenerative syndrome, represents one of the most significant public health challenges of the 21st century. It is characterized by a progressive and irreversible decline in cognitive functions, including memory, reasoning, and language, which severely impacts an individual's daily life and autonomy. With an aging global population, the prevalence of dementia is escalating at an alarming rate, yet effective therapeutic options remain profoundly limited. Current pharmacological interventions, such as acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (e.g., donepezil) and N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor antagonists (e.g., memantine), offer only modest symptomatic relief and are often accompanied by adverse side effects. Consequently, there is a pressing need for novel, safer, and more effective preventative or therapeutic strategies. In this context, natural products and functional foods have garnered considerable attention as promising sources for developing cognitive enhancers, often referred to as nootropics.

The cholinergic hypothesis, which posits that cognitive decline is largely attributable to a deficit in cholinergic neurotransmission, has been a cornerstone of Alzheimer's disease (AD) research and drug development. Scopolamine, a potent muscarinic acetylcholine receptor antagonist, is widely used to experimentally induce a temporary state of cognitive impairment in animal models that closely mimics the memory deficits seen in dementia. By blocking cholinergic signaling, scopolamine disrupts crucial processes for learning and memory, particularly in the hippocampus, a brain region essential for memory consolidation. This model provides a robust and reliable platform for screening potential cognitive-enhancing agents and for investigating their underlying mechanisms of action.

Beyond cholinergic dysfunction, oxidative stress is increasingly recognized as a key pathological mechanism in the development and progression of neurodegenerative diseases. An imbalance between the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and the brain's endogenous antioxidant defenses can lead to cellular damage, neuronal dysfunction, and impaired synaptic plasticity. This oxidative milieu can disrupt critical intracellular signaling cascades that are vital for learning and memory. Among these, the extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) pathway plays a central role. ERK phosphorylation (p-ERK) initiates a signaling cascade that leads to the activation of the transcription factor cAMP response element-binding protein (CREB) via phosphorylation (p-CREB). Activated CREB, in turn, upregulates the expression of various genes crucial for neuronal survival and synaptic plasticity, most notably brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). BDNF is a key neurotrophin that supports neuronal growth, differentiation, and survival, and is indispensable for long-term potentiation (LTP), a cellular correlate of memory. Therefore, agents that can mitigate oxidative stress and concurrently activate the ERK-CREB-BDNF signaling pathway hold significant therapeutic promise for combating cognitive decline.

Natural marine resources are a vast and largely untapped reservoir of bioactive compounds with diverse pharmacological properties. Among these, microalgae, particularly Spirulina species, have emerged as a "superfood" due to their rich content of proteins, vitamins, minerals, and potent antioxidant pigments like phycocyanin and β-carotene. *Spirulina maxima*, a cyanobacterium, is known for its strong antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities. While extracts of *S. maxima* have demonstrated various health benefits, their direct cognitive-enhancing effects and the underlying molecular mechanisms have not been fully elucidated. Furthermore, the bioavailability and bioactivity of compounds from raw plant or algal sources can be limited. Fermentation, particularly with lactic acid bacteria (LAB), is a traditional and effective bioprocessing technique used to enhance the nutritional value, digestibility, and bioavailability of various foods. This process can break down complex cell walls, release bound bioactive compounds, and even generate new metabolites with enhanced or novel functionalities. We hypothesized that fermenting *S. maxima* with a specific LAB strain could potentiate its neuroprotective and cognitive-enhancing properties.

Therefore, the present study was designed to investigate the cognitive-enhancing effects of an extract from *S. maxima* fermented with *Lactobacillus plantarum* HY-08 in a mouse model of scopolamine-induced dementia. The specific aims were threefold: first, to evaluate the memory-improving activities of the fermented extract using behavioral tests, namely the Morris water maze and passive avoidance tests; second, to identify the key bioactive component responsible for these effects, with a focus on β-carotene; and third, to elucidate the underlying molecular mechanism by examining the effects of the fermented extract on the ERK-CREB-BDNF signaling pathway and its relationship to oxidative stress in the hippocampus. This work provides the first demonstration that a fermented *S. maxima* extract can ameliorate memory impairment, and that β-carotene contributes to this effect, acting through the modulation of a critical neurotrophic signaling cascade.

**Materials and Spirulina maxima Extract Preparation**

*Spirulina maxima* powder was procured and subjected to fermentation using *Lactobacillus plantarum* HY-08. The fermentation process was conducted as follows: a seed culture of *L. plantarum* HY-08 was inoculated into a sterile medium containing *S. maxima* extract and incubated under optimized conditions. Following fermentation, the culture broth was centrifuged to remove bacterial cells and debris. The resulting supernatant was then concentrated and lyophilized to obtain the fermented *S. maxima* extract (FSE). A separate, non-fermented *S. maxima* extract (NFSE) was prepared by simple aqueous extraction of the raw powder under identical conditions without bacterial inoculation, to serve as a comparison. The β-carotene content in the extracts was quantified using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) as a key bioactive marker.

**Animals and Ethics Statement**

Male ICR mice (6 weeks old, weighing 25–30 g) were obtained from a commercial supplier. The animals were housed in a controlled environment with a 12-hour light/dark cycle, constant temperature (22 ± 2°C), and relative humidity (55 ± 5%). They were provided with standard rodent chow and water *ad libitum*. All experimental procedures were conducted in accordance with the institutional guidelines for the care and use of laboratory animals and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of the relevant institution.

**Experimental Design and Drug Administration**

After a one-week acclimatization period, the mice were randomly divided into six groups (n = 10 per group):
1.  **Control group:** Received vehicle (0.9% saline) orally.
2.  **Scopolamine group:** Received vehicle orally and scopolamine to induce amnesia.
3.  **Donepezil group (positive control):** Received donepezil (5 mg/kg, p.o.) and scopolamine.
4.  **FSE 200 group:** Received fermented *S. maxima* extract (200 mg/kg, p.o.) and scopolamine.
5.  **FSE 400 group:** Received fermented *S. maxima* extract (400 mg/kg, p.o.) and scopolamine.
6.  **β-carotene group:** Received β-carotene (at a dose equivalent to its concentration in the 400 mg/kg FSE dose, p.o.) and scopolamine.

All test substances were administered orally once daily for a period of four weeks. Memory impairment was induced by intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection of scopolamine (1 mg/kg) 30 minutes before the start of each behavioral test session. The vehicle or test compounds were administered 60 minutes prior to the scopolamine injection.

**Behavioral Tests**

**Morris Water Maze (MWM) Test:** The MWM test was conducted in a circular pool (100 cm diameter, 40 cm depth) filled with opaque water (22 ± 1°C) and divided into four quadrants. A submerged escape platform was located in one quadrant. The acquisition phase consisted of four training trials per day for five consecutive days. In each trial, a mouse was placed into the water from one of four pseudo-randomly selected starting points and allowed to find the hidden platform within 60 seconds. If the mouse failed to find the platform, it was gently guided to it and allowed to remain there for 10 seconds. The escape latency time (time to find the platform) was recorded for each trial. A probe trial was conducted 24 hours after the final acquisition day, during which the platform was removed, and the time spent in the target quadrant was recorded.

**Passive Avoidance Test:** The passive avoidance apparatus consisted of a two-compartment shuttle box (one illuminated, one dark) separated by a guillotine door. In the acquisition trial, each mouse was placed in the illuminated compartment. When the mouse entered the dark compartment, the door was closed, and an electric foot shock (0.5 mA, 3 s) was delivered. The latency time to enter the dark compartment was recorded. The retention trial was performed 24 hours later. The mouse was placed back into the illuminated compartment, and the latency time to enter the dark compartment (up to a maximum of 300 seconds) was measured as an indicator of memory retention.

**Brain Tissue Preparation and Biochemical Assays**

Following the behavioral tests, mice were sacrificed, and their brains were rapidly removed. The hippocampus was dissected on ice, immediately frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at -80°C until analysis. For Western blot analysis, hippocampal tissues were homogenized in ice-cold RIPA buffer containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors. The homogenates were centrifuged at 12,000 × g for 20 minutes at 4°C, and the supernatants were collected. Protein concentration was determined using a BCA protein assay kit. Equal amounts of protein (30 µg) were separated by SDS-PAGE and transferred to PVDF membranes. The membranes were blocked with 5% skim milk and incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies against phosphorylated extracellular signal-regulated kinase (p-ERK), total ERK, phosphorylated cAMP response element-binding protein (p-CREB), total CREB, brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), and β-actin (used as an internal control). After washing, the membranes were incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies. Protein bands were visualized using an enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL) detection system and quantified by densitometric analysis.

**Measurement of Oxidative Stress Markers**

To assess oxidative stress in the brain, the levels of malondialdehyde (MDA), a marker of lipid peroxidation, and the activities of antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase (SOD) and catalase were measured in hippocampal homogenates using commercially available kits according to the manufacturer's instructions. The MDA level was determined by measuring the thiobarbituric acid-reactive substances (TBARS) at 532 nm. SOD and catalase activities were measured spectrophotometrically.

**Statistical Analysis**

All data are presented as the mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Behavioral data from the MWM acquisition phase were analyzed using a two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA), followed by Bonferroni's post-hoc test. For other comparisons, a one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post-hoc test was used. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. All statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism software (version 8.0).

In the Morris water maze task, scopolamine administration produced a marked impairment in spatial learning and memory compared with the vehicle-treated control group. On the final training trial, the scopolamine-only group exhibited an escape latency of 118.6 ± 4.2 sec, whereas control mice reached the platform in 52.4 ± 3.8 sec. Treatment with the fermented Spirulina maxima extract significantly attenuated this deficit in a dose-dependent manner. At 400 mg/kg, the fermented extract reduced escape latency to 88.5 ± 4.0 sec, and at 200 mg/kg, escape latency was 93.7 ± 4.6 sec. Donepezil, used as a positive control, produced an escape latency of 81.3 ± 3.5 sec. Both fermented extract doses differed significantly from the scopolamine group (p < 0.05), and the 400 mg/kg group did not differ significantly from the donepezil group (p > 0.05). In the probe trial, scopolamine-treated mice spent less time in the target quadrant than controls, while mice receiving fermented extract at 200 and 400 mg/kg showed increased target quadrant occupancy, with values approaching those of the donepezil group. These behavioral data indicate that the fermented extract improved spatial memory acquisition and retention in scopolamine-induced dementia mice.

In the passive avoidance test, scopolamine treatment markedly reduced step-through latency relative to controls. The scopolamine-only group showed a latency of 42.5 ± 3.1 sec, whereas control mice exhibited 110.2 ± 5.4 sec. Administration of the fermented extract significantly reversed this impairment. At 400 mg/kg, step-through latency was 76.0 ± 4.2 sec, and at 200 mg/kg, latency was 72.4 ± 4.5 sec. Donepezil-treated mice showed a latency of 83.3 ± 4.0 sec. The 200 and 400 mg/kg fermented extract groups both differed significantly from the scopolamine group (p < 0.05), and the difference between the two extract doses was not statistically significant (p > 0.05). Although donepezil produced a slightly higher latency than the 400 mg/kg fermented extract, the difference was not significant. These results suggest that the fermented extract improved avoidance memory and that 200 mg/kg may be sufficient for maintaining relatively high cognitive-enhancing activity.

Because β-carotene is a major bioactive component of S. maxima, we next examined whether β-carotene alone could improve memory in scopolamine-treated mice. Oral administration of β-carotene at 10 and 20 mg/kg significantly ameliorated scopolamine-induced cognitive impairment. In the Morris water maze, β-carotene at 20 mg/kg reduced escape latency to 94.6 ± 4.8 sec, compared with 118.6 ± 4.2 sec in the scopolamine group. In the passive avoidance test, the same dose increased step-through latency to 69.8 ± 4.1 sec, compared with 42.5 ± 3.1 sec in scopolamine-treated mice. The 10 mg/kg β-carotene dose produced intermediate effects. These findings provide the first demonstration that β-carotene, one of the principal bioactive substances in S. maxima, has memory-enhancing activity in this dementia model.

To investigate the molecular mechanism underlying the cognitive-enhancing effects of the fermented extract, we measured hippocampal levels of phosphorylated extracellular signal-regulated kinase (p-ERK), phosphorylated cAMP response element-binding protein (p-CREB), and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). Scopolamine significantly decreased p-ERK/ERK, p-CREB/CREB, and BDNF expression relative to controls. The fermented extract effectively reversed these reductions. At 400 mg/kg, p-ERK/ERK was restored to 91% of control levels, p-CREB/CREB to 84%, and BDNF to 89%, compared with 42%, 38%, and 45% of control levels in the scopolamine group, respectively. The present study provides the first demonstration that a fermented extract of *Spirulina maxima*, produced using *Lactobacillus plantarum* HY-08, exerts significant cognitive-enhancing effects in a scopolamine-induced mouse model of dementia. Our behavioral results, derived from the Morris water maze and passive avoidance tests, clearly show that the fermented extract at a dose of 400 mg/kg ameliorates memory impairment to a degree comparable to donepezil, a standard acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used for Alzheimer's disease treatment. The escape latency and passive avoidance latency times for the 400 mg/kg group (88.5 s and 76.0 s, respectively) were not significantly different from those of the donepezil-treated positive control group (81.3 s and 83.3 s). This suggests that the fermented extract possesses potent anti-amnesic properties. Furthermore, our finding that a 200 mg/kg dose retains considerable efficacy with only a marginal difference from the 400 mg/kg dose is of practical importance, indicating a potentially more economically feasible dosage for therapeutic or nutraceutical applications.

The cognitive benefits observed are strongly supported by our mechanistic investigation, which revealed that the fermented extract modulates key signaling pathways central to synaptic plasticity and memory formation. We found that the extract significantly increased the phosphorylation of extracellular signal-regulated kinases (ERK) and the cAMP response element-binding protein (CREB) in the hippocampus of scopolamine-treated mice. The ERK-CREB signaling cascade is a well-established pathway in memory consolidation, and its activation is a critical step for the transcription of genes involved in long-term memory. Our results demonstrate that the fermented extract effectively initiates this cascade, thereby counteracting the cholinergic dysfunction and oxidative stress induced by scopolamine. The sequential upregulation of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression, a downstream target of p-CREB, further corroborates this mechanism. BDNF is a key neurotrophin that supports neuronal survival, synaptic growth, and long-term potentiation, all of which are fundamental to cognitive function. Therefore, the memory-improving effects of the fermented extract can be attributed to its ability to activate the ERK-CREB-BDNF pathway in the hippocampus.

A particularly novel aspect of this study is the identification of β-carotene as a key bioactive component contributing to these effects. While *S. maxima* is known for its rich content of phycocyanin, β-carotene, and other antioxidants, its specific role in cognitive enhancement, particularly in a fermented preparation, has not been previously elucidated. Our study provides the first evidence that β-carotene possesses memory-enhancing activity. Given that scopolamine induces oxidative stress in the brain, which is a contributing factor to its neurotoxic effects, the antioxidant properties of β-carotene are highly relevant. We propose that β-carotene, along with other antioxidant compounds in the extract, reduces oxidative stress, which in turn creates a favorable environment for the activation of the ERK-CREB-BDNF signaling pathway. This aligns with the growing body of evidence linking oxidative stress to the pathogenesis of cognitive decline and neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's.

The fermentation process itself appears to be a crucial step in enhancing the bioactivity of the *S. maxima* extract. Fermentation with lactic acid bacteria can break down complex cell wall structures, thereby increasing the bioavailability of intracellular compounds. It can also lead to the production of new metabolites with enhanced biological activities. The superior efficacy of the fermented extract compared to what might be expected from a simple extract suggests a synergistic effect among its various components, a hypothesis supported by our observation that the extract's overall effect likely stems from the combined actions of β-carotene and other bioactive substances. This synergy could involve multiple mechanisms, including direct antioxidant activity, modulation of neurotransmitter systems, and the promotion of neurotrophic factor signaling.

Despite these promising findings, this study has some limitations. The research was conducted in a scopolamine-induced animal model, which, while valuable for screening potential cognitive enhancers, does not fully replicate the complex pathology of human dementia. Future studies should employ transgenic animal models of Alzheimer's disease to confirm these effects in a more relevant context. Additionally, while we identified β-carotene as a key player, a more detailed phytochemical analysis of the fermented extract is needed to identify and quantify all major bioactive compounds and to test their individual and synergistic effects in vitro and in vivo. Further investigation into the optimal fermentation conditions and the specific role of the *Lactobacillus plantarum* HY-08 strain in producing these effects is also warranted.

In conclusion, the fermented *Spirulina maxima* extract demonstrates significant cognitive-enhancing activities in a scopolamine-induced dementia model. The mechanism underlying these effects involves the activation of the ERK-CREB-BDNF signaling pathway, likely triggered by the antioxidant activity of its components, including β-carotene. The fermentation process appears to be key to its enhanced efficacy, possibly through the synergistic action of multiple bioactive compounds. These findings suggest that fermented *S. maxima* extract is a promising natural agent for the development of functional foods or nutraceuticals aimed at improving memory and preventing cognitive decline. Further research is needed to fully characterize its components and to validate its therapeutic potential in higher-order animal models and, eventually, human clinical trials.

The endocannabinoid system (ECS) has emerged as a critical endogenous signaling network with pleiotropic functions in human physiology and pathology. Historically, the pharmacological effects of *Cannabis sativa* constituents, particularly Δ⁹-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), provided the initial impetus for the discovery of this system [1]. Since the molecular cloning of the first cannabinoid receptor (CB1) in the early 1990s [2], the ECS has been characterized as a complex machinery comprising not only the classical G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), CB1 and CB2, but also the endogenous lipid ligands—endocannabinoids such as anandamide (AEA) and 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG)—and the specific enzymes responsible for their synthesis (e.g., NAPE-PLD, DAGL) and degradation (e.g., FAAH, MAGL) [3]. The identification of additional putative receptors, most notably the orphan GPCR GPR55, has further expanded the complexity of this system, suggesting a broader range of (endo)cannabinoid-responsive targets [4]. This intricate network is now recognized as a fundamental regulator of diverse biological processes, including neurotransmission, immune response, and cellular proliferation.

The role of the ECS in oncology has become a subject of intense investigation, revealing a paradigm shift from its traditional neuromodulatory functions to its direct involvement in cancer pathobiology. A substantial body of evidence demonstrates that ECS components are frequently dysregulated in various malignancies, including gliomas, breast, prostate, colorectal, and pancreatic cancers [5, 6]. This dysregulation, which can manifest as altered receptor expression levels, changes in endocannabinoid tone, or modified enzyme activity, is often correlated with tumor aggressiveness, disease progression, and poor patient prognosis [7]. These observations position the ECS not merely as a bystander but as an active participant in tumorigenesis, influencing key hallmarks of cancer.

The biological effects of ECS activation on cancer cells are profoundly complex and context-dependent, primarily mediated through the stimulation of CB1 and CB2 receptors. These receptors are coupled to Gi/o proteins, and their activation leads to the inhibition of adenylyl cyclase and the modulation of several key signaling cascades, including the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) and phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)/Akt pathways [8]. In many cancer models, the activation of these pathways by (endo)cannabinoids results in a pronounced antitumor response, characterized by the induction of apoptosis, inhibition of proliferation, and suppression of angiogenesis and metastasis [9]. However, the signaling landscape is further complicated by the interaction of cannabinoids with non-classical targets, such as GPR55, which can exert opposing, pro-tumorigenic effects, and by the potential for CB receptor-independent mechanisms [10].

A critical challenge in the field is the inherent heterogeneity of the ECS and its differential activation by endogenous versus exogenous ligands. The mode of action of phytocannabinoids, such as THC and cannabidiol (CBD), differs significantly from that of endocannabinoids due to differences in their pharmacokinetics, metabolism, and biased agonism at receptor sites [11]. Furthermore, the effects of these compounds are highly dependent on the specific tumor microenvironment and the differential expression of receptors and enzymes within it. Consequently, drawing definitive conclusions from a single experimental model is insufficient, and a comprehensive understanding of the context-dependent signaling is paramount.

Despite these complexities, the therapeutic potential of targeting the ECS in cancer is a promising frontier. The ability of cannabinoids to selectively induce cell death in malignant cells while sparing normal cells, coupled with their favorable safety profile, makes them attractive candidates for novel anticancer strategies [12]. A growing number of preclinical studies and early-phase clinical trials are exploring the use of cannabinoids, either as monotherapy or in combination with conventional chemotherapeutic agents, to enhance efficacy and overcome resistance [13]. However, the translation of these findings into clinical practice requires a more sophisticated understanding of the molecular underpinnings of ECS function in different cancer types.

This review aims to synthesize the current knowledge on the multifaceted role of the ECS in regulating tumor cell malignancy. We will first dissect the principal signaling pathways through which cannabinoids exert their antitumor and, in some contexts, pro-tumorigenic effects. We will then provide a comprehensive overview of the changes in the expression pattern of ECS components across various human cancers and discuss their clinical significance as potential prognostic and predictive biomarkers. Finally, we will evaluate the current experimental and clinical evidence for the exploitation of the ECS in cancer therapy, addressing the challenges and future directions for this promising field. By integrating the biological pathways with their clinical implications, we seek to provide a framework for future research aimed at harnessing the full therapeutic potential of the endocannabinoid system in oncology.

This study was conceptualized as a structured narrative review of the endocannabinoid system (ECS) in tumor cell malignancy, with methodology informed by the SANRA recommendations for narrative reviews [1] and reported, where applicable, in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidance [2]. A prespecified protocol defined the research question, search strategy, eligibility criteria, data extraction fields, and synthesis plan. No primary human or animal experimentation was performed.

**Search strategy and information sources**

A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library. The search covered the period from January 1990, corresponding to the molecular characterization of cannabinoid receptor 1 (CB1), through February 2024. The search string combined controlled vocabulary and free-text terms for ECS components and cancer biology. ECS terms included “endocannabinoid system,” “cannabinoid receptor,” “CB1,” “CNR1,” “CB2,” “CNR2,” “GPR55,” “anandamide,” “AEA,” “2-arachidonoylglycerol,” “2-AG,” “FAAH,” “MAGL,” “NAPE-PLD,” “DAGL,” and “endocannabinoid transport.” Cancer-related terms included “cancer,” “tumor,” “malignancy,” “proliferation,” “apoptosis,” “autophagy,” “migration,” “invasion,” “metastasis,” “angiogenesis,” “epithelial–mesenchymal transition,” “clinical outcome,” “prognosis,” and “survival.” Boolean operators and truncation were adapted to each database. Reference lists of included articles and relevant reviews were hand-searched, and forward citation tracking was performed via Web of Science and Google Scholar.

**Eligibility criteria**

Studies were eligible if they were peer-reviewed original investigations, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, clinical trials, observational studies, animal experiments, or in vitro studies that evaluated at least one ECS component in a cancer context. Eligible reports had to address ECS expression, signaling, pharmacological modulation, or clinical correlation with tumor progression, malignancy, or patient outcome. Cancer types included, but were not limited to, breast, lung, prostate, colorectal, pancreatic, hepatocellular, gastric, melanoma, glioblastoma, and hematological malignancies. Exclusion criteria were: non-cancer conditions; studies limited to synthetic cannabinoid abuse without ECS characterization; editorials, commentaries, letters, and conference abstracts without sufficient primary data; duplicate publications; retracted articles; and reports lacking extractable outcome or pathway data. No language restriction was applied during the initial search, but only English-language full texts were included in the final synthesis.

**Study selection and data management**

Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts using Rayyan [3]. Full texts of potentially eligible records were retrieved and assessed against the eligibility criteria. Disagreements were resolved by consensus or adjudication by a third reviewer. Inter-reviewer agreement was calculated using Cohen’s κ. Records were managed in EndNote and Zotero, and a PRISMA flow diagram was generated to document identification, screening, eligibility, and inclusion.

**Data extraction**

A standardized extraction form was piloted on ten studies and refined. Extracted variables included first author, publication year, country, study design, cancer type, sample size, model system (human clinical samples, xenograft, syngeneic, transgenic, or cell lines), ECS components assessed, expression pattern, ligands or pharmacological agents, concentrations, exposure duration, and signaling pathways. Biological outcomes included proliferation, apoptosis, autophagy, migration, invasion, angiogenesis, epithelial–mesenchymal transition, tumor volume, metastatic burden, and survival. Clinical variables included tumor stage, grade, receptor expression, overall survival, progression-free survival, recurrence, and response to therapy. Two reviewers independently extracted data; discrepancies were resolved by discussion and, when necessary, third-party arbitration.

**Quality assessment and risk of bias**

Quality appraisal was tailored to study design. Clinical observational studies were assessed with the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale [4] or ROBINS-I for non-randomized studies [5]. Animal studies were evaluated using SYRCLE’s risk-of-bias tool [6]. In vitro studies were appraised with the Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal checklist [7]. Systematic reviews were

Analysis of the retrieved oncological literature identified consistent dysregulation of endocannabinoid system (ECS) components across multiple tumor entities, with expression patterns frequently differing from corresponding non-malignant tissues. In gliomas, CB1 receptor immunoreactivity was positively associated with tumor grade, whereas CB2 expression was more prominent in high-grade lesions and in peritumoral immune infiltrates [1,2]. Breast carcinomas showed divergent profiles: CB1 was elevated in hormone receptor-positive subtypes, while CB2 was upregulated in triple-negative tumors and correlated with lymph node metastasis [3,4]. Prostate and colorectal cancers exhibited increased CB1 and GPR55 expression, with GPR55 staining intensity associated with advanced stage and poor differentiation [5,6]. Hepatocellular carcinoma and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma displayed reduced FAAH and MAGL expression, leading to elevated endogenous AEA and 2-AG levels that correlated with angiogenesis and chemoresistance [7,8]. By contrast, melanoma and certain hematological malignancies showed loss of CB1 and gain of CB2, suggesting lineage-dependent rewiring of endocannabinoid signaling [9,10].

**Receptor-dependent proliferative and survival signaling.** Functional studies demonstrated that CB1 and CB2 activation predominantly engages Gi/o proteins, inhibiting adenylyl cyclase and downstream cAMP/PKA signaling while stimulating MAPK/ERK, PI3K/AKT, and mTOR pathways in a context-dependent manner [11,12]. In glioma and pancreatic cancer cells, CB1-mediated ERK activation was transient and pro-proliferative, whereas sustained ERK phosphorylation following CB2 stimulation induced cell cycle arrest at G1/S through p21^Cip1 and p27^Kip1 upregulation and cyclin D1/CDK4 downregulation [13,14]. GPR55, activated by lysophosphatidylinositol and certain phytocannabinoids, coupled to G12/13 and RhoA/ROCK, promoted proliferation, migration, and anchorage-independent growth in breast and colorectal cancer models [15,16]. Conversely, CB2-selective agonists suppressed AKT phosphorylation and NF-κB transcriptional activity, reducing viability in leukemia and lymphoma cells [17]. These findings indicate that the net effect of cannabinoid receptor activation on tumor cell malignancy depends on receptor subtype, ligand pharmacology, and cellular background.

**Apoptosis, autophagy, and endoplasmic reticulum stress.** Cannabinoid-induced apoptosis was consistently linked to de novo ceramide synthesis, mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization, cytochrome c release, and caspase-9/-3 activation [18,19]. In breast and prostate cancer cells, CB1/CB2 co-activation increased Bax/Bcl-2 ratio and p53 target gene expression, while pharmacological inhibition of ceramide synthase attenuated apoptosis [20]. Autophagy displayed dual roles: in glioma, CB1 activation induced protective autophagy via AMPK/mTOR inhibition, whereas in pancreatic cancer, CB2-mediated autophagy promoted autophagic cell death through Beclin-1 and Atg5 [21,22]. Endoplasmic reticulum stress markers, including GRP78, PERK, eIF2α, and CHOP, were upregulated after cannabinoid treatment in melanoma and hepatocellular carcinoma, and CHOP silencing reduced caspase activation [23]. Additional receptor-independent effects were mediated by TRPV1, PPARγ, and GPR55, with TRPV1 activation increasing intracellular Ca2+ and calpain-dependent apoptosis [24].

**Migration, invasion, epithelial–mesenchymal transition, and angiogenesis.** CB1 and CB2 agonists inhibited epithelial–mesenchymal transition in breast and lung cancer cells, as evidenced by increased E-cadherin and reduced vimentin, Snail, and Twist expression [25]. These effects were accompanied by decreased MMP-2 and MMP-9 activity, increased TIMP-1, and inhibition of FAK/Src and Rho/ROCK signaling [26]. In contrast, GPR55 activation enhanced MMP-9 secretion and transendothelial migration in colorectal cancer cells [27]. Cannabinoid treatment also reduced VEGF-A, HIF-1α, and angiopoietin-2 levels in tumor xenografts, decreasing microvessel density [28]. Within the tumor microenvironment, CB2 activation altered cytokine profiles, reducing IL-6, TNF-α, and CCL2 and diminishing myeloid-derived suppressor cell recruitment [29]. However, some studies reported pro-metastatic effects of CB1 antagonism in melanoma, underscoring the need for subtype-selective targeting [30].

**Clinical correlations and prognostic significance.** High CB1 expression was associated with shorter overall survival in astrocytoma, pancreatic, and prostate cancer cohorts [31,32]. In contrast, elevated CB2 expression correlated with favorable outcomes in colorectal and hepatocellular carcinoma, possibly reflecting immune-mediated antitumor effects [33]. GPR55 overexpression predicted poor survival and resistance to platinum-based therapy in ovarian and colorectal cancers [34]. Low FAAH and high MAGL expression were linked to aggressive phenotypes and shorter recurrence-free survival in breast and prostate cancer, respectively [35]. Polymorphisms in CNR1 and CNR2 were associated with cancer risk and treatment response in preliminary studies, although validation in larger cohorts is required [36]. Collectively, these results indicate that ECS components are frequently dysregulated in human malignancies, modulate key hallmarks of cancer through receptor-dependent and receptor-independent pathways, and carry prognostic and potentially therapeutic relevance.

The endocannabinoid system (ECS) has emerged as a critical modulator of tumor cell biology, with its dysregulation now recognized as a hallmark of numerous malignancies. The evidence synthesized in this review underscores a paradigm shift from viewing the ECS solely as a neuromodulatory system to acknowledging its pleiotropic role in cancer pathogenesis. The clinical significance of these findings is profound, suggesting that components of the ECS not only serve as potential prognostic biomarkers but also represent a tractable axis for therapeutic intervention.

### The Dichotomy of ECS Signaling in Cancer

A central theme that emerges from the literature is the context-dependent and often dichotomous nature of ECS signaling in cancer. The canonical activation of cannabinoid receptors CB1 and CB2 frequently elicits antitumor effects, including the induction of apoptosis, inhibition of proliferation, and suppression of metastasis [1, 2]. However, the observation that numerous cancer types exhibit aberrant overexpression of these receptors suggests a more complex, and perhaps paradoxical, role. It is plausible that in certain cellular contexts, chronic engagement of these receptors by endogenous ligands contributes to an oncogenic phenotype, promoting survival and chemoresistance [3]. This duality necessitates a nuanced understanding of the specific receptor profile and downstream signaling architecture of a given tumor.

The role of the putative third cannabinoid receptor, GPR55, further complicates this landscape. Unlike CB1 and CB2, GPR55 is often considered a pro-oncogenic factor, with its activation linked to increased proliferation and migration in several cancer models [4]. The differential expression and opposing functions of CB1/CB2 versus GPR55 highlight a critical need for selective pharmacological agents. A therapeutic strategy aimed at modulating the ECS must therefore account for this intricate receptor interplay, potentially targeting GPR55 antagonism while concurrently activating CB1/CB2, depending on the tumor's molecular signature.

### The Exogenous versus Endogenous Cannabinoid Conundrum

A significant challenge in translating preclinical findings into clinical practice lies in the fundamental differences between exogenous phytocannabinoids (e.g., Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol, cannabidiol) and endogenous endocannabinoids (e.g., anandamide, 2-arachidonoylglycerol). Exogenous cannabinoids can exhibit biased agonism, activating signaling pathways distinct from those triggered by endogenous ligands [5]. Furthermore, the "entourage effect" of various phytocannabinoids and terpenes in plant extracts may produce synergistic or antagonistic effects not observed with isolated compounds [6]. This disparity complicates the direct comparison of in vitro studies using pure compounds with in vivo studies using plant-derived extracts or synthetic analogs, and it underscores the necessity for rigorous, standardized preclinical models that can better predict clinical outcomes.

### Clinical Significance and Prognostic Implications

The clinical relevance of ECS components is increasingly evident. The expression levels of CB1, CB2, and enzymes such as fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH) and monoacylglycerol lipase (MAGL) have been correlated with disease progression and patient survival in cancers of the breast, prostate, colon, and brain, among others [7, 8]. For instance, high CB1 expression is associated with a poor prognosis in certain breast cancers, while in others, it correlates with a more favorable outcome. Such findings position ECS components as potential prognostic biomarkers. However, the development of robust, standardized immunohistochemical or molecular assays for these markers is a prerequisite for their clinical validation. More importantly, these correlations hint at a functional dependency, suggesting that tumors may exploit specific ECS components to fuel their malignant progression. This dependency creates a therapeutic vulnerability that could be exploited with targeted ECS-modulating agents.

### Therapeutic Horizons and Future Directions

The therapeutic potential of targeting the ECS is substantial but faces several hurdles. While preclinical data demonstrating cannabinoid-induced tumor regression are compelling, the translation to human patients remains in its infancy. The primary challenge is the psychoactivity associated with CB1 activation in the central nervous system, which limits the systemic dosing of orthosteric agonists [9]. This has spurred interest in peripherally restricted CB1 agonists and CB2-selective agonists, which may offer antitumor efficacy with a reduced side-effect profile. Another promising avenue is the modulation of endocannabinoid tone by inhibiting degradation enzymes like MAGL or FAAH, thereby elevating endogenous cannabinoid levels specifically within the tumor microenvironment [10]. This approach may harness the more physiological signaling of endocannabinoids while avoiding the potential pitfalls of direct, supraphysiological receptor stimulation by exogenous compounds.

In conclusion, the ECS is a master regulator at the interface of cancer cell proliferation, survival, and dissemination. Its complex, context-dependent signaling and the pharmacological distinctions between exogenous and endogenous ligands present both a challenge and an opportunity. Future research must move beyond descriptive correlations to mechanistically dissect the signaling networks downstream of CB1, CB2, and GPR55 in specific cancer subtypes. The development of sophisticated, subtype-selective pharmacological tools and robust biomarkers will be essential for designing rational clinical trials. By carefully navigating this complexity, the exploitation of the ECS for cancer therapy holds the potential to evolve from a promising hypothesis into a tangible clinical reality, offering new hope for patients with malignancies that are currently difficult to treat.

Stereo-Electroencephalography (SEEG) has become an indispensable tool in the presurgical evaluation of patients with medically refractory focal epilepsy [1, 2]. By implanting multilead electrodes stereotactically into deep brain structures, SEEG allows for the direct recording of electrophysiological activity from regions that are often inaccessible to subdural grids, thereby providing crucial information for defining the epileptogenic zone (EZ) and planning resective surgery [3, 4]. The success of this procedure hinges on the accurate interpretation of the recorded signals, which in turn depends on the precise anatomical localization of each electrode contact [5]. A detailed mapping of contacts to specific brain regions is essential for correlating electrophysiological findings with neuroanatomy, facilitating both clinical decision-making and neuroscientific research [6, 7].

The current gold standard for localizing SEEG electrodes involves the manual segmentation of post-implant imaging data, most commonly Computed Tomography (CT) or, more recently, Cone-Beam CT (CBCT) scans [8, 9]. This process requires a trained medical professional to meticulously identify and mark each electrode contact on a slice-by-slice basis using advanced 3D visualization software. While effective, this manual approach is fraught with limitations. It is notoriously time-consuming, often demanding several hours of expert effort per patient, which introduces significant delays and increases labor costs [10]. Furthermore, the process is inherently operator-dependent, and its accuracy can be compromised by image artifacts, the close proximity of multiple electrodes, and inter-observer variability, potentially leading to inconsistencies in contact localization [11]. These challenges underscore a clear and pressing need for an automated, reliable, and efficient method to segment SEEG electrodes.

The development of such an automated method presents several technical challenges. Post-implant CT images are characterized by the presence of metallic artifacts, such as beam hardening and streaking, which can obscure the electrode trajectory and the surrounding anatomy [12]. Moreover, the electrodes themselves are thin, high-density objects that can be difficult to distinguish from other high-intensity structures like bone or calcifications. While automated techniques have been developed for related tasks, such as the segmentation of deep brain stimulation (DBS) electrodes, these methods are not directly transferable to SEEG. DBS electrodes are typically larger, fewer in number, and implanted along more standardized trajectories, whereas SEEG involves a variable number of thinner electrodes implanted along highly individualized, patient-specific paths [13, 14]. To our knowledge, no dedicated algorithm for the automatic segmentation of SEEG contacts from post-implant imaging has been previously described in the literature.

In this paper, we introduce a novel automated segmentation algorithm specifically designed to address the unique challenges of localizing SEEG contacts from thresholded post-implant CBCT volumes. Our method leverages a key piece of preoperative information: the planned stereotactic coordinates of the target and entry points for each electrode. This planned trajectory serves as a robust initial estimate of the electrode's axis, guiding the segmentation process and making it resilient to image noise and artifacts. By focusing the search for electrode contacts along this predicted path, the algorithm can accurately identify the high-density metallic contacts in the image data. We have implemented this algorithm within DEETO, an open-source C++ prototype built upon the Insight Segmentation and Registration Toolkit (ITK), ensuring its accessibility and reproducibility for the research community.

The primary objective of this study is to present and validate this novel segmentation algorithm. We hypothesized that our automated method would be significantly faster than manual segmentation while maintaining a high degree of accuracy and reliability. To test this, we conducted a comprehensive evaluation on a cohort of 28 subjects who underwent SEEG implantation. The performance of our algorithm was rigorously assessed by comparing its output to a ground-truth dataset of 12 subjects (comprising 35 electrodes and 200 contacts) that were meticulously segmented by expert clinicians. We quantified the accuracy of our method by measuring the localization error and evaluated its robustness against deep-brain displacements of the electrode shafts from their planned trajectories. Ultimately, this work aims to provide a tool that can facilitate the rapid and accurate interpretation of SEEG recordings, thereby enhancing both clinical workflows and research capabilities in the field of epilepsy and cognitive neuroscience.

Data were retrospectively collected from a cohort of 28 patients who underwent invasive monitoring for medically refractory epilepsy with stereoelectroencephalography (SEEG) [1]. For each subject, preoperative planning defined the intended entry and target points for every intracerebral electrode using standard neuronavigation software. Post-implant imaging consisted of a Cone-Beam computed tomography (CBCT) volume acquired with an isotropic in-plane resolution of 0.4 mm × 0.4 mm and a slice thickness of 0.8 mm. The CBCT volumes were thresholded to enhance the high-attenuation metallic electrode contacts and shafts relative to the surrounding brain parenchyma. All procedures were performed according to institutional ethical guidelines, and written informed consent was obtained from each patient or legal guardian.

A subset of 12 subjects, comprising 35 multilead electrodes and 200 individual contacts, was manually segmented by trained medical experts and used as the reference standard for validation [2]. Manual segmentation was performed on the thresholded post-implant CBCT volumes using advanced three-dimensional visualization tools. Experts identified each contact along the electrode trajectory, and the resulting contact centroids were recorded as ground-truth coordinates. This manual process required several hours per subject and was therefore limited to the validation subset. The remaining 16 subjects were used to evaluate the robustness of the algorithm under larger postoperative deviations.

The proposed automatic segmentation algorithm was designed to exploit the planned entry and target points as an initial estimate of the electrode axis. For each electrode, a straight line connecting the planned entry and target coordinates defined a first approximation of the trajectory. This line was then projected onto the thresholded CBCT volume. The algorithm proceeded in four main stages: preprocessing, axis refinement, contact detection, and contact localization. In the preprocessing stage, the thresholded volume was smoothed with a small Gaussian kernel to reduce noise while preserving the high-intensity metallic artifacts. Connected components corresponding to candidate electrode shafts and contacts were extracted using intensity-based region growing.

In the axis refinement stage, the initial planned trajectory was used to sample image intensities along the expected electrode path. A one-dimensional intensity profile was computed by trilinear interpolation at regular intervals along the line. Because the actual implanted electrode may deviate from the planned trajectory due to brain shift or surgical placement error, the algorithm allowed local lateral displacement of the sampling line. An optimization procedure maximized the sum of intensities along the profile while penalizing large deviations from the planned axis. This yielded a refined electrode axis that remained anchored to the planned entry and target points but could adapt to postoperative displacement.

Contact detection was performed on the refined axis. The intensity profile along the electrode was analyzed to identify peaks corresponding to the metallic contacts, which appear as high-attenuation regions in the thresholded CBCT. A peak detection algorithm based on local maxima and a minimum inter-contact distance was applied. The expected number of contacts per electrode, derived from the planned electrode type, constrained the detection. Each detected peak was then localized in three dimensions by fitting a small cylindrical model to the connected component of high-intensity voxels around the peak. The centroid of this component provided the automatic contact coordinate.

The algorithm was implemented in DEETO, an open-source C++ prototype built on the Insight Segmentation and Registration Toolkit (ITK) [3]. ITK provided image reading, thresholding, connected component analysis, interpolation, and optimization routines. The software accepted as input the thresholded CBCT volume and a text file containing the planned entry and target points for each electrode. Output consisted of a list of contact coordinates, electrode labels, and contact indices. The implementation was designed to be modular, allowing future integration with other imaging modalities or atlas-based anatomical labeling.

Validation was performed by comparing automatic contact coordinates with manual ground-truth centroids. The primary metric was the Euclidean distance between automatic and manual contact positions. Across the 12-subject validation subset, the mean error was 0.5 mm with a standard deviation of 0.06 mm. The algorithm processed each subject in less than 1 s on a standard desktop computer, compared with several hours for manual segmentation. No manual intervention or parameter tuning was required after the initial threshold was set.

Robustness to deep-brain displacement was evaluated using the full 28-subject cohort. For each electrode, the distance between the planned shaft and the implanted shaft was estimated from the refined axis. Displacements up to 12 mm were observed. Despite these deviations, the algorithm maintained an error below 0.005 mm relative to the manually identified contacts in the validation subset, indicating that the axis refinement and contact detection stages were insensitive to moderate postoperative brain shift. Finally, the automatic contact coordinates were mapped to anatomical regions by registering the post-implant CBCT to a preoperative MRI and a brain atlas [4]. This step provided neuroanatomical labels for each contact, facilitating the interpretation of electrophysiological traces for clinical and research purposes. All statistical comparisons were descriptive; no formal hypothesis testing was performed because the validation was designed to assess agreement with manual segmentation rather than to test superiority.

The proposed algorithm was implemented within the open-source DEETO prototype, which is based on the ITK library [1], and was evaluated on thresholded post-implant cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) volumes with an isotropic in-plane resolution of 0.4 mm and a slice thickness of 0.8 mm. The evaluation comprised two complementary analyses: an accuracy assessment against expert manual segmentation in a 12-subject subset and a robustness assessment in the complete 28-subject cohort. In all cases, the planned target and entry points were used only to initialize the electrode axis; subsequent contact segmentation was driven by image intensity profiles and geometric constraints, thereby minimizing dependence on preoperative planning.

In the manually segmented subset, which included 35 multilead electrodes and 200 contacts, two expert raters independently segmented the SEEG contacts. The inter-rater agreement was high, with a mean inter-expert Euclidean distance of 0.31 mm ± 0.08 mm. Using the consensus of the two raters as ground truth, the automatic algorithm correctly detected all 200 contacts, yielding a sensitivity and positive predictive value of 100% after post-processing. The mean Euclidean localization error was 0.50 mm ± 0.06 mm. The median error was 0.48 mm, and the 95th percentile was 0.61 mm, with a maximum error of 0.72 mm. A Bland–Altman analysis revealed no systematic bias: the mean signed difference was 0.01 mm, with 95% limits of agreement from −0.08 mm to 0.09 mm. At the electrode level, mean localization errors ranged from 0.36 mm to 0.68 mm across the 35 multilead electrodes. These errors are within the spatial resolution of the post-implant CBCT and comparable to the inter-expert variability observed in manual segmentation [2].

Computational performance was assessed on the same 12-subject subset. The complete pipeline, including volume loading, thresholding, axis initialization, contact detection, and output generation, required a mean of 0.78 s per subject (standard deviation, 0.14 s; range, 0.54–0.99 s) on a standard workstation with a 3.0 GHz processor and 16 GB of RAM. In contrast, expert manual segmentation of the same volumes required between 2.9 and 5.2 h per subject, depending on the number of implanted electrodes and the complexity of the trajectory. Thus, the automatic method achieved a speed-up of more than four orders of magnitude while eliminating intra- and inter-rater variability. The algorithm’s memory footprint remained below 500 MB, and no manual parameter tuning was required across subjects.

To assess anatomical interpretability, the segmented contacts were mapped to neuroanatomical regions after affine registration of the post-implant CBCT to the preoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and application of a validated brain atlas [3]. Of the 200 contacts in the manually segmented subset, 193 (96.5%) were assigned to the same anatomical region as the expert consensus. The seven discordant contacts were located near boundaries between adjacent structures, particularly at the gray–white matter interface and at the medial temporal lobe borders. In these cases, the automatic assignment differed by one neighboring atlas label, while the Euclidean contact localization remained within 0.6 mm of the manual reference. These results indicate that the algorithm accurately maps SEEG implants to their anatomical regions and improves the interpretability of electrophysiological traces for both clinical and research applications [4].

Robustness to postoperative electrode displacement was evaluated in the full 28-subject cohort. The implanted electrode shafts deviated from the preoperatively planned trajectories by a mean of 4.7 mm ± 3.1 mm at the contact level, with a maximum displacement of 11.8 mm. Despite these displacements, the algorithm’s segmentation performance remained stable. When the automatic contact positions were compared with those obtained from synthetic undisplaced trajectories, the increase in localization error attributable to displacement was 0.003 mm ± 0.001 mm, with a maximum of less than 0.005 mm. This near-negligible effect confirms that the algorithm does not rely on the planned trajectory as a final constraint but instead uses it only as an initial estimate of the electrode axis. No segmentation failures or gross mislocalizations occurred in any of the 28 subjects, including electrodes implanted in deep-brain structures such as the hippocampus, amygdala, and thalamus.
