Exposure-age constraints on Pliocene interior thickening

Our new cosmogenic nuclide exposure ages, together with previously published datasets [1–3], provide direct geological evidence that sectors of the East Antarctic interior were thicker during the Pliocene than at present. These ages are derived from glacially transported and bedrock surfaces now exposed at high elevations, and they require ice-surface configurations that cannot be explained by present-day ice thickness alone. The spatial distribution of exposure ages indicates that interior thickening was not a localized phenomenon but affected broad sectors of the EAIS. Importantly, the preservation of these surfaces requires that subsequent thinning was sufficient to expose them, yet not so rapid or erosive as to reset the nuclide inventory. This pattern is difficult to reconcile with a simple, uniform retreat of the EAIS during the Pliocene. Instead, it supports a more complex configuration in which interior accumulation increased while marine-based margins retreated.

Model-data synthesis and basin-scale melt

Mid-Pliocene simulations employing boundary conditions consistent with warmer-than-present sea-surface temperatures, reduced sea-ice extent, and elevated atmospheric CO₂ [4,5] reproduce the first-order pattern of interior thickening. Increased atmospheric moisture availability and enhanced poleward transport promote greater snowfall over the continental interior, leading to higher ice-surface elevations. At the same time, the model predicts substantial grounding-line retreat and melt in the Wilkes Subglacial and Aurora Basins. These marine-based basins are highly sensitive to ocean thermal forcing and are underlain by bed topography that permits marine ice-sheet instability [6,7]. Their partial or near-complete loss contributes to sea-level rise and offsets the positive volume anomaly associated with interior thickening. The coexistence of interior growth and marginal basin melt is therefore a key dynamic of the Pliocene EAIS.

This model-data synthesis has important implications for sea-level reconstructions. If only interior thickening is considered, the EAIS would appear to have gained mass during the Pliocene. If only marine-basin retreat is considered, the EAIS would appear to have lost mass. The net contribution depends on the relative magnitudes of these opposing changes. When contributions from West Antarctica and Greenland are included [8,9], our results are consistent with the most recent IPCC AR5 estimate that Pliocene sea level likely did not exceed +20 m on Milankovitch timescales [10]. This consistency does not imply a precise sea-level budget, but it does suggest that interior thickening acted as a partial buffer against marine-margin melt. The buffering is, however, finite and depends on the rate at which interior accumulation can compensate for rapid grounding-line retreat.

Climatic transition after ~3 Ma

The inception of colder climate since ∼3 Myr [11,12] fundamentally altered the moisture regime of the Antarctic ice sheet. Expanded sea-ice cover reduced evaporation from the Southern Ocean and inhibited active moisture transport to the continent. As a result, accumulation over the EAIS declined, particularly in coastal sectors where moisture delivery is most direct. Reduced accumulation, combined with unchanged or increased ablation at marine margins, led to reduced ice-sheet thickness, at least in coastal areas. This mechanism may explain the transition from Pliocene interior thickening to thinner ice surfaces recorded by younger exposure ages. It also implies that the EAIS is not solely temperature-limited; rather, it is strongly moisture-limited in its interior. Colder conditions can therefore lead to a thinner ice sheet if moisture supply is suppressed, even without substantial oceanic melting.

This moisture-limitation framework helps reconcile apparently contradictory proxy signals. Some marine records indicate expanded ice volume after ∼3 Ma, whereas exposure ages from coastal and interior nunataks indicate lower ice surfaces. These observations can be reconciled if ice volume increased in some sectors, such as West Antarctica, while the East Antarctic interior thinned because of reduced snowfall. The spatial heterogeneity of EAIS response is therefore critical. It also highlights the need to distinguish between ice-volume changes and ice-surface elevation changes when interpreting geological archives.

Conclusions

Our integrated exposure-age and ice-sheet modeling study demonstrates that Pliocene EAIS dynamics cannot be captured by a single, continent-wide response. Interior thickening, driven by enhanced moisture transport under warm conditions, occurred alongside substantial melt of the Wilkes Subglacial and Aurora Basins. These opposing changes partly offset one another, yielding a net sea-level contribution consistent with the IPCC AR5 upper estimate of +20 m on Milankovitch timescales. Following the onset of colder climate after ∼3 Ma, increased sea-ice cover and reduced moisture transport led to lower accumulation and thinner ice, especially in coastal areas. The EAIS therefore appears to have been sensitive to both oceanic forcing at its marine margins and atmospheric moisture supply in its interior.

These findings have implications for future warming. Increased moisture transport could again promote interior thickening, while ocean warming and sea-ice retreat destabilize marine-based basins. The net sea-level response will depend on the balance between these processes, as well as on subglacial topography, ocean heat uptake, and the rate of grounding-line retreat. Reducing uncertainties requires improved constraints on Pliocene boundary conditions, better exposure-age chronologies that account for inheritance and erosion, and coupled ice-sheet–ocean–atmosphere models capable of resolving basin-scale dynamics. Nevertheless, the Pliocene remains a powerful analogue for understanding how the EAIS may respond to a warmer world, and our results argue for a spatially complex, moisture-sensitive ice sheet rather than a simple, uniform retreat.

Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains one of the most common malignancies and a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide [1,2]. Despite improvements in surveillance and curative treatment modalities such as surgical resection, liver transplantation, and local ablation, a large proportion of patients are diagnosed at intermediate or advanced stages, when curative options are limited and prognosis remains poor [3,4]. The Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) staging system recommends transcatheter hepatic arterial chemoembolization (TACE) for selected patients with intermediate-stage HCC and preserved liver function [5,6]. TACE combines intra-arterial delivery of cytotoxic chemotherapy with selective embolization of tumor-feeding vessels, thereby producing ischemic and chemotherapeutic injury within the hypervascular tumor while limiting systemic drug exposure [7]. Randomized trials and meta-analyses have demonstrated survival advantages for TACE compared with best supportive care, and TACE is now widely accepted as a standard locoregional therapy for unresectable HCC [8,9]. Nevertheless, TACE rarely achieves complete pathological necrosis, and many patients subsequently develop residual viable tumor, local recurrence, or distant progression [10,11].

The biological effects of TACE may paradoxically promote tumor progression. Embolization induces hypoxia within the tumor microenvironment, leading to upregulation of hypoxia-inducible factor 1α and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), which stimulate angiogenesis and may accelerate the growth of residual disease [12,13]. Elevated circulating VEGF and platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) levels after TACE have been associated with poorer clinical outcomes [14]. These observations provided a strong rationale for combining TACE with antiangiogenic systemic therapy to suppress the postembolization angiogenic surge and to control occult micrometastatic disease [15].

Sorafenib is an oral multikinase inhibitor that targets Raf-1, B-Raf, VEGF receptor 1/2/3, PDGF receptor-β, and several other kinases involved in tumor proliferation and angiogenesis [16]. In the pivotal SHARP and Asia-Pacific randomized trials, sorafenib improved overall survival (OS) compared with placebo in patients with advanced HCC, establishing it as the first systemic agent for this disease [17,18]. However, the survival benefit was modest, and sorafenib is associated with adverse events such as hand-foot skin reaction (HFSR), rash, fatigue, diarrhea, hypertension, and nausea [19]. Because TACE and sorafenib have potentially complementary mechanisms—locoregional cytoreduction and systemic angiogenesis inhibition—their combination has been extensively investigated. Early-phase studies suggested that concurrent or sequential TACE plus sorafenib was feasible and might prolong time to disease progression (TTP) [20,21].

Subsequent randomized controlled trials (RCTs), however, have yielded inconsistent results. Some trials reported improved TTP or progression-free survival with TACE plus sorafenib, whereas others failed to demonstrate an OS benefit [22,23]. Differences in trial design, patient selection, TACE technique, sorafenib dose, timing of initiation, and duration of treatment may explain these discrepancies [24]. In addition, safety concerns are prominent, because combining an embolic procedure with a multikinase inhibitor may increase hepatotoxicity, fatigue, skin toxicity, and gastrointestinal symptoms, potentially compromising tolerability and quality of life [25]. Prior meta-analyses have addressed this combination, but many pooled studies with heterogeneous designs, including open-label trials and retrospective series, which may introduce performance and detection bias, particularly for subjective adverse events and progression endpoints [26,27].

Double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials provide the most rigorous evidence for treatment effects and safety. However, to our knowledge, a focused meta-analysis of double-blind RCTs evaluating TACE plus sorafenib specifically for HCC has not been comprehensively synthesized. Such an analysis is clinically relevant because it can clarify whether the addition of sorafenib to TACE provides a reproducible benefit in TTP or OS and can quantify the incremental risk of sorafenib-related adverse events under blinded conditions. Therefore, we performed a meta-analysis of randomized, double-blind controlled trials to compare TACE plus sorafenib with TACE plus placebo in patients with HCC. The primary objectives were to assess TTP and OS; secondary objectives were to evaluate the risks of HFSR, rash, fatigue, diarrhea, and nausea. We hypothesized that TACE plus sorafenib would improve TTP but that its effect on OS would remain uncertain, with a significantly higher burden of adverse events. The findings are intended to inform clinical decision-making and future trial design regarding combination locoregional and systemic therapy for HCC.

A systematic review and meta-analysis was performed in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement [1] and the recommendations of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [2]. A review protocol was developed a priori to define the search strategy, eligibility criteria, primary and secondary outcomes, data extraction process, risk-of-bias assessment, and statistical analysis plan. Because the present study used only published aggregate data and did not involve direct contact with human participants, ethical approval and informed consent were not required.

We systematically searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Web of Science, and ClinicalTrials.gov from database inception to the date of the final search. The search strategy combined Medical Subject Headings and free-text terms, including (“transcatheter hepatic arterial chemoembolization” OR “transarterial chemoembolization” OR TACE) AND (“sorafenib” OR Nexavar) AND (“hepatocellular carcinoma” OR HCC OR “liver cancer” OR “hepatic carcinoma”) AND (“randomized controlled trial” OR RCT OR “double-blind” OR “placebo”). No language restriction was applied. Reference lists of eligible trials, previous systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and relevant conference proceedings were also hand-searched to identify additional potentially eligible studies.

Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts, followed by full-text assessment of potentially relevant articles. Any disagreements were resolved through discussion or adjudication by a third reviewer. Studies were considered eligible if they were randomized, double-blind, controlled trials; enrolled adult patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) diagnosed by histopathology, cytology, or accepted imaging criteria; compared transcatheter hepatic arterial chemoembolization (TACE) combined with sorafenib (experimental group) with TACE combined with placebo (control group); and reported at least one outcome of interest, including time to disease progression (TTP), overall survival (OS), or sorafenib-related adverse events. Four double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials [1–4] met the prespecified eligibility criteria and were included in the final meta-analysis. These trials collectively randomized 877 patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) who were treated with transcatheter hepatic arterial chemoembolization (TACE) combined with sorafenib (experimental groups) or TACE combined with placebo (control groups). The studies were multicenter and multinational, with participating sites across 14 countries, including China and the USA. Baseline characteristics, including age, sex, etiology of liver disease, Child–Pugh status, Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer stage, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status, and prior TACE exposure, were generally balanced between the experimental and control groups within each trial [1–4]. All included trials were judged to have a low risk of bias with respect to random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and personnel, blinding of outcome assessment, incomplete outcome data, and selective reporting. The duration of follow-up and outcome definitions were sufficiently comparable to permit pooled analyses.

Time to disease progression (TTP) was reported in all four trials and was defined as the interval from randomization to first documented radiologic progression or death from any cause. The pooled analysis demonstrated that TTP was significantly longer in the experimental groups than in the control groups (hazard ratio [HR]: 0.82; 95% CI: 0.69–0.97; p = 0.02). This corresponded to an 18% relative reduction in the hazard of disease progression or death among patients receiving TACE plus sorafenib. Statistical heterogeneity for TTP was not significant (I² = 0%, p = 0.58), suggesting consistency of the treatment effect across the included trials [1–4]. Leave-one-out sensitivity analysis did not materially alter the direction or statistical significance of this finding, although the confidence interval widened when any single trial was omitted.

Overall survival (OS), defined as the time from randomization to death from any cause, was also evaluated in all four trials. In contrast to the TTP result, the pooled analysis showed no statistically significant improvement in OS for the experimental groups compared with the control groups (HR: 0.97; 95% CI: 0.72–1.29; p = 0.82). There was no evidence of significant between-study heterogeneity for OS (I² = 0%, p = 0.91). Sensitivity analyses excluding one trial at a time consistently yielded nonsignificant pooled estimates, and no individual trial demonstrated a statistically significant OS benefit that was masked in the overall analysis [1–4]. Subgroup analyses based on available trial-level characteristics, including geographic region and baseline liver function, did not identify a consistent subgroup with a clear OS advantage, although these analyses were limited by the small number of included studies.

Safety analyses included all 877 randomized patients and assessed sorafenib-related adverse events. The risks of hand and foot skin reaction (HFSR), rash, fatigue, and diarrhea were significantly greater in the experimental groups than in the control groups

The present meta-analysis of four double-blind, randomized controlled trials demonstrates that the combination of transcatheter hepatic arterial chemoembolization (TACE) and sorafenib significantly prolongs time to disease progression (TTP) in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) compared to TACE plus placebo. However, this improvement in a surrogate endpoint did not translate into a statistically significant overall survival (OS) benefit. Furthermore, the combination therapy was associated with a markedly increased risk of several adverse events, most notably hand and foot skin reactions (HFSR). These findings underscore the complex risk-benefit profile of combining anti-angiogenic therapy with locoregional treatment in HCC and highlight the critical need to interpret progression-free survival (PFS) or TTP data with caution when OS is the ultimate goal.

The discordance between TTP and OS observed in our analysis is a central and clinically significant finding. While the TTP benefit suggests that the addition of sorafenib does indeed delay tumor progression, the lack of OS improvement may be attributable to several factors. First, the advanced stage of disease in the enrolled patient populations is a likely contributor. In patients with more advanced HCC, the aggressive nature of the disease and underlying liver dysfunction may lead to mortality from causes other than direct tumor progression, thereby diluting any potential OS benefit from improved tumor control [1]. Second, the phenomenon of post-progression survival can confound the relationship between TTP and OS. Patients in the control group who experienced progression may have received subsequent lines of effective therapy, including sorafenib itself, which could have equalized the long-term survival outcomes between the two groups [2]. This is a common challenge in oncology trials where effective salvage therapies exist.

Our safety analysis revealed a substantial increase in toxicity for patients receiving the combination therapy. The risk of HFSR was particularly pronounced, with a risk ratio exceeding five. This finding is consistent with the established safety profile of sorafenib, a multi-kinase inhibitor known to cause dermatologic toxicities [3]. The high rates of rash, fatigue, and diarrhea further contribute to the treatment burden. These adverse events are not merely quality-of-life issues; they can lead to dose reductions, treatment interruptions, and premature discontinuation, which may ultimately compromise the efficacy of the entire treatment regimen [4]. The management of these toxicities is paramount in clinical practice and must be carefully weighed against the modest TTP benefit observed. The statistically similar risk of nausea between the groups is a minor point, but the overall toxicity profile necessitates a thorough discussion between clinicians and patients regarding the goals of therapy.

The strengths of this meta-analysis lie in its inclusion of only double-blind, randomized controlled trials, which minimizes selection and performance bias. The multi-national patient cohort also enhances the generalizability of the findings. However, several limitations must be acknowledged. The analysis included only four trials, and the potential for publication bias cannot be excluded. Furthermore, the patient populations across the trials may have had differences in baseline characteristics, such as etiology of liver disease, tumor burden, and prior treatments, which could contribute to heterogeneity. While our subgroup analysis for HFSR addressed heterogeneity, a similar exploration for survival outcomes was not feasible with the available data. The specific TACE protocols and sorafenib dosing schedules may also have varied across studies, introducing another potential source of variability.

The clinical implications of these findings are twofold. On one hand, the significant TTP benefit provides a rationale for considering this combination in patients where delaying progression is a primary objective, such as those awaiting liver transplantation or those with a limited expected survival due to comorbidities. On the other hand, the lack of an OS benefit and the considerable toxicity demand a highly selective approach. Identifying biomarkers that can predict which patients are most likely to derive a survival benefit without experiencing prohibitive toxicity is a critical unmet need. Future research should focus on refining patient selection criteria and exploring optimal sequencing and combination strategies with newer systemic agents, such as immune checkpoint inhibitors, which may offer a better efficacy and safety profile [5].

In conclusion, the combination of TACE and sorafenib for intermediate-to-advanced HCC significantly improves TTP but fails to provide a clear OS advantage over TACE alone. This benefit is counterbalanced by a substantial increase in clinically significant adverse events, particularly HFSR. Therefore, the routine use of this combination is not supported by the current evidence. The decision to use TACE plus sorafenib should be individualized, carefully considering the patient's performance status, liver function, tumor characteristics, and, most importantly, their ability to tolerate the associated toxicity. The therapeutic landscape for HCC is rapidly evolving, and future efforts should be directed toward developing more effective and better-tolerated combination regimens and identifying predictive biomarkers to guide personalized treatment.

Human action recognition has become a central problem in computer vision, with applications ranging from video surveillance and human–computer interaction to sports analytics and assistive living [1], [2]. Among the available modalities, skeleton sequences are particularly attractive because they encode motion as a compact set of joint trajectories, thereby reducing sensitivity to background clutter, illumination changes, and viewpoint variation [3]. Early skeleton-based methods commonly relied on hand-crafted descriptors or recurrent neural networks to model temporal dynamics. More recently, graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have emerged as the dominant paradigm, since the human skeleton can be naturally represented as a graph whose nodes correspond to joints and whose edges describe anatomical or learned connections [4]. Architectures such as spatial–temporal graph convolutional networks, attention-enhanced GCNs, and multi-stream GCNs have produced substantial gains on large-scale benchmarks, including NTU RGB+D [5]–[7].

Despite this progress, most existing GCN-based approaches are developed under an implicit assumption that every joint is reliably observed throughout the sequence. This assumption rarely holds in unconstrained real-world deployments. Depth sensors, markerless pose estimators, and wearable motion capture systems frequently produce incomplete skeletons due to self-occlusion, object occlusion, truncation at image boundaries, motion blur, and sensor noise [8]. Missing joints are not merely absent values; they alter the graph topology and disrupt the message-passing mechanism of GCNs. When a joint is missing, its incident edges no longer transmit reliable information, and the convolutional aggregation at neighboring nodes becomes biased or incomplete. Consequently, even high-capacity models trained on complete skeletons can experience sharp accuracy degradation when tested on incomplete data [9].

A common remedy is to reconstruct or impute missing joints before recognition. While such preprocessing can be effective for small gaps or predictable motion patterns, it often introduces artifacts, requires additional assumptions, and may discard discriminative cues that remain in the observed joints [10]. Alternative strategies use attention mechanisms, masking, or graph rewiring to reduce the influence of unreliable joints [11], [12]. These methods improve robustness to a degree, but they typically operate within a single-stream architecture and still concentrate on a limited subset of joints. In skeleton-based action recognition, class activation maps (CAMs) reveal that only a small number of joints are highly activated for a given action class. If those salient joints are occluded or missing, the model lacks complementary evidence from other body parts. Simply increasing network depth or adding parallel streams does not necessarily solve this problem, because multiple streams may converge to similar activated joints and thus provide redundant rather than complementary information.

This paper addresses the above limitation by introducing a richly activated graph convolutional network (RA-GCN) for action recognition with incomplete skeletons. The central idea is to explicitly diversify the joints from which discriminative features are learned across multiple network streams. The first stream is trained conventionally and yields a CAM that identifies the joints most responsible for its prediction. These activated joints are then treated as unavailable for the next stream, forcing it to learn from the currently unactivated joints. By repeating this procedure, each stream specializes in a different subset of the skeleton, and the union of activated joints expands substantially compared with traditional single-stream models. This CAM-guided activation scheduling encourages the network to discover complementary motion cues distributed over the entire skeleton, rather than relying on a few vulnerable joints.

The proposed RA-GCN offers several advantages. First, it does not require explicit imputation of missing joints; instead, it learns robust representations from whatever joints remain observable. Second, the multi-stream design is modular and can be integrated with various graph convolutional backbones. Third, the CAM-based masking mechanism provides an interpretable way to analyze which body parts contribute to recognition under different occlusion patterns. Extensive experiments on the NTU RGB+D dataset show that RA-GCN achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods when skeletons are complete. More importantly, on a synthetic occlusion benchmark, the proposed method significantly alleviates the performance deterioration caused by missing joints, demonstrating improved robustness in realistic incomplete-skeleton scenarios.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work on skeleton-based action recognition and robust learning with incomplete data. Section III presents the proposed RA-GCN, including the CAM-guided multi-stream architecture and training procedure. Section IV reports experimental results and ablation studies. Section V concludes the paper and discusses future directions.

3.1 Problem formulation and graph representation
Let a skeleton sequence be represented as \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times N \times C}\), where \(T\) denotes the number of frames, \(N\) is the number of body joints, and \(C\) is the feature dimension, typically comprising 3D coordinates and confidence scores. Each skeleton is modeled as a spatio-temporal graph \(\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E})\), where \(\mathcal{V}\) contains all joint nodes across frames and \(\mathcal{E}\) contains intra-body physical connections and inter-frame temporal connections. Following graph convolutional action recognition frameworks [1], [2], the spatial graph is normalized as \(\hat{A}=D^{-1/2}(A+I)D^{-1/2}\), where \(A\) is the adjacency matrix, \(I\) is the identity matrix, and \(D\) is the degree matrix. A graph convolution layer is formulated as
\[
H^{(l+1)}=\sigma\left(\hat{A}H^{(l)}W^{(l)}\right),
\]
where \(H^{(l)}\) denotes node features at layer \(l\), \(W^{(l)}\) is a learnable transformation, and \(\sigma(\cdot)\) is a nonlinear activation. Temporal dependencies are captured by temporal convolutions, yielding a backbone similar to spatio-temporal GCNs [1], [3].

3.2 Baseline stream and class activation maps
The first stream of RA-GCN is trained on the complete skeleton and serves as a baseline classifier. Given its final spatio-temporal feature maps \(F \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times N \times K}\) and the classification weights \(w_c \in \mathbb{R}^{K}\) for action class \(c\), the class activation map (CAM) over joints is computed as
\[
M_c(n)=\mathrm{ReLU}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{K} w_{c,k}\, \bar{F}_k(n)\right),
\]
where \(\bar{F}_k(n)\) denotes the temporally pooled response of channel \(k\) at joint \(n\). In contrast to conventional CAM usage for visual localization [4], we employ CAMs as a joint-routing mechanism. For a threshold \(\tau\), the activated joint set of stream \(s\) is defined as
\[
\mathcal{A}_s=\{n \mid M_c(n)>\tau\}.
\]
These joints are regarded as sufficiently informative for the current stream’s decision. The remaining joints, \(\mathcal{U}_s=\mathcal{V}\setminus \bigcup_{r<s}\mathcal{A}_r\), are considered unactivated and are passed to subsequent streams.

These results are comparable to the strongest published methods, including 2s-AGCN [3] and SGN [4], while exceeding AS-GCN [2] by a clear margin. The experimental evidence indicates that the proposed richly activated graph convolutional network (RA-GCN) addresses a central weakness of conventional skeleton-based action recognition pipelines: their implicit dependence on a relatively small set of highly discriminative joints. Standard graph convolutional networks, such as ST-GCN [1], AS-GCN [2], and MS-G3D [3], learn joint importance jointly with action classification and often concentrate activation on anatomically salient regions. When skeletons are complete, this concentration is beneficial. Under incomplete observations, however, it becomes a liability because missing or corrupted joints may coincide with the most activated regions. The RA-GCN mitigates this issue by explicitly redistributing learning across joint subsets through class activation map (CAM) [9] guidance. Instead of allowing all streams to compete for the same dominant joints, each stream is assigned to currently unactivated joints identified by preceding streams. This sequential activation mechanism encourages broader joint coverage and yields representations that are less dependent on any single anatomical cue.

A key observation is that the proposed method attains accuracy on the NTU RGB+D dataset [4] that is comparable to state-of-the-art GCNs while providing substantially improved robustness on synthetically occluded skeletons. This pattern is informative. On fully observed data, the additional streams do not introduce a decisive accuracy advantage, which suggests that complete skeletons already expose sufficient discriminative information for strong models. The value of RA-GCN therefore lies primarily in its generalization behavior rather than in absolute performance on clean benchmarks. The occlusion experiments demonstrate that when joints are removed or degraded, the performance deterioration is alleviated significantly relative to traditional models. This improvement can be attributed to the richer activation patterns discovered across streams: if a highly informative joint is unavailable, other streams retain the capacity to extract discriminative features from joints that would otherwise remain underexplored. In this sense, RA-GCN functions as a structured feature diversification mechanism rather than a simple ensemble of independent classifiers.

The CAM-based stream assignment also provides a useful conceptual bridge between attention-based skeleton models and missing-data robustness. Prior work has explored spatial attention, temporal attention, and adaptive graph topologies to improve recognition [2], [3], but these mechanisms are usually optimized for complete inputs. By contrast, RA-GCN treats activation itself as a resource to be distributed across joints. This is related to broader observations in deep representation learning that redundancy and distributed coding can improve tolerance to input corruption [5]. The method does not attempt to reconstruct missing joints or impute their coordinates, which avoids the risk of hallucinating physically implausible motion. Instead, it learns to exploit the joints that remain observable. This design choice is particularly relevant for real-world systems using depth sensors or pose estimators, where missing joints often arise from self-occlusion, truncation, low resolution, or tracking failure [6].

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the occlusion experiments are synthetic and may not fully reflect the temporal and spatial statistics of real incomplete skeletons. Real-world missingness can affect entire limbs, consecutive frames, or multiple interacting subjects, and it may be coupled with coordinate noise rather than clean joint removal. We formulate document modelling as a Bayesian latent-variable problem. Let a document be represented by a bag-of-words count vector \(\mathbf{x}_d = (x_{d1},\ldots,x_{dV})\), where \(V\) is the vocabulary size and \(x_{dv}\) denotes the count of word \(v\) in document \(d\). We introduce a continuous latent document embedding \(\mathbf{z}_d \in \mathbb{R}^K\), with \(K \ll V\). In the proposed Bayesian subspace multinomial model (Bayesian SMM), each document is generated from a log-linear multinomial distribution whose natural parameters are obtained by projecting the latent embedding through a global word-embedding matrix \(\mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times K}\) and a bias vector \(\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^{V}\). Formally, the generative process for document \(d\) is
\[
\mathbf{z}_d \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}), \qquad
p(\mathbf{x}_d \mid \mathbf{z}_d) = \mathrm{Multinomial}\!\left(\mathbf{x}_d \,\middle|\, \mathrm{softmax}(\mathbf{W}\mathbf{z}_d + \mathbf{b})\right).

We evaluated the proposed Bayesian subspace multinomial model (Bayesian SMM) on two corpora: the Fisher speech corpus and the 20Newsgroups text collection. For Fisher, we used the provided transcripts, removed stopwords, applied lowercasing and tokenization, and retained a vocabulary of the 10,000 most frequent terms. For 20Newsgroups, we followed the standard train–test split, removed headers and footers, and used the same preprocessing pipeline. Unless otherwise stated, all models were trained with 50 topics or latent dimensions, and perplexity was computed on held-out documents. Lower perplexity indicates better model fit. We compared Bayesian SMM against latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) [2], the subspace multinomial model (SMM) [3], the neural variational document model (NVDM) [1], and ProdLDA [4]. The proposed model achieved the best intrinsic performance on both corpora. On Fisher, Bayesian SMM obtained a held-out perplexity of 318.4, compared with 356.7 for NVDM, 389.2 for SMM, 402.1 for ProdLDA, and 421.5 for LDA. On 20Newsgroups, Bayesian SMM reached 1042.3, whereas NVDM, SMM, ProdLDA, and LDA yielded 1128.9, 1196.4, 1213.5, and 1247.8, respectively. These correspond to relative perplexity reductions of 10.7% on Fisher and 7.7% on 20Newsgroups over the strongest neural variational baseline [1]. Paired t-tests over ten random restarts indicated that the improvements were statistically significant at p < 0.01.

Beyond aggregate perplexity, we examined whether the learned Gaussian embeddings encoded meaningful uncertainty. For each held-out document, we computed the trace of the posterior covariance and compared it with per-document reconstruction error and topic-classification confidence. Across both corpora, higher covariance traces were associated with higher reconstruction error and lower classification confidence. On 20Newsgroups, the Pearson correlation between covariance trace and per-document perplexity was r = 0.68; on Fisher, it was r = 0.61. This supports the interpretation that the covariance captures ambiguity in document representation rather than acting as a nuisance parameter. We also assessed calibration by binning documents according to predicted variance and comparing average predicted variance with observed squared error. Bayesian SMM showed lower expected calibration error than an ensemble of point-estimate models constructed from NVDM [1], suggesting that the variational posterior provides useful uncertainty estimates.

For topic identification, we used the proposed generative Gaussian linear classifier, which consumes both the mean and covariance of each document embedding. On the 20Newsgroups 20-class task, Bayesian SMM with the uncertainty-aware classifier achieved 78.4% accuracy and 76.9% macro-F1. Unsupervised topic-model baselines were substantially lower: LDA [2] obtained 64.7% accuracy, ProdLDA [4] 67.9%, NVDM [1] 69.8%, and SMM [3] 71.5%. The proposed model therefore outperformed state-of-the-art unsupervised topic models by a clear margin. Fully supervised discriminative models trained directly on bag-of-words features performed slightly better, with an SVM [5] reaching 79.2% and a convolutional neural network [6] reaching 80.1%. The Bayesian SMM results were thus comparable to these supervised baselines, despite using a generative topic representation rather than end-to-end discriminative training. On Fisher, using ten topic labels, Bayesian SMM achieved 84.6% accuracy and 83.2% macro-F1, compared with 72.3% for LDA, 74.5% for ProdLDA, 76.8% for NVDM, and 79.1% for SMM. The SVM and CNN baselines reached 85.9% and 86.7%, respectively, again placing Bayesian SMM in the same performance band as fully supervised methods.

The results reported in this study support the central premise that document embeddings should be represented as probability distributions rather than as deterministic point estimates. By learning Gaussian document representations, the proposed Bayesian subspace multinomial model (Bayesian SMM) encodes not only the semantic content of a document but also the uncertainty associated with that representation. This distinction is important because documents are often short, noisy, ambiguous, or topically mixed, and a single vector cannot adequately express such variability [1], [2]. The covariance structure learned by Bayesian SMM provides a principled way to quantify this ambiguity, while the Bayesian treatment regularizes the model and reduces the risk of overfitting, particularly in sparse or heterogeneous corpora [3], [4].

The intrinsic evaluation using perplexity demonstrates that Bayesian SMM fits the data better than the state-of-the-art neural variational document model on both the Fisher speech and 20Newsgroups text corpora [5]. This improvement is notable because perplexity measures how well a model predicts held-out documents, and lower perplexity indicates a better-calibrated generative process. The advantage of Bayesian SMM may arise from two complementary factors. First, the generative log-linear formulation provides a flexible mapping from latent Gaussian variables to categorical word distributions, allowing the model to capture complex lexical dependencies. Second, the Bayesian framework imposes priors that shrink unreliable estimates and encourage smoother posterior distributions [6], [7]. Together, these properties enable Bayesian SMM to represent documents in a way that is both expressive and robust.

A key methodological contribution of this work is the treatment of intractability in variational inference for mixed-logit models. Such models are widely used in discrete choice and text modelling, but their posterior expectations often lack closed forms, making standard variational updates difficult to apply [8], [9]. The proposed inference procedure addresses this issue while preserving the uncertainty encoded in the document embeddings. This is significant because approximate inference methods that ignore or oversimplify the logit-normal structure can underestimate posterior variance and produce overconfident embeddings [10]. By contrast, Bayesian SMM retains a distributional representation that reflects the inherent uncertainty of the inference process.

The topic identification experiments further illustrate the practical value of uncertainty-aware document embeddings. The proposed generative Gaussian linear classifier exploits the covariance of each document embedding, allowing predictions to be adjusted according to how confident the model is about the representation. This classifier outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised topic models and achieves results comparable to fully supervised discriminative models [11], [12]. More importantly, the proposed systems are robust to overfitting on unseen test data. This robustness is particularly desirable in real-world topic identification, where documents may be ambiguous, domain-shifted, or only weakly associated with a single topic. By leveraging uncertainty, the classifier can down-weight unreliable embeddings and avoid making overly confident predictions based on noisy evidence.

Despite these promising results, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the Gaussian assumption, while convenient and computationally attractive, may not capture multimodal, skewed, or heavy-tailed posterior distributions that can arise in complex document collections [13]. Second, variational inference provides a lower bound on the marginal likelihood, and the quality of the approximation depends on the flexibility of the variational family. More expressive posterior approximations, such as normalizing flows or hierarchical variational models, could yield better uncertainty estimates [14]. Third, the computational cost of Bayesian inference may be higher than that of point-estimate neural models, especially for very large corpora. Fourth, the empirical evaluation is limited to two datasets, and further validation is needed across languages, domains, document lengths, and genre-specific corpora. Finally, perplexity and topic identification accuracy do not fully characterize the usefulness of uncertainty; calibration, coverage, and decision-theoretic utility should also be examined in future work.

Several directions for future research emerge from this study. One promising avenue is to relax the Gaussian assumption and explore richer posterior families, including mixtures, elliptical distributions, or normalizing flows, while maintaining tractable inference. Another is to develop scalable stochastic variational inference and amortized inference networks that can handle massive text collections without sacrificing uncertainty calibration [15]. It would also be valuable to incorporate hierarchical priors over topics and documents, enabling information sharing across related domains. Beyond topic identification, uncertainty-aware document embeddings could be applied to information retrieval, active learning, clustering, sentiment analysis, and domain adaptation, where knowing when a representation is unreliable can guide downstream decisions. Finally, interpretability methods for distributional embeddings could help practitioners understand which aspects of a document contribute most to its uncertainty.

In conclusion, this paper introduced Bayesian SMM, a generative log-linear model that learns Gaussian document embeddings and their uncertainties, and a Gaussian linear classifier that exploits these uncertainties for topic identification. The proposed approach addresses a key inference challenge in mixed-logit models and demonstrates improved data fit over a strong neural variational baseline on Fisher speech and 20Newsgroups. The topic identification results show that uncertainty-aware representations are robust to overfitting and competitive with both unsupervised and supervised alternatives. These findings suggest that distributional document embeddings provide a principled and practical foundation for probabilistic text modelling, and they open several avenues for future work on richer posterior approximations, scalable inference, and uncertainty-aware downstream applications.

Cryptococcosis is an invasive fungal infection caused by encapsulated basidiomycetous yeasts of the Cryptococcus neoformans and Cryptococcus gattii species complexes [Kwon-Chung et al., 2014]. Although C. neoformans remains the predominant cause of cryptococcal meningitis in immunocompromised populations, C. gattii is increasingly recognized as a primary pathogen capable of causing severe pulmonary and central nervous system disease in apparently immunocompetent hosts [Perfect, 2012]. The C. gattii species complex is genetically and antigenically heterogeneous, comprising four major molecular types, VGI, VGII, VGIII, and VGIV, which correlate imperfectly with serotype B and serotype C antigenic profiles and exhibit distinct geographic distributions [Hagen et al., 2015]. The emergence of highly virulent VGII strains on Vancouver Island and in the Pacific Northwest of North America demonstrated that C. gattii can cause large outbreaks in temperate climates and has stimulated substantial interest in the virulence attributes of this species complex [Fraser et al., 2005; Byrnes et al., 2010]. However, most molecular, immunological, and pathogenicity studies have focused on serotype B isolates, particularly VGII outbreak strains, whereas serotype C isolates belonging to molecular types VGIII and VGIV remain comparatively neglected.

The epidemiological and clinical significance of VGIII and VGIV C. gattii is increasingly apparent. VGIII isolates have been recovered from patients in Mexico, Colombia, the southwestern United States, and California, where they may cause disease in both HIV-infected and non-HIV-infected individuals [Litvintseva et al., 2006; Escandón et al., 2006]. VGIV isolates, although less frequently reported, have been described in sub-Saharan Africa, India, and other regions, and may exhibit substantial phenotypic and genotypic diversity [Meyer et al., 2009; Hagen et al., 2015]. These observations suggest that the pathogenic potential of serotype C C. gattii is not uniform and that molecular type alone may not fully predict clinical behavior. Nevertheless, comparative data on virulence determinants among VGIII and VGIV isolates are scarce, and the extent to which strain-specific phenotypic differences translate into differential host outcomes remains poorly defined.

### Phenotypic and molecular confirmation of isolate identity

The three serotype C *Cryptococcus gattii* isolates used in this study were confirmed by URA5-RFLP and multilocus sequence typing to belong to molecular types VGIII (ATCC 24066) and VGIV (WM 779 and 106.97), consistent with previous molecular surveys of serotype C populations [1,2]. All isolates grew at 30°C and 37°C, although ATCC 24066 exhibited a modestly longer lag phase at 37°C than WM 779 and 106.97 (data not shown). Because growth temperature is a recognized virulence determinant in *C. gattii* [3], subsequent phenotypic assays were performed under standardized conditions at 30°C for capsule and cell wall analyses and at 37°C for host interaction experiments.

### Capsule architecture and CAP gene expression

Capsule dimensions differed markedly among the isolates. India ink staining followed by ImageJ quantification revealed that ATCC 24066 produced significantly larger capsules than WM 779 and 106.97 under capsule-inducing conditions (low iron, 5% CO₂). Mean capsule diameters were 5.2 ± 0.7 µm for ATCC 24066, compared with 2.9 ± 0.4 µm for WM 779 and 3.1 ± 0.5 µm for 106.97 (P < 0.01 for both comparisons). This difference was maintained after 24 h and 48 h of induction. Consistent with these morphological data, quantitative RT-PCR showed that ATCC 24066 expressed higher transcript levels of CAP10 and CAP64 than the two VGIV isolates, with 3.5-fold and 4.1-fold increases, respectively, relative to WM 779. CAP59 and CAP60 expression was less variable, although ATCC 24066 still showed a 1.8-fold increase in CAP60 compared with 106.97. Capsular heterogeneity and antigenic variation were prominent among the serotype C isolates examined here. Although capsule size and CAP gene expression are well-established correlates of cryptococcal virulence, our data indicate that VGIII and VGIV isolates can diverge substantially in these traits. The capsule remains a central virulence determinant because it interferes with phagocytosis, complement deposition, and cytokine polarization, and because capsular glucuronoxylomannan (GXM) modulates interactions with host cells [1,2]. The distinct antibody reactivity patterns against GXM observed among ATCC 24066, WM 779, and 106.97 suggest that serotype C isolates may express structurally or conformationally different GXM epitopes. Such antigenic diversity could influence immune recognition, antibody-mediated clearance, and the performance of GXM-based diagnostic assays [3,4]. It also implies that capsule-mediated virulence is not a fixed property of molecular type VGIII or VGIV but is strain-specific and possibly shaped by post-transcriptional regulation of CAP genes, capsule shedding, and extracellular matrix remodeling [5,6].

Cell wall composition and host chitinase induction further distinguished ATCC 24066 from the VGIV isolates. Chitin and chitosan are essential for cell wall integrity and are recognized by pattern recognition receptors, while chitooligomers can modulate inflammatory and type 2 immune responses [7,8]. The differential distribution of chitooligomers and the corresponding differences in host chitinase activity may reflect distinct strategies for evading or exploiting host chitinolytic pathways. Because chitinases can degrade fungal cell wall components and influence tissue inflammation, isolate-specific chitin profiles could affect pulmonary persistence, immune pathology, and dissemination [9]. In this context, the reduced ability of ATCC 24066 to reach the brain may not result solely from capsule differences but may also involve altered cell wall–host interactions that restrict extrapulmonary spread.

Sickle cell disease (SCD) is an inherited hemoglobinopathy characterized by the production of abnormal hemoglobin S (HbS), leading to chronic hemolytic anemia, vaso-occlusion, and a wide spectrum of clinical complications. It is among the most common severe monogenic disorders worldwide, with a particularly high prevalence among individuals of African descent. In the United States alone, more than 100,000 people are affected, and despite advances in newborn screening, prophylactic antibiotics, and disease-modifying therapies, SCD remains a life-limiting condition associated with substantial morbidity and early mortality. While the hallmark acute manifestations—vaso-occlusive pain episodes and acute chest syndrome (ACS)—have historically dominated clinical and research attention, there is growing recognition that chronic respiratory complications contribute significantly to the disease burden and may serve as important markers of disease severity and prognosis.

Respiratory involvement in SCD is protean, encompassing abnormalities in pulmonary function, sleep-disordered breathing, pulmonary hypertension, and airway hyperreactivity. Among these, the relationship between SCD and asthma has generated considerable interest and controversy. Epidemiological studies have consistently demonstrated a higher prevalence of asthma among individuals with SCD compared to the general population, and asthma has been associated with an increased risk of vaso-occlusive crises, ACS, and even premature death. However, the clinical overlap between asthma and SCD-related pulmonary manifestations is substantial, and distinguishing between the two poses a significant diagnostic challenge. Wheezing, a cardinal symptom of asthma, is frequently reported by patients with SCD, yet it may occur in the absence of an asthma diagnosis. Similarly, objective measures such as airway obstruction on spirometry and airway hyperresponsiveness (AHR) on bronchoprovocation testing are common in SCD, even among individuals without typical asthma symptoms. These features often present in isolation, failing to fulfill the conventional diagnostic criteria for asthma, which typically require a combination of symptoms, variable airflow limitation, and evidence of reversibility or hyperresponsiveness.

This diagnostic ambiguity has important clinical implications. If asthma is under-recognized in SCD, patients may be denied effective anti-inflammatory therapy, leading to preventable morbidity. Conversely, if wheezing and airway obstruction are indiscriminately attributed to asthma, patients may be exposed to unnecessary medications and their associated risks, while other contributing mechanisms—such as SCD-related pulmonary vascular disease or recurrent infection—are overlooked. The distinction is further complicated by the fact that asthma itself is a heterogeneous condition, and the phenotypes observed in SCD may differ from those in the general population. For example, airway inflammation in SCD may be driven by unique mechanisms related to hemolysis, oxidative stress, and endothelial dysfunction, rather than the classic type 2 inflammatory pathways that predominate in many asthmatics. Understanding these distinctions is essential for developing targeted therapies and improving outcomes.

The pathophysiological links between SCD and airway disease are multifaceted. Chronic hemolysis releases free hemoglobin and arginase, which deplete nitric oxide (NO) and contribute to endothelial dysfunction and airway smooth muscle dysregulation. Additionally, recurrent episodes of ACS and pulmonary infection may lead to airway remodeling and persistent obstruction. Platelet activation, leukocyte adhesion, and cytokine release—all features of SCD—may further promote airway inflammation and hyperresponsiveness. These mechanisms suggest that wheezing and airway obstruction in SCD may not simply represent comorbid asthma, but rather a distinct pulmonary phenotype driven by the underlying hematological disorder. This has led to the hypothesis that wheezing, even in the absence of an asthma diagnosis, may serve as a clinical marker of SCD severity and a predictor of adverse outcomes.

Despite the growing body of literature, several critical gaps remain. The epidemiology of asthma, wheezing, airway obstruction, and AHR in SCD has not been uniformly characterized, with studies varying in their definitions, populations, and methodologies. The extent to which these respiratory features are associated with specific SCD complications, such as pain crises, ACS, and mortality, requires further clarification. Moreover, the optimal approach to diagnosing and managing asthma in patients with SCD is uncertain, as standard diagnostic algorithms may not perform well in this population, and treatment strategies have not been rigorously evaluated in large, prospective trials. Finally, the underlying mechanisms linking SCD to airway inflammation and hyperreactivity are incompletely understood, hindering the development of targeted interventions.

In this review, we aim to synthesize the current evidence on the intersection of SCD and airway disease. We will first summarize the epidemiology of asthma, wheezing, airway obstruction, and airway responsiveness among patients with SCD, highlighting the variability in prevalence estimates and the challenges in case definition. We will then examine the evidence supporting associations between these respiratory features and SCD morbidity, including pain, ACS, and mortality. Next, we will explore our current understanding of the pathophysiology of airway inflammation in SCD, focusing on the roles of hemolysis, NO depletion, and inflammatory mediators. We will subsequently discuss current approaches to diagnosis and management of asthma in SCD, including the limitations of standard diagnostic tests and the evidence for various therapeutic options. Finally, we will outline future directions for research, emphasizing the need for prospective studies, standardized definitions, and mechanistic investigations. By clarifying the relationship between SCD and airway disease, we hope to inform clinical practice and stimulate further research aimed at reducing the respiratory burden of this devastating condition.

This review was designed to synthesize the available evidence on the epidemiology, clinical associations, pathophysiology, diagnosis, and management of asthma and wheezing among patients with sickle cell disease (SCD). Because the literature spans pediatric and adult hematology, pulmonology, allergy, and primary care, we used a broad search strategy and a narrative synthesis approach. The review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines where applicable, although it was not registered as a systematic review because the primary aim was to provide an integrated overview rather than a quantitative pooled estimate. No ethical approval was required because only published, de-identified data were used.

We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, the Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Scopus, and CINAHL from database inception through March 1, 2024. The search combined terms for SCD and terms for asthma, wheeze, airway obstruction, airway hyperresponsiveness, and lung function. The SCD search string included “sickle cell disease,” “sickle cell anemia,” “sickle cell disorders,” “hemoglobin SS,” “HbSS,” “hemoglobin SC,” “HbSC,” “sickle beta thalassemia,” and “SCD.” The respiratory search string included “asthma,” “wheeze,” “wheezing,” “reactive airway disease,” “airway obstruction,” “airflow obstruction,” “airway hyperresponsiveness,” “bronchial hyperreactivity,” “bronchial hyperresponsiveness,” “pulmonary function,” “lung function,” “spirometry,” “FEV1,” “methacholine challenge,” and “exercise challenge.” To capture SCD-related morbidity, we added “acute chest syndrome,” “vaso-occlusive crisis,” “pain crisis,” “hospitalization,” “mortality,” and

The prevalence of respiratory symptoms and asthma in patients with sickle cell disease (SCD) is substantially higher than in the general population, with studies reporting asthma prevalence rates ranging from 20% to over 50%, depending on the diagnostic criteria used. A landmark cooperative study found that asthma was diagnosed in 28% of children with SCD compared to 12% of controls, and more recent analyses have confirmed this elevated risk. However, the true prevalence of asthma in SCD remains difficult to ascertain due to overlapping clinical features. Wheezing, a hallmark symptom of asthma, is reported in 20-40% of patients with SCD, even in the absence of a formal asthma diagnosis. This high prevalence of wheezing is a critical finding, as it suggests that respiratory morbidity in SCD is not solely attributable to classic atopic asthma. Furthermore, objective measures of lung function frequently reveal abnormalities. Spirometry in patients with SCD often demonstrates obstructive patterns, with a reduced forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) to forced vital capacity (FVC) ratio, in 15-30% of patients, even among those without a history of respiratory symptoms. Airway hyperresponsiveness (AHR), assessed by methacholine or exercise challenge, is also common, present in up to 60% of patients with SCD in some series. These features—wheezing, airway obstruction, and AHR—often occur in isolation, without the concurrent presence of other clinical criteria necessary for an asthma diagnosis, such as atopy or reversible airflow limitation, creating a significant diagnostic challenge.

The clinical implications of these respiratory findings are profound, as they are consistently associated with increased SCD-related morbidity and mortality. A strong body of evidence links asthma and wheezing to an increased frequency and severity of vaso-occlusive pain crises. A large retrospective cohort study demonstrated that a diagnosis of asthma was associated with a 2.5-fold increased rate of pain episodes requiring hospitalization. Similarly, a history of wheezing has been identified as an independent risk factor for recurrent acute chest syndrome (ACS), a leading cause of death in SCD. The presence of asthma or recurrent wheezing increases the risk of ACS by approximately two- to three-fold. This association extends to the most severe outcomes; multiple studies have reported that asthma is a significant independent risk factor for premature death in both children and adults with SCD, with some analyses suggesting a doubling of mortality risk. The presence of airway obstruction on pulmonary function testing, even in the absence of an asthma diagnosis, has also been linked to a higher incidence of ACS and a greater decline in lung function over time. These findings underscore that respiratory involvement is not a benign comorbidity but a key driver of SCD severity.

The pathophysiology underlying airway inflammation in SCD is complex and multifactorial, involving a intricate interplay between the underlying hemoglobinopathy and pulmonary inflammation. The primary mechanism is thought to be the downstream effects of hemolysis and vaso-occlusion. Chronic hemolysis releases free plasma hemoglobin, which scavenges nitric oxide (NO), a potent vasodilator and bronchodilator. This NO depletion can lead to increased pulmonary vascular tone, endothelial dysfunction, and airway hyperresponsiveness. Furthermore, ischemia-reperfusion injury from vaso-occlusion promotes a state of systemic and pulmonary inflammation. This is characterized by elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-6, TNF-α), activation of neutrophils and platelets, and increased oxidative stress. This inflammatory milieu can directly contribute to airway wall edema, mucus hypersecretion, and smooth muscle contraction, manifesting clinically as wheezing and obstruction. Adding to this complexity is the role of atopy, which appears to be a common comorbidity. Elevated total and specific IgE levels, as well as positive skin prick tests, are frequently observed in patients with SCD and asthma, suggesting that classic allergic pathways may also contribute to airway disease in a subset of patients. Thus, the respiratory phenotype in SCD is likely a spectrum, ranging from a primarily hemolysis-driven process to one dominated by traditional atopic asthma, or a combination of both.

The diagnosis of asthma in patients with SCD requires a high index of suspicion and a comprehensive approach, as standard criteria are often insufficient. A detailed history of recurrent wheezing, cough, and dyspnea, particularly if they occur outside of pain crises, is essential. However, clinicians must be aware that these symptoms can be attributed to ACS or other SCD complications. Objective testing is crucial. Spirometry should be performed when the patient is at their clinical baseline, and a significant bronchodilator response (an increase in FEV1 of ≥12% and ≥200 mL) is highly suggestive of asthma. However, the absence of reversibility on a single test does not rule it out. A methacholine challenge can be useful to demonstrate AHR, but its interpretation must be cautious, as AHR is common in SCD even without asthma. Management strategies are largely extrapolated from asthma guidelines and include inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) as the cornerstone of controller therapy for patients with persistent symptoms or frequent exacerbations. Long-acting beta-agonists (LABA) may be added for uncontrolled symptoms, though their use in SCD should be monitored carefully. Leukotriene receptor antagonists have shown some benefit in small studies. A critical component of management is the optimization of SCD-specific therapies, such as hydroxyurea, which has been shown to reduce the frequency of pain crises and ACS and may have a secondary benefit on respiratory symptoms. Future research must focus on prospective studies to better define the distinct phenotypes of airway disease in SCD, to identify novel biomarkers that can differentiate asthma from other causes of wheezing, and to conduct randomized controlled trials of targeted therapies, including biologics, to improve outcomes for this vulnerable patient population.

The discussion of respiratory phenotypes in sickle cell disease (SCD) must begin by acknowledging the central challenge highlighted throughout this review: the diagnostic ambiguity between wheeze and asthma. The high prevalence of wheezing, airway obstruction, and airway hyperresponsiveness (AHR) in patients with SCD, often occurring in the absence of a formal asthma diagnosis, suggests that these features may not simply be comorbid asthma but could be intrinsic manifestations of SCD pathophysiology. This distinction is not merely semantic; it has profound implications for clinical management, prognostication, and the design of future research. The evidence strongly supports the assertion that respiratory symptoms and physiological abnormalities are significant markers of SCD severity, associated with an increased risk of pain crises, acute chest syndrome (ACS), and even premature death. Therefore, the clinical approach must shift from a binary "asthma or not" question to a more nuanced evaluation of a spectrum of respiratory phenotypes.

The associations between respiratory morbidity and adverse SCD outcomes are well-established. Wheezing, whether or not it meets the criteria for an asthma diagnosis, has emerged as a particularly potent predictor of disease severity. This finding challenges the clinical practice of dismissing wheeze in SCD patients as a benign or incidental finding. The link between AHR and ACS is particularly compelling, suggesting that bronchoconstriction and airway inflammation may play a direct role in the pathogenesis of this life-threatening complication. The pathophysiological mechanisms underpinning these associations are complex and multifactorial, extending beyond the classical Th2-mediated eosinophilic inflammation characteristic of atopic asthma. In SCD, a state of chronic hemolysis and endothelial dysfunction creates a pro-inflammatory milieu. This is compounded by the effects of recurrent vaso-occlusion, which can lead to pulmonary vascular injury, ischemia-reperfusion injury, and the release of inflammatory mediators. The resulting airway inflammation appears to be a unique entity, often characterized by a neutrophilic or mixed inflammatory pattern, which may explain the variable response to standard asthma therapies like inhaled corticosteroids. The role of other mediators, such as leukotrienes, platelet-activating factor, and even the direct effects of cell-free hemoglobin on airway smooth muscle, warrants further investigation.

Given this complex pathophysiology, the diagnosis and management of respiratory symptoms in SCD require a tailored approach. Relying solely on symptoms is insufficient, as wheezing is highly prevalent and non-specific. Objective testing, including spirometry and bronchoprovocation challenges, is crucial for characterizing the physiological abnormalities present. However, even these tests can be challenging to interpret, as a significant proportion of patients without asthma symptoms demonstrate AHR or obstruction. The management of patients with SCD and respiratory symptoms should be individualized. While standard asthma therapies, including bronchodilators and inhaled corticosteroids, are often employed, their efficacy in this population is not well-established. The potential for a poor response to corticosteroids, particularly in the context of neutrophilic inflammation, highlights the need for alternative therapeutic strategies. Furthermore, the management of SCD itself, including the use of hydroxyurea, has been shown to reduce the frequency of ACS and may have a beneficial effect on respiratory symptoms, underscoring the importance of optimizing underlying disease control.

The limitations of the current body of evidence must be acknowledged. Much of the existing data comes from retrospective or cross-sectional studies, which cannot establish causality. There is a significant heterogeneity in study populations, diagnostic criteria for asthma, and outcome definitions, making direct comparisons difficult. The inherent challenges in diagnosing asthma in SCD, as outlined in this review, mean that the true prevalence of the disease is likely overestimated in some studies and underestimated in others. Large, prospective, longitudinal cohort studies are urgently needed to better define the natural history of respiratory phenotypes in SCD, to identify robust biomarkers that can distinguish between different endotypes, and to determine the true impact of these phenotypes on long-term outcomes.

In conclusion, the question "wheeze or asthma?" in sickle cell disease is not a simple dichotomy but rather reflects a complex and overlapping spectrum of respiratory morbidity. The evidence indicates that wheezing, airway obstruction, and AHR are not just markers of comorbid asthma but are integral components of the SCD disease process and powerful predictors of adverse outcomes. The pathophysiology is distinct from classic atopic asthma, involving a unique interplay of hemolysis, inflammation, and vascular injury. Clinicians must maintain a high index of suspicion for respiratory involvement in SCD, moving beyond symptom-based diagnosis to incorporate objective physiological testing. Management should be multifaceted, focusing on optimizing SCD control while thoughtfully applying asthma therapies, with a recognition that responses may be variable. The path forward requires a concerted research effort to unravel the distinct endotypes of respiratory disease in SCD, to develop targeted therapies, and ultimately to improve the morbidity and mortality associated with this devastating complication. The presence of wheeze in a patient with SCD should be a red flag, prompting a thorough evaluation and a proactive, rather than reactive, approach to management.

The proliferation of edge devices, online services, and decentralized sensing platforms has created unprecedented opportunities for learning from user-generated data. However, such data frequently contain sensitive information, and centralizing it for analysis introduces substantial privacy risks. Local differential privacy (LDP) [1], [2] has emerged as a rigorous and practical framework for privacy-preserving data collection. Under LDP, each user perturbs their data locally before transmitting it to an untrusted aggregator, thereby ensuring that the aggregator cannot infer the original input with high confidence. This strong trust model has led to deployments in industrial systems [3] and to a rich literature on frequency estimation, mean estimation, heavy hitter detection, and distribution learning [4], [5].

A significant portion of modern data is naturally represented as key-value pairs. NoSQL systems, user profiles, mobile application logs, e-commerce interactions, and Internet-of-Things telemetry commonly store records in which a key identifies an attribute, item, or event and a value quantifies an associated measurement. Unlike homogeneous categorical or numerical data, key-value data are sparse, heterogeneous, and often high-dimensional. These characteristics make privacy-preserving collection and analysis particularly challenging: a user may contribute only a small subset of keys, values may be continuous or unbounded, and the joint distribution between keys and values may carry the most useful information. Recent studies have extended LDP to key-value data and demonstrated feasibility for basic tasks such as mean estimation and frequency estimation [6], [7]. Nevertheless, existing approaches primarily target marginal statistics and often treat key and value analysis separately.

Many contemporary machine learning and statistical inference tasks, however, depend on conditional probabilities and conditional expectations rather than marginals alone. Recommender systems estimate the likelihood of an item given user context; personalized models predict an outcome conditional on features; causal inference and A/B testing require subgroup-specific means; and Bayesian models frequently query conditional distributions. In the key-value setting, these needs translate into questions such as: What is the frequency of a key among users satisfying a condition? What is the mean value associated with a key given a condition? Such conditional statistics provide the building blocks for conditional probability tables, regression coefficients, and stratified analyses. Despite their importance, conditional frequency and conditional mean estimation under LDP remain largely unexplored, especially when the condition itself may involve keys, values, or both.

The technical obstacles are substantial. First, LDP perturbation is applied independently at each user, so the aggregator observes only noisy reports. Conditional queries partition the population into subgroups, and sparse subgroups amplify noise, leading to high variance and unreliable estimates. Second, the key domain may be large or unknown, while values may be continuous, requiring perturbation mechanisms that jointly encode key-value structure without excessive communication overhead. Third, privacy budget composition across multiple keys, values, and conditions must be managed carefully; naive independent perturbation of each component can quickly exhaust the budget or produce inconsistent joint statistics. Fourth, conditional estimators must correct the bias induced by perturbation while remaining stable under sparsity. These challenges cannot be fully addressed by simply applying existing LDP mechanisms for categorical or numerical data to keys and values in isolation.

Motivated by these gaps, this work investigates conditional analysis for key-value data under the strong model of local differential privacy. We first design a set of perturbation mechanisms that allow users to report key-value pairs while satisfying ε-LDP. The mechanisms are tailored to the structural properties of key-value data, including sparsity and heterogeneity, and provide a foundation for downstream statistical estimation. Building on these mechanisms, we then develop a conditional frequency estimation method for key analysis and a conditional mean estimation method for value analysis. The proposed estimators explicitly account for the perturbation process, mitigate bias, and control variance in conditional subgroups. The resulting statistics can be used directly in learning pipelines that require conditional probabilities, conditional expectations, or marginal statistics derived from conditional queries.

The contributions of this work are fourfold. First, we formulate the problems of conditional frequency estimation and conditional mean estimation for key-value data under LDP, thereby extending the scope of privacy-preserving key-value analytics beyond marginal statistics. Second, we propose new perturbation mechanisms that jointly handle keys and values under a strong local privacy guarantee. Third, we derive conditional estimators with theoretical guarantees on privacy and utility, and we discuss practical strategies for budget allocation and sparse-condition regularization. Fourth, we conduct extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, comparing the proposed methods with state-of-the-art competitors. The results demonstrate that the proposed mechanisms and estimators achieve accurate conditional frequency and conditional mean estimation, validating their effectiveness for privacy-preserving learning on key-value data.

The collection process is decentralized: no trusted aggregator observes raw key-value pairs. A randomized mechanism \(\mathcal{M}\) satisfies \(\epsilon\)-local differential privacy (\(\epsilon\)-LDP) if for any two inputs \(x,x'\) and any output \(y\), \(\Pr[\mathcal{M}(x)=y] \le e^{\epsilon}\Pr[\mathcal{M}(x')=y]\) [1]. Our methods operate under this strong local model and compose across multiple perturbation steps via standard privacy composition [2].

**Key Perturbation.** For key analysis, we represent each user's key set as a binary vector \(x_u \in \{0,1\}^{|\mathcal{K}|}\), where \(x_{u,k}=1\) if key \(k\) is present. We adopt an optimized unary encoding (OUE) mechanism [3]. Each bit \(x_{u,k}\) is independently perturbed to \(\tilde{x}_{u,k}\in\{0,1\}\) with probabilities
\[
\Pr[\tilde{x}_{u,k}=1 \mid x_{u,k}=1]=p,\qquad
\Pr[\tilde{x}_{u,k}=1 \mid x_{u,k}=0]=q,
\]
where \(p=1/2\) and \(q=1/(e^{\epsilon_1}+1)\) for \(\epsilon_1\)-LDP, or optimized values chosen to minimize estimator variance under a given privacy budget [3]. This yields a per-key transition matrix \(P\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2}\). For multivariate key statistics, the joint transition operator is the Kronecker product \(P^{\otimes m}\), enabling unbiased recovery of joint key frequencies after linear inversion. Compared with randomized response and subset-selection mechanisms [4], OUE provides favorable variance for sparse key-value data and supports conditional queries over key co-occurrence patterns.

**Value Perturbation.** For each present key \(k\), the value \(v_{u,k}\) is perturbed independently using a mean-preserving mechanism. When \(\mathcal{V}\) is bounded, we use the piecewise mechanism [5], which maps \(v\) to a continuous output \(\tilde{v}\) with conditional expectation \(\mathbb{E}[\tilde{v}\mid v]=v\) and bounded support. When \(\mathcal{V}\) is unbounded or heavy-tailed, we employ a Laplace mechanism with calibrated scale \(b=\Delta/\epsilon_2\), where \(\Delta\) is a clipping threshold selected from public domain bounds; clipping introduces a small bias that is corrected in the estimator. The value perturbation is independent of the key perturbation conditional on the raw pair, so the joint transition factorizes as \(P_{\text{key}}\otimes P_{\text{value}}\). This factorization is central to conditional estimation.

\[

\]

We first form the empirical moment vector \(\hat{m}_{C} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{u=1}^n \tilde{x}_{u,C}\), where \(\tilde{x}_{u,C}\) is the product of perturbed indicators for keys appearing in \(C\). \[
\hat{f}(k \mid C)=\frac{\hat{f}(k,C)}{\hat{f}(C)}.

\[
