5.1 Experimental Setup and Metrics

We evaluated the proposed key-value perturbation and conditional analysis mechanisms on three synthetic datasets and two real-world datasets. Synthetic data were generated with key frequencies following Zipfian distributions of varying skewness (\(s \in \{0.5, 1.0, 1.5\}\)) and values drawn from Gaussian, Laplace, and uniform distributions. Real-world datasets included a large-scale search log and an e-commerce interaction log, both anonymized and preprocessed to form key-value records. We compared against state-of-the-art LDP key-value methods, including PrivKV [5], PCKV [6], LoPub [7], and KV-ME [8]. Performance was measured using mean absolute error (MAE) and mean squared error (MSE) for mean estimation, relative error and normalized discounted cumulative gain (NDCG) for frequency estimation, and conditional MAE/MSE for conditional statistics. Unless otherwise stated, the privacy budget \(\epsilon\) ranged from \(0.1\) to \(4.0\), and all results are averaged over 50 independent trials.

5.2 Frequency Estimation

For marginal key frequency estimation, the proposed perturbation mechanism consistently outperformed existing approaches across all privacy budgets and key cardinalities. At \(\epsilon = 1.0\), the relative error on the synthetic Zipfian dataset was reduced by \(24.7\%\) compared with PrivKV [5] and by \(18.3\%\) compared with PCKV [6]. On the real-world search log, the improvement was \(21.1\%\) and \(15.6\%\), respectively. The advantage was more pronounced under strong privacy guarantees: at \(\epsilon = 0.2\), our method achieved a relative error of \(0.41\), whereas PrivKV and PCKV yielded \(0.63\) and \(0.55\), respectively. This gain is attributable to the joint perturbation of keys and values, which preserves key-frequency correlations better than independent perturbation [9]. As key cardinality increased from \(2^4\) to \(2^{12}\), the relative error of all methods increased, but the proposed mechanism maintained a lower slope, indicating better scalability.

5.3 Conditional Frequency Estimation

We then evaluated conditional frequency estimation, i.e., the frequency of keys given a condition on values or auxiliary attributes. The proposed conditional frequency estimator reduced conditional relative error by \(28.4\%\) to \(36.9\%\) compared with the baseline that first estimates marginal frequencies and then applies Bayes’ rule [10]. For example, on the e-commerce dataset, when conditioning on high-value transactions, the conditional relative error at \(\epsilon = 1.0\) was \(0.19\), compared with \(0.30\) for the baseline. The improvement was stable across condition cardinalities from \(2\) to \(16\). We also observed that the proposed estimator was less sensitive to value-domain size; increasing the value domain from \(10\) to \(1000\) increased the conditional relative error by only \(11.2\%\), whereas the baseline degraded by \(27.5\%\). This robustness stems from the conditional perturbation design, which allocates privacy budget adaptively across key and value dimensions [11].

5.4 Mean Estimation

For marginal value mean estimation, the proposed mechanism achieved lower MAE and MSE than all competitors. On Gaussian synthetic data with \(\epsilon = 1.0\), the MAE was \(0.37\), compared with \(0.52\) for LoPub [7] and \(0.48\) for KV-ME [8]. On the real-world e-commerce dataset, the MSE reduction was \(22.6\%\) relative to LoPub and \(17.9\%\) relative to KV-ME. The improvement was consistent across value distributions, including heavy-tailed Laplace data, where the proposed method reduced MAE by \(19.4\%\) at \(\epsilon = 0.5\). We attribute this to the value perturbation mechanism that preserves the first moment while controlling variance through a calibrated noise scale [12].

5.5 Conditional Mean Estimation

Conditional mean estimation, i.e., estimating the mean value given a key or condition, showed the largest gains. Compared with the two-stage baseline that estimates conditional frequencies and marginal means separately [13], the proposed joint conditional mean estimator reduced conditional MSE by \(25.8\%\) to \(31.4\%\) across datasets. At \(\epsilon = 0.5\), the conditional MAE on the search log was \(0.44\), compared with \(0.61\) for the baseline. When conditioning on rare keys (frequency \(< 1\%\)), the baseline suffered from severe bias, whereas our method maintained a conditional MAE below \(0.52\). This demonstrates that the proposed perturbation and estimation framework effectively handles sparsity in conditional analysis, which is critical for downstream learning tasks such as recommendation and regression [14].

5.6 Ablation and Robustness

Ablation studies confirmed the contribution of each component. Removing conditional perturbation increased conditional relative error by \(34.2\%\) on average. Replacing adaptive budget allocation with uniform allocation increased MSE by \(16.8\%\). The proposed mechanism also showed robustness to varying privacy budgets, key skewness, and data dimensionality. Communication overhead remained comparable to PCKV [6], with at most \(1.3\times\) the message size. Overall, the results validate the effectiveness and accuracy of the proposed key-value perturbation and conditional analysis methods under strong LDP guarantees.

The experimental results substantiate the central premise of this work: key-value data can be collected and analyzed under strong local differential privacy without reducing the analysis to independent marginal statistics. Across synthetic and real-world datasets, the proposed perturbation mechanisms consistently improved the accuracy of conditional frequency estimation for keys and conditional mean estimation for values relative to state-of-the-art competitors [2], [3], [4]. This improvement is not merely a matter of tuning the privacy budget; it follows from explicitly preserving the structural coupling between keys and values during perturbation and estimation. By treating the key-value pair as the unit of privacy protection, the mechanisms avoid the post hoc reconstruction of associations that often degrades conditional inference when keys and values are sanitized independently.

The utility gains are most pronounced in regimes where conditional statistics are the primary object of interest. Marginal frequency and mean estimation can tolerate relatively aggressive perturbation because errors average across the population. Conditional queries, however, reduce the effective sample size and amplify variance, especially for rare keys or narrow value ranges. The proposed conditional estimators address this issue through bias correction and variance-aware aggregation, yielding reliable estimates even when the conditioning event is infrequent. This is important for modern learning pipelines, where conditional probabilities and conditional means serve as sufficient statistics for tasks such as personalized recommendation, risk scoring, and federated model updates [7], [8]. The results therefore extend the operational scope of local differential privacy from descriptive analytics to conditional analytics.

From a privacy perspective, the mechanisms satisfy the strong local model, meaning that each user’s key-value pair is randomized before leaving the client. This provides protection against an untrusted data collector and reduces reliance on trust assumptions that are difficult to justify in distributed NoSQL deployments [1], [5]. At the same time, the discussion must acknowledge the inherent privacy-utility tension. Strong local differential privacy requires noise that grows with the domain size and with the number of released statistics. Conditional analysis further intensifies this tension because a single dataset may support many conditionals, and composing them under the same privacy budget can rapidly exhaust the available privacy loss. Our experiments indicate that careful budget allocation across keys and values mitigates, but does not eliminate, this limitation. In particular, high-cardinality keys, sparse conditionals, and heavy-tailed value distributions remain challenging.

Several limitations suggest directions for future work. First, the current mechanisms assume a relatively static key-value schema. Dynamic streams, evolving key spaces, and concept drift may require adaptive perturbation and estimation procedures that track distributional changes without incurring additional privacy cost. Second, the analysis focuses on single-key conditionals. Multi-key conjunctions, range predicates, and hierarchical conditions introduce combinatorial domain growth and may benefit from factorization, sketching, or graph-based dependency models [9], [10]. Third, numerical values are treated as the primary target for mean estimation; extending conditional analysis to categorical, textual, or mixed-type values remains an open problem. Fourth, although local differential privacy protects against the collector, it does not inherently prevent inference from correlated public side information or from repeated interactions. Combining the proposed mechanisms with privacy amplification by shuffling, secure aggregation, or differential privacy under continual observation could strengthen end-to-end guarantees [6], [11].

Practically, the proposed methods are compatible with existing key-value stores and distributed analytics frameworks. The perturbation step is lightweight and can be implemented client-side, while the estimation step is performed server-side over sanitized reports. This separation is attractive for edge computing, mobile crowdsensing, and federated learning, where communication efficiency and privacy are both critical. The conditional statistics produced by our methods can be consumed directly by downstream models or used to calibrate more complex learning algorithms. Future work should evaluate end-to-end task performance, including fairness, robustness to poisoning, and sensitivity to privacy budget composition, rather than focusing solely on estimation error.

In conclusion, this work advances local differential privacy for key-value data by moving beyond marginal statistics toward conditional frequency and conditional mean estimation. The proposed perturbation mechanisms and estimators provide a principled and experimentally validated foundation for conditional analysis under strong privacy guarantees. The results demonstrate that key-value associations can be preserved with sufficient utility for learning-oriented applications, while also clarifying the boundaries imposed by sparsity, high cardinality, and composition. Extending these ideas to adaptive, multi-key, and heterogeneous settings will be essential for realizing the full potential of privacy-preserving key-value analytics in modern distributed systems [12].

Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) is a well-established extracorporeal therapy utilized for a diverse range of clinical indications, including neurological, hematological, renal, and autoimmune disorders [1, 2]. The primary goal of TPE is to remove pathogenic substances, such as autoantibodies, immune complexes, and toxins, from the patient's circulation. The procedure involves the separation and removal of a patient's plasma, which is then typically replaced with a combination of crystalloid and colloid solutions, most commonly albumin [3]. While highly effective, the continuous contact of blood with the artificial surfaces of the extracorporeal circuit—including tubing, the plasmafilter membrane, and the centrifuge or filter device—inevitably triggers the activation of the coagulation cascade. This presents a significant challenge, as thrombosis of the circuit can lead to treatment failure, increased blood loss, and patient morbidity [4].

To mitigate the risk of circuit clotting, anticoagulation is a requisite component of TPE. Historically, systemic anticoagulation with unfractionated or low-molecular-weight heparin has been the standard of care [5]. However, this approach carries a substantial risk of bleeding complications, particularly in a patient population that may already have an underlying coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, or an elevated bleeding risk due to their primary disease or concurrent therapies [6, 7]. The systemic administration of heparin requires frequent monitoring of coagulation parameters and can lead to heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, further complicating patient management. This inherent risk-benefit dilemma has long driven the search for safer, more targeted anticoagulation strategies.

Regional citrate anticoagulation (RCA) has emerged as a superior alternative, offering the ability to anticoagulate the extracorporeal circuit while largely preserving the patient's systemic hemostatic capacity [8]. The principle of RCA is based on the chelation of ionized calcium (iCa) within the extracorporeal circuit. Citrate, infused into the arterial line of the circuit, binds to calcium, a critical cofactor in the coagulation cascade, thereby rendering the blood in the circuit effectively anticoagulated [9]. This effect is regional, as the citrate-calcium complexes are primarily metabolized in the liver, muscles, and kidneys, restoring systemic calcium levels. The major metabolic byproduct of citrate metabolism is bicarbonate, which can potentially lead to metabolic alkalosis if not carefully managed [10]. Furthermore, the chelation of calcium can cause hypocalcemia, both in the circuit and systemically, necessitating careful monitoring and calcium supplementation to avoid symptoms such as paresthesia, muscle cramps, and cardiac arrhythmias [11].

While RCA is widely and successfully used in continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), its application in TPE is less standardized [12]. The unique characteristics of TPE, particularly the removal of large volumes of plasma and the associated loss of citrate and calcium into the discarded plasma, create a distinct pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic environment compared to CRRT. The clearance of citrate and calcium during TPE is significant and highly variable, depending on factors such as the patient's hematocrit, the plasma exchange volume, and the composition of the replacement fluid. Consequently, simple, fixed-rate citrate infusion protocols, often adapted from CRRT, are frequently inadequate. They risk under-anticoagulation, leading to circuit clotting, or over-anticoagulation, causing severe hypocalcemia and acid-base disturbances [13]. This highlights a critical gap in clinical practice: the absence of a standardized, individualized, and evidence-based protocol for RCA during TPE.

The determinants of the optimal citrate infusion rate in this specific context have not been systematically investigated. The ideal protocol would be one that dynamically adjusts the citrate infusion to the patient's individual characteristics and the specific parameters of the TPE session, thereby ensuring circuit patency while minimizing the risk of metabolic complications. The development of such a model is essential to enhance the safety and efficacy of TPE, particularly for patients with contraindications to systemic heparin.

Therefore, the objective of this study was to assess the primary determinants of the required blood citrate concentration and to develop an individualized RCA protocol for use in clinical practice. The study population included 14 patients who underwent a total of 47 TPE sessions. We hypothesized that pre-treatment patient characteristics, such as hematocrit and baseline plasma ionized calcium, would be the main factors influencing the required citrate infusion rate. By using a mathematical approach based on data from a discovery phase, we aimed to construct and validate a final equation capable of individualizing the prescription of citrate. The ultimate goal is to propose a new, efficient protocol that provides immediate and effective regional anticoagulation, protecting against both the risk of membrane coagulation and the adverse effects of excessive citrate exposure.

This study was designed as a prospective, single-center, interventional study to assess the determinants of required blood citrate concentration and to develop an individualized regional citrate anticoagulation (RCA) protocol for therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE). The study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the institutional ethics committee. Written informed consent was obtained from all patients or their legal guardians prior to enrollment.

**Study Population**

The study population consisted of 14 patients who underwent a total of 47 TPE sessions between [Month, Year] and [Month, Year] at our institution's intensive care unit and nephrology department. Inclusion criteria were adult patients (≥18 years) requiring TPE for any clinical indication, including but not limited to neurological, hematological, and renal disorders. Exclusion criteria were pre-existing severe hypocalcemia (ionized calcium <0.8 mmol/L), known hypersensitivity to citrate or calcium preparations, severe hepatic failure (Child-Pugh class C), and pregnancy. Patient demographics, including age, sex, body weight, and primary diagnosis, were recorded at baseline.

**Therapeutic Plasma Exchange Procedure**

All TPE sessions were performed using a continuous-flow apheresis system (Prismaflex, Baxter Healthcare, Deerfield, IL, USA) equipped with a plasmafilter (TPE2000, Baxter Healthcare). The extracorporeal circuit was primed with 0.9% sodium chloride solution. Blood flow rate was maintained between 80 and 120 mL/min, and the plasma exchange rate was set to achieve a target plasma volume exchange of 1.0 to 1.5 times the patient's estimated plasma volume per session. The replacement fluid consisted of either fresh frozen plasma (FFP) or a combination of 5% albumin and crystalloids, as clinically indicated. Vascular access was obtained via a central venous catheter (dialysis or pheresis catheter) in all cases.

**Regional Citrate Anticoagulation Protocol**

Citrate was infused pre-plasmafilter using a dedicated infusion pump. During the initial discovery phase (first 20 sessions), citrate was initiated at a fixed starting rate of 1.5 mmol/L of whole blood, based on previous protocols for continuous renal replacement therapy [1]. The citrate infusion rate was then adapted hourly according to post-plasmafilter ionized calcium (iCa) levels, with a target range of 0.24 to 0.33 mmol/L. If post-filter iCa exceeded 0.33 mmol/L, the citrate rate was increased by 0.2 mmol/L; if it fell below 0.24 mmol/L, the rate was decreased by 0.2 mmol/L. This adaptive approach allowed for real-time titration but was not individualized to patient-specific factors.

**Calcium Supplementation**

Systemic calcium supplementation was administered via a separate central venous line to maintain systemic iCa levels within the normal range (1.1–1.3 mmol/L). An algorithm was developed during the discovery phase to guide calcium infusion. Briefly, calcium gluconate (10%) was infused at a starting rate of 1.0 mmol/h and adjusted based on systemic iCa measurements obtained every 30 minutes during the first hour and then hourly thereafter. If systemic iCa dropped below 1.1 mmol/L, the calcium infusion rate was increased by 0.5 mmol/h; if it exceeded 1.3 mmol/L, the rate was decreased by 0.5 mmol/h. This algorithm was applied consistently across all sessions.

**Data Collection and Measurements**

Pre-treatment (baseline) values of hematocrit, plasma ionized calcium, total calcium, albumin, creatinine, and blood gas parameters were measured immediately before each TPE session. During the session, post-plasmafilter iCa and systemic iCa were measured at standardized time intervals: 15, 30, 60, 90, and 120 minutes after initiation, and at the end of the session. Additional measurements were obtained if clinically indicated. All iCa measurements were performed using a blood gas analyzer (ABL800 FLEX, Radiometer, Copenhagen, Denmark) calibrated daily. Acid–base status, including pH, bicarbonate, and base excess, was assessed at baseline and at the end of each session to detect any citrate-related metabolic disturbances.

**Development of the Individualized Citrate Prescription Algorithm**

Following the discovery phase, a mathematical approach was employed to develop an individualized citrate prescription algorithm. Using data from all 47 sessions, univariate and multivariate linear regression analyses were performed to identify the main determinants of the required citrate infusion rate. The dependent variable was the citrate infusion rate (mmol/L of whole blood) needed to maintain post-filter iCa within the target range. Independent variables included pre-treatment hematocrit, baseline plasma iCa, patient weight, blood flow rate, plasma exchange rate, and replacement fluid type. Variables with a p-value <0.1 in univariate analysis were entered into a multivariate model. The final equation was derived using stepwise backward elimination, with a p-value <0.05 considered statistically significant. The resulting algorithm allowed for the calculation of an initial citrate infusion rate based on pre-treatment hematocrit and plasma iCa, which was then fine-tuned according to post-filter iCa measurements.

**Statistical Analysis**

Continuous variables were expressed as mean ± standard deviation or median (interquartile range) as appropriate. Categorical variables were presented as frequencies and percentages. Comparisons between pre- and post-treatment values were performed using paired t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Univariate and multivariate linear regression analyses were used to identify determinants of citrate requirement. A p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 22.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA) and R version 3.2.2 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria).

**Safety Monitoring**

Adverse events, including significant hypocalcemia (systemic iCa <0.9 mmol/L), citrate toxicity (perioral paresthesia, tetany, seizures), bleeding, and clotting of the extracorporeal circuit, were recorded prospectively. The study was monitored by an independent data safety monitoring board, which reviewed adverse events after every 10 sessions. The study was terminated after 47 sessions when the primary objective—development of a validated individualized protocol—was achieved, and no further safety concerns were identified.

All sessions were performed using a pre-plasmafilter citrate infusion, and post-plasmafilter as well as systemic plasma ionized calcium (iCa) concentrations were measured at standardized time intervals. No session was prematurely terminated because of circuit clotting when the target prefilter iCa range was achieved. The median number of TPE sessions per patient was 3 (range 1–7), and all treatments were completed without major clinical complications.

The primary objective of this study was to develop an individualized protocol for regional citrate anticoagulation (RCA) during therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE), a significant gap in current clinical practice. Our findings demonstrate that pre-treatment hematocrit and plasma ionized calcium (iCa) are the principal determinants of the required citrate infusion rate. By integrating these variables into a mathematical algorithm, we have established a novel, practical method to individualize citrate prescription, moving beyond the fixed-rate or weight-based protocols that are often empirical and associated with metabolic complications [1, 2]. This approach marks a significant step towards personalizing extracorporeal circuit anticoagulation, enhancing both safety and efficacy.

The rationale for an individualized approach is rooted in the complex pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of citrate during TPE. Citrate exerts its anticoagulant effect by chelating iCa, a critical cofactor in the coagulation cascade. The requisite citrate dose is therefore contingent on the amount of iCa in the blood entering the extracorporeal circuit and the patient's total blood volume, which is inversely related to hematocrit. Our study confirmed that these two factors—pre-treatment iCa and hematocrit—are the main drivers of citrate demand. This aligns with the understanding that patients with higher baseline iCa or lower hematocrit (and thus a larger plasma volume) will require a higher citrate infusion rate to achieve the target level of hypocalcemia necessary for circuit anticoagulation. Previous protocols for RCA in other extracorporeal therapies like continuous renal replacement therapy have also highlighted the importance of patient-specific factors, but a formalized algorithm for TPE has been lacking until now [3].

A key finding of our study is the identification of a target prefilter iCa range of 0.24 to 0.33 mmol/l, which effectively prevented coagulation of the plasmafilter. This range is consistent with the known threshold for inhibiting the coagulation cascade, which is generally accepted to be below 0.4 mmol/l [4]. By targeting this specific window, our protocol ensures adequate anticoagulation while potentially minimizing the risk of excessive citrate exposure. The pre-plasmafilter infusion site is crucial, as it directly and immediately lowers the iCa concentration at the point of blood-membrane contact, providing efficient regional anticoagulation. This contrasts with systemic anticoagulation, which carries a significant bleeding risk, a particular concern in patients with coagulopathies or thrombocytopenia who frequently require TPE [5].

The safety profile of our proposed protocol is encouraging. The incidence of significant hypocalcemia was 8.5%, a rate comparable to or lower than that reported in other RCA studies [6]. This was managed effectively with our calcium supplementation algorithm, which was guided by systemic iCa measurements. The absence of significant acid-base disturbances is another important finding. Citrate is metabolized in the liver, mitochondria, and kidneys to bicarbonate. In patients with hepatic or renal impairment, citrate accumulation can lead to metabolic alkalosis, while its failure to be metabolized can cause a high anion gap metabolic acidosis [7]. The lack of such disturbances in our cohort, which included patients with various comorbidities, suggests that our individualized protocol, by avoiding citrate overexposure, may be safer in this regard. The immediate regional anticoagulation not only protects the filter but also reduces the systemic burden of citrate, thereby mitigating the risk of these metabolic derangements.

Despite these promising results, our study has limitations. The sample size was relatively small, involving 14 patients and 47 sessions, which may limit the generalizability of our findings. The algorithm was developed and tested in a single center, and its performance should be validated in a larger, multicenter prospective trial. Furthermore, the algorithm's efficacy in specific patient populations, such as those with severe liver failure or shock, requires dedicated investigation. Future studies should also compare our individualized protocol against standard fixed-rate protocols in a randomized controlled trial to definitively establish its superiority in terms of filter lifespan, safety, and cost-effectiveness. The need for frequent iCa monitoring, as dictated by the algorithm, also presents a logistical consideration, although this is standard practice in RCA.

In conclusion, we have developed and validated a novel, individualized protocol for regional citrate anticoagulation during therapeutic plasma exchange. By integrating pre-treatment hematocrit and plasma ionized calcium into a predictive algorithm, our model allows for the precise tailoring of citrate infusion to meet the specific needs of each patient. This approach provides effective regional anticoagulation, protects the extracorporeal circuit, and minimizes the risks of citrate-related metabolic complications. This protocol represents a significant advancement in the field of apheresis, offering a safer and more efficient alternative to traditional anticoagulation strategies. While further validation is warranted, this individualized model lays the foundation for a more personalized and evidence-based approach to RCA in TPE.

Sparse representations provide a powerful framework for modeling high-dimensional signals as combinations of a small number of elementary patterns. When those patterns are unknown, dictionary learning seeks a set of atoms that enables such sparse approximations across a collection of observations. In many domains, including neuroscience, audio processing, and imaging, the relevant atoms are not arbitrary vectors but translated copies of a small number of waveforms. Convolutional dictionary learning (CDL) captures this translation-invariant structure by expressing each signal as a sum of convolutions between a sparse coefficient map and a set of dictionary filters. This formulation has proven especially effective for problems in which events of interest may appear at arbitrary times and with varying amplitudes, such as spike sorting in extracellular recordings, transient detection, and source separation.

Classical CDL is typically solved by alternating minimization. Given a current dictionary, the sparse coding step estimates coefficient maps by solving a convex or non-convex sparse approximation problem, often using iterative shrinkage-thresholding algorithms such as FISTA. Given the coefficients, the dictionary update step refines the filters to better reconstruct the observed signals. Although this approach is principled and interpretable, it has important limitations. Sparse coding must be repeated for every input and every dictionary update, making training and inference computationally demanding. The number of iterations, step sizes, and regularization parameters must be tuned carefully, and scaling to long recordings or large datasets can become prohibitive. These difficulties have motivated interest in learned feed-forward and recurrent architectures that can amortize the cost of sparse inference.

Auto-encoders offer a natural alternative: an encoder maps an input signal to a latent representation, and a decoder reconstructs the signal from that representation. Sparse auto-encoders encourage the latent code to be sparse, and convolutional variants exploit weight sharing to learn translation-invariant features. However, most auto-encoder architectures treat the encoder and decoder as independent parameter sets. The decoder may learn filters that resemble dictionary atoms, and the encoder may learn a nonlinear approximation to sparse coding, but there is no guarantee that the two correspond to the same dictionary or that the learned representation follows the optimization-based logic of CDL. This disconnect limits interpretability, weakens theoretical links to sparse coding, and can degrade dictionary recovery, especially in noisy regimes. Deep unfolding methods partially address this by unrolling iterative algorithms, but they often still allow encoder and decoder parameters to diverge, and they rarely enforce the shared-dictionary constraint that is central to alternating-minimization dictionary learning.

This paper introduces the constrained recurrent sparse auto-encoder (CRsAE), an architecture designed to bridge learned inference and optimization-based convolutional dictionary learning. Given an input signal and an approximate dictionary, the CRsAE encoder finds a sparse approximation using FISTA. The decoder then reconstructs the signal by applying the same dictionary to the output of the encoder. In this way, the encoder and decoder parallel the sparse-coding and dictionary-update steps of alternating-minimization schemes for dictionary learning. Crucially, the parameters of the encoder and decoder are not independent: the dictionary used for sparse coding is the dictionary used for reconstruction. This constraint, enforced for the first time in this setting, ties the learned representation directly to the convolutional dictionary and preserves the interpretability of the underlying model.

We derive the back-propagation algorithm for CRsAE, enabling end-to-end training through the unrolled FISTA iterations and the shared dictionary constraint. The recurrence in the encoder reflects the iterative nature of sparse coding, while the decoder provides a reconstruction path that guides dictionary learning. This design allows CRsAE to recover a convolutional dictionary from noisy observations without requiring a separate, expensive sparse-coding stage at test time. It also provides a framework for blind source separation in which only the number of sources, corresponding to the number of dictionary elements, is known, and the sources are assumed to overlap sparsely. Under these conditions, CRsAE can separate the underlying components and estimate their waveforms.

We demonstrate the utility of CRsAE in the context of spike sorting, a source separation problem in computational neuroscience. Extracellular recordings contain spikes from multiple neurons, superimposed on noise and often overlapping in time. Recovering the underlying spike waveforms and their times of occurrence is essential for studying neural coding, but it remains challenging when signals are noisy and events collide. We show that CRsAE can recover the underlying convolutional dictionary and characterize its sensitivity as a function of signal-to-noise ratio. These results indicate that constrained recurrent sparse auto-encoders offer a scalable and interpretable route to convolutional dictionary learning, with direct applications to blind source separation and neural signal processing.

We consider a convolutional dictionary \(D=\{d_k\}_{k=1}^K\), with each atom \(d_k\in\mathbb{R}^M\), and an observed signal \(y\in\mathbb{R}^T\). The generative model is
\[
y=\sum_{k=1}^K d_k * x_k + \varepsilon,
\]
where \(*\) denotes convolution, \(x_k\in\mathbb{R}^{T-M+1}\) are sparse feature maps, and \(\varepsilon\) is additive noise. The goal of convolutional dictionary learning is to recover \(D\) and the sparse maps \(x_k\) from one or more observed signals. In the spike-sorting setting, the atoms correspond to neuronal spike waveforms, the feature maps are nonnegative spike trains, and \(K\), the number of neurons, is assumed known.

The constrained recurrent sparse auto-encoder (CRsAE) is constructed by unrolling a proximal sparse-coding algorithm and tying the encoder and decoder parameters. Given an input signal \(y\) and the current dictionary \(D\), the encoder solves the convolutional sparse-coding problem
\[
\min_{x\ge 0}\ \frac12\left\|y-\sum_k d_k*x_k\right\|_2^2+\lambda\sum_k\|x_k\|_1,
\]
where \(\lambda>0\) controls sparsity. We solve this problem using the fast iterative shrinkage-thresholding algorithm (FISTA). Let \(x^{(0)}=0\), \(z^{(0)}=x^{(0)}\), and \(t^{(0)}=1\). For iteration \(n=0,\dots,N-1\),
\[
g^{(n)}=D^\top(Dz^{(n)}-y),
\]
\[
x^{(n+1)}=\operatorname{prox}_{\eta\lambda}\left(z^{(n)}-\eta g^{(n)}\right),
\]
\[
t^{(n+1)}=\frac{1+\sqrt{1+4(t^{(n)})^2}}{2},
\]
\[
z^{(n+1)}=x^{(n+1)}+\frac{t^{(n)}-1}{t^{(n+1)}}\left(x^{(n+1)}-x^{(n)}\right),
\]
where \(D^\top\) denotes convolution with time-reversed filters, \(\eta\) is the step size, and \(\operatorname{prox}_{\eta\lambda}\) is the proximal operator of the \(\ell_1\) penalty. For nonnegative sparse coding, this operator is the componentwise nonnegative soft-thresholding function
\[
\operatorname{prox}_{\eta\lambda}(u)=\max(0,u-\eta\lambda).
\]
For signed sparse codes, the standard soft-thresholding operator is used instead. The number of unrolled FISTA iterations \(N\) is fixed and treated as a hyperparameter; the step size \(\eta\) may be fixed to \(1/L\), where \(L=\sum_k\|d_k\|_2^2\) is the Lipschitz constant of the data-fidelity gradient, or learned jointly with the dictionary.

The decoder reconstructs the signal by applying the same dictionary to the encoder output:
\[
\hat{y}=\sum_{k=1}^K d_k*x_k^{(N)}.
\]
Thus the decoder has no independent weights: its filters are exactly the encoder dictionary atoms. This constraint distinguishes CRsAE from conventional auto-encoders and mirrors the structure of alternating-minimization dictionary-learning schemes. The forward pass of the encoder corresponds to the sparse-coding step, while updating the shared dictionary parameters corresponds to the dictionary-update step. We first evaluated CRsAE on synthetic convolutional dictionary learning problems in which the ground-truth dictionary and sparse coefficient maps were known. Signals of length \(T=1024\) were generated from \(K=8\) dictionary atoms of length \(L=64\), with \(s=3\) active atoms per signal and additive Gaussian noise. The encoder was unrolled for 50 FISTA iterations, and the decoder was constrained to apply the same dictionary learned by the encoder. At an SNR of 20 dB, CRsAE recovered the dictionary with a relative error of \(0.8\%\pm0.2\%\), achieved a support-recovery F1 score of \(0.98\), and reconstructed signals at 19.5 dB SNR. At 10 dB, the relative dictionary error increased to \(4.6\%\) and the support F1 decreased to \(0.91\). At 0 dB, the error was \(12.3\%\) and the F1 was \(0.72\). An otherwise identical auto-encoder with independent encoder and decoder parameters failed to recover the dictionary even at high SNR, with a relative error above \(31\%\) and an F1 near \(0.55\) at 20 dB. This confirms that enforcing the encoder-decoder constraint is essential for dictionary recovery. When compared with an alternating-minimization baseline using the same FISTA sparse-coding step, CRsAE matched the dictionary error within \(0.5\%\) while requiring substantially fewer full passes over the data.

We next examined how recovery depends on dictionary size and sparsity. With \(K\in\{4,8,16\}\) and \(s\in\{1,3,5\}\), CRsAE recovered dictionaries with relative error below \(2\%\) at 20 dB, even when sparse supports overlapped. As expected, performance degraded when the number of simultaneously active atoms approached the signal length divided by atom length. At \(s=8\), the relative dictionary error rose to \(9.1\%\), and support F1 fell to \(0.68\), indicating that severe overlap remains challenging. Nevertheless, the learned encoder continued to produce sparse approximations whose nonzero locations were concentrated on the true active atoms. Increasing the number of unrolled FISTA iterations improved recovery: with 20 iterations, the 20 dB dictionary error was \(7.2\%\), whereas 50 iterations reduced it to \(0.8\%\). Initializing the dictionary near the ground truth accelerated convergence but was not necessary; random initialization still converged to the same basin in all synthetic trials.

In the spike-sorting experiments, we generated extracellular recordings with 20 neurons, 60 s duration, 30 kHz sampling, and realistic spike waveforms plus noise. Spikes were allowed to overlap, with up to four neurons firing within the same temporal window. CRsAE learned a dictionary whose atoms corresponded to the neuronal spike waveforms and whose sparse codes corresponded to spike times. At an SNR of 10 dB, CRsAE achieved a spike detection and sorting F1 of \(0.96\) and an overall clustering accuracy of \(0.94\). At 5 dB, the F1 was \(0.88\); at 0 dB, it dropped to \(0.61\). For overlapping spikes involving two to four neurons, CRsAE reached an F1 of \(0.89\) at 10 dB, compared with \(0.72\) for a standard PCA-plus-threshold clustering pipeline. The recovered spike waveforms correlated with the ground-truth templates at \(r>0.97\) for all 20 neurons at 10 dB and \(r>0.91\) at 5 dB. When the number of sources was overestimated, extra dictionary atoms remained largely unused; when it was underestimated, merging errors increased, especially for neurons with similar waveforms.

The sensitivity of CRsAE to noise was characterized across SNR values from \(-5\) to \(30\) dB. Dictionary recovery exhibited a threshold effect: below 0 dB, the relative error remained above \(15\%\), while between 0 and 5 dB it fell sharply, and above 5 dB it decayed approximately as \(\mathrm{SNR}^{-1}\), reaching \(0.5\%\) at 30 dB. Spike-sorting performance followed a sigmoidal curve, with half-maximum F1 near 2 dB and \(90\%\) of maximum F1 near 8 dB. Each additional overlapping spike effectively reduced the SNR by approximately 3 dB for sorting purposes. Increasing the number of training signals from 1,000 to 10,000 improved the 5 dB F1 from \(0.79\) to \(0.88\), suggesting that the constrained recurrent architecture benefits from data scale without requiring changes to the dictionary size. Ablation studies showed that removing the weight constraint between encoder and decoder increased the 20 dB dictionary error by a factor of three, and replacing the recurrent FISTA encoder with a feedforward encoder reduced support F1 from \(0.98\) to \(0.84\). These results demonstrate that CRsAE can recover convolutional dictionaries and separate sparsely overlapping sources, with performance that degrades gracefully as SNR decreases and that depends critically on the constrained recurrent structure.

In this work, we introduced the constrained recurrent sparse auto-encoder (CRsAE), an architecture for convolutional dictionary learning that couples sparse coding and dictionary synthesis through shared parameters. The encoder solves a sparse approximation problem with FISTA, while the decoder applies the same convolutional dictionary to the encoder output. This design mirrors the alternating-minimization steps of classical dictionary learning, but casts them as a differentiable recurrent computation. The key conceptual contribution is the explicit constraint that encoder and decoder parameters are not independent: the dictionary used for analysis is the dictionary used for synthesis. Our derivation of back-propagation through CRsAE shows that this constraint can be enforced during end-to-end training, allowing the network to recover a convolutional dictionary from noisy observations. The empirical results, including application to spike sorting, support the premise that a carefully designed auto-encoder can indeed recover the dictionary and separate sources when only the number of dictionary elements is known and overlaps are sparse.

The significance of CRsAE lies in bridging two usually separate worlds. Optimization-based dictionary learning offers interpretability, theoretical grounding, and explicit sparsity, but can be computationally demanding and sensitive to initialization. Deep auto-encoders offer scalability and flexibility, but often lack interpretability and may learn representations that do not correspond to a generative dictionary. CRsAE combines these strengths. Its encoder is not an arbitrary black-box feature extractor; it is an unrolled sparse-coding algorithm. Its decoder is not a separate reconstruction network; it is the dictionary synthesis operator. Consequently, the learned parameters have direct meaning as dictionary elements, and the latent code has a direct interpretation as sparse coefficients. This makes CRsAE particularly attractive for scientific domains where the goal is not merely reconstruction but discovery of interpretable structure.

The application to spike sorting illustrates this advantage. Spike sorting is a source separation problem in which extracellular recordings contain overlapping action potentials from multiple neurons. CRsAE, knowing only the number of sources and assuming sparsely many can overlap, is able to separate them and recover waveforms. This is notable because spike sorting traditionally relies on hand-engineered features, clustering, and careful preprocessing. CRsAE instead learns a convolutional dictionary of spike waveforms and performs sparse coding jointly. The sensitivity analysis as a function of SNR further clarifies when the method can be trusted: performance is high in favorable noise conditions and degrades gracefully as noise increases, with a transition region where dictionary recovery and source separation become unreliable. This behavior is consistent with the intuition that sparse dictionary recovery requires sufficient signal-to-noise ratio and enough sparse events to constrain the dictionary.

Several limitations remain. First, CRsAE assumes a convolutional dictionary model and a known number of dictionary elements. In many real blind source separation problems, neither the number of sources nor the convolutional structure is known a priori. Second, the method relies on sparse overlap; if sources overlap densely, the sparse-coding step becomes ill-posed and the encoder may not produce a unique or stable representation. Third, the unrolled FISTA iterations introduce hyperparameters, including step size, sparsity regularization, and number of iterations, which affect both training and inference. Although end-to-end training can learn some of these, the architecture still requires careful tuning. Fourth, while we derived back-propagation and demonstrated dictionary recovery, a complete theoretical characterization of identifiability, convergence, and sample complexity under noise is not yet available. Finally, the spike-sorting experiments, while encouraging, are not a substitute for broad validation across recording modalities, electrode geometries, and nonstationary noise.

Future work should proceed along both theoretical and practical lines. Theoretically, it would be valuable to establish conditions under which CRsAE recovers the true convolutional dictionary up to scaling and permutation, and to quantify how recovery depends on SNR, sparsity, dictionary coherence, and the number of observations. Practically, CRsAE can be extended to nonnegative dictionaries, multi-channel and multidimensional convolutions, and structured sparsity. Adaptive sparsity penalties or learned thresholds could replace fixed regularization, and stochastic or online training could make the method scalable to long recordings. It would also be interesting to combine CRsAE with recurrent architectures beyond FISTA, such as learned iterative shrinkage-thresholding or plug-and-play priors, while preserving the encoder-decoder constraint. Applications beyond spike sorting include EEG/MEG source separation, calcium imaging, audio source separation, radar, and communication systems, wherever convolutional sparse models are plausible.

In conclusion, CRsAE demonstrates that constraining an auto-encoder to follow the structure of alternating-minimization dictionary learning enables scalable and interpretable convolutional dictionary learning. By tying the encoder and decoder through a shared dictionary and unrolling sparse coding with FISTA, the method recovers dictionaries and separates sources in noisy settings, as shown in spike sorting. The approach does not solve all blind source separation problems, and important theoretical and practical questions remain. Nevertheless, it provides a principled framework for combining optimization-based sparse coding with end-to-end learning, and it suggests a broader research direction: designing auto-encoders whose latent computations and parameters are explicitly constrained to match the inverse problem they are meant to solve.

Parkinson’s Disease (PD) is a chronic, progressive neurodegenerative disorder that affects millions of individuals worldwide, with prevalence rates rising sharply with age. In the United States alone, tens of millions of Americans are impacted by PD, either directly or through caregiving. The disease is characterized by a broad spectrum of motor symptoms—such as tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, and postural instability—as well as non-motor manifestations including cognitive decline, depression, and autonomic dysfunction. Critically, PD is highly heterogeneous: its clinical presentation, rate of progression, and underlying pathophysiology vary substantially across patients. This heterogeneity poses major challenges for early diagnosis, prognosis, and the development of disease-modifying therapies. Consequently, there is an urgent need for objective, sensitive, and reproducible biomarkers that can distinguish PD cases from healthy controls and track disease progression over time.

In recent years, considerable research efforts have focused on predictive and disease progression modeling of PD using clinical assessments and fluid biomarkers, such as cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) measures of alpha-synuclein, tau, and amyloid-beta. While these approaches have provided valuable insights, they often suffer from limited sensitivity and specificity, particularly in early disease stages. Neuroimaging has emerged as another powerful information source for neurodegenerative disease research. Structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI), and positron emission tomography (PET) with tracers for dopamine transporter or metabolic activity can reveal subtle brain alterations associated with PD. These modalities capture complementary aspects of brain structure, function, and metabolism, and their combination—multimodal fusion—has the potential to improve diagnostic and predictive accuracy. However, effectively integrating heterogeneous brain imaging data remains a formidable challenge due to high dimensionality, small sample sizes, inter-subject variability, and complex, non-linear relationships among imaging features.

Traditional approaches to multimodal neuroimage analysis often rely on dimensionality reduction techniques such as principal component analysis (PCA), followed by classical machine learning classifiers. While simple and interpretable, these methods typically assume linear relationships and treat each modality independently before concatenation, which may fail to capture the intricate interplay between different imaging views. Moreover, they often ignore the intrinsic topological structure of the brain, where regions of interest (ROIs) can be regarded as nodes and their structural or functional connectivity as edges. Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have recently emerged as a powerful deep learning framework for learning representations from graph-structured data. By aggregating information from neighboring nodes, GCNs can effectively exploit both node features and the underlying graph topology. This makes them particularly well-suited for brain imaging data, where connectivity matrices naturally define a graph across brain regions.

Despite the promise of GCNs, most existing approaches focus on a single imaging modality or a single graph view. Yet, as noted, PD pathology is multi-faceted, and different imaging modalities provide distinct, complementary views of the same underlying brain network. For example, structural MRI reveals atrophy patterns, DTI captures white matter integrity, and rs-fMRI reflects functional connectivity—each of which may be altered in PD but in different ways. A naive concatenation of features from these modalities ignores the fact that each modality may have its own graph structure and that cross-modality interactions are essential for accurate classification. Therefore, there is a clear gap: a principled deep learning method that can simultaneously leverage multiple graph views derived from different brain imaging modalities and fuse them for relationship prediction, such as distinguishing PD patients from healthy controls.

To address this gap, we propose a novel Multi-View Graph Convolutional Network (MV-GCN) for neuroimage analysis in Parkinson’s disease. Our method models each imaging modality as a separate graph, where nodes correspond to brain regions and edges encode connectivity strengths or similarities. Each view undergoes dedicated graph convolution operations to learn view-specific node embeddings. These embeddings are then fused through a multi-view integration mechanism that allows the model to learn complementary representations across modalities. The fused representation is finally used for relationship prediction—specifically, classifying subjects as PD or control. By jointly optimizing the graph convolutions and the fusion process, our approach can capture both intra-view topological patterns and inter-view dependencies in an end-to-end manner.

We evaluate our proposed MV-GCN on the Parkinson’s Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) cohort, a large, longitudinal, multi-center observational study that includes comprehensive clinical, imaging, and biomarker data. On the task of distinguishing PD cases from controls, our approach achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.9537 ± 0.0587. In contrast, a traditional PCA-based baseline achieved only 0.6443 ± 0.0223 AUC. This substantial improvement demonstrates the effectiveness of multi-view graph convolution for fusing brain imaging modalities. The high AUC also suggests that our method can extract discriminative patterns that are not captured by linear dimensionality reduction techniques.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. We first review related work on neuroimaging in PD and graph convolutional networks. Then we describe the PPMI dataset and our preprocessing pipeline. Next, we detail the architecture of the Multi-View Graph Convolutional Network, including graph construction, convolution layers, and multi-view fusion. We present experimental results, compare with baseline methods, and provide ablation studies to analyze the contribution of each view and fusion strategy. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for PD diagnosis and future directions for multi-view graph learning in neurodegenerative disease research.

We used data from the Parkinson’s Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) cohort, a longitudinal observational study of Parkinson’s disease (PD) and healthy controls. Participants were included if they had baseline neuroimaging data from at least two of the following modalities: T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), and dopamine transporter SPECT (DaTSCAN). Subjects with severe motion artifacts, incomplete preprocessing, or missing clinical diagnosis were excluded. Diagnostic labels were defined as PD versus healthy control according to PPMI criteria. All images were preprocessed using standard pipelines. T1-weighted MRI scans were processed with FreeSurfer and parcellated into 116 regions of interest (ROIs) using the Automated Anatomical Labeling atlas. For each ROI, we extracted gray matter volume, cortical thickness, and surface area. DTI scans were corrected for eddy currents and head motion using FSL, registered to the T1 image, and used to compute fractional anisotropy (FA) within each ROI.
