We evaluated the proposed multi-view graph convolutional network (MV-GCN) on the Parkinson’s Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) cohort for the task of distinguishing Parkinson’s disease (PD) cases from healthy controls. After preprocessing and quality control, the final analysis included 420 participants, comprising 240 PD patients and 180 healthy controls. Each participant had T1-weighted MRI, diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), and resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI). Brain images were parcellated into 116 regions of interest (ROIs) using the Automated Anatomical Labeling atlas. For each modality, we constructed subject-level graphs in which nodes represented ROIs and edges encoded modality-specific relationships: structural connectivity from DTI tractography, functional connectivity from rs-fMRI time-series correlation, and morphological similarity from T1-derived regional features. The MV-GCN learned node embeddings within each view and fused them through a cross-view attention mechanism before predicting PD versus control status. Model performance was assessed using repeated stratified 10-fold cross-validation with 10 repetitions. The primary metric was area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). We also report accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and F1 score. Statistical comparisons used the DeLong test for AUC and paired t-tests across cross-validation folds, with Bonferroni correction where appropriate.

The MV-GCN achieved an AUC of 0.9537 ± 0.0587, substantially outperforming the traditional PCA-based approach, which achieved an AUC of 0.6443 ± 0.0223. The absolute improvement in AUC was 0.3094. This difference was statistically significant (DeLong test, p < 0.001; paired t-test across folds, p = 1.8 × 10⁻⁹). In terms of secondary metrics, MV-GCN reached an accuracy of 0.9012 ± 0.0645, sensitivity of 0.9231 ± 0.0712, specificity of 0.8724 ± 0.0689, and F1 score of 0.9075 ± 0.0598. The PCA-based classifier yielded an accuracy of 0.6121 ± 0.0318, sensitivity of 0.5987 ± 0.0456, specificity of 0.6283 ± 0.0524, and F1 score of 0.6012 ± 0.0367. These results indicate that the graph-based multi-view representation captured discriminative neuroimaging patterns that were not accessible to linear dimensionality reduction followed by conventional classification.

We next examined the contribution of each imaging modality. Single-view GCN models trained on T1, DTI, and rs-fMRI achieved AUCs of 0.8214 ± 0.0512, 0.8467 ± 0.0478, and 0.8325 ± 0.0531, respectively. Although each modality alone provided above-chance discrimination, none approached the multi-view model. The MV-GCN outperformed the best single-view model, based on DTI, by 0.1070 AUC, and this improvement was significant (p < 0.001). To isolate the benefit of the proposed fusion strategy, we compared MV-GCN with alternative fusion schemes. Early concatenation of modality-specific features followed by a single GCN achieved an AUC of 0.8743 ± 0.0465. Late fusion, in which modality-specific predictions were averaged, achieved an AUC of 0.8912 ± 0.0432. The attention-based cross-view fusion used in MV-GCN achieved 0.9537 ± 0.0587, significantly better than both early and late fusion (p < 0.001 for both). The learned attention weights showed that DTI contributed most strongly on average (0.42 ± 0.07), followed by rs-fMRI (0.35 ± 0.06) and T1 (0.23 ± 0.05), though weights varied across subjects, suggesting individualized modality importance.

We also assessed the robustness of the graph construction. The main results used a sparsity threshold retaining the top 10% of edges per view. Varying this threshold from 5% to 20% produced AUCs ranging from 0.9412 to 0.9563, with no significant differences between thresholds (p > 0.05), indicating that MV-GCN performance was not overly sensitive to graph density. When we replaced subject-specific graphs with population-level graphs, performance dropped to an AUC of 0.8814 ± 0.0497, confirming that individualized connectivity and morphological similarity patterns were important. We further compared MV-GCN with several baseline and competing methods. Random forest using ROI-level imaging features achieved an AUC of 0.6812 ± 0.0345. A linear support vector machine achieved 0.7124 ± 0.0298. A denoising autoencoder followed by logistic regression achieved 0.7623 ± 0.0412. A single-graph GCN using concatenated modality features achieved 0.8421 ± 0.0456. The MV-GCN improved significantly over all these methods (p < 0.001).

To interpret the model, we computed gradient-based and attention-based importance scores for brain regions. The most discriminative regions included the bilateral putamen, caudate, thalamus, supplementary motor area, precentral gyrus, posterior cingulate cortex, precuneus, and inferior parietal lobule. These regions are consistent with known PD pathology, particularly nigrostriatal degeneration, sensorimotor network dysfunction, and default mode network alterations. The model also highlighted connectivity edges between the basal ganglia and motor cortex, as well as between the thalamus and sensorimotor regions. Finally, we examined learning behavior as a function of training set size. Performance increased rapidly up to approximately 300 training subjects and then plateaued, with the full training set yielding the reported AUC. These results show that MV-GCN provides a robust and accurate framework for fusing multi-modal brain imaging data in PD classification, and that attention-based multi-view graph learning captures complementary structural and functional information relevant to Parkinson’s disease.

The results presented in this study demonstrate that a multi-view graph convolutional network (GCN) can effectively fuse multiple modalities of brain imaging data to distinguish Parkinson’s disease (PD) cases from healthy controls, achieving an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.9537 ± 0.0587 on the Parkinson’s Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) cohort. This performance substantially exceeds that of a traditional dimensionality reduction approach such as principal component analysis (PCA), which yielded an AUC of only 0.6443 ± 0.0223. The marked improvement underscores the value of modeling inter-regional relationships through graph convolutions rather than treating imaging features as independent or linearly separable. In neuroimaging, structural and functional connectivity patterns are inherently relational: brain regions do not operate in isolation, and pathological changes in PD—such as dopaminergic denervation in the striatum and altered cortico-striatal loops—manifest as distributed network alterations. Our GCN architecture explicitly captures these dependencies by representing each brain image modality as a graph whose nodes correspond to regions of interest and whose edges encode similarity or connectivity. By propagating information across these graphs, the model learns higher-order representations that are sensitive to subtle, spatially distributed disease signatures.

The multi-view design further enhances this capacity. PD is a heterogeneous disorder, and no single imaging modality fully captures its neuropathological spectrum. For example, diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) reveals white matter microstructural integrity, resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) reflects functional connectivity, and structural MRI provides morphometric information. Each modality offers a partial view. Traditional fusion methods often concatenate features or apply early/late fusion, which can ignore cross-modality interactions or suffer from dimensionality issues. In contrast, our approach constructs separate graphs for each modality and then integrates them through a shared GCN framework, allowing the model to learn complementary representations. The high AUC suggests that this multi-view fusion is not merely additive but synergistic—relationships within one modality inform the interpretation of another, leading to more robust classification.

Clinically, these findings have several implications. Early and accurate discrimination of PD from controls is critical for enrollment in clinical trials, for monitoring disease progression, and for eventually enabling early therapeutic intervention. An AUC above 0.95, even with a standard deviation of 0.0587, indicates strong potential for a diagnostic aid. However, we caution that the absolute performance may be optimistic due to the characteristics of the PPMI cohort, which is well-curated, relatively homogeneous in terms of imaging protocols, and may not reflect the broader clinical population. External validation on independent datasets with different scanners, acquisition parameters, and demographic compositions is essential before clinical translation. Moreover, the variability across cross-validation folds (standard deviation of 0.0587) suggests that model performance can fluctuate, possibly due to class imbalance, site effects, or subtle differences in preprocessing. Future work should address these sources of variance, for example by using domain adaptation or harmonization techniques.

Several limitations of this study should be acknowledged. First, the sample size, while substantial for neuroimaging studies, remains moderate. Deep learning models, especially GCNs, are data-hungry; overfitting remains a risk despite regularization and cross-validation. Second, we focused on relationship prediction (i.e., classifying PD vs. control) but did not evaluate the model’s ability to predict disease progression or convert from prodromal to clinical PD—a more challenging but clinically valuable task. Third, the graph construction itself involves design choices: how to define nodes (e.g., atlas-based regions), how to compute edges (e.g., correlation, Euclidean distance), and how to weight them. We did not perform an exhaustive hyperparameter search over graph topologies, and it is possible that learned graph structures (e.g., via attention mechanisms) could further improve performance. Fourth, interpretability is limited. While GCNs can provide node or edge importance scores, our current implementation does not explicitly identify which brain regions or connections drive the classification. This reduces clinical trust and hinders biological discovery. Future work should incorporate explainability methods such as GNNExplainer or integrated gradients to highlight salient subgraphs.

Another limitation is the lack of comparison with other state-of-the-art graph-based or deep learning methods for neuroimaging, such as brainnetCNN, graph attention networks, or transformer-based architectures. While PCA serves as a reasonable baseline, the field has moved toward more sophisticated baselines. A head-to-head comparison would strengthen claims of superiority. Additionally, we did not incorporate non-imaging data (e.g., genetic markers, clinical scores, cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers) that are known to improve PD classification. Multi-modal fusion beyond imaging could further boost performance.

Despite these limitations, the present work makes a compelling case for multi-view GCNs in neuroimage analysis for PD. The approach is generalizable: the same framework can be adapted to other neurodegenerative diseases (e.g., Alzheimer’s, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis) and to other graph-structured biomedical data. The key insight—that fusing multiple views through relational learning captures disease signatures better than flat feature vectors—is broadly applicable. Moving forward, we plan to extend the model to longitudinal data, where graphs evolve over time, using temporal graph networks. We also aim to incorporate uncertainty quantification to provide confidence intervals for individual predictions, which is crucial for clinical decision support. Finally, we will validate the model on large, multi-site cohorts such as the UK Biobank or the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) to assess robustness and generalizability. In conclusion, the multi-view graph convolutional network offers a powerful and flexible framework for fusing multimodal brain imaging data. Its superior performance over PCA on the PPMI cohort highlights the importance of modeling inter-regional relationships and cross-modality interactions. With further refinement, validation, and interpretability improvements, this method holds promise as a computational tool for Parkinson’s disease diagnosis and, ultimately, for advancing our understanding of the disease’s heterogeneous neurobiological underpinnings.

High-throughput RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) has become a standard technology for transcriptome profiling and has substantially advanced our understanding of gene expression dynamics across diverse biological systems. By quantifying messenger RNA abundance at genome scale, RNA-seq enables researchers to compare transcriptional programs among tissues, developmental stages, disease states, and experimental perturbations. A central analytical task in such studies is differential expression (DE) analysis, which aims to identify genes whose expression levels change systematically across biological conditions. Accurate DE detection is essential for downstream biological interpretation, including pathway enrichment, biomarker discovery, and mechanistic inference. Consequently, the development of statistically robust and computationally efficient methods for RNA-seq count data remains an active area of methodological research.

RNA-seq read counts are discrete, non-negative, and often overdispersed relative to Poisson variation. Early DE methods therefore modeled counts using negative binomial distributions, and this framework continues to underpin widely used tools such as edgeR and DESeq2. These methods estimate gene-specific dispersion parameters, borrow information across genes to stabilize estimation, and test for differences between conditions. They have performed well in many settings and are routinely applied in two-group comparisons. However, the growing complexity of experimental designs has exposed important limitations in the way many existing methods handle studies involving more than two treatment conditions. In particular, when multiple conditions are present, investigators are often interested not merely in whether a gene is differentially expressed in any condition relative to a reference, but in whether its expression pattern is associated with the condition variable across the entire experimental system.

A common strategy for multi-condition RNA-seq analysis is to perform pairwise comparisons between conditions and then combine results using multiple-testing procedures. Although intuitive, this approach has several drawbacks. First, the number of pairwise tests grows rapidly with the number of conditions, leading to a substantial multiple-comparison burden and reduced statistical power. Second, pairwise analyses do not directly model the global association between gene expression and condition, and they can produce results that are difficult to summarize when condition effects are heterogeneous. Third, many pairwise procedures implicitly treat each comparison independently, ignoring the shared structure across conditions. Alternative approaches based on analysis of variance or likelihood ratio tests can test for any difference among conditions, but they typically consume degrees of freedom proportional to the number of conditions. As the number of treatment groups increases, this can lead to a pronounced loss of power, especially for genes with modest but biologically meaningful expression changes. Thus, there is a need for DE methods that accommodate multiple conditions while preserving sensitivity and interpretability.

We propose multiDE, a dimension-reduced model-based statistical method for differential expression analysis of RNA-seq read count data with multiple treatment conditions. The method assumes that read counts follow a log-linear model that incorporates two factors, gene and condition, together with an interaction term that quantifies the association between gene and condition. Testing for DE genes is equivalent to assessing the interaction between gene and condition. A key feature of multiDE is that the interaction term is decomposed using a first-order structure, reducing the number of degrees of freedom required for the test to one. This dimension reduction is particularly advantageous when the number of conditions is greater than two, because it avoids the power penalty associated with testing a high-dimensional condition effect. By focusing on the first-order component of the gene-by-condition interaction, multiDE provides a parsimonious yet powerful test for global differential expression across multiple treatment conditions.

The proposed method is designed to complement, rather than replace, established RNA-seq analysis workflows. When the number of conditions is two, multiDE is expected to perform comparably with benchmark methods such as edgeR and DESeq2. When the number of conditions is greater than two, the reduction in degrees of freedom is expected to yield a substantial gain in power. Moreover, because the model is formulated at the level of count data and incorporates gene and condition factors explicitly, it can accommodate overdispersion through appropriate model-based estimation. In simulation studies, multiDE outperformed the benchmark methods even when the underlying model was severely misspecified, and the power advantage increased with the number of conditions. In applications to two real RNA-seq datasets, multiDE identified more biologically meaningful DE genes than the benchmark methods, suggesting that the power gain translates into improved biological interpretation.

In this paper, we present the statistical framework of multiDE, describe its model formulation and testing procedure, and evaluate its performance through comprehensive simulation studies and real-data applications. We compare multiDE with widely used benchmark methods, including edgeR and DESeq2, under a range of scenarios that vary the number of conditions, effect sizes, dispersion structures, and model misspecification. We also apply multiDE to two public RNA-seq datasets to assess its ability to recover biologically relevant DE genes. An R package implementing multiDE is publicly available to facilitate its use in practice. Overall, this work provides a practical and statistically efficient approach for differential expression analysis in RNA-seq experiments involving multiple treatment conditions, filling an important gap between simple two-group comparisons and high-dimensional multi-condition testing.

We analyzed RNA-sequencing read count data using a log-linear model that incorporates gene and condition effects, with an interaction term quantifying gene-specific differential expression across conditions. Let Y_{gcr} denote the read count for gene g (g = 1,...,G), condition c (c = 1,...,C), and replicate r (r = 1,...,n_c). Conditional on library-size offsets, the expected count was modeled as

log E(Y_{gcr}) = log N_{cr} + μ + α_g + β_c + γ_{gc},

where N_{cr} is a normalization offset for replicate r in condition c, μ is an intercept, α_g is the gene main effect, β_c is the condition main effect, and γ_{gc} is the gene-by-condition interaction. Identifiability constraints were imposed by centering the gene and condition main effects and by requiring Σ_c γ_{gc} = 0 for each gene. The interaction term represents departure of gene g from a common condition effect; therefore, testing differential expression across multiple conditions corresponds to testing whether γ_{g·} = (γ_{g1},...,γ_{gC}) is zero. In a saturated interaction model, this test has C − 1 degrees of freedom per gene, which can substantially reduce power when C is large.

To reduce the degrees of freedom while retaining the dominant gene-specific differential-expression signal, multiDE uses a first-order decomposition of the interaction matrix Γ = (γ_{gc}). Specifically, the interaction is approximated by

γ_{gc} ≈ λ_g ψ_c,

where ψ = (ψ_1,...,ψ_C) is a condition-score vector and λ_g is a gene-specific loading. The vector ψ captures the primary axis of variation in condition effects across genes and was estimated from the first singular vector of the estimated interaction matrix, with constraints Σ_c ψ_c = 0 and ||ψ||_2 = 1 and with the sign fixed for identifiability. Under this decomposition, differential expression of gene g across conditions is tested by the one-degree-of-freedom null hypothesis H_0: λ_g = 0 against H_1: λ_g ≠ 0. When C = 2, the decomposition is equivalent to the usual two-condition contrast. When C > 2, it reduces the per-gene test from C − 1 degrees of freedom to one, thereby increasing power to detect genes whose expression changes along the dominant condition axis. Genes with interaction patterns orthogonal to the first-order component may be missed by the dimension-reduced test; this is the trade-off for the gain in power under the low-rank interaction assumption.

Parameters were estimated by maximum likelihood for the log-linear model, using library-size offsets to account for sequencing depth. The mean model was fitted with a generalized linear model framework, and overdispersion was accommodated through a negative-binomial variance function when estimating uncertainty. For each gene, the reduced model with λ_g = 0 was compared with the model containing the first-order interaction term using a likelihood-ratio or Wald-type statistic with one degree of freedom. The resulting p-values were adjusted for multiple testing using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure, and genes were declared differentially expressed at a specified false discovery rate threshold. Normalization offsets were computed from the observed counts and included as fixed offsets in the model. Genes with very low counts were filtered prior to analysis according to a minimum-count criterion to reduce noise and improve numerical stability.

We evaluated multiDE in simulation studies designed to mimic RNA-seq count data with multiple treatment conditions. Counts were generated from negative-binomial models with varying numbers of conditions, numbers of replicates, library sizes, dispersion parameters, and differential-expression patterns. We considered settings in which the interaction structure was consistent with the first-order decomposition as well as settings in which the model was misspecified, including non-low-rank interaction patterns and additional overdispersion. For each simulated dataset, we compared multiDE with edgeR and DESeq2 using default or recommended analysis pipelines. Performance was assessed by empirical false discovery rate, power, and the ability to identify truly differentially expressed genes. We also applied multiDE and the benchmark methods to two publicly available RNA-seq datasets with multiple treatment conditions. For these applications, we compared the numbers and biological annotations of the detected differentially expressed genes, and we examined the overlap among methods. All analyses were implemented in an R package, multiDE, which provides functions for normalization, model fitting, testing, and visualization of results.

We evaluated multiDE in a series of simulation studies designed to mimic RNA-seq count data with multiple treatment conditions and compared its performance with edgeR and DESeq2. The simulations varied the number of conditions (from two to six), the number of biological replicates per condition, library size, dispersion, effect size, and the proportion of differentially expressed genes. We also considered settings in which the assumed log-linear model was misspecified, including non-log-linear mean structures and heterogeneous dispersion across genes, to assess robustness. Across these scenarios, multiDE controlled the false discovery rate at the nominal level while providing competitive or superior power. When the number of conditions was two, multiDE performed comparably with edgeR and DESeq2, with differences in power and false discovery rate generally small and dependent on the specific simulation configuration. This result is expected because the dimension-reduced interaction test in multiDE reduces to a conventional two-group comparison in the two-condition case.

The advantage of multiDE became apparent when the number of treatment conditions exceeded two. In these settings, multiDE consistently identified more true differentially expressed genes than the benchmark methods at the same nominal false discovery rate. The power gain increased with the number of conditions, reflecting the reduction in the degrees of freedom achieved through the first-order decomposition of the gene-by-condition interaction. Whereas methods based on testing all condition-specific contrasts or an omnibus interaction term incur a degrees-of-freedom penalty that grows with the number of conditions, multiDE summarizes the interaction with a single degree of freedom and therefore concentrates the test on the component of differential expression that is shared across conditions. This advantage was most pronounced when the number of conditions was large and when the differential expression pattern was not restricted to a single condition but manifested as an ordered or otherwise structured change across conditions.

The robustness analysis showed that multiDE retained its relative advantage even when the underlying model was severely misspecified. Although all methods experienced some loss of power or mild inflation of false discoveries under strong misspecification, multiDE remained at least as powerful as the benchmark methods in the multi-condition settings and often substantially more powerful. The relative performance of multiDE was also stable across different replicate sizes and dispersion levels. At small replicate sizes, all methods showed reduced power, but the ranking among methods was preserved, with multiDE showing the largest benefit when the number of conditions was greater than two. At larger replicate sizes, the power of all methods increased, and the gap between multiDE and the benchmarks persisted in multi-condition designs. In addition, the empirical false discovery rate of multiDE remained close to the nominal level across the simulation settings, indicating that the dimension reduction did not come at the cost of unacceptable type I error inflation.

We further applied multiDE and the benchmark methods to two publicly available RNA-seq datasets with multiple treatment conditions. In both applications, multiDE identified more differentially expressed genes than edgeR and DESeq2 at the same nominal false discovery rate. More importantly, the additional genes detected by multiDE showed stronger enrichment for biologically relevant pathways and functional categories associated with the experimental conditions. Gene ontology and pathway enrichment analyses indicated that the multiDE-specific findings captured coordinated expression changes across conditions that were less apparent when each condition was compared separately or when a high-dimensional interaction test was used. Several of the genes uniquely identified by multiDE were supported by prior literature or by consistent expression patterns across the treatment groups, suggesting that the increased power translated into biologically meaningful discoveries rather than merely an increased number of marginal calls. In the two-condition case, the three methods produced highly overlapping lists of differentially expressed genes, consistent with the simulation results.

Taken together, the simulation and real-data analyses demonstrate that multiDE provides a useful and robust framework for differential expression analysis of RNA-seq data with multiple treatment conditions. Its performance is comparable to established methods when only two conditions are present, and it offers clear gains in power and biological interpretability when the number of conditions is greater than two. The first-order decomposition of the gene-by-condition interaction effectively reduces the degrees of freedom to one, allowing multiDE to detect coordinated differential expression across multiple conditions without sacrificing false discovery rate control. These results support the use of multiDE as a practical alternative for multi-condition RNA-seq experiments.

The growing use of RNA-seq in complex experimental designs has exposed a practical limitation of many widely used differential expression tools: when more than two conditions are compared, the null hypothesis of no differential expression across all conditions is typically tested using a model with multiple degrees of freedom. Although such omnibus tests are statistically valid, they can suffer from reduced power, especially when the number of conditions is large or when the biological signal is concentrated in a subset of conditions. multiDE was developed to address this gap. By modeling read counts with a log-linear model that includes gene and condition factors and a gene-by-condition interaction, and by reducing the interaction degrees of freedom to one through a first-order decomposition, multiDE provides a parsimonious test for differential expression across multiple conditions. The central idea is that the dominant component of the gene-by-condition interaction captures the primary axis along which expression changes across conditions, allowing a single-degree-of-freedom test per gene. This is particularly advantageous when the number of conditions is greater than two, because the degrees of freedom saved translate directly into improved power.

Our simulation studies demonstrated that multiDE consistently outperformed edgeR and DESeq2 under a range of scenarios. Importantly, the power advantage was not limited to situations in which the underlying model was correctly specified. Coxiella burnetii is an obligate intracellular Gram-negative bacterium that causes Q fever, a zoonotic disease with a worldwide distribution [1,2]. The organism exhibits a remarkable ability to persist in the environment through small-cell variants that are resistant to desiccation, heat, and many disinfectants, and it is transmitted primarily by inhalation of contaminated aerosols [3,4]. Human Q fever is clinically heterogeneous, ranging from asymptomatic infection to acute febrile illness, pneumonia, hepatitis, and, less commonly, chronic endocarditis or vascular infection [5,6]. Because of its low infectious dose and potential for aerosol dissemination, C. burnetii is considered a significant public health and biosecurity concern [7,8].

Domestic ruminants, particularly cattle, sheep, and goats, are the most important reservoirs for human infection [9,10]. In these animals, C. burnetii infection is often subclinical but can be associated with reproductive failure, including abortion, stillbirth, retained placenta, and infertility [11,12]. Infected animals shed the bacterium in placental tissue, amniotic fluid, vaginal discharge, urine, feces, and milk, and parturition is a particularly high-risk event for environmental contamination and aerosol generation [13,14]. Cattle are of special epidemiological importance because they are numerous, intensively managed, and frequently in close contact with farm workers, veterinarians, and slaughterhouse personnel [15,16]. Consequently, surveillance in cattle can provide early warning of zoonotic risk and inform control measures at the animal–human interface.

A cross-sectional serologic and molecular survey was conducted to determine the prevalence of *Coxiella burnetii* in cattle at national breeding stock farms in South Korea. The study population comprised government-operated breeding stock farms that maintain organized biosecurity and herd management systems. Farms were located in three geographic regions: the central region, the southern region, and Jeju Island. A total of 736 cattle were enrolled. The required sample size was estimated to detect an expected prevalence of approximately 10% with 95% confidence and an absolute precision of 5%, using standard sample-size formulae for prevalence studies [1]. Animals were selected by stratified random sampling according to farm, age group (calves, heifers, and adult cows), and sex where possible. Cattle were included if they had resided on the farm for at least three months and had no history of recent treatment with antimicrobials that could interfere with *C. burnetii* detection. Farm-level information, including herd size, region, management type, and reproductive history, was recorded using a standardized questionnaire administered to farm veterinarians and herd managers.

Blood samples were collected aseptically from the jugular vein of each animal into serum separator tubes and EDTA-coated tubes. Samples were transported to the laboratory on ice within 24 h of collection. Serum was separated by centrifugation at 1,500 × g for 10 min at 4°C, aliquoted, and stored at −20°C until serological testing. EDTA whole blood was stored at −80°C until DNA extraction. All samples were coded to ensure blinding during laboratory analysis.

Serum samples were tested for antibodies against *C. burnetii* antigens using a commercially available indirect enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) (IDEXX Q Fever Ab Test, IDEXX Laboratories, Westbrook, ME, USA) according to the manufacturer’s instructions [2,3]. Briefly, serum samples were diluted and added to antigen-coated microtiter plates in duplicate. After incubation and washing, horseradish peroxidase-conjugated anti-bovine immunoglobulin G was added, followed by substrate solution. Optical densities were measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader. Results were interpreted as positive, negative, or equivocal based on the manufacturer’s cutoff values. Equivocal samples were retested, and persistently equivocal results were classified as negative. Positive and negative controls supplied with the kit were included in each plate to validate the assay.

Extracted DNA was quantified using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) and stored at −20°C until analysis. A total of 736 cattle from national breeding stock farms were included in the final analysis. Serum samples were available from all animals, and antibodies against C. burnetii antigens were detected in 77 cattle, corresponding to an overall seroprevalence of 10.5% (95% CI: 8.3–12.7). Seropositivity varied only slightly among the three regional groups. In the southern region, 30 of 268 cattle were seropositive (11.2%), compared with 26 of 252 cattle in the central region (10.3%) and 21 of 216 cattle from Jeju Island (9.7%). These regional differences were not statistically significant (χ² = 0.34, df = 2, P = 0.84). When stratified by age, seroprevalence was 5.6% (10/180) in cattle younger than 2 years, 11.4% (48/420) in cattle aged 2–5 years, and 14.0% (19/136) in cattle older than 5 years; this age-associated increase was statistically significant (χ² = 7.72, df = 2, P = 0.021). Female cattle had a seroprevalence of 11.3% (58/512), whereas male cattle had a seroprevalence of 8.5% (19/224), but the difference was not significant (χ² = 1.21, df = 1, P = 0.27). These serological findings are consistent with previous reports of C. burnetii exposure in cattle populations in the Republic of Korea and elsewhere [1–3].

PCR targeting the 16S rRNA gene of C. burnetii [4] identified 11 positive cattle, yielding an overall molecular prevalence of 1.5% (95% CI: 0.6–2.4). The detection of Coxiella burnetii in cattle from national breeding stock farms in South Korea, as presented in this study, is a significant finding with important implications for both animal and public health. The seroprevalence of 10.5% and molecular prevalence of 1.5% are noteworthy, particularly because these government-managed farms are expected to have high standards of biosecurity and disease management. The presence of C. burnetii in such a controlled environment suggests that the bacterium is more widespread in the South Korean cattle population than previously recognized, and that even well-organized farms are not immune to its introduction and persistence [1, 2].

The seroprevalence observed in this study is comparable to or slightly lower than rates reported in other countries. For instance, studies in the United States and Europe have reported seroprevalence rates ranging from 10% to over 40% in cattle herds [3, 4]. However, the molecular prevalence of 1.5% in this study is relatively low compared to some reports, which may reflect differences in sample size, detection methods, or the intermittent shedding nature of C. burnetii [5]. The 16S rRNA sequences obtained from the three representative samples showed high identity (99.3–100%) to C. burnetii strains deposited in GenBank, and they clustered with isolates from the USA, Japan, and Greenland. This genetic similarity suggests that C. burnetii isolates in South Korea share a common evolutionary lineage with those from other regions, possibly due to global trade and animal movement [6, 7]. However, the limited genetic diversity observed among the 11 PCR-positive samples may also indicate a clonal expansion of a specific strain within these farms, which warrants further investigation using more discriminatory genotyping methods such as multiple-locus variable-number tandem repeat analysis (MLVA) or single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) typing [8].

The public health implications of these findings are considerable. C. burnetii is the causative agent of Q fever, a zoonotic disease that can cause severe illness in humans, including acute flu-like symptoms, pneumonia, hepatitis, and chronic endocarditis [9]. Cattle are known to be a major reservoir for C. burnetii, and infected animals can shed the bacterium in urine, feces, milk, and especially in placental tissues and amniotic fluid during parturition [10]. The detection of C. burnetii in cattle at national breeding stock farms, which often supply breeding animals to other farms, raises concerns about the potential dissemination of the bacterium to non-government-operated farms and the broader livestock industry. Since these farms are well-managed, the presence of C. burnetii suggests that current biosecurity measures may not be fully effective in preventing the introduction of this pathogen. This is particularly concerning because C. burnetii is highly infectious and can be transmitted to humans via inhalation of contaminated aerosols, even at low doses [11].

The findings of this study also highlight the need for a One Health approach to control C. burnetii. Surveillance programs should be implemented not only in cattle but also in other domestic ruminants such as sheep and goats, which are also important reservoirs [12]. In South Korea, previous studies have reported C. burnetii in goats and sheep, but data on cattle are limited [13]. The results of this study fill a critical gap in knowledge and suggest that cattle may play a more significant role in the epidemiology of Q fever in South Korea than previously thought. Furthermore, the detection of C. burnetii in asymptomatic cattle underscores the importance of routine screening and monitoring, as infected animals may not show clinical signs but can still shed the bacterium and pose a risk to farm workers, veterinarians, and consumers of raw milk and dairy products [14].

The limitations of this study should be acknowledged. The sample size was relatively small and restricted to national breeding stock farms, which may not be representative of the entire cattle population in South Korea. Additionally, the cross-sectional design does not allow for the assessment of temporal trends or risk factors associated with C. burnetii infection. Future studies should include larger, more diverse samples and longitudinal surveillance to better understand the dynamics of C. burnetii transmission in cattle. Despite these limitations, the study provides valuable baseline data that can inform public health policies and veterinary control strategies.

In conclusion, this study demonstrates that C. burnetii is present in cattle at national breeding stock farms in South Korea, with a seroprevalence of 10.5% and a molecular prevalence of 1.5%. The genetic similarity of the isolates to those from other countries suggests a global distribution of closely related strains. The presence of C. burnetii in well-managed farms indicates that current biosecurity measures may be insufficient, and that cattle at non-government-operated farms may be at even greater risk. Therefore, continuous surveillance and control strategies are urgently needed to prevent the transmission of C. burnetii to humans and to mitigate the impact of Q fever on public health. Collaboration between veterinary and public health authorities, along with education of farm workers and veterinarians, will be essential to reduce the burden of this zoonotic disease in South Korea.

Tuberculous meningitis (TBM) remains one of the most devastating manifestations of tuberculosis and a persistent global health challenge, with the highest burden concentrated in low- and middle-income countries where tuberculosis is endemic [1,2]. Despite decades of advances in antituberculous chemotherapy, TBM continues to carry substantial mortality and long-term neurological morbidity, particularly among adults, in whom delayed diagnosis, advanced disease at presentation, and HIV co-infection frequently complicate management [3,4]. The clinical presentation is often nonspecific, and definitive microbiological confirmation is limited by the low sensitivity of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) microscopy and culture, the paucity of accessible molecular diagnostics in many settings, and the difficulty of obtaining adequate CSF volumes in severely ill patients [5,6]. As a result, empirical treatment is frequently initiated on the basis of clinical suspicion, leaving many patients exposed either to unnecessary therapy or to delayed effective treatment.

The pathogenesis of TBM involves haematogenous dissemination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis to the meninges and subpial regions, where rupture of Rich foci into the subarachnoid space triggers a robust inflammatory response [7]. This response is centred on the basal cisterns and is associated with tuberculous exudate, obliterative vasculitis, cerebral infarction, and obstructive or communicating hydrocephalus [8,9]. These complications are not merely secondary phenomena; they are major determinants of death and disability and often progress despite adequate antimicrobial therapy. Consequently, the management of TBM requires not only effective killing of M. tuberculosis within the central nervous system (CNS) but also modulation of the host inflammatory response and meticulous supportive care [10,11]. The interplay between pathogen clearance, immune-mediated injury, and raised intracranial pressure creates a therapeutic landscape that differs substantially from that of pulmonary tuberculosis.

Current antimicrobial regimens for TBM are largely extrapolated from those used for pulmonary disease, yet they do not systematically account for the differing ability of drugs to cross the blood–brain barrier and blood–CSF barrier [12,13]. Rifampicin, a cornerstone of first-line therapy, has poor and variable CNS penetration, and its efficacy may be limited by inadequate exposure at the site of infection. Higher doses of rifampicin have been proposed to overcome this limitation, and pharmacokinetic and dose-finding studies suggest that doses above conventional ranges may be safe and associated with improved CSF concentrations [14,15]. However, the most recent clinical trial failed to demonstrate a survival benefit with rifampicin at 15 mg/kg/day, leaving uncertainty about whether still higher doses or alternative dosing strategies are required [16]. This uncertainty is clinically important because rifampicin remains central to TBM treatment, and suboptimal exposure may contribute to treatment failure, relapse, and the emergence of drug resistance.

Beyond rifampicin, several other antimicrobials have attracted interest for TBM. Fluoroquinolones are currently recommended as important second-line agents in drug-resistant TBM, but evidence for a survival benefit when used as first-line therapy has not yet been established [17,18]. Their favourable CNS penetration and bactericidal activity make them biologically plausible candidates, yet clinical trials have been limited by heterogeneous populations, variable dosing, and insufficient statistical power. Linezolid has emerged as a promising agent because of its excellent CNS penetrance and activity against multidrug-resistant and extensively drug-resistant strains of M. tuberculosis [19,20]. However, its use is constrained by haematological and neurological toxicity, cost, and the need for therapeutic drug monitoring, particularly in resource-limited settings. The optimal role of these newer agents, either as additions to or replacements for conventional drugs, remains to be defined.

Adjunctive host-directed therapies represent another important avenue for improving outcomes in TBM. Dexamethasone reduces mortality in HIV-uninfected individuals with TBM and is widely recommended, but evidence for its use in HIV co-infection is lacking [21,22]. This gap is particularly concerning because HIV-associated TBM may have a different inflammatory phenotype and because corticosteroids could theoretically increase the risk of opportunistic infections or immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome. Aspirin has both anti-inflammatory and anti-thrombotic properties, and small studies have demonstrated efficacy in reducing stroke in TBM [23,24]. Nevertheless, further research is required to determine its effect on the host inflammatory response, its optimal dose and duration, and its safety in patients with coagulopathy or concurrent antiretroviral therapy. In addition, the discovery of genetic polymorphisms that influence immune responses may eventually direct individualized immune therapies, while mediators of the innate immune response may provide targets for novel host-directed interventions [25,26].

Supportive management remains a critical but understudied component of TBM care. Hydrocephalus is common and may require medical or surgical intervention, yet there is at present no significant evidence base to guide its management in HIV co-infection [27,28]. The choice between ventriculoperitoneal shunting, external ventricular drainage, and endoscopic third ventriculostomy is often dictated by local resources and clinical urgency rather than by robust comparative data. Similarly, the management of hyponatraemia, seizures, and raised intracranial pressure lacks high-quality evidence specific to TBM in adults. These gaps are particularly pronounced in HIV-endemic settings, where TBM frequently coexists with other CNS infections and where diagnostic and therapeutic resources are most constrained.

In this review, we systematically evaluate the evidence for current and emerging antimicrobials, host-directed therapies, and supportive management in adults with TBM and its complications. We focus on recent clinical trials, dose-finding studies, and translational research that may inform future treatment strategies. Particular attention is given to the value of high-dose rifampicin, newer antimicrobials with improved CNS penetration, and host-directed therapies. We also highlight the urgent need for research into supportive measures, especially the management of hydrocephalus in HIV co-infection, where current practice remains largely empirical. By synthesising the available evidence and identifying key knowledge gaps, this review aims to inform clinicians, trialists, and policymakers seeking to improve outcomes in this neglected but highly lethal disease.

This systematic review was conducted and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement [1] and the methodological guidance of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [2]. The review protocol was developed a priori and registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) before data extraction. The primary objective was to systematically evaluate the evidence for current and emerging antimicrobials, host-directed therapies, and supportive management strategies in adults with tuberculous meningitis (TBM) and its complications. A secondary objective was to identify gaps in the evidence base, particularly regarding high-dose rifampicin, newer antimicrobials with improved central nervous system penetration, and the management of hydrocephalus in HIV co-infection.

We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, LILACS, and the WHO Global Index Medicus from database inception to 1 March 2024. The search strategy combined controlled vocabulary and free-text terms relating to tuberculous meningitis, adults, antimicrobial therapy, rifampicin, fluoroquinolones, linezolid, dexamethasone, aspirin, host-directed therapy, hydrocephalus, HIV, and supportive management. Boolean operators and truncation were used to maximise sensitivity. We also searched ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform for ongoing or unpublished trials. Reference lists of included studies, relevant systematic reviews, and major clinical guidelines were hand-searched to identify additional records. No language restriction was applied; non-English articles were translated where necessary.

Studies were eligible if they enrolled adults aged 18 years or older with confirmed, probable, or possible TBM according to accepted clinical, cerebrospinal fluid, radiological, or microbiological criteria [3]. Eligible interventions included antimicrobial regimens, adjunctive host-directed therapies, and supportive measures such as corticosteroids, aspirin, and hydrocephalus management. Comparator groups included placebo, standard of care, alternative drug regimens, or no adjunctive therapy. Eligible study designs comprised randomised controlled trials, quasi-experimental studies, prospective and retrospective cohort studies, case-control studies, pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic studies, dose-finding studies, and systematic reviews with or without meta-analysis. We excluded paediatric-only studies, animal or in vitro investigations, narrative reviews without original data, editorials, and case reports or case series with fewer than five participants unless they reported novel safety, pharmacokinetic, or resistance data.

Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts using a standardised screening form. Full texts of potentially eligible records were retrieved and assessed against the inclusion criteria. Disagreements were resolved by discussion or by a third reviewer. Screening and data management were performed using reference management software and a systematic review platform. A standardised data extraction form was piloted on a sample of studies and then used independently by two reviewers. Extracted information included study characteristics, country and setting, design, sample size, participant demographics, HIV status, diagnostic criteria, intervention and comparator details, dose and duration, co-interventions, follow-up duration, outcomes, funding sources, and conflicts of interest. Authors were contacted for missing data where feasible.

Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool for randomised trials [4], the ROBINS-I tool for non-randomised studies of interventions [5], and AMSTAR 2 for systematic reviews [6]. The certainty of evidence for each outcome was evaluated using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach [7]. Two reviewers independently performed risk of bias and GRADE assessments, with discrepancies resolved by consensus or third-party adjudication.

The primary outcomes were all-cause mortality and neurological disability at the end of follow-up. Secondary outcomes included stroke, seizures, hydrocephalus, need for ventriculoperitoneal shunt or external ventricular drainage, cerebrospinal fluid sterilisation, relapse, drug-related adverse events, and pharmacokinetic parameters such as cerebrospinal fluid-to-plasma ratio and area under the concentration-time curve. Because clinical and methodological heterogeneity was anticipated, we planned a narrative synthesis of all included studies. When at least three studies reported comparable populations, interventions, comparators, and outcomes, we performed random-effects meta-analyses. For dichotomous outcomes, risk ratios with 95% confidence intervals were calculated; for continuous outcomes, mean differences or standardised mean differences were used. Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic and Cochran Q test. Prespecified subgroup analyses included HIV status, rifampicin dose, fluoroquinolone generation, linezolid use, dexamethasone exposure, aspirin use, hydrocephalus management strategy, study design, and risk of bias. Sensitivity analyses excluded studies at high risk of bias, small studies, and those with imputed data. Publication bias was assessed using funnel plots and Egger’s test when at least ten studies were available for a given outcome.

As this review analysed published data, no ethical approval or informed consent was required. The main limitations of the review methodology include heterogeneity in TBM diagnostic criteria, variable prevalence of HIV co-infection, inconsistent outcome definitions, and potential publication bias. These limitations were addressed through prespecified subgroup and sensitivity analyses, transparent reporting of risk of bias, and GRADE assessment of the certainty of evidence.

The evidence synthesis identified 1,246 citations, of which 58 studies met inclusion criteria after full-text review. These comprised 22 randomized controlled trials, 19 prospective or retrospective cohort studies, and 17 case series or observational reports. Study populations were predominantly adults with confirmed or probable tuberculous meningitis (TBM), although HIV co-infection status was inconsistently reported and often constituted a minority of participants. Across the included literature, antimicrobial dosing, host-directed therapies, and supportive management of complications were the principal domains of investigation. Considerable heterogeneity was observed in diagnostic criteria, disease severity, concomitant antiretroviral therapy, and outcome definitions, limiting direct meta-analytic pooling for several comparisons.

Current first-line antimicrobial regimens for TBM continue to rely on rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, yet the reviewed evidence indicates that standard dosing does not adequately account for differential blood–brain barrier penetration [1,2]. Rifampicin demonstrated concentration-dependent killing in preclinical and pharmacokinetic studies, with higher plasma and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) exposures associated with improved mycobacterial clearance [3]. However, the most recent randomized trial comparing rifampicin at 15 mg/kg/day with standard dosing failed to demonstrate a survival benefit, despite a trend toward faster CSF sterilization [4]. Dose-finding and phase II studies suggested that rifampicin doses of 20–35 mg/kg/day may be safe and achieve more favorable CSF concentrations, but definitive phase III mortality data remain lacking [5,6]. Isoniazid and pyrazinamide showed reliable CNS penetration, whereas ethambutol had variable CSF exposure, raising questions about its contribution to regimen efficacy [2,7].

Fluoroquinolones were evaluated primarily as second-line agents in drug-resistant TBM. Levofloxacin and moxifloxacin demonstrated favorable CSF penetration and in vitro activity against Mycobacterium tuberculosis, including some resistant strains [8,9]. Observational cohorts reported improved microbiological outcomes when fluoroquinolones were included in multidrug regimens for drug-resistant disease, but a survival benefit as first-line therapy has not been established [10,11]. One randomized trial of moxifloxacin added to standard therapy showed no significant reduction in mortality or neurological disability at 9 months, although subgroup analyses suggested potential benefit in patients with less severe disease [12]. Linezolid emerged as a promising antimicrobial with excellent CNS penetrance and activity against multidrug-resistant isolates [13]. Case series and small prospective studies reported favorable clinical responses, but myelosuppression, peripheral neuropathy, and optic neuritis were notable adverse events, and optimal dosing and duration remain uncertain [14,15].

Host-directed therapies were investigated as adjuncts to antimicrobial treatment. Dexamethasone significantly reduced mortality in HIV-uninfected adults with TBM, particularly in those with mild to moderate disease, consistent with earlier trial data [16,17]. However, evidence for its use in HIV co-infection was limited and conflicting; no randomized trial has demonstrated a clear survival advantage in this population, and concerns regarding immunosuppression and opportunistic infections persist [18,19]. Aspirin, possessing anti-inflammatory and anti-thrombotic properties, was associated with reduced incidence of stroke in small observational and pilot studies [20,21]. These studies also suggested modulation of host inflammatory markers, including interleukin-6 and C-reactive protein, but sample sizes were insufficient to assess mortality or functional outcomes [22]. Genetic polymorphisms in genes regulating innate immunity, such as TLR2, TREM1, and LTA4H, were associated with differential inflammatory responses and may inform individualized immune therapy [23,24]. Mediators of the innate immune response, including tumor necrosis factor-alpha and matrix metalloproteinases, were identified as potential therapeutic targets, though clinical trial data are lacking [25,26].

Supportive management of TBM complications was inconsistently studied. Hydrocephalus, a common and morbid complication, was managed with ventriculoperitoneal shunting, external ventricular drainage, or osmotic therapy, but comparative evidence was sparse [27,28]. In HIV co-infection, the management of hydrocephalus was particularly understudied; no significant evidence base was identified to guide decisions regarding shunt timing, corticosteroid use, or antiretroviral optimization [29,30]. Stroke, hyponatremia, seizures, and tuberculoma expansion were frequently reported complications, yet most studies were retrospective and underpowered to determine optimal interventions [31,32]. Among the included studies, few stratified outcomes by HIV status, baseline Glasgow Coma Scale, or drug resistance, limiting generalizability. Overall, the results indicate that high-dose rifampicin, newer antimicrobials with improved CNS penetration, and host-directed therapies remain promising but unproven, while supportive measures—especially hydrocephalus management in HIV co-infection—represent a critical evidence gap requiring future randomized investigation [33,34].

The management of tuberculous meningitis (TBM) remains a formidable challenge, underscored by persistently high rates of mortality and neurological sequelae despite the availability of effective anti-tuberculous therapy. The current review highlights a critical disconnect between standard antimicrobial regimens and the unique pharmacological demands of treating an infection sequestered behind the blood-brain barrier (BBB). The finding that current regimens do not adequately account for differing drug penetration into the central nervous system (CNS) is a pivotal issue [1]. This pharmacokinetic limitation may be a primary driver of suboptimal outcomes, suggesting that a re-evaluation of standard dosing is not just warranted, but essential.

The role of rifampicin, a cornerstone of TBM therapy, serves as a prime example of this therapeutic dilemma. While its efficacy is concentration-dependent, standard dosing may yield sub-therapeutic CNS concentrations. The recent clinical trial that failed to demonstrate a survival benefit with a 15 mg/kg/day dose is a sobering reminder of the gap between pharmacological theory and clinical reality [2]. However, this should not be interpreted as a definitive refutation of the high-dose strategy. Rather, it likely reflects the complex interplay of drug exposure, toxicity, and patient-specific factors. Dose-finding studies suggesting that even higher doses may be safe and more effective open a crucial avenue for future research [3]. The path forward requires carefully designed trials that not only escalate doses but also incorporate therapeutic drug monitoring to ensure adequate CNS exposure, while meticulously tracking potential hepatotoxicity and other adverse events.

Beyond optimizing existing agents, the investigation of newer antimicrobials with enhanced CNS penetrance is a high priority. Linezolid, with its favorable pharmacokinetic profile, represents a promising candidate [4]. Its role, particularly in the context of drug-resistant TBM, needs to be defined through robust clinical trials. Similarly, while fluoroquinolones are established second-line agents, their potential as first-line therapy to improve outcomes has yet to be substantiated by a demonstrated survival benefit [5]. The prospect of designing regimens with drugs that reliably achieve bactericidal concentrations in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is a key strategy to improve treatment efficacy and potentially shorten therapy duration.

The paradigm of TBM treatment is expanding beyond direct antimicrobial killing to include host-directed therapies that modulate the often destructive immune response. Dexamethasone remains the standard of care for HIV-uninfected individuals, based on evidence showing a mortality benefit [6]. However, its role in HIV co-infection is a critical knowledge gap, creating significant uncertainty in a patient population with high TBM prevalence. The potential for steroids to exacerbate immunosuppression in this group necessitates dedicated research. Aspirin, with its anti-inflammatory and anti-thrombotic properties, offers another intriguing avenue. Small studies demonstrating a reduction in stroke—a major cause of TBM morbidity—are encouraging but preliminary [7]. The dual mechanism of aspirin raises questions about whether its benefit derives primarily from preventing thrombosis or from modulating the inflammatory cascade that drives vasculopathy. Future research must aim to disentangle these effects and identify the optimal dose and duration of therapy.

Looking ahead, the field is moving towards more personalized and targeted interventions. The discovery of genetic polymorphisms that influence the host immune response could pave the way for individualized immune therapies, allowing clinicians to tailor adjunctive treatments based on a patient's genetic predisposition [8]. Furthermore, a deeper understanding of the innate immune response may yield novel therapeutic targets. Mediators of inflammation, such as specific cytokines or inflammasome components, could be targeted with precision to dampen immunopathology without compromising pathogen clearance. This represents a sophisticated, next-generation approach to managing the complications of TBM.

A glaring omission in the current evidence base, as highlighted in the review, is the management of hydrocephalus, particularly in the context of HIV co-infection. Hydrocephalus is a common and devastating complication of TBM, yet there is a profound lack of high-quality data to guide its management. The optimal timing and type of neurosurgical intervention (e.g., ventriculoperitoneal shunt vs. endoscopic third ventriculostomy) and the role of medical management with acetazolamide or corticosteroids remain areas of debate, with even less clarity for the HIV-positive population [9]. This is a critical area for future research, as improved management of hydrocephalus could significantly reduce TBM-related mortality and long-term disability.

In conclusion, while the core principles of TBM treatment are established, significant opportunities exist to improve patient outcomes. The primary challenge is to optimize antimicrobial therapy by overcoming the barrier of poor CNS drug penetration. This will require a multipronged approach encompassing high-dose rifampicin trials, investigation of newer agents like linezolid, and a re-evaluation of fluoroquinolones. Simultaneously, the field must advance the use of host-directed therapies, moving from broad immunosuppression with dexamethasone to more targeted and personalized interventions based on a clearer understanding of TBM immunopathology. Finally, the management of hydrocephalus, especially in HIV co-infection, must be elevated as a research priority. Addressing these gaps through collaborative, well-designed clinical trials is paramount to reducing the global burden of this devastating disease.

Ochratoxin A (OTA) is a secondary metabolite produced mainly by several species of Aspergillus and Penicillium, particularly Aspergillus ochraceus, Aspergillus carbonarius, Aspergillus niger, and Penicillium verrucosum. Since its discovery, OTA has been recognized as one of the most important mycotoxins contaminating a wide range of agricultural commodities and processed foods, including cereals, cereal products, coffee, cocoa, dried fruits, spices, beer, and wine. Its presence in food and feed represents a global food safety concern because OTA exhibits nephrotoxic, hepatotoxic, immunotoxic, teratogenic, and carcinogenic properties. The International Agency for Research on Cancer has classified OTA as a possible human carcinogen (Group 2B). Human exposure occurs mainly through the ingestion of contaminated plant-derived foods and beverages, and chronic exposure has been linked to Balkan endemic nephropathy and urinary tract tumors. Consequently, many countries have established maximum permissible levels for OTA in various food commodities, and the wine industry has become increasingly concerned with reducing OTA contamination to meet regulatory and consumer expectations.

Red wine is particularly susceptible to OTA contamination because grapes can be infected by ochratoxigenic fungi, especially black aspergilli such as Aspergillus carbonarius, in the vineyard. The mycotoxin can persist through vinification and may be transferred into the final wine, although concentrations are generally low. Nevertheless, because wine is widely consumed and OTA has cumulative toxic effects, even low levels are of concern. Several strategies have been proposed to control OTA in wine, including preventive measures in the vineyard, sorting of grapes, and post-harvest treatments such as adsorption with fining agents, filtration, and chemical treatments. However, these approaches can be costly, may alter wine quality, or have limited efficiency. Therefore, there is growing interest in biological methods for OTA detoxification, particularly using microorganisms or their enzymes, as environmentally friendly and sustainable alternatives.

Microbial biocontrol has emerged as a promising approach for reducing mycotoxin contamination in food and feed. Lactic acid bacteria, yeasts, and some Bacillus species have been reported to bind or degrade various mycotoxins, including aflatoxins, zearalenone, deoxynivalenol, and OTA. Among these, Bacillus subtilis is a Gram-positive, spore-forming bacterium with a long history of safe use in food fermentation and as a probiotic. It produces a variety of extracellular enzymes and antimicrobial compounds, and its spores are highly resistant to adverse conditions, making it attractive for biotechnological applications. Several studies have shown that Bacillus strains can reduce OTA levels in culture media, although the mechanisms remain unclear and may involve cell wall binding, enzymatic degradation, or metabolic transformation. Importantly, the OTA-reducing activity may differ depending on whether whole cells, intracellular extracts, or extracellular metabolites are used, and whether the cells are viable or non-viable. Understanding these aspects is critical for developing practical biocontrol formulations.

Korean traditional fermented foods, such as kimchi, are rich sources of diverse microorganisms with potential functional properties. Kimchi is produced through spontaneous fermentation of vegetables, mainly cabbage, with various seasonings, and its microbial community includes lactic acid bacteria, yeasts, and Bacillus species. Several Bacillus strains isolated from kimchi have shown probiotic, antimicrobial, and enzyme-producing activities. However, the potential of kimchi-derived Bacillus subtilis for mycotoxin reduction, especially OTA, has not been extensively investigated. Given the safety and functional attributes of kimchi-associated microorganisms, they may provide novel biocontrol agents suitable for food applications. In particular, a Bacillus subtilis strain isolated from kimchi could offer advantages such as adaptability to food environments and acceptability in fermented foods.

In the present study, a new Bacillus subtilis strain, KU-153, was isolated from Korean traditional fermented food kimchi and evaluated for its ability to reduce OTA in culture medium and in artificially contaminated red wine. The specific objectives were: (i) to isolate and identify the strain by 16S rRNA gene sequencing; (ii) to examine the growth kinetics of B. subtilis KU-153 in relation to OTA reduction; (iii) to compare the OTA-reducing activity of whole cells, heat-killed cells, intracellular extracts, and extracellular extracts; and (iv) to assess the practical potential of the strain for reducing OTA in red wine. The results demonstrated that viable and heat-killed cells, but not cell extracts, significantly reduced OTA, with heat-killed cells showing higher activity. Furthermore, heat-killed B. subtilis KU-153 reduced OTA in red wine by approximately 90%, highlighting its potential as a biocontrol agent for OTA mitigation in food and beverages. This study provides new insights into the use of kimchi-derived Bacillus subtilis for mycotoxin control and supports further development of safe and effective biological strategies to reduce OTA contamination.

Samples of Korean traditional fermented food Kimchi were collected aseptically and homogenized in sterile physiological saline. Serial tenfold dilutions were prepared and spread onto nutrient agar plates, which were incubated at 37°C for 24–48 h. Individual colonies were purified by repeated streaking and stored in nutrient broth containing 20% glycerol at −80°C. A total of 153 isolates were screened for antifungal and ochratoxin A (OTA)-reducing activity, and the isolate designated KU-153 was selected for further study because of its pronounced OTA reduction ability. For molecular identification, genomic DNA was extracted from an overnight culture of KU-153 using a commercial genomic DNA extraction kit according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The 16S rRNA gene was amplified by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) with the universal primers 27F (5′-AGAGTTTGATCMTGGCTCAG-3′) and 1492R (5′-TACGGYTACCTTGTTACGACTT-3′). Each 50-µL PCR mixture contained 1× PCR buffer, 2 mM MgCl₂, 200 µM each dNTP, 0.5 µM each primer, 1.25 U Taq DNA polymerase, and approximately 50 ng template DNA. Amplification was performed with an initial denaturation at 95°C for 5 min, followed by 30 cycles of 95°C for 30 s, 55°C for 30 s, and 72°C for 90 s, with a final extension at 72°C for 10 min. The PCR product was purified, sequenced commercially, and compared with sequences in the NCBI GenBank database using BLAST. Phylogenetic analysis was conducted using MEGA software after alignment with closely related Bacillus species. The results identified KU-153 as Bacillus subtilis.

The growth kinetics of B. subtilis KU-153 were examined in nutrient broth at 37°C with shaking at 150 rpm. An overnight preculture was inoculated at 1% (v/v) into fresh nutrient broth containing OTA at a final concentration of 1 µg/mL. Culture samples were taken at 0, 6, 12, 24, 36, and 48 h. Bacterial growth was monitored by measuring optical density at 600 nm (OD₆₀₀) and by determining viable colony counts on nutrient agar. At each time point, the culture supernatant was collected by centrifugation at 10,000 × g for 10 min at 4°C and analyzed for residual OTA by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). The OTA reduction was calculated relative to an uninoculated OTA-containing medium control incubated under the same conditions.

To prepare whole-cell and extract fractions, B. subtilis KU-153 was grown in nutrient broth at 37°C for 24 h with shaking at 150 rpm. Viable cells were harvested by centrifugation, washed twice with sterile phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, pH 7.2), and resuspended in PBS to an OD₆₀₀ of 1.0, corresponding to approximately 1 × 10⁸ CFU/mL. Heat-killed cells were prepared by heating the viable cell suspension at 80°C for 30 min, followed by rapid cooling on ice. The absence of viable cells was confirmed by plating 100 µL of the heat-treated suspension onto nutrient agar and incubating at 37°C for 48 h. Extracellular extracts were obtained from the cell-free culture supernatant after centrifugation at 10,000 × g for 15 min at 4°C, followed by filtration through a 0.22-µm membrane. Intracellular extracts were prepared by resuspending washed cells in PBS and disrupting them by sonication at 20 kHz for 5 min on ice with intermittent pulses. The lysate was centrifuged at 12,000 × g for 20 min at 4°C, and the supernatant was filter-sterilized through a 0.22-µm membrane. The protein concentration of intracellular extracts was determined using a Bradford assay.

OTA reduction assays were performed in sterile nutrient broth containing OTA at a final concentration of 1 µg/mL. Viable cells, heat-killed cells, extracellular extracts, or intracellular extracts were added to separate OTA-containing medium samples. The final cell density for whole-cell treatments was adjusted to an OD₆₀₀ of 0.1, while extracts were added at a final protein concentration of 100 µg/mL. Uninoculated OTA-containing medium served as the control. All samples were incubated at 37°C with shaking at 150 rpm for 24 h. After incubation, samples were centrifuged at 10,000 × g for 10 min, and the supernatants were collected for OTA quantification. OTA was extracted from the culture supernatants by liquid–liquid extraction with chloroform. The organic phase was evaporated to dryness under a gentle stream of nitrogen, and the residue was reconstituted in methanol. OTA was quantified by HPLC using a C₁₈ reversed-phase column with a mobile phase consisting of acetonitrile:water:acetic acid (57:41:2, v/v/v) at a flow rate of 1.0 mL/min. Fluorescence detection was performed at an excitation wavelength of 333 nm and an emission wavelength of 460 nm. The injection volume was 20 µL, and OTA was identified and quantified by comparison with an external OTA standard curve. The percentage of OTA reduction was calculated as follows: reduction (%) = [(OTA control − OTA treatment)/OTA control] × 100.
