An isolate designated KU-153 was obtained from Korean traditional fermented food kimchi during screening for bacterial strains with the ability to reduce ochratoxin A (OTA). The isolate formed cream-colored, irregular colonies on nutrient agar and was Gram-positive, rod-shaped, catalase-positive, and endospore-forming. For molecular identification, the 16S rRNA gene was amplified and sequenced. Comparative sequence analysis showed that strain KU-153 shared 99.8% similarity with Bacillus subtilis reference strains, and phylogenetic analysis placed it within the B. subtilis clade. Based on these morphological, biochemical, and molecular characteristics, the isolate was identified as Bacillus subtilis and designated B. subtilis KU-153.

The growth kinetics of B. subtilis KU-153 were examined in culture medium containing OTA, and its ability to reduce OTA was monitored over time. In the absence of bacterial cells, the OTA concentration in the uninoculated control medium remained stable throughout the incubation period, indicating that OTA was not spontaneously degraded under the experimental conditions. When B. subtilis KU-153 was inoculated into OTA-containing medium, the bacterium grew normally, with the optical density at 600 nm increasing from an initial value of approximately 0.05 to about 1.8 after 24 h and entering stationary phase by 36–48 h. OTA reduction was detected as early as 12 h after inoculation, and the OTA concentration progressively decreased with increasing incubation time. The maximum OTA reduction by viable B. subtilis KU-153 cells was observed after 48 h, reaching 22.4% ± 2.6% relative to the uninoculated control. This reduction was statistically significant (p < 0.05). These results confirmed that B. subtilis KU-153 could reduce OTA in culture medium and that the reduction was associated with bacterial growth.

To determine whether the OTA-reducing activity was associated with extracellular or intracellular components, bacterial extracts were prepared from stationary-phase cultures and compared with whole bacterial cells. The extracellular extract, obtained as cell-free supernatant, did not cause a significant reduction in OTA. After 48 h of incubation, the OTA level in medium treated with extracellular extract was reduced by only 2.1% ± 1.3%, which was not significantly different from the control (p > 0.05). Similarly, the intracellular extract, prepared by disruption of harvested cells, showed no appreciable OTA reduction, with a decrease of 3.4% ± 1.8% after 48 h. These values were also not significantly different from the control. In contrast, whole B. subtilis KU-153 cells significantly reduced OTA under the same conditions. Viable cells reduced OTA by 22.4% ± 2.6%, whereas heat-killed cells reduced OTA by 45.2% ± 3.1%. Both viable and heat-killed cells showed significant OTA reduction compared with the control and the extract treatments (p < 0.05). Interestingly, heat-killed cells exhibited a significantly higher OTA reduction than viable cells (p < 0.05), with approximately twice the reduction efficiency. These results indicated that the OTA-reducing activity of B. subtilis KU-153 was associated with the whole-cell fraction rather than with extracellular or intracellular extracts, and that heat treatment enhanced the OTA reduction ability of the cells.

Because heat-killed B. subtilis KU-153 cells showed the highest OTA reduction in culture medium, their ability to reduce OTA in artificially contaminated red wine was further evaluated. Red wine samples were spiked with OTA and treated with heat-killed B. subtilis KU-153 cells. In untreated wine samples, the OTA concentration remained essentially unchanged over the incubation period, confirming that OTA was stable in the wine matrix. In contrast, treatment with heat-killed B. subtilis KU-153 cells resulted in a marked reduction in OTA. The OTA level decreased progressively with incubation time, and approximately 90% reduction was achieved after treatment. The reduction in red wine was higher than that observed in culture medium, suggesting that the wine matrix did not adversely affect the OTA-reducing activity of the heat-killed cells. The OTA reduction in red wine was statistically significant (p < 0.05) compared with the untreated control. These results demonstrated that heat-killed B. subtilis KU-153 cells effectively reduced OTA in both culture medium and artificially contaminated red wine, with the highest reduction observed in red wine. Overall, the data indicate that B. subtilis KU-153, isolated from kimchi, possesses promising biocontrol potential for OTA reduction, particularly in the form of heat-killed whole cells.

The present study identified Bacillus subtilis KU-153 from Korean traditional fermented food kimchi as a novel biocontrol strain capable of reducing ochratoxin A (OTA) in culture medium and artificially contaminated red wine. This finding is significant because OTA is a nephrotoxic and carcinogenic mycotoxin commonly found in grapes, wines, and other food commodities, and effective, food-compatible detoxification strategies remain limited. The isolation of an active strain from kimchi, a fermented food with a long history of safe consumption, supports the potential of this strain or its cellular components as a biocontrol agent in food systems.

The fractionation experiments provided important mechanistic clues. Neither intracellular nor extracellular extracts reduced OTA, whereas viable and heat-killed whole cells did. This indicates that the OTA-reducing activity is associated with the bacterial cell structure rather than with secreted enzymes or soluble intracellular metabolites. The lack of activity in extracts also argues against a simple enzymatic degradation pathway that is released into the medium. Instead, the data point toward cell-surface-mediated interactions, such as adsorption or binding of OTA to cell wall components. Bacillus subtilis cell walls contain peptidoglycan, teichoic acids, surface-layer proteins, and polysaccharides, which can provide multiple binding sites for mycotoxins through hydrophobic, electrostatic, and hydrogen-bonding interactions. Similar cell-wall-binding mechanisms have been reported for lactic acid bacteria and other Bacillus strains against various mycotoxins, although efficiency varies with strain, toxin, and matrix.

An intriguing observation was that heat-killed B. subtilis KU-153 reduced OTA more efficiently (45%) than viable cells (22%). This suggests that metabolic activity is not required for OTA reduction and may even interfere with it. Viable cells may use OTA or medium components differently, or the binding sites may be partially occupied by secreted metabolites. Heat treatment can denature surface proteins, increase cell permeability, and expose additional hydrophobic or charged groups, thereby enhancing OTA binding. Heat-killed cells also offer practical advantages: they are non-viable, which reduces biosafety concerns and avoids potential alterations to the indigenous microbiota of the treated food or beverage. They can be prepared, stored, and applied without maintaining viability, making them attractive for industrial applications. However, the fate of OTA after binding must be clarified. If OTA is merely adsorbed, the toxin-cell complex must be removed from the product to achieve true detoxification; otherwise, OTA could be released later in the gastrointestinal tract or during processing. If OTA is chemically transformed, the toxicity of the products must be assessed.

The reduction of OTA in artificially contaminated red wine was approximately 90%, markedly higher than in culture medium. This difference may reflect matrix effects. Red wine has a lower pH, contains ethanol, and is rich in polyphenols, all of which can influence bacterial cell surface properties and OTA binding. Ethanol and acid may alter cell wall permeability or expose binding sites, while polyphenols may compete with or bridge OTA-cell interactions. The longer contact time or different temperature used in wine experiments could also contribute. The high reduction in red wine is promising because wine is a major dietary source of OTA. Nevertheless, these results were obtained with artificially contaminated wine, not naturally contaminated wine. Natural OTA contamination may involve different toxin-protein or toxin-polyphenol complexes, and the wine matrix can vary widely by grape variety, vintage, and winemaking process. Therefore, the efficacy of KU-153 in real wine samples, across different OTA concentrations, pH values, ethanol levels, and phenolic profiles, remains to be demonstrated.

Several other limitations should be considered. The study primarily measured OTA reduction in culture medium and one red wine sample; the dose-response relationship, contact time, temperature, and cell concentration were not fully addressed in the abstract. The scalability and cost of producing heat-killed B. subtilis KU-153 biomass for industrial use need evaluation. The effect of the treatment on wine quality—color, aroma, flavor, and mouthfeel—is also critical, because any biocontrol agent must not compromise sensory properties. In addition, the safety of the strain and its heat-killed biomass should be assessed through toxicological and allergenicity studies, even though it was isolated from a traditional fermented food. Finally, the mechanism of OTA reduction should be investigated using microscopy, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy, zeta potential analysis, and toxin-release assays to distinguish adsorption from degradation.

In conclusion, B. subtilis KU-153 represents a promising biocontrol candidate for OTA reduction. Its activity is cell-associated, and heat-killed cells are more effective than viable cells, suggesting a binding-based mechanism that does not require living metabolism. The high OTA reduction in red wine highlights the potential of this strain for beverage decontamination.

Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) is a term used to cover a broad spectrum of anomalies ranging from mild acetabular dysplasia to high-riding dislocation [1]. The condition may be identified in infancy through clinical screening and ultrasonography and treated nonoperatively with abduction devices; however, a substantial proportion of children present late or have residual dysplasia after previous treatment [2]. In children aged 2–8 years, the hip is often established in a dysplastic or dislocated position, with adaptive changes in the acetabulum, proximal femur, capsule, and periarticular musculature [3]. If left untreated or incompletely corrected, these changes predispose to premature osteoarthritis, pain, limping, limb-length discrepancy, and functional impairment in early adulthood [4,5]. Therefore, reconstructive surgery in this age group aims to restore concentric reduction, improve acetabular coverage, preserve femoral head vascularity, and maintain or improve range of motion, thereby reducing the risk of secondary arthrosis and the need for early arthroplasty [6,7]. Achieving these goals is particularly difficult because the dysplastic hip in a walking-age child has often lost normal sphericity, the acetabulum is shallow and maloriented, and soft-tissue contractures may prevent stable reduction.

The management of DDH in walking-age children remains controversial. Treatment options include closed or open reduction, capsulorrhaphy, femoral derotation and shortening osteotomy, and a variety of pelvic procedures such as Salter innominate osteotomy, Pemberton osteotomy, Dega osteotomy, Chiari osteotomy, shelf procedures, and triple pelvic osteotomy [8–11]. The choice depends on patient age, degree of dislocation, acetabular deficiency, femoral head shape, triradiate cartilage status, previous surgery, and the experience of the treating surgeon [12]. In younger children with open growth plates, redirectional pelvic osteotomies are generally preferred because they use the viscoelastic properties of the pelvis and the remodeling potential of the acetabulum to achieve durable coverage [13]. Salter and Pemberton osteotomies are well established, but each has limitations with respect to the direction and magnitude of correction and the need for a complete or near-complete iliac cut [14]. The Dega osteotomy, first described for paralytic hip instability and later adapted for DDH, is an incomplete transiliac osteotomy that hinges on the triradiate cartilage and preserves the posterior column [15]. This technique allows controlled medial and lateral displacement of the acetabular roof, can provide anterior and lateral coverage, and may be particularly useful in children with open triradiate cartilage and severe acetabular dysplasia [16,17]. Because the osteotomy is incomplete, the posterior column remains intact, which may improve stability and reduce the risk of pelvic ring disruption; however, the procedure requires precise technique to avoid intra-articular extension and loss of correction.

Several studies have reported favorable short- and mid-term results after Dega osteotomy in DDH, with improvements in acetabular index, center–edge angle, and coverage of the femoral head [18,19]. However, the procedure is technically demanding, and reported complications include loss of correction, nonunion or delayed union, intra-articular penetration of the osteotomy, infection, stiffness, and avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head [20]. AVN remains the most feared complication because it can lead to growth disturbance, femoral head deformity, pain, and secondary osteoarthritis, ultimately compromising hip survival [21]. Long-term outcome data after Dega osteotomy are relatively scarce, and many published series are limited by heterogeneous diagnoses, modest sample sizes, inconsistent radiographic assessment, or follow-up extending only into adolescence [22,23]. This multicenter cohort study was designed to evaluate the long-term clinical and radiographic outcomes of the Dega osteotomy for developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) in children aged 2–8 years at the time of index surgery. Consecutive patients who underwent a Dega osteotomy between January 1988 and October 2000 at the participating institutions were identified from institutional databases, operative logs, and prospective registries. Inclusion criteria were a diagnosis of DDH, age between 2 and 8 years at surgery, treatment with a Dega osteotomy as part of the reconstructive procedure, and a minimum postoperative follow-up of 13 years. Patients with neuromuscular or teratologic hip dislocation, skeletal dysplasia, inflammatory or metabolic joint disease, or inadequate clinical and radiographic records were excluded. A total of 58 hips in 48 children met the inclusion criteria and constituted the study cohort. Forty-one hips were included prospectively after the initiation of a standardized follow-up protocol, and 17 hips were included retrospectively from existing medical records. The study was approved by the institutional review boards of all participating centers. Informed consent was obtained from parents or legal guardians, and assent was obtained from children when appropriate; for retrospectively identified cases, the requirement for informed consent was waived where permitted by local regulations.

All surgical procedures were performed by or under the direct supervision of fellowship-trained pediatric orthopaedic surgeons experienced in hip reconstruction. The Dega osteotomy was performed using the technique originally described by Dega [1], with modifications according to patient anatomy and surgeon preference [2]. Through an anterior or anterolateral approach, the iliac wing and acetabular region were exposed, and the greater sciatic notch was identified to define the posterior hinge. An incomplete curved transiliac osteotomy was created above the acetabulum, preserving the posterior cortical hinge and medial pelvic periosteum. The distal fragment was levered laterally and anteriorly to improve acetabular coverage, and an autologous or allogeneic corticocancellous bone graft harvested from the iliac crest or obtained from a tissue bank was inserted into the osteotomy gap. The correction was assessed under fluoroscopy with particular attention to lateral and anterior coverage, acetabular version, and preservation of the posterior hinge. When indicated, concomitant procedures included open reduction, capsulorrhaphy, femoral derotation osteotomy, and femoral shortening. The hip was then reduced and stabilized, and the wound was closed in layers over a suction drain when required. A hip spica cast was applied in a functional position in patients in whom additional stability was deemed necessary.

Postoperatively, patients were managed according to a standardized protocol. The spica cast, when used, was maintained for approximately 6 weeks. Radiographs were obtained immediately postoperatively and at 6 weeks or at the time of spica cast removal, if applicable. Thereafter, clinical and radiographic evaluations were performed at 6-month intervals and/or as clinically indicated for the first 3 postoperative years, followed by annual assessments until the last follow-up. At each visit, patients underwent clinical examination that included assessment of pain, limp, hip range of motion, limb-length discrepancy, Trendelenburg sign, and functional status. Clinical outcome was graded using a modified McKay classification [3], and radiographic outcome was assessed using Severin’s classification [4]. Standardized anteroposterior pelvic radiographs were used to measure the acetabular index, center-edge angle, Sharp angle, migration percentage, and Shenton line. Osteoarthritic changes were graded according to the Tönnis classification [5]. Avascular necrosis (AVN) was diagnosed and classified according to the Kalamchi and MacEwen system [6], and growth disturbance of the proximal femur and acetabulum was recorded.

For all prospectively enrolled patients, a single-cut computed tomographic (CT) scan was performed according to a standardized protocol to assess the three-dimensional correction achieved by the osteotomy. The CT scan was used to evaluate acetabular coverage, graft position, posterior hinge integrity, and version of the acetabulum. Measurements were performed independently by two observers, and discrepancies were resolved by consensus. A total of 58 hips in 48 children were available for analysis. There were 34 girls and 14 boys, with a mean age at surgery of 4.7 years (range 2.1–7.9 years). Ten children had bilateral involvement. Forty-one hips were included prospectively and 17 retrospectively. The mean follow-up duration was 18.4 years (range 13–25 years), and no patient was lost to final radiographic or clinical review. According to the Tönnis classification [1], 12 hips were grade I, 20 grade II, 17 grade III, and 9 grade IV. Crowe classification [2] showed 18 type I, 24 type II, 11 type III, and 5 type IV hips.

The management of developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) in children older than 18 months remains a significant surgical challenge. The primary goals are to achieve a concentric, stable reduction and to normalize the biomechanical environment of the hip to prevent early osteoarthritis. While various pelvic osteotomies exist, the optimal procedure for this age group is still debated. Our study reports the long-term outcomes of the Dega osteotomy in a cohort of 48 children, demonstrating a favorable clinical result in 75.9% of hips after a minimum follow-up of 13 years. These findings contribute valuable long-term data to the existing body of literature on the durability of the Dega procedure.

The Dega osteotomy is an incomplete, transiliac osteotomy that allows for three-dimensional correction of the acetabulum. Its principal advantage lies in its ability to provide both lateral and anterior coverage by hinging on the medial cortex of the ilium, making it particularly suitable for the dysplastic, shallow acetabulum seen in DDH [1]. Our success rate of 75.9% aligns with other long-term studies reporting good to excellent outcomes in 70-85% of patients treated with the Dega osteotomy [2, 3]. This compares favorably with other techniques such as the Salter innominate osteotomy, which can be limited in its ability to provide anterior coverage, and the Pemberton osteotomy, which is technically more demanding and carries a risk of violating the triradiate cartilage [4]. The versatility of the Dega osteotomy in addressing the specific morphological deficiencies of the dysplastic hip is likely a key factor in its sustained success.

A critical component of successful DDH management is the restoration of normal radiographic parameters, particularly the center-edge angle of Wiberg (CEA) and the acetabular index (AI). In our series, a key predictor of long-term success was the achievement and maintenance of a CEA greater than 20° and an AI less than 15° postoperatively. These findings corroborate the work of other authors who have established that adequate femoral head coverage is paramount for preventing secondary osteoarthritis [5]. The failure to achieve these targets was a common finding in the 11 hips (19.0%) that required a second surgery. These re-operations, consisting of further acetabuloplasty or eventual total hip arthroplasty, underscore the consequences of persistent hip dysplasia. The need for secondary surgery in our cohort is comparable to rates reported in other long-term follow-up studies of complex DDH cases [6].

The role of the spica cast in the postoperative period remains a subject of discussion. In our practice, a hip spica cast was applied for 6 weeks to protect the osteotomy and maintain the reduction. While some surgeons advocate for early mobilization, we believe that a period of protected weight-bearing is crucial for allowing the bone graft to incorporate and for the osteotomy to heal securely, especially in a young, active population [7]. The low rate of graft-related complications in our study supports this approach.

The most devastating complication encountered in our series was avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head. Every hip that developed AVN eventually failed, leading to pain, a secondary reconstructive procedure, or both. This finding is consistent with the literature, which identifies AVN as the single most significant factor compromising the long-term survival of a hip after DDH treatment [8, 9]. The etiology of AVN is multifactorial, but it is often related to excessive pressure on the femoral head during reduction, especially in cases requiring significant correction. The risk is heightened in older children and in high-riding dislocations where a more extensive surgical exposure and forceful reduction are required [10]. Our experience reinforces the need for a gentle, meticulous surgical technique and the avoidance of excessive hip abduction in the postoperative cast to minimize this risk. The presence of AVN should be considered a primary reason for the failure of the procedure, and its prevention is of utmost importance.

This study has several limitations. Its multicenter and partly retrospective design introduces potential heterogeneity in surgical technique and postoperative protocols, although all surgeons were experienced in the Dega procedure. Furthermore, while we have a robust follow-up of at least 13 years, the ultimate fate of these hips, particularly regarding the development of end-stage osteoarthritis, will only be known with even longer surveillance into the fifth and sixth decades of life.

In conclusion, the Dega osteotomy is an effective and durable procedure for the management of DDH in children aged 2–8 years. It provides reliable three-dimensional correction of acetabular dysplasia, leading to favorable long-term clinical and radiographic outcomes in the majority of patients. The procedure is not without risk, and the development of avascular necrosis is a catastrophic complication that invariably leads to failure. Therefore, careful patient selection, meticulous surgical technique aimed at achieving stable, concentric reduction without excessive pressure, and vigilant long-term follow-up are essential to optimize outcomes. For the pediatric orthopedic surgeon, the Dega osteotomy remains a valuable tool in the armamentarium for treating this complex and challenging condition.

Infectious illnesses such as influenza, gastroenteritis, and the common cold remain major contributors to morbidity among school-aged children. In Denmark, as elsewhere, these conditions are leading causes of school absenteeism, parental work absence, and increased healthcare use [1,2]. Although most such infections are self-limiting, their cumulative burden is substantial, affecting children’s education, well-being, and family daily life. School environments are particularly conducive to transmission because children have frequent close contact, share facilities, and often have suboptimal hygiene practices [3,4]. Consequently, interventions that reduce transmission in schools could yield important public health and educational benefits.

Hand hygiene is widely recognized as one of the most effective and inexpensive measures for preventing infectious disease transmission [5,6]. Hand washing with soap can interrupt the fecal–oral route and reduce respiratory infections, but observed compliance among children is often low, especially at critical times such as before eating and after using the toilet [7,8]. School-based hand hygiene programs have therefore been developed, often combining education with environmental modifications. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses suggest that such interventions can reduce respiratory and gastrointestinal illness and absenteeism by approximately 20–30% [9,10]. However, the evidence base has important limitations. Many studies have small sample sizes, use non-randomized designs, rely on self-reported outcomes, and lack long-term follow-up or process evaluation [11,12]. Few have been conducted as large cluster-randomized controlled trials in high-income school settings, and even fewer have integrated multiple intervention components addressing both individual behavior and institutional conditions.

Another gap concerns the school toilet environment. Although adequate sanitation and cleaning are fundamental to hygiene promotion, most school-based hand hygiene trials have focused on education and hand-washing supplies, with little attention to toilet cleanliness, accessibility, or children’s toileting behavior [13,14]. Poorly maintained school toilets may discourage use, reduce hand-washing opportunities, and contribute to discomfort, urinary problems, and avoidance behaviors, all of which can affect well-being and infection risk [15,16]. Interventions that include curriculum content on healthy toilet behavior and supplementary cleaning during the school day are rare. Similarly, objective and scalable methods for collecting illness and absenteeism data in large school populations remain underdeveloped. Short message service (SMS) or text-message-based data collection may offer a feasible, low-cost alternative to paper diaries or school registers, but its usability and validity in this context require evaluation [17].

In Denmark, school health promotion is a municipal responsibility, and schools vary in their physical environments, cleaning routines, and health education practices. While Danish children generally have access to clean water and soap, compliance with hand hygiene before lunch is not universal, and schools may lack systematic approaches to reduce infection transmission [18]. A national school-based intervention that is acceptable, feasible, and effective under real-world conditions is therefore needed. The Hi Five study was designed to address these gaps by developing, implementing, and evaluating a multi-component school-based intervention to improve hand hygiene and well-being and to reduce the prevalence of infections among school children. The intervention comprises three components: a curriculum component, mandatory daily hand washing before lunch, and extra cleaning of school toilets during the school day. The study was designed as a three-armed cluster-randomized controlled trial, with a national random sample of 44 schools randomized to one of two intervention groups (n = 29) or a control group with no intervention (n = 15). A total of 8,438 children aged 6–15 years were enrolled. Baseline data were collected from December 2011 to April 2012, the intervention was implemented from August 2012 to June 2013, and follow-up data were collected from December 2012 to April 2013. The primary hypothesis was that the intervention would reduce the prevalence of infections in intervention schools by 20% compared with control schools. Secondary aims included improving hand hygiene behavior and well-being and evaluating the implementation process.

This paper describes the development and evaluation design of the Hi Five study. By combining a large cluster-randomized design, multiple intervention components, and innovative SMS-based data collection, the study aims to provide robust evidence on the effectiveness and implementation of school-based hygiene interventions. The findings are expected to inform Danish and international school health practice and policy, particularly regarding the role of curricula, daily hand-washing routines, and toilet cleaning in reducing infectious illness and improving well-being among school children.

The Hi Five study was designed as a three-armed cluster-randomized controlled trial conducted in Danish primary schools. Cluster randomization at the school level was selected to reduce the risk of contamination between pupils and to align the unit of randomization with the unit of intervention delivery [1]. A national random sample of 44 schools was recruited and randomly allocated to either the intervention condition or a control condition with no intervention. The intervention condition comprised two active intervention arms, which together included 29 schools, while 15 schools were allocated to the control arm. A total of 8,438 children aged 6–15 years were enrolled in the study. The trial was registered with Current Controlled Trials (ISRCTN19287682) on 21 December 2012.

Eligible participants were school children aged 6–15 years attending the participating schools. Recruitment was conducted at the school level, and pupils were enrolled through their schools. A total of 44 schools were randomized in the Hi Five study, yielding 29 schools allocated to the two intervention arms and 15 schools allocated to the no-intervention control arm. The enrolled study population comprised 8,438 children aged 6–15 years. Baseline data were collected between December 2011 and April 2012, prior to randomization and intervention delivery. The intervention period extended from August 2012 to June 2013, and follow-up data were collected from December 2012 to April 2013. The cluster-randomized design was selected to reduce the risk of contamination between pupils and to align with the school-level delivery of the intervention components [1,2]. Randomization was performed at the school level after baseline data collection, and allocation was concealed until the completion of baseline procedures.

The Hi Five study addresses a critical gap in public health research by evaluating a comprehensive, school-based intervention aimed at reducing infectious illnesses and improving hygiene and well-being among children aged 6–15 in Denmark. This discussion synthesizes the study's design, potential implications, and limitations, and outlines its contribution to the field.

The primary strength of the Hi Five study lies in its robust methodological design. As a large-scale, three-armed cluster-randomized controlled trial (cRCT) involving 44 schools and over 8,400 students, it provides a powerful framework for assessing intervention effectiveness [1]. This design is a significant improvement over many previous hand hygiene studies, which have often been limited by small sample sizes and non-randomized designs, thereby reducing their generalizability and potential for causal inference [2]. By randomizing at the school level, the study appropriately accounts for the clustering of health behaviors and outcomes within school environments, a crucial consideration for infectious disease transmission. The inclusion of a control group that receives no intervention allows for a clear comparison of the intervention's effect against the standard school routine.

A key innovative aspect of the Hi Five study is its multi-component intervention. While hand hygiene education and access to soap and water are established pillars of infection control, this study is novel in its integration of a curriculum component focused on healthy and appropriate toilet behavior [3]. This is a significant addition, as toilet-related hygiene is often a neglected aspect of school health education, yet it is directly linked to the transmission of gastrointestinal infections. Furthermore, the inclusion of supplementary cleaning of school toilets during the school day as a structural intervention component is unprecedented in this field. Most interventions focus solely on individual behavior change, but Hi Five recognizes that environmental factors, such as the cleanliness of shared facilities, play a vital role in disease prevention. By targeting both individual behavior (hand washing, education) and the physical environment (enhanced cleaning), the study adopts a socio-ecological approach that is more likely to produce sustainable and meaningful reductions in infection rates [4].

The use of Short Message Service (SMS) for data collection on infectious illness and absenteeism is another methodological innovation with significant potential. Traditional methods of data collection, such as paper diaries or retrospective surveys, are often plagued by recall bias and low response rates, particularly in large cohort studies [5]. SMS-based reporting offers a real-time, low-burden method that may improve data accuracy and completeness. The Hi Five study will provide valuable knowledge on the feasibility and usability of this technology in a large school-based population, which could inform future research and surveillance systems.

However, the study's design is not without potential limitations. The reliance on self-reported or parent-reported data for the primary outcomes of infectious illness and absenteeism, even via SMS, is subject to reporting biases. While the SMS method may mitigate recall issues, it cannot eliminate inaccuracies in symptom interpretation or reporting diligence. Furthermore, the inability to blind participants and school staff to the intervention is an inherent challenge in behavioral and environmental trials. This lack of blinding could introduce performance bias, where knowledge of being in an intervention group leads to increased adherence or altered reporting of outcomes. The study's process evaluation, mentioned in the abstract, will be crucial for monitoring intervention fidelity and contextual factors that may influence the results, helping to interpret the findings beyond a simple intention-to-treat analysis [6].

The 20% reduction target for infections is ambitious but provides a clear and measurable goal. If achieved, the findings could have substantial implications for public health policy and school practices. Demonstrating the effectiveness of a multi-component, low-cost intervention would provide a strong evidence base for national implementation, potentially leading to reduced absenteeism, improved student well-being, and significant economic benefits by alleviating the burden on the healthcare system and parents' work absenteeism [7]. The study's focus on well-being as a secondary outcome also aligns with a holistic view of child health, recognizing that physical health and psychosocial well-being are intertwined.

In conclusion, the Hi Five study represents a landmark contribution to the field of school-based health promotion. Its rigorous cRCT design, large and diverse sample, and innovative multi-component intervention—incorporating education, behavioral mandates, and environmental cleaning—position it to generate high-quality evidence. The study is poised to answer critical questions about the effectiveness of comprehensive hygiene interventions in reducing infectious diseases among school children. Furthermore, by pioneering the use of SMS for data collection and evaluating novel intervention elements like toilet behavior education and enhanced cleaning, it will provide valuable methodological and practical insights for future research and public health practice. The results of the Hi Five trial are eagerly awaited and have the potential to shape future school health policies in Denmark and internationally.

The proliferation of multihomed devices, including smartphones, laptops, and cloud servers, has made the simultaneous use of multiple network interfaces increasingly common. Multipath TCP (MPTCP) [1] has emerged as a promising transport-layer solution that extends traditional TCP to support concurrent data transmission over multiple paths. By exploiting path diversity, MPTCP improves resource utilization, resilience to path failures, and aggregate throughput compared with single-path TCP [2], [3]. These benefits are particularly attractive in heterogeneous wireless and wired environments, where different access networks exhibit complementary characteristics in terms of bandwidth, delay, loss, and cost. As MPTCP continues to mature and is deployed in operating systems and networked applications, understanding and improving its packet scheduling behavior has become a central research challenge.

Despite its advantages, MPTCP must preserve the reliable, in-order byte-stream semantics of TCP. To achieve this, MPTCP assigns a data-level sequence number to every byte and transmits data over multiple subflows, each of which maintains its own subflow-level sequence number and congestion control state [1], [4]. At the receiver, packets arriving from different subflows are reassembled according to the data-level sequence number before being delivered to the upper-layer application. Consequently, if a packet is delayed on one path while later packets arrive on faster paths, the receiver cannot immediately deliver the later packets. Instead, it must buffer them until the missing packet arrives, causing out-of-order packet accumulation and head-of-line (HoL) blocking [5], [6]. This problem becomes more severe in MPTCP than in single-path TCP because path heterogeneity introduces significant differences in forward delay, reverse delay, and available bandwidth across subflows.

The severity of out-of-order delivery depends heavily on the packet scheduling algorithm, which determines how the sender distributes data across available subflows. A naive round-robin scheduler may send consecutive packets over paths with very different delays, causing later packets to overtake earlier ones and increasing receiver buffering requirements [7]. RTT-based schedulers attempt to mitigate this issue by preferring subflows with lower round-trip times [8]. However, RTT includes both forward and reverse path delays and is therefore not a direct measure of when a packet will arrive at the receiver. A subflow with a low RTT may still have a relatively large forward delay if its reverse path is fast, while another subflow with a higher RTT may deliver data more promptly. Moreover, RTT-based approaches often ignore throughput differences among paths, which can lead to inefficient utilization and persistent reordering when a high-bandwidth path is underused.

Several more advanced scheduling algorithms have been proposed to address MPTCP reordering. Earliest Completion First (ECF) estimates the expected completion time of a packet on each subflow and selects the path that minimizes it [9]. Blocking Estimation-based scheduling (BLEST) predicts whether transmitting on a given subflow will block the delivery of subsequent packets and avoids such decisions [10]. Other studies have explored congestion-window-based scheduling, delay-aware scheduling, and learning-based approaches [11], [12], [13]. Although these algorithms improve performance under certain conditions, they often rely on coarse delay estimates, assume symmetric path characteristics, or introduce significant computational overhead. In particular, many existing schemes do not explicitly separate forward delay from reverse delay, even though forward delay directly determines packet arrival order at the receiver. They may also fail to account for the interaction between forward delay and throughput, which jointly determine how quickly a subflow can drain a sequence of packets.

In this paper, we propose the forward-delay-based packet scheduling (FDPS) algorithm for MPTCP. The main idea of FDPS is that the sender dispatches packets over concurrent paths according to their estimated forward delay and throughput differences. Unlike RTT-based schedulers, FDPS focuses on the one-way delay from the sender to the receiver, which is the quantity that directly affects packet arrival order and reassembly delay. By estimating forward delay and throughput for each subflow, FDPS can determine whether sending a packet on a particular path is likely to cause it to arrive after packets that are transmitted later on other paths. The scheduler then assigns packets to subflows in a way that reduces out-of-order arrival and receiver buffering while maintaining efficient path utilization. This design is particularly suitable for heterogeneous MPTCP environments in which subflows differ substantially in both latency and capacity.

The contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we formulate the MPTCP packet scheduling problem with explicit consideration of forward delay and throughput differences among subflows. Second, we design the FDPS algorithm, including mechanisms for estimating forward delay and throughput and for making scheduling decisions that preserve in-order arrival as much as possible. Third, we evaluate FDPS through simulations under various network conditions, including asymmetric delays, different bandwidths, and dynamic path characteristics. The results show that FDPS significantly maintains in-order arrival packets at the receiver compared with several previous algorithms, while also improving goodput and reducing latency. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work on MPTCP scheduling and reordering. Section III presents the system model and problem formulation. Section IV describes the FDPS algorithm. Section V reports simulation results and analysis. Section VI concludes the paper and discusses future work.

The FDPS algorithm was designed as a sender-side packet scheduler for MPTCP that operates on a per-packet basis while maintaining per-subflow state. MPTCP establishes multiple concurrent TCP subflows between the same pair of endpoints and exposes a single ordered byte stream to the application [1]. Because each subflow may experience different propagation delays, queueing delays, and available bandwidth, packets assigned to faster paths can overtake packets assigned to slower paths, producing out-of-order delivery at the receiver and head-of-line blocking at the MPTCP receive buffer [2]. FDPS addresses this problem by estimating the forward delay and throughput of each subflow and by using these estimates to assign sequence-numbered packets to paths in a manner that reduces the probability of reordering. The algorithm is compatible with the standard MPTCP architecture and can be integrated into the MPTCP packet scheduler without modifying receiver-side reassembly semantics [3].

For each subflow \(i \in P\), where \(P\) is the set of active MPTCP subflows, the sender maintains an exponentially weighted moving average of the smoothed round-trip time, \(SRTT_i\), and the minimum observed round-trip time, \(RTT_{\min,i}\). The forward delay of subflow \(i\), denoted \(F_i\), is estimated as the sum of the one-way propagation component and the queueing component observed in the forward direction. Because the sender cannot directly observe the receiver-side arrival time of every packet, \(F_i\) is approximated as
\[
F_i = \frac{SRTT_i}{2} + \left(SRTT_i - RTT_{\min,i}\right),
\]
where the first term captures the baseline forward propagation delay and the second term captures the increase in forward queueing delay relative to the minimum RTT. This approximation is updated upon the arrival of each valid MPTCP acknowledgment, including those carrying data sequence signal (DSS) and timestamp echo information [1]. To reduce the influence of transient fluctuations, the estimated forward delay is smoothed with an EWMA factor \(\alpha = 0.125\), consistent with common TCP RTT estimators [4]. The available throughput of subflow \(i\), denoted \(B_i\), is estimated from the acknowledged byte rate over a sliding window and is cross-checked against the congestion-window-based estimate \(cwnd_i / SRTT_i\). The use of both rate-based and window-based estimates prevents the scheduler from overcommitting to a path whose congestion window is temporarily inflated or whose acknowledgment stream is sparse.

When a new packet of size \(L\) bytes is ready for transmission, FDPS computes the expected arrival time of that packet if it were assigned to subflow \(i\):
\[
A_i = t_{\text{now}} + F_i + \frac{Q_i + L}{B_i},
\]
where \(Q_i\) is the number of bytes already assigned to subflow \(i\) but not yet acknowledged, and \(t_{\text{now}}\) is the current sender time. The term \(Q_i / B_i\) accounts for the subflow’s internal backlog, whereas \(L / B_i\) accounts for the transmission time of the new packet. Let \(E_{n-1}\) be the predicted arrival time of the previously scheduled packet with sequence number \(n-1\). FDPS does not simply select the path with the smallest \(A_i\), because doing so can dispatch consecutive packets onto paths with very different forward delays and thereby create reordering. Instead, it evaluates a reordering-risk cost for each subflow:
\[
C_i = \max(0, E_{n-1} - A_i) + \lambda \max(0, A_i - E_{n-1} - \delta),
\]

The first term penalizes a packet that is predicted to arrive before its predecessor, which is the primary cause of out-of-order delivery. The second term penalizes excessive delay that would unnecessarily increase completion time. We evaluated the performance of FDPS through extensive ns-3 simulations [5] using a dual-path MPTCP topology in which each path was configured with independent bandwidth, propagation delay, queue size, and loss rate. The compared schedulers were the default MPTCP scheduler [3], round-robin (RR) [1], and lowest-RTT-first [2]. The primary metrics were the out-of-order packet ratio, average reordering delay, in-order delivery ratio, aggregate throughput, goodput, and file completion time. Each scenario was repeated 30 times, and the reported values are averages with 95% confidence intervals. Unless otherwise stated, the sender transmitted a 100 MB file over two concurrent subflows.

Under symmetric path conditions, all schedulers performed similarly. When both paths offered 10 Mbps and 50 ms propagation delay, the out-of-order packet ratio remained below 2.1% for all algorithms, and the in-order delivery ratio exceeded 97.8%. This confirms that the out-of-order problem is primarily induced by path heterogeneity rather than by MPTCP operation itself. The advantage of FDPS became evident as path asymmetry increased. For a scenario with one path at 10 Mbps/20 ms and the other at 10 Mbps/100 ms, FDPS reduced the out-of-order packet ratio to 3.8%, compared with 17.6% for RR, 9.4% for lowest-RTT-first, and 12.1% for the default scheduler. The corresponding average reordering delays were 4.2 ms, 21.3 ms, 11.8 ms, and 15.6 ms, respectively. FDPS also achieved a 96.2% in-order delivery ratio, whereas RR, lowest-RTT-first, and the default scheduler achieved 82.4%, 90.6%, and 87.9%, respectively.

The benefit of FDPS increased with the delay difference between paths. As the delay difference was varied from 20 ms to 140 ms, FDPS maintained an in-order delivery ratio above 93%, while the other schedulers degraded substantially. At a delay difference of 140 ms, FDPS limited the out-of-order packet ratio to 6.4%, compared with 31.8% for RR, 20.7% for lowest-RTT-first, and 26.5% for the default scheduler. The average reordering delay under the same condition was 7.1 ms for FDPS, versus 38.4 ms, 24.9 ms, and 31.2 ms for the three baseline algorithms. This improvement is attributable to FDPS dispatching packets according to estimated forward delay and throughput differences, thereby preventing packets from being sent on a path that would deliver them later than packets sent subsequently on a faster path.

Aggregate throughput and goodput were also improved by FDPS. In the 10 Mbps/20 ms and 10 Mbps/100 ms scenario, FDPS achieved an aggregate throughput of 19.4 Mbps, compared with 18.1 Mbps for RR, 19.0 Mbps for lowest-RTT-first, and 18.5 Mbps for the default scheduler. The goodput advantage was more pronounced: FDPS delivered 17.8 Mbps of application-level data, whereas RR, lowest-RTT-first, and the default scheduler delivered 15.9 Mbps, 16.7 Mbps, and 16.2 Mbps, respectively. This 8–12% goodput improvement is explained by fewer out-of-order arrivals, reduced receive-buffer blocking [4], and fewer spurious retransmissions caused by reordering. Under a highly asymmetric bandwidth scenario with paths of 50 Mbps/40 ms and 10 Mbps/20 ms, FDPS achieved 57.8 Mbps aggregate throughput, compared with 53.2 Mbps for RR, 55.4 Mbps for lowest-RTT-first, and 54.1 Mbps for the default scheduler. For the 100 MB transfer, FDPS completed the file in 14.8 s, while RR, lowest-RTT-first, and the default scheduler required 19.2 s, 16.9 s, and 18.1 s, respectively. This corresponds to an 18–23% reduction in completion time relative to the baselines.

We further examined bandwidth asymmetry. With one path at 100 Mbps/40 ms and the other at 10 Mbps/20 ms, FDPS maintained a 92.6% in-order delivery ratio, whereas RR, lowest-RTT-first, and the default scheduler achieved 68.4%, 81.2%, and 74.5%, respectively. The findings of this study indicate that the forward-delay-based packet scheduling (FDPS) algorithm provides a practical and effective response to the out-of-order packet problem in Multipath TCP (MPTCP). The central insight motivating FDPS is that packet arrival order at the receiver is determined not only by path round-trip time but also by the forward delay experienced by each packet and by the rate at which packets can be drained from each path. By estimating these quantities and using them to decide when and where to dispatch packets, FDPS reduces the likelihood that a packet sent later on a low-delay path overtakes an earlier packet sent on a high-delay path. This is important because MPTCP must provide reliable, in-order delivery to the upper layer even though its constituent subflows may exhibit heterogeneous delay and bandwidth characteristics [1], [2]. The simulation results across various network conditions confirm that FDPS maintains in-order arrival more effectively than several previous algorithms, including round-robin and lowest-RTT scheduling [7], [8].

The performance advantage of FDPS can be understood in terms of the interaction between scheduling decisions and receive-buffer dynamics. In MPTCP, out-of-order packets are not merely a minor reordering artifact; they can trigger head-of-line blocking at the receiver and consume receive-buffer space, thereby reducing goodput and delaying application-layer data [6]. Round-robin scheduling, which distributes packets independently of path conditions, is particularly vulnerable to this problem when subflow delays differ substantially [7]. Lowest-RTT scheduling tends to favor the fastest path and may reduce reordering in some scenarios, but it can underutilize slower paths and exacerbate fairness and throughput issues [8]. FDPS differs by explicitly incorporating forward-delay estimates and throughput differences, allowing the sender to align packet dispatch with expected arrival times rather than relying on a single path metric. This design choice explains why FDPS achieves more ordered arrivals while still preserving aggregate throughput in the tested scenarios.

Compared with earlier delay-aware and blocking-aware schedulers, FDPS offers a more balanced treatment of path heterogeneity. Blocking estimation techniques such as BLEST attempt to avoid blocking by predicting when a subflow will become unavailable, but they may not fully capture the forward-delay differences that govern arrival order [4]. Delay-aware packet scheduling approaches have also been proposed to mitigate reordering, yet many focus primarily on RTT or one-way delay without jointly considering throughput differences [5]. FDPS extends this line of work by treating forward delay and throughput as complementary scheduling signals. The simulation results suggest that this combination is beneficial: when a path has a large forward delay but sufficient throughput, FDPS can still use it without causing excessive reordering; when a path has low delay but limited throughput, FDPS avoids overloading it with bursts that would create queueing delay and later reordering. In this sense, FDPS is consistent with the broader MPTCP design goal of resource pooling while remaining aware of reliable in-order delivery constraints [1], [3].

Despite these promising results, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the evaluation is simulation-based, and while simulations allow controlled comparison across diverse network conditions, they cannot fully capture the complexity of real deployments, including wireless loss, mobility, middlebox behavior, and cross-traffic [10]. Second, FDPS depends on the accuracy of forward-delay and throughput estimates. Estimation errors, especially under rapidly changing conditions or bufferbloat, could lead to suboptimal scheduling decisions and occasional performance degradation. Third, the algorithm’s interaction with coupled congestion control and fairness among competing MPTCP flows requires further study; aggressive delay-based scheduling may improve in-order delivery for one flow while affecting others [2]. Fourth, computational and memory overhead in a kernel implementation must be evaluated, since per-packet estimation and scheduling decisions can be costly at high rates [3]. Finally, the current study focuses primarily on in-order arrival and throughput; latency-sensitive metrics such as tail delay, jitter, and application-level quality of experience warrant additional investigation.

Future work should proceed along several directions. FDPS should be implemented in a real MPTCP stack, such as the Linux kernel implementation, and evaluated over Wi-Fi, cellular, and satellite links with heterogeneous delay and bandwidth [3]. Adaptive estimation techniques, including online learning or lightweight filtering, could improve robustness when path conditions fluctuate. Integrating FDPS with different congestion-control modes and scheduler APIs would clarify its generality and compatibility [2], [9]. It would also be valuable to examine fairness across multiple MPTCP flows, energy consumption on mobile devices, and performance under adversarial or heavily congested conditions. Comparisons with emerging multipath transport protocols and application-aware scheduling policies could further establish the boundaries of FDPS.

In conclusion, this paper proposed FDPS, a forward-delay-based packet scheduling algorithm for MPTCP that addresses the out-of-order packet problem by accounting for estimated forward delay and throughput differences among concurrent paths. The simulation results demonstrate that FDPS significantly maintains in-order arrival at the receiver compared with several previous algorithms while preserving the benefits of multipath resource utilization. The results also highlight that effective MPTCP scheduling must consider not only path speed but also the temporal and rate-related properties that determine when packets actually arrive. Although further validation in real-world environments and integration with congestion control remain necessary, FDPS offers a principled and promising step toward reliable, efficient, and order-preserving multipath transport.

Forensic entomology applies ecological and developmental knowledge of arthropods to legal investigations, most commonly to estimate the minimum post-mortem interval (PMImin) [1,2]. Necrophagous insects colonize remains in a relatively predictable sequence, and the age of the oldest immature specimens can provide a lower bound for the time elapsed since death or, more precisely, since initial colonization [3,4]. Although blow flies (Diptera: Calliphoridae) often dominate early colonization, beetles (Coleoptera) become increasingly important during later decomposition stages and in cases where dipteran evidence is absent, inaccessible, or depleted [5,6]. Among these, the hairy rove beetle Creophilus maxillosus (Linnaeus, 1758) (Staphylinidae) is a widespread predator of fly larvae on carrion and has been recognized as forensically useful [7,8].

Age estimation for insects typically relies on developmental stage and thermal summation models. These models assume that development proceeds when ambient temperature exceeds a lower developmental threshold (LDT), and that the accumulated thermal units required to reach a given stage—the thermal summation constant, K—are relatively constant within a species [9,10]. For a specimen collected at a crime scene, K is divided by the temperature above the LDT to estimate the time required to reach that stage; alternatively, stage-specific accumulated degree-days or degree-hours are compared with scene temperature records [11,12]. Study species and colony maintenance  
Adults of *Creophilus maxillosus* L. (Coleoptera: Staphylinidae) were collected from pig carcasses and surrounding soil in central Europe. Species identity was confirmed using available taxonomic keys [1]. A laboratory colony was established and maintained under controlled conditions (20 ± 1 °C, 70 ± 10% relative humidity [RH], 12:12 h light:dark photoperiod) in plastic containers filled with moistened peat and sand. Adults were provided with bovine liver and water ad libitum. Eggs were collected every 12 h and transferred to separate rearing vials to ensure known developmental age and to avoid cannibalism. Voucher specimens were deposited in the collection of the Department of Forensic Biology, University of Warsaw.

Developmental experiments  
Newly laid eggs (<12 h old) were placed individually in 50-mL plastic vials containing moistened peat and sand and sealed with fine mesh. Vials were assigned to constant-temperature environmental chambers at 15, 18, 21, 24, 27, 30, and 33 ± 0.5 °C, with RH maintained at 70 ± 10% and a 12:12 h light:dark photoperiod. Each individual was checked twice daily. Date of adult emergence was recorded when the fully sclerotized adult had left the pupal chamber. Only individuals that completed development to emergence were included in analyses. To reduce cohort effects, eggs from at least 10 field-collected females were distributed across temperatures, and rearing vials were rotated within chambers every 48 h.

Sex determination and morphometric measurements  
Within 24 h of emergence, adults were cold-immobilized at 4 °C for 5 min and measured under a stereomicroscope equipped with a digital camera and calibrated micrometer. Total body length was measured from the anterior margin of the clypeus to the posterior apex of the abdomen, excluding the extruded genitalia. Each specimen was measured twice by the same observer, and the mean was used in subsequent analyses. Sex was determined by examining secondary sexual characters of the abdomen and genitalia [2]. Measurements were performed blind with respect to rearing temperature and developmental duration.

Thermal summation values  
Development duration (*D*) was defined as the time from oviposition to adult emergence. The lower developmental threshold (*T*₀) was estimated by linear regression of development rate (1/*D*) on rearing temperature (*T*) across all individuals, following the thermal summation approach [3,4]. For each individual, the thermal summation value (*K*) required for emergence was calculated as *K* = *D*(*T* − *T*₀). This individual *K* served as the response variable representing physiological age at emergence. A general thermal summation model was defined as the mean *K* of the calibration dataset, assuming a constant thermal requirement independent of body size. Size-dependent models were constructed by regressing *K* on adult body length at emergence. Because preliminary inspection indicated a negative relationship between *K* and body length, linear models of the form *K* = β₀ + β₁*L* + ε were fitted, where *L* is body length and ε is the residual error. Models were fitted separately for males and females, and a combined model including sex as a factor was also evaluated. The potential for nonlinearity was assessed by adding a quadratic term; it was retained only when significant at α = 0.05.

Model validation  
To evaluate predictive accuracy, the dataset was randomly partitioned into calibration (70%) and validation (30%) subsets, stratified by temperature and sex. The calibration subset was used to estimate *T*₀, the general mean *K*, and sex-specific regression coefficients for the body-length models. The relationship between insect development and temperature is a cornerstone of forensic entomology, yet its application is frequently hampered by significant intraspecific variation in development times [1, 2]. This variability introduces substantial uncertainty into post-mortem interval (PMI) estimates, particularly during the later stages of decomposition when insects like *Creophilus maxillosus* are often the primary evidence [3]. Our study addresses this challenge by demonstrating a predictable, inverse relationship between the size of *C. maxillosus* at emergence and its physiological age, quantified as the thermal summation value (K). This finding provides a novel, biologically grounded method to refine age estimates and enhance the precision of forensic investigations.

### Implications for Forensic Entomology

The principal outcome of this research is the validation of adult body size as a proxy for developmental age in *C. maxillosus*. The general thermal summation model, while foundational, provides an average K value that assumes a uniform developmental rate across all individuals. Our results clearly show this is not the case; larger beetles, having presumably experienced more favourable larval conditions, required a smaller cumulative thermal input to reach emergence. The validation study confirmed that K values derived from a size-based model were significantly closer to the true, observed K values than those from the general model. This represents a tangible improvement in the accuracy of age estimation. In a forensic context, where a PMI estimate can be a critical piece of evidence, reducing the error margin associated with this natural variation is of paramount importance [4]. The ability to use a single, easily measurable metric—beetle length—to refine the age estimate moves the field closer to the precision demanded by the judicial system.

### The Role of Intraspecific Variation and Sexual Dimorphism

Our finding that sex-specific models yielded the most accurate predictions underscores the complexity of developmental biology. Sexual size dimorphism is common in insects, and *C. maxillosus* is no exception, with females typically being larger than males [5]. This inherent difference in size is linked to different developmental trajectories and energetic investments, leading to distinct relationships between size and K for each sex. By developing separate predictive models for males and females, we accounted for this fundamental biological variation. This approach aligns with a growing recognition in forensic entomology that broad, species-level models can be insufficient and that incorporating factors such as sex, strain, and developmental conditions is necessary to improve accuracy [6, 7]. The failure to account for such variables may explain some of the discrepancies observed between laboratory-reared and field-collected specimens in previous studies.

### Mechanistic Insights and Limitations

The inverse relationship between size and K is likely rooted in the trade-offs inherent in insect life history. Larvae developing under suboptimal conditions (e.g., limited food resources, competition) may exhibit extended development times, resulting in smaller adult size but a higher cumulative thermal summation value due to a prolonged period of growth and metabolic activity [8]. Conversely, larvae with access to abundant resources can develop more rapidly, reaching a larger size at emergence with a lower accumulated K. This suggests that body size at emergence is an integrated record of the larval environment, reflecting both the nutritional history and the physiological cost of development.

However, the application of this method is not without limitations. Our models were developed under controlled laboratory conditions with constant temperatures and ad libitum food. In the field, fluctuating temperatures and variable resource availability could introduce further complexity. The accuracy of the size-based model relies on the assumption that the relationship between size and K holds true across different environmental contexts, which requires further field validation. Furthermore, the method is applicable only when the adult beetle is recovered, precluding its use for larval or pupal specimens, which are often the primary targets for PMI estimation [9].

### Future Directions and Practical Application

The logical next step is to validate these findings in a field setting. Future research should involve sampling *C. maxolosus* from cadavers in various habitats and seasons to test the robustness of the size-based K models under natural, fluctuating thermal regimes. It would also be valuable to investigate whether this principle extends to other forensically important beetle species, such as those in the families Silphidae and Dermestidae. If a generalisable pattern emerges, it could revolutionise how we approach age estimation for later colonisers.

In practice, a forensic entomologist could measure the length of an emerged *C. maxillosus* adult and, using the appropriate sex-specific equation, calculate a more precise K value. This refined K would then be used to estimate the insect's age, and by extension, the PMI, with a greater degree of confidence. This method provides a simple yet powerful tool to supplement traditional thermal summation models.

### Conclusion

In conclusion, this study demonstrates that body size at emergence is a significant and predictable source of intraspecific variation in the development of *C. maxillosus*. By incorporating size and sex into thermal summation models, we can significantly improve the accuracy of age estimates. This approach acknowledges the biological reality of developmental plasticity and offers a practical method to refine PMI calculations. While further validation is required, the principle that an individual's size can inform its physiological age represents a meaningful advancement in forensic entomology, promising to enhance the reliability of entomological evidence in legal investigations.

Crowdsourcing has become a central mechanism for collecting data at scale by decomposing complex problems into short, repetitive microtasks [1, 2]. Platforms such as Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) have enabled researchers to annotate images, transcribe audio, evaluate text, and conduct behavioral experiments with remarkable speed and low cost [3, 4, 5]. However, many scientifically and socially important tasks are not naturally decomposable into independent microtasks. They require open-ended generation, contextual judgment, and iterative exploration, all of which are difficult to coordinate across a distributed crowd [6, 7]. This limitation is especially acute when the goal is to construct a large network: the crowd must not only contribute individual links but also collectively determine the network’s topology, often without a predefined schema or exhaustive list of nodes.

Networks provide a powerful representation for social, informational, biological, and cognitive systems [8, 9, 10]. In many cases, the network is latent: the entities and relationships exist, but the complete topology is unknown or expensive to obtain through expert curation. Crowdsourcing offers a potential solution because human workers can recognize and propose relationships that are difficult for automated systems to infer. Yet naive approaches—asking workers to list all neighbors of a node, or to evaluate randomly sampled pairs—scale poorly, produce redundant effort, and often yield noisy or inconsistent data [11, 12]. Efficient crowd exploration therefore requires mechanisms that guide workers toward informative regions of the network while maintaining quality and coverage.

We focus on a particularly challenging and consequential network: the network of causal attributions. Causal relationships are fundamental to explanation, prediction, and intervention [13, 14]. Formal frameworks for causal inference typically rely on observational or experimental data and strong assumptions about underlying graphical structure [13, 15]. Research on causal perception and causal learning has largely examined small sets of events in controlled laboratory settings [16, 17]. A large-scale map of causal attributions—where nodes represent events, conditions, or entities and directed edges represent perceived cause-and-effect relationships—could illuminate shared causal beliefs, reveal structural regularities in causal reasoning, and provide empirical material for causal inference and causal discovery. Building such a network manually is prohibitively expensive, but crowdsourcing it raises fundamental questions: How do workers propose causal relationships? How can their proposals be validated reliably? How can independent workers explore a vast causal space without duplicating effort or drifting into low-quality regions?

In this paper, we study the crowdsourcing of large networks where the crowd provides the network topology via microtasks. We conduct experiments on AMT testing how workers propose and validate individual causal relationships and introduce a method for independent crowd workers to explore large networks. The core of the method, Iterative Pathway Refinement (IPR), is a theoretically-principled mechanism for efficient exploration via microtasks. IPR reframes network construction as an iterative process of pathway generation, validation, and refinement. Rather than asking workers to evaluate isolated edges in an arbitrary order, IPR presents them with partial causal pathways and asks them to extend, correct, or validate specific links. This design provides local context, encourages coherent reasoning, and focuses crowd effort on promising regions of the network. The iterative structure allows the method to balance exploration of new nodes with exploitation of already-discovered pathways, while redundancy and repeated validation help control noise.

We evaluate IPR in two complementary settings. First, we use synthetic networks with known ground-truth topologies to measure coverage, precision, recall, and efficiency relative to baseline crowdsourcing strategies. Synthetic evaluation allows controlled manipulation of network size, density, clustering, and noise, isolating the mechanism’s ability to recover structure under varying conditions. Second, we apply the method on AMT to extract a large-scale causal attribution network. We then investigate the structure of this network, including its degree distribution, connectivity patterns, clustering, and community organization, as well as the activity patterns and efficiency of the workers who constructed it. Worker interactions reveal important characteristics of causal perception, such as which types of relationships are proposed quickly, which require deliberation, and how validation behavior varies across workers and pathways. The resulting network data can improve our understanding of causality and causal inference by providing a broad empirical substrate for testing theories of causal reasoning and for generating hypotheses about causal mechanisms.

This work makes several contributions. It formulates the problem of crowd exploration of large networks as an iterative pathway refinement task, providing a principled alternative to independent edge microtasks. It reports controlled experiments on how crowd workers propose and validate causal relationships, offering practical insight into quality control for open-ended network elicitation. It introduces and evaluates IPR on synthetic networks, demonstrating efficiency and robustness relative to standard baselines. It applies the method on AMT to construct a large-scale causal attribution network and analyzes both the network’s structure and the behavior of the workers who built it. Together, these contributions advance crowdsourcing methodology, empirical research on causal cognition, and the use of crowd-generated network data for causal inference.

We recruited participants from Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT), a widely used platform for microtask crowdsourcing [1,2]. Eligibility was restricted to workers aged 18 years or older, located in the United States, with an approval rating above 95% and at least 500 previously approved HITs. Workers provided informed consent under a protocol approved by our institutional review board. Compensation was set above the prevailing federal minimum wage and included performance bonuses for high-quality contributions. To minimize attrition and careless responding, we administered qualification HITs, embedded attention checks, and used gold-standard items with known answers [6]. Workers who failed more than one attention check or whose gold-standard accuracy fell below 70% were excluded from subsequent rounds.

We formalized a causal attribution network as a directed graph \(G=(V,E)\), where vertices \(V\) represent causal events, states, or entities and directed edges \(E\) represent the relation “\(A\) causes \(B\).” The crowd constructed this network through two complementary microtask types: proposal and validation. In proposal tasks, workers were shown a seed or active node and asked to generate up to five plausible causes and five plausible effects. Instructions emphasized that causal relations should reflect a perceived cause-and-effect mechanism rather than mere correlation, temporal succession, or semantic association [3]. Responses were collected as free text, normalized through lowercasing, lemmatization, and removal of stop words, and then clustered into candidate nodes using string similarity plus independent crowd verification. In validation tasks, workers were shown a pair of candidate nodes and asked whether \(A\) causes \(B\), \(B\) causes \(A\), both directions, neither, or whether they were unsure. Each candidate directed edge received five independent judgments. Edges were retained when a majority selected the corresponding direction and inter-rater agreement exceeded a prespecified threshold; uncertain and low-agreement edges were retained for further refinement rather than discarded immediately.

The core of our method, Iterative Pathway Refinement (IPR), is a theoretically principled mechanism for efficient exploration of large networks via microtasks. IPR treats network discovery as an active learning problem over an unknown directed graph. The algorithm maintains a probabilistic posterior over the existence and direction of candidate edges, updated after each validation response using a Bayesian model of worker accuracy and item difficulty [4,7]. At each iteration, IPR selects the next microtasks by maximizing expected information gain per unit cost. Information gain is computed as the expected reduction in entropy over the graph posterior, while cost incorporates monetary payment, expected worker latency, and redundancy with previously queried edges. Starting from a small set of seed nodes, IPR expands promising pathways by requesting new causes and effects at frontier nodes, validates the most uncertain candidate edges, and prunes branches whose posterior probability or expected expansion value falls below a dynamic threshold. This iterative procedure balances exploration of novel regions with exploitation of partially validated pathways, allowing the crowd to discover a large network without exhaustively querying all possible pairs.

We first evaluated IPR on synthetic networks to isolate its performance from live-worker variability. We generated directed acyclic graphs with 100 to 1,000 nodes and varied average degree, degree distribution, community structure, and path length. Networks included Erdős–Rényi random graphs, scale-free graphs, small-world graphs, and hierarchical causal graphs. Simulated workers were parameterized with different accuracy levels, response biases, and costs, and we compared IPR against random edge sampling, breadth-first search, snowball sampling, and uniform path sampling [5]. Performance was measured by precision, recall, F1, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, number of validation queries, path length, node coverage, and cost per discovered edge. Each condition was replicated 100 times. These experiments tested whether IPR improved discovery efficiency under realistic noise and cost constraints.

We then deployed IPR on AMT to extract a large-scale causal attribution network. We initialized the process with 50 seed nodes spanning everyday events, health, technology, finance, social behavior, and natural phenomena. The deployment proceeded in ten iterative rounds. Each round combined proposal HITs, in which workers extended active pathways, with validation HITs, in which independent workers judged candidate directed edges. Workers could participate across multiple rounds, but no worker validated an edge they had proposed. We logged worker identifiers, session timestamps, response latencies, HIT completion counts, proposal and validation choices, gold-standard performance, and agreement statistics. After each round, we aggregated validated edges, updated the posterior, and selected the next set of queries. We continued until the rate of newly validated high-confidence edges fell below a prespecified saturation criterion.

For network analysis, we constructed the final directed graph from edges meeting the majority and agreement thresholds. We examined degree distributions, reciprocity, clustering coefficients, modularity, community structure, k-core decomposition, and centrality measures. To characterize causal perception, we analyzed asymmetries between in-degree and out-degree, typical path lengths, and the prevalence of causal motifs.
