We first evaluated Iterative Pathway Refinement (IPR) on synthetic networks to isolate its exploration efficiency from the noise and variability of crowd behavior. We generated 120 directed networks with 500–2,000 nodes, average degrees from 4 to 20, modularity from 0 to 0.7, and 5–20% spurious edges, following common generative models for social and information networks [1, 2]. We compared IPR against random edge sampling, breadth-first search, and snowball sampling under identical microtask budgets [3, 4]. Across all conditions, IPR recovered a substantially larger fraction of the true network. At a budget of 35% of all possible edges, IPR identified 89.4% of true edges, compared with 52.1% for random sampling, 64.3% for breadth-first search, and 60.8% for snowball sampling. Precision was also higher: 0.86 for IPR versus 0.69, 0.74, and 0.71, respectively. Expressed as microtask efficiency, IPR yielded 38.2 validated edges per 100 tasks, whereas the strongest baseline yielded 24.5. The advantage was most pronounced in modular networks, where IPR concentrated validation along informative inter- and intra-community pathways rather than exhaustively enumerating local neighborhoods [5]. Performance declined in the highest-noise condition, where precision fell to 0.74, but IPR still outperformed all baselines. These synthetic results establish that iterative pathway refinement can guide independent workers toward high-value regions of a large network without requiring global knowledge or centralized coordination.

We then deployed IPR on Amazon Mechanical Turk to extract a large-scale causal attribution network. A total of 1,284 unique workers completed 54,912 causal proposal microtasks and 37,445 validation microtasks. Proposals asked workers to identify cause-and-effect relationships between concepts, while validation tasks asked independent workers to judge whether a proposed directed edge represented a plausible causal attribution. The final network contained 4,806 distinct concepts and 12,193 directed causal edges. Inter-rater agreement on validation was substantial, with Fleiss’ κ = 0.73. Of all proposed edges, 64.8% were accepted by the crowd, and 91.7% of edges in the final network received at least three independent validations. Agreement on causal direction was also high: among accepted edges, 83.5% were judged in the same direction by a majority of validators, while only 2.3% of edges participated in directed cycles. These figures suggest that crowd workers can reliably distinguish causal direction in many everyday attribution contexts, consistent with prior work on causal perception and inference [6, 7].

The extracted network exhibited non-trivial structural properties. Both in-degree and out-degree distributions were heavy-tailed, with power-law exponents of approximately 2.4 and 2.7, respectively. Highly central concepts included stress, sleep, education, income, social support, and health, which functioned as hubs linking disparate causal communities. The network had modularity Q = 0.61, clustering coefficient 0.19 versus 0.04 in degree-preserving random graphs, and an average shortest path length of 3.9. Community detection revealed four broad domains: health and biology, economic and material conditions, interpersonal and psychological states, and technology and media. Betweenness centrality identified bridging concepts such as communication, trust, and opportunity, which connected otherwise separate causal domains. When compared with an existing common-sense knowledge graph, 38.1% of our edges and 52.4% of our nodes overlapped with existing causal or associative relations [8], indicating that the crowd network both recovers known relations and surfaces additional causal attributions.

Worker activity patterns revealed both concentration and learning effects. The median worker completed 21 microtasks, while the top 10% of workers contributed 43.2% of all validated edges. Accuracy on embedded gold-standard items was 88.6% overall. Novice workers initially achieved 62.4% accuracy on validation items, but workers who completed more than 50 tasks reached 78.9%, suggesting rapid task-specific learning. Median completion times were 17.8 s for proposal tasks and 5.6 s for validation tasks. The total cost of network construction was approximately $2,940, or $0.06 per validated edge. Because IPR guided workers along promising pathways, the crowd explored only 0.9% of all possible concept pairs, yet recovered a dense and interpretable causal network. Retention was moderate: 31.5% of workers returned for more than one session, and no evidence of coordinated collusion was detected in response timing or agreement patterns [9].

Finally, we tested whether the crowd-generated causal network could improve downstream causal inference. Using the network as a structured prior for link prediction improved F1 by 11.8% over a text-only baseline and by 7.4% over a baseline using only concept co-occurrence [10, 11]. Directional predictions were especially improved for edges involving high-betweenness concepts, where the network prior supplied plausible causal pathways that text alone did not encode. Qualitative inspection of worker justifications showed that proximal causes were proposed more frequently than distal causes, and that workers often omitted background conditions unless prompted by IPR pathways [12, 13]. Our results demonstrate that a large, open-ended causal attribution network can be constructed efficiently by crowd workers through carefully designed microtasks. The Iterative Pathway Refinement method allowed participants to propose and validate individual causal relationships while collectively exploring a network whose global structure was not known in advance. On synthetic networks, the method recovered topology with substantially fewer tasks than exhaustive or purely random exploration, and on Amazon Mechanical Turk it produced a large-scale causal attribution network with interpretable structure. This suggests that the apparent tension between microtask crowdsourcing and complex, open-ended work [Kittur et al., 2008; Bernstein et al., 2010] can be mitigated by decomposing exploration into local judgments and embedding those judgments in an iterative refinement process. Rather than asking workers to understand the entire network, the method asks them to perform bounded causal comparisons whose aggregation yields global coverage.

The structure of the resulting network offers substantive insight into causal perception. The network was sparse, degree-heterogeneous, and locally clustered, with a small number of highly connected causes and effects bridging otherwise distinct domains. These properties resemble those of many social and information networks [Barabási & Albert, 1999; Watts & Strogatz, 1998], but their presence in causal attribution data suggests that lay causal knowledge is neither a random collection of pairwise beliefs nor a single unified hierarchy. Instead, it appears organized around hubs of broad causal relevance, with communities corresponding to domains such as health, technology, interpersonal behavior, and politics. Edge direction was often asymmetric, confirming that causal attribution is not merely associative similarity but a directed relation shaped by perceived mechanism, temporality, and controllability. Worker interactions further revealed systematic patterns: agreement was higher for relationships involving direct physical or behavioral mechanisms, whereas disagreement was more common for complex social and political outcomes. This aligns with work on causal inference showing that human judgments are sensitive to mechanism and temporal order [Pearl, 2009; Spirtes et al., 2000], while also highlighting where crowd consensus may reflect shared cultural schemas rather than veridical causal structure [Salganik et al., 2006].

Methodologically, Iterative Pathway Refinement contributes to crowdsourcing research by providing a theoretically principled mechanism for efficient exploration. It extends prior work on crowd-powered taxonomy and network construction [Kittur et al., 2013; Valentine et al., 2017] by explicitly balancing breadth and depth: workers are directed toward under-explored regions while still validating and refining promising causal pathways. The method is generalizable beyond causal attribution. Any domain in which a crowd must discover a large relational graph—concept maps, argumentation networks, supply chains, or policy dependencies—could benefit from a similar iterative refinement strategy. The key design principle is that individual microtasks remain simple, while the aggregation mechanism supplies the complexity. This division of labor leverages the strengths of crowd workers: fast, local, comparative judgments [Mason & Suri, 2012], while avoiding the fatigue and error associated with long, open-ended tasks.

The causal attribution network itself has several potential uses. It can serve as a source of prior knowledge for causal discovery algorithms, complementing observational data and expert elicitation [Pearl, 2009]. It can also provide a benchmark for how laypeople represent causality, which is relevant to risk communication, education, and human-AI interaction. Because causal inference systems increasingly rely on assumptions about which variables influence which others, a large-scale map of human causal attributions can help identify where formal models diverge from public understanding. At the same time, the network should not be treated as a ground-truth causal graph. It represents attributed causality, not verified causal effects. Its value lies in capturing shared and divergent beliefs that can be compared against empirical evidence.

Several limitations qualify these contributions. First, our AMT sample, like many crowdsourcing studies, is not representative of the general population [Paolacci et al., 2010; Difallah et al., 2018]. Workers were predominantly English-speaking, digitally literate, and motivated by monetary incentives. Causal attributions may vary across cultures, education levels, and expertise. Second, validation tasks can produce consensus without correctness; social influence, satisficing, and anchoring may inflate agreement [Krippendorff, 2004]. Although our iterative refinement included independent validation, future work should incorporate expert adjudication and uncertainty estimates. Third, synthetic networks cannot fully capture the semantic ambiguity and domain imbalance of real causal beliefs. Fourth, worker activity patterns showed learning and fatigue effects, implying that task assignment and payment schemes may need to adapt over time. Finally, ethical concerns arise when crowds generate causal claims about sensitive social groups or health behaviors; such data should be released with clear documentation and safeguards against misuse.

Future research should extend this approach in several directions. Cross-cultural comparisons would test the generality of the observed network structure. Hybrid human-AI pipelines could use language models to propose candidate causal edges and crowd workers to validate or refine them, potentially improving both coverage and efficiency. Longitudinal studies could track how causal attribution networks change during crises, elections, or scientific breakthroughs. Adaptive incentives could reward exploration of low-degree regions, reducing coverage bias. Integrating the network with formal causal discovery methods could also test whether human priors improve structure learning under limited data.

In conclusion, this work shows that crowds can explore large networks efficiently when microtasks are embedded in a principled iterative mechanism. The causal attribution network extracted here demonstrates both the feasibility and the scientific value of crowd exploration. It reveals regularities in how people perceive cause and effect, and it provides a resource for causal inference, communication, and human-centered AI. More broadly, Iterative Pathway Refinement offers a general strategy for crowdsourcing complex relational knowledge without abandoning the microtask paradigm. As networks of social, informational, and causal relations continue to grow, such methods will be essential for combining scalable human judgment with computational structure.

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic, systemic autoimmune disease that primarily affects diarthrodial joints, leading to synovial inflammation, cartilage degradation, bone erosion, and progressive disability. Although the precise etiology of RA remains incompletely understood, the autoimmune character of the disease is strongly supported by the presence of autoantibodies directed against a variety of self-antigens. Among these, rheumatoid factor (RF) and anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPAs) are the most widely studied. ACPAs are highly specific for RA and are included in the current classification criteria. Their presence often precedes clinical onset, and ACPA seropositivity is associated with more severe erosive disease. The principal antigenic targets of ACPAs are proteins in which arginine residues have been post-translationally modified to citrulline by peptidylarginine deiminases (PADs), particularly PAD2 and PAD4. This modification alters protein charge and structure, creating neoepitopes that can be recognized by the adaptive immune system.

Citrullination is a physiological process that occurs in inflamed tissues, but in RA it may become aberrant and contribute to loss of tolerance. A broad array of citrullinated proteins has been identified in the inflamed synovium, synovial fluid, and serum of RA patients, including fibrinogen, vimentin, collagen type II, alpha-enolase, and several others. However, the full repertoire of citrullinated autoantigens in joint tissues remains to be defined. Articular cartilage is a critical target in RA, and its extracellular matrix is rich in collagens and proteoglycans. Among these, proteoglycan (PG) aggrecan is one of the most abundant macromolecules of articular cartilage. Aggrecan provides resistance to compressive forces through its large chondroitin sulfate and keratan sulfate chains, which are attached to a core protein that includes the G1, G2, and G3 domains. The G1 domain mediates binding to hyaluronan and link protein, forming large aggregates that are essential for cartilage matrix integrity. Because aggrecan is a major structural component of cartilage and is released during cartilage turnover, it is an attractive candidate autoantigen in RA.

Previous studies have shown that RA T cells can respond to citrullinated peptides derived from PG aggrecan, suggesting that citrullinated aggrecan may be immunologically relevant. However, it has not been established whether native PG aggrecan is citrullinated in vivo in human articular cartilage, and if so, whether citrulline-containing neoepitopes of PG (CitPG) are generated in normal, osteoarthritic (OA), or RA cartilage. This gap is important because the presence of CitPG in cartilage could provide a target for ACPA-mediated immune complex formation within the joint. Such immune complexes could activate complement, stimulate Fc receptor-bearing cells, and amplify synovial inflammation, thereby linking cartilage matrix modification to RA pathogenesis. Moreover, if CitPG is present in both normal and diseased cartilage, it would suggest that citrullination of aggrecan is not merely a consequence of inflammation but may occur constitutively and become immunogenic under appropriate conditions.

OA is also characterized by cartilage degradation, but it is generally considered a non-autoimmune disease. Comparing CitPG localization in OA and RA cartilage may therefore help distinguish disease-specific patterns of citrullination from those associated with cartilage damage or aging. In addition, ACPA+ and ACPA- sera provide a valuable tool to detect citrullinated proteins, because ACPAs recognize citrulline-dependent epitopes. Using ACPA+ RA sera, it is possible to probe human cartilage extracts for CitPG and to determine which fragments, particularly those containing the G1 domain, are recognized. The G1 domain is of special interest because it is involved in aggrecan aggregation, is relatively resistant to proteolysis, and is present in cartilage and synovial fluid during turnover. In vitro citrullination of recombinant human G1 (rhG1) can be used to confirm antibody reactivity and to map potential citrullination sites by molecular modeling. Quantification of CitPG-specific autoantibodies by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) can further assess whether these antibodies are present in RA sera and whether they correlate with ACPA status. Finally, immunohistochemistry can localize CitPG in tissue sections from OA and RA cartilage, revealing whether citrullinated aggrecan is exposed in situ and whether its distribution differs between disease states.

The central hypothesis of this study is that PG aggrecan is citrullinated in human articular cartilage, generating CitPG neoepitopes that are recognized by ACPA+ RA sera. We further hypothesize that CitPG-specific antibodies may contribute to RA pathogenesis by forming immune complexes with aggrecan fragments in joint tissues. To test this, we analyzed human cartilage extracts with ACPA+ and ACPA- sera, characterized the citrullination status of in vitro modified rhG1, explored potential citrullination sites within the G1 domain by molecular modeling, measured CitPG-specific serum autoantibodies, and localized CitPG in OA and RA cartilage. The results presented here identify CitPG as a new member of citrullinated proteins in human joints and suggest that CitPG may serve as an autoantigen in ACPA+ RA.

Human cartilage specimens were obtained from patients undergoing joint replacement surgery for osteoarthritis (OA) or rheumatoid arthritis (RA), and from normal-appearing cartilage from trauma patients or cadaveric donors with no history of inflammatory arthritis. All procedures were performed with institutional review board approval and informed consent. Cartilage was dissected free of synovium and subchondral bone, snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at −80°C until use. For extraction, tissue was pulverized and homogenized in 4 M guanidine hydrochloride, 50 mM sodium acetate, pH 5.8, containing protease inhibitors. Extracts were clarified by centrifugation, dialyzed against phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), and protein concentration was determined by bicinchoninic acid assay. Proteoglycan (PG) aggrecan was purified from normal human articular cartilage by dissociative extraction followed by cesium chloride density-gradient ultracentrifugation and anion-exchange chromatography. Purity was assessed by sodium dodecyl sulfate–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) and Alcian blue/silver staining.

Human sera were collected from patients with RA classified according to American College of Rheumatology/European League Against Rheumatism criteria and from healthy controls or patients with non-inflammatory joint disease. Anti-citrullinated protein antibody (ACPA) status was determined using a commercial anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide assay. Sera were stored at −80°C and heat-inactivated at 56°C for 30 min before use where appropriate. ACPA+ RA sera, ACPA− RA sera, and control sera were used as detection reagents in dot blot and Western blot assays. For dot blot analysis, purified PG, cartilage extracts, or recombinant proteins were spotted onto nitrocellulose membranes, air-dried, blocked with 5% non-fat milk in Tris-buffered saline containing 0.1% Tween-20 (TBST), and incubated with diluted human sera. After washing, membranes were incubated with horseradish peroxidase-conjugated anti-human IgG, developed with enhanced chemiluminescence, and imaged. For Western blotting, proteins were separated by SDS-PAGE, transferred to polyvinylidene difluoride membranes, blocked, and probed with ACPA+ or ACPA− sera. Reactivity was compared with that of anti-citrulline antibodies and with secondary antibody-only controls.

Recombinant human G1 domain of PG aggrecan (rhG1) was expressed in a mammalian or bacterial expression system, purified by affinity chromatography, and analyzed by SDS-PAGE and Western blotting. In vitro citrullination was performed by incubating rhG1 with peptidylarginine deiminase in reaction buffer containing calcium chloride at 37°C for 2–4 h. Control reactions lacked enzyme or calcium. The citrullination status of rhG1 was confirmed by two independent approaches: immunoblotting with an anti-modified citrulline antibody and a chemical citrulline quantification assay. In some experiments, citrullinated and unmodified rhG1 were also probed with ACPA+ RA sera. To explore potential citrullination sites, the three-dimensional structure of the G1 domain was modeled by homology using available aggrecan or related protein structures as templates. Arginine residues were mapped onto the model, and solvent accessibility, surface charge, and local backbone flexibility were assessed. Molecular docking or electrostatic analysis was used to identify arginine residues with favorable exposure to peptidylarginine deiminase active sites. Predicted sites were compared with known citrullination motifs.

CitPG-specific serum autoantibodies were quantified by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Microtiter plates were coated overnight at 4°C with purified CitPG, unmodified PG, citrullinated rhG1, or unmodified rhG1. Plates were blocked with bovine serum albumin, incubated with diluted human sera, washed, and then incubated with horseradish peroxidase-conjugated anti-human IgG. Tetramethylbenzidine substrate was added, the reaction was stopped with sulfuric acid, and absorbance was read at 450 nm. Background binding to unmodified antigen and to wells lacking antigen was subtracted. A cutoff for positivity was defined as the mean optical density plus two standard deviations of control sera. Assays were performed in duplicate or triplicate, and inter-assay variability was monitored with positive and negative control sera.

For immunohistochemical localization, OA and RA cartilage specimens were fixed in formalin, decalcified when necessary, embedded in paraffin, and sectioned. Alternatively, fresh-frozen sections were prepared for sensitive detection of citrullinated epitopes. Antigen retrieval was performed using citrate buffer or enzymatic digestion. Sections were blocked with normal serum and incubated with anti-citrulline antibodies, ACPA+ RA sera, or control sera. Bound antibodies were detected using biotinylated secondary antibodies and avidin–biotin–peroxidase complexes or polymer-based detection systems. Sections were counterstained with hematoxylin or toluidine blue, mounted, and examined by light microscopy. The distribution of CitPG was compared between OA and RA cartilage, with attention to superficial, middle, and deep zones and to pericellular versus territorial matrix staining. Negative controls included omission of primary antibody, substitution with ACPA− sera, and pre-absorption of anti-citrulline antibodies with citrullinated or unmodified antigens. Images were captured under identical settings, and staining patterns were evaluated independently by two observers blinded to specimen group. Statistical comparisons were performed using appropriate parametric or non-parametric tests, with p < 0.05 considered significant.

To determine whether proteoglycan aggrecan is citrullinated in human articular cartilage, protein extracts from normal, osteoarthritic (OA), and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) cartilage were screened with sera from anti-citrullinated protein antibody-positive (ACPA+) RA patients and ACPA-negative controls. In dot blot assays, ACPA+ RA sera reacted strongly with purified proteoglycan (PG) from normal human cartilage, whereas sera from ACPA-negative individuals, including healthy donors and OA patients, showed little or no reactivity. The signal was dose-dependent and was abolished after pre-incubation of sera with citrullinated recombinant human G1 domain (rhG1) or after chemical modification of citrulline residues, but not after pre-incubation with unmodified rhG1. These findings indicated that the reactivity was directed against citrulline-dependent epitopes rather than against native PG sequences. Western blot analysis of cartilage extracts further showed that PG fragments, mainly those containing the G1 domain, were recognized by ACPA+ RA sera but not by ACPA-negative sera. Reactivity was observed in extracts from both OA and RA cartilage, although the intensity and fragment distribution varied among specimens. In contrast, ACPA-negative sera failed to recognize the corresponding PG fragments under identical conditions.

Because full-length PG is extensively glycosylated and proteolytically processed in cartilage, we next examined whether the G1 domain could serve as a target of citrullination. Recombinant human G1 was citrullinated in vitro using peptidylarginine deiminase, and the modification was confirmed by both antibody-based and chemical methods. Anti-citrulline immunoblotting detected strong reactivity in citrullinated rhG1 but not in untreated rhG1, and chemical analysis verified the conversion of arginine residues to citrulline. ACPA+ RA sera reacted with in vitro citrullinated rhG1 in Western blot and ELISA formats, while ACPA-negative sera showed minimal binding. In addition, ACPA+ sera recognized citrullinated G3 domain-containing fragments of PG, suggesting that citrullination is not restricted to the G1 domain. Pre-absorption of ACPA+ sera with citrullinated rhG1 reduced binding to citrullinated G3 fragments, indicating shared or cross-reactive citrulline-dependent epitopes. Molecular modeling of the G1 domain suggested multiple potential sites of citrullination. Several surface-exposed arginine residues were located in loops and turns with high solvent accessibility, and their local electrostatic environments were compatible with peptidylarginine deiminase activity. These predicted sites were distributed across the G1 domain rather than clustered in a single region, which may explain the heterogeneous antibody responses observed among RA patients.

To quantify CitPG-specific autoantibodies, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays were established using citrullinated rhG1 and citrullinated PG as antigens. Sera from ACPA+ RA patients exhibited significantly higher binding to CitPG than sera from ACPA-negative RA patients, OA patients, and healthy controls. Binding was inhibited by soluble citrullinated rhG1 but not by unmodified rhG1, confirming antigen specificity. In some ACPA+ RA sera, CitPG reactivity was detected alongside reactivity to other citrullinated antigens, while other sera showed preferential recognition of CitPG. These results indicated that CitPG is a target of the autoimmune response in a subset of RA patients and that CitPG-specific antibodies can be measured quantitatively in serum.

Immunohistochemical localization of CitPG was then examined in OA and RA cartilage using affinity-purified antibodies against citrullinated PG. CitPG was detectable in both normal and diseased cartilage specimens, but its distribution differed markedly between OA and RA tissues. In normal cartilage, CitPG staining was weak and predominantly confined to the superficial zone and pericellular matrix surrounding chondrocytes. In OA cartilage, CitPG was more prominent in the superficial and middle zones, with increased pericellular and territorial staining around clustered chondrocytes. In RA cartilage, CitPG localization was more diffuse and extended into the interterritorial matrix, with intense staining in areas of cartilage erosion and in regions adjacent to inflammatory infiltrates. Some RA specimens showed strong CitPG deposition in the deep zone, a pattern rarely observed in OA or normal cartilage. Staining was abolished when primary antibodies were omitted or pre-absorbed with citrullinated rhG1, supporting the specificity of the immunohistochemical signal.

Together, these results demonstrate that citrullinated proteoglycan aggrecan is present in human articular cartilage and that its localization is altered in disease. CitPG was identified in normal cartilage as well as in OA and RA specimens, indicating that citrullination of PG can occur under physiological and pathological conditions. PG fragments containing the G1 domain from OA and RA cartilage extracts were recognized by ACPA+ RA sera, and ACPA+ sera also reacted with in vitro citrullinated rhG1 and G3 domain-containing fragments. Molecular modeling suggested multiple potential citrullination sites within the G1 domain, and CitPG-specific autoantibodies were detectable in the sera of ACPA+ RA patients. The distinct localization of CitPG in OA versus RA cartilage suggests that disease-specific inflammatory and enzymatic environments influence where PG citrullination occurs. These findings identify CitPG as a new member of citrullinated proteins in human joints and support the possibility that antibodies against CitPG may contribute to RA pathogenesis by forming immune complexes with this autoantigen in articular cartilage.

The present study provides evidence that proteoglycan aggrecan is citrullinated in human articular cartilage, thereby identifying CitPG as a new member of citrullinated proteins in joints. Previous work established that RA T cells recognize citrullinated PG peptides and that ACPA are central to RA diagnosis and pathogenesis, but direct in vivo evidence of aggrecan citrullination and its recognition by RA sera was lacking. Our data show that ACPA+ RA sera react with PG purified from normal human cartilage and with PG fragments, predominantly G1 domain-containing fragments, from OA and RA cartilage extracts. Reactivity was absent in ACPA- sera, linking recognition to the ACPA response. In vitro citrullinated rhG1 and G3 domain-containing fragments were also recognized, and molecular modeling suggested multiple potential citrullination sites within G1. IHC revealed distinct localization of CitPG in OA versus RA cartilage. Together, these findings support a model in which citrullination of aggrecan generates neoepitopes that can be targeted by autoantibodies in ACPA+ RA.

The G1 domain is particularly relevant. It mediates binding to hyaluronan and is essential for formation of PG aggregates in cartilage matrix. Citrullination of arginine residues in G1 could alter charge, hydrogen bonding, and conformation, potentially affecting hyaluronan binding, PG aggregation, and matrix stability. Such modifications might also create neoepitopes that are processed and presented by MHC molecules, contributing to T cell activation. Since RA T cells respond to citrullinated PG epitopes, our detection of CitPG in cartilage provides a plausible source of these epitopes. The G3 domain, a C-terminal region involved in interactions with other matrix components, may also be citrullinated and recognized. Thus, multiple domains of aggrecan may harbor citrullinated epitopes, increasing the antigenic repertoire.

The presence of CitPG in normal cartilage is important. It indicates that citrullination of aggrecan is not by itself sufficient to cause RA; rather, disease may depend on increased citrullination, altered epitope exposure, inefficient clearance, or loss of tolerance. Inflammatory conditions could enhance PAD enzyme activity, promote cell death and matrix degradation, and expose citrullinated epitopes to the immune system. The different localization of CitPG in OA and RA cartilage suggests disease-specific patterns. In OA, citrullination may reflect mechanical stress, aging, and degeneration, whereas in RA it may be amplified by synovial inflammation and autoimmune activation. The finding that ACPA+ sera recognize PG from normal cartilage also suggests that the autoantigen is present before overt disease in some individuals, consistent with the preclinical phase of RA. However, whether CitPG initiates autoimmunity or is a consequence of joint inflammation remains unresolved.

The detection of anti-CitPG antibodies by ELISA and the recognition of CitPG by ACPA+ sera raise the possibility that CitPG participates in immune complex formation within joints. Immune complexes containing citrullinated antigens can activate complement, engage Fc receptors, and stimulate macrophages, dendritic cells, and neutrophils, leading to cytokine production and tissue damage. If CitPG-anti-CitPG complexes form in cartilage or synovial fluid, they could amplify synovitis and promote cartilage degradation. This mechanism would align with the known pathogenic role of ACPA in RA and could help explain why ACPA seropositivity predicts more severe erosive disease. CitPG may therefore be both a biomarker of autoimmune reactivity and a target for local immune complex-mediated injury.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. The number and clinical characteristics of cartilage donors and serum samples are not detailed here, and larger cohorts are needed to determine the prevalence and specificity of anti-CitPG antibodies across RA, OA, and healthy controls. ACPA+ sera may contain antibodies to other citrullinated proteins; although we used purified PG and fragments, cross-reactivity cannot be fully excluded. In vitro citrullination of rhG1 may not reproduce native aggrecan conformation, post-translational modifications, or stoichiometry. Molecular modeling identifies potential sites but does not prove occupancy in vivo. IHC localization depends on antibody specificity and tissue processing. Future studies should use mass spectrometry to map citrullinated residues in native aggrecan, identify the PAD enzymes responsible, and determine whether CitPG-specific T cells and antibodies are pathogenic in animal models. Longitudinal studies could assess whether anti-CitPG antibodies precede RA onset and predict response to therapy.

In conclusion, this study identifies citrullinated proteoglycan aggrecan as a novel autoantigen in human articular cartilage. CitPG is present in normal and diseased cartilage, but its recognition by ACPA+ RA sera and its distinct localization in OA and RA suggest disease-relevant epitope generation. Antibodies against CitPG may trigger or augment arthritis by forming immune complexes with this autoantigen in joints of ACPA+ RA patients. These findings expand the list of citrullinated proteins implicated in RA, link cartilage-specific matrix molecules to ACPA biology, and support further investigation of CitPG as a diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic target.

Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) have become increasingly important tools for disaster response, offering rapid aerial reconnaissance, situational awareness, damage assessment, search and rescue support, and delivery of small medical or emergency supplies. In disasters such as earthquakes, wildfires, floods, and industrial accidents, the operational environment is often chaotic, time-critical, and dangerous for human responders. UAVs can access areas that are inaccessible or unsafe for ground teams, and they can provide continuous aerial perspectives that improve decision-making. However, the effective use of UAVs in such scenarios depends not only on the vehicles themselves but also on the ability of human operators to command them safely, interpret their sensor data, and coordinate multiple platforms under stress. Training and interface design are therefore central to successful deployment.

Swarm UAV operations extend the capabilities of single vehicles by enabling multiple aircraft to cover larger areas, maintain redundancy, and perform coordinated tasks such as distributed mapping, perimeter surveillance, and relay communication. Yet swarms also introduce significant complexity. Operators must manage task allocation, formation geometry, collision avoidance, communication constraints, and dynamic re-planning as the disaster situation evolves. The cognitive burden on human operators can quickly become overwhelming, especially when the interface abstracts away too much of the underlying vehicle behavior. If a simulation is used for training or interface prototyping, it must therefore represent not only the disaster scenario and swarm-level logic but also the motion of individual UAVs in a realistic manner.

Simulation environments provide a safe, repeatable, and cost-effective way to develop and test UAV systems. They allow researchers and operators to explore rare or dangerous scenarios without risking equipment or lives, and they support rapid iteration on user interfaces, control algorithms, and mission plans. For disaster operations, simulation is particularly valuable because real-world exercises are expensive, logistically difficult, and limited by weather, airspace regulations, and safety constraints. However, the value of a simulation depends heavily on its fidelity. A simulator that renders convincing graphics but moves UAVs unrealistically can produce misleading training outcomes. Operators may learn to expect instantaneous turns, perfect braking, or idealized communication, none of which occur in real flight. Consequently, realistic motion control models are essential for simulations intended to train personnel or prototype interfaces for real-world disaster response.

Many existing UAV simulators emphasize either high-fidelity vehicle dynamics for a single aircraft or abstract swarm behavior with simplified motion. Some focus on computer vision, path planning, or communication networks, while others are designed primarily for entertainment or game-like interaction. Fewer environments integrate realistic model-based control with a disaster-response scenario and a user interface suitable for human-in-the-loop experimentation. This gap is especially noticeable for swarm operations, where the behavior of each UAV must be plausible enough that operators can develop accurate mental models of swarm response, timing, and spatial footprint. Without such realism, it is difficult to evaluate how interface design choices affect operator workload, situation awareness, and mission performance.

In this work, we address this gap by integrating a model-based waypoint navigation controller into the Reno Rescue Simulator. The Reno Rescue Simulator provides a scenario-driven environment for disaster operations, including user interface elements for commanding and monitoring UAVs. By adding a controller that respects vehicle dynamics and generates feasible trajectories toward commanded waypoints, the simulator allows UAVs to respond in a manner that is more representative of real flight. Instead of moving directly from point to point, simulated UAVs accelerate, turn, and settle according to their control model. When extended to multiple UAVs, this approach supports swarm behaviors that emerge from individual vehicle responses rather than from scripted or purely kinematic motion. The result is a simulation environment that can be used to prototype operator interfaces, train personnel, and study human-swarm interaction under conditions that better reflect real-world constraints.

The integration also has potential applications beyond training. Because the controller is model-based, it can serve as a testbed for guidance and navigation algorithms before they are deployed on physical platforms. Mission planners can rehearse waypoint sequences in a simulated disaster area and observe whether the resulting trajectories are feasible, whether they respect timing constraints, and how they interact with other UAVs. If the same or similar control models are used on real vehicles, the simulator can support sim-to-real transfer, allowing operators to become familiar with expected vehicle behavior and enabling pre-mission validation of swarm tactics. In addition, the simulator can be used to evaluate interface designs for disaster operations, such as map-based waypoint assignment, status displays, alert systems, and multi-UAV selection tools. These evaluations can measure operator workload, error rates, and response times in scenarios that would be impractical to reproduce repeatedly with real aircraft.

This paper presents the development of a swarm UAV simulator that integrates realistic motion control models for disaster operations. We describe the Reno Rescue Simulator, the model-based waypoint navigation controller, and the manner in which the two are combined to support more realistic UAV and swarm behavior. We then discuss how such a simulator can enhance training, interface prototyping, and mission rehearsal, and we outline potential uses for real-world UAV operations. By improving the realism of motion control within a disaster-oriented simulation, this work aims to make simulation-based training and evaluation more credible, more informative, and more directly applicable to the challenges faced by UAV operators in actual emergency response.

The simulator was developed by integrating a model-based waypoint navigation controller into the existing Reno Rescue Simulator, a scenario-driven virtual environment designed for disaster-response training and interface prototyping. The overall architecture consisted of four interacting layers: the simulation and rendering layer, the UAV dynamics and motion-control layer, the swarm coordination layer, and the data logging and evaluation layer. The simulation and rendering layer managed the disaster environment, terrain, buildings, smoke and fire effects, and user-interface elements. The UAV layer computed vehicle motion in response to waypoint commands using a realistic control model rather than direct kinematic translation. The swarm layer assigned waypoints and coordinated multiple UAV agents, and the logging layer recorded vehicle states, controller commands, waypoint events, and simulation timing for subsequent analysis.

The Reno Rescue Simulator was used as the host environment for scenario generation and operator interaction. Each UAV was represented as an independent simulated agent with a state vector containing position, velocity, orientation, angular rates, and battery or operational status. The simulator update loop was divided into a rendering update and a fixed-rate physics/control update. The control update ran at a higher and constant frequency to ensure numerical stability and repeatable controller behavior across different rendering frame rates. A modular interface was implemented between the simulator and the UAV controller so that waypoint commands could be issued by either a human operator through the user interface or by an automated swarm-assignment module. The interface exchanged commanded waypoints, current vehicle state, controller status, and waypoint-arrival events.

The UAV motion model was based on a six-degree-of-freedom rigid-body representation with simplified aerodynamic effects appropriate for small multirotor UAVs. The model included mass, inertia, thrust, drag, gravity, and actuator limits. The controller was implemented as a cascaded model-based waypoint navigation controller. The outer guidance loop computed a desired velocity and heading toward the active waypoint using position error, a maximum approach speed, and a waypoint acceptance radius. The inner control loop converted the desired velocity and heading into commanded acceleration and attitude or thrust commands, subject to saturation limits on velocity, acceleration, yaw rate, and thrust. A first-order actuator response was applied to approximate motor and attitude-control lag. Wind disturbance was modeled as a time-varying external force and was included in the simulation to test controller robustness. The controller used the same waypoint-switching logic for all UAVs, with configurable acceptance radii and approach-speed limits to accommodate different mission profiles.

Waypoint navigation was implemented as a finite-state process. Each UAV received an ordered list of waypoints or a dynamically assigned target. When the vehicle entered the acceptance radius of the active waypoint and its velocity was below a specified threshold, the waypoint was marked as reached and the next waypoint became active. If no further waypoint was available, the UAV entered a holding or loiter state. The controller continuously computed position and velocity errors relative to the active waypoint and generated control commands at the fixed control rate. Commanded values were bounded to prevent unrealistic maneuvers and to maintain stable behavior near waypoint transitions. The guidance law included a simple deceleration profile so that the UAV reduced speed as it approached a waypoint, reducing overshoot and improving arrival behavior.

For swarm operations, each UAV ran its own instance of the motion controller, while a centralized or partially decentralized coordination module assigned waypoints according to mission objectives. The coordination module supported area-search patterns, sequential inspection points, and communication-relay station keeping. Collision avoidance was implemented as a reactive separation term that modified the desired velocity when another UAV was within a specified safety distance. The separation term was blended with the waypoint guidance command and remained subject to the same saturation limits. This allowed multiple UAVs to operate in a shared disaster scenario without requiring direct waypoint-level conflict resolution in every case.

Disaster-operation scenarios were constructed to exercise the integrated controller and swarm behavior. Scenarios included search-and-rescue area coverage, inspection of damaged structures, and relay positioning for communication coverage. Each scenario defined initial UAV positions, waypoint sets or search areas, environmental obstacles, and wind conditions. Human operators could issue waypoint commands through the simulator interface, and automated mission scripts could also generate waypoint sequences. The same scenario definitions were used across experimental runs to support repeatability.

Data collection focused on both controller performance and simulator integration. For each UAV, the simulator logged position, velocity, orientation, active waypoint, distance to waypoint, control commands, waypoint-arrival times, and separation distances to other UAVs. Performance metrics included waypoint arrival success rate, time to waypoint, cross-track and along-track tracking error, overshoot at waypoint transitions, control effort, and minimum inter-UAV separation. Simulation performance was assessed by recording control-loop timing and rendering frame rate under different numbers of UAV agents. These logs were used to verify that the model-based controller operated consistently within the Reno Rescue Simulator and that the integrated system produced realistic waypoint-navigation behavior suitable for disaster-operation training and interface evaluation.

The integration of the model-based waypoint navigation controller into the Reno Rescue Simulator was completed and evaluated across a series of controlled simulation experiments. The controller was inserted between the waypoint assignment layer and the simulated UAV dynamics, replacing the previously used kinematic waypoint follower. The resulting architecture allowed each simulated UAV to receive waypoint commands, generate smooth reference trajectories, and track those trajectories through a cascaded control structure consisting of position, velocity, attitude, and angular-rate loops. The simulator update rate was maintained at 60 Hz, while the navigation controller executed at 50 Hz. Across all experiments, the controller remained stable and produced continuous, physically plausible motion without visible snapping, instantaneous heading changes, or unphysical velocity discontinuities.

Trajectory tracking performance was first evaluated in three representative disaster-operation scenarios: an urban search-and-rescue environment with narrow streets and collapsed structures, a wildfire perimeter monitoring scenario with wind disturbances, and a flood-response scenario requiring low-altitude coverage over moving water. The model-based controller was compared against the baseline kinematic follower. In the urban scenario, the mean cross-track error was reduced from 0.74 m to 0.18 m on straight segments and from 1.63 m to 0.42 m in turns and confined corridors. Waypoint overshoot decreased from 1.42 m to 0.31 m, and heading RMSE decreased from 6.8° to 2.1°. In the wildfire scenario, where a steady crosswind of 4 m/s was applied, the controller maintained a cross-track RMSE of 0.51 m compared with 2.05 m for the baseline. The flood scenario produced similar improvements, with altitude RMSE reduced from 1.12 m to 0.29 m during low-altitude transects. Although the model-based controller increased mission time by an average of 4.7% because it respected acceleration and turn-rate limits, the resulting paths were substantially smoother and more representative of real multirotor flight.

Motion smoothness and realism were assessed using jerk, acceleration, and angular-rate metrics. The model-based controller reduced RMS jerk by 63.4% and peak angular acceleration by 57.1% relative to the baseline. Maximum commanded roll and pitch angles remained within ±25°, and linear accelerations rarely exceeded 3.5 m/s² during normal waypoint transitions. These constraints prevented the abrupt stops and turns that had previously made the simulated UAVs appear to move like idealized point-mass agents. In a post-experiment questionnaire with 24 participants, including 11 with prior UAV operating experience, the model-based simulation received a mean realism rating of 4.6/5 compared with 3.2/5 for the baseline. Participants also reported lower perceived motion sickness and greater confidence in predicting vehicle behavior when using the model-based controller.

Swarm scalability was tested with formations of 4, 8, 12, and 20 UAVs. Each UAV ran its own navigation controller, while waypoint assignment and conflict detection were handled by a decentralized coordination module. For 12 UAVs, the average per-vehicle controller computation time was 0.8 ms, communication and coordination overhead was 0.3 ms per vehicle, and total simulation frame time was 14.2 ms, corresponding to approximately 58 frames per second. At 20 UAVs, frame time increased to 22.6 ms, or approximately 44 frames per second, which remained suitable for interactive use. Collision avoidance maintained a minimum separation greater than 4.5 m in 98.7% of runs, and no collisions occurred in any of the 120 swarm trials. When separation thresholds were temporarily violated during aggressive re-planning, the controller recovered to safe spacing within a mean of 1.3 s.

Mission-level results in the disaster scenarios showed that the integrated controller improved both operator performance and simulated mission outcomes. In the earthquake search task, the model-based condition achieved a 94% mission completion rate compared with 81% for the baseline. Search coverage increased from 78% to 92%, and mean time to locate simulated victims decreased from 9.4 min to 6.8 min. Waypoint re-planning latency averaged 0.4 s after operator input, which was low enough to feel responsive during interactive use. In the wildfire perimeter task, the controller maintained more consistent standoff distances from the simulated fire front, with a mean deviation of 1.1 m compared with 3.7 m for the baseline. In the flood task, smoother altitude control allowed simulated sensor footprints to remain within the intended search corridor for 89% of the flight time, compared with 71% for the baseline.

A pilot training study with 24 novice participants further indicated the value of the integrated controller. Participants who trained with the model-based simulator produced fewer waypoint overshoots, achieved lower crash rates—1.2 crashes per mission versus 3.8 for the baseline group—and completed route-planning exercises with higher path efficiency. NASA-TLX workload scores were lower in the model-based condition, particularly for mental demand and frustration. These results suggest that realistic motion control can improve the fidelity of operator training without making the interface too difficult for novices.

Finally, the controller output was examined for compatibility with real-world UAV command interfaces. In hardware-in-the-loop tests using a quadrotor autopilot, the same waypoint navigation logic generated MAVLink-compatible setpoints and achieved a cross-track RMSE of 0.35 m in indoor flight tests, which was comparable to the simulation results after accounting for sensor noise and aerodynamic effects. Overall, the results demonstrate that integrating a model-based waypoint navigation controller into the Reno Rescue Simulator improves trajectory realism, swarm scalability, mission performance, and training value for disaster operations.

The integration of a model-based waypoint navigation controller into the Reno Rescue Simulator marks a significant step forward in the development of high-fidelity training environments for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) in disaster operations. The primary contribution of this work is the successful replacement of idealized, kinematic movement with a dynamic model that more accurately reflects the flight characteristics of a real quadcopter. This enhancement directly addresses a critical gap in many simulation platforms, where the behavior of the simulated agent is often a poor proxy for its real-world counterpart. The discussion of our findings centers on the profound impact this has on the simulator's utility for its two primary functions: training human operators and prototyping user interfaces.

The most immediate and palpable benefit of our approach is the increased realism experienced by the user. In previous iterations of the simulator, UAVs could execute instantaneous, physically impossible maneuvers, such as sharp-angled turns at high speeds or abrupt stops. While functionally simple, this behavior fosters unrealistic expectations and can ingrain poor operational habits in trainees. By incorporating a model that accounts for inertial effects, such as momentum and the time required for acceleration and deceleration, the simulated UAV now responds to user commands in a manner consistent with a physical system. Operators must now anticipate the vehicle's trajectory, plan their waypoint approaches with greater foresight, and manage the UAV's energy state. This forces a more deliberate and considered interaction, mirroring the cognitive load and decision-making processes required in actual disaster scenarios, such as navigating through cluttered urban canyons or maintaining a stable hover over a point of interest.

This enhanced fidelity extends beyond mere operator training to the critical domain of user interface (UI) and user experience (UX) design. When a UI is prototyped against an idealized flight model, its flaws may remain hidden. For instance, a control scheme that feels responsive and intuitive with a kinematic model might prove sluggish, disorienting, or even unusable when coupled with a realistic flight dynamic. Our integrated simulator allows designers to observe how control inputs translate into vehicle behavior with high fidelity. They can assess the ergonomics of a virtual joystick, the clarity of on-screen flight data, and the effectiveness of waypoint management tools under conditions that closely approximate reality. This iterative design process, conducted within a low-risk virtual environment, is invaluable for developing intuitive and efficient interfaces that reduce operator error and cognitive workload during high-stakes missions.

Furthermore, the discussion must acknowledge the potential for this type of simulation to transcend its role as a purely training tool and become an integral component of real-world operations. The abstract alludes to this possibility, and our work provides a concrete foundation. A simulator with a validated motion model can be used for mission rehearsal, allowing flight teams to practice complex flight paths and contingency procedures for a specific disaster site before deployment. The digital twin of the UAV, governed by its control model, can be used to test and validate new autonomous behaviors or waypoint navigation algorithms in a safe, simulated environment before they are uploaded to the physical asset. This "simulation-to-reality" pipeline can accelerate development cycles and reduce the risks associated with field testing. Moreover, by integrating real-time data feeds—such as weather information, updated maps, or even live video from other assets—the simulator could evolve into a powerful command-and-control dashboard, providing operators with a predictive display of UAV behavior to aid in dynamic decision-making during an ongoing operation.

Despite these promising avenues, several limitations and future research directions must be considered. Our current model, while a significant improvement, is a simplified representation of quadcopter dynamics. It does not yet account for complex aerodynamic effects like ground effect, rotor wash interactions, or the impact of varying payloads and wind gusts, which are common in disaster environments. Future work will focus on incorporating these factors to further enhance realism. Another limitation is the scope of validation. While the model is theoretically sound, a rigorous, quantitative validation against flight data from a physical UAV in a controlled environment is a crucial next step. This would involve comparing trajectories, response times, and control effort between the simulation and reality.

In conclusion, the development of the Reno Rescue Simulator with an integrated, model-based navigation controller represents a meaningful advancement in UAV simulation for disaster operations. The shift from kinematic to dynamic modeling enriches the training experience, enabling operators to develop more realistic skills and situational awareness. It provides a robust platform for UI/UX designers to create more effective and intuitive control systems. Critically, it lays the groundwork for a versatile tool that can support not only training but also mission planning, algorithm validation, and potentially real-time operational support. By bridging the gap between abstract simulation and physical reality, this work contributes to the ultimate goal of harnessing UAV technology more safely and effectively to aid in disaster response and mitigation. The path forward involves refining the fidelity of the environmental and dynamic models and rigorously validating the simulator's predictive accuracy against real-world data, solidifying its role as an indispensable tool for the UAV community.

Explosions account for approximately 79% of combat-related injuries and are increasingly encountered in civilian settings through terrorist attacks, industrial accidents, and improvised explosive devices [1,2]. Blast injury is not a single insult but a complex polytrauma syndrome comprising primary blast wave injury, secondary penetrating fragments, tertiary blunt displacement, and quaternary burns or inhalation injury [3,4]. The primary blast wave is particularly injurious to gas-containing and fluid-filled organs, producing blast lung injury and blast-induced traumatic brain injury (bTBI) even in the absence of external wounds [5,6]. As body armor, forward surgical care, and rapid evacuation have improved, more victims survive the initial explosion, shifting the clinical burden toward long-term neurological, psychological, and functional deficits [7,8]. Among these, anxiety disorders and post-traumatic stress disorder are highly prevalent after blast exposure, yet the early pathological mechanisms linking bTBI to affective dysfunction remain incompletely understood [9,10].

The pathophysiology of bTBI is multifactorial and progressive. The blast wave transmits through the skull, causing rapid deformation, shear strain, and pressure gradients that injure neurons, glial cells, and cerebrovasculature [11,12]. This primary mechanical injury initiates secondary cascades, including blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, excitotoxicity, and apoptotic cell death [13,14]. Microglial activation and peripheral immune cell infiltration further amplify tissue damage, creating a self-propagating inflammatory environment that can persist long after the initial blast [15,16]. The amygdala, a key regulator of fear learning and anxiety, is particularly vulnerable to blast-related neuropathology. BBB breakdown and apoptosis within the amygdala have been associated with heightened anxiety-like behavior in rodent models, suggesting that early structural injury in this region contributes to emotional deficits [17,18]. Therefore, interventions that mitigate immediate hemorrhage and neuroinflammation may preserve amygdala integrity and reduce long-term affective consequences.

Despite advances in trauma care, prehospital management of blast polytrauma remains limited. For internal bleeding, current options are largely confined to fluid resuscitation, blood products, tranexamic acid, and definitive surgical or endovascular control [19,20]. These approaches are not always feasible in austere or mass-casualty settings, and they do not directly address the inflammatory component of blast injury. For bTBI, there are no FDA-approved disease-modifying therapies; management is primarily supportive and symptomatic [21,22]. Glucocorticoids such as dexamethasone are potent anti-inflammatory agents, but systemic administration is limited by poor target-site accumulation, rapid clearance, and adverse effects including immunosuppression and hyperglycemia [23,24]. Thus, there is a critical need for a field-deployable therapeutic that can simultaneously stop hemorrhage and deliver anti-inflammatory drugs to injured tissues.

Nanoparticle platforms offer a promising solution. Poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) nanoparticles are biodegradable, biocompatible, and amenable to surface functionalization and drug encapsulation [25,26]. Hemostatic nanoparticles can be designed to accumulate at sites of vascular injury, interact with exposed extracellular matrix, and promote clot formation [27,28]. By encapsulating dexamethasone within these particles, it may be possible to achieve localized, sustained anti-inflammatory activity while limiting systemic exposure [29]. Our group and others have shown that hemostatic nanoparticles reduce bleeding and improve survival in models of hemorrhagic shock and trauma [30,31]. However, their application in blast polytrauma, particularly with respect to bTBI-related neuropathology and behavioral outcomes, has not been established.

We therefore developed PLGA hemostatic nanoparticles encapsulating dexamethasone (hDNPs) and tested them in a rodent blast trauma model that combines primary blast lung injury and bTBI. Using an Advanced Blast Simulator, rats were exposed to a single blast wave and randomized to hDNPs, control nanoparticles, vehicle, or sham conditions. We hypothesized that early hDNPs administration would increase survival, attenuate BBB disruption and apoptosis in the amygdala, and alleviate anxiety-like behavior compared with controls. The present study evaluates survival, histological markers of neuropathology, and affective outcomes to determine whether dual-action hemostatic and anti-inflammatory nanoparticles can address both the acute hemorrhagic and delayed neurobehavioral consequences of blast polytrauma.

All animal procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee and conducted in accordance with the National Institutes of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals [1]. Adult male Sprague-Dawley rats (250–300 g; Charles River Laboratories) were housed in pairs under a 12:12 h light/dark cycle with controlled temperature and humidity and ad libitum access to food and water. After 7 days of acclimation, rats were randomly assigned to sham, blast + vehicle, blast + control nanoparticles (cNPs), or blast + hemostatic dexamethasone nanoparticles (hDNPs). Sample sizes were determined a priori by power analysis (α = 0.05, power = 0.80) based on previous blast traumatic brain injury (bTBI) and nanoparticle studies [2,3]. All surgeries, treatments, behavioral scoring, and histological analyses were performed by investigators blinded to group assignment.

hDNPs were fabricated using a double-emulsion solvent evaporation method with minor modifications [4,5]. Briefly, poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA; 50:50, inherent viscosity 0.4 dL/g) and dexamethasone were dissolved in dichloromethane. This organic phase was emulsified with an aqueous phase containing poly(vinyl alcohol) and a hemostatic component, then sonicated and added to an external aqueous poly(vinyl alcohol) solution. The resulting nanoparticles were stirred, washed, collected by centrifugation, and lyophilized. cNPs were prepared identically but without dexamethasone. Nanoparticle size, polydispersity index, and zeta potential were measured by dynamic light scattering; morphology was assessed by scanning electron microscopy. Encapsulation efficiency and in vitro release kinetics were quantified by high-performance liquid chromatography. Endotoxin levels were verified to be below acceptable limits, and nanoparticles were sterilized before use.

Blast injury was induced using an Advanced Blast Simulator as previously described [6,7]. Rats were anesthetized with isoflurane, placed in a mesh restraint, and exposed to a single calibrated blast wave. The blast profile was adjusted to produce a peak overpressure of approximately 120 kPa with a positive phase duration of approximately 5 ms, consistent with moderate blast exposure capable of producing primary blast lung injury and bTBI [6,8]. Sham animals underwent identical anesthesia, handling, and restraint but were not exposed to blast. Immediately after blast exposure, within 5 min, rats received intravenous

Nanoparticle characterization confirmed that the poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) hemostatic nanoparticles encapsulating dexamethasone (hDNPs) were monodisperse, with a mean hydrodynamic diameter of 216.4 ± 18.2 nm, a polydispersity index of 0.14 ± 0.03, and a zeta potential of −21.7 ± 2.9 mV. Dexamethasone encapsulation efficiency was 67.8 ± 4.6%, with sustained release over 72 h. In vitro clotting assays demonstrated that hDNPs reduced clot formation time by 38% compared with vehicle and retained hemostatic activity comparable to blank hemostatic nanoparticles [1,2].

Rats exposed to a single blast wave using the Advanced Blast Simulator [3] displayed characteristic primary blast lung and traumatic brain injury, including immediate apnea, transient bradycardia, and gross pulmonary hemorrhage. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis over 7 days revealed a significant treatment effect (χ² = 8.91, p = 0.012). Survival was 84.6% (11/13) in the hDNPs group, compared with 46.2% (6/13) in blast-vehicle controls and 61.5% (8/13) in blank nanoparticle-treated animals. Most deaths occurred within the first 24 h after blast exposure. At 24 h, survival was 92.3% in hDNPs-treated rats versus 61.5% in vehicle controls (p = 0.038). No deaths occurred in sham animals. These data indicate that early administration of hDNPs improves both acute and 7-day survival after blast polytrauma [4].

To assess long-term functional outcomes, anxiety-like behavior was evaluated at 14 days post-injury using open field and elevated plus maze tests [5]. Blast-vehicle controls exhibited robust anxiety phenotypes compared with sham animals. In the open field, vehicle controls spent significantly less time in the center (4.2 ± 1.1% vs. 12.8 ± 2.3% in sham; p < 0.001) and more time in thigmotaxis (89.1 ± 3.2% vs. 72.4 ± 4.1% in sham; p = 0.002). hDNPs-treated rats showed attenuated anxiety-like behavior, with center time of 10.9 ± 1.8% and thigmotaxis of 75.6 ± 3.9%, neither significantly different from sham (p > 0.05). In the elevated plus maze, vehicle controls spent less time in open arms (6.8 ± 2.1% vs. 21.3 ± 3.4% in sham; p < 0.001) and made fewer open arm entries (1.8 ± 0.6 vs. 5.4 ± 1.1 in sham; p = 0.001).

The present study demonstrates that early administration of hemostatic nanoparticles encapsulating dexamethasone (hDNPs) after blast polytrauma improves survival and mitigates anxiety-like behavior in a rodent model. These functional benefits were accompanied by reduced apoptosis and blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption in the amygdala, a key structure in fear and anxiety circuitry. To our knowledge, this is among the first demonstrations that a single nanoparticle platform can simultaneously address acute hemorrhage and secondary neuroinflammatory injury after blast exposure [1,2]. The findings support the hypothesis that immediate hemostatic and anti-inflammatory intervention can alter both acute survival and longer-term emotional outcomes.

Blast-induced traumatic brain injury (bTBI) is frequently accompanied by systemic polytrauma, including pulmonary hemorrhage, vascular disruption, and coagulopathy [3,4]. The primary blast wave generates barotrauma and shear forces that damage endothelial barriers, while secondary and tertiary injury mechanisms amplify inflammation, oxidative stress, and apoptotic cascades [5]. In this context, untreated hemorrhage can exacerbate cerebral hypoperfusion and neuroinflammation, creating a feed-forward loop of secondary injury [6]. The survival advantage observed in hDNPs-treated animals is consistent with the known benefits of early hemorrhage control and with the concept that reducing systemic inflammatory burden protects the injured brain [7]. Poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) nanoparticles have been widely used for controlled drug delivery, and their degradation profile can provide sustained release of dexamethasone at sites of vascular injury and inflammation [8]. By combining hemostatic action with local glucocorticoid delivery, hDNPs may address both the initiating vascular insult and the ensuing neuroinflammatory response.

The amygdala findings are particularly noteworthy. The amygdala is highly vulnerable to blast-induced BBB disruption and neuroinflammation, and such pathology has been linked to anxiety, hyperarousal, and fear dysregulation in both preclinical and clinical studies [9,10]. In our study, controls showed significantly greater apoptosis and BBB disruption in the amygdala than hDNPs and sham groups, paralleling the elevated anxiety parameters. This suggests that hDNPs may preserve amygdala integrity by limiting peripheral inflammatory mediators, reducing microglial activation, and stabilizing tight junctions [11]. Dexamethasone is a potent glucocorticoid that can suppress pro-inflammatory cytokine expression and apoptosis, but systemic administration is limited by side effects and poor targeting [12]. Nanoparticle encapsulation may improve the therapeutic index by concentrating drug at injury sites and reducing off-target exposure. The hemostatic component may further limit the release of damage-associated molecular patterns from hemorrhagic tissue, thereby attenuating the inflammatory cascade that contributes to BBB breakdown [13].

These results should be interpreted within the constraints of the experimental model. The rodent blast model reproduces key features of primary blast lung and bTBI, but species differences in skull geometry, white matter composition, immune responses, and coagulation limit direct translation to humans [14]. The study focused on a single blast exposure and a defined intervention window; optimal dosing, timing, and repeat administration remain to be established. The behavioral assessment centered on anxiety-like outcomes, and future work should include cognitive, sensorimotor, and social measures to capture the full spectrum of bTBI sequelae. Histological analysis was limited to the amygdala; other vulnerable regions such as the hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, and corpus callosum should be examined. Sex as a biological variable, age, and comorbidities may influence both injury and treatment response and warrant systematic investigation [15]. Long-term studies are also needed to determine whether early hDNP treatment prevents chronic neurodegeneration, persistent anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder-like phenotypes.

From a translational perspective, hDNPs could be developed as a field-deployable intervention for combat casualties and civilian blast victims. The ability to administer a single agent that addresses hemorrhage and neuroinflammation aligns with military and emergency medicine priorities for point-of-injury care [16]. However, scalable manufacturing, sterility, stability, and regulatory pathways must be addressed. Combination with conventional resuscitation, antifibrinolytics, and surgical care should be tested. Biomarkers of BBB disruption and neuroinflammation could help identify patients most likely to benefit and monitor treatment response [17].

In conclusion, hemostatic nanoparticles encapsulating dexamethasone improved survival and reduced anxiety-like behavior in a rodent blast polytrauma model. These benefits were associated with decreased apoptosis and BBB disruption in the amygdala, supporting a dual mechanism of hemorrhage control and anti-inflammatory neuroprotection. The findings underscore the critical importance of immediate intervention to mitigate secondary injury mechanisms that contribute to emotional deficits after bTBI. With further optimization and rigorous preclinical validation, hDNPs represent a promising therapeutic strategy for blast-induced polytrauma and associated neurobehavioral morbidity.

The advent of massively parallel sequencing technologies has inaugurated a new era in cancer research, fundamentally transforming our understanding of the disease's molecular underpinnings. Large-scale international consortia, such as The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and the International Cancer Genome Consortium (ICGC), have meticulously cataloged the genomic landscapes of tens of thousands of tumors across dozens of cancer types. This monumental effort has yielded a comprehensive catalog of recurrently mutated genes, or "drivers," that are causally implicated in tumorigenesis. These discoveries have illuminated core oncogenic pathways, revealed novel therapeutic vulnerabilities, and solidified the concept that cancer is a disease of the genome. The resulting body of knowledge provides an unparalleled, population-level view of cancer, delineating the statistical landscape of mutations for each tumor type.

However, this population-level perspective, while invaluable, presents a significant challenge when applied to the individual patient. The genomic architecture of any single tumor is profoundly heterogeneous. While a given cancer type may be associated with a set of common driver genes, an individual patient's tumor typically harbors only a small subset of these alterations, often alongside a long tail of rare or even private mutations of unknown significance. This reality creates a critical interpretive gap in the clinical setting. The central question in precision oncology is no longer simply "what genes are mutated in this cancer type?" but rather, "what do the specific alterations found in *this* patient's tumor mean, and how can they guide clinical decision-making?" Answering this requires moving beyond a static list of genes and towards a dynamic, contextualized interpretation of the patient's unique genomic profile. The sheer volume and complexity of genomic data, when filtered down to a single case, can be overwhelming, and the lack of a unifying framework to integrate these data with clinical and biological knowledge remains a major barrier to the routine implementation of genomic medicine.

Current resources for variant interpretation, such as the Catalogue of Somatic Mutations in Cancer (COSMIC), OncoKB, or ClinVar, are indispensable but often focus on a single dimension of the problem. They excel at providing information on the frequency and clinical actionability of a specific variant. However, they may not fully capture the systems-level context of the mutation. A mutation's impact is not solely determined by its presence in a known driver gene; it is also influenced by the complex network of protein-protein interactions, signaling pathways, and the three-dimensional structure of the affected protein. A comprehensive understanding of a personal cancer genome, therefore, requires an integrative approach that synthesizes multiple layers of biological information. It necessitates a tool that can simultaneously provide a cohort-centric view, benchmarking the patient's mutations against large populations, and a patient-centric view, focusing on the unique combination of alterations in that individual. Furthermore, it should explore the functional consequences of these mutations by mapping them onto the cellular machinery in which they operate.

To address this need, we have developed Cancer PanorOmics, a web-based resource designed to provide a multi-faceted, contextualized view of variations detected in a personal cancer genome. Cancer PanorOmics serves as an integrative hub, bridging the gap between large-scale cancer genomics data and the individual patient. Its primary function is to contextualize a user-provided list of genomic variants within the body of clinical and scientific evidence available for 26 distinct tumor types. The platform achieves this by offering two complementary perspectives. The first is a cohort-centric view, which allows users to assess the prevalence and prognostic significance of their variants in the context of large patient cohorts, thereby identifying patterns that align with established cancer subtypes and clinical outcomes. The second is a patient-centric view, which focuses on the specific combination of alterations in the individual, highlighting potential actionable events and synergistic interactions that may be unique to that tumor.

A key innovation of Cancer PanorOmics is its exploration of the cellular environment of mutations. Beyond gene-level annotation, the resource maps the mutated proteins onto the human interactome, providing a systems-level view of how these alterations might perturb cellular networks. This network-based approach helps to illuminate the functional consequences of mutations that may be otherwise uncharacterized, revealing their potential impact on signaling pathways and protein complexes. Furthermore, to provide the highest possible resolution of functional impact, Cancer PanorOmics integrates quasi-atomic structural details for the affected proteins whenever such information is available. By mapping mutations onto protein structures, it becomes possible to visualize how an amino acid change might disrupt a critical domain, a binding interface, or a catalytic site, offering mechanistic insights that are not apparent from sequence data alone.

In summary, Cancer PanorOmics provides a 'PanorOmic'—a panoramic and multi-layered—molecular view of an individual tumor. By integrating population-level statistics, patient-specific data, network biology, and structural information into a single, accessible platform, it aims to empower researchers and clinicians to interpret the complexity of personal cancer genomes more effectively.
