We envision that this resource, when used in conjunction with appropriate genetic counseling and expert medical advice, will contribute to the identification of clinically actionable alterations, ultimately helping to guide the clinical decision-making process and advance the practice of precision oncology.

Cancer PanorOmics was constructed as an integrated web-based resource to contextualize somatic and germline variations detected in individual cancer genomes against cohort-level and patient-level evidence across 26 tumor types. Molecular and clinical data were assembled from public and semi-public repositories, including The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), the International Cancer Genome Consortium (ICGC), the Pan-Cancer Analysis of Whole Genomes (PCAWG), the AACR Project GENIE, cBioPortal, and the MSK-IMPACT clinical sequencing cohort. Only datasets with appropriate consent and de-identified clinical annotations were included. Tumor types were selected to cover the most common solid and hematological malignancies for which sufficient genomic and clinical data were available. Variants were harmonized to GRCh38 and annotated at transcript and protein levels using Ensembl, RefSeq, VEP, ANNOVAR, and Oncotator. Somatic single-nucleotide variants, small insertions and deletions, copy-number alterations, and gene fusions were processed through standardized pipelines. Germline variants were included only when they were classified as pathogenic or likely pathogenic in ClinVar or when they were explicitly reported as clinically relevant in the source dataset.

Tumor-type-specific driver genes were compiled from IntOGen, the Cancer Gene Census, OncoKB, and published pan-cancer analyses. For each tumor type, we calculated mutation frequencies, recurrence rates, and significance using MutSigCV, OncodriveFML, and dNdScv. Actionability was assessed using the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (ESCAT), OncoKB levels of evidence, CIViC evidence statements, and FDA/NCCN therapeutic annotations. Variants were classified into tiers ranging from clinically actionable biomarkers to variants of uncertain significance. Clinical evidence was linked to specific tumor types, drugs, and resistance mechanisms. When multiple evidence sources disagreed, we prioritized curated clinical guidelines and regulatory approvals, followed by high-level curated databases, and recorded provenance for each annotation.

The patient-centric view accepts variant calls in VCF, MAF, or CSV format. After upload, variants are mapped to canonical transcripts, normalized, and filtered by tumor type. The system reports the frequency of each alteration in the selected cohort, co-occurring and mutually exclusive alterations, and associations with clinical variables such as stage, age, sex, and survival. For each variant, the resource provides an evidence summary, including actionable therapeutic options, prognostic implications, and diagnostic or predisposing associations. Patient-centric analyses are performed transiently, and no personally identifiable information is stored. Users can also explore a “virtual tumor board” summary that ranks alterations by actionability and evidence level.

The cohort-centric view provides precomputed statistics for each of the 26 tumor types. We calculated mutation frequencies, pairwise co-occurrence and mutual exclusivity using Fisher’s exact test, and pathway enrichment using Reactome and MSigDB gene sets. Survival analyses were performed with Kaplan-Meier estimates, log-rank tests, and Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for available clinical covariates. Multiple testing correction was applied using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. Results are displayed as interactive heatmaps, lollipop plots, survival curves, and network diagrams. Users can compare an individual patient’s alteration profile with the cohort distribution and identify whether observed combinations are expected by chance or are statistically enriched.

To explore the cellular environment of mutations, we assembled a human interactome from BioGRID, HIPPIE, IntAct, STRING, and Reactome, retaining physical and functional interactions with confidence scores above predefined thresholds. Mutated genes were mapped onto this network, and network proximity to known cancer genes was computed using random walk with restart, shortest-path distances, and network propagation. We identified enriched subnetworks and communities using the Louvain algorithm and assessed significance by permutation testing. Pathway-level analyses were performed with Reactome and WikiPathways. For each mutated protein, we mapped residues to experimental structures from the Protein Data Bank and, when unavailable, to AlphaFold2 models. Residue mapping was performed with SIFTS, and structural features were calculated using DSSP, FreeSASA, and PDBePISA. We annotated solvent accessibility, secondary structure, domain boundaries from Pfam and CATH, post-translational modification sites, ligand-binding residues, and protein-protein interfaces. Quasi-atomic details include distances to catalytic residues, interface participation, and predicted destabilization scores from FoldX and Rosetta. Structural confidence was reported using pLDDT for AlphaFold models and resolution for experimental structures.

The web resource was implemented with a Python/Django backend, PostgreSQL for relational data, Neo4j for network queries, and a React frontend with D3.js, igv.js, and NGL Viewer for visualization. A RESTful API enables programmatic access. Uploaded data are processed in isolated containers, and results are cached only for the duration of the session. We validated the resource by benchmarking against known actionable alterations from clinical cases, comparing driver gene lists with published pan-cancer studies, and testing network and structural annotations against experimentally characterized cancer mutations. User acceptance testing was performed with oncologists and molecular biologists. Cancer PanorOmics is freely available at http://panoromics.irbbarcelona.org.

Cancer PanorOmics was implemented as an integrated web resource that contextualizes somatic alterations from individual cancer genomes within cohort-level and patient-level evidence. The current release incorporates 26 tumor types and aggregates 1,248,317 somatic variants from 38,412 tumors, including single-nucleotide variants, small insertions and deletions, copy-number alterations, and gene fusions. For each tumor type, the cohort-centric module provides mutation frequencies, recurrently altered genes, pathway enrichment, co-occurrence and mutual-exclusivity patterns, and clinical annotation. Users can browse tumor-type landscapes or query specific genes and variants. The resource includes 1,142 genes with significant recurrence in at least one tumor type, of which 287 are annotated as actionable or potentially actionable by at least one clinical evidence source. Across the 26 tumor types, the most frequently altered pathways were TP53/cell-cycle, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, MAPK, DNA repair, and Wnt/β-catenin, although the relative contribution of each pathway varied substantially by tumor type.

The cohort-centric view allows direct comparison of a personal variant with the background mutation spectrum of the same tumor type. For example, in lung adenocarcinoma, EGFR, KRAS, TP53, STK11, and KEAP1 were among the most recurrently altered genes, whereas in breast carcinoma, PIK3CA, TP53, CDH1, and GATA3 dominated the mutational landscape. The interface displays allele frequencies, mutation types, and clinical evidence levels, and it supports filtering by pathway, actionability tier, and variant class. Mutual-exclusivity analysis identified known relationships, such as the tendency of EGFR and KRAS mutations to occur in distinct subsets of lung adenocarcinoma, and co-occurrence patterns such as TP53 and PIK3CA alterations in breast cancer. These cohort-level summaries provide the baseline against which a patient’s variants can be interpreted, but they also highlight the central challenge of precision oncology: most individual tumors harbor few or no highly recurrent actionable drivers.

The patient-centric module addresses this challenge by accepting variant call format or mutation annotation format files, as well as manual entry of individual variants. Each alteration is annotated with population frequency, predicted functional impact, and clinical evidence from curated sources. Variants are classified into tiers ranging from strong clinical actionability to variants of uncertain significance. The patient view then projects the uploaded variants onto the cohort landscape, indicating whether each alteration is recurrent, whether it is a known driver, and whether it has therapeutic, prognostic, or diagnostic implications. In a representative colorectal cancer case, a KRAS G12C mutation was flagged as actionable because of investigational KRAS G12C inhibitors, while also being marked as a predictor of resistance to anti-EGFR antibodies. In a separate melanoma case, BRAF V600E was linked to approved BRAF/MEK inhibitor combinations, and a co-occurring PTEN loss was highlighted as a potential modifier of response. The patient-centric view therefore complements cohort frequencies by prioritizing alterations that may be rare but clinically meaningful.

To capture the cellular environment of mutations, Cancer PanorOmics maps altered genes onto a human interactome comprising 15,731 proteins and 248,946 high-confidence interactions. For each patient, the mutated proteins are projected onto the network, and the resource identifies affected modules, hub proteins, and paths between altered genes. This network view revealed that mutations in apparently unrelated genes often converge on common complexes or signaling cascades. For instance, in tumors without a canonical driver, network analysis frequently highlighted MAPK or PI3K pathway activation through combinations of less recurrent events. The interactome module also supports enrichment analysis for biological processes and identifies network proximity to known drug targets, which can suggest repurposing opportunities or combination strategies.

Whenever available, mutations are mapped onto quasi-atomic protein structures derived from the Protein Data Bank or predicted by AlphaFold. The structural viewer displays the mutated residue in the context of domains, interfaces, and binding pockets. This allowed us to annotate known structural mechanisms, such as the destabilization of the TP53 DNA-binding domain by R175H, the disruption of inhibitory contacts between PIK3CA and p85α by E545K, and the localization of EGFR L858R within the kinase activation loop. For variants without experimental structures, AlphaFold models provided residue-level context and interface predictions, although these were labeled as lower confidence. The combination of interactome and structural mapping transforms a list of variants into a mechanistic hypothesis about how a personal tumor may be wired.

Finally, we integrated cohort recurrence, clinical actionability, network centrality, and structural impact into a single prioritization score. In a retrospective evaluation of 500 cases across the 26 tumor types, the resource identified at least one actionable alteration in 62% of patients, consistent with expert curation. In 18% of cases without a cohort-level actionable driver, network or structural analysis nominated a plausible pathway-level vulnerability, such as MAPK activation through co-occurring NF1 truncation and BRAF amplification. The web interface provides interactive visualizations, downloadable reports, and a programmatic API, with median query times under 10 seconds for typical variant lists. Cancer PanorOmics is freely available at http://panoromics.irbbarcelona.org and is updated quarterly to incorporate new clinical evidence, tumor-type cohorts, and structural data.

The advent of massively parallel sequencing has irrevocably altered the landscape of cancer research and clinical oncology. We now possess an unprecedented catalog of genetic alterations across thousands of tumors, a resource that has illuminated the core signaling pathways and driver genes responsible for oncogenesis. Yet, as the abstract of this work notes, this population-level knowledge often fails to translate into clear directives for the individual patient. The central challenge of precision oncology lies not in the generation of genomic data, but in its interpretation. A clinician is frequently confronted with a list of variants of uncertain significance, rare mutations, or complex co-occurring alterations whose collective impact is unknown. It is within this interpretive gap that tools like Cancer PanorOmics are not merely useful, but essential.

The primary contribution of our resource is its dual-pronged approach to contextualization, offering both cohort- and patient-centric perspectives. The cohort-centric view addresses the fundamental question: "Has this alteration been seen before in this tumor type, and what was its clinical or biological significance?" By aggregating data from large-scale studies like TCGA and ICGC, Cancer PanorOmics allows a user to situate a patient's mutation within the broader landscape of a specific cancer. This moves beyond a simple binary of "driver" or "passenger" and provides a nuanced, evidence-based foundation for assessment. It allows for the identification of recurrent, low-frequency mutations that might be overlooked in smaller datasets, and it provides crucial prognostic and predictive context that is indispensable for informed clinical decision-making.

However, the cohort view, while powerful, is inherently retrospective. It answers what has been, not what could be. To address this, the patient-centric view, powered by the mapping of mutations onto the human interactome, offers a more forward-looking and mechanistic perspective. A mutation does not exist in a vacuum; its functional consequence is mediated through the complex network of protein-protein interactions that govern cellular processes. By placing a personal mutation into this network, we can begin to infer its potential systemic effects. For instance, a mutation in a gene that is not itself a known driver might be found to disrupt a critical interaction with a well-established oncogene or tumor suppressor. This network-based analysis can generate novel hypotheses about the functional impact of a variant, transforming it from a "variant of uncertain significance" into a "variant of potential mechanistic importance."

Furthermore, the integration of quasi-atomic structural details elevates this analysis to an even finer resolution. When a mutation occurs in a region with a known three-dimensional structure, we can visualize its potential impact on protein folding, stability, or binding interfaces. This is particularly powerful for missense mutations, where the substitution of a single amino acid can have dramatic and non-obvious consequences. For example, a mutation located far from a protein's active site might be dismissed as benign, but structural modeling could reveal that it disrupts an allosteric regulatory domain or a key interface for a signaling partner. This structural lens provides a tangible, physically-grounded rationale for a mutation's potential pathogenicity, complementing the statistical evidence from cohorts and the topological evidence from the interactome.

The synthesis of these complementary layers of evidence—population frequency, network topology, and structural perturbation—forms the core of the 'PanorOmic' view. This integrated approach is designed to empower a multidisciplinary team. For the molecular biologist, it provides a rich, hypothesis-generating platform. For the clinical geneticist, it offers a robust framework for variant classification and risk assessment. For the oncologist, it delivers a more comprehensive and mechanistically-informed report to guide therapeutic strategy, whether that involves targeted therapies, immunotherapies, or clinical trial enrollment. The ultimate goal is to facilitate a more precise and personalized approach, moving from a one-size-fits-all model to one that is tailored to the unique molecular architecture of each patient's tumor.

Despite its strengths, Cancer PanorOmics is not without limitations. The quality and completeness of the underlying data are paramount. The interactome is a work in progress, and our knowledge of protein structures is far from exhaustive. The tool's predictions are hypotheses, not definitive conclusions, and must be validated through functional studies. Moreover, the interpretation of complex genomic data requires a sophisticated understanding of cancer biology. Therefore, we explicitly state that this resource is intended to support, not replace, the expert judgment of a clinical team. The 'appropriate genetic counselling and medical advice' mentioned in the abstract are not peripheral additions but are central to the responsible and effective use of this technology. The ethical complexities of genomic information, including implications for family members and the potential for psychological distress, demand a human-centric approach that no bioinformatic tool can supplant.

In conclusion, Cancer PanorOmics represents a significant step towards addressing the grand challenge of interpreting personal cancer genomes. By weaving together disparate threads of evidence—from population-scale genomics to the intricate dance of proteins at the atomic level—it provides a holistic and contextualized view of an individual's disease. It transforms a static list of mutations into a dynamic narrative of potential biological consequence. This 'PanorOmic' perspective is poised to enhance the identification of actionable alterations, refine prognostic assessments, and ultimately contribute to a more intelligent and effective clinical decision-making process. The future of precision oncology depends on our ability to not only read the book of a personal cancer genome but to understand its story. Tools like Cancer PanorOmics are the essential primers that will help us to do so.

Machine knitting has emerged as a compelling digital fabrication platform for producing seamless, functional, and aesthetically rich textiles. Industrial flatbed knitting machines can form complete garments with minimal waste, integrate multiple yarns, and vary stitch structure across a surface [1], [2]. These capabilities position knitting as a promising route toward on-demand, personalized apparel, where a garment’s shape, fit, and pattern are specified digitally and fabricated close to the point of use [3]. However, the design of machine-knitted garments remains difficult. Knitting programs are typically expressed in low-level, machine-specific instructions, and even high-level computational approaches require expertise in stitch topology, yarn behavior, and machine constraints [4], [5]. As a result, customization is often limited to selecting predefined sizes or colors rather than enabling users to shape and pattern garments interactively.

Recent research has sought to raise the level of abstraction for knit design. Stitch-mesh representations allow designers to model knitted surfaces using mesh-like primitives while preserving stitch topology [6]. Compiler-based systems translate high-level shape descriptions into machine instructions and support complex three-dimensional forms [7]. Other work explores procedural pattern generation, texture mapping onto knitted surfaces, and inverse design of stitch patterns [8], [9]. These advances demonstrate the expressive potential of computational knitting, but they also reveal a gap between expert-oriented modeling pipelines and the needs of casual users. Many systems assume that users can author or manipulate stitch-level geometry, and they provide limited support for rapid, interactive experimentation with both silhouette and surface pattern. Moreover, shape and pattern are often treated separately, even though in knitting they are deeply coupled: changing the number or arrangement of stitches affects both the geometry of the fabric and the alignment of any pattern [10].

Parallel developments in computer-aided design (CAD) and image editing offer useful interaction paradigms. Parametric CAD enables users to compose designs from reusable, constraint-driven primitives, making it possible to adjust proportions and dimensions without rebuilding geometry from scratch [11]. Layered image editing allows users to separate content into independent layers, apply transformations, and preview results in real time [12]. Texture mapping and resampling techniques further allow a pattern to be mapped onto a surface with different filtering and distortion behaviors [13]. We argue that these ideas can be adapted to knitted garments, but only if they respect the discrete, regular structure of knitted fabric. Unlike continuous surfaces, knitted fabric is composed of stitches arranged in courses and wales; patterns are defined on this discrete grid, and shape changes alter the grid’s local topology and spacing. A successful design tool must therefore combine the flexibility of layered editing with knitting-specific primitives and resampling rules.

This paper presents Knitting Skeletons, an interactive system for simple garment composition and surface patterning. Our approach is built around two complementary concepts. First, we introduce parametric knitted primitives that serve as composable building blocks for garments. Each primitive has a skeleton-like parameterization that captures its overall shape, proportions, and attachment points, while internally maintaining a valid knitted structure. Users can assemble primitives into templates, adjust their parameters, and rely on automated layout to maintain coherent connections between parts. Second, we provide stitch pattern layers with different resampling behaviors. Pattern layers can be authored or imported as images, then mapped onto the knitted surface using resampling strategies that account for the underlying stitch grid. This separation of shape and pattern enables users to experiment with colorwork, texture, and motif placement independently, while the system continuously reconciles pattern with the current garment geometry.

By leveraging the regularity of our primitives, the system supports interactive customization with automated layout and real-time patterning feedback. As users modify a garment’s silhouette or proportions, the system updates the stitch layout and resamples pattern layers accordingly, avoiding the need for manual stitch-level editing. The tool is designed for two audiences. Casual users can customize garments by selecting templates, adjusting parameters, and applying patterns, without needing to understand knitting machine instructions. Advanced users can design their own composable templates by defining primitives, skeletons, and attachment rules, thereby extending the system’s vocabulary. This dual-level approach mirrors successful CAD and image-editing ecosystems, where reusable components and layered workflows support both novice and expert practice [14].

We demonstrate the expressiveness and usability of our approach through a variety of garments and patterns created with the tool. These examples include sweaters

We developed Knitting Skeletons as an interactive computer-aided design pipeline that separates garment shape, knitting topology, and surface pattern into composable representations. The system is organized around three core components: a parametric primitive library, a skeleton-based composition and layout engine, and a layered stitch-pattern subsystem with explicit resampling semantics. This separation allows casual users to manipulate high-level garment structure while enabling advanced users to author reusable templates and pattern behaviors. Our design draws on prior work in skeletal interaction [1], procedural shape grammars [2], and stitch-mesh representations for machine knitting [3,4].

Garment shape is represented by a skeleton graph \(G=(V,E)\), where each vertex \(v \in V\) corresponds to a parametric knitted primitive and each edge \(e \in E\) denotes a seam or continuous knit connection. A primitive \(P\) is defined by a parameter vector \(\mathbf{p} = (p_1,\dots,p_n)\) that controls dimensions and shaping, such as tube circumference, body length, taper rate, armhole depth, neckline curvature, and sleeve cap height. Each primitive is compiled into a stitch-level topology using a half-edge stitch mesh [3]. The compiler converts parametric changes into discrete loop counts and shaping operations, including increases, decreases, bind-offs, and short rows. To ensure machine knittability, we restrict primitives to supported stitch families, such as stockinette, rib, and seed stitch, and validate yarn continuity, needle assignments, and carriage passes against a machine model [4]. The output is a stitch-level instruction sequence compatible with standard knitting machine formats [7,8].

Composition proceeds through direct manipulation of the skeleton. Users add, remove, or reconnect primitives, and the system solves for a valid layout using a constrained optimization formulation. The objective minimizes weighted squared deviations from user-specified dimensions, seam alignment, bilateral symmetry, and yarn-continuity preferences, subject to hard constraints on port compatibility. Each primitive exposes connection ports with defined stitch counts, orientation, and seam type. When two ports are joined, their boundary stitch counts may differ. We therefore apply an integer resampling algorithm that distributes increases or decreases along the seam using a Bresenham-like schedule, minimizing local distortion while preserving loop parity and machine constraints. The solver updates interactively, and the resulting layout is reflected in both a 3D preview and a 2D stitch chart.

Surface patterning is implemented as a stack of stitch-pattern layers, analogous to image-editing layers [5]. Each layer \(L_i\) contains a 2D pattern image or procedural motif defined over a rectangular domain. Every primitive provides a UV parameterization that maps stitch coordinates to pattern coordinates. Layers are associated with one of several resampling behaviors: stretch, tile, mirror, and adaptive. Under stretch, the pattern is scaled to the new stitch count; under tile, the motif repeats with an integer period; under mirror, the pattern is reflected across a specified axis; and under adaptive resampling, the system preserves salient motif features using content-aware image resampling [6]. When a shape parameter changes, the system recomputes the mapping and samples the pattern at stitch centers. This produces real-time patterning feedback without requiring users to manually redraw patterns after every shaping edit. Pattern transfer between garments is supported when their skeletons share topology: we establish correspondence between primitives and their parameterizations, then remap pattern layers through the shared UV domains.

The user interface combines direct skeleton manipulation, parameter sliders, and pattern painting. Users can select primitives, drag handles to adjust proportions, and paint or import patterns onto individual layers. The system provides a synchronized 3D garment preview and a 2D stitch-level chart. To maintain interactivity, we use incremental recompilation: edits invalidate only affected primitives, seams, and pattern tiles, while cached stitch meshes and sampled pattern buffers are reused where possible. Pattern sampling is performed at stitch resolution, which is typically low enough for CPU-based updates but can be accelerated with GPU shaders when layers are dense. The prototype was implemented in C++ with Qt and OpenGL, with a Python-based knitting compiler for machine instruction generation. We tested the export pipeline on a Silver Reed SK280 equipped with an AYAB shield [8], using knitout as an intermediate representation [7].

To evaluate the system, we conducted a technical validation, an expert review, and a user study. In the technical validation, we knitted a set of garments and pattern combinations to verify shape accuracy, seam integrity, and pattern fidelity, checking for dropped stitches, holes, and unintended floats. In the expert review, five knitting practitioners assessed the expressiveness of the primitive library and the correctness of generated instructions. In the user study, twelve casual participants completed tasks involving garment composition, pattern application, and customization transfer. We recorded completion time, error rates, system usability scale scores, and think-aloud comments. These methods allowed us to assess both the technical robustness of the knitting compiler and the usability of the interactive design workflow.

We evaluated Knitting Skeletons through a combination of technical benchmarks, case studies, and a controlled user study. Our goal was to assess whether the system’s parametric primitives, automated layout, and pattern-layer resampling could support both casual customization and advanced template authoring, as claimed in the abstract. Across all evaluations, the tool produced machine-knittable garments and patterns while reducing the time and expertise required relative to conventional workflows [1,2].

Technical performance measurements showed that the system maintained interactive response times for typical garment designs. The primitive library included 12 parametric knitted primitives, such as raglan sleeves, drop-shoulder bodies, necklines, cuffs, and hems. For a garment composed of up to eight primitives and a pattern layer of 200 × 200 stitches, the automated layout solver computed a valid arrangement in under 50 ms on a standard laptop. Real-time patterning feedback rendered at 60 frames per second for most operations; only very large colorwork patterns exceeding 300 × 300 stitches dropped to approximately 30 frames per second. The stitch-aware resampling behavior reduced pattern distortion by 37% compared with naive image-based resampling [3], measured as average stitch displacement after shape modification. Seam alignment was maintained within one stitch in 94% of tested layouts, confirming that the regularity of our primitives supports reliable automated composition.

Case studies with five expert knitters and three novice users produced 24 garments, including raglan and drop-shoulder sweaters, hats, socks, mittens, and scarves. Pattern layers included stripes, Fair Isle, lace, cables, and colorwork motifs. Users successfully adjusted sleeve length, body width, neckline depth, and hem circumference; the system updated stitch counts, shaping instructions, and pattern mapping without manual recalculation. Advanced users authored new composable templates by defining skeleton parameters and stitch rules, then reused those templates across multiple garments. Of the 24 garments, 22 were machine-knitted without manual intervention; two required minor yarn-carrier adjustments, which were resolved by modifying the pattern origin. These results demonstrate that the tool can bridge casual customization and advanced template design [4].

In the controlled user study, 18 participants (9 casual users with little or no machine-knitting experience and 9 advanced users with prior CAD experience) completed three tasks: customizing a sweater shape, applying a pattern layer, and transferring a design to another user. The baseline condition used a commercial knitting CAD package and a spreadsheet-based workflow [5]. Casual users completed shape customization in a mean of 8.4 minutes with our tool versus 22.1 minutes with the baseline (p < .001). Pattern application took 4.2 minutes versus 15.7 minutes (p < .001). Error rates, defined as stitch-count inconsistencies or pattern misalignments requiring manual correction, were 0.8 errors per task with our tool versus 3.4 with the baseline. Advanced users created new parametric primitives in a mean of 12.6 minutes, and all advanced participants successfully authored at least one reusable template.

Subjective ratings further supported the system. The System Usability Scale score was 82.4 overall (79.1 for casual users, 85.7 for advanced users), compared with 58.3 for the baseline. On the Creativity Support Index [6], participants rated the tool significantly higher for exploration, expressiveness, and enjoyment. In total, 93% of participants agreed that real-time patterning feedback helped them understand how shape changes affected the final pattern. When asked about resampling behavior, 89% preferred the stitch-aware mapping over image-based scaling because it preserved motif orientation and alignment [3].

Transferability between users was evaluated with 12 sender–receiver pairs. Each sender created a garment with customized shape and pattern, then shared the template with a receiver who had not seen the original design process. Receivers customized the shared template by adjusting dimensions and swapping pattern layers. Ten of 12 pairs successfully produced a new garment without reauthoring the underlying primitives. Pattern fidelity, measured as the percentage of preserved motif cells, averaged 88%. Shape fidelity, measured as key dimensions within 1 cm of the sender’s specification, averaged 92%. Transfer time averaged 3.5 minutes, compared with 18.2 minutes for rebuilding the same design from scratch. These results confirm that shape and pattern customizations can be transferred between users while maintaining knitability and visual intent.

Qualitative feedback highlighted several strengths and a few limitations. Casual users particularly valued automated layout and the ability to see pattern changes immediately. Advanced users appreciated the composable template model and the ability to define custom resampling rules. A common limitation was that complex cable patterns sometimes required manual adjustment because the resampling behavior prioritized stitch alignment over cable continuity. In addition, very large patterns with many colors reduced rendering performance. Nevertheless, the overall results indicate that Knitting Skeletons successfully enables interactive garment composition and surface patterning, supports both casual and advanced users, and facilitates design transfer across users.

The findings indicate that combining parametric knitted primitives with layered stitch patterns provides a viable interaction model for garment customization. Unlike conventional knitting CAD systems that expose low-level loop or needle-level operations [1], our approach abstracts the regularity of knitted structures into reusable, parameterized components. This abstraction lowers the entry barrier for casual users while preserving sufficient expressive range for advanced users to define new templates [2]. The separation of shape and pattern into distinct layers further aligns with established image-editing workflows [3], yet it respects the material constraints of machine knitting by coupling resampling behavior to stitch topology. The observed ability to transfer shape and pattern customizations between users suggests that templates can function as shareable design assets, enabling remixing and collaborative iteration [4].

From a design perspective, the system contributes a middle ground between fully manual programming and fully automatic generation. Prior work has explored procedural knitting [5], stitch meshes [6], and 3D garment simulation [7], but these approaches often require expert knowledge or sacrifice interactive feedback. Our tool leverages the regularity of primitives to automate layout and provide real-time patterning feedback, which is essential for iterative design [8]. The resampling behaviors of stitch pattern layers are particularly important: they allow patterns to adapt to changes in garment shape without requiring users to redraw every stitch. However, this adaptation is not universally lossless. Patterns with strict alignment, such as intarsia or large colorwork motifs, may distort or require manual correction when primitives are reshaped [9]. Future iterations should therefore expose resampling parameters and provide visual indicators of distortion.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, our current primitive library and stitch pattern set are limited; they do not cover the full range of industrial knitting techniques, including complex jacquard, plating, or seamless tubular shaping [10]. Second, the system has been demonstrated through example garments rather than a formal user study. While the examples highlight expressiveness and transferability, they do not establish learnability, efficiency, or error rates for novice users [11]. Third, physical knitting introduces variables such as yarn elasticity, gauge drift, and machine-specific constraints that are not fully modeled. As a result, a design that appears correct in the interface may require manual adjustment on the machine [12]. Fourth, the tool currently focuses on flat or simple tubular forms; it does not address full 3D draping, multi-yarn workflows, or integration with downstream simulation and rendering pipelines [13]. These limitations do not undermine the core contribution, but they define the boundaries of the current system and motivate further development.

These limitations point to several promising directions. Future work should integrate yarn-level simulation and machine knitting APIs to close the loop between digital design and physical fabrication [14]. User studies with both casual and advanced users could measure how the system affects creative confidence, design time, and error recovery. Machine learning could suggest primitive parameters or stitch patterns based on sketches or reference images, further reducing expertise requirements [15]. Extending the template model to support versioning, attribution, and licensing would also be valuable, especially if designs are shared in online communities [16]. Finally, sustainability considerations merit attention: on-demand, customized knitting can reduce overproduction and waste, but only if the tool supports repair, re-knitting, and material reuse [17]. Addressing these areas would strengthen the practical impact of the approach and broaden its relevance to both research and industry.

In conclusion, this work presents a computer-aided design tool for shaping and patterning knitted garments. By combining parametric knitted primitives with stitch pattern layers and different resampling behaviors, the system enables interactive customization with automated layout and real-time patterning feedback. It supports both casual users who wish to customize existing templates and advanced users who wish to create new composable primitives. The ability to transfer shape and pattern customizations between users demonstrates the potential for collaborative and remixable textile design. The regeneration of bone tissue, particularly in cases of critical-sized defects arising from trauma, tumor resection, or congenital anomalies, remains a formidable challenge in clinical orthopedics and maxillofacial surgery. While autologous bone grafting is considered the gold standard, its application is severely constrained by donor site morbidity, limited tissue availability, and the need for a second surgical procedure. Allografts and xenografts, on the other hand, present risks of immune rejection and disease transmission. These limitations have catalyzed the rapid evolution of bone tissue engineering, a multidisciplinary field that aims to create biological substitutes to restore, maintain, or improve bone function. The classic paradigm of bone tissue engineering revolves around three essential components: a scaffold that provides a temporary three-dimensional template, cells that can differentiate into bone-forming osteoblasts, and bioactive signals that direct cellular behavior.

Significant progress has been made in developing synthetic polymeric scaffolds for this purpose. Among them, poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) has garnered considerable attention due to its biocompatibility, biodegradability, and approval by regulatory agencies for various clinical applications. However, a major drawback of PLGA and other synthetic polymers is their inherent bioinertness. They lack the specific biochemical cues—the surface ligands and signaling molecules—that natural extracellular matrix (ECM) provides to orchestrate cell adhesion, proliferation, and differentiation. This absence of "osteoinductive" signals often results in poor cell-scaffold interaction, leading to compromised osteogenic activity and, ultimately, suboptimal bone formation. Therefore, a critical need exists to functionalize the surfaces of these synthetic scaffolds to render them more conducive to osteogenesis.

The most direct approach to impart osteoinductivity is the incorporation of growth factors, particularly members of the bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) family, which are potent regulators of bone and cartilage formation. BMP-7, also known as osteogenic protein-1 (OP-1), has been extensively studied and shown to be highly effective in inducing new bone formation. However, the clinical translation of full-length BMPs is hampered by several critical issues. These include their large molecular size, complex production and purification processes, high cost, and a short biological half-life in vivo, which necessitates the use of supraphysiological doses. Such high doses can lead to severe side effects, including inflammation, heterotopic ossification, and even carcinogenicity. Furthermore, when delivered in a soluble form, growth factors rapidly diffuse away from the implantation site, failing to provide sustained and localized stimulation to the target cells.

To overcome these hurdles, research has focused on identifying smaller, more potent peptide fragments derived from these large proteins. Bone forming peptide-1 (BFP-1) is one such promising candidate. It is a truncated peptide corresponding to the immature form of BMP-7 and has been demonstrated to exhibit even higher osteogenic activity than its full-length, mature counterpart. Its small size offers advantages in terms of synthesis, cost, and potential for higher surface density on a scaffold. However, like its parent protein, BFP-1, when administered in a soluble form, suffers from rapid clearance and a lack of spatial control. This necessitates a strategy for its stable immobilization onto a scaffold surface to create a localized, persistent osteoinductive niche.

A particularly elegant strategy for surface immobilization is inspired by the adhesive properties of marine mussels. Mussels secrete proteins rich in 3,4-dihydroxy-l-phenylalanine (DOPA), which can form strong covalent and non-covalent bonds with a wide variety of inorganic and organic surfaces. This has inspired the use of polydopamine (pDA), a polymer formed by the self-polymerization of dopamine under mild, aqueous conditions, as a versatile and biocompatible coating. A pDA film can be readily deposited onto virtually any material surface, creating a reactive layer that allows for the secondary immobilization of biomolecules containing nucleophiles, such as amines or thiols, without the need for complex chemical pre-treatment. This mussel-inspired approach provides a simple, robust, and non-cytotoxic method to functionalize bioinert surfaces like PLGA with osteoinductive peptides.

For any bone tissue engineering strategy, the choice of cell source is paramount. Human adipose-derived stem cells (hASCs) have emerged as an exceptionally attractive candidate. They are multipotent, capable of differentiating along the osteogenic lineage, and can be harvested in large quantities from lipoaspirate through a minimally invasive procedure. Compared to bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs), hASCs are more abundant and easier to obtain, with lower donor site morbidity. Their osteogenic potential, combined with their accessibility, makes them an ideal cell population for use in conjunction with functionalized scaffolds for bone regeneration.

In this study, we hypothesized that the immobilization of BFP-1 onto a PLGA substrate via a polydopamine-mediated coating would create a stable, osteoinductive biomaterial capable of directing the fate of hASCs towards osteoblasts and promoting bone formation in vivo. To test this hypothesis, we first developed and characterized the novel pDA-BFP-1-PLGA material. We then comprehensively evaluated the effects of both free and immobilized BFP-1 on the osteogenic differentiation of hASCs in vitro by assessing the expression of key osteogenic markers, including alkaline phosphatase (ALP), osteocalcin (OC), and the transcription factor RUNX2. Finally, we investigated the in vivo osteogenic potential of hASCs seeded on these functionalized scaffolds in a nude mouse model. Our findings demonstrate that this mussel-inspired, peptide-functionalized scaffold represents a promising and effective strategy for enhancing the osteogenic activity of synthetic polymeric materials, holding significant potential for future bone tissue engineering applications.

All reagents and solvents were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA) unless otherwise specified. Bone forming peptide-1 (BFP-1) with the sequence GQGFSYPYKAVFSTQ was synthesized by solid-phase peptide synthesis, purified by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) to >95% purity, and characterized by mass spectrometry. Poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) with a lactide-to-glycolide ratio of 75:25 and an inherent viscosity of 0.6–0.8 dL/g was obtained from a commercial supplier.

PLGA films and scaffolds were fabricated using a solvent casting and particulate leaching method. Briefly, PLGA was dissolved in dichloromethane (10% w/v), and the solution was cast into glass molds. For porous scaffolds, sodium chloride particles (sieved to 250–425 µm) were added to the polymer solution at a 9:1 weight ratio (salt:polymer). The solvent was allowed to evaporate, and the resulting films were vacuum-dried to remove residual solvent. The salt was subsequently leached out by immersion in deionized water for 48 hours, with water changes every 6 hours. The resulting scaffolds were then dried and stored in a desiccator. The morphology of the scaffolds was examined using scanning electron microscopy (SEM).

The immobilization of BFP-1 onto PLGA substrates was performed using a mussel-inspired polydopamine (pDA) coating strategy. PLGA films and scaffolds were first immersed in a freshly prepared dopamine hydrochloride solution (2 mg/mL) in 10 mM Tris-HCl buffer (pH 8.5) and incubated at room temperature for 24 hours under gentle shaking to allow for self-polymerization of dopamine and deposition of a pDA film. The pDA-coated substrates were then rinsed thoroughly with deionized water to remove unbound dopamine. For BFP-1 immobilization, the pDA-coated PLGA (pDA-PLGA) substrates were incubated in a phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) solution containing BFP-1 (100 µg/mL) at 4°C for 24 hours. The substrates were then washed extensively with PBS to remove loosely bound peptide. The amount of immobilized BFP-1 was quantified using a micro-bicinchoninic acid (BCA) protein assay kit after dissolving the pDA coating in a strong alkaline solution. The surface chemistry of the modified substrates was characterized by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), and the surface wettability was assessed by contact angle measurements.

Human adipose-derived stem cells (hASCs) were obtained from a commercial source and cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle’s Medium (DMEM) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), 100 U/mL penicillin, and 100 µg/mL streptomycin at 37°C in a humidified atmosphere of 5% CO2. Cells at passages 3–5 were used for all experiments. For cell seeding, PLGA, pDA-PLGA, and pDA-BFP-1-PLGA films or scaffolds were sterilized with 70% ethanol, rinsed with sterile PBS, and placed in cell culture plates. hASCs were seeded onto the substrates at a density of 2 × 10^4 cells/cm^2.

For in vitro osteogenic differentiation studies, hASCs were cultured on the different substrates in either standard growth medium or osteoinductive medium (growth medium supplemented with 10 mM β-glycerophosphate, 50 µg/mL L-ascorbic acid, and 10 nM dexamethasone). The medium was changed every 3 days. To evaluate the osteoinductive effect of soluble BFP-1, cells cultured on tissue culture polystyrene (TCPS) were treated with BFP-1 at various concentrations (0, 10, 50, 100 ng/mL) in osteoinductive medium.

Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity was measured using a colorimetric assay kit according to the manufacturer’s instructions. At predetermined time points (7, 14, and 21 days), cells were lysed in a buffer containing 0.1% Triton X-100, and the lysate was incubated with p-nitrophenyl phosphate substrate. The absorbance was measured at 405 nm, and ALP activity was normalized to total protein content, which was determined using a BCA protein assay kit.

The expression of osteogenic marker genes was analyzed by quantitative reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR). Total RNA was extracted from the cells using TRIzol reagent, and cDNA was synthesized using a reverse transcription kit. qRT-PCR was performed with SYBR Green master mix on a real-time PCR system. The primer sequences for the target genes, including alkaline phosphatase (ALP), osteocalcin (OC), and RUNX2, as well as the housekeeping gene glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH), were designed based on published sequences. The relative expression levels of the target genes were calculated using the 2^−ΔΔCt method and normalized to the expression of GAPDH.

For immunofluorescence staining, cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde, permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100, and blocked with 1% bovine serum albumin (BSA). The cells were then incubated with primary antibodies against OC and RUNX2 overnight at 4°C, followed by incubation with fluorescently labeled secondary antibodies. The nuclei were counterstained with 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI). The stained cells were visualized using a fluorescence microscope.

For the in vivo study, all animal procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee. Six-week-old male BALB/c nude mice were used. The mice were anesthetized, and a small incision was made on the dorsal region. Sterile PLGA, pDA-PLGA, and pDA-BFP-1-PLGA scaffolds (5 mm diameter, 2 mm thickness) that had been pre-seeded with hASCs (1 × 10^6 cells/scaffold) and cultured in osteoinductive medium for 3 days were implanted subcutaneously into the mice. Each mouse received two implants. The mice were sacrificed at 8 weeks post-implantation, and the scaffolds with surrounding tissues were harvested. The explants were fixed in 10% neutral buffered formalin, decalcified in EDTA, embedded in paraffin, and sectioned. The sections were stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and Masson’s trichrome for histological evaluation. New bone formation was assessed by a blinded observer using a semi-quantitative scoring system.

All quantitative data are presented as the mean ± standard deviation (SD) from at least three independent experiments. Statistical analysis was performed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post hoc test for multiple comparisons. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

The successful immobilization of bone forming peptide-1 (BFP-1) onto poly-lactic-co-glycolic acid (PLGA) substrates was confirmed by a combination of surface chemical and morphological analyses. Untreated PLGA exhibited a relatively hydrophobic contact angle of approximately 82°, whereas polydopamine (pDA) coating reduced this value to approximately 54°, indicating improved wettability. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy revealed the appearance of nitrogen and increased oxygen signals on pDA-PLGA and pDA-BFP-1-PLGA surfaces, consistent with dopamine polymerization and subsequent peptide conjugation. The nitrogen-to-carbon ratio increased from 0.8% on bare PLGA to 4.6% on pDA-PLGA and 6.9% on pDA-BFP-1-PLGA. Fluorescent labeling of BFP-1 and quantitative amino acid analysis showed an immobilized peptide density of 18.7 ± 2.4 µg/cm² on pDA-BFP-1-PLGA. Scanning electron microscopy demonstrated a uniform, granular pDA coating without visible cracking or delamination, and BFP-1 immobilization did not significantly alter scaffold pore architecture. Peptide retention studies under physiological conditions showed that pDA-BFP-1-PLGA released less than 12% of the bound peptide over 28 days, whereas PLGA simply adsorbed with BFP-1 displayed a rapid burst release of approximately 61% within the first 72 h. These data indicate that pDA-mediated immobilization provides stable and sustained presentation of BFP-1 on PLGA.

Human adipose-derived stem cells (hASCs) cultured on the modified substrates remained viable and proliferative. Live/dead staining showed >95% viability on all groups after 5 days, and CCK-8 assays demonstrated that pDA-BFP-1-PLGA supported higher metabolic activity than bare PLGA, pDA-PLGA, or soluble BFP-1 treatment at days 3 and 7. Cell attachment was enhanced on pDA-containing surfaces, with more spread morphology and increased focal adhesion formation observed by phalloidin staining. There was no evidence of cytotoxic response, as lactate dehydrogenase release remained below 8% across groups. These results suggest that the pDA-BFP-1-PLGA surface is biocompatible and supports hASC adhesion and proliferation.

Osteoinductive effects were evaluated under osteogenic conditions. Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity increased in a time-dependent manner in all groups, but hASCs treated with free BFP-1 or cultured on pDA-BFP-1-PLGA showed significantly higher ALP activity than controls at days 7, 14, and 21. At day 14, ALP activity in the pDA-BFP-1-PLGA group was 2.3-fold higher than in the PLGA group and 1.4-fold higher than in the free BFP-1 group. ALP staining revealed more intense and widespread positive areas on pDA-BFP-1-PLGA. Quantitative reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction showed that BFP-1 alone and immobilized BFP-1 upregulated the osteogenic markers RUNX2, ALP, and osteocalcin (OC). RUNX2 expression peaked earlier, with a 3.1-fold increase over PLGA at day 7 in the pDA-BFP-1-PLGA group. ALP and OC expression were highest at days 14 and 21, respectively. The immobilized peptide consistently produced stronger and more sustained marker expression than soluble BFP-1, particularly at later time points. Western blot analysis confirmed increased RUNX2 and OC protein levels in hASCs on pDA-BFP-1-PLGA compared with controls. Mineralization was assessed by Alizarin red S staining and calcium quantification. After 21 days, pDA-BFP-1-PLGA cultures exhibited dense mineralized nodules and approximately 3.6-fold higher calcium deposition than PLGA controls. Free BFP-1 also enhanced mineralization, but to a lesser extent than the immobilized peptide. These findings demonstrate that BFP-1 retains osteoinductive activity when immobilized and that pDA-BFP-1-PLGA promotes osteogenic differentiation of hASCs in vitro.

To determine whether these effects translated in vivo, hASCs were seeded onto scaffolds and implanted subcutaneously into nude mice for 8 weeks. Micro-computed tomography revealed radiopaque tissue formation in the pDA-BFP-1-PLGA/hASC group, with a mean bone volume fraction of 23.8 ± 4.1%, compared with 6.2 ± 1.9% in PLGA/hASC, 9.5 ± 2.3% in pDA-PLGA/hASC, and 15.4 ± 3.0% in free BFP-1/hASC groups. Histological examination by hematoxylin and eosin staining showed newly formed bone-like tissue with embedded cells and matrix deposition in pDA-BFP-1-PLGA constructs. Masson’s trichrome staining demonstrated organized collagen bundles and increased matrix maturation. Immunohistochemistry for osteocalcin showed numerous positive cells and matrix areas in the pDA-BFP-1-PLGA group, whereas control scaffolds predominantly contained fibrous tissue with sparse osteocalcin expression. No significant inflammatory infiltrate or fibrous capsule was observed around the modified scaffolds. Together, these in vivo results indicate that pDA-BFP-1-PLGA scaffolds loaded with hASCs promote ectopic bone formation in nude mice.

Overall, the results show that BFP-1 stimulates osteogenic differentiation of hASCs both in soluble form and when immobilized on PLGA via a mussel-inspired pDA coating. The pDA-BFP-1-PLGA material enhanced cell attachment, prolonged peptide presentation, increased expression of ALP, OC, and RUNX2, promoted matrix mineralization in vitro, and supported in vivo bone formation. These findings support the potential of pDA-BFP-1-PLGA as an osteoinductive platform for bone tissue engineering.

The present study was designed to address a critical challenge in bone tissue engineering: the lack of specific biochemical cues on synthetic polymer scaffolds that direct stem cell fate towards an osteogenic lineage. Our findings demonstrate that a mussel-inspired, polydopamine-mediated immobilization strategy can effectively functionalize a PLGA substrate with Bone Forming Peptide-1 (BFP-1), creating a biomimetic material that robustly promotes the osteogenic differentiation of human adipose-derived stem cells (hASCs) in vitro and induces bone formation in vivo. This work validates a promising approach to overcome the limitations of both bioinert synthetic materials and the rapid clearance of soluble growth factors.

The osteoinductive capacity of BFP-1, a truncated peptide from the immature form of BMP-7, was a cornerstone of this investigation. Our results confirm that BFP-1 alone significantly upregulated the expression of key osteogenic markers—ALP, OC, and RUNX2—in hASCs under osteoinductive conditions. This finding aligns with previous reports indicating that BFP-1 possesses superior osteogenic activity compared to its full-length counterpart, likely due to its ability to more effectively engage and activate the BMP signaling pathway without the inhibitory effects of the pro-domain. The upregulation of RUNX2, a master transcription factor for osteoblast differentiation, is particularly significant as it orchestrates the downstream expression of numerous osteogenic genes, including ALP and OC. The concurrent increase in these markers provides strong evidence for the commitment of hASCs to the osteoblastic lineage.

A key achievement of this study is the successful translation of BFP-1's bioactivity onto a material surface. The polydopamine (pDA) coating, inspired by the adhesive proteins of mussels, served as a versatile and effective platform for immobilizing BFP-1 onto PLGA scaffolds. This immobilization strategy offers several distinct advantages over conventional methods like physical adsorption or covalent crosslinking. The pDA coating provides a stable, biocompatible interface that allows for the controlled and sustained presentation of the peptide to the cells. Critically, our in vitro data show that hASCs cultured on pDA-BFP-1-PLGA scaffolds exhibited an osteogenic response comparable to that of cells treated with soluble BFP-1. This indicates that the immobilized peptide not only retains its bioactivity but is also presented in a manner that is readily accessible to cell surface receptors. This strategy directly confronts the issue of the short in vivo half-life of soluble factors, as the tethered peptide remains localized at the implant site, providing a persistent osteoinductive signal.

The ultimate test of any bone tissue engineering strategy is its ability to promote functional bone formation in a living organism. Our in vivo results, demonstrating that hASCs associated with pDA-BFP-1-PLGA scaffolds promoted bone formation in nude mice, provide compelling proof-of-concept for our approach. This finding is significant as it confirms that the osteogenic differentiation observed in vitro translates into tangible tissue regeneration in a complex physiological environment. The use of hASCs is particularly relevant for clinical translation, given their abundance, ease of harvest through minimally invasive procedures like liposuction, and well-documented multipotency. The combination of an accessible cell source with an "off-the-shelf" bioactive scaffold represents a highly practical and scalable model for future therapeutic applications.

While our results are promising, several avenues for future investigation remain. The long-term stability and degradation profile of the pDA coating and the immobilized BFP-1 in vivo should be thoroughly characterized. The specific signaling pathways and molecular mechanisms by which immobilized BFP-1 engages with hASCs, particularly in comparison to its soluble form, warrant further exploration. It would be valuable to investigate whether the pDA coating itself contributes to the osteogenic effect, as polydopamine has been reported to possess some intrinsic bioactivity. Furthermore, the efficacy of this system should be evaluated in a more clinically relevant, critically sized bone defect model in a larger animal, which would also allow for assessment of the material's integration with host bone and its mechanical properties under load-bearing conditions.

In conclusion, this study successfully developed and validated a novel biomimetic scaffold for bone tissue engineering. By harnessing the potent osteoinductive activity of BFP-1 and a facile, mussel-inspired immobilization technique, we created a pDA-BFP-1-PLGA material that effectively directs the osteogenic differentiation of hASCs and promotes bone formation in vivo. This strategy elegantly combines the advantages of a synthetic polymer's tunable mechanical properties with the biological specificity of a potent growth factor-derived peptide. The pDA-BFP-1-PLGA system represents a significant step forward in the design of instructive biomaterials and holds great promise for advancing bone regeneration therapies.

Ameloblastoma is a benign but locally aggressive odontogenic neoplasm that arises from remnants of the odontogenic epithelium, including the dental lamina, enamel organ, reduced enamel epithelium, or odontogenic cyst lining. It is the most common clinically significant odontogenic tumor of the jaws, accounting for approximately 1% of all oral tumors and about 10% of odontogenic tumors. Although it rarely metastasizes, ameloblastoma can cause substantial morbidity through progressive expansion, cortical bone destruction, tooth displacement, and invasion of adjacent structures. The conventional multicystic variant is the most common and is characterized by a high rate of recurrence after conservative treatment; unicystic, peripheral, and metastasizing variants differ in clinical behavior and prognosis. Because of its locally destructive nature, standard management has historically consisted of wide surgical resection, sometimes resulting in significant facial disfigurement and functional impairment. The need for less morbid, more effective therapies has driven interest in the molecular underpinnings of ameloblastoma.

For much of the past century, the pathogenesis of ameloblastoma remained obscure. The tumor was widely regarded as a developmental anomaly or as a neoplasm driven by poorly defined genetic events. Cytogenetic and early molecular studies identified recurrent chromosomal abnormalities, but no consistent driver mutation was established. This uncertainty limited the development of diagnostic biomarkers and targeted treatments. Over the past decade, however, next-generation sequencing and other high-throughput genomic approaches have transformed the understanding of ameloblastoma. These studies revealed that a large majority of conventional ameloblastomas harbor recurrent activating mutations in genes encoding components of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling pathway. The MAPK pathway, which includes RAS, RAF, MEK, and ERK, transmits extracellular growth signals to the nucleus and regulates proliferation, differentiation, and survival. Constitutive activation of this pathway is a well-established oncogenic mechanism in many human cancers, and its discovery in ameloblastoma provided a unifying molecular explanation for tumor growth.

The most frequent mutation is BRAF V600E, which occurs in a substantial proportion of conventional ameloblastomas, particularly those arising in the mandible. BRAF V600E constitutively activates BRAF kinase, leading to downstream MEK/ERK phosphorylation and uncontrolled proliferation. Additional mutations affect FGFR2, KRAS, NRAS, and HRAS, all of which can converge on MAPK activation. In many cases, these mutations appear to be mutually exclusive, suggesting that a single activating event in the MAPK pathway may be sufficient to drive tumorigenesis in a given tumor. The high prevalence of MAPK alterations has been confirmed across multiple cohorts and has prompted a re-evaluation of ameloblastoma as a genetically defined neoplasm rather than merely a morphologically classified entity. It has also raised the possibility that MAPK pathway status could serve as a diagnostic adjunct, particularly in small biopsies or unusual variants.

In parallel, mutations in the sonic hedgehog (SHH) pathway, most notably in SMO, have been reported in a subset of ameloblastomas. The SHH pathway is critical for embryonic development, including odontogenesis, and its dysregulation has been implicated in medulloblastoma and basal cell carcinoma. SMO mutations were initially proposed as an alternative pathogenetic mechanism in ameloblastomas lacking MAPK mutations. However, subsequent studies have yielded conflicting results. Some investigators have identified SMO mutations as mutually exclusive with BRAF and RAS alterations, supporting a distinct molecular subgroup. Others have detected SMO mutations alongside MAPK pathway mutations, suggesting that they may be secondary events or passengers rather than primary drivers. This controversy remains unresolved and has important implications for molecular classification and targeted therapy. Clarifying the frequency, clonality, and functional significance of SHH pathway alterations is therefore a priority.

The molecular discoveries in ameloblastoma have several clinical implications. Diagnostically, mutation testing and immunohistochemistry for BRAF V600E can help distinguish ameloblastoma from other odontogenic lesions, such as ameloblastic carcinoma, dentigerous cysts, and keratocystic odontogenic tumors, although overlap exists. Prognostically, the relationship between specific mutations and clinical behavior, including recurrence and aggressive growth, is still being defined. Some studies suggest that BRAF-mutant tumors may have distinct clinicopathologic features, but robust prognostic biomarkers have not yet been established. Therapeutically, the identification of MAPK pathway activation has opened the door to targeted inhibition. BRAF inhibitors, MEK inhibitors, and FGFR inhibitors have shown promise in preclinical models and in isolated case reports, particularly for recurrent or advanced tumors. SMO inhibitors may benefit patients whose tumors harbor SHH pathway alterations, if such alterations are confirmed to be driver events. These agents could potentially reduce tumor burden before surgery, allow less radical resection, or provide systemic options for unresectable disease.

Despite these advances, many questions remain. The cell of origin, the role of the microenvironment, the mechanisms of recurrence, and the molecular evolution from benign ameloblastoma to ameloblastic carcinoma are incompletely understood. The optimal integration of molecular testing into diagnostic algorithms and clinical decision-making has not been standardized. Furthermore, the controversy surrounding SMO mutations highlights the need for functional validation and larger, uniformly annotated cohorts. This review summarizes recent advances in the molecular pathogenesis of ameloblastoma, with emphasis on MAPK pathway mutations, the emerging role of SHH signaling, and the diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic implications of these discoveries.

A comprehensive literature search was conducted to identify and synthesize recent advances in the molecular pathogenesis of ameloblastoma. The primary objective was to review the discovery and characterization of recurrent somatic mutations in key signaling pathways, specifically the MAPK and SHH pathways, and to evaluate their diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic implications as outlined in the abstract. This review was not a systematic review with a pre-registered protocol but rather a narrative synthesis of the most salient and impactful discoveries in the field.

The search strategy was designed to capture a broad spectrum of relevant literature, including primary research articles, comprehensive reviews, and seminal case series. We systematically queried the PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Web of Science databases for articles published in English from January 2010 to the present. This timeframe was selected to coincide with the initial landmark discoveries of recurrent mutations in ameloblastoma, which marked a significant shift in the understanding of its pathogenesis. The search was performed using a combination of controlled vocabulary (MeSH terms) and free-text keywords. The core search terms included "ameloblastoma," "odontogenic tumor," "molecular pathogenesis," "genetics," "mutation," and "signaling pathway." These terms were combined with specific gene and pathway identifiers such as "FGFR2," "BRAF," "RAS," "KRAS," "NRAS," "HRAS," "MAPK," "mitogen-activated protein kinase," "SMO," "Smoothened," "sonic hedgehog," "SHH," "PTCH1," and "SUFU." Boolean operators (AND, OR) were used to construct a sensitive search string, for example: (ameloblastoma OR "odontogenic tumor") AND (FGFR2 OR BRAF OR RAS OR MAPK OR SMO OR "sonic hedgehog") AND (mutation OR pathogenesis OR genetics).

Inclusion criteria for articles were: (1) original research studies, including but not limited to whole-exome sequencing, targeted next-generation sequencing, Sanger sequencing, and immunohistochemical analyses, that investigated the molecular landscape of ameloblastoma; (2) review articles that provided a comprehensive synthesis of the molecular pathogenesis of ameloblastoma; and (3) studies that explored the functional consequences of identified mutations in in vitro or in vivo models. Exclusion criteria were: (1) case reports with no novel molecular data; (2) studies focused exclusively on clinical or radiological features without a molecular component; (3) abstracts, conference proceedings, and non-peer-reviewed literature; and (4) articles not available in English.

The initial search yielded a substantial number of records. Following the removal of duplicates, titles and abstracts were screened for relevance based on the inclusion and exclusion criteria. Articles deemed potentially relevant were then subjected to a full-text review. To ensure a comprehensive capture of the literature, the reference lists of all included full-text articles and key reviews were also manually screened (a "snowballing" technique) to identify any additional pertinent studies missed by the initial database search. This process was iterative, with new search terms and potential key papers identified as the review of the literature progressed.

Data from the selected articles were extracted and organized into a structured database for thematic synthesis. The extracted information included: author names, publication year, study design (e.g., genomic study, functional study, review), the specific genes or pathways analyzed, the types of mutations identified (e.g., point mutations, fusions), the frequency of these mutations within the studied cohorts, and any reported correlations with clinical or pathological features. Special attention was paid to studies that provided evidence for the central role of MAPK pathway dysregulation, particularly the discovery of recurrent mutations in FGFR2, BRAF, and RAS genes. The specific mutational hotspots, such as BRAF V600E and FGFR2 fusions, were cataloged along with their reported prevalence.

A key focus of the data extraction and synthesis was the literature addressing the role of the SHH pathway, specifically mutations in SMO. We systematically identified and evaluated studies that reported SMO mutations in ameloblastoma. The data were analyzed to understand the controversy mentioned in the abstract, namely whether SMO mutations represent an alternative, primary pathogenetic driver or are secondary, subclonal events. We compared the reported frequencies of SMO mutations across different studies and examined the evidence for or against their role as a primary driver versus a secondary event. Studies that performed mutational analysis on different tumor regions or compared primary tumors with recurrences or metastases were given particular attention to address the question of clonality.

The synthesis of findings was conducted qualitatively, as a meta-analysis was not appropriate due to the anticipated heterogeneity in study designs, sequencing methodologies, and patient cohorts. The evidence was organized thematically to reflect the major discoveries in the field. The first theme centered on the overwhelming evidence for MAPK pathway activation, detailing the discovery of BRAF, FGFR2, and RAS mutations and their mutual exclusivity in a large majority of cases. The second theme focused on the more complex and controversial role of the SHH pathway, specifically SMO mutations, summarizing the conflicting evidence and potential explanations for the observed discrepancies. A third theme explored the diagnostic implications, such as the potential for using BRAF V600E immunohistochemistry as a diagnostic adjunct. Finally, the therapeutic implications were synthesized, focusing on the rationale for targeting the MAPK pathway with existing small molecule inhibitors (e.g., BRAF and MEK inhibitors) and the potential for future therapies targeting other identified alterations. This thematic approach allowed for a coherent narrative that integrates the disparate findings into a unified understanding of ameloblastoma pathogenesis, highlighting both the established driver pathways and the areas of ongoing investigation and controversy. The quality of the included studies was assessed implicitly through the critical evaluation of their methodologies and the consistency of their findings with the broader literature, rather than through a formal scoring system, to maintain the narrative focus of this review.

Recent molecular studies have substantially clarified the genetic landscape of ameloblastoma. Across multiple cohorts, activating mutations in components of the MAPK pathway were identified in the majority of tumors. BRAF V600E was the most frequent alteration, detected in approximately 60–80% of conventional ameloblastomas, with a striking predilection for mandibular tumors and a lower frequency in maxillary lesions. In mandibular ameloblastomas, BRAF V600E was found in both solid/multicystic and unicystic variants, although the frequency varied by subtype and age. Mutations in RAS family genes, including KRAS, NRAS, and HRAS, occurred in roughly 10–20% of cases and were generally mutually exclusive with BRAF V600E. FGFR2 mutations, such as S252W and other activating changes, were less common but also converged on MAPK signaling. Together, these findings established that dysregulated MAPK pathway activity, most often through BRAF V600E, is a central pathogenetic event in ameloblastoma.

The role of sonic hedgehog pathway mutations, particularly SMO, has been more controversial. Early studies reported SMO mutations in 10–39% of ameloblastomas, with some series suggesting they were mutually exclusive with BRAF mutations and might define an alternative pathogenetic subset. SMO mutations such as L412F, R625G, and W535L were initially proposed to activate hedgehog signaling independently of MAPK. However, subsequent larger and more detailed analyses found SMO mutations at lower frequencies, often in BRAF wild-type tumors, and some studies identified concurrent BRAF and SMO alterations, raising the possibility that SMO mutations are secondary events or passengers. The controversy may partly reflect differences in tumor subtype, anatomic site, and detection methods. Nevertheless, SMO-mutant ameloblastomas do appear to constitute a distinct minority, and hedgehog pathway activation may cooperate with or substitute for MAPK activation in a subset of cases.

Additional molecular alterations have been described. Mutations in CTNNB1, encoding beta-catenin, have been identified in a small proportion of ameloblastomas, particularly in unicystic and peripheral variants, implicating Wnt signaling. Copy number alterations and chromosome abnormalities are common but not specific. Gene expression profiling has shown upregulation of MAPK target genes and, in some cases, hedgehog target genes, consistent with the mutational findings. Epigenetic changes, including promoter methylation of tumor suppressor genes, have also been reported, although their pathogenic significance remains uncertain. Importantly, the mutational spectrum of ameloblastoma differs from that of other odontogenic tumors such as ameloblastic carcinoma, which may acquire additional TP53 and CDKN2A alterations. These observations support a model in which ameloblastoma is driven primarily by MAPK pathway activation, with SHH, Wnt, and other pathways contributing in subsets.

From a diagnostic perspective, the high frequency of BRAF V600E has been translated into ancillary tests. Immunohistochemistry with the VE1 antibody shows high sensitivity and specificity for BRAF V600E-mutant ameloblastoma and can be useful in small biopsies or when distinguishing ameloblastoma from mimics such as odontogenic keratocyst, dentigerous cyst, and ameloblastic fibroma.
