Our findings fundamentally challenge the long-held assumption that voltage-gated sodium channel (Nav) α-subunits function as independent monomers [1,2]. The evidence presented here demonstrates that Nav α-subunits not only physically associate but assemble, function, and gate as dimers. This observation reconciles a growing body of literature that has been difficult to explain within a strict monomeric framework, including reports of cooperative gating, dominant-negative effects of mutant subunits, and unexpected pharmacological modulation [3-5]. Unlike voltage-gated potassium channels, whose pore-forming α-subunits assemble as tetramers [6], Nav α-subunits contain four homologous domains (DI–DIV) within a single polypeptide and were therefore widely regarded as complete functional units. Our data indicate that this pseudotetrameric architecture represents only one level of organization: two Nav α-subunits associate to form a dimeric channel complex. Such an arrangement creates a higher-order gating machine in which conformational transitions in one α-subunit can influence those in its partner, thereby expanding the regulatory repertoire of sodium channels beyond that predicted by a monomeric model.

The identification of the dimerization region provides a molecular basis for this assembly. Although the precise structural details remain to be resolved at atomic resolution, the mapped interface offers a starting point for understanding how Nav α-subunits recognize and stabilize one another. It is likely that this region operates in concert with auxiliary β-subunits, which are known to modulate trafficking, gating, and cell-surface expression [7]. However, the present work suggests that α–α interactions are not merely incidental but are central to channel function. This raises the possibility that dimerization occurs early in the secretory pathway and influences subsequent processing, membrane targeting, and stability. Future structural studies, including cryo-electron microscopy and single-molecule imaging, will be required to determine whether the dimer is obligate or dynamic, whether it adopts a symmetric or asymmetric configuration, and how the interface rearranges during activation and inactivation.

A particularly important finding is that 14-3-3 protein mediates the coupled gating of Nav dimers. 14-3-3 proteins are dimeric phosphoserine/phosphothreonine-binding scaffolds that regulate numerous signaling proteins [8]. Their involvement suggests that coupled gating is not a fixed property but a phosphorylation-dependent and potentially reversible process. This has broad implications for excitable tissues, where kinase and phosphatase activity constantly tune sodium channel behavior. Coupled gating may contribute to use-dependent modulation, action potential broadening, and arrhythmogenesis under conditions of altered phosphorylation. It may also explain why mutations distant from the pore can produce pronounced gain- or loss-of-function phenotypes: by disrupting the dimer interface or the 14-3-3 interaction, such mutations could uncouple gating between subunits and destabilize the channel complex.

The conservation of this mechanism among mammalian sodium channels is striking. Despite substantial divergence in their cytoplasmic domains and tissue-specific expression patterns, Nav1.1–Nav1.9 appear to retain the capacity for dimerization and coupled gating. This suggests that dimeric assembly is an ancient and fundamental feature of the Nav channel family rather than an isoform-specific peculiarity. The finding has direct relevance to sodium channelopathies, which include epilepsies, cardiac arrhythmias, skeletal muscle disorders, and chronic pain syndromes [9,10]. In a dimeric context, a mutant α-subunit may exert dominant-negative or dominant-positive effects on its partner, thereby modifying disease severity, penetrance, and response to therapy. This could help explain the clinical heterogeneity often observed among patients carrying identical Nav mutations. Moreover, the dimer interface and the 14-3-3 binding site represent previously unrecognized therapeutic targets. Small molecules or peptides that stabilize or disrupt these interactions could modulate sodium channel gating in a manner distinct from classical pore blockers or state-dependent antagonists.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. The present study establishes dimerization and coupled gating across multiple experimental systems, but the stoichiometry of native channels in intact tissues remains to be definitively established. It will be important to determine whether dimerization is influenced by β-subunits, alternative splicing, post-translational modifications, or disease-associated mutations. In addition, the relative contribution of 14-3-3 isoforms and the identity of the kinases and phosphatases that regulate the interaction require further investigation. It also remains possible that some Nav complexes exist in higher-order assemblies or in dynamic equilibrium between monomeric and dimeric states. Addressing these questions will require complementary structural, biochemical, and electrophysiological approaches, ideally in native excitable cells.

In conclusion, this study shifts the conventional paradigm of sodium channel assembly, structure, and function. Nav α-subunits physically interact, assemble as dimers, and gate in a coupled manner, with 14-3-3 protein serving as a key mediator of biophysical coupling. This mechanism is conserved among mammalian sodium channels and provides a new conceptual framework for understanding sodium channel physiology and pathophysiology. The discovery of the dimerization interface and the 14-3-3–dependent coupling mechanism opens the door to new approaches and targets for treating or preventing sodium channelopathies. Future work aimed at resolving the dimeric structure, defining its regulation in vivo, and developing modulators of α–α coupling may yield novel therapeutic strategies for epilepsy, cardiac arrhythmia, pain, and other excitability disorders.

Professional values constitute the normative foundation of nursing practice, shaping how nurses interpret ethical obligations, make clinical decisions, and interact with patients, families, and interdisciplinary teams [1,2]. In contemporary healthcare systems, nurses are expected not only to possess technical competence but also to demonstrate moral agency, accountability, and advocacy in complex and often resource-constrained environments [3]. Professional values have been conceptualized as enduring beliefs about what is worthwhile and desirable in the profession, guiding conduct and providing criteria for evaluating practice [4]. Within nursing, these values are commonly articulated through codes of ethics, professional standards, and socialization processes that transmit the profession’s collective identity from one generation of practitioners to the next [5,6]. The International Council of Nurses and national nursing organizations emphasize values such as respect for human dignity, patient autonomy, confidentiality, privacy, social justice, and professional integrity [7]. When these values are internalized and enacted, they support safe, high-quality, person-centered care; when they are neglected or compromised, ethical distress, moral injury, and diminished care quality may ensue [8,9].

The measurement of professional values has received considerable attention in nursing research. The Nursing Professional Values Scale-Revised, developed by Weis and Schank, is among the most widely used instruments for assessing nurses’ valuation of professional standards [10]. The scale operationalizes values across domains including caring, activism, professionalism, trust, and justice. Studies using this and related tools have reported variation in how nurses prioritize different values. Values associated with direct patient care, such as maintaining confidentiality and safeguarding privacy, are often rated highly, whereas values linked to broader professional responsibilities, such as participation in research, engagement with professional associations, and influencing health policy, may receive lower priority [11,12]. Such discrepancies are consequential because the profession’s capacity to advance evidence-based practice, shape healthcare policy, and address structural determinants of health depends on nurses’ commitment to these less immediate but systemically important values [13].

Multiple factors influence nurses’ professional values. Demographic and professional characteristics, including age, educational preparation, years of clinical experience, specialty area, and prior ethics training, have been associated with differences in value orientation [14,15]. Organizational context also matters: supportive ethical climates, visible nursing leadership, shared governance, and opportunities for continuing education can reinforce professional values, whereas heavy workloads, staff shortages, hierarchical decision-making, and limited autonomy can constrain their expression [16,17]. In addition, cultural, religious, and legal contexts shape how values are understood and prioritized. For example, confidentiality and privacy may be interpreted through both professional codes and local norms concerning family involvement, gender, and disclosure [18]. Therefore, assessing professional values from the perspective of clinical nurses is essential for designing context-sensitive ethics education, improving practice environments, and aligning institutional policies with the profession’s moral commitments [19].

In Iran, nursing has undergone significant educational and professional development, yet clinical nurses continue to face persistent challenges, including workforce shortages, high patient acuity, administrative burdens, and limited participation in policy-making [20,21]. Iranian hospitals affiliated with medical universities serve as major centers for clinical education, research, and service delivery, and the values held by nurses in these settings influence both student socialization and patient outcomes [22]. Although professional values are embedded in Iranian nursing curricula and regulated through national ethical guidelines, empirical evidence regarding how clinical nurses prioritize these values remains limited and somewhat fragmented [23]. Much of the existing literature has been conducted in Western contexts, where professional socialization, regulatory frameworks, and cultural expectations may differ substantially from those in Iran [24]. Consequently, there is a need for studies that examine professional values among Iranian clinical nurses using validated instruments and that consider local organizational and cultural realities.

Understanding the importance that clinical nurses assign to professional values is not merely an academic exercise. It has direct implications for clinical decision-making, patient advocacy, confidentiality protection, informed consent, end-of-life care, and equitable resource allocation [25]. It also informs the development of continuing education programs, ethics consultation services, and policies that support moral agency. Moreover, identifying values that are perceived as less important can help educators and managers target curricular and organizational interventions. Given the evolving ethical landscape of healthcare, including technological advances, patient rights movements, and increasing public expectations for accountability, a current assessment of professional values is timely [26]. The present study therefore aimed to investigate the importance of professional values from the perspective of clinical nurses in four educational hospitals affiliated with Kerman University of Medical Sciences, Iran. By examining nurses’ valuations of professional values and their relationship with selected demographic and professional characteristics, the study seeks to provide evidence that can guide ethics education, nursing management, and future instrument development for evaluating values in practice.

This cross-sectional, descriptive-analytical study was conducted in 2016 among clinical nurses employed in four educational hospitals affiliated with Kerman University of Medical Sciences, Iran. The study aimed to determine the importance of professional values from the perspective of clinical nurses. The design and reporting of the study were guided by the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) recommendations for cross-sectional studies [1].

**Study Setting and Participants**

The study was conducted in four teaching hospitals that provide secondary and tertiary care services in Kerman, Iran. The target population comprised all registered nurses who were directly involved in clinical patient care at the time of data collection. Eligible participants were required to be registered nurses, have at least six months of clinical work experience, be currently employed in a clinical ward, and provide written informed consent to participate. Nurses working exclusively in managerial, supervisory, or non-clinical administrative positions, those on prolonged leave, and those who returned incomplete questionnaires were excluded. The sample consisted of 250 clinical nurses. Sample size was determined based on Cochran’s formula for cross-sectional studies, assuming a 95% confidence level, a 5% margin of error, and an anticipated proportion of 0.5 for the main outcome, while accounting for potential non-response [2].

**Sampling Procedure**

A stratified random sampling method was used. The four participating hospitals were treated as primary strata. Within each hospital, clinical wards were considered secondary strata, including medical, surgical, intensive care, pediatric, obstetric, and emergency units. The number of nurses allocated to each stratum was proportional to the total number of eligible nurses in that stratum. Within each ward, participants were selected using a computer-generated random number table from the list of employed nurses. This approach was intended to ensure representativeness across hospitals and clinical specialties and to reduce selection bias [3].

**Instrument**

Data were collected using the Persian version of the Nursing Professional Values Scale-Revised (NPVS-R), originally developed by Weis and Schank [4]. The NPVS-R is a 26-item instrument designed to measure nurses’ perceptions of the importance of professional values. Each item is rated on a five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (“not important”) to 5 (“very important”). The total score ranges from 26 to 130, with higher scores indicating greater perceived importance of professional values. The original instrument includes five dimensions: caring, activism, trust, professionalism, and justice [4]. The Persian version of the NPVS-R has been previously translated and validated, with acceptable content validity, face validity, and internal consistency [5]. In the present study, the internal consistency of the total scale was assessed using Cronbach’s alpha, which was 0.89, indicating good reliability. In addition to the NPVS-R, a researcher-developed demographic and professional characteristics questionnaire was used to collect data on age, sex, marital status, educational level, work experience, clinical ward, hospital, and participation in professional ethics training courses.

**Data Collection Procedure**

Following approval from the Ethics Committee of Kerman University of Medical Sciences and obtaining official permissions from the administrators of the participating hospitals, the researcher approached eligible nurses in their clinical wards. The purpose of the study was explained, and nurses who agreed to participate received the questionnaire package. Participants were assured that participation was voluntary and that their responses would remain anonymous and confidential. The self-administered questionnaires were completed in a quiet setting during non-urgent working hours or outside working hours, according to the participants’ preference. The average completion time was 20 to 30 minutes. Completed questionnaires were returned in sealed, unmarked envelopes to protect confidentiality. To minimize missing data, the researcher checked returned questionnaires for completeness and, where necessary, invited participants to complete missing items. No identifying information was recorded on the questionnaires.

**Ethical Considerations**

The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Kerman University of Medical Sciences (approval number: [insert code]). All participants provided written informed consent before data collection. They were informed of the study objectives, the voluntary nature of participation, and their right to withdraw at any stage without any consequence. Confidentiality and anonymity were maintained throughout data handling and analysis. All data were stored in a locked cabinet and on a password-protected computer accessible only to the research team.

**Data Analysis**

Data were analyzed using SPSS version 22 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA) [6]. Descriptive statistics, including means, standard deviations, frequencies, and percentages, were used to summarize demographic characteristics and NPVS-R scores. The Kolmogorov–Smirnov test was used to assess the normality of continuous variables. Independent-samples t-tests and one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) were used to compare NPVS-R mean scores across dichotomous and categorical variables, respectively. Pearson correlation coefficients were calculated to examine relationships between NPVS-R scores and continuous variables such as age and work experience. Multiple linear regression analysis was performed to identify variables independently associated with professional values scores. Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05. Missing data were handled using listwise deletion, as the proportion of missing responses was low.

Sample characteristics. Of the 270 questionnaires distributed, 250 were returned with complete data, yielding an analyzable response rate of 92.6%. The mean age of participants was 34.2 ± 7.8 years (range 22–56 years), and the mean length of clinical work experience was 9.6 ± 6.9 years. The majority were female (82.4%), married (63.2%), and held a Bachelor of Science in Nursing (88.0%); the remaining 12.0% held a Master of Science in Nursing. Participants were distributed across four educational hospitals (31.2%, 26.4%, 23.6%, and 18.8%, respectively). Most respondents were staff nurses (78.4%), followed by head nurses (12.8%) and supervisors (8.8%). Rotating shift work was reported by 61.6% of nurses

The present findings indicate that clinical nurses in the studied hospitals generally attach high importance to professional values, a result consistent with international evidence suggesting that nurses across diverse health systems regard ethical principles as central to their professional identity [1,2]. This overall endorsement is encouraging, because professional values shape moral reasoning, clinical decision-making, and the quality of patient-centred care [3]. Nevertheless, the item-level variability observed in this study is more instructive than the composite score alone. The relatively greater importance assigned to maintaining patient confidentiality and safeguarding privacy reflects foundational deontological commitments and aligns with the ethical mandates embedded in nursing codes and regulatory frameworks [4]. In the Iranian context, these values may also be reinforced by cultural and religious emphases on dignity, modesty, and trust, which can intensify nurses’ sensitivity to privacy-related obligations [5]. Conversely, the lower ranking of recognising professional nursing associations in shaping healthcare policy and participating in nursing research or implementing research findings suggests a narrower, predominantly bedside-oriented conceptualisation of professional values. This pattern has been reported elsewhere and may reflect heavy clinical workloads, limited research capacity, hierarchical organisational cultures, and the historically physician-dominated nature of health policy in some settings [6,7]. When nurses do not view policy engagement and research utilisation as core professional values, the profession risks remaining excluded from decisions that directly affect practice environments and patient outcomes [8].

The statistically significant associations between professional values and age, work experience, and participation in professional ethical training merit careful interpretation. Greater age and clinical experience may facilitate professional socialisation, ethical sensitivity, and the accumulation of tacit moral knowledge through repeated exposure to complex care situations [9]. Similarly, ethics training can enhance moral agency, reflective capacity, and value internalisation, enabling nurses to move from rule-following to ethically engaged practice [10]. However, because the design was cross-sectional, causality cannot be established. It is equally plausible that nurses with stronger pre-existing professional values are more likely to seek ethics training, or that generational and educational differences confound the observed relationships. Longitudinal and intervention studies are therefore needed to determine whether targeted ethics education produces durable changes in value orientation and, ultimately, in clinical behaviour.

Several implications follow from these findings. First, undergraduate and continuing nursing curricula should explicitly address the full spectrum of professional values rather than emphasising only direct patient-care duties. Case-based ethics discussions, reflective journals, simulation, and role-modelling by senior nurses can help students and clinicians integrate confidentiality, privacy, advocacy, research utilisation, and policy participation into a coherent professional identity [11]. Second, healthcare organisations should create ethical climates that support nurses in enacting these values. This includes visible leadership commitment to ethical practice, access to ethics consultation, protected time for research and evidence-based practice activities, and recognition of nurses’ contributions to policy committees [12]. Third, nursing associations and regulatory bodies should strengthen their visibility and influence, and schools of nursing should foster student membership and mentorship in professional organisations. Without such structural support, calls for greater policy engagement may remain rhetorical [13].

The study also highlights a measurement gap. The Nursing Professional Values Scale-Revised assesses the perceived importance of values, not their enactment in everyday practice [1]. A nurse may rate a value highly while being unable to implement it because of resource constraints, organisational pressure, or interpersonal conflict. Future research should therefore adopt mixed methods designs to capture both the priority assigned to values and the contextual factors that facilitate or impede their translation into action. Qualitative interviews, observations, and participatory instrument development could produce culturally grounded tools that evaluate value-based practice rather than value endorsement alone [14]. Such tools would be valuable for evaluating educational interventions and for identifying organisational barriers to ethical care.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. The cross-sectional, self-report design is vulnerable to social desirability bias, and the sample was drawn from four educational hospitals affiliated with one medical university, which may limit generalisability to other regions, private hospitals, or community settings. The Persian version of the NPVS-R, although validated, may not capture all culturally specific professional values. Additionally, the study did not measure patient outcomes or actual ethical behaviour, so the clinical significance of the reported value priorities remains inferential. Despite these limitations, the findings provide a useful foundation for targeted educational and organisational interventions.

In conclusion, although nurses in this study valued professional values highly overall, the relative neglect of professional associations and research participation reveals important gaps in the profession’s ethical and political formation. Addressing these gaps requires coordinated action across education, practice, management, and policy. By strengthening ethics training, fostering research capacity, supporting professional associations, and developing context-sensitive instruments that assess the use of values in practice, nursing can better meet emerging ethical challenges and sustain safe, high-quality, patient-centred care.

The transition from marine to freshwater habitats requires profound adjustments in ion and water balance. In teleost fishes, the gill, intestine, kidney, and integument collectively regulate hydromineral homeostasis across salinities ranging from ion-poor fresh water to hypersaline marine environments [1,2]. At the cellular level, mitochondrion-rich ionocytes in the gill epithelium orchestrate ion transport through apical channels and basolateral transporters, with Na+/K+-ATPase (NKA) providing the electrochemical gradient that drives Na+ and Cl− movement [3,4]. In freshwater, fish face passive ion loss and water influx; they compensate by active ion uptake and dilute urine production. In seawater, they experience osmotic water loss and ion gain; they drink, absorb ions intestinally, and secrete excess ions across the gill [2,5]. The capacity to remodel these mechanisms, either reversibly through acclimation or heritably through adaptation, determines the success of habitat shifts.

Diadromous and amphidromous life cycles expose fishes to multiple osmotic environments, but also provide routes for colonization of fresh waters. When migratory connections are severed, landlocked populations can arise and persist entirely in freshwater. Such populations offer natural experiments for testing how osmoregulatory systems diverge following geographic isolation, reduced gene flow, and novel selective regimes [6,7]. Because landlocked lineages often originate from small founder groups, they may experience reduced genetic diversity, drift, and strong selection on physiological traits. The resulting divergence can involve not only salinity tolerance breadth but also the underlying molecular machinery, including ATPase enzymes, ionocyte composition, and intestinal transport [8,9].

Galaxias maculatus (Jenyns, 1848) is a small amphidromous osmeriform fish widely distributed across southern South America, Australia, New Zealand, and associated islands [10,11]. In coastal rivers and estuaries, adults spawn in habitats influenced by tides, and larvae spend an early marine phase before recruiting back to fresh water. This life history is thought to facilitate dispersal and gene flow among catchments. Nevertheless, numerous landlocked populations have been reported, particularly in lakes of the Andean region formed or exposed during deglaciation [12,13]. These populations complete their life cycle entirely in freshwater and are often morphologically and ecologically distinct from diadromous conspecifics. The degree to which such shifts are accompanied by changes in osmoregulatory performance, and whether those changes reflect plasticity or evolved divergence, remains poorly resolved for G. maculatus.

From a phylogeographic perspective, landlocked populations provide an opportunity to infer the timing and direction of colonization. Mitochondrial DNA sequences are particularly useful for reconstructing maternal lineages, detecting founder events, and estimating genetic differentiation between migratory and resident stocks [14,15]. **Study populations and sampling.** Adult *Galaxias maculatus* were collected from two contrasting habitats in southern South America: a landlocked population from a postglacial Andean lake and an amphidromous population from a nearby coastal river–estuary system. The lake population has been isolated since the last deglaciation, whereas the riverine population maintains a migratory life cycle between freshwater and estuarine environments [1,2]. Fish were captured using baited minnow traps and seine nets during austral spring and summer. Immediately after capture, a subset of individuals was euthanized with an overdose of MS-222 (250 mg L⁻¹), and fin clips were preserved in 95% ethanol for molecular analyses. Live fish destined for physiological experiments were transported in aerated, temperature-controlled containers to the laboratory within 6 h. Sampling was conducted under institutional ethical approval and national collection permits.

**Mitochondrial DNA amplification and sequencing.** Total genomic DNA was extracted from fin tissue using a standard salting-out protocol or silica-membrane spin columns following the manufacturer’s instructions. A 650-bp fragment of the mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) control region was amplified by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) using published primers [3]. Each 25-µL reaction contained 1× PCR buffer, 2.5 mM MgCl₂, 0.2 mM each dNTP, 0.4 µM each primer, 1 U *Taq* DNA polymerase, and approximately 50 ng template DNA. Thermal cycling consisted of an initial denaturation at 94 °C for 3 min, followed by 35 cycles of 94 °C for 30 s, 55 °C for 30 s, and 72 °C for 45 s, with a final extension at 72 °C for 5 min. PCR products were visualized on 1.5% agarose gels, purified with exonuclease I and shrimp alkaline phosphatase, and sequenced in both directions using BigDye Terminator v3.1 chemistry on an ABI 3730xl automated sequencer. Chromatograms were edited manually and aligned using ClustalW implemented in MEGA [4]. Unique haplotypes were identified and deposited in GenBank.

**Population genetic analyses.** Standard diversity indices, including the average number of nucleotide differences (Π) and haplotype diversity (H), were calculated in DnaSP v5 [5]. Pairwise genetic differentiation between populations was estimated using GST and NST with Arlequin v3.5 [6]. Statistical significance was assessed with 10,000 permutations, and sequential Bonferroni correction was applied where appropriate. Haplotype genealogy was reconstructed using a median-joining network in Network v4.6 [7], with positions weighted according to the number of mutations. Mismatch distributions and neutrality tests (Tajima’s D and Fu’s Fs) were used to infer demographic expansion following founder events. The landlocked population was tested for signatures of a recent bottleneck and subsequent expansion from the amphidromous stock.

**Acclimation and salinity challenge.** Fish were held in recirculating aquaria at 15 ppt salinity, 18 ± 1 °C, and a 12 h light:12 h dark photoperiod for 14 days before experimentation. They were fed commercial pellets daily, and water quality (ammonia, nitrite, pH, and dissolved oxygen) was monitored every 48 h. After acclimation, fish were subjected to a progressive salinity change of 5 ppt every 12 h until reaching target salinities of 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, or 30 ppt. Fish were then maintained at the target salinity for 8 days. Each population–salinity combination was tested in three replicate tanks, with 10 fish per tank. Survival was recorded every 12 h, and dead individuals were removed immediately. Water temperature, pH, and salinity were measured daily using calibrated meters.

### Genetic diversity and historical demography
A total of 1,142 bp of mitochondrial DNA, comprising partial cytochrome *b* and the control region, was resolved for 182 individuals: 94 from the landlocked lake population and 88 from the diadromous estuarine-river population. Across all samples, 31 haplotypes were identified. The diadromous population retained substantially higher genetic diversity than the landlocked population, with haplotype diversity (*H*) of 0.91 ± 0.02 versus 0.48 ± 0.06 and nucleotide diversity (π) of 0.0048 ± 0.0004 versus 0.0007 ± 0.0001, respectively. The average number of nucleotide differences was also greater in the diadromous population (5.42 ± 2.61) than in the landlocked population (0.81 ± 0.62). These differences were statistically significant (Mann–Whitney *U* test, *P* < 0.001), indicating a pronounced reduction in genetic variability following colonization of the lake.

Population differentiation was marked. Pairwise *G*ST was 0.31, whereas *N*ST was 0.54; the significantly greater value of *N*ST relative to *G*ST (*P* = 0.018) indicated that differentiation was not solely due to haplotype frequency differences but also reflected genealogical separation among haplotypes [1]. AMOVA attributed 43.6% of the total molecular variance to among-population divergence (ΦST = 0.436, *P* < 0.001). ### Discussion

The results of this study provide a compelling case of rapid, isolation-driven adaptive divergence in the osmoregulatory physiology of *Galaxias maculatus*. The integration of genetic and physiological data allows for a nuanced interpretation of the colonization event and its consequences, highlighting a striking shift in environmental tolerance over a geologically brief period.

#### Genetic Signature of a Recent Colonization

The genetic data are consistent with a scenario of recent colonization of the Andean lake by a small propagule from the diadromous stock. The significantly lower genetic diversity (Π and H) and the evidence of a recent founder effect in the landlocked population are characteristic signatures of a population bottleneck followed by expansion [1, 2]. The statistically significant pairwise GST and NST values confirm that the two populations are now genetically distinct, likely due to a combination of founder effects and subsequent genetic drift in the isolated lake environment [3]. The genealogy of haplotypes, evidencing an expansion process from the diadromous stock, further supports a model where a few individuals successfully established a new, self-sustaining population after the last deglaciation [4]. This genetic isolation is the foundational event upon which the observed physiological divergence was built.

#### Divergence in Osmoregulatory Capacity and Tolerance

The most striking finding is the landlocked population's surprisingly wider tolerance to salinity. Its 100% survival across a broad range of hypoosmotic conditions (0 to 20 ppt), in contrast to the diadromous population's narrow tolerance (10 to 15 ppt), represents a fundamental shift in osmoregulatory strategy. This divergence is particularly noteworthy given the short evolutionary timescale of a few thousand years [5]. The diadromous life cycle of *G. maculatus* necessitates a high degree of euryhalinity to migrate between freshwater rivers and the marine environment [6]. However, our common-garden acclimation experiment reveals that this plasticity is not sufficient to cope with the extreme and stable freshwater conditions of the lake. The landlocked population has apparently evolved a more robust hyper-osmoregulatory capacity, allowing it to maintain homeostasis in ion-poor waters.

#### Mechanistic Insights and Unresolved Questions

The analysis of ATPase activities in gills and intestine provides a partial, but incomplete, view of the underlying mechanisms. The detection of differences in ATPase activity at the lowest salinities confirms that the divergence has a cellular and biochemical basis. The differential activity of Na+/K+-ATPase (NKA) and H+-ATPase (HA) between populations suggests a remodeling of the ion-transporting machinery in key osmoregulatory tissues [7]. For instance, a shift towards greater reliance on HA and other ATPases could reflect an adaptation for active ion uptake in extremely dilute media, a common strategy in stenohaline freshwater fish [8].

However, a critical discrepancy emerges: population differences in mortality are not directly reflected in the measured enzyme activity. This decoupling suggests that survival in near-distilled water is not solely a function of the maximum transport capacity of these two key enzymes. Other factors are likely at play. These could include: (i) differences in the regulation of paracellular permeability in the gill epithelium to limit passive ion loss [9]; (ii) modifications in the expression or function of other ion transporters and channels (e.g., Na+/Cl- cotransporters, aquaporins); (iii) divergence in hormonal control pathways (e.g., cortisol, prolactin, growth hormone) that orchestrate the osmoregulatory response [10]; or (iv) differences in cellular stress responses and metabolic reorganization. The activity differences in "ATPases other than NKA and HA" hint at this broader physiological remodeling, which warrants further investigation using transcriptomic or proteomic approaches.

### Conclusion

This study demonstrates that the isolation of a diadromous fish population in a novel freshwater habitat can drive the rapid evolution of a fundamentally different osmoregulatory phenotype. The landlocked *G. maculatus* population has not merely acclimated to its new environment but has adapted, evolving a significantly enhanced tolerance to ion-poor water. This divergence occurred on a timescale of just a few thousand years, underscoring the potent evolutionary pressure exerted by a shift in habitat and life cycle. The adaptive changes appear to involve a complex reorganization of the osmoregulatory system that extends beyond simple changes in the activity of key ATPases. These findings contribute significantly to our understanding of the mechanisms of rapid adaptation and speciation in freshwater ecosystems. Future research should aim to unravel the full suite of molecular and physiological changes that confer this remarkable tolerance, providing deeper insight into the genetic and regulatory basis of osmoregulatory evolution.

The persistent global burden of cancer necessitates the continuous discovery and development of novel therapeutic agents. Despite significant advancements in oncology, challenges such as drug resistance, severe side effects, and the limited efficacy of current treatments against certain cancer types underscore the urgent need for new chemical scaffolds with unique mechanisms of action. For decades, natural products have served as an invaluable source of inspiration for drug discovery, contributing to a vast array of clinically used antitumor agents. A significant portion of these compounds originates from microorganisms, which possess an extraordinary metabolic diversity capable of producing complex bioactive molecules. However, the traditional reservoirs for microbial natural product discovery, such as terrestrial soils, have been extensively mined, leading to a high rate of rediscovery of known compounds. This has prompted a global search for novel microbial resources in underexplored and extreme environments, which are often hotspots for unique biodiversity and, consequently, novel biochemistry.

Among these extreme environments, the Antarctic stands out as a potentially important and largely untapped library of microbial resources and new bioactive substances. This vast, isolated continent and its surrounding Southern Ocean are characterized by a combination of extreme conditions, including persistently low temperatures, high salinity, intense ultraviolet radiation, and prolonged periods of darkness. Microorganisms that have successfully adapted to these harsh conditions, particularly those inhabiting the marine environment, have evolved unique physiological and metabolic strategies for survival. These adaptations often involve the production of secondary metabolites with unprecedented chemical structures and potent biological activities, making Antarctic marine microorganisms a promising frontier for bioprospecting. The unique evolutionary pressures of this environment increase the probability of discovering novel compounds with pharmaceutical potential, including new antibiotics, antioxidants, and anticancer agents.

Marine bacteria, in particular, have emerged as prolific producers of secondary metabolites. Within this group, the genus *Bacillus* is well-known for its ability to synthesize a wide spectrum of bioactive compounds, such as lipopeptides, polyketides, and peptides, many of which exhibit significant antimicrobial, antiviral, and cytotoxic properties. The isolation and characterization of novel *Bacillus* strains from unique environments like the Antarctic could therefore yield new and effective antitumor lead compounds. To efficiently identify these valuable resources, robust and reliable screening methodologies are essential. The 3-(4,5-dimethyl-2-thiazolyl)-2,5-diphenyl-2H-tetrazolium bromide (MTT) assay is a widely adopted, colorimetric method for assessing cell viability and proliferation. Its application as a cytotoxicity-tracking method allows for the rapid and high-throughput screening of microbial extracts or fermented products to identify those with potent inhibitory effects on cancer cell lines, thereby streamlining the discovery pipeline for antitumor lead compounds.

The objective of this study was to discover novel antitumor lead compounds from Antarctic marine microorganisms. To achieve this, we isolated a diverse collection of microorganisms from surface water samples collected at different sites in the Antarctic. We then employed an MTT assay-based cytotoxicity-tracking method to screen these isolates for their ability to produce metabolites with cytotoxic activity against a panel of human cancer cell lines. This screening effort led to the identification of 129 Antarctic microorganism strains, of which twelve displayed potent cytotoxic activities. Among these promising candidates, a Gram-negative, rod-shaped bacterium, designated as N11-8, was selected for further in-depth investigation. Phylogenetic analysis based on its 16S rRNA gene sequence revealed that this strain belongs to the genus *Bacillus*. We focused on characterizing the fermented active products from this Antarctic marine *Bacillus* sp. N11-8, evaluating their inhibitory effects on various cancer cell lines, including BEL-7402 human hepatocellular carcinoma cells, U251 human glioma cells, RKO human colon carcinoma cells, A549 human lung carcinoma cells, and MCF-7 human breast carcinoma cells. Crucially, we also assessed their cytotoxicity against HFL1 human normal fibroblast lung cells to determine their selectivity and safety profile. Furthermore, we investigated the stability of these active products under different pH and temperature conditions to evaluate their potential for development. This paper details the isolation, screening, and characterization of these cytotoxic metabolites, highlighting the potential of Antarctic marine microorganisms, and specifically *Bacillus* sp. N11-8, as a promising source for the discovery of novel antitumor bioactive substances for the prevention and treatment of cancer.

Surface water samples were collected aseptically from different sites in the Antarctic, including coastal and open-water stations. At each site, surface water was obtained from the upper 1 m using sterile polycarbonate bottles. Samples were transported under cold conditions and processed as soon as possible after arrival. For microbial isolation, aliquots of each water sample were serially diluted in sterile aged seawater and spread onto marine agar 2216 and seawater-based oligotrophic agar plates. Plates were incubated at 4, 10, 15, and 20°C for 7–30 days to allow growth of psychrophilic, psychrotolerant, and mesophilic microorganisms. Colonies with distinct morphological characteristics were picked and purified by repeated streaking on fresh marine agar. Purified strains were maintained on marine agar slants at 4°C and in glycerol stocks at −80°C. A total of 129 Antarctic microorganism strains were isolated and catalogued.

Primary screening for cytotoxic activity was performed using an MTT assay-based cytotoxicity-tracking method. Each isolate was inoculated into 50 mL marine broth in 250 mL Erlenmeyer flasks and incubated at 15°C with shaking at 150 rpm for 5–7 days. Culture broths were centrifuged at 10,000 × g for 20 min at 4°C, and supernatants were filtered through 0.22 µm sterile filters. The human hepatocellular carcinoma cell line BEL-7402 was used as the initial screening model. Cells were seeded in 96-well plates at a density of 5 × 10³ cells per well in RPMI-1640 medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum, 100 U/mL penicillin, and 100 µg/mL streptomycin, and incubated at 37°C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO₂. After 24 h, cells were treated with culture supernatants or serial dilutions thereof. After 48 h, 20 µL MTT solution (5 mg/mL in phosphate-buffered saline) was added to each well, and plates were incubated for an additional 4 h. Formazan crystals were dissolved in dimethyl sulfoxide, and absorbance was measured at 570 nm using a microplate reader. Inhibition rates were calculated relative to untreated controls. Strains showing potent cytotoxic activity were selected for further study, and among them, the isolate designated N11-8 was chosen for detailed characterization.
