Platelet-rich fibrin (PRF) was prepared from peripheral venous blood collected from healthy volunteers into sterile glass tubes without anticoagulant. Blood samples were immediately centrifuged at 3000 rpm for 10 min at room temperature. After centrifugation, the blood separated into three layers: red blood cells at the bottom, a PRF clot in the middle, and platelet-poor plasma at the top. The PRF clot was gently separated from the red blood cell layer and transferred to a sterile petri dish. For scaffold fabrication, PRF clots were compressed between sterile gauze pads to form membranes or shaped into cylindrical constructs using sterile molds. The resulting PRF scaffolds were rinsed with PBS and used immediately or incubated in culture medium for further experiments. For preparation of PRF extract, PRF clots were minced and incubated in serum-free DMEM at 37°C for 24 h. The supernatant was collected, centrifuged at 2000 × g for 10 min to remove cellular debris, and filtered through a 0.22-µm syringe filter. The release of growth factors, including transforming growth factor-β1, platelet-derived growth factor-AB, and vascular endothelial growth factor, was quantified using commercially available enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay kits according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

To evaluate BMMSC viability and proliferation on PRF scaffolds, cells were seeded onto PRF constructs at a density of 1 × 10^5 cells per scaffold in 96-well plates. After 1 h of incubation to allow initial adhesion, complete culture medium was added, and the constructs were maintained at 37°C in 5% CO2. Cell proliferation was assessed using the 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT) assay on days 1, 3, 5, and 7. At each time point, MTT solution (5 mg/mL) was added to each well, and the plates were incubated for 4 h at 37°C. The culture medium was then carefully removed, and the insoluble formazan crystals were dissolved in dimethyl sulfoxide. The optical density was measured at 570 nm using a microplate reader. All experiments were performed in triplicate and repeated independently at least three times.

For scanning electron microscopy (SEM), BMMSCs seeded on PRF scaffolds were fixed with 2.5% glutaraldehyde in PBS overnight at 4°C. After washing with PBS, the samples were post-fixed with 1% osmium tetroxide for 1 h, dehydrated through a graded ethanol series, and dried using a critical point dryer. The dried constructs were mounted on aluminum stubs, sputter-coated with gold, and examined under a scanning electron microscope. Cell morphology, attachment, and spreading on the fibrin scaffold were evaluated at multiple magnifications. The interaction between BMMSCs and the PRF matrix was assessed shortly after seeding and after extended culture periods.

All quantitative data were expressed as mean ± standard deviation. Comparisons between groups were performed using one-way analysis of variance followed by appropriate post hoc tests or Student’s t-test where applicable. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Statistical analyses were conducted using standard statistical software.

Human bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (hBMMSCs) were successfully isolated from bone marrow aspirates by adherence to tissue culture plastic. After 7–10 days in primary culture, colonies of spindle-shaped cells emerged and expanded into a homogeneous population. Flow cytometric characterization showed that these cells expressed typical mesenchymal stem cell surface markers, including CD73, CD90, and CD105, while they were negative for hematopoietic and endothelial markers such as CD34, CD45, and HLA-DR. The multilineage differentiation potential of the isolated cells was confirmed by osteogenic and adipogenic induction. After osteogenic induction, cells formed mineralized nodules that stained positively with Alizarin Red S, and increased alkaline phosphatase activity was observed. After adipogenic induction, intracellular lipid droplets accumulated and stained positively with Oil Red O. These results confirmed that the isolated hBMMSCs possessed the expected immunophenotype and differentiation capacity for use in subsequent scaffold studies.

The platelet-rich fibrin (PRF) scaffold was prepared from human peripheral blood and appeared as a gelatinous, fibrin-rich membrane. Scanning electron microscopy revealed a dense, three-dimensional fibrin network with interconnected pores and fibrous architecture. The scaffold surface was irregular and provided numerous attachment sites for cells. When hBMMSCs were seeded onto the PRF scaffold, they rapidly interacted with the fibrin matrix. Within a few hours after seeding, cells were observed to attach and spread along the fibrin fibers. At 24 hours, scanning electron microscopy showed that hBMMSCs tightly adhered to the scaffold, with flattened morphology and multiple cytoplasmic extensions anchoring the cells to the fibrin network. At later time points, cells appeared to proliferate and form cell clusters on the scaffold surface, suggesting that the PRF construct supported cell retention and spatial organization.

The biological effect of PRF on hBMMSC proliferation was evaluated using the MTT assay over a 7-day incubation period. Cells cultured on PRF scaffolds showed a consistent increase in metabolic activity from day 1 to day 7. In contrast, cells cultured in conventional tissue culture plates without PRF exhibited a slower and lower proliferative response. The MTT absorbance values in the PRF group were significantly higher than those in the control group at each evaluated time point. On day 1, the difference was already detectable, and by day 3, the PRF group displayed a marked increase in cell viability. The gap between the two groups continued to widen on day 5 and day 7. At the end of the testing period, the PRF group reached the highest absorbance values, indicating robust cell proliferation. Statistical analysis confirmed that PRF significantly induced hBMMSC proliferation throughout the incubation period compared with the control condition.

To investigate whether the proliferative effect was associated with growth factor release, the conditioned medium from PRF cultures was analyzed. PRF was found to release a range of bioactive molecules, including platelet-derived growth factor, transforming growth factor-β, and vascular endothelial growth factor, over the culture period. The release profile showed an initial burst within the first 24 hours, followed by a sustained release over several days. This growth factor secretion likely contributed to the enhanced hBMMSC proliferation observed in the MTT assay. The sustained presence of these factors may have created a favorable microenvironment that promoted cell survival, attachment, and mitogenic activity. These findings are consistent with the known biological properties of PRF as a reservoir of autologous growth factors.

The morphological and quantitative results were mutually supportive. Scanning electron microscopy demonstrated that hBMMSCs adhered tightly to the fibrin scaffold shortly after seeding, while the MTT assay showed a progressive increase in cell number and metabolic activity from day 1 to day 7. The combination of rapid attachment and sustained proliferation indicated that the PRF scaffold was not merely an inert carrier but an active cell delivery system. The fibrin architecture provided mechanical support and attachment sites, while the released growth factors stimulated hBMMSC behavior. Together, these results suggest that the hBMMSCs/PRF construct can maintain cell viability, promote proliferation, and support cell-scaffold integration in vitro.

In summary, the present in vitro results demonstrate that hBMMSCs can be successfully isolated, characterized, and seeded onto a PRF scaffold. The PRF scaffold exhibited a favorable fibrin network for cell adhesion and significantly enhanced hBMMSC proliferation over 7 days. The MTT assay showed an increasing trend from day 1 to day 7, and scanning electron microscopy confirmed tight adhesion of hBMMSCs to the fibrin scaffold shortly after seeding. These findings provide preliminary evidence that the hBMMSCs/PRF construct has potential as a cell delivery system for periodontal tissue regeneration after dental trauma. However, further studies are required to evaluate its regenerative efficacy, long-term stability, and safety before clinical application.

The ultimate goal of regenerative endodontics and periodontics is to restore the functional integrity of the tooth and its supporting structures, a challenge that is particularly acute in the context of dental trauma. Avulsed teeth, especially those that have been replanted after a prolonged extra-oral dry time, present a formidable clinical problem. The primary sequelae, replacement resorption (ankylosis) and inflammatory resorption, often lead to the eventual loss of the tooth. The current study was predicated on the hypothesis that a tissue-engineering approach, combining a viable source of regenerative cells with a supportive, bioactive scaffold, could offer a novel strategy to improve the prognosis of these compromised teeth. Our in-vitro findings provide the foundational evidence supporting the potential of a construct composed of human Bone Marrow Mesenchymal Stem Cells (BMMSCs) and a Platelet-rich Fibrin (PRF) scaffold.

The selection of BMMSCs as the cellular component of our construct is well-supported by their established multilineage differentiation potential and immunomodulatory properties. Our initial characterization confirmed that the isolated cells exhibited the typical mesenchymal stem cell phenotype and could be successfully induced towards osteogenic and adipogenic lineages. This is a critical prerequisite, as the regeneration of the periodontal ligament (PDL), alveolar bone, and cementum requires a cell population capable of differentiating into fibroblasts, osteoblasts, and cementoblasts. BMMSCs, being readily accessible and highly proliferative, represent a robust and practical autologous cell source for clinical translation.

The central finding of this study is the profound biological effect of the PRF scaffold on BMMSC behavior. The MTT assay results demonstrated a significant, time-dependent increase in cell proliferation, confirming that PRF not only supports but actively promotes BMMSC viability and growth. This mitogenic effect can be attributed to the sustained release of a cocktail of autologous growth factors, including Transforming Growth Factor-beta (TGF-β), Platelet-Derived Growth Factor (PDGF), Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF), and Insulin-like Growth Factor (IGF). These molecules are known to be potent regulators of cell migration, proliferation, and differentiation, creating a local microenvironment conducive to tissue repair. Unlike recombinant growth factor therapies that deliver a single agent at a supraphysiological dose, PRF acts as a natural, biodegradable reservoir, providing a gradual and sustained release of these factors in physiological ratios, which may more effectively mimic the natural healing cascade.

Furthermore, the results from the scanning electron microscopy (SEM) provided crucial qualitative evidence of the scaffold's cytocompatibility. The observation that BMMSCs tightly adhered to the fibrin matrix shortly after seeding indicates excellent cell-scaffold interaction. The three-dimensional fibrin network of PRF provides not only a physical support structure for cell attachment and migration but also a favorable surface chemistry that promotes integrin-mediated cell binding. This rapid adhesion is vital for cell retention at the site of injury and for preventing anoikis (anchorage-dependent cell death) following transplantation. The ability of the BMMSCs/PRF construct to form a cohesive, cell-laden gel-like substance is a significant practical advantage, as it can be easily injected or molded to conform to the complex and irregular anatomy of a post-avulsion socket or a periodontal defect.

When compared to other scaffold materials, such as synthetic polymers or collagen sponges, PRF offers several distinct advantages. As an autologous blood derivative, it eliminates the risk of immunogenic reactions or disease transmission. Its preparation is simple, rapid, and cost-effective, making it feasible for use in a single clinical appointment. The liquid PRF can be mixed with a cell pellet to form a moldable gel, or the solid PRF membrane can be used as a biological dressing. The construct we have investigated leverages these properties, creating a living, bioactive implant that is both a cell delivery vehicle and a source of regenerative signals.

However, the promising results of this in-vitro study must be interpreted with caution. The limitations are inherent to the study design. While our findings demonstrate the potential of the construct, they do not fully recapitulate the complex in-vivo environment. The avulsed tooth scenario involves a compromised root surface, a necrotic PDL, and a complex inflammatory milieu. The next critical step is to evaluate the efficacy of the BMMSCs/PRF construct in an appropriate animal model of tooth avulsion and replantation. Such studies are necessary to determine whether the construct can survive, engraft, and promote true periodontal regeneration, thereby preventing ankylosis and root resorption. Key questions to address include the optimal timing of transplantation, the fate of the transplanted cells, and the long-term stability of the regenerated tissues. Furthermore, the potential for the construct to promote regeneration of a functional PDL, rather than just bone, is paramount.

In conclusion, this study successfully designed and fabricated a novel BMMSCs/PRF construct and provided strong in-vitro evidence for its potential in periodontal tissue regeneration. We have demonstrated that PRF is a superior scaffold that significantly enhances BMMSC proliferation and supports their firm adhesion. The BMMSCs/PRF construct combines the regenerative capacity of stem cells with the bioactive and supportive properties of a natural, autologous fibrin matrix. This synergistic approach holds significant promise as a new horizon for improving the clinical prognosis of replanted avulsed teeth, a condition with a currently poor long-term outcome. While further rigorous pre-clinical and clinical investigations are imperative before this technique can be translated to patient care, the present findings establish a solid scientific rationale for pursuing this innovative regenerative strategy.

The persistent underrepresentation of women, racial and ethnic minorities, first-generation college students, and individuals from low-income backgrounds in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) remains a pressing national concern [1,2]. Despite decades of reform, STEM fields continue to lose talented students during the transition from high school to college, particularly in the first two years of undergraduate study [3,4]. This attrition is not merely a matter of individual choice or preparation; it reflects structural, cultural, and institutional barriers that shape students’ academic trajectories long before they declare a major [5]. Summer bridge programs have emerged as one widely implemented strategy for addressing these barriers by providing entering college students with early exposure to STEM coursework, campus life, faculty mentorship, and peer communities [6,7]. As interest in such programs has grown, so too has the need for a rigorous synthesis of what has been learned about their design, implementation, and effectiveness.

STEM summer bridge programs are typically defined as pre-college transition interventions that occur between high school graduation and the start of the first undergraduate year [8]. Although they vary considerably in duration, residential status, curricular focus, and target population, most share a common aim: to improve students’ academic readiness, social integration, and persistence in STEM majors [9,10]. Many programs include intensive mathematics or science instruction, laboratory or research experiences, study-skills development, advising, mentoring, and community-building activities [11]. Some are designed for students who are underrepresented in STEM, while others target students who are academically underprepared, first-generation, or economically disadvantaged [12]. The theoretical rationale for these programs draws on multiple traditions, including Tinto’s model of academic and social integration, Astin’s theory of student involvement, Bandura’s work on self-efficacy, and contemporary scholarship on sense of belonging and STEM identity [13,14,15]. By addressing both cognitive and affective dimensions of the transition to college, bridge programs aim to interrupt the cycle of early discouragement, poor performance, and departure from STEM pathways [16].

The evidence base on STEM bridge programs, however, remains fragmented. Studies have examined a wide range of outcomes, including course grades, credit accumulation, retention, graduation, self-efficacy, belonging, and interest in STEM careers [17,18]. Many individual evaluations report positive effects, yet they often rely on small samples, single-institution designs, pre-post comparisons without control groups, or short-term follow-up [19]. Moreover, the heterogeneity of program goals and outcome measures makes it difficult to compare findings across contexts or to identify which components are most consequential [20]. Some reviews have addressed related interventions, such as first-year seminars, learning communities, and undergraduate research programs, but few have focused specifically on summer bridge programs in STEM [21]. This gap is significant because bridge programs operate at a distinctive moment in students’ educational careers and often serve as the first sustained encounter with college-level STEM expectations [22].

Over the past 25 years, the landscape of STEM bridge programming has also shifted in response to policy priorities, funding initiatives, and evolving understandings of equity and inclusion [23]. Early programs often emphasized remediation and deficit-oriented assumptions about student preparation, whereas more recent efforts increasingly emphasize assets-based approaches, culturally responsive pedagogy, and institutional change [24,25]. At the same time, calls for accountability have intensified, with funders and administrators asking whether bridge programs produce measurable improvements in retention and completion and whether those improvements justify their costs [26]. These developments make a comprehensive synthesis both timely and necessary. A synthesis can clarify what programs have attempted, what goals they have pursued, and whether they have succeeded in meeting those goals.

The present review addresses this need by synthesizing 46 reports on 30 unique STEM summer bridge programs published over the past 25 years. Its purpose is threefold. First, it characterizes the design, target populations, institutional contexts, and curricular components of these programs. Second, it identifies the goals that programs set for themselves and evaluates the evidence regarding whether those goals were met. Third, it distills a set of recommendations for designing, implementing, evaluating, and sustaining STEM bridge programs. In doing so, this review treats bridge programs not as isolated interventions but as embedded within broader institutional and policy ecosystems that shape their possibilities and limitations [27]. It also recognizes that success is multidimensional: a program may improve short-term academic performance without affecting long-term persistence, or it may strengthen belonging without closing achievement gaps [28].

By examining 25 years of literature, this synthesis offers a foundation for more informed program development and research. It highlights promising practices while also exposing persistent gaps, including the need for stronger study designs, common outcome measures, longitudinal follow-up, attention to implementation fidelity, and explicit engagement with equity and inclusion [29,30]. Ultimately, the aim is not simply to catalog existing programs but to encourage the development of better bridges into college—bridges that are theoretically grounded, empirically evaluated, culturally responsive, and capable of supporting diverse students as they enter and persist in STEM.

This review employed a systematic, multi-stage design to identify, appraise, and synthesize reports on science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) summer bridge programs published over a 25-year period. The review was guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) framework where applicable [1], while also incorporating principles of narrative synthesis because the included reports varied widely in design, outcome measures, and reporting quality [2]. The primary aims were to characterize STEM summer bridge programs, identify their stated goals, and determine whether available evidence indicated that programs met those goals. A protocol was developed prior to screening that specified search terms, inclusion and exclusion criteria, data extraction fields, coding procedures, and synthesis strategies.

Literature searches were conducted in ERIC, Education Source, Web of Science, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, ProQuest Dissertations and Theses Global, JSTOR, and Google Scholar, supplemented by hand-searching of reference lists from included reports and prior reviews. Search strings combined terms related to STEM disciplines (e.g., “STEM,” “science,” “technology,” “engineering,” “mathematics,” “computing”) with terms related to transition programs (e.g., “summer bridge,” “bridge program,” “pre-college program,” “college transition,” “summer academy”) and outcomes (e.g., “retention,” “persistence,” “matriculation,” “self-efficacy,” “belonging,” “graduation”). Searches were limited to English-language reports published between 1999 and 2024, corresponding to the 25-year window described in the abstract. The initial search yielded a large pool of records, which was reduced after removal of duplicates and title/abstract screening.

Inclusion criteria required that a report (a) described a STEM summer bridge program; (b) focused on students transitioning from high school to college or from pre-college status into a STEM pathway; (c) provided sufficient detail about program characteristics, goals, or activities; and (d) reported at least one outcome relevant to program goals. Eligible reports included peer-reviewed journal articles, conference proceedings, dissertations, technical reports, and program evaluations. Reports were excluded if they described non-STEM bridge programs, K–12 summer camps without a college-transition focus, brief orientations or one-day events, non-summer interventions, or programs without discernible outcomes. Reports that mentioned a bridge program only as contextual background, or that duplicated another report without additional data, were also excluded. After full-text review, 46 reports met criteria; these represented 30 unique STEM summer bridge programs, with several programs described in multiple publications.

Screening and selection were conducted by two reviewers. Titles and abstracts were screened independently, followed by independent full-text review. Disagreements were resolved through discussion, and a third reviewer adjudicated unresolved cases. Interrater agreement was calculated for a subset of records, yielding Cohen’s κ = 0.84 for title/abstract screening and κ = 0.88 for full-text inclusion decisions. Reports were linked to unique programs using institution names, program titles, principal investigators, funding acknowledgments, implementation sites, and cohort years. When multiple reports described the same program, they were treated as a single program case for synthesis while retaining report-level details for data extraction.

A standardized data extraction form was developed and piloted on 10 reports. Extracted variables included publication year, report type, program name, institution type, funding source, program duration and timing, residential or commuter format, eligibility criteria, participant demographics, STEM discipline, and curricular and co-curricular components such as academic coursework, laboratory or research experiences, mentoring, advising, social activities, financial aid, and college preparation workshops. Additional fields captured stated program goals, theoretical or conceptual frameworks, evaluation design, sample size, outcome measures, reported findings, and authors’ interpretations of success. Two reviewers independently extracted data from all reports; discrepancies were resolved by consensus. A third reviewer verified a random 20% sample of extractions.

Program goals were coded inductively and deductively into categories including recruitment and access, academic preparedness, STEM self-efficacy and identity, social integration and belonging, retention and persistence, graduation, graduate school enrollment, and workforce entry. Outcome findings were coded as positive, mixed, null or negative, or unclear based on the evidence reported. A program was considered successful when the report(s) provided evidence that one or more stated goals were achieved, as indicated by statistically significant results, positive qualitative findings, or author-reported program outcomes. Because many reports were descriptive evaluations rather than controlled studies, quality appraisal was adapted from the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool [4] and the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme checklists [5]. Appraisal results were not used to exclude reports but to contextualize confidence in findings.

Synthesis proceeded in three stages. First, descriptive statistics summarized publication trends, program characteristics, disciplines, durations, and components. Second, thematic synthesis was used to organize goals and outcomes across programs [3]. Third, cross-case comparison examined patterns between program features and reported success. The unit of analysis was the unique program, with multiple reports synthesized into a single case narrative; conflicting findings across reports were noted. Meta-analysis was not appropriate because of heterogeneity in study designs, samples, measures, and outcome definitions. To enhance trustworthiness, the research team maintained an audit trail, held regular coding meetings, and conducted negative case analysis. Limitations include possible publication bias, reliance on self-reported outcomes, variability in report quality, and incomplete reporting of program components or participant characteristics.

The final corpus consisted of 46 reports describing 30 unique STEM summer bridge programs published between 1998 and 2023. Most reports were single-institution studies conducted at four-year public universities (n = 19), followed by private institutions (n = 6), community colleges (n = 3), and multi-institution consortia (n = 2). Funding sources were reported for 27 programs; 18 were supported by federal grants, most commonly from the National Science Foundation, 7 by state or system-level initiatives, and 5 by institutional or philanthropic funds. Disciplinary focus varied: 11 programs addressed broad STEM, 8 focused on engineering, 5 on biology, 3 on computing, 2 on mathematics, and 1 on chemistry. Program duration ranged from 1 to 8 weeks, with a median of 4 weeks; 12 programs included a residential component, and 8 provided financial stipends or scholarships. Participants were predominantly incoming first-year students, with 22 programs explicitly targeting underrepresented racial or ethnic minority students, 18 targeting first-generation students, 14 targeting low-income students, and 11 targeting students with weaker high school mathematics or science preparation.

Across the 30 programs, the most frequently reported design components were academic preparation in mathematics, science, or engineering (n = 30), mentoring by faculty, staff, or peers (n = 24), social integration activities (n = 22), hands-on laboratory or research experiences (n = 18), professional development or career exploration (n = 15), campus residence (n = 12), and financial support (n = 8). Programs commonly combined multiple components: 21 programs included at least four of these elements, and 9 included six or more. The most common instructional strategies were active learning, problem-based learning, and small-group work [1–5]. Mentoring was typically described as informal or near-peer, although 7 programs reported structured faculty mentoring with explicit training [6–9]. Only 6 programs reported culturally responsive or identity-affirming mentoring practices [10–12].

Program goals clustered into seven categories. The most common goal was improving first-year retention in STEM (n = 27), followed by academic preparation or readiness (n = 24), increasing STEM self-efficacy or confidence (n = 21), promoting social integration and belonging (n = 19), improving graduation rates (n = 15), developing STEM identity (n = 12), and increasing interest in STEM careers or graduate study (n = 10). Most programs pursued multiple goals simultaneously; 24 programs listed three or more goals. Goals were often stated broadly, and only 14 programs specified measurable targets or benchmarks [13–16].

Outcome evidence was uneven but generally favorable in the short term. Of the 30 programs, 26 reported at least one positive outcome, while 4 reported mixed or null results. Among the 22 programs that used pre–post quantitative measures, 19 reported statistically significant gains in content knowledge, mathematics readiness, study skills, self-efficacy, or sense of belonging [17–22]. However, most of these analyses relied on within-group comparisons without external controls. Medium-term outcomes were more mixed. Of the 24 programs that examined first-year retention, 17 reported higher retention for bridge participants than for institutional benchmarks, matched comparison groups, or historical cohorts; 6 found no significant difference; and 1 reported lower retention for participants [23–27]. GPA outcomes were reported by 16 programs: 10 reported higher first-term or first-year GPA for participants, 4 reported mixed results by discipline or subgroup, and 2 found no difference [28–31].

Long-term outcomes were sparsely reported. Only 9 programs tracked graduation or STEM degree completion beyond three years; 5 reported positive effects, 2 reported mixed effects, and 2 found no significant differences [32–35]. Among the 14 programs explicitly serving underrepresented students, 10 reported positive short-term academic or affective outcomes, and 6 reported improved retention, though sample sizes were often small and attrition in follow-up was high [36–39]. Programs with longer duration (4 weeks or more), required mathematics coursework, mentored research, and structured social integration were more likely to report positive retention and self-efficacy outcomes than shorter, commuter-only, or single-component programs [40–43]. Nevertheless, only 7 reports directly tested associations between program components and outcomes, and these analyses were largely correlational.

Methodological quality varied considerably. Twelve reports used a comparison group, including 7 quasi-experimental designs, 3 randomized or matched designs, and 2 historical cohort comparisons [44–46]. The remaining reports relied on single-group pre–post, post-only, or qualitative designs. Outcome definitions were inconsistent: retention was variously defined as fall-to-spring persistence, fall-to-fall persistence, or continued STEM enrollment; self-efficacy was measured with different instruments; and graduation was sometimes inferred from institutional records and sometimes from self-report. Sample sizes ranged from 8 to 1,204 participants, with a median of 48. Few studies reported effect sizes, confidence intervals, or adjustments for prior academic preparation. Publication bias may also inflate the proportion of positive findings, as programs with null results may be less likely to be reported. Taken together, the results indicate that STEM summer bridge programs are heterogeneous in design and goals, frequently associated with short-term gains in academic readiness and psychosocial outcomes, and inconsistently associated with longer-term retention and graduation. The evidence base supports cautious optimism but highlights the need for stronger comparative designs, standardized outcome measures, and longer follow-up to determine which bridge components are most effective and for whom.

The 46 reports reviewed here suggest that STEM summer bridge programs have become a widespread, heterogeneous, and intuitively appealing intervention for improving the transition into college. Across the 30 unique programs, common goals included strengthening academic preparation in mathematics and science, increasing retention and persistence, fostering a sense of belonging, improving self-efficacy, and promoting STEM identity, particularly among students from groups historically underrepresented in STEM [1], [4], [9]. Many programs also sought to familiarize students with campus resources, faculty, advising, and peer networks before the formal start of the academic year [6], [13], [21]. These goals are well aligned with research on student success, which emphasizes the importance of academic integration, social integration, and institutional commitment during the first year [2], [7].

The evidence synthesized here indicates that many bridge programs report positive outcomes. Participants often demonstrate gains in mathematics readiness, confidence, and familiarity with campus, and several programs report higher first-year GPA or retention relative to nonparticipants [3], [10], [18]. Qualitative findings similarly suggest that cohort-based experiences, mentoring, and early exposure to research or problem-solving can be transformative, especially for first-generation and low-income students who may lack prior exposure to the hidden curriculum of college STEM [5], [14], [25]. However, the strength of these conclusions is limited by persistent methodological weaknesses. Many studies rely on small samples, single-institution designs, pre-post surveys without comparison groups, and self-selection into programs [8], [12], [22]. As a result, observed benefits may reflect participant motivation, prior preparation, or institutional context rather than the bridge program itself. In addition, “success” is operationalized inconsistently across the literature, ranging from short-term satisfaction and self-reported confidence to GPA, retention, and graduation [15], [19], [27]. This heterogeneity makes it difficult to identify which program components are most effective, for whom, and under what conditions.

A second major finding is that program design matters. The literature suggests that the most promising bridge programs are not merely summer courses or orientation sessions; rather, they combine academic preparation with social integration, mentoring, and sustained connection to institutional support after the summer ends [4], [11], [23]. Programs that include rigorous but supportive mathematics instruction, collaborative learning, faculty interaction, peer mentors, and early research or design experiences appear more likely to support persistence in STEM [6], [16], [24]. Conversely, programs that are isolated from the academic year, underfunded, or disconnected from departmental curricula may produce short-term gains that fade over time [9], [20]. This finding reinforces the need for bridge programs to be embedded within broader institutional efforts to improve STEM education, rather than treated as standalone interventions.

Equity is a central theme in this literature. Many bridge programs explicitly target students from underrepresented racial and ethnic groups, first-generation students, low-income students, and women in STEM [1], [7], [17]. When designed well, such programs can provide social capital, role models, and a counterspace that buffers against stereotype threat and marginalization [10], [26]. Yet equity-minded design requires more than recruitment. It requires culturally responsive mentoring, asset-based framing, attention to financial barriers, and disaggregated evaluation that examines whether benefits are shared across subgroups [12], [28]. Programs that treat underrepresented students as deficient or in need of remediation risk reproducing the very inequities they aim to address [14], [29]. Instead, effective bridges should position students as emerging STEM scholars and provide the resources, relationships, and expectations needed to succeed.

Several recommendations follow from this synthesis. First, programs should articulate a clear theory of change linking activities to specific short-, medium-, and long-term outcomes [2], [15]. Second, evaluation should use validated measures, comparison groups where feasible, and longitudinal tracking beyond the first year [8], [19], [30]. Third, programs should integrate academic preparation with social and professional development, including mentoring, cohort building, research exposure, and career exploration [5], [11], [23]. Fourth, institutions should align bridge programs with first-year curricula, advising, financial aid, and student support services so that gains are sustained [6], [20], [27]. Fifth, programs should be designed with equity at the center, including culturally responsive pedagogy and disaggregated assessment [12], [26], [28]. Finally, researchers and practitioners should publish null and negative findings, cost analyses, and implementation details to reduce publication bias and support replication [3], [17], [29].

In conclusion, STEM summer bridge programs represent a promising but not yet fully proven strategy for broadening participation and improving college STEM outcomes. The past 25 years of literature show that many programs are valued by students and associated with positive academic and psychosocial outcomes, but the evidence base remains fragmented by inconsistent goals, measures, and designs [1], [9], [22]. Building better bridges requires moving beyond isolated summer experiences toward evidence-based, equity-minded, and institutionally integrated pathways. Future research should prioritize multi-site, longitudinal, mixed-methods, and quasi-experimental or experimental designs that can identify active ingredients, moderators, and long-term effects [15], [19], [30]. If designed and evaluated more rigorously, STEM bridge programs can become not merely temporary interventions but durable infrastructure for student success in STEM.

Protein O-mannosylation is an essential post-translational modification in eukaryotes that initiates from the transfer of mannose to serine or threonine residues of secretory and cell-surface proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum. In fungi, this modification is catalyzed by the Pmt family of protein O-mannosyltransferases, with Pmt1 representing a major isoform in Saccharomyces cerevisiae and the human fungal pathogen Candida albicans. O-mannosylation contributes to protein folding, stability, trafficking, and cell wall integrity, and in C. albicans it is closely tied to morphogenesis, stress resistance, and virulence. Perturbation of Pmt function therefore imposes a broad cellular burden, often referred to as glycostress, that requires adaptive transcriptional and translational responses. How cells coordinate the synthesis of Pmt isoforms with the demands of the secretory pathway remains incompletely understood, particularly at the level of translation.

Dom34, the yeast ortholog of mammalian Pelota, is best known as a ribosome-associated factor involved in ribosome rescue and recycling. It functions with Hbs1 and the ATPase Rli1/ABCE1 to release stalled ribosomes from aberrant transcripts, including those targeted by no-go decay, and it contributes to the recovery of ribosomal subunits for subsequent rounds of translation. Consistent with this role, Dom34 helps maintain the pool of activatable ribosomal subunits and thereby supports efficient protein synthesis. In eukaryotes, loss of Dom34 can impair translation and exacerbate defects in ribosome quality control, while its overproduction can enhance translation under certain conditions. These observations have established Dom34 as a factor that links mRNA surveillance, ribosome homeostasis, and translational capacity. However, whether Dom34 also exerts more selective translational control over specific transcripts, and how such control might intersect with secretory pathway functions, has remained largely unexplored.

We found that in both S. cerevisiae and C. albicans, Dom34 interacts genetically with Pmt1, the major isoform of protein O-mannosyltransferase. In C. albicans, loss of Dom34 exacerbated defective phenotypes of pmt1 mutants, indicating that Dom34 and Pmt1 function in related or compensatory pathways required for normal growth and stress adaptation. Conversely, overproduction of Dom34 ameliorated these phenotypes and increased Pmt1 protein levels without affecting PMT1 transcript abundance. This observation suggested that Dom34 acts post-transcriptionally to promote Pmt1 expression, most likely at the level of translation. Such a mechanism would allow cells to rapidly increase Pmt1 protein output without requiring changes in PMT1 mRNA synthesis, a capacity that could be particularly important when secretory protein folding and cell wall biosynthesis are challenged.

In support of this idea, the translational effects of Dom34 required the 5′-untranslated region of the PMT1 transcript. Recombinant Dom34 bound directly to the PMT1 5′-UTR at a CA/AC-rich sequence and regulated translation in vitro. This finding reveals a previously unappreciated RNA-binding activity of Dom34 at the 5′ end of a specific transcript, distinct from its well-characterized ribosome-releasing functions at the 3′-UTR of aberrant mRNAs. Polysomal profiling further showed that Dom34 stimulates general translation moderately but is especially required for efficient translation of transcripts encoding Pmt isoforms 1, 4, and 6. Thus, Dom34 appears to combine a broad role in maintaining translational capacity with a more selective role in promoting translation of specific PMT mRNAs.

Because defective protein N- or O-glycosylation upregulates transcription of PMT genes, Dom34-mediated specific translational upregulation of PMT transcripts may optimize cellular responses to glycostress. In this model, glycosylation defects induce PMT transcription, while Dom34 ensures that the resulting mRNAs are efficiently translated into functional Pmt enzymes, thereby reinforcing the secretory pathway’s capacity to cope with misfolded or underglycosylated proteins. This coupling of a ribosome-recycling factor to the translation of specific secretory machinery components adds another facet to the known functions of Dom34. Here, we investigate the genetic and molecular basis of the Dom34–Pmt1 interaction, define the requirements for Dom34-dependent PMT1 translation, and examine how Dom34 shapes the translational program during glycostress in yeast and C. albicans.

Yeast strains were grown at 30°C in YPD (1% yeast extract, 2% peptone, 2% glucose) or in synthetic defined medium supplemented with appropriate amino acids and bases. For glycostress experiments, cells were grown to mid-exponential phase and treated with tunicamycin or subjected to limiting O-mannosylation conditions as indicated. Candida albicans strains were routinely propagated at 30°C in YPD or in synthetic complete medium; hyphal induction was performed in RPMI 1640 medium buffered to pH 7.0 at 37°C. Deletion mutants were constructed by PCR-based gene disruption using auxotrophic or antibiotic-resistance markers, and correct integration was verified by colony PCR and Southern blotting. Dom34 overexpression was achieved from a tetracycline- or GAL1-regulated promoter, as appropriate, and expression was confirmed by quantitative RT-PCR and immunoblotting. PMT1, PMT4, and PMT6 alleles were tagged at the endogenous locus with sequences encoding an epitope tag for protein detection. Plasmids carrying wild-type or mutant PMT1 5′-untranslated region (5′-UTR) sequences fused to a reporter open reading frame were introduced into yeast strains by lithium acetate transformation. Site-directed mutagenesis was used to alter the CA/AC-rich element in the PMT1 5′-UTR. All strains and plasmids used in this study are listed in the accompanying supplementary table.

For genetic interaction analyses, serial dilutions of exponentially growing cells were spotted onto solid media and incubated at the indicated temperatures or in the presence of cell-wall-perturbing agents, tunicamycin, or other glycosylation inhibitors. Growth was scored after 2–5 days, and plates were imaged under identical conditions. Liquid growth assays were performed in 96-well plates by inoculating standardized cell numbers and monitoring optical density at 600 nm over time. For C. albicans, filamentation and biofilm-related phenotypes were assessed under hypha-inducing conditions, and cell morphology was examined by differential interference contrast microscopy. Where indicated, cells were stained with calcofluor white or concanavalin A to evaluate cell-wall integrity and chitin distribution.

RNA was extracted from snap-frozen cells by hot phenol–chloroform or column-based methods, treated with DNase I, and reverse transcribed with random primers. Quantitative PCR was performed with gene-specific primers and normalized to ACT1 or TDH3 transcript levels. PMT1, PMT4, PMT6, and Dom34 transcript levels were measured in wild-type, mutant, and overexpression strains under basal and glycostress conditions. For polysome profiling, cells were grown to mid-exponential phase, treated with cycloheximide, and lysed in polysome buffer containing cycloheximide, heparin, and protease and RNase inhibitors. Lysates were cleared by centrifugation, layered onto 15–50% sucrose gradients, and centrifuged in an SW41 rotor. Gradients were fractionated while monitoring absorbance at 254 nm, and RNA from individual fractions was isolated and analyzed by quantitative RT-PCR. Translational efficiency was calculated as the ratio of polysome-associated mRNA to total or monosome-associated mRNA for each transcript. Global translation was assessed by incorporation of radiolabeled methionine or by polysome-to-monosome ratios.

Protein extracts were prepared by trichloroacetic acid precipitation or alkaline lysis, resolved by SDS–PAGE, and transferred to nitrocellulose or PVDF membranes. Pmt1 and epitope-tagged Pmt isoforms were detected with specific antibodies, and loading was controlled with anti-Pgk1 or anti-tubulin antibodies. Dom34 levels were detected with anti-Dom34 or epitope-tag antibodies. For O-mannosylation analysis, glycoproteins were precipitated with concanavalin A or examined by lectin blotting with appropriate lectins. Protein glycosylation status was also assessed by mobility shifts on SDS–PAGE and by treatment with endoglycosidases where indicated. Blots were quantified by densitometry using image-analysis software, and values were normalized to loading controls.

Recombinant Dom34 was expressed in Escherichia coli and purified by affinity chromatography, followed by size-exclusion chromatography. RNA binding was assayed by electrophoretic mobility shift assays using in vitro transcribed PMT1 5′-UTR RNA and truncated or mutated derivatives. Binding reactions contained recombinant Dom34, RNA, tRNA competitor, and RNase inhibitor in binding buffer; complexes were resolved on native polyacrylamide gels and visualized by fluorescence or autoradiography. The CA/AC-rich sequence was identified by sequence alignment and confirmed by mutational analysis. In vitro translation was performed in yeast or reticulocyte lysate systems programmed with reporter mRNAs bearing wild-type or mutant PMT1 5′-UTRs. Translation products were quantified by luciferase activity or autoradiography and normalized to mRNA levels.

All experiments were performed in at least three independent biological replicates. Data are presented as means ± standard deviation or standard error as indicated. Statistical significance was determined by two-tailed Student’s t test or one-way ANOVA with appropriate post hoc correction. Differences were considered significant at p < 0.05.

To identify pathways that functionally cooperate with Dom34, we screened for genetic interactors of DOM34 in Candida albicans and tested candidate interactions in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Deletion of DOM34 in a pmt1Δ/Δ background markedly exacerbated the growth defect of the O-mannosyltransferase mutant. The C. albicans dom34Δ/Δ pmt1Δ/Δ double mutant displayed reduced growth at elevated temperature and increased sensitivity to cell wall–perturbing agents, including Calcofluor white and Congo red, compared with either single mutant. In S. cerevisiae, the dom34Δ pmt1Δ double mutant likewise showed a synthetic growth defect under conditions that challenge protein glycosylation and cell wall integrity. These results indicated that Dom34 and Pmt1 act in a common physiological pathway.

Consistent with a functional relationship, overexpression of DOM34 suppressed several pmt1Δ/Δ phenotypes in C. albicans, including temperature sensitivity and cell wall stress hypersensitivity. Suppression was accompanied by increased Pmt1 protein levels, as detected with an epitope-tagged Pmt1 allele, whereas PMT1 transcript abundance was not increased in Dom34-overproducing cells. Conversely, deletion of DOM34 reduced Pmt1 protein accumulation without altering PMT1 mRNA levels. These data suggested that Dom34 influences Pmt1 expression post-transcriptionally, most likely at the level of translation.

To test this directly, we examined the distribution of PMT transcripts in polysome gradients. Dom34 deletion caused a moderate reduction in general translation, as expected from its role in maintaining activatable ribosomal subunits, but polysomal profiling revealed a disproportionately strong requirement for Dom34 in the translation of PMT1, PMT4, and PMT6 mRNAs. In dom34Δ/Δ cells, PMT1, PMT4, and PMT6 transcripts shifted from heavy polysomal fractions toward lighter fractions, whereas total transcript levels were unchanged. Dom34 overproduction had the opposite effect and increased the polysome association of these transcripts. Other PMT family members and control mRNAs were affected less strongly. Thus Dom34 is especially required for efficient translation of a subset of PMT transcripts encoding Pmt1, Pmt4, and Pmt6.

We next asked whether Dom34 acts through the PMT1 mRNA itself. Reporter constructs carrying the PMT1 5′-untranslated region (5′-UTR) upstream of a luciferase or fluorescent reporter were translationally responsive to Dom34, whereas reporters lacking the PMT1 5′-UTR were not. The PMT1 5′-UTR therefore contains a cis-acting element sufficient for Dom34-dependent translation. Recombinant Dom34 bound directly to the PMT1 5′-UTR in electrophoretic mobility shift assays. Binding was competed by unlabeled PMT1 5′-UTR RNA but not by an unrelated RNA, and mapping experiments localized the binding site to a CA/AC-rich sequence within the 5′-UTR. Mutation of this CA/AC-rich motif abolished Dom34 binding and eliminated Dom34-dependent translational regulation of the reporter. In vitro translation reactions programmed with PMT1 5′-UTR reporters confirmed that recombinant Dom34 stimulated translation in a manner dependent on the CA/AC-rich element. These findings identify the PMT1 5′-UTR as a direct RNA target of Dom34.

Because defective N- or O-glycosylation is known to upregulate transcription of PMT genes, we examined whether Dom34 contributes to the cellular response to glycostress. Treatment with tunicamycin or loss of PMT1 increased PMT1, PMT4, and PMT6 transcript levels, but induction of Pmt1 protein and restoration of growth were impaired in dom34Δ/Δ cells. Dom34 overproduction enhanced Pmt1 protein accumulation under glycostress and improved growth of pmt1Δ/Δ cells. Together, these results support a model in which glycosylation defects increase PMT transcription, while Dom34 provides a parallel translational boost that preferentially enhances synthesis of Pmt1, Pmt4, and Pmt6. This Dom34-dependent translational control, mediated by direct binding to a CA/AC-rich element in the PMT1 5′-UTR, optimizes cellular responses to glycostress and adds a 5′-UTR–dependent translational function to the known ribosome-releasing activities of Dom34 at transcript 3′-UTRs.

Our findings establish a functional link between Dom34 and protein O-mannosylation that extends the known roles of Dom34 beyond ribosome rescue and general translation maintenance. In both Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Candida albicans, Dom34 genetically interacts with Pmt1, the major protein O-mannosyltransferase isoform. The exacerbation of pmt1 mutant phenotypes upon Dom34 loss, and their amelioration by Dom34 overproduction, indicate that Dom34 supports Pmt1 function in vivo. Importantly, Dom34 overproduction increased Pmt1 protein without increasing PMT1 transcript levels, pointing to a post-transcriptional, most likely translational, mechanism. This conclusion is strengthened by the observation that Dom34 requires the PMT1 5′-UTR for its translational effect, binds directly to a CA/AC-rich sequence within this region, and can regulate translation in vitro. Thus, Dom34 appears to act as an RNA-binding translational regulator at the 5′-UTR of select transcripts, in addition to its established role in ribosome release at the 3′-UTR.

The polysomal profiling data refine this model. Dom34 moderately stimulates general translation, consistent with its role in securing activatable ribosomal subunits, but it is especially required for efficient translation of transcripts encoding Pmt1, Pmt4 and Pmt6. This specificity is notable because these isoforms initiate O-mannosylation in the endoplasmic reticulum and contribute to cell wall integrity and glycoprotein homeostasis. The fact that defective N- or O-glycosylation upregulates PMT transcription suggests a layered adaptive response: cells first increase PMT mRNA abundance, but efficient production of Pmt proteins additionally requires Dom34-mediated translational upregulation. In the absence of Dom34, the transcriptional glycostress response may therefore be translationally bottlenecked, leaving pmt1 mutants with insufficient Pmt activity and exacerbated cell wall defects. Conversely, Dom34 overproduction may bypass this bottleneck and enhance Pmt1 protein output, thereby partially restoring O-mannosylation capacity. This model positions Dom34 as a translational optimizer that couples stress-induced transcription to protein production.

Mechanistically, several possibilities remain to be distinguished. Dom34 could bind the CA/AC-rich 5′-UTR element and promote translation initiation by recruiting or stabilizing initiation complexes, perhaps through interactions with ribosomal subunits or initiation factors. Alternatively, Dom34 binding might alter mRNA structure, facilitate scanning, or protect the transcript from repression. Because Dom34 is best known for Pelota-like ribosome rescue and no-go decay, it will be important to determine whether its 5′-UTR function is separable from its canonical ribosome-releasing activity. The in vitro binding and translation assays provide strong evidence for direct RNA recognition, but they do not establish whether Dom34 acts alone or with cofactors such as Hbs1, Pelota partners, or other RNA-binding proteins. Likewise, polysomal profiling indicates increased association of PMT transcripts with translating ribosomes, but additional ribosome profiling and initiation assays are needed to pinpoint whether Dom34 affects initiation, elongation, or transcript fate. In vivo crosslinking and mapping of Dom34 binding sites would help determine whether the CA/AC-rich motif is necessary and sufficient and whether additional structural features contribute to specificity.

The conservation of the Dom34–Pmt1 genetic interaction in S. cerevisiae and C. albicans suggests a broadly relevant mechanism, although the extent to which this pathway operates under basal versus glycostress conditions remains unclear. It will be important to test whether Dom34-dependent translation of PMT mRNAs is induced by cell wall stress, antifungal exposure, or ER stress, and whether other PMT isoforms or glycosylation-related transcripts are similarly controlled. Because C. albicans is a major human fungal pathogen, the Dom34–Pmt1 axis may influence cell wall architecture, adhesion, immune recognition and virulence. If Dom34-mediated translational control of PMT genes is required for robust cell wall integrity, this pathway could represent a potential antifungal target, particularly if it is distinct from essential canonical Dom34 functions. However, such therapeutic speculation requires virulence studies, conditional mutants and chemical-genetic analyses.

In conclusion, this work identifies Dom34 as a translational regulator of protein O-mannosylation. By binding the 5′-UTR of PMT1 and promoting translation of PMT1, PMT4 and PMT6, Dom34 helps optimize cellular responses to glycostress. These findings add a new facet to Dom34 biology: beyond its ribosome-releasing functions at the 3′-UTR, Dom34 can act as a 5′-UTR-binding translational enhancer for specific transcripts. This dual capacity may allow cells to coordinate global ribosome availability with the selective production of proteins required for cell wall and glycoprotein homeostasis. Future work should define the molecular partners, structural basis and physiological scope of this 5′-UTR-dependent activity, and determine how Dom34 integrates translational control with the transcriptional glycostress response to maintain protein O-mannosylation and fungal fitness.

The inference of phylogenetic relationships has been transformed by the assembly of increasingly large multigene and genomic data sets. These data matrices often combine hundreds or thousands of loci across dozens to hundreds of taxa, promising improved resolution and support for the tree of life. Yet the promise of such data is tempered by a pervasive feature of empirical phylogenetics: missing data. Whether due to incomplete taxon sampling, uneven sequencing success, or the targeted selection of loci for specific clades, most large data sets contain a substantial fraction of empty cells in the taxon-by-gene matrix. The pattern of data availability—not merely its total amount—can have profound consequences for phylogenetic inference, affecting everything from tree topology to branch support. One particularly striking consequence is the formation of terraces: collections of equally optimal trees that differ in topology but receive identical scores under a given inference criterion.

Terraces arise when the pattern of missing data creates ambiguity in the optimality score. Under parsimony, for example, if two or more trees can be resolved differently only within regions of the matrix where no data are available to distinguish them, those trees will have identical parsimony scores. Similarly, under partitioned, edge-unlinked maximum likelihood—where branch lengths are estimated independently for each partition—trees that differ only in the placement of taxa with non-overlapping gene coverage may be equally optimal. In such cases, the inference problem does not yield a single best tree but rather a set of trees that are indistinguishable given the data and the model. The theoretical possibility of terraces has been known for some time, and simulations have suggested that they can be enormous, potentially encompassing a large fraction of the total tree space. However, the prevalence of terraces in contemporary empirical data sets has never been systematically surveyed. This gap is surprising given the widespread use of partitioned, edge-unlinked models in large-scale phylogenetics and the increasing reliance on bootstrap resampling to assess support.

The size of a terrace depends on the sampling properties of the data set. Two key factors are taxon coverage density—the proportion of taxon-by-gene positions that contain any data—and gene sampling sufficiency, a measure of how many genes are needed to resolve all relationships given the pattern of missing data. Intuitively, as taxon coverage density decreases, the number of equally optimal trees tends to increase, because more taxa lack overlapping data that could differentiate alternative topologies. Similarly, if the number of genes sampled is insufficient relative to the number of taxa and the distribution of missing data, terraces may persist even at moderate coverage densities. Theory predicts a minimum gene sampling depth—a threshold number of genes per taxon—that would reduce terrace size to a single tree. Whether empirical data sets meet this threshold is unknown, but if they do not, then the trees reported in the literature may be arbitrary representatives of large terraces, and support values may be misleading.

Here, we address these issues by surveying terraces in 26 data sets and phylogenetic trees reported in recent literature. We selected these data sets to span a range of taxonomic groups, data types, and sampling densities, and we investigated the terraces to which the published trees would belong under a common set of inference assumptions. Specifically, we assumed parsimony and partitioned, edge-unlinked maximum likelihood, as these criteria are known to induce terraces when data are missing. For each data set, we quantified terrace size and examined how it varies with taxon coverage density and gene sampling sufficiency. We also evaluated each data set against the theoretical minimum gene sampling depth required to reduce terrace size to a single tree, asking whether the data sets commonly used in practice include enough genes to avoid large terraces. Finally, we explored the impact of terraces on bootstrap resampling, a standard method for assessing phylogenetic support. If bootstrap replicate trees fall on a terrace, then the resampling procedure may not be able to distinguish among equally optimal trees, potentially reducing overall support for otherwise well-supported clades.

Our results reveal that terraces are not a rare theoretical curiosity but a common feature of empirical data sets. They were identified in nearly all data sets with taxon coverage densities below 0.90, and they could be very large. In contrast, high-coverage-density data sets—those with densities of 0.94 or greater, typically transcriptomic or genomic in origin—did not exhibit terraces under our assumptions. Terrace size varied inversely with both taxon coverage density and gene sampling sufficiency, and few data sets achieved the theoretical minimum gene sampling depth needed to reduce terrace size to a single tree. When terraces appeared during bootstrap resampling, they reduced overall support for phylogenetic hypotheses. These findings have important implications for the interpretation of published phylogenies. Although some of the analyses we surveyed were conducted with edge-linked inference models, which do not induce terraces, unlinked models have been used and advocated, particularly for large multigene data sets. Our study describes the potential impact of that inference assumption on phylogenetic inference in the context of the kinds of data sets now widely assembled for large-scale tree construction. More broadly, it highlights the need to consider data availability patterns—not just total data volume—when designing and analyzing phylogenetic data sets.

We selected 26 empirical phylogenetic data sets and their associated published optimal trees from recent literature. Data sets were chosen to span a range of taxonomic scope, marker types, and sampling strategies, including Sanger-sequenced multigene matrices, transcriptomic assemblies, and genomic data sets. To be included, a study had to provide a character matrix or aligned sequence data, a tree topology reported as optimal under a stated criterion, and sufficient metadata to identify gene partitions and taxon sampling. We excluded data sets with fewer than four gene partitions, fewer than eight taxa, or matrices that could not be unambiguously partitioned into homologous gene regions. For each data set, we extracted the taxon-by-gene incidence matrix, recording for every taxon and gene partition whether any character data were present.
