We assembled 26 empirical data sets from recently published phylogenetic studies, spanning plants, animals, fungi, and microbes, with matrix sizes from 18 to 412 taxa and 3 to 1,102 gene partitions. Taxon coverage density, defined as the proportion of taxon-by-gene cells containing any data, ranged from 0.31 to 0.99. Gene sampling sufficiency, a measure of the number of genes sampled relative to the theoretical minimum needed to resolve all relationships under the observed missing-data pattern, ranged from 0.08 to 1.00. We evaluated each data set under a common set of inference assumptions: parsimony and partitioned, edge-unlinked maximum likelihood. Under these assumptions, terraces—collections of equally optimal trees—were identified in 19 of the 20 data sets with taxon coverage densities below 0.90. The single low-density exception had an unusually uniform gene-coverage pattern, with nearly every taxon sampled for the same subset of genes, which reduced the opportunity for terrace formation. No terraces were detected in the six data sets with taxon coverage densities of 0.94 or higher, all of which were transcriptomic or genomic data sets with dense taxon-by-gene sampling. No data set fell in the 0.90–0.93 coverage interval.

Terrace sizes were often large. Among the 19 affected data sets, the number of equally optimal trees per terrace ranged from 2 to approximately 1.1 × 10^6 under parsimony and from 2 to approximately 3.4 × 10^5 under partitioned, edge-unlinked maximum likelihood. The median terrace size was 144 trees under parsimony and 96 trees under maximum likelihood. The largest terraces occurred in data sets with taxon coverage densities between 0.35 and 0.55 and with many taxa represented by only one or two genes. In several cases, the terrace contained trees that differed only by rearrangements among taxa with non-overlapping gene coverage, while the well-sampled core topology remained constant. This pattern indicates that terraces were driven primarily by taxon-by-gene sampling gaps rather than by conflict among gene trees.

Terrace size varied inversely with taxon coverage density. Across all data sets, log10-transformed terrace size was negatively correlated with coverage density (Spearman’s ρ = −0.81, P < 0.001). Data sets with coverage densities below 0.70 typically had terraces containing more than 1,000 equally optimal trees, whereas those with densities above 0.85 had terraces of fewer than 50 trees. The relationship was nonlinear: terrace size increased sharply as coverage density fell below approximately 0.75. A similar negative relationship was found between terrace size and gene sampling sufficiency (ρ = −0.67, P < 0.001). Data sets with sufficiency values above 0.80 generally had small terraces or none, while those below 0.40 had consistently large terraces. These results suggest that both the breadth of taxon coverage and the depth of gene sampling jointly determine the extent of terrace ambiguity.

We next compared observed gene sampling to the theoretical minimum gene sampling depth required to reduce each terrace to a single tree under the same coverage pattern. Few data sets achieved this minimum. Only 4 of 26 data sets met or exceeded the theoretical minimum, and all four had taxon coverage densities of at least 0.94. Among the 19 terrace-bearing data sets, the median shortfall was 2.8-fold, meaning that roughly three times as many genes would have been needed to collapse the terrace to one tree. The shortfall ranged from 1.2-fold to 11.4-fold. In the most extreme case, a 96-taxon data set with 14 genes and a coverage density of 0.38 would have required at least 160 genes under the observed sampling pattern to eliminate the terrace. These results indicate that most contemporary multigene data sets, as sampled, are far from the theoretical threshold needed to guarantee a single optimal tree under edge-unlinked inference.

Terraces also affected bootstrap resampling. For the 19 data sets with terraces, we mapped bootstrap replicate trees onto the terraces of the original data set. In 14 data sets, at least one bootstrap replicate tree belonged to a terrace, and in 7 data sets more than 25% of replicate trees fell on a terrace. When replicate trees lay on a terrace, support for clades that were not shared by all terrace members was reduced. Across affected data sets, the mean bootstrap support for clades whose resolution varied within the terrace was 62%, compared with 81% for clades outside the terrace (paired difference = 19 percentage points; P < 0.001). In one data set, a clade that received 95% bootstrap support under an edge-linked analysis dropped to 54% under the edge-unlinked analysis because replicate trees were distributed among equally optimal terrace topologies. Thus, terraces encountered during bootstrap resampling can deflate support for otherwise well-supported phylogenetic hypotheses.

High-coverage transcriptomic and genomic data sets showed no terraces under the same inference assumptions, and their bootstrap support values were correspondingly stable. In contrast, the low- and moderate-coverage data sets that dominate many published multigene analyses frequently belonged to large terraces of equally optimal trees. The prevalence of terraces was closely tied to taxon coverage density and gene sampling sufficiency, and most data sets did not include enough genes to reduce terrace size to a single tree. These results demonstrate that terrace formation is not a rare theoretical curiosity but a common property of empirical phylogenetic data sets when edge-unlinked inference assumptions are applied.

The results of this survey demonstrate that terraces are not a theoretical curiosity but a common feature of contemporary multigene phylogenetic data sets when trees are inferred under parsimony or partitioned, edge-unlinked maximum likelihood. Nearly all data sets with taxon coverage densities below 0.90 contained terraces, whereas high-coverage transcriptomic and genomic data sets (≥0.94) did not. Terrace size varied inversely with taxon coverage density and gene sampling sufficiency, and few data sets achieved the theoretical minimum gene sampling depth required to reduce terrace size to a single tree. These patterns suggest that many published trees may represent one arbitrarily selected member of a potentially large collection of equally optimal trees. In such cases, the inferred topology is not uniquely determined by the data under the assumed model, even though the tree may be reported as a single best estimate.

The formation of terraces is closely tied to missing data and the way inference models treat branch lengths across partitions. When a taxon is absent from some genes, those genes provide no information about its placement relative to other taxa. Under edge-unlinked models, each partition has its own set of edge lengths, so alternative resolutions of poorly sampled taxa can achieve identical optimal scores. The resulting terrace can be large, and its members may differ in ways that are biologically meaningful. Edge-linked models, in which branch lengths are shared across partitions, impose additional constraints that can collapse terraces to a single tree. However, edge-linked models may be misspecified when rates of evolution vary substantially among genes, and unlinked models have been used and advocated precisely to accommodate such heterogeneity. Our findings highlight a tradeoff: the flexibility of edge-unlinked models can come at the cost of reduced topological identifiability.

Taxon coverage density and gene sampling sufficiency emerge as useful predictors of terrace size. Data sets with denser taxon-by-gene matrices and more genes per taxon are less likely to contain large terraces. Yet many empirical data sets, including those assembled for large-scale tree construction, remain sparse because of incomplete sequencing, missing taxa in individual loci, or deliberate sampling strategies. The theoretical minimum gene sampling depth needed to reduce terrace size to one tree was rarely achieved in the surveyed data sets. This implies that simply adding more taxa or genes may not eliminate terraces unless sampling is sufficiently complete across the matrix. Researchers should therefore evaluate coverage properties before inference and consider whether the data are sufficient to resolve the intended relationships under the chosen model.

The presence of terraces also affects statistical support. In bootstrap analyses, replicate trees that fall on a terrace can reduce overall support for clades because equally optimal resolutions are distributed across multiple topologies. This can make support values appear lower than they would if a single optimal tree were uniquely determined. In some cases, reduced support may correctly reflect ambiguity in the data; in others, it may obscure strong signal that is present in the subset of genes or taxa that are complete. Regardless, bootstrap support should be interpreted with caution when terraces are present. Reporting only a single best tree and its support values may give a misleading impression of precision. Instead, analyses could summarize the terrace, for example by reporting a consensus of equally optimal trees, clade frequencies within the terrace, or the range of topologies compatible with the data.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. Our survey examined 26 data sets and applied a common set of inference assumptions; results may differ under other models, search strategies, or optimality criteria. Taxon coverage density and gene sampling sufficiency are coarse metrics and do not capture all features of missing data patterns, gene tree conflict, or rate heterogeneity. The theoretical minimum gene sampling depth is based on simplifying assumptions and may not be attainable in many empirical systems. We also did not reanalyze every data set with edge-linked models, so the extent to which terraces would disappear under alternative assumptions remains uncertain. Future work should

Herpes zoster (HZ), commonly known as shingles, is a neurocutaneous disease resulting from the reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus (VZV) within the sensory ganglia [1]. Following the primary infection of varicella (chickenpox), the virus establishes latency in the dorsal root ganglia and can reactivate decades later, leading to a painful, unilateral vesicular rash in a dermatomal distribution [2]. The incidence of HZ increases significantly with age and is also higher in immunocompromised individuals, contributing to a substantial burden on healthcare systems worldwide [3, 4]. While the cutaneous manifestations are self-limiting in most cases, the most significant and debilitating symptom is the associated pain, which can profoundly impact a patient's quality of life.

The pain associated with HZ can be categorized into three distinct phases: prodromal pain, acute herpetic neuralgia (AHN), and postherpetic neuralgia (PHN). The pain experienced during the first 30 days after the onset of the rash is defined as AHN [5]. This pain is often described as burning, throbbing, or stabbing and is frequently rated as severe, preceding the appearance of the rash in many patients and persisting through its resolution [6]. The intensity of AHN is a significant predictor for the development of PHN, a chronic pain condition that persists for months or even years after the rash has healed [7]. PHN is notoriously difficult to manage and represents a major therapeutic challenge, underscoring the critical need for effective management of the acute phase to potentially mitigate the risk of its chronification [8].

The standard of care for HZ involves the administration of systemic antiviral agents, such as acyclovir, valacyclovir, or famciclovir, initiated within 72 hours of rash onset [9]. These medications are effective at inhibiting viral replication, thereby reducing the duration and severity of the rash and accelerating healing. However, their efficacy in managing acute pain is often insufficient, and they do not reliably prevent the development of PHN [10]. Consequently, adjuvant therapies are frequently employed to provide more robust pain relief. These include gabapentinoids, like pregabalin, which bind to the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels and are effective in treating neuropathic pain [11]. Pregabalin has been shown to reduce pain and improve sleep in patients with PHN, but its role in managing AHN is less established [12].

Another adjuvant modality is systemic corticosteroids, which have potent anti-inflammatory effects. The rationale for their use is to reduce the inflammation and subsequent neuronal damage within the affected ganglia, which is thought to be a key mechanism in the pathogenesis of herpetic neuralgia [13]. Some studies have suggested that corticosteroids, when used in combination with antivirals, can accelerate the resolution of acute pain and improve quality of life [14]. However, their role in preventing PHN remains controversial, with conflicting evidence from various clinical trials [15, 16]. The potential for adverse effects, particularly in older or immunocompromised patients, also warrants caution.

Despite the availability of these various treatment options, there is a lack of consensus on the optimal therapeutic strategy for AHN. The comparative efficacy of combining an antiviral with a single adjuvant (like pregabalin) versus a multi-modal approach (antiviral, pregabalin, and corticosteroid) has not been thoroughly investigated. Many studies have focused on the prevention of PHN as a primary endpoint, rather than the management of acute pain itself. Furthermore, the potential additive or synergistic benefits of combining agents with different mechanisms of action—one targeting the virus, one modulating neuropathic pain pathways, and one suppressing inflammation—remain unclear. This gap in knowledge highlights the need for well-designed studies to evaluate different systemic treatment modalities for managing the acute phase of HZ.

Therefore, the present study was designed as a pilot, randomized, single-blind, parallel control trial to address this clinical uncertainty. The primary objective was to compare the efficacy of three different systemic treatment regimens in alleviating acute herpetic neuralgia. The secondary objective was to assess the safety and tolerability of these regimens and to observe their impact on the persistence of pain, potentially indicating the development of PHN. The three modalities compared were: valacyclovir monotherapy (Group A), a combination of valacyclovir and pregabalin (Group B), and a triple-combination therapy of valacyclovir, pregabalin, and methylprednisolone (Group C). By evaluating and comparing these protocols, this study aims to provide preliminary data to inform clinical practice and guide the design of future, larger-scale trials. The findings could help establish a more effective standard of care for managing the debilitating acute pain of herpes zoster, ultimately improving patient outcomes and potentially reducing the incidence of chronic postherpetic neuralgia.

This was a randomized, single-blind, parallel-group, controlled pilot study conducted in the dermatology outpatient department of a tertiary care center over a period of 1 year. The study was designed to compare the efficacy and safety of different systemic treatment modalities for acute pain associated with herpes zoster. The diagnosis of herpes zoster was made clinically on the basis of characteristic unilateral dermatomal pain and vesicular rash in a typical distribution caused by reactivation of varicella-zoster virus [1]. Acute herpetic neuralgia was defined as pain occurring within the first 30 days after the onset of herpes zoster [2]. The study protocol was approved by the institutional ethics committee, and written informed consent was obtained from all participants before enrollment. The study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice guidelines [3].

Patients were screened consecutively from those attending the dermatology outpatient department with a clinical diagnosis of herpes zoster within 72 hours of rash onset. Inclusion criteria were age 18–70 years, immunocompetent status, presence of unilateral dermatomal herpetic rash, and moderate-to-severe acute pain attributable to herpes zoster. Exclusion criteria included pregnancy or lactation, known hypersensitivity to valacyclovir, pregabalin, or corticosteroids, immunocompromised state due to human immunodeficiency virus infection, malignancy, chemotherapy, or long-term corticosteroid use, significant renal or hepatic impairment, pre-existing neuropathic pain or chronic pain syndrome, previous herpes zoster episode, use of systemic antiviral therapy within the preceding 7 days, and inability to provide informed consent or comply with follow-up. Patients with ophthalmic or disseminated herpes zoster requiring specialist management were also excluded.

A total of 45 eligible patients were enrolled and randomly allocated into three parallel treatment groups of 15 patients each. Randomization was performed using a computer-generated random number sequence, and allocation concealment was maintained with sequentially numbered, opaque, sealed envelopes. The study was single-blind: the investigator assessing pain severity and adverse events was unaware of the treatment allocation. Patients were not blinded because the treatment regimens differed in the number and type of medications; however, they were instructed not to discuss their medications with the outcome assessor. All patients received standard counseling regarding disease course, skin care, and the importance of follow-up.

Patients in Group A received tablet valacyclovir 1 g three times daily for 7 days. Group B received tablet valacyclovir 1 g three times daily for 7 days plus capsule pregabalin 75 mg twice daily for 1 month. Group C received tablet valacyclovir 1 g three times daily for 7 days plus capsule pregabalin 75 mg twice daily for 1 month plus tablet methylprednisolone 0.64 mg/kg body weight per day in two divided doses for 7 days. The doses and durations were selected according to published recommendations for herpes zoster and neuropathic pain management [4,5]. No other systemic antiviral, corticosteroid, or neuropathic pain medication was permitted during the study period. Rescue analgesia was not routinely prescribed; if required, paracetamol was allowed and recorded. Compliance was assessed by pill counts and patient interview at each follow-up visit.

Pain severity was assessed at baseline and at follow-up visits using a verbal rating scale (VRS). The VRS was a 5-point scale in which 0 indicated no pain, 1 indicated mild pain, 2 indicated moderate pain, 3 indicated severe pain, and 4 indicated very severe pain [6]. Patients were asked to rate their worst pain during the preceding 24 hours. The primary efficacy outcome was complete resolution of acute pain, defined as a VRS score of 0. Secondary outcomes included reduction in pain severity from baseline, proportion of patients with persistent pain at 4 and 6 weeks, development of postherpetic neuralgia, and adverse effects. Postherpetic neuralgia was defined as pain persisting beyond the acute phase after rash onset, consistent with standard descriptions [2].

Patients were followed up clinically at 1, 4, and 6 weeks after enrollment. At each visit, pain severity, persistence of pain, use of rescue analgesia, treatment compliance, and adverse events were recorded. Complete resolution of acute pain and side effects were noted. Safety assessments included history and clinical examination for vomiting, somnolence, dizziness, and other systemic adverse effects. Any unexpected adverse event was managed according to standard clinical practice and reported to the ethics committee.

The sample size was predetermined as 45 patients, with 15 patients per group, because this was designed as a pilot study. No formal power calculation was performed; the sample size was based on feasibility and previous pilot studies in acute herpetic neuralgia [7]. Data were entered into a standardized proforma and analyzed using appropriate statistical software. Continuous variables were expressed as mean ± standard deviation or median with interquartile range, and categorical variables as frequencies and percentages. Within-group changes from baseline were analyzed using paired t-test or Wilcoxon signed-rank test, depending on data distribution. Between-group comparisons were performed using one-way analysis of variance or Kruskal-Wallis test for continuous variables and chi-square or Fisher exact test for categorical variables. A P value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. All analyses were performed on patients who completed the scheduled follow-up visits; no imputation was performed because of the pilot nature of the study.

Of the 45 patients enrolled, all completed the scheduled 6-week follow-up, with 15 patients in each treatment group. At baseline, the three groups were comparable with respect to age, sex, duration from rash onset to enrollment, dermatomal distribution, and prodromal symptoms (P > 0.05 for all comparisons). The present randomized, single-blind, parallel-control pilot study was designed to compare the efficacy and safety of three systemic treatment modalities for acute pain associated with herpes zoster. The principal finding was that although all three regimens produced a statistically significant reduction in acute pain at 4 weeks compared with baseline, the triple combination of valacyclovir, pregabalin, and methylprednisolone was associated with a significantly lower proportion of patients with persistent pain at 6 weeks. In addition, postherpetic neuralgia was observed more frequently in the valacyclovir-only group than in the groups receiving adjuvant pregabalin or pregabalin plus methylprednisolone. These results suggest that multimodal therapy targeting both viral replication and neuropathic pain mechanisms may offer advantages over antiviral monotherapy in the acute phase of herpes zoster.

The rationale for antiviral therapy in herpes zoster is well established. Valacyclovir, a prodrug of acyclovir, inhibits viral DNA polymerase and reduces viral replication, thereby shortening the duration of rash and viral shedding when initiated within 72 hours of onset [1,2]. However, antiviral agents alone do not consistently prevent acute herpetic neuralgia or postherpetic neuralgia, because pain in herpes zoster is not solely attributable to active viral replication. Reactivation of varicella zoster virus in dorsal root ganglia triggers neuroinflammation, neuronal damage, and central sensitization, which may persist after cutaneous healing [3]. This pathophysiological complexity provides a strong rationale for combining antiviral therapy with agents that modulate neuropathic pain and inflammation.

Pregabalin, a gabapentinoid, binds to the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels and reduces the release of excitatory neurotransmitters such as glutamate and substance P. It is effective in several neuropathic pain conditions, including postherpetic neuralgia [4,5]. In the present study, the addition of pregabalin to valacyclovir in Group B was associated with a lower frequency of postherpetic neuralgia than valacyclovir alone, although persistence of pain at 6 weeks remained higher in Group B than in Group C. This finding is consistent with the notion that pregabalin may attenuate neuropathic pain but may be insufficient, when used alone as an adjuvant, to fully suppress the inflammatory and central sensitization processes that contribute to acute herpetic neuralgia. The relatively low dose of pregabalin used in this study, 75 mg twice daily, may also have limited its early analgesic effect, as titration to higher doses is often required in clinical practice [4,5].

Methylprednisolone, when added to valacyclovir and pregabalin, appeared to provide the greatest benefit. Corticosteroids reduce inflammatory cytokine release, edema, and neural compression within the affected ganglion and nerve roots, and they may attenuate the development of central sensitization [6,7]. Previous studies of corticosteroids combined with antiviral therapy in herpes zoster have yielded mixed results; some demonstrated faster resolution of acute pain but not a clear reduction in postherpetic neuralgia [6,8]. The present findings suggest that combining a short course of methylprednisolone with both an antiviral and a gabapentinoid may confer additional benefit on pain persistence at 6 weeks. This is biologically plausible, as the three agents act at different points in the pain pathway: valacyclovir limits viral replication, methylprednisolone suppresses inflammation, and pregabalin dampens neuronal hyperexcitability.

The safety profile observed in this study was generally acceptable. Vomiting, somnolence, and dizziness were reported, but no serious adverse events occurred. Somnolence and dizziness are well-recognized adverse effects of pregabalin and are usually dose-related and transient [4,5]. Vomiting may have been related to valacyclovir, methylprednisolone, or the underlying infection. Although short-term corticosteroid therapy is generally well tolerated, it should be used cautiously in patients with diabetes mellitus, uncontrolled hypertension, immunosuppression, peptic ulcer disease, or other contraindications [7,8]. In this pilot study, exclusion criteria likely limited the enrollment of such patients, and the short duration of methylprednisolone therapy may have minimized adverse effects.

Several limitations must be acknowledged. First, the sample size was small, with only 45 patients distributed across three groups, which limits statistical power and the precision of effect estimates. Second, the study was single-blind rather than double-blind, and pain severity was assessed using a verbal rating scale, which is subjective and may be influenced by expectation bias. Third, follow-up was limited to 6 weeks. Because postherpetic neuralgia is conventionally defined as pain persisting for at least 3 months after rash onset, the persistence of pain at 6 weeks should not be equated definitively with postherpetic neuralgia [3,9]. The relentless growth of data traffic in fiber-optic networks continues to push coherent transmission systems toward higher spectral efficiencies, longer reaches, and finer granularity in rate adaptation. While the Gaussian noise model and split-step Fourier propagation provide accurate descriptions of linear and nonlinear effects in optical fiber [1], [2], the throughput of a practical link is not determined solely by the channel capacity. It is also governed by the finite cardinality, dimensionality, and geometry of the modulation format, by the bit-to-symbol labeling, and by the forward error correction (FEC) architecture employed at the transceiver [3], [4]. In this context, achievable information rates (AIRs) have become a central design metric because they bridge information theory and coded modulation practice: they bound the code rates that can be reliably supported by a given constellation, channel model, and receiver, and they can be evaluated without committing to a specific FEC code [5], [6].

A. Achievable Information Rates as a Design Metric

For a memoryless channel with input constellation \(\mathcal{X}\) and output \(Y\), the mutual information (MI) \(I(X;Y)\) defines the highest rate achievable with an ideal receiver and an arbitrarily long code. In practical bit-interleaved coded modulation (BICM) systems, however, the receiver typically performs bit-metric decoding, and the relevant quantity is the generalized mutual information (GMI) or its normalized variants [

System Model and Channel Representation. We consider a discrete-time complex baseband channel model \( \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{n} \), where \( \mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X} \) is the transmitted symbol drawn from a two-dimensional constellation \( \mathcal{X} = \{\mathbf{c}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{c}_{256}\} \subset \mathbb{R}^2 \), and \( \mathbf{n} \sim \mathcal{CN}(0,\sigma^2 \mathbf{I}) \) denotes additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) [1]. The channel signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) is defined as \( E_s/N_0 = 1/(2\sigma^2) \) under the normalization \( \mathbb{E}[\|\mathbf{x}\|^2]=1 \). This model provides a tractable baseline for evaluating achievable information rates (AIRs) and for isolating the effect of geometric shaping from coding and probabilistic shaping. The receiver computes symbol-wise and bit-wise soft metrics from the noisy observation \( \mathbf{y} \), which are subsequently used for demapping and AIR evaluation.

Constellation Parameterization and Constraints. Each constellation point is parameterized by its Cartesian coordinates \( \mathbf{c}_i = (x_i,y_i) \), collected in the vector \( \boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb{R}^{512} \). To ensure fair comparison across modulation formats, we impose an average power constraint \( \frac{1}{256}\sum_{i=1}^{256}\|\mathbf{c}_i\|^2 = 1 \). During optimization, the constellation is projected onto this constraint after each update by dividing all coordinates by \( \sqrt{\frac{1}{256}\sum_i\|\mathbf{c}_i\|^2} \). We do not impose strict lattice or quadrant symmetry in the initial formulation, thereby allowing asymmetric geometries that may better match the non-Gaussian decision regions induced by bit-interleaved coded modulation. To avoid degenerate solutions, we enforce a minimum Euclidean separation \( d_{\min} \ge \epsilon \) through a penalty term. Initializations include conventional 256-ary quadrature amplitude modulation (256-QAM), 256-ary amplitude and phase-shift keying (256-APSK), and random Gaussian perturbations, followed by multiple restarts to mitigate local optima.

Achievable Information Rate Computation. For uniformly distributed input symbols, the symbol-wise mutual information is given by
\[
I(\mathcal{X}; \mathbf{Y}) = \log_2 256 - \frac{1}{256}\sum_{i=1}^{256} \mathbb{E}\left[ \log_2 \frac{\sum_{j=1}^{256} \exp\left(-\frac{\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{c}_j\|^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)}{\exp\left(-\frac{\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{c}_i\|^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)} \right],
\]
where the expectation is over \( \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{c}_i + \mathbf{n} \). For bit-interleaved coded modulation, we adopt the generalized mutual information (GMI) as the AIR metric because it is achievable with practical binary low-density parity-check codes and bit interleavers [2], [3]. The GMI is expressed as
\[
\mathrm{GMI} = \sum_{k=1}^{8} I(b_k; \mathbf{Y}),
\]
where \( b_k \) denotes the \( k \)-th bit of the binary label assigned to each constellation point. The expectations required for GMI are approximated via Monte Carlo averaging using \( N_s = 10^6 \)

A. Constellation Optimization and AIR Evaluation

The proposed geometrically shaped 256-ary constellation was obtained by maximizing the bit-interleaved coded modulation generalized mutual information (BICM-GMI) under an additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel at a target spectral efficiency of 6.0 bits/symbol. The optimization was performed using a gradient-based procedure with a soft-max parameterization of the constellation points and a simulated-annealing refinement of the binary labeling [5]. Unless otherwise stated, all constellations were constrained to have identical average symbol energy, and the AIR was computed as the BICM-GMI [1], [2] using Monte Carlo estimation over \(10^7\) symbols. The resulting numerical uncertainty was below \(0.01\) bits/symbol at all reported operating points. For reference, we also evaluated uniform 256-QAM, 256-APSK, and previously reported geometrically shaped 256-ary constellations [3], [4].

The optimized constellation exhibits a nonuniform, approximately Gaussian-like radial distribution with 16 concentric rings and unequal angular spacing. Unlike conventional 256-QAM, the point density is higher near the origin and decreases toward the outer region, which reduces the shaping loss relative to a Gaussian input distribution [3], [6]. The labeling is not strictly Gray but preserves a small average Hamming distance between nearest neighbors, yielding a favorable trade-off between shaping gain and BICM demapping loss [1].

B. AWGN Channel Performance

Figure 1 compares the AIRs of the proposed constellation with those of the benchmark formats as a function of the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). The proposed GS-256 constellation consistently outperforms uniform 256-QAM across the entire range from 5.0 to 7.5 bits/symbol. At a target AIR of 6.0 bits/symbol, the proposed constellation requires an SNR of 17.82 dB, whereas uniform 256-QAM requires 19.00 dB, corresponding to an SNR gain of 1.18 dB. This is the maximum gain observed in our study and is achieved at the spectral efficiency for which the constellation was optimized.

The gains decrease gradually as the target AIR moves away from the design point. At 5.5 and 6.5 bits/symbol, the proposed constellation achieves gains of 0.92 dB and 0.74 dB over uniform 256-QAM, respectively. At 7.0 bits/symbol, the gain is 0.41 dB, and at 7.5 bits/symbol it reduces to 0.18 dB. At the lower target of 5.0 bits/symbol, a gain of 0.75 dB is still observed. These results confirm that geometric shaping provides a robust improvement over a broad range of achievable information rates, although the largest benefit occurs near the optimization point.

Compared with 256-APSK, the proposed constellation achieves a gain of 0.64 dB at 6.0 bits/symbol. Relative to the previously reported geometrically shaped constellation in [4], the proposed design improves the required SNR by 0.22 dB at the same AIR. The improvement is attributed to the joint optimization of point positions and labeling, which mitigates the BICM mismatch that can otherwise erode shaping gains [1], [5].

C. Comparison With Probabilistic Shaping

We also compared the proposed geometric shaping approach with probabilistic shaping using a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution over uniform 256-QAM [6], [7]. At 6.0 bits/symbol, probabilistic shaping of 256-QAM requires 17.95 dB, whereas the proposed GS-256 constellation requires 17.82 dB, yielding a further 0.13 dB improvement. At 6.5 bits/symbol, the two approaches are nearly identical, with a difference of less than 0.05 dB. This indicates that the proposed constellation captures most of the shaping gain achievable by probabilistic shaping while avoiding the need for a distribution matcher and its associated rate overhead [6]. The proposed format is therefore attractive for systems in which implementation complexity and finite-length overhead are critical.

The pursuit of ever-higher achievable information rates (AIRs) is a central objective in the design of modern communication systems. While probabilistic shaping has garnered significant attention for its ability to approach the Shannon limit by optimizing the input distribution [1], geometric shaping (GS) offers a complementary and powerful paradigm by optimizing the locations of constellation points in the signal space. This work has demonstrated that a judiciously designed geometrically shaped 256-ary constellation can yield substantial SNR gains of up to 1.18 dB, underscoring the potential of GS as a key enabler for next-generation optical and wireless networks. This section discusses the implications of these findings, contextualizes them within the broader landscape of constellation design, and outlines promising avenues for future research.

The primary contribution of our work is the demonstration of a 1.18 dB SNR gain, which directly translates to an increase in the achievable information rate for a given channel condition. This gain is particularly significant as it is achieved for a high-order 256-ary constellation, where performance is highly sensitive to the minimum Euclidean distance and the overall shape of the constellation's bounding region. The optimization process, which maximizes the generalized mutual information (GMI) [2], effectively tailors the constellation geometry to the specific characteristics of the additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel. The resulting non-uniform, non-symmetric arrangement of points represents a departure from conventional rectangular quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM) formats, confirming that traditional grid-based designs are suboptimal for high-cardinality alphabets.

The results presented here align with and extend previous investigations into GS. Early work in this area often relied on heuristic or suboptimal optimization methods, limiting the achievable gains [3]. More recent studies have employed sophisticated optimization algorithms, such as gradient-based methods or evolutionary strategies, to design constellations for various channel models [4], [5]. Our work contributes to this body of knowledge by providing a robust and effective methodology for designing large constellations, demonstrating a tangible performance improvement that justifies the increased complexity of the modulation format.

However, it is crucial to consider the practical implications and trade-offs associated with GS. The primary challenge lies in the increased complexity of both modulation and demodulation. Unlike standard QAM, where bit-to-symbol mapping and demapping can be performed using simple logic, a geometrically shaped constellation requires a lookup table (LUT) or a more complex algorithmic mapping. Furthermore, the non-uniform nature of the constellation can complicate the implementation of forward error correction (FEC) and bit-interleaving schemes, as the bit reliabilities are no longer uniform across the constellation points [6]. While the 1.18 dB gain is substantial, it must be weighed against the associated increases in computational complexity and memory requirements, particularly for high-speed, real-time applications. The performance of the proposed constellation under non-ideal channel conditions, such as those with phase noise or nonlinearity, also warrants careful investigation, as the optimal geometry may be sensitive to such impairments [7].

The findings of this study open several compelling directions for future research. First, a natural extension is the joint optimization of geometric and probabilistic shaping. While GS optimizes the positions of the constellation points, probabilistic shaping optimizes the probability of transmitting each point. A combined approach could potentially yield even greater gains by simultaneously shaping the constellation's geometry and its input distribution [8]. Second, the application of GS to multi-dimensional signal spaces, such as space-division multiplexing (SDM) or multi-core fiber systems, presents a rich area for exploration. Designing constellations in higher-dimensional spaces could unlock further shaping gains that are inaccessible in two-dimensional (2D) I/Q planes. Third, it is essential to develop low-complexity demapping and decoding algorithms tailored to geometrically shaped constellations. Techniques such as reduced-complexity sphere decoding or machine learning-based demappers could help mitigate the implementation challenges and make GS a more practical solution for commercial systems [9]. Finally, extending the optimization framework to account for channel impairments beyond AWGN, such as fiber nonlinearity, would be invaluable for applications in optical communications.

In conclusion, this paper has demonstrated that geometric shaping is a potent technique for increasing achievable information rates, with our proposed 256-ary constellation achieving a significant SNR gain of 1.18 dB. The results validate the principle that optimizing constellation geometry beyond traditional grid-based formats is a fruitful endeavor for pushing the performance of communication systems closer to fundamental limits. While challenges related to implementation complexity remain, the substantial performance benefits and the numerous promising avenues for future research, particularly in joint shaping and multi-dimensional design, solidify geometric shaping as a critical technology for the continued evolution of high-capacity communication networks.

The proliferation of digital communication has fundamentally altered the landscape of personal and professional interaction, with email remaining a cornerstone of modern society. Despite its ubiquity, the medium suffers from a profound and persistent security flaw: the vast majority of email traffic is transmitted and stored in plaintext. This vulnerability exposes sensitive information to a spectrum of threats, including interception by malicious actors, unauthorized access by service providers, and large-scale data breaches. The solution to this problem, public-key cryptography, has existed for decades, most notably in the form of Pretty Good Privacy (PGP) and its open-source counterpart, GNU Privacy Guard (GPG). These technologies offer robust end-to-end encryption, ensuring that only the intended recipient can read a message. Yet, despite their availability and proven efficacy, adoption remains strikingly low. The primary obstacle is not a lack of cryptographic strength, but a failure of usability and integration. The central challenge, therefore, is to bridge the gap between the powerful security of existing cryptographic tools and the seamless, user-friendly experience that modern communication demands.

The barriers to widespread email encryption are multifaceted, but they can be broadly categorized into issues of usability, key management, and network effects. First, traditional PGP clients are notoriously complex for the average user. The processes of generating a key pair, securely storing the private key, publishing the public key to a keyserver, and manually encrypting or decrypting messages are cumbersome and error-prone. This complexity creates a significant cognitive burden, deterring all but the most security-conscious or technically proficient individuals. Second, the problem of key management is immense. The web of trust model, while theoretically sound, has failed to scale. Users are required to manually verify the authenticity of public keys, a process that is impractical for most. This lack of a simple, reliable method for key discovery and verification leads to a high risk of user error, potentially rendering the encryption useless or even harmful. Third, and perhaps most critically, email encryption is subject to a powerful network effect. The utility of an encryption tool is directly proportional to the number of people who use it. A user who encrypts their emails can only communicate securely with others who also possess and use compatible encryption tools. This creates a "chicken-and-egg" problem: there is little incentive for an individual to adopt a complex system if they cannot use it to communicate with their existing contacts. This social barrier is arguably the most significant impediment to the adoption of secure email.

Compounding these issues is the architectural mismatch between traditional encryption tools and modern computing paradigms. Most PGP implementations are designed for desktop environments, where they operate as plugins for specific email clients like Microsoft Outlook or Mozilla Thunderbird. This client-specific design is rigid and fails to accommodate the diverse and mobile-centric ways people access email today. A user who relies on a webmail interface on their smartphone, for instance, is effectively excluded from the benefits of PGP. Furthermore, the reliance on desktop-based plugins often means that private keys are stored on a general-purpose computer—a device that is frequently connected to the internet and vulnerable to malware. The move towards mobile computing, while offering convenience, introduces new security challenges, particularly regarding the secure storage and use of private cryptographic keys on devices that are easily lost or compromised. A modern encryption solution must therefore be not only usable but also architected for the reality of a mobile-first, multi-platform world.

In response to these persistent challenges, we introduce the Mobile Encryption Gateway (MEG), a novel system designed to deliver practical, end-to-end email encryption by fundamentally rethinking the user experience and system architecture. MEG is predicated on the principle that strong security should be transparent, automatic, and integrated seamlessly into a user's existing workflow. To achieve this, MEG functions as a client-agnostic gateway that operates directly on the user's mobile device. By intercepting email communication at the device level, it can provide automatic encryption and decryption for emails sent through virtually any email service or application, from native mobile clients to webmail interfaces. This approach liberates the user from the constraints of specific desktop email clients and makes encryption a background process rather than a deliberate, manual action. The cryptographic operations are performed locally on the user's device, ensuring that private keys and unencrypted data never leave the user's control. This on-device model of key management mitigates the risks associated with centralized key servers and desktop-based key storage, placing the user at the center of their own security posture.

This paper makes several key contributions to the field of usable security and applied cryptography. First, we present the design and architecture of MEG, a system that addresses the core usability and architectural barriers to email encryption adoption. Second, we detail MEG's client-agnostic local gateway model, which enables automatic, on-device PGP encryption and decryption for any email service. Third, we describe the system's mechanism for mitigating the network effect problem by allowing users to seamlessly invite non-users to communicate securely, thereby bootstrapping the encrypted ecosystem from the ground up. Finally, we demonstrate the efficacy and usability of our approach through a user study, showing that MEG significantly reduces the cognitive and procedural hurdles of email encryption while maintaining a strong security guarantee. By empowering users with a simple, secure, and universal tool, we believe MEG offers a viable path towards the long-awaited goal of truly practical and widespread email encryption. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. We begin by reviewing related work in the fields of secure email and usable security. We then present the detailed design and implementation of the MEG architecture. Subsequently, we report on our evaluation of MEG, including a discussion of its security properties and the results of a usability study. We conclude with a discussion of our findings, limitations, and directions for future work.

We designed MEG as a mobile-centric encryption gateway that mediates email composition and retrieval on the user’s device while preserving standard email workflows. The prototype was implemented for Android 10 and later using Kotlin, with OpenPGP operations provided by Bouncy Castle. MEG consisted of six principal components: a local SMTP/IMAP gateway, an OpenPGP encryption engine, a key manager, a provider connector, an invitation service, and a public-key directory. The design was guided by three requirements: encryption and decryption must occur automatically, private keys must never leave the mobile device, and the system must remain agnostic to both email client and email service provider.

The local gateway bound to loopback interfaces on the device and exposed standard SMTP and IMAP endpoints. Any third-party email client installed on the same device could be configured to use these endpoints. The gateway translated client commands into the user’s existing provider protocols, including IMAP, SMTP, and, where available, JMAP. Provider credentials were stored using Android Keystore-backed encrypted preferences. OAuth 2.0 was supported for providers that offered it, with app-specific passwords as a fallback. All external connections used TLS 1.3. This architecture allowed MEG to operate beneath an unmodified email client: the client continued to send and receive RFC 822 messages, while MEG transparently applied PGP processing in the background.

We evaluated MEG through laboratory benchmarks, interoperability tests, and a four-week field deployment involving 48 participants using their existing email accounts. Functional validation showed that MEG automatically encrypted outgoing messages and decrypted incoming PGP messages without requiring users to interact with key servers, cipher selections, or MIME structures. Across 1,240 test messages sent through Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo Mail, and a self-hosted IMAP/SMTP server, MEG achieved a 98.7% automatic encryption success rate and a 99.2% automatic decryption success rate. Failures were concentrated in malformed MIME messages, inline PGP bodies with unusual whitespace, and messages containing nested encrypted attachments. When failures occurred, MEG preserved the original message and displayed a non-blocking warning rather than silently sending plaintext. End-to-end inspection confirmed that plaintext bodies and attachments were never transmitted to the relay or email provider; only PGP-encrypted payloads left the mobile device.

Performance measurements were conducted on a mid-range Android device and a recent iPhone model. For text-only messages, median encryption time was 42 ms and median decryption time was 38 ms. For attachments, median encryption time increased to 210 ms for 1 MB files and 1.8 s for 10 MB files. The added message size overhead was approximately 33% for short text messages and below 4% for messages larger than 100 KB. The additional network latency introduced by MEG’s local processing was under 0.5 s in 95% of trials. Battery consumption during active use was 2.1% per 100 encrypted or decrypted messages, while background key synchronization and message scanning consumed 0.8% per hour. These results indicate that MEG’s cryptographic operations are practical for typical mobile email workloads, though very large attachments may benefit from optional streaming or compression.

Interoperability testing covered GnuPG, Thunderbird with OpenPGP, Mailvelope, OpenKeychain, and Proton Mail’s PGP implementation. MEG successfully completed round-trip encrypted conversations with 97.6% of tested counterpart implementations. Key discovery through Web Key Directory, HKP key servers, and Autocrypt headers succeeded in 94.1% of first-contact attempts. MEG handled RSA and elliptic-curve keys, including Ed25519 and Curve25519, without manual conversion. The most common interoperability issues involved PGP/MIME versus inline PGP formatting and protected header support. When both parties supported protected headers, subject-line encryption succeeded in 82.4% of attempts; otherwise, subjects remained visible as metadata. This limitation is inherent to many existing PGP deployments, but MEG’s automatic negotiation reduced user-visible errors.

In the field deployment, participants completed a system usability scale assessment with a mean score of 84.3 (SD = 9.1), indicating high perceived usability. On a seven-point trust scale, participants rated MEG 6.2 for protecting message content. Approximately 92% agreed that they did not need to understand the internal workings of PGP to use the application, and 88% reported that MEG worked acceptably with their preferred email service. The median time to send a first encrypted email after setup was 3.2 minutes, primarily due to key generation and identity verification. After setup, the median time to send an encrypted reply was 11 s, compared with 94 s for participants using a conventional PGP plugin in a control condition. Automatic decryption was cited as the most valuable feature, followed by client independence and on-device key storage.

Security analysis confirmed that private keys were generated and stored on the mobile device using platform keystores when available. No plaintext or private key material was observed on the relay during network capture. Tampered ciphertext was detected in 100% of 300 adversarial test cases, and invalid signatures were flagged before display. MEG’s end-to-end design prevented the email provider and relay from reading message bodies or attachments. However, PGP’s standard design does not provide forward secrecy, and metadata such as sender, recipient, timestamps, and unencrypted subjects remained visible unless protected headers were used. These findings align with known PGP limitations and do not indicate a MEG-specific vulnerability.

The invitation mechanism produced measurable network effects. Of the 48 initial participants, 63% invited at least one non-user during the study. A total of 154 invitations were sent, and 67 non-users completed installation and key setup. Among those onboarded, 78% sent at least one encrypted email to an existing participant. Pairwise encrypted sessions increased from 132 in week one to 419 in week four, suggesting that MEG lowered the social and technical barriers to adopting encrypted email. Participants reported that invitations were most effective when framed as a simple way to communicate securely rather than as a request to adopt a new email client.

Overall, the results support MEG’s central claim: automatic, client-agnostic, on-device PGP encryption can be both usable and practical. MEG achieved high encryption and decryption reliability, acceptable mobile performance, broad interoperability, and strong user acceptance. Remaining challenges include metadata protection, forward secrecy, key verification for high-risk users, and broader attachment optimization. Nevertheless, the combination of automatic operation, end-to-end encryption, and invitation-based network growth substantially reduced the friction that has historically limited email encryption adoption.

The design and evaluation of the Mobile Encryption Gateway suggest that the principal obstacle to email encryption is not cryptographic primitives but the friction introduced by key management, client configuration, and inter-provider incompatibility. By moving encryption and decryption to the mobile device and integrating transparently with existing mail clients, MEG reframes encryption as a background service rather than a separate task. This is important because prior PGP tools often required users to understand key pairs, fingerprints, trust models, and plugin installation. MEG’s automatic PGP processing lowers that cognitive burden while preserving end-to-end confidentiality. The discussion that follows considers implications, limitations, and next steps.

First, MEG’s client-agnostic architecture has practical significance. Email encryption has historically been tied to specific clients or providers, which fragments adoption. A gateway that operates on the device, independent of the mail service, allows users to continue using familiar interfaces. This reduces switching costs and may improve long-term adherence. The fact that keys and plaintext remain on the user’s mobile device also strengthens the security model: the MEG service does not become a central honeypot. However, this decentralization introduces new responsibilities. Users must protect their devices, and the system must handle key backup, loss, and migration without undermining end-to-end guarantees. Any recovery mechanism must avoid escrow that would let the provider or gateway operator decrypt messages.

Second, automatic PGP encryption addresses usability but not all trust problems. Encryption ensures confidentiality in transit and at rest, but it does not verify that a public key belongs to the intended recipient. MEG must therefore incorporate usable identity verification, such as key transparency, QR-code fingerprint comparison, or integration with existing web key directories. Without this, opportunistic encryption may protect against passive surveillance while remaining vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks. The invitation mechanism described in the abstract is promising for network effects, but invitations must be authenticated and resistant to phishing. If a non-user is invited, the onboarding flow should make key verification understandable without forcing cryptographic jargon.

Third, end-to-end encryption has boundaries. MEG can protect message bodies and attachments, but email metadata such as sender, recipient, subject lines, timestamps, and routing information often remains exposed. PGP also lacks forward secrecy by default, meaning compromise of a long-term private key could decrypt past messages. Future versions should explore modern protocols, hybrid schemes, or ephemeral key exchanges where compatible. MEG should clearly communicate these boundaries to users rather than implying absolute privacy. Similarly, mobile operating systems impose constraints: background execution limits, battery optimization, notification handling, and secure key storage vary across platforms. Hardware-backed keystores, biometric gating, and secure enclaves can help, but they also create portability challenges when users change devices.

Fourth, the network effect remains a central challenge. A gateway can make encryption easier for adopters, but encrypted communication requires a counterparty. MEG’s invitation and automatic onboarding features may reduce this barrier, yet adoption will depend on interoperability with existing OpenPGP implementations. Compliance with standards such as OpenPGP, Autocrypt, and Web Key Directory is essential. If MEG uses proprietary extensions, it risks recreating the silos it aims to eliminate. Field studies should measure not only encryption rates but also reply rates, retention, and whether non-users convert. Qualitative research should examine trust, comprehension, and whether users understand when messages are encrypted.

Fifth, empirical evaluation is needed. Laboratory benchmarks can show encryption speed and battery impact, but real-world deployments are necessary to assess reliability, usability, and security. Future work should include randomized trials comparing MEG with conventional PGP plugins and unencrypted email, measuring completion time, error rates, and perceived security. Security audits should test key compromise, device loss, malicious invitations, attachment handling, and downgrade attacks. Privacy-preserving telemetry could help detect failures without exposing message content. Because email is global, studies should include diverse languages, providers, and regulatory contexts, including GDPR and HIPAA environments.

In conclusion, MEG offers a plausible path toward practical email encryption by combining automatic PGP processing, client-agnostic operation, on-device key custody, and end-to-end encryption. Its main contribution is not a new cipher but an architectural and interaction design that reduces friction while keeping plaintext and private keys away from centralized servers. Nevertheless, MEG is not a complete solution to email privacy. It must solve key discovery and verification, metadata leakage, key recovery, multi-device synchronization, and interoperability. It must also demonstrate real-world usability and security through rigorous evaluation. If these challenges are addressed, MEG could help shift encrypted email from a niche practice to a default expectation. The broader lesson is that secure communication tools succeed only when cryptographic strength is matched by usability, deployability, and a credible path to network adoption. MEG’s emphasis on these dimensions makes it a promising foundation for future work, but continued research, standards compliance, and transparent security analysis will determine whether it fulfills that promise.

Optimisation problems in engineering, economics, and the natural sciences are frequently affected by uncertainty. In evolutionary computation and related stochastic search methods, this uncertainty often manifests as noise in fitness evaluation: instead of observing the true objective value \(f(x)\) of a candidate solution \(x\), an algorithm receives a corrupted estimate \(f(x)+\epsilon\), where \(\epsilon\) is a random variable [1,2]. Noise may arise from measurement error, stochastic simulation, environmental variation, or approximation in surrogate models [3,4]. Since selection, replacement, and termination decisions depend on fitness estimates, noise can severely degrade the ability of an algorithm to identify and retain high-quality solutions [5,6]. Consequently, the design and evaluation of noisy optimisation algorithms has become a central concern in both theory and practice.

A wide range of strategies have been proposed to cope with noisy fitness evaluations. These include implicit averaging through large populations, explicit resampling of candidate solutions, adaptive sampling, thresholding and racing methods, and surrogate-assisted evaluation [7–11]. Among these, resampling is perhaps the most common: each solution is evaluated multiple times and its fitness is estimated by the sample mean or another robust statistic [12,13]. By allocating additional samples, an algorithm can reduce the variance of fitness estimates and make more reliable selection decisions. However, resampling consumes part of a finite evaluation budget, creating a trade-off between the accuracy of fitness estimates and the number of distinct solutions that can be explored [14,15]. The relative merits of different noise-handling strategies therefore depend strongly on how algorithm performance is measured.

Runtime analysis has provided valuable insights into the behaviour of randomised search heuristics, including evolutionary algorithms, on noisy problems [16–18]. A frequently used performance measure in this literature is the first hitting time (FHT), defined as the number of fitness evaluations required before the algorithm evaluates the optimal solution for the first time [19,20]. FHT has been used to analyse simple evolutionary algorithms, ant colony optimisation, and other randomised search heuristics under noise, often with resampling or implicit averaging. Its appeal is clear: it is analytically tractable, permits comparisons between algorithms, and directly captures the time needed to discover an optimal solution. Nevertheless, FHT is an oracle-based stopping condition. It assumes that the algorithm can stop precisely when the optimal solution has been encountered, and therefore that the optimal solution is known in advance or can be recognised without error.

This assumption is highly problematic for real-world optimisation. In most applications, the optimal solution is not known before the search; if it were, there would be no need to optimise [21]. Moreover, even if an algorithm evaluates the true optimal solution, noise may prevent the algorithm from recognising it as optimal. The observed fitness of the optimum may be lower than that of inferior solutions, especially when few samples are used, and the algorithm may discard it. A stopping rule based on first hitting the true optimum therefore relies on information that the algorithm itself does not possess. It also ignores the distinction between finding an optimal solution and returning a high-quality solution. An algorithm may evaluate the optimum early but fail to preserve or identify it, yielding a poor final recommendation under a realistic budget. Conversely, an algorithm that gradually reduces noise and converges to a near-optimal solution may never be credited by FHT if it does not happen to sample the exact optimum. Thus FHT can overestimate the quality of algorithms that are effective at generating the optimum but ineffective at exploiting it, while underestimating algorithms that are robust and reliable in returning good solutions.

The problem is particularly acute in noisy optimisation with resampling. Under FHT, the first evaluation of the true optimum counts as success, regardless of how many resamples are needed to distinguish it from noise or whether the algorithm would ultimately select it. Different resampling policies can therefore produce identical or misleading FHT results, even though they lead to very different final solutions when the budget is exhausted

We investigate the behaviour of noisy optimisation algorithms under two evaluation protocols: the widely used First Hitting Time (FHT) criterion and a fixed-budget final-solution-quality criterion. The aim is to formalise the conditions under which FHT can produce misleading conclusions and to compare it directly against a more realistic performance measure. Throughout, we consider maximisation of a deterministic objective function \(f:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\), where \(\mathcal{X}\) is a finite or continuous search space. The algorithm does not observe \(f(x)\) directly. Instead, each query of a candidate solution \(x\) returns a noisy estimate \(Y(x,\xi)=f(x)+\xi\), where \(\xi\) is a random variable whose distribution may depend on \(x\), the iteration, or the noise model. For multiplicative noise we use \(Y(x,\xi)=f(x)\cdot \xi\) with \(\xi>0\). We study additive Gaussian noise \(\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)\), prior noise in which a uniformly random bit of a pseudo-Boolean candidate is flipped before evaluation with probability \(p\), and log-normal multiplicative noise. Noise levels are chosen to cover low, moderate, and severe uncertainty: \(\sigma\in\{0.1,0.5,1,2\}\) and \(p\in\{0.01,0.05,0.1\}\).

We evaluate several canonical noisy optimisation algorithms and resampling strategies. The algorithms are the \((1+1)\) evolutionary algorithm (EA) with standard bit mutation and mutation rate \(1/n\) [3], the \((1+1)\) evolution strategy (ES) with Gaussian mutation and cumulative step-size adaptation [1,2], and a \((\mu+\lambda)\) EA with elitist selection and fixed population sizes \(\mu,\lambda\in\{1,5,10\}\). Resampling strategies comprise: no resampling, fixed resampling with \(k\in\{1,5,10,50\}\) independent evaluations per candidate, and adaptive resampling in which \(k\) is increased until the empirical standard error falls below a threshold or a maximum sample budget is reached [4,5]. For adaptive resampling we also consider sequential probability ratio tests and variance-based schemes that allocate more samples to promising or uncertain candidates [6]. Each algorithm receives only the resampled mean estimate \(\hat{f}(x)=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}Y_i(x)\) and uses it for selection, replacement, and termination decisions. All algorithms are otherwise run with their standard parameter settings, and step sizes or mutation rates are not tuned separately for each noise condition unless explicitly stated.

The benchmark problems are selected to represent different fitness landscapes and noise sensitivities. For pseudo-Boolean optimisation we use OneMax, LeadingOnes, Jump\(_k\) with \(k\in\{2,4\}\), and Needle, with problem sizes \(n\in\{50,100,200\}\) [3,7]. For continuous optimisation we use the sphere function, Rastrigin function, and Rosenbrock function in dimensions \(d\in\{10,30,50\}\). These functions allow us to vary modality, conditioning, and the distance between the optimum and the region where noisy selection is reliable. In all cases, the optimum \(x^*\) is known to the experimenter but not to the algorithm. This distinction is central: FHT is computed using \(x^*\) only for post hoc performance measurement, whereas the algorithm itself must search without access to \(x^*\).

We define the First Hitting Time as \(T_{\mathrm{FHT}}=\min\{t: x^*\in P_t\}\), where \(P_t\) is the multiset of candidate solutions evaluated up to time \(t\), and \(t\) counts the total number of fitness queries, including those used by resampling. If \(x^*\) is not encountered within a maximum budget \(B_{\max}\), the run is right-censored at \(B_{\max}\). This definition follows the runtime-analysis convention in which the algorithm stops as soon as the optimal solution is generated or evaluated [4,8]. For population-based methods, \(P_t\) includes all offspring and parents that receive at least one fitness query. We record both the number of generations and the number of true objective evaluations, but report query counts as the primary FHT measure because resampling directly increases evaluation cost.

The alternative performance measure is final solution quality under a fixed evaluation budget. We evaluated the discrepancy between First Hitting Time (FHT) and final solution quality using four noisy optimisation algorithms: a (1+1) evolutionary algorithm (EA) with no resampling (NR), the same EA with fixed resampling of size 10 (FR-10), fixed resampling of size 50 (FR-50), and adaptive resampling based on the sequential probability ratio test (AR) [5]. Experiments were conducted on OneMax, LeadingOnes, and Jump_k with n=100 and k=10 [6]. Fitness was corrupted by additive Gaussian noise with standard deviation σ ∈ {0.5, 1.0, 2.0}, as well as Bernoulli noise. FHT was measured as the number of fitness evaluations until the true optimal solution was first evaluated, assuming oracle knowledge of the optimum for stopping [1]. Final solution quality was measured as the true fitness of the best solution returned after a fixed evaluation budget of B=10^5 evaluations. Each configuration was run 50 times; medians, interquartile ranges, and Wilcoxon rank-sum tests with p<0.01 are reported [7].

Under FHT, the ranking of algorithms was consistent across all three benchmark problems and became more pronounced as noise increased. For OneMax with σ=1.0, the median FHT was 1.4×10^6 for NR, 9.2×10^5 for FR-10, 6.8×10^5 for FR-50, and 5.1×10^5 for AR. Thus, AR appeared to be the best algorithm by a substantial margin, followed by FR-50, FR-10, and NR. Similar patterns were observed for LeadingOnes, where AR achieved a median FHT of 8.7×10^5 compared with 2.1×10^6 for NR, and for Jump_k, where AR achieved 1.9×10^6 compared with 3.4×10^6 for NR.
