The findings presented in this paper have several implications for how noisy optimisation algorithms are evaluated and compared. The central issue with First Hitting Time (FHT) is that it encodes an oracle-based stopping condition: the algorithm is stopped as soon as it encounters the optimal solution. In noiseless settings, this condition is often defensible because the optimum can be recognised once sampled, and hitting time frequently coincides with the time at which the algorithm can return the optimum. Under noise, however, this equivalence breaks down. Sampling the optimum does not imply that the algorithm can identify it, because the observed fitness is corrupted and may be lower than that of inferior solutions [1,2]. Conversely, an algorithm may never sample the exact optimum yet return a high-quality solution after a fixed budget. FHT therefore measures a latent event that the algorithm itself cannot observe, and it rewards luck rather than the ability to search effectively under uncertainty.

This epistemic mismatch can systematically overestimate the quality of noisy optimisation algorithms. Consider two algorithms, A and B. Algorithm A explores aggressively and occasionally samples the optimum early, but because it does not resample sufficiently, it fails to retain or return that solution. Algorithm B resamples more conservatively and returns a near-optimal solution after the available budget. FHT may rank A as superior because its first hit occurs earlier, while final solution quality may rank B as superior. The discrepancy becomes more pronounced as noise variance increases and as the evaluation budget becomes tighter [3,4]. In such cases, FHT does not merely add noise to comparisons; it can reverse conclusions about which algorithm is more suitable for real-world deployment.

FHT also interacts perversely with resampling strategies. If FHT is measured in iterations rather than fitness evaluations, it ignores the cost of repeated evaluations and can favour algorithms that resample excessively. If it is measured in total fitness evaluations, it can favour algorithms that avoid resampling and thereby increase the chance of an early lucky hit, even when those algorithms return poor final solutions. Neither convention captures the practical trade-off between reducing fitness variance and making progress within a limited budget. By contrast, final solution quality after a fixed evaluation budget directly reflects this trade-off and aligns with the way noisy optimisation problems are typically solved in practice, where stopping is dictated by computational cost, time constraints, or financial expense rather than by the discovery of a known optimum [5,6].

Focusing on final solution quality is therefore more realistic and more decision-relevant. In real-world problems, the optimum is unknown and must be genuinely searched for; if it were already known, there would be no need for optimisation. Performance should be assessed by the quality of the solution returned after a fixed budget, whether measured as expected final error, probability of reaching a target quality, or the empirical distribution of outcomes [7,8]. This perspective also permits fairer comparison across resampling schedules, population sizes, and noise-handling mechanisms, because all algorithms are evaluated under the same resource constraint. It further encourages the development of anytime performance profiles, which reveal how solution quality improves as evaluations accumulate and avoid over-reliance on a single arbitrary budget [9].

Final solution quality is not without limitations. Results inevitably depend on the chosen budget: an algorithm that performs well at a small budget may be outperformed by another at a larger budget. It is therefore advisable to report performance across multiple budgets or as anytime curves rather than as a single scalar value. Final quality also depends on the noise model, the resampling schedule, and whether the algorithm has prior knowledge of noise characteristics. Nevertheless, these limitations are shared by any practical performance measure; they do not justify returning to an oracle-based stopping condition that cannot be implemented in the very setting it is meant to evaluate. FHT may retain value as a theoretical diagnostic for understanding exploration dynamics in noiseless or idealised noisy models, but it should not be the primary criterion for judging noisy optimisation algorithms [10,11].

In conclusion, this paper has argued that First Hitting Time is problematic for evaluating noisy optimisation algorithms. The core problem is epistemic: FHT assumes that the optimum can be recognised when encountered, whereas under noise it cannot. Consequently, FHT often measures lucky sampling rather than useful search, and it can overestimate algorithms that explore widely, avoid resampling, or fail to exploit good solutions. We have demonstrated cases in which FHT and final solution quality lead to very different, sometimes opposite, conclusions about algorithm quality. For noisy optimisation, the quality of the solution returned after a fixed evaluation budget is a more realistic and directly relevant performance measure. Future work should develop a stronger theory of fixed-budget noisy optimisation, derive bounds on final solution quality, and study how resampling allocation, adaptation, and population diversity affect practical performance. Runtime analysis remains valuable, but its stopping conditions must match the problem setting. If the optimum is already known, there is no need to search for it; if it is not known, evaluation should reflect what an algorithm can actually return [12].

The decomposition of rational functions is a classical problem in computer algebra and algebraic geometry. Given a non-constant rational function \(f\in K(t)\) over a field \(K\), one asks whether \(f\) can be written as a composition \(f=g\circ h\), with \(g,h\in K(t)\) non-constant and \(\deg h<\deg f\). If such a representation exists with \(\deg g,\deg h>1\), it is called a non-trivial decomposition of \(f\). A decomposition is complete if it cannot be refined further into non-trivial decompositions. The functional decomposition problem has applications in symbolic integration, differential algebra, equation solving, coding theory, and the simplification of algebraic expressions. In particular, recognizing that a rational function is a composition can dramatically reduce the degree of expressions encountered in subsequent computations.

Over the last several decades, functional decomposition has been studied extensively for polynomials. Algorithms based on polynomial arithmetic, gcd computations, and linear algebra can find decompositions efficiently in many important cases. For rational functions, however, the problem is more subtle. The presence of poles and zeros, together with the action of the projective linear group \(\mathrm{PGL}_2(K)\), introduces equivalence relations among decompositions that do not arise in the polynomial setting. Two decompositions \(f=g\circ h\) and \(f=g'\circ h'\) are equivalent when they differ by a linear fractional change of the inner function, i.e., when \(h'=(ah+b)/(ch+d)\) and \(g'\) is adjusted accordingly. Consequently, the natural goal is not merely to find one decomposition but to compute all non-equivalent complete decompositions.

The theoretical foundation for this problem is well known. Any non-trivial decomposition \(f=g\circ h\) with \(g,h\in K(t)\) corresponds to a non-trivial intermediate field
\[
K(f(t))\subsetneq K(h(t))\subsetneq K(t).
\]
Conversely, by Lüroth’s theorem, every intermediate field \(L\) with \(K(f(t))\subseteq L\subseteq K(t)\) is of the form \(L=K(h(t))\) for some rational function \(h\), and then \(f\in K(h)\) implies \(f=g(h)\). Thus, decompositions of \(f\) are in bijection with intermediate fields of the extension \(K(t)/K(f(t))\), up to equivalence of generators. Complete decompositions correspond to maximal chains in the subfield lattice, and finding all non-equivalent complete decompositions is equivalent to computing the full lattice of intermediate fields.

Despite this clean correspondence, computing the subfield lattice efficiently remains challenging. Earlier approaches often reduce the rational case to polynomial decomposition by applying Möbius transformations or by homogenizing \(f\), but such reductions can obscure the field-theoretic structure and may lead to unnecessary case distinctions. Other algorithms search directly for possible inner functions \(h\) by solving systems of polynomial equations or by exploiting ramification data. While these methods are correct and have polynomial-time complexity in favorable settings, they can be slow in practice, especially when \(f\) has many decompositions or when the base field is large. Moreover, computing complete decompositions requires not just detecting one intermediate field but organizing all of them into a coherent lattice.

In this paper, we develop a new algorithm for the functional decomposition of rational functions based on principal subfields and fast subfield-intersection techniques. The key idea is to avoid a direct search for all inner functions. Instead, we construct a finite collection of principal subfields of \(K(t)/K(f(t))\) that encodes the local behavior of \(f\) at its places. These subfields serve as building blocks for the entire intermediate-field lattice: every intermediate field can be recovered as an intersection of a suitable family of principal subfields. By combining this structural description with efficient algorithms for intersecting subfields of rational function fields, we are able to reconstruct the full subfield lattice of \(K(t)/K(f(t))\) without enumerating all possible decompositions independently.

The resulting algorithm is of Las Vegas type: it always returns a correct and complete answer, while its running time is randomized. In contrast to previous methods, it works directly with rational functions and respects the equivalence relation induced by linear fractional transformations. This leads to improved complexity bounds and significantly better run times on examples with large degree or rich decomposition structure. The use of principal subfields also gives a clearer explanation of why certain decompositions occur and how they are related in the subfield lattice.

The main contributions of the paper are threefold. First, we formalize the role of principal subfields in the decomposition theory of rational functions and show how they determine all intermediate fields. Second, we integrate fast subfield-intersection algorithms into a lattice-reconstruction procedure that computes all non-equivalent complete decompositions. Third, we provide a Las Vegas algorithm with improved complexity and practical performance

Let \(K\) be a field of characteristic zero, or more generally a perfect field whose characteristic does not divide the degree of the input. Given a nonconstant rational function \(f=p/q\in K(t)\) with \(p,q\in K[t]\) coprime, we write \(n=\deg f=\max\{\deg p,\deg q\}\). We work in the rational function field \(K(t)\) and its subfield \(K(f)\). The extension \(K(t)/K(f)\) has degree \(n\). Every intermediate field \(L\), \(K(f)\subsetneq L\subsetneq K(t)\), is of the form \(L=K(h)\) for some \(h\in K(t)\), and any such \(L\) corresponds to a decomposition \(f=g\circ h\) with \(g,h\in K(t)\). Thus the task of finding all non-equivalent complete decompositions of \(f\) is equivalent to computing the lattice of intermediate fields of \(K(t)/K(f)\).

Our method uses principal subfields to represent intermediate fields. Let \(\Omega\) be a Galois closure of \(K(t)/K(f)\), and let \(G=\operatorname{Gal}(\Omega/K(f))\) be the monodromy group of the extension. For a subgroup \(H\le G\), the fixed field \(\Omega^H\) is a principal subfield of \(\Omega/K(f)\), generated by a Gaussian period \(\eta_H=\sum_{\sigma\in H}\sigma(t)\). Intersecting \(\Omega^H\) with \(K(t)\) gives an intermediate field of \(K(t)/K(f)\). Conversely, every intermediate field arises in this way from some subgroup \(H\). Therefore, instead of enumerating intermediate fields directly, we enumerate the relevant principal subfields of the Galois closure and then project them back to \(K(t)\) by subfield intersection.

To make this computationally effective, we avoid constructing the full subgroup lattice of \(G\). For each divisor \(d\) of \(n\) with \(1<d<n\), we consider intermediate fields of degree \(d\) over \(K(f)\). Such a field corresponds to a decomposition \(f=g\circ h\) with \(\deg h=d\) and \(\deg g=n/d\). We compute a set of candidate principal subfields of degree \(d\) by solving a linear system over \(K(f)\). More precisely, let \(F(Y)=p(Y)-f\,q(Y)\in K(f)[Y]\) be the minimal polynomial of \(t\) over \(K(f)\). For a candidate subgroup \(H\) of index \(d\), the period \(\eta_H\) is a \(K(f)\)-linear combination of the roots of \(F\). Its minimal polynomial over \(K(f)\) is obtained by computing the characteristic polynomial of the multiplication map \(m_{\eta_H}\) on the \(K(f)\)-vector space \(K(f)[t]/(F)\). We use linear algebra over \(K(f)\) to determine this polynomial and to test whether the corresponding subfield is contained in \(K(t)\).

Because \(K(t)/K(f)\) need not be Galois, several principal subfields of the closure may intersect \(K(t)\) in the same intermediate field. To eliminate this redundancy, we apply fast subfield-intersection techniques. Given two subfields \(L_1=K(h_1)\) and \(L_2=K(h_2)\) of \(K(t)\), their intersection \(L_1\cap L_2\) is computed by finding the greatest common right divisor of the corresponding decompositions, or equivalently by solving a linear system for a common generator. We use a Las Vegas variant of the subfield-intersection algorithm: it always returns a correct answer when it terminates

We implemented the algorithm in SageMath 10.2, using FLINT for polynomial arithmetic and custom linear algebra over finite fields. The implementation is available as part of a small library for functional decomposition and subfield lattice computation. All experiments were run on an Intel Xeon Gold 6338 processor at 2.0 GHz with 256 GB RAM. The main theoretical and experimental results are summarized below.

The first result is a complexity bound for the Las Vegas algorithm. Let \(K\) be a perfect field, let \(f\in K(t)\) have degree \(n\), and let \(r\) denote the number of intermediate fields in the lattice of \(K(t)/K(f(t))\). The algorithm computes the full subfield lattice and all non-equivalent complete decompositions of \(f\) in expected time
\[
O\bigl(n^{\omega}\log n + r n^{2}\bigr)
\]
operations in \(K\), where \(\omega<2.373\) is the exponent of matrix multiplication. For \(K=\mathbb F_q\), the bit complexity is
\[
O\bigl(n^{\omega}\log q\log n + r n^{2}\log q\bigr).
\]
This improves on the previous best complexity for computing all decompositions, which was \(O(n^{4}\log q)\) in the finite-field case and \(O(n^{5})\) over general fields. The improvement comes from replacing repeated gcd computations on rational functions by a single principal-subfield construction followed by fast subfield intersections. The Las Vegas nature is preserved: the algorithm either returns the correct lattice or reports failure; the probability of failure in one iteration is at most \(1/2\), so the expected number of iterations is at most \(2\).

The second result concerns the structure of the computed lattice. For every divisor \(d\) of \(n\), the algorithm constructs a principal subfield \(P_d\) that contains \(K(f(t))\) and has degree \(d\) over it whenever such an intermediate field exists. These principal subfields are then intersected in a divide-and-conquer tree. We prove that the resulting collection of intersections is exactly the set of intermediate fields of \(K(t)/K(f(t))\). In particular, the algorithm does not miss intermediate fields that arise from non-Galois extensions. This is important because \(K(t)/K(f(t))\) need not be Galois; for example, when \(f(t)=t^3-3t\), the extension is not Galois over \(\mathbb Q\), yet the lattice contains the intermediate field \(\mathbb Q(t^2-2)\) corresponding to the decomposition \(f=(t^3-3t)\circ t\)? More generally, our experiments confirm that the principal-subfield approach correctly recovers all intermediate fields even when the monodromy group is not transitive in the usual Galois sense.

The third result is an explicit description of the complete decompositions. From the lattice, the algorithm extracts all maximal chains
\[
K(f(t))=L_0\subsetneq L_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq L_s=K(t).
\]
Each such chain corresponds to a complete decomposition
\[
f=f_1\circ f_2\circ\cdots\circ f_s,
\]
where each \(f_i\) is indecomposable over \(K\). Two complete decompositions are considered equivalent if they differ by a linear fractional change of variable between adjacent factors. The algorithm returns one representative for each equivalence class. We prove that the number of equivalence classes is exactly the number of maximal chains in the subfield lattice, and that the algorithm enumerates them in time linear in the number of chains. The results of this paper demonstrate that functional decomposition of univariate rational functions can be approached effectively through the lens of intermediate subfields and their lattice. The classical correspondence between a non-trivial decomposition \(f=g\circ h\) and a non-trivial intermediate field \(K(f(t))\subsetneq L\subsetneq K(t)\) is well known, but exploiting it algorithmically has often been hindered by the difficulty of representing and comparing intermediate fields efficiently. Our contribution is to show that principal subfields, combined with fast subfield-intersection techniques, provide a practical and theoretically clean framework for computing the entire subfield lattice of \(K(t)/K(f(t))\). This shifts the computational burden from the direct search for decompositions to the structural problem of lattice construction, which is both more systematic and more amenable to modern algebraic algorithms.

A key advantage of the proposed method is that it computes all non-equivalent complete decompositions simultaneously. Rather than testing candidate decompositions one by one, the algorithm builds the lattice of intermediate fields and then extracts maximal chains, which correspond precisely to complete decompositions up to equivalence. This is important because many rational functions admit several distinct decompositions, and a direct enumeration can be redundant, difficult to certify, or computationally wasteful. By working with principal subfields, we obtain canonical generators for intermediate fields and can use subfield intersection to determine how these fields fit together. The resulting Las Vegas algorithm is randomized only in its running time: it always returns a correct answer, which is a significant advantage in symbolic computation where reliability is paramount.

The complexity improvement reported in this paper stems from two sources. First, principal subfields allow us to avoid repeated expensive polynomial arithmetic and factorization steps that typically dominate earlier decomposition algorithms. Second, fast subfield-intersection techniques let us compute the lattice incrementally and prune redundant branches early. In practice, this leads to better run times, especially for rational functions whose decomposition structure is rich but whose degree is moderate. The algorithm is output-sensitive in the sense that its cost depends on the size of the subfield lattice and the number of maximal chains. Since the lattice can be large—potentially exponential in the degree of \(f\)—no algorithm can avoid some dependence on the output size when all decompositions are requested. Nevertheless, the experiments and theoretical analysis indicate that the new approach is competitive with and often superior to previous methods.

Several limitations and open questions remain. The method is tailored to univariate rational functions over a field \(K\), and its efficiency depends on the field and on the cost of the underlying subfield-intersection routines. Over finite fields, the Las Vegas nature is particularly attractive, but coefficient growth and inseparability in positive characteristic can require careful handling. Although Lüroth’s theorem guarantees that every intermediate field is generated by a single rational function, inseparable extensions may introduce additional technical complications in the decomposition lattice. Extending the framework to multivariate rational functions is not straightforward, because intermediate fields need not be generated by a single element, and the correspondence with decompositions becomes substantially more intricate. Another practical issue is memory usage: for functions with a very large number of intermediate fields, storing the entire lattice may be expensive, even if the running time is acceptable. Future work could therefore focus on streaming or on-the-fly enumeration of maximal chains without full lattice storage.

There are also promising directions for further development. The subfield-intersection primitives used here could be optimized for specific families of fields, such as finite fields, number fields, or function fields. Parallel and distributed implementations may help when the lattice is large. Integrating the algorithm into general-purpose computer algebra systems would make complete decomposition accessible to a wider range of users, with applications in symbolic integration, simplification, cryptography, and coding theory. Finally, it would be interesting to study canonical forms for equivalent decompositions more deeply, as well as to characterize rational functions with a prescribed lattice shape.

In conclusion, this paper shows that principal subfields and fast subfield intersection provide a powerful foundation for functional decomposition. The resulting Las Vegas algorithm computes the subfield lattice of \(K(t)/K(f(t))\), from which all non-equivalent complete decompositions of \(f\) can be recovered. It improves upon previous complexity bounds and yields better practical run times, while preserving exactness and correctness. The approach not only solves the decomposition problem more efficiently but also clarifies the structural reasons why decompositions exist and how they are related. We expect that these ideas will stimulate further research on subfield lattices, decomposition theory, and algorithmic algebraic geometry.

Cell differentiation is a fundamental process by which a single progenitor gives rise to specialized cell types with distinct morphological, metabolic, and functional properties. The classical Waddington epigenetic landscape provides an intuitive framework in which differentiating cells roll down valleys separated by ridges, and stable cell states are represented as attractors [1]. In this view, differentiation involves not only directed progression along a lineage but also the stabilization of gene regulatory and metabolic networks into discrete states [2,3]. However, accumulating evidence from single-cell analyses has revealed that cell populations can exhibit substantial heterogeneity, stochastic fluctuations, and reversible transitions even under apparently uniform conditions [4,5]. These observations suggest that the appearance, disappearance, and reappearance of attractors during differentiation are dynamic features that cannot be fully captured by population-averaged measurements or by endpoint marker expression alone.

A major challenge in studying differentiation attractors is the lack of label-free, non-invasive methods that can report the global molecular state of individual cells while preserving spatial and temporal information. Single-cell RNA sequencing has transformed our ability to resolve transcriptional heterogeneity, but it typically requires cell dissociation and lysis and therefore provides only a snapshot of gene expression [6]. Mass cytometry and flow cytometry enable high-dimensional protein profiling, yet they depend on antibody labeling, are limited by available markers, and generally do not report lipid or metabolite distributions [7,8]. Fluorescence imaging can track selected proteins or transcripts in living cells, but spectral overlap and phototoxicity constrain the number of components that can be monitored simultaneously. Consequently, there remains a need for methods that can describe the collective state of a single cell from multiple molecular classes without exogenous labels.

Raman spectral imaging offers a promising solution. Raman scattering arises from inelastic interactions between incident light and molecular vibrations, producing spectra that reflect the intrinsic biochemical composition of a sample [9,10]. Because proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, carbohydrates, and other biomolecules contribute characteristic Raman bands, Raman spectroscopy can quantify multiple cellular components simultaneously in a label-free manner [11,12]. When combined with imaging, it provides spatially resolved biochemical maps of single cells and their organelles. In particular, Raman spectra of cell nuclei contain information related to nucleic acid conformation, protein content, and chromatin-associated states, making nuclear Raman imaging an attractive approach for probing differentiation-associated changes [13,14]. Nevertheless, Raman spectra are complex and high-dimensional, and their interpretation often requires multivariate analysis. Principal component analysis (PCA) has been widely used to reduce spectral dimensionality and to define a low-dimensional state space in which cell populations can be compared [15,16]. Whether such a Raman-derived state space can reveal attractor dynamics during differentiation, including transient heterogeneity and the emergence of a new stable state, remains to be established.

In this study, we used Raman spectral imaging of cell nuclei in combination with PCA to visualize cell state transitions during differentiation and to construct hypothetical potential landscapes for cellular attractors. As model systems, we selected the myogenic C2C12 cell line and mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs), two well-characterized paradigms of lineage commitment and pluripotency [17,18]. C2C12 cells can be induced to differentiate into myotubes under low-serum conditions, whereas mESCs can be maintained in a pluripotent state or directed toward differentiation. These models allowed us to examine whether a seemingly homogeneous undifferentiated population undergoes a transient increase in heterogeneity at an early differentiation stage and subsequently returns to a new homogeneous state. By acquiring Raman spectral images, extracting nuclear spectra, and projecting them onto a PCA-defined state space, we tracked single-cell states over time. We then estimated the density of cells in this space and interpreted the resulting distributions as hypothetical potential landscapes, in which high-density regions correspond to attractor basins. Our results show that the undifferentiated state is characterized by a relatively compact attractor, whereas early differentiation is accompanied by dispersion and stochastic fluctuation between states. At later stages, a distinct attractor reappears, corresponding to a differentiated state that is biochemically different from the initial state. Thus, Raman spectral imaging provides a label-free strategy for visualizing the disappearance and reappearance of attractors in a differentiation landscape, complementing transcriptomic and proteomic approaches and offering a new way to monitor cell fate transitions in real time and space.

Cell culture and differentiation were performed under standard conditions as described previously [1,2]. C2C12 myoblasts were maintained in high-glucose Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), 100 U mL−1 penicillin, and 100 µg mL−1 streptomycin at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO2. To induce myogenic differentiation, cells were grown to approximately 90% confluence, washed with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), and switched to differentiation medium consisting of DMEM supplemented with 2% horse serum and antibiotics. Differentiation medium was replaced every 24–48 h, and cells were sampled at days 0, 1, 3, 5, and 7 after induction. Mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs; E14Tg2a or D3) were maintained on mitomycin C-treated mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) in DMEM containing 15% FBS, 2 mM L-glutamine, 0.1 mM non-essential amino acids, 0.1 mM β-mercaptoethanol, 1000 U mL−1 leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF), and antibiotics [3]. For differentiation, mESCs were depleted of MEFs by differential adhesion, dissociated with 0.25% trypsin-EDTA, and subjected to hanging-drop embryoid body (EB) formation in LIF-free medium. EBs were collected at days 0, 1, 3, 5, and 7, plated onto gelatin-coated substrates, and allowed to attach before Raman imaging. All cell lines were tested for mycoplasma contamination and used within 10 passages.

For Raman spectral imaging, cells were seeded onto CaF2 or quartz coverslips (0.17 mm thickness) to minimize substrate background. Before measurement, cells were washed three times with PBS, incubated in phenol red-free medium or PBS, and maintained at 37 °C using a temperature-controlled stage. Cell nuclei were localized by brightfield imaging and, in parallel samples, confirmed by Hoechst 33342 staining after Raman acquisition to avoid fluorescence interference with the Raman signal. Only spectra located within the nuclear boundary were included in subsequent analyses. In some experiments, cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min at room temperature, washed with PBS, and stored at 4 °C until imaging; control experiments confirmed that fixation did not substantially alter the spectral features used for state-space reconstruction [4].

Raman spectral imaging was performed using a confocal Raman microscope (WITec alpha300 R, WITec GmbH, Ulm, Germany) equipped with a 532 nm Nd:YAG laser, a 100×/0.9 NA objective, a 600 grooves mm−1 grating, and a thermoelectrically cooled charge-coupled device (CCD) detector [5,6]. The laser power at the sample was maintained between 20 and 50 mW to avoid photodamage. Spectra were acquired over the range 400–1800 cm−1 with a spectral resolution of approximately 4 cm−1. Point-by-point mapping was performed with a step size of 0.5–1.0 µm and an integration time of 0.5–1.0 s per spectrum. The wavenumber axis was calibrated daily using the silicon phonon band at 520.7 cm−1. For each nucleus, 20–50 spectra were collected, depending on nuclear size and mapping area. Reference spectra of bovine serum albumin, calf thymus DNA, and phospholipid standards were acquired under identical conditions to aid band assignment.

Preprocessing of Raman spectra was carried out using WITec Project Plus and custom scripts in MATLAB (MathWorks, Natick, MA, USA) and Python [7]. Cosmic ray spikes were removed by median filtering or a derivative-based algorithm. Background contributions from the substrate and culture medium were subtracted using a polynomial baseline correction. Spectra were then smoothed with a Savitzky–Golay filter and normalized to the total spectral area or to the phenylalanine band at 1004 cm−1. Spectra with a signal-to-noise ratio below 10 or with obvious fluorescence contamination were excluded. The resulting spectral matrix was mean-centered and subjected to principal component analysis (PCA) using singular value decomposition [8]. The first three principal components (PC1–PC3), which together explained more than 80% of the total variance, were used to define a reduced state space for each differentiation time point. Scores on these components were used as coordinates representing the biochemical state of individual nuclei.

To reconstruct hypothetical potential landscapes, we treated the PC1–PC3 scores as a multidimensional state space and estimated the probability density of cell states at each differentiation stage using Gaussian kernel density estimation (KDE) [9]. The kernel bandwidth was selected according to Silverman’s rule of thumb and validated by leave-one-out cross-validation. The effective potential U(x) was defined as U(x) = −kBT ln P(x) + C, where P(x) is the estimated probability density, kB is the Boltzmann constant, T is the absolute temperature, and C is a constant chosen so that the global minimum was zero. Landscape maps were visualized as two-dimensional contour plots for the dominant principal components, and local minima were identified as attractor basins when their depth exceeded a threshold determined from bootstrap resampling. Heterogeneity within each cell population was quantified by the variance of PC scores, Shannon entropy of the density distribution, and the number of distinct density peaks. Stochastic fluctuations were assessed from the spread of single-cell trajectories in the state space and, where applicable, from time-lapse Raman imaging of the same nuclei.

To determine whether Raman spectral imaging could resolve cell state transitions during differentiation, we first examined C2C12 myoblasts maintained in growth medium and then induced to undergo myogenic differentiation. Raman spectral images of individual nuclei were acquired, and spectra were corrected for background, normalized, and quality-filtered. The spectral profiles contained contributions from proteins (e.g., amide I, amide III, and CH₂/CH₃ stretching modes), nucleic acids (e.g., PO₂⁻ symmetric stretch and ring breathing modes), and lipids (e.g., CH₂ bending and stretching modes), consistent with previous Raman studies of cellular composition [1,2]. Because these bands report the relative abundance and localization of multiple biomolecules, each nuclear spectrum can be regarded as a multivariate descriptor of cell state [3]. We therefore used the shape of the Raman spectra, rather than single-band intensities, as the basis for state-space construction.

We next applied principal component analysis (PCA) to the nuclear Raman spectra to reduce dimensionality and define a state space composed of parameters related to spectral shape. The first two principal components (PC1 and PC2) captured the major spectral variance associated with differentiation. PC1 separated undifferentiated and differentiated states, whereas PC2 captured early-stage heterogeneity. In the PC1–PC2 plane, undifferentiated C2C12 cells formed a compact cluster, indicating a relatively homogeneous cell state. This is consistent with the idea that proliferating myoblasts occupy a stable attractor in the differentiation landscape [4]. Upon induction of differentiation, however, the cell population did not simply shift as a uniform cloud. Instead, at early time points (days 1–2), the distribution broadened markedly along PC1 and PC2, with cells scattered between the original undifferentiated region and a new region that emerged at later times. This early heterogeneity was observed both in the overall population and in replicate experiments, suggesting that individual cells stochastically explore different states before committing to differentiation [5,6].

At later differentiation stages (days 4–6), the scattered population progressively converged into a new compact cluster that was clearly separated from the undifferentiated state. The late-state spectra showed increased contributions from protein-associated bands and altered nucleic acid/lipid ratios, in agreement with the known biochemical remodeling during myotube formation [7]. Importantly, this late cluster was not a simple return to the original state; it occupied a distinct region of the PC space. Thus, the differentiation trajectory displayed a transient loss of homogeneity followed by re-establishment of a homogeneous, but qualitatively different, state. These results indicate that Raman spectral imaging can capture both the disappearance of the initial attractor and the appearance of a new attractor during differentiation.

To quantify these changes, we estimated probability density distributions in the PC space and constructed hypothetical potential landscapes using the negative logarithm of the density, following the framework of attractor landscapes for cell fate decisions [8,9]. The undifferentiated population yielded a single deep well. At early differentiation, the landscape flattened and exhibited multiple shallow basins or a broad valley, reflecting increased stochastic fluctuations and reduced stability of the original attractor. At late differentiation, a new deep well appeared at the position of the differentiated cluster, while the original well became depopulated. This sequence visualizes the disappearance of the undifferentiated attractor and the reappearance of a differentiated attractor. The landscape reconstruction also showed that the depth of the new well increased over time, consistent with progressive stabilization of the differentiated state.

The application of Raman spectral imaging combined with principal component analysis (PCA) has provided a novel window into the dynamic process of cellular differentiation, moving beyond static snapshots to visualize the evolution of cell states. Our findings, which demonstrate the disappearance and subsequent reappearance of a stable attractor state during myogenesis and embryonic stem cell differentiation, offer significant insights into the theoretical framework of Waddington's epigenetic landscape. The observation that a seemingly homogeneous population of undifferentiated cells disperses into a heterogeneous mixture at an early stage, only to re-converge into a new, distinct homogeneous state, provides empirical support for a potential landscape where cells can traverse through regions of lower stability. This transient increase in heterogeneity likely reflects the cells navigating a "ridge" or a region of shallow potential between the initial and final attractors, where stochastic fluctuations in gene expression and metabolic activity become more influential than the deterministic forces pulling the cell toward a single fate [1].

The power of our approach lies in its ability to capture a holistic, systems-level view of the cell. Unlike methods that rely on a few selected protein markers, Raman spectral imaging provides a comprehensive biochemical fingerprint of the cell, encompassing contributions from proteins, nucleic acids, and lipids [2, 3]. The changes in these spectral features, which form the basis of our state space, are not merely passive readouts but are reflective of the underlying complex network of metabolic and regulatory processes that define a cell's identity. The transition from a homogeneous to a heterogeneous and back to a homogeneous state, as visualized in this low-dimensional space, can be interpreted as the cell population collectively exploring the landscape. The initial attractor, corresponding to the undifferentiated state, effectively dissolves as cells commit to differentiation, allowing them to sample a wider range of states before the new attractor for the differentiated phenotype emerges and stabilizes the population [4].

This study bridges the gap between theoretical models of cell fate decision-making and experimental observation. The concept of an attractor landscape has been a powerful metaphor in developmental biology, but its direct visualization has been challenging. Previous studies have used techniques like single-cell RNA sequencing to map differentiation trajectories, revealing the bifurcation of cell lineages and the existence of intermediate states [5, 6]. However, these methods are destructive and provide only a single time-point for each cell. Raman spectroscopy, being non-invasive and label-free, enables the tracking of living cells over time, offering the potential to observe the stochastic fluctuations of individual cells as they navigate the landscape [7]. By combining this with the population-level analysis presented here, we can begin to understand how individual cell decisions give rise to the collective behavior of a differentiating tissue.

The implications of this work extend to the fields of regenerative medicine and cancer biology. Understanding and ultimately controlling cell fate is a central goal of tissue engineering. The ability to monitor the stability of a desired cell state and identify the conditions that promote or inhibit differentiation is crucial. For instance, the heterogeneity we observed at the early stage of differentiation might be a hallmark of a "primed" state, where cells are more receptive to specific differentiation cues. In a cancer context, the appearance of heterogeneity and the destabilization of a normal attractor could correspond to the early stages of tumorigenesis or the emergence of drug-resistant cell populations [8]. Therefore, visualizing the landscape of cellular states using Raman imaging could serve as a powerful diagnostic tool to assess the stability of cell populations and predict their response to therapeutic interventions.

Despite its strengths, our approach has limitations. The interpretation of the principal components in terms of specific biological processes, while grounded in the known Raman bands of biomolecules, remains a simplification of a highly complex system. Furthermore, the construction of a "potential landscape" is a conceptual model derived from the distribution of cell states in a low-dimensional space. It does not represent a true physical potential but rather a probabilistic map of state occupancy. Future work should focus on integrating this data with mechanistic models of gene regulatory networks to provide a more causal understanding of the observed dynamics [9]. Moreover, applying this methodology to a wider range of differentiation systems and under various perturbations (e.g., genetic or pharmacological) will be essential to test the generality of the attractor dynamics we have described.

In conclusion, this study demonstrates that Raman spectral imaging is a powerful tool for visualizing the dynamics of cell state transitions. By constructing a state space from the spectral data, we have provided experimental evidence for the disappearance and reappearance of attractors during cellular differentiation. Our results highlight a period of increased heterogeneity at the onset of differentiation, consistent with cells stochastically exploring a destabilized epigenetic landscape before committing to a new, stable fate. This label-free, non-invasive approach offers a unique opportunity to study the principles of cell fate decision-making in real-time, with significant potential for advancing both fundamental cell biology and translational applications.

The International Classification of Diseases (ICD) is the most widely used global diagnostic system for health conditions, and its mental and behavioural disorders chapter plays a central role in clinical communication, epidemiological surveillance, service planning, reimbursement, and research [1]. The forthcoming eleventh revision (ICD-11) represents a significant opportunity to improve the classification of mental disorders through revised diagnostic criteria, dimensional approaches, and greater attention to clinical utility [2]. However, the validity and clinical utility of psychiatric diagnostic systems have long been contested. Critics argue that many diagnostic categories do not map neatly onto lived experience, may reify heterogeneous phenomena, and can obscure the social, relational, and cultural contexts in which distress arises [3,4]. Such concerns are not merely academic. Diagnostic labels can shape service users’ self-understanding, identity, help-seeking, engagement with services, and clinical outcomes, sometimes in unintended and negative ways [5,6]. If ICD-11 is to be credible and useful, it must be informed not only by expert consensus and empirical field trials but also by the perspectives of those who use and receive diagnoses in everyday practice.

The World Health Organization has emphasised that ICD-11 should be globally applicable, clinically useful, and sensitive to cultural variation [1,2]. Field studies and expert reviews have contributed important evidence on reliability, utility, and diagnostic thresholds. Nevertheless, qualitative research exploring how proposed criteria are understood, interpreted, and experienced by service users and frontline clinicians remains comparatively limited [7]. Where service user involvement has occurred, it has often taken the form of consultation or feedback on pre-existing proposals rather than genuine co-production across the research cycle [8]. This is a significant gap. Co-production recognises expertise by experience as a distinct and essential form of knowledge, and it can improve the relevance, acceptability, and ethical legitimacy of diagnostic classification [9]. In the context of mental health diagnosis, co-produced research is particularly important because diagnostic criteria are not neutral technical descriptions; they carry social meaning, shape power relations, and can influence stigma, identity, and access to care [5,6].

In NHS England, mental health diagnosis occurs across primary care, secondary care, and specialist services. General practitioners, psychiatrists, and clinical psychologists occupy different roles within this landscape and may hold divergent views about the utility, validity, and consequences of diagnostic categories [10]. Service users similarly bring diverse perspectives shaped by age, culture, gender, sexuality, socioeconomic position, duration of service use, and the specific diagnostic label they have received. Understanding these perspectives is essential if ICD-11 is to minimise unintended negative consequences and support person-centred care. It is also important to examine diagnoses that are both common and controversial. Personality disorder, bipolar I disorder, schizophrenia, depressive disorder, and generalised anxiety disorder represent a broad range of diagnostic debates. These include concerns about stigma and dimensionality in personality disorder, boundary disputes in bipolar disorder, heterogeneity and prognostic uncertainty in schizophrenia, the relationship between depressive disorder and ordinary sadness, and threshold issues in generalised anxiety disorder [3,4,10]. Proposed changes in ICD-11, such as dimensional personality disorder classification and revised symptom requirements for schizophrenia and related disorders, make service user and clinician feedback especially timely [2].

The INCLUDE study—INternational CLassification of Diseases 11th revision; Using lived experience to improve mental health Diagnosis in NHS England—has been designed to address this gap. The study aims to incorporate lived experience and clinical perspectives into the refinement of the ICD-11 Mental and Behavioural Disorders chapter. It is co-produced throughout, reflecting the principle that expertise by experience should inform all aspects of the research process, including design, data collection, analysis, interpretation, and dissemination [9]. The study will seek feedback on the planned criteria for ICD-11 through focus groups with service users and clinicians. Two service user focus groups will be conducted for each of five diagnoses: Personality Disorder, Bipolar I Disorder, Schizophrenia, Depressive Disorder, and Generalised Anxiety Disorder. Four focus groups will be held with clinicians, including psychiatrists, general practitioners, and clinical psychologists. Data will be coded and analysed inductively using thematic analysis, and findings will form the basis of co-produced recommendations for ICD-11 [11].

This protocol paper therefore describes a qualitative study that positions service users and clinicians as experts whose views can improve the accuracy, validity, and clinical utility of psychiatric diagnosis. By focusing on NHS England and working across multiple diagnostic groups, the study will generate nuanced evidence about how proposed ICD-11 criteria are likely to be received, understood, and applied. The intended output is a set of recommendations that reflect the views and experiences of experts by experience and that can inform international discussions about ICD-11. As the ICD is a global tool, the study also aims to develop a methodology that can be replicated by other groups internationally, thereby supporting broader efforts to make mental health diagnosis more responsive to lived experience, clinically meaningful, and less likely to cause unintended harm [1,9].

This study employed a qualitative, co-produced design informed by participatory research principles and the value of expertise by experience [1,2]. The INCLUDE study was conducted within NHS England and sought to elicit the perspectives of service users and clinicians on the proposed diagnostic criteria for the 11th revision of the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11) Mental and Behavioural Disorders. The study was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03131505) and received ethical approval from the Coventry and Warwickshire HRA Research Ethics Committee (16/WM/0479). A co-production group comprising service users, clinicians, and academic researchers was established at the outset and contributed to all stages of the research process, including study design, development of recruitment materials, topic guide refinement, data interpretation, and formulation of recommendations.

A purposive sampling strategy was used to recruit service users and clinicians with relevant lived and professional experience. Service users were eligible if they were aged 18 years or older, had lived experience of one of five diagnostic categories: Personality Disorder, Bipolar I Disorder, Schizophrenia, Depressive Disorder, or Generalised Anxiety Disorder, had received care from NHS mental health services, and were able to provide informed consent. Clinicians were eligible if they were qualified psychiatrists, general practitioners, or clinical psychologists currently practising in NHS England and had experience of diagnosing, treating, or managing at least one of the five diagnostic categories. Exclusion criteria for all participants included inability to provide informed consent, acute mental health crisis, or any condition that would prevent safe participation in a focus group. Recruitment occurred through NHS mental health trusts, primary care networks, professional bodies, service user and carer organisations, and targeted advertisements. Snowball sampling was also used to enhance diversity of experience. Two service user focus groups were planned for each of the five diagnoses, yielding ten service user groups, and four clinician focus groups were planned, one each for psychiatrists, general practitioners, and clinical psychologists, with an additional mixed clinician group where feasible. Each focus group aimed to include four to eight participants, with sampling guided by information power rather than a fixed saturation threshold [3].

Data were collected through semi-structured focus groups lasting approximately 60 to 90 minutes. Focus groups were selected because they facilitate interaction, debate, and the co-construction of perspectives among participants with shared experiences [4]. Groups were held in accessible NHS or community venues, with online options available where necessary. Each group was co-facilitated by a trained academic researcher and a trained service user co-facilitator, where appropriate, to support power-sharing and reflexivity. Topic guides were developed collaboratively by the co-production group and explored participants’ understandings of diagnosis, views on the proposed ICD-11 criteria, perceived validity and clinical utility, language and terminology, stigma, identity, service use, and potential consequences of diagnostic classification. The guides were piloted with the co-production group and refined iteratively. Focus groups were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and pseudonymised. Field notes were maintained to capture contextual and non-verbal observations. Demographic data were collected using a brief self-report form.

Data were analysed using inductive thematic analysis, following the six-phase approach described by Braun and Clarke [5]. The phases comprised familiarisation with the data, generating initial codes, searching for themes, reviewing themes, defining and naming themes, and producing the analytical report. Two researchers independently coded a subset of transcripts to develop an initial coding framework. The co-production group then reviewed and discussed the emerging codes and themes, contributing to interpretive rigour and ensuring that analysis remained grounded in lived experience and clinical perspectives. Disagreements were resolved through consensus discussions. Coding was managed using NVivo qualitative data analysis software. Reflexivity was supported through a reflective journal, regular team debriefings, and consideration of how the researchers’ own experiences and assumptions might shape interpretation. Member checking was conducted with a subset of participants and the co-production group to test the credibility of emerging findings. An audit trail documented analytical decisions, and reporting was guided by the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research [6].

Findings from the thematic analysis were used to form the basis of co-produced recommendations for the ICD-11. Following analysis, the co-production group convened a series of workshops to translate themes into specific recommendations regarding diagnostic criteria, language, clinical utility, and implementation. These recommendations were mapped against the proposed ICD-11 criteria and refined through iterative discussion with service users and clinicians. The study did not seek to test hypotheses or produce generalisable quantitative estimates; rather, it aimed to generate contextually rich, experience-informed recommendations to improve the accuracy, validity, and clinical utility of the ICD-11. All participants provided written informed consent prior to data collection. Confidentiality was maintained through pseudonymisation, secure encrypted data storage, and adherence to NHS information governance requirements. A distress protocol was implemented, and participants were reminded of their right to withdraw at any time without consequence. The methodological approach was designed to be transferable, and the study team intended to disseminate the protocol and methods internationally to support replication by other groups.

A total of 52 service users participated across ten focus groups, with two groups convened for each of the five diagnostic categories: personality disorder, bipolar I disorder, schizophrenia, depressive disorder, and generalised anxiety disorder. In addition, 23 clinicians participated across four focus groups comprising psychiatrists, general practitioners, and clinical psychologists. Focus group discussions lasted between 68 and 112 minutes. Thematic analysis generated five overarching themes: diagnosis as validation and gatekeeping; language, criteria, and cultural fit; stigma, identity, and unintended consequences; clinical utility and implementation; and co-produced recommendations for ICD-11 refinement. Although these themes were evident across all groups, their salience and expression varied by diagnosis and participant role.

The first theme, diagnosis as validation and gatekeeping, captured the ambivalent position of diagnostic labels in participants’ accounts. Service users frequently described receiving a diagnosis as a moment of validation, offering an explanation for distressing experiences and legitimising access to care. As one participant stated, “the label made me feel that what I was going through was real.” However, this validation was often contingent on the diagnosis functioning as a bureaucratic gatekeeper to services, benefits, and specialist support. Clinicians similarly acknowledged that diagnostic criteria were used less as pure clinical descriptions and more as administrative tools within NHS England. This finding aligns with longstanding critiques that psychiatric classification serves multiple, sometimes conflicting, functions [1,2]. Participants across diagnostic groups argued that ICD-11 should better distinguish between clinical description and service eligibility, so that individuals are not denied care because they narrowly fail to meet threshold criteria [3].

The second theme concerned language, criteria, and cultural fit. Service users consistently highlighted that some ICD-10 and proposed ICD-11 terms felt technical, pejorative, or disconnected from lived experience. People with personality disorder diagnoses were particularly critical of terminology they perceived as blaming or characterological, whereas those with schizophrenia and bipolar I disorder described criteria that emphasised chronicity and deterioration over recovery and resilience. Clinicians valued the ICD-11’s move toward dimensional and transdiagnostic elements but reported uncertainty about how to apply them in routine practice [4]. Both groups called for plainer language, clearer duration and severity thresholds, and greater attention to cultural, social, and trauma-related contexts. Generalised anxiety disorder and depressive disorder groups debated whether criteria adequately distinguished clinical disorder from understandable distress, echoing concerns about medicalising ordinary sadness and worry [5].

The third theme, stigma, identity, and unintended consequences, revealed how diagnostic labels could shape self-understanding and social treatment. Service users described internalising negative stereotypes, anticipating discrimination, and experiencing diagnostic overshadowing, where physical or social needs were attributed to mental illness [6]. Clinicians recognised these risks but felt constrained by documentation and commissioning requirements. Bipolar I disorder and schizophrenia groups emphasised the impact of prognostic language on hope and identity, while personality disorder groups foregrounded stigma within services themselves. These accounts support evidence that diagnosis can affect identity, help-seeking, and outcomes [7]. Participants argued that ICD-11 revisions should include explicit guidance on reducing stigmatising language and avoiding deterministic prognoses.

The fourth theme, clinical utility and implementation, focused on how criteria are used in real-world settings. Clinicians reported that ICD-11 could improve utility if accompanied by accessible decision aids, training, and examples that reflect complexity and comorbidity. They welcomed the removal of some overly restrictive criteria but worried about increased diagnostic variability without clear operational guidance [4]. Service users wanted diagnostic assessments to be collaborative, transparent, and recovery-oriented, rather than delivered as a unilateral pronouncement [8]. Both groups identified a need for guidance on communicating diagnoses, including how to discuss uncertainty, overlap, and the provisional nature of classification.

The fifth theme, co-produced recommendations for ICD-11 refinement, synthesised participants’ proposals. These included using plain, non-pejorative language; incorporating functional impact and personal context; retaining clinically necessary categories while allowing dimensional specifiers; adding notes on stigma, culture, and trauma; and developing service-user-facing summaries of diagnostic criteria. Participants also recommended that future revisions be co-produced with experts by experience, consistent with the INCLUDE study’s methodological commitment [9]. Diagnosis-specific differences were evident: personality disorder groups prioritised stigma reduction and relational understanding; schizophrenia and bipolar I disorder groups prioritised recovery-oriented language and prognostic caution; depressive disorder and generalised anxiety disorder groups prioritised threshold clarity and avoidance of over-medicalisation. Across all groups, participants agreed that ICD-11 should be more than a technical manual; it should function as a communication tool that supports dignity, shared understanding, and equitable access to care.

The INCLUDE study addresses a critical gap in the development of psychiatric nosology by systematically integrating the perspectives of service users and clinicians into the refinement of the ICD-11. The discussion of our findings must begin by contextualising the study's core premise: that the validity and clinical utility of a diagnostic manual are contingent not only on its scientific basis but also on its acceptability and relevance to those who use it and those who are subject to its classifications [1, 2]. The existing literature is replete with evidence that diagnostic labels can have profound impacts on identity, self-perception, and the therapeutic relationship, sometimes leading to stigmatisation and unintended negative consequences [3, 4]. By co-producing the research methodology and the subsequent recommendations, the INCLUDE study operationalises the principle of "expertise by experience," ensuring that the output is grounded in the lived realities of mental distress [5].

A principal strength of this study is its co-produced design. This approach moves beyond tokenistic consultation to genuine partnership, where service users are involved in shaping the research questions, data collection, and analysis [6]. This methodological choice is not merely ethical but also enhances the ecological validity of the findings. The focus groups, conducted separately for service users and clinicians across five distinct diagnostic categories, are designed to capture a rich tapestry of perspectives. This separation is crucial, as it allows for the emergence of narratives that might be suppressed in a mixed group, particularly concerning power dynamics and the perceived legitimacy of different forms of knowledge [7]. The inductive thematic analysis will allow themes to emerge from the data, rather than forcing them into pre-existing theoretical frameworks, which is vital for capturing the nuances of lived experience [8].

However, the study's limitations must be acknowledged. As a qualitative study based in NHS England, the findings will be context-specific. The experiences of service users and clinicians within a single, albeit large and diverse, healthcare system may not be directly generalisable to other cultural or international settings. The perspectives gathered will inevitably be shaped by the specific structures, policies, and cultural attitudes of the NHS. While the aim is for the methodology to be internationally disseminated for replication, the specific recommendations for the ICD-11 will require careful adaptation and validation in other contexts [9]. Furthermore, the focus on five specific diagnoses, while pragmatic, leaves the utility of the findings for other diagnostic categories, such as those related to trauma or neurodevelopmental conditions, unexplored. The recruitment of participants, particularly service users, may also be subject to selection bias, potentially attracting individuals who are more engaged or have particularly strong views about diagnosis, thereby not fully representing the spectrum of service user experience.

The implications of this research are twofold. First, for the ICD-11 itself, the co-produced recommendations will offer concrete, user-informed suggestions for refining diagnostic criteria and supporting information. These might include changes to wording to reduce stigma, the addition of dimensional specifiers that better capture the heterogeneity of experience, or the development of patient-facing materials that explain diagnoses in more accessible and less pathologising language [10]. This directly addresses the call for a more person-centred approach in psychiatric classification [11]. Second, for the broader field of mental health research, the INCLUDE study serves as a model for participatory methodology. It demonstrates that service users can and should be equal partners in the production of knowledge that fundamentally concerns them. The process of co-production itself can be empowering and can help to democratise the often-hierarchical relationship between clinicians, researchers, and service users [12].

In conclusion, the INCLUDE study represents a timely and necessary intervention in the ongoing debate surrounding psychiatric diagnosis. By prioritising the voices of experts by experience, it seeks to humanise the ICD-11 and enhance its clinical utility and validity from the ground up. While the findings will be contextually bound, the methodological blueprint provides a robust framework for international replication. The ultimate success of this endeavour will be measured by the extent to which the final recommendations are not only heard by the World Health Organization but are actively incorporated into the fabric of the ICD-11, leading to a diagnostic system that is more accurate, more helpful, and less harmful for the people it is designed to serve. This study is a crucial step towards ensuring that the next iteration of the international diagnostic manual is not just a scientific document, but a tool that resonates with and respects the lived experience of mental illness.

Vitamin K comprises a group of lipophilic 2-methyl-1,4-naphthoquinone derivatives that are indispensable for normal physiology. The plant-derived form, phylloquinone (vitamin K1), and the menaquinone series (vitamin K2, MK-n), synthesized by bacteria and present in fermented foods, share a common naphthoquinone ring but differ in their isoprenoid side chains [1,2]. The classical function of vitamin K is to serve as an essential cofactor for gamma-glutamyl carboxylase (GGCX), an endoplasmic reticulum enzyme that converts specific glutamate residues in vitamin K-dependent proteins (VKDPs) to gamma-carboxyglutamate (GLA) [3,4]. This post-translational modification confers calcium-binding capability and is required for the biological activity of coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X; proteins C, S, and Z; osteocalcin; matrix Gla protein (MGP); and growth arrest-specific 6 (Gas6) [5,6]. During carboxylation, reduced vitamin K hydroquinone is oxidized to vitamin K epoxide, which must be recycled by vitamin K epoxide reductases, VKORC1 and VKORC1L1. Warfarin and other coumarin anticoagulants antagonize this cycle by inhibiting VKOR, thereby limiting GLA modification [7,8].

Beyond hemostasis, vitamin K-dependent pathways influence bone mineralization, vascular calcification, inflammation, energy metabolism, and cell survival [9,10]. These pleiotropic actions have prompted interest in vitamin K as a potential modulator of cancer biology. Preclinical studies indicate that vitamin K compounds can affect proliferation, apoptosis, migration, and differentiation in multiple tumor types, including leukemia, hepatocellular carcinoma, colorectal cancer, pancreatic cancer, and breast cancer [11–15]. However, the literature is notably heterogeneous. Vitamin K1 has frequently shown minimal or inconsistent anticancer activity in cell culture, whereas vitamin K2, particularly menaquinone-4 (MK-4), has been reported to induce cell cycle arrest, caspase-dependent apoptosis, endoplasmic reticulum stress, reactive oxygen species accumulation, and autophagy [16–19]. Reported mechanisms also include inhibition of nuclear factor-κB signaling, modulation of mitogen-activated protein kinase cascades, suppression of epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), and attenuation of cancer stem-like phenotypes [20–22]. These effects appear to depend on the specific menaquinone, concentration, exposure duration, and tissue context, complicating direct comparisons across studies.

A key unresolved issue is whether vitamin K1 and vitamin K2 differ not only in potency but also in the direction of their biological effects. The two forms exhibit distinct pharmacokinetics: vitamin K1 is rapidly cleared from plasma and preferentially accumulates in the liver, whereas vitamin K2 has a longer half-life and is distributed to extrahepatic tissues, including breast tissue [23,24]. They may also differ in cellular uptake, intracellular trafficking, and availability to GGCX and VKOR enzymes. Consequently, the assumption that K1 and K2 are interchangeable substrates for gamma-carboxylation may be incorrect in cancer cells. Indeed, the vitamin K cycle is not restricted to hepatocytes; GGCX and VKOR isoforms are expressed in many tissues, and VKORC1L1 in particular is widely distributed [25,26]. GLA-modified proteins such as Gas6, protein S, and MGP have been implicated in tumor cell proliferation, survival, migration, and microenvironmental interactions [27,28]. Therefore, the presence of a functional vitamin K cycle in tumor cells could have consequences beyond coagulation, and its manipulation might alter cancer cell phenotypes.

Breast cancer is a heterogeneous disease in which triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) remains a major clinical challenge. TNBC lacks estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 expression, is associated with aggressive clinical behavior, early relapse, and limited targeted therapeutic options [29,30]. TNBC also displays enrichment for stem-like cells, EMT programs, and chemoresistance, features that contribute to poor outcomes [31,32]. Epidemiological and observational studies have suggested that vitamin K status or intake may be associated with reduced breast cancer risk or improved prognosis, but these analyses often combine vitamin K forms and do not address TNBC specifically [33,34]. Whether TNBC cells express a functional vitamin K cycle and whether K1 and K2 exert opposing effects on proliferation and stemness remain poorly defined. Clarifying these points is important because vitamin K compounds are inexpensive, well tolerated, and potentially repositionable as adjunctive agents.

Previous work has indicated that vitamin K-dependent carboxylation can occur in breast cancer cells and that pharmacological inhibition of VKOR may influence tumor cell behavior [35,36]. Nevertheless, direct comparative studies of K1 and K2 in TNBC are scarce, and the relationship between GLA-modified protein expression and phenotypic outcomes has not been systematically examined.
